items.t: 1 · What this notebook is
items.x: A personal study and revision notebook for Modern Indian History, built only from the material you provided: the Sarrthi IAS handout chapters (the "book") and the class slides with the teacher's board notes. Nothing is added from outside. Where the teacher's slide and the handout differ, the notebook says so in a note box instead of quietly choosing one. Each chapter follows the same pattern: sections in the order of the class, the teacher's ink in teacher boxes, traps in alert boxes, then a mind map, timeline, flow charts, tables, connections, recall sheet, quiz and flash cards. Teacher: Source for this course = only the Sarrthi IAS handout. After the batch is over, add the new NCERTs (from the Sarrthi IAS Foundation YouTube channel).

items.t: 2 · The box colours
items.x: Teacher: Saffron box: what the teacher wrote or said on the board or slide. Red box: a trap, a Prelims alert or a common mistake. Blue box: a note, a clarification, or a difference between the handout and the slides. Green box: a takeaway to memorise. Mnemonic: Purple box: a memory hook (acronym, rhyme, story or peg) for a war, treaty, year, list or sequence. Each chapter also ends its notes with one "chapter in one breath" story. The Mnemonics page collects all of them.

items.t: 3 · The teacher's study method
items.x: Keep total sync between the uploaded chapters and the PPTs after class. Reading before class: read the chapters without making gists. Reading after class: make gists. Make gists in the side margins of the chapter; the second option is the PPT margins. Do fast reading without highlighting. MMP (the expansion is not clear on the slides) is another reading of the gists and PPTs, used to make flowcharts of Mains PYQs. Prelims short notes = gists plus the PPT. Each chapter has PYQs/FYQs (Prelims 1995-2026, Mains 2013-26). This notebook's recall sheet and flash cards at the end of each chapter are built for step 2 (quick gists) and step 6 (Prelims short notes).

items.x: Teacher: Chapter 1 is marked not important. It is the vocabulary chapter (power, state, sovereignty, centralisation) that later chapters use. PYQs: none is quoted in the handout or slides for this chapter. Read it once for the terms; do not spend revision time here.

items.t: 1 · Basics first: power, state, sovereignty
items.x: The teacher opens with vocabulary. Every later chapter uses these words (power, state, sovereignty, centralisation), so this section is worth reading slowly once. Teacher: Source for this course = only the Sarrthi IAS handout (the "book"). After the batch is over, add the new NCERTs (go to the Sarrthi IAS Foundation YouTube channel for those). Feudal, non-modern and modern Feudal = old in time and regressive. Modern = usually new in time and progressive / better / more efficient. Old is not always feudal or backward. Old can be gold (the handout's example: Lata Mangeshkar). Raja Ram Mohun Roy, the Father of Modern India, wanted a return to the pure past of Vedantic traditions. Teacher's ladder: Feudal → Non-modern (the transition period) → Modern.  Feudal is old in time and regressive; non-modern is the transition period; modern is usually new and progressive. Power and its six forms Power = Economic + Political (decision-making) + Military + Social (influence over people, or awe in their hearts) + Intellectual/Technological + Spiritual. A rise or fall in one form of power drives a rise or fall in the others. Example from the handout: a social-media influencer's popularity raises his or her economic power, while a scandal can hurt a politician's political power. Mnemonic: Six forms of power. "Every Pandit Makes Sweet Tea Slowly." Decode: Economic, Political, Military, Social, Tech (Intellectual/Technological), Spiritual, in the chapter's order. Why it sticks: a pandit slowly stirring sweet tea is easy to picture, and the six words keep the order.  Power and its six forms (W1 to W6), with the teacher's notes: Mao, "person-power fit", and the joint-family example. Teacher: Person-power fit. Think of a joint family. The strong personality of the grandparents holds all the power. After years a weak personality follows, and power gets decentralised. Teacher: Mao: power flows from the barrel of a gun (written beside Military). Teacher: Baba Ramdev example: social power turns into money power (Patanjali, plus coaching). One power rising lifts another. It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality Power centralises itself in a strong personality. That personality can be a human or an institution. When the personality weakens, power leaves in one of two ways: vertically downwards (decentralisation) or by horizontal displacement (another personality replaces it). Teacher's example of horizontal displacement by an institution: Kodak → smartphones. Mnemonic: Vertical vs horizontal (when power leaves). Vertical = the Vault door opens downward; Horizontal = a Heir steps in beside. Decode: Vertical = power flows down, so decentralisation (grandparents to the family). Horizontal = another personality replaces the weak one at the same level (Kodak → smartphones). Why it sticks: V goes Down (V points down), H goes Across (H has a crossbar).  Rise and fall of super-powers: a wave between centralisation and decentralisation. Mughals strong till 1707, then regional powers, Marathas by the 1750s, Third Battle of Panipat 1761, then the EIC. Teacher: Reading the wave. Till 1707: strong Mughal emperors (all-India power). After 1707: decline of the Mughals, decentralisation of power to regional powers. Then the Maratha empire by the 1750s, broken at the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761, and then the EIC (circled in red) rises. The teacher draws a grandparent with four children as the Mughal picture. Beside it are the initials "SS, RS, AA", which I could not decode from the handwriting. Check your own notebook. Country, nation, state Country = territory (Desh). State = the organisation that rules or governs a country and its people (Rajya). To rule = to make laws, implement them and settle disputes (L, E, J) over domestic affairs. That is also called governance. Nation = the summation of people who are one (fraternity), equal (equality) and supreme (liberty). This is the definition given by the French Revolution (1789). The teacher links it to "We the People" in the Preamble = Nation (Rashtra).  Teacher's board: State = organisation that rules a territory (country) and its people (nation). Nation = people who are or feel one, equal and supreme. State rules a territory and its people. Country = the territory. Nation = the people. The State talks, trades or fights with the outside world, but it *rules* only its own country and people. Mnemonic: Country, Nation, State: C-T, N-P, S-O. "Country = Territory, Nation = People, State = Organisation." Decode: Country (Desh) is the land; Nation (Rashtra) is the people who are one, equal and supreme; State (Rajya) is the organisation that rules both. Why it sticks: the State is the only one that *does* something (rules); the other two just *are*. State structure  Teacher's board: State structure. The symbolic sovereign (the President, Head of State) over Legislature, Executive and Judiciary, at Centre and Province. Teacher's tree: Symbolic sovereign (= President, Head of State) sits over the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. This structure repeats at the Centre and at the Province. The Executive = the Council of Ministers, which works through military servants and civil servants. The handout says the primary purpose of any constitution is to create the State structure. A modern State structure has separation of power, a well-defined internal structure with clear goals and functions, and mechanisms that keep the whole structure stable from top to bottom. A non-modern State structure has no institutional separation of power and is prone to instability. Student confusion resolved (handout). NCERT says a Modern State has "centralised power exercised over a clearly defined territory". In class we say a Modern State has separation of power. Both are right. A State can be vertically centralised (a strong Union Government with authority over the provinces) and at the same time have horizontal separation of powers at the Union level: Parliament makes laws, the Prime Minister implements them, the Supreme Court resolves disputes. Like parents who centralise power over the home, yet divide it between mother and father. Teacher: The word "province" is better than "state" for the units of a federation, otherwise it causes confusion with State = the ruling organisation. "Republic of India" and the point of Modern Indian History  Teacher's board: "Republic of India" is the name of the State (organisation) ruling the territory and people of India since 26 January 1950. "Republic of India" = the name of the State (organisation) ruling the Territory and People of India since 26 January 1950. Key goal of the Constitution = to define and create this State (organisation). MIH = the history of the States that ruled the territory of India and its people, for example the Mughal State, the Maratha State, the Awadh State, and the Company State by the EIC. INM (Indian National Movement) = a people's movement. Its goal: end the British colonial State and establish the Nation State (the Republic of India). Teacher: Keep one picture: a State is an organisation. Every dynasty in this course is just one such organisation, and each can be studied by the same questions: who rules, over what territory, with what structure, and why did it weaken? Types of State   Type   What it means    --- ---    Military State   Set up and sustained by military power     Police State   Sustained by overuse of the police     Kingdom / Empire   Head of State decided by bloodline. An Empire = a sum of kingdoms     Company State   Set up by a company, for example the EIC's Company State (1765–1858) in India     Nation State   Set up by the people / nation   Mnemonic: Five types of State. "My Police Keep Calm Nightly." Decode: Military, Police, Kingdom/Empire (bloodline; an empire = a sum of kingdoms), Company (EIC, 1765–1858), Nation State (set up by the people). Why it sticks: the list runs from force (Military, Police) to bloodline to business to the people, in the chapter's order.  Types of State, with the teacher's notes: a Military State is established by military victory and ended by defeat; all States until 1950 were of this kind. Teacher: Military State = established by military victory, ended by defeat. Example: all States until 1950. Teacher: Game of Thrones picture: an empire = seven kingdoms. Each kingdom has a king (or queen), and the emperor or empress sits above K1, K2 ... Kn. Teacher: Dynasty = bloodline-based succession for the Head of State. It is named on the basis of family, name or ethnicity (example: the Bourbon dynasty). Dynastic rule = monarchy. By contrast, a Head of State who is a representative of the public = Republic.  Teacher's board: dynasty = bloodline-based succession of the Head of State; a Head of State who represents the public = Republic. Organisations and their motives   Organisation   Motive    --- ---    Family   Welfare of its members     Private company   Profit for shareholders     NGO   A social motive     Political party   Power over the State (the 1886 INC rule: take up only political issues, not social issues, so the INC is a political party, not an NGO)     State   Territory, and ideally the people's welfare (example: a Nation State)   The common man does not want to be an MP, MLA or minister. She wants security: physical, economic, socio-cultural and spiritual. Teacher: The State's motive is territory. A State will make no compromise with its own territory (defensive), but it may also seek territorial expansion (offensive).  Organisations by motive, with the teacher's note that the State's territorial motive has a defensive and an offensive side. Teacher: Social power and the common man. The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural: religion, language, art and so on). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises. If social power rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example given: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the hit song of the time. Sovereignty Sovereignty = symbolic sovereignty + the power to make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (legislative, executive, judicial power), over external and domestic sovereign functions.   Aspect   Meaning    --- ---    Symbolic sovereignty   Who is the head of the State     The three powers   Make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (L, E, J)     External sovereign functions   Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs: war and diplomacy (including trade)     Domestic sovereign functions   Everything else: Home, Finance, Agriculture, Industry, Infrastructure, Health, Education, Transport and so on     "Rule" / "Govern"   Always means exercising those powers over domestic affairs   Sovereign functions are also called subjects or affairs. The 7th Schedule of the Constitution (COI 1950) divides the domestic affairs between the Centre and the provinces.  What is Sovereignty? Teacher's notes: symbolic sovereignty (real power = 0), the power to do L, E, J on external sovereign functions and on domestic affairs. Teacher: Symbolic sovereignty: real power = 0. (The head of State is only a symbol.) Second part: the power to do L, E, J on (a) external sovereign functions = D, C, FA and (b) internal / domestic affairs = Home, Finance, Education, Health. Teacher: Affairs = subjects = sovereign functions = the items in the 7th Schedule of the COI.  External functions: Defence goes to the Defence Minister (war). Communications and Foreign Affairs go to the MEA (diplomacy plus trade). Foreign Affairs has an economic and a political side. Teacher: External functions map to ministers like this. D (Defence) → Defence Minister → war. C (Communications) and FA (Foreign Affairs) → MEA → diplomacy + trade. Foreign Affairs has an economic and a political side. Mnemonic: External functions: D, C, FA. "Defence fights, Communications and Foreign Affairs talk and trade at the MEA." Decode: D (Defence) → Defence Minister → war. C (Communications) + FA (Foreign Affairs) → MEA → diplomacy + trade. Symbolic sovereignty = real power 0; L, E, J are the three powers over these and over domestic affairs. Why it sticks: one minister fights, the other talks, and you only need two ministries for three letters. Separation of powers in a modern State  Teacher's board: modern State structure. Symbolic Head of State over L, E, J, at Centre and provinces. Neither over-centralisation nor an over-weak centre.  Teacher's board, "Today": a modern State has horizontal separation of powers (L, E, J) and vertical separation of powers (federalism). Modern State structure = symbolic Head of State over L, E and J, at the Centre and provinces. The aim is separation of power, with neither over-centralisation nor an over-weak centre. Horizontal SoP = L / E / J. Vertical SoP = federalism. Inside the executive too: Head of State, PM, Council of Ministers, then the military servants ("gun power") and the civil servants ("political power"). Teacher: notice the separation of powers here also, for example a DM and an SP (more than one civil servant) share district power. Teacher: Non-modern State (example: Mughal). An absolute monarch, extremely powerful, with ministers, aristocrats and mansabdars below him. The mark is excessive centralisation. Teacher: Feudal State. The king is powerless, and feudal lords, ministers or aristocrats are powerful. There is no centralisation of power in the king: a very weak central authority.  The non-modern (Mughal) and feudal states compared with the modern structure. Modern INM: the phases  Modern INM (1857 to 1947) in five phases: Moderates, Extremists, Revolutionaries, Gandhian Era, Many Voices of the Nation.   Phase   Years   Tag    --- --- ---    Moderates   1857–1905   "the Pen"     Extremists   1905–20   "the People"     Revolutionaries   1907–47   "the Gun"     Gandhian Era   1920–47   —     Many Voices of the Nation   —   Working class, women's empowerment, Dalit issues   Mnemonic: INM phases: Pen, People, Gun, then Gandhi. "The Pen wrote (1857–1905), the People marched (1905–20), the Gun fired (1907–47), then Gandhi led (1920–47)." Decode: Moderates = Pen; Extremists = People; Revolutionaries = Gun; Gandhian Era 1920–47; the fifth phase is the Many Voices (working class, women, Dalits). Why it sticks: Revolutionaries start in 1907 (overlapping the Extremists) and run to 1947, the same end year as the Gandhian Era. How the teacher says to remember battles and wars  Teacher's method: remember every battle or war by its Geography/Place, Duration, Participants and Reason. A war is the sum of battles. War = Σ (the sum) of battles. For any named battle or war, hold four things: Geography / place, Duration (example: the Seven Years' War), Participants, and Reason (example: the Austrian War of Succession, 1740–48). Mnemonic: Remember any war: G-D-P-R. "Great Drummers Play Rhythms" (Geography, Duration, Participants, Reason). Decode: for every war ask where (Geography/place), how long (Duration, e.g. Seven Years' War), who (Participants), why (Reason, e.g. Austrian War of Succession 1740–48). A war = the sum of its battles. Why it sticks: use it as a four-box grid every time a new battle appears in later chapters. Passages: how regions connect  Passages: natural (passes on land, straits on water) and man-made (bridges, tunnels, canals). Khyber Pass is India's entry from the North-West. Khyber Pass = India's entry pathway from the North-West. A passage can be natural: on land a pass (Khyber); on water a strait (Gibraltar; the Dardanelles linking the Black and Mediterranean Seas). Or man-made: on land bridges and tunnels; on water canals (the Suez; the Panama Canal). Two places that are strategically important are joined by a passage, and the passage makes them so (teacher's sketch of A and B with a link, natural or man-made). Mnemonic: Passages: natural = P-S, man-made = B-T-C. "Nature gives a Pass and a Strait; people build Bridges, Tunnels and Canals." Decode: Natural land = pass (Khyber, India's North-West entry); natural water = strait (Gibraltar joins Europe and Africa; the Dardanelles). Man-made land = bridges and tunnels; man-made water = canals (Suez, Panama; Panama 1914 = key to the rise of the USA). Why it sticks: Khyber is the only pass you need to name, Gibraltar the first strait. Teacher: Gibraltar joins Europe and Africa. 1914 = the most important development in the rise of the USA (written next to the Panama Canal).
