Each code's second number is the next ruler's first number, like a baton passed on the track: Babur 26-30 → Humayun 30-40 ... Akbar 56-05 → Jahangir 05-27 → Shahjahan 27-58 → Aurangzeb 58-07 → Bahadur Shah 07-12 → Jahandar Shah 12-13 → Farukhsiyar 13-19 → Muhammad Shah 19-48 → Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54 → Alamgir II 54-59. Decode: only two dropped batons. Humayun 30-40 to Akbar 56-05 (the Suri gap), and Alamgir II 54-59 to Shah Alam II 60-06 (starts 60). Then Shah Alam II 60-06 → Akbar II 06-37 → Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 is smooth again. Why it sticks: if your next code does not start where the last one ended, you have found a gap. Mnemonic: The first six: B-H-A-J-S-A. "Bhaji, Sa-ab?" = Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shahjahan, Aurangzeb. Decode: Babur 26-30, Humayun 30-40, Akbar 56-05, Jahangir 05-27, Shahjahan 27-58, Aurangzeb 58-07 are #1 to #6. The Later Mughals (#7 to #15) begin with Bahadur Shah 07-12 in 1707, the year Aurangzeb 58-07 died. Why it sticks: 6 great + 9 later = 15 monarchs.  The teacher's heading for this table: "Heads of Mughal State". Humayun 30-40 is the only Mughal ruler with two reign periods: overthrown by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 in 1540, in exile for years, back on the throne in 1555, dead the following year. The list ends in 1857, the year of the great uprising. The last powerful emperor, Aurangzeb 58-07 (Alamgir), died in 1707. His successors, from Bahadur Shah to Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 (Bahadur Shah II), are the Later Mughals, ruling with ever-shrinking authority until 1857, when Zafar was deposed and exiled by the British. The Mughal State began with a cannon blast at Panipat in 1526 and ended with cannon blasts in Delhi. Mnemonic: Humayun 30-40 = "Hum-do" (two reigns). "Hum do reigns: 30-40, then back for 1555–56." Decode: Humayun 30-40 is the only Mughal with two reign periods. Overthrown by Sher Shah 40-45 in 1540, in exile, back on the throne in 1555, dead the following year. Why it sticks: "Hum-ayun" literally contains "hum", and he is the one who came back ("ayun"). Teacher: Simple picture of the Mughal State. Mughal State = 1526–1858, with an intermission 1540–55. The teacher's line-by-line: 1526 set up; 1540 demolished; 1555 re-established; Jan 1556 demolished (Humayun 30-40 dies); 1556 re-established. Akbar 56-05's reign is marked 49 years. Mnemonic: The Mughal see-saw: up, down, up, down, up. 1526 UP (set up), 1540 DOWN (demolished), 1555 UP (re-established), Jan 1556 DOWN (Humayun 30-40 dies), 1556 UP (re-established). Decode: the State is 1526–1858 with an intermission 1540–55 (the Suri gap, "a gap in the Mughal movie"). The handout's monarch list ends 1857; the teacher writes 1858, when the Company State ended. Why it sticks: five beats on a see-saw; the two DOWNs are Kanauj-era 1540 and the death in Jan 1556. The handout's monarch list ends in 1857, while the teacher writes the State as 1526–1858 (the year the Company State ended). Keep both in mind.  Teacher's board: Mughal State 1526-1858, intermission 1540-55. The State was set up in 1526, demolished in 1540, re-established in 1555, demolished in Jan 1556 and re-established in 1556.

items.t: 3 · Mughal take-over from the Lodis (Babur 26-30)
items.x: Who were the Mughals? Babur 26-30 was born in 1483 to Umar Shaikh Mirza, ruler of Fergana, a semi-autonomous State in present-day Uzbekistan, roughly half the size of modern Haryana. Fergana belonged to the Timurid Empire, and Babur 26-30 was a descendant of Timur (Tamerlane). "Mughal" is a Persian corruption of "Mongol". The Mughals were a Turko-Mongol dynasty.   Side   Ancestor   Empire    --- --- ---    Maternal   Genghis Khan (1206–27)   Mongol Empire (1206–1368)     Paternal   Timur (Tamerlane) (1370–1405)   Timurid Empire (1370–1507)     Self-identity   Timurids   Pride in Timur, who had captured Delhi in 1398   They took greater pride in the paternal ancestor, so they called themselves Timurids, not Mughals. Mnemonic: Mother Mongol, Father Timur. "Ma = Mongol (Genghis Khan 1206–27), Pa = Timur (1370–1405). The child chose Papa's name." Decode: maternal side = Genghis Khan, Mongol Empire (1206–1368); paternal side = Timur (Tamerlane), Timurid Empire (1370–1507). They took greater pride in Timur, who captured Delhi in 1398, so they called themselves Timurids. "Mughal" = Persian corruption of "Mongol". Why it sticks: pride goes to the ancestor who actually took Delhi.  Khanates of the Mongol Empire, about 1300 (handout figure).  Map: lands of the Empire of Timur (campaigns 1379 to 1405). Delhi is marked as sacked in 1398-99.  Map: the Fergana Valley, Babur's homeland (Kokand, Andijan, Osh, Namangan, Fergana, Jodzend). Why Babur 26-30 turned to India Babur 26-30 came to power young but could not hold Fergana; by 1512 his Central Asian ambitions had collapsed. He held Kabul (captured 1504), but Kabul was economically poor. India was wealthy but politically fragile under the Lodi dynasty. With artillery support from the Ottoman Empire (expert gunners), Babur 26-30 began attacking the Delhi Sultanate from 1519. Mnemonic: Babur 26-30's road: 83, 04, 12, 19, 26. Born 83; Kabul 04 (poor); Fergana lost 12; attacks start 19; Panipat 26. Decode: 1483 born in Fergana; 1504 captured Kabul (economically poor); 1512 Central Asian ambitions collapse; 1519 begins attacking the Delhi Sultanate with Ottoman gunners; 1526 First Panipat. Why it sticks: after Kabul 04, the gaps are +8, +7, +7 (04 → 12 → 19 → 26).  Map: the conquests of Babur, 1516 to 1529 (Kabul 1504, Khyber Pass, Panipat 1526, Agra 1528, Gwalior and the east 1529). The teacher marks Kabul as economically poor. Teacher: Babur 26-30's map: Kabul = "eco" (poor). The Khyber Pass is underlined. The dates 1526 (Panipat), 1528 (Agra) and 1529 (Gwalior and the march east) are underlined. First Battle of Panipat (1526) Babur 26-30 entered India through the Khyber Pass and met Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty (1451–1526), on the plains of Panipat. Babur 26-30's army was smaller (about 12,000 men), but his small bronze cannons were decisive, a technology the Lodis could not match. Lodi was killed, the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) ended and the Mughal Kingdom was born. This was still a kingdom, not yet an empire. It became an empire under Akbar 56-05 and reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07. Mnemonic: First Panipat 1526: small gun, big result. "A dozen thousand men, but bronze guns go BOOM: Lodi falls, a Kingdom is born." Decode: Babur 26-30 had about 12,000 men and small bronze cannons (Ottoman gunners) against Ibrahim Lodi, last of the Lodis (1451–1526). The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) ended. Tech power beat numbers. Why it sticks: Babur 26-30 = Kingdom (K), Akbar 56-05 = Empire (E), Aurangzeb 58-07 = greatest Extent (E): "K-E-E".  First Battle of Panipat 1526: Babur's edge (small bronze cannons, Ottoman gunners), the battle, and the outcome. Teacher writes: Tech Power.  First Battle of Panipat, 1526: Mughal miniature of Babur against Ibrahim Lodi. Teacher: Tech power. Babur 26-30's edge over a fragile Lodi Sultanate was technology, not numbers. The teacher underlines "small bronze cannons", "about 12,000" and "Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)". Why three great battles happened at Panipat Three of the most consequential battles in Indian history, 1526, 1556 and 1761, were all fought at Panipat. Geography chose Panipat; the commanders merely followed: Panipat lay close to the Khyber Pass, the primary invasion route from Central Asia. It sat in the narrow corridor between the Thar Desert (south) and the Himalayan foothills (north), a natural bottleneck. The Yamuna to the east acted as a defensive choke-point, ruling out flanking manoeuvres. The Kala Amb memorial in Haryana commemorates the 1761 Third Battle, not the 1526 one. Mnemonic: Three Panipats: 26, 56, 61. "Twenty-six, fifty-six, sixty-one: Babur 26-30's gun, Bairam's win, Kala Amb for the last one." Decode: 1526 (First, Babur 26-30 beats Lodi), 1556 (Second, Bairam Khan beats Hemu), 1761 (Third; the Kala Amb memorial in Haryana is for this one, not 1526). The first two share "15"; the third jumps to 17. Why it sticks: Kala Amb = the late one, 61. Mnemonic: Why Panipat? Three locks: K-T-Y. "Khyber door, Thar-Himalaya tunnel, Yamuna wall." Decode: close to the Khyber Pass (invasion route); a narrow corridor between the Thar Desert (south) and Himalayan foothills (north); the Yamuna to the east rules out flanking. Why it sticks: the invader enters the door, walks the tunnel and hits the wall right at Panipat. Babur 26-30 in Fergana; Timurid descendant, loses Fergana by 1512 (warn) Kabul held from 1504; economically poor India: rich but politically fragile under the Lodis Ottoman gunners and small bronze cannons; attacks from 1519 First Battle of Panipat 1526; Babur 26-30 (about 12,000) defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi (good) Delhi Sultanate ends; the Mughal Kingdom is born (a kingdom, not yet an empire)

items.t: 4 · Humayun 30-40 and Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: Babur 26-30 died in 1530; his son Humayun 30-40 succeeded. Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 was an Afghan-Pathan, born Farid Khan in Bihar, c. 1486. He was no foreign invader: his ancestors migrated to India under the Lodis and settled as Jagirdars in Bihar. He won the title Sher Khan by killing a tiger single-handed while serving Bahar Khan Lohani (Governor of Bihar under the Lodis till 1526, then independent Sultan Md Lohani, who refused Mughal sovereignty). Sher Shah 40-45 defeated Humayun 30-40 at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540), founded the Suri dynasty (1540–55) and pushed the Mughals out of India entirely.  Humayun's loss and return: 1530 succession, 1539 Chausa, 1540 Kanauj, 1555 Sirhind, Jan 1556 death and Hemu seizes Delhi. Teacher: a gap or intermission in the Mughal movie. Teacher: Two defeats: Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540). The Suri interregnum 1540–55 is a gap / intermission in the Mughal movie. Sirhind (1555) is boxed. Mnemonic: Humayun 30-40's battles go A-B-C: C, K, S. Alphabetical = chronological: Chausa 1539 (lose), Kanauj 1540 (lose), Sirhind 1555 (win). Decode: Chausa and Kanauj were his two defeats by Sher Shah 40-45; Sirhind was his win over the Suris with Safavid help. The Suri dynasty (1540–55) fills the gap between K and S. Why it sticks: C, K, S never swap places, so the quiz order is just the alphabet. Two Ls then one W. Sher Shah 40-45's three reforms The Suri dynasty lasted only fifteen years, but Sher Shah 40-45's administrative innovations outlasted it: Revenue. A standardised system of land measurement and revenue assessment, the precursor to Akbar 56-05's Zabti system. Each peasant got a Patta specifying his revenue obligation, and the State took a Qabuliyat, a written agreement, from the peasant. The two-document system gave both State and cultivator an enforceable record. Currency. The silver Rupiya, a coin of standardised weight and purity, the ancestor of the modern Indian rupee. Infrastructure. He upgraded the Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Sonargaon in Bengal, transforming communication and trade across the subcontinent. Mnemonic: Sher Shah 40-45's three Rs. "Records, Rupiya, Road." Decode: Records = Patta + Qabuliyat (revenue; precursor to Akbar 56-05's Zabti). Rupiya = silver coin of fixed weight and purity. Road = Grand Trunk Road, Peshawar to Sonargaon (Bengal). Why it sticks: "P to S" for the road, Peshawar to Sonargaon. He ruled the Suri dynasty only 1540–55, fifteen years. Patta and Qabuliyat. The Patta is a document given by the State to the ryot: land details, ryot's name, the LR to be paid. The Qabuliyat is proof that the ryot agreed to pay the LR; it is given by the ryot to the State. Sher Shah 40-45 was the first to introduce this bilateral / mutual agreement system. In ancient times a Patta existed but it was not two-sided: the State gave the Patta (Tamra Patra, a copper inscription). Mnemonic: Patta vs Qabuliyat: "Qabool hai!" The State hands over the Patta; the ryot says "Qabool hai" and signs the Qabuliyat. Decode: Patta = title deed from State to ryot (his field, his name, the LR to pay; a check on over-extraction). Qabuliyat = acceptance deed signed by the ryot and given back, promising to pay the LR on the Patta. Sher Shah 40-45 was first to make it two-sided. Why it sticks: like a wedding, both sides must say yes. Sher Shah 40-45 died in 1545. The Suri dynasty held Delhi until 1555, when Humayun 30-40 recaptured the throne. Much of what Akbar 56-05 later systematised had its roots in Sher Shah 40-45's innovations. Humayun 30-40 returns, with Safavid help To retake his throne, Humayun 30-40 turned to the Safavid dynasty of Iran. The Safavids agreed at a political price: Humayun 30-40 had to adopt Shia practices and outward observances, cede Kandahar to Iran, and promote Persian culture in India. Whether this was genuine conversion is debated; Humayun 30-40 publicly assumed Shia forms as the price of the alliance. Lasting consequences: Persian language and art became embedded in Mughal court culture, and a distinct Irani group of Mansabdars later emerged in the Mughal administration. Mnemonic: Persia's bill: Shirt, Key, Poem (S-K-P). Humayun 30-40 pays for Safavid help with a Shirt, a Key and a Poem. Decode: Shirt = adopt Shia forms; Key = cede Kandahar to Iran; Poem = promote Persian culture (so an Irani group of Mansabdars follows). The help: 14,000 Iranian troops, win at Sirhind 1555. Why it sticks: three things to hand over, one picture each.  Teacher's board: the Safavid dynasty of Persia's conditions for helping Humayun: convert to Shia, promote Persian culture, make Persians mansabdars (link: the Irani group). With 14,000 Iranian troops, Humayun 30-40 defeated the Suris at the Battle of Sirhind (Punjab, 1555). In January 1556 Humayun 30-40 fell from the stairs of his library, struck his head and died. Hemchandra Vikramaditya (Hemu), from Rewari in present-day Haryana, who had served as chief commander and minister of the Suris, seized Delhi and declared himself Samrat.

items.t: 5 · How the Mughal Kingdom was re-established (Panipat 1556)
items.x: On one side stood Hemu, controlling Delhi. On the other, the Mughal army under Bairam Khan: general, strategist and guardian to the thirteen-year-old Akbar 56-05. Hemu was defeated. The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) secured the Mughal State in India for the next 150 years. Mnemonic: 1556: one year, three events, one code. "Fifty-six: Humayun 30-40 falls (Jan), Hemu crowns himself, Bairam wins, and Akbar 56-05's code starts with 56." Decode: Jan 1556 Humayun 30-40 falls from his library stairs; Hemu (from Rewari, ex-Suri commander) declares himself Samrat; Second Panipat 1556, Bairam Khan (guardian of 13-year-old Akbar 56-05) defeats him. Why it sticks: Akbar 56-05's code begins with the year of the battle, and "Bairam = Guardian" because the boy was only 13.  Second Battle of Panipat 1556: Hemu (declares himself Samrat; teacher: a powerful military general and minister of the Suris, 1540-55), Bairam Khan defeats him, the Mughal State is secured for about 150 years. Babur 26-30 enters through the Khyber Pass; First Panipat 1526 Humayun 30-40 defeated by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 (Chausa 1539, Kanauj 1540) (bad) Suri dynasty 1540–55; Mughals lose India Safavid alliance; 14,000 Iranian troops; Sirhind 1555 Humayun 30-40 dies Jan 1556; Hemu seizes Delhi (good) Second Panipat 1556: Bairam Khan defeats Hemu; Akbar 56-05's reign secured

items.t: 6 · How Akbar 56-05 built the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System
items.x: Babur 26-30 founded the Mughal Kingdom. Humayun 30-40 nearly lost it. Akbar 56-05, ruling for fifty years (1556–1605), built the machinery of the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System, a military-bureaucracy that decided how the State was administered, how its army was maintained and how the King kept control over a vast and diverse territory. What is a Mansabdar? Mansab = a post or rank. Mansabdar = the holder of the post. Every Mansabdar had a dual function: military and civil-administrative. The same man who commanded troops also governed territory. That is why it is called a military-bureaucracy.  Teacher's board: the Mughal Emperor over Mansabdars (= ministers and senior officers). A post = mansab; a DM or minister = mansabdar; DMship or ministership = mansab. Teacher: Posts in the State structure. "O" = a post = mansab. A DM or minister = mansabdar; DM-ship or minister-ship = mansab. Mansabdars = the ministers and senior officers of the Mughal State. Five questions the teacher sets for the topic: *What is a mansab? What is a mansabdar? Salary? Ranks? How to become a mansabdar?* Rank: Zat + Sawar Each Mansabdar carried two ranks: Zat = personal rank, governing seniority and status. Sawar = the number of horsemen he must maintain and provide to the King. Net rank = Zat + Sawar. Example: Zat 2,000 + Sawar 3,000 = net rank 5,000. Mnemonic: Zat = Zaat (status), Sawar = Sawari (riders). "Zat is who you are; Sawar is who rides for you." Decode: Mansab = post/rank, Mansabdar = holder. Zat = personal rank (seniority, status). Sawar = number of horsemen to maintain. Net rank = Zat + Sawar (2,000 + 3,000 = 5,000). Why it sticks: "Sawari" is the Hindi word for a ride, so Sawar = horse-riders.  Mansabdari, Zat plus Sawar. Teacher's notes: no separation of power between civil and military; Zat = A (like today), Sawar = B (army), net = A+B; eligibility primary = hereditary, exception Birbal; Piyush and Anshu on a Zat-Sawar graph. Teacher: No separation of power between civil and military. Zat is like today's rank (A); Sawar = the army, i.e. the horsemen (B); net rank = A + B. Teacher: Eligibility. "Lineage, not merit" in most cases. The primary rule was hereditary, with the exception of Birbal, who was not from an aristocratic family. Teacher: Zat-Sawar graph. Most nobles lie on the rising line (more Zat, more Sawar). Outliers: the favourite of the emperor = "Anshu" and the distrusted = "Piyush". The teacher's two names sit at opposite corners of the graph (Piyush high on Zat, Anshu high on Sawar). Mnemonic: Anshu = Army, Piyush = Paper. Anshu (the emperor's favourite) is high on Sawar, the army; Piyush (the distrusted) is high on Zat, rank only. Decode: the teacher's two outliers on the Zat-Sawar graph. Most nobles lie on the rising line (more Zat, more Sawar). Favourite = Anshu (high Sawar); distrusted = Piyush (high Zat). Why it sticks: the trusted get the Army, the distrusted get Paper. Who could become a Mansabdar? Lineage, not merit. If your ancestors had been Mansabdars, you had the opportunity. Talent alone was not enough, not unlike pre-revolutionary France, where only sons of nobles could enter the nobility. This rigidity later became a serious weakness. How Mansabdars were paid: Jagir, Khalisa, Inam A Mansabdar could be paid in cash (a Naqdi Mansabdar) or by a Jagir: a specific piece of land whose land revenue he pocketed directly. This revenue paid his salary and covered the cost of maintaining his army. A Jagir given in lieu of salary = a Tankha Jagir; its holder = a Jagirdar. Iqtadar of the Delhi Sultanate is like the Jagirdar Mansabdar of the Mughals. (Iqta = Jagir in Persian.) Mughal land was divided into these categories: Jagir land: revenue to Mansabdars. Khalisa land: royal land. Revenue goes directly to the King and pays Naqdi Mansabdars plus other State expenses. Inam land: gifted land. Revenue goes to a chosen beneficiary (for example a man of exceptional talent) to sustain himself. Mashrut Jagir: a temporary "top-up" or extra allowance given to an official to cover the extra costs of a specific, difficult assignment. It is revoked automatically when the assignment ends. (Like "base salary" versus "the bonus".) Mnemonic: Four land types: J-K-I-M. Jagir = Jagirdar's; Khalisa = King's; Inam = I'm-chosen gift; Mashrut = Mission bonus. Decode: Jagir land: revenue to Mansabdars. Khalisa: royal land, revenue straight to the King, pays Naqdi Mansabdars. Inam: gifted land for a beneficiary (exceptional talent). Mashrut Jagir: a temporary top-up for a difficult assignment, revoked when it ends. Why it sticks: J and K are the big two; I and M are the small extras.  Mughal land classification: Jagir (Tankha and Watan), Khalisa, Inam, Mashrut Jagir. By the early 18th century there were over 8,000 Mansabdars, and four-fifths of all LR came from Jagirs, only one-fifth from Khalisa land. Mnemonic: Four fingers and a thumb: 4/5 Jagir, 1/5 Khalisa. The Mansabdars hold four fingers of the revenue; the King holds only the thumb. Decode: four-fifths of all LR came from Jagirs, only one-fifth from Khalisa land (teacher's 80 to 20). So the richest *single* person was still the King. Why it sticks: the thumb is one finger, and the King is one person.  Teacher's board: land of the Mughal empire. Khalisa land = 1/5 of total LR; Jagir lands = 4/5, with a small Watan Jagir block (10% to the king, 90% to the Jagirdar). Teacher: Salary in those times. The key source of power was control over land and its resources (today it is money). Mansabdars were about 4,000 to 5,000 at the peak of Mughal power (17th century); about 80 out of every 100 of LR went to them and about 20 to the King. Therefore the richest single person was the King. Teacher: Worked example for LR: ₹100 of wheat is cultivated by the ryot / peasant / Khudkasht. Tax = LR = 1/3 to 2/3 of gross produce. (For the changing LR share by era, see section 7.)  Teacher's board: salary is cash (Naqdi Mansabdar) or allocation of a Tankha Jagir (Jagirdar Mansabdar). LR of a Jagir goes to the Mansabdar. LR = 1/3 to 2/3 of gross produce. Three rules for Tankha Jagirs Transferable. The King could rotate Jagirs among Mansabdars, or convert a Jagirdar into a Naqdi Mansabdar at will. Capped extraction. A Jagirdar could collect only the pre-determined LR, not a rupee more. Royal supervision existed to prevent oppression of peasants and zamindars. Confiscation on death. On the death of a Tankha Jagirdar, both the Jagir and all accumulated wealth were confiscated. The predictable result: Mansabdars spent lavishly in their lifetimes, since saving made little sense. Mnemonic: Tankha Jagir rules: T-C-C. "Tossed around, Capped, Confiscated." Decode: Transferable (King can rotate it or turn the holder into a Naqdi Mansabdar); Capped (collect only the fixed LR, not a rupee more); Confiscated on death (Jagir and wealth both). Result: Mansabdars spent lavishly. Why it sticks: a tenant who knows the house will be taken back spends everything on parties.  Tankha Jagir: the King gets his army from it. Of a Jagir's LR, 30 is for personal salary and 70 must be used for maintaining the army as per Sawar. Military corruption after 1707 = the expected army not being maintained. Teacher: From a Tankha Jagir the King gets his army. Teacher's example split: LR = ₹30 pays for personal salary; LR = ₹70 must be used to maintain the army as per Sawar. Military corruption (post-1707) = the expected army is not being maintained. Watan Jagir Watan = hereditary and permanent. Unlike Tankha Jagirs, a Watan Jagir could be passed down and was not subject to rotation or confiscation. Given mainly to Rajput chieftains and autonomous rulers who had submitted to the Emperor, so they could collect revenue in their ancestral domains in exchange for military service and loyalty. The holder paid 10% of LR to the King as Peshkash (tribute), acknowledging the King's ultimate authority and compensating him for giving up his right to reclaim the Jagir. Do not confuse an ordinary Zamindar's Milkiyat (hereditary personal property within his zamindari tract) with a Watan Jagir (a political grant to a chieftain, carrying sovereign-like privileges). Inam vs Watan: Inam is a pure gift and is confiscated after death like Tankha Jagir. Watan is hereditary, given to a Mansabdar doing duty for the King, and passes to heirs.   Axis   Tankha Jagir   Watan Jagir    --- --- ---    Nature   Salary grant   Hereditary, permanent grant     Heritability   Confiscated on the holder's death   Passes to heirs     Transfer   King could rotate it at will   Not rotated     Typical holder   Any Mansabdar   Rajput chiefs / rulers who submitted     Tribute   —   Pays 10% of LR as Peshkash to the King   Mnemonic: Tankha = Temporary, Watan = Waris (heir). "Tankha is Taken back; Watan is Willed on." Decode: Tankha Jagir = salary grant, rotated at will, confiscated on death; Jagirdar takes 100% of the LR. Watan = hereditary, permanent, not rotated; given to Rajput chiefs and submitted rulers; holder keeps 90% and pays 10% as Peshkash (tribute). Why it sticks: Tankha's salary split (teacher's example) is 30 for self, 70 for the army: "thirty for me, seventy for my men".  Tankha vs Watan Jagir.  Teacher's board: power of a Mansabdar. Jagirdar Mansabdars hold Tankha Jagir (all LR to the mansabdar) and sometimes Watan Jagir (90% to the mansabdar, 10% to the king); Naqdi Mansabdars get cash. Teacher: W = Watan / Vatan = hereditary = permanent = 10% of LR to the King as tribute. TJ = temporary = the emperor can take it away = transferable. In the teacher's picture, a Jagirdar with both gets 90% of the LR of the Watan portion, the king taking 10%; on Tankha land the Jagirdar takes 100% of the LR. What held the system together, and its fatal weakness The system ran on a patron-client relationship: the King gave rank and Jagir, and the Mansabdar pledged personal loyalty and maintained the army. This co-opted powerful individuals who might have challenged royal authority. But the loyalty was personal, not institutional. A Mansabdar's loyalty was to the King as a person, not to the State as an institution or to any law. It was transactional and conditional: give and take. If the King could not deliver Mansab and Jagir (land shortage, financial pressure, weak authority), the loyalty dissolved, and dissolved loyalty meant political instability. This differs from a modern State, where bureaucrats and military officers owe their position to merit and service rules: impersonal loyalty to institution and law. Because the whole military strength depended on Mansabdars actually maintaining the Sawar armies, weakened royal supervision meant hollowed-out armies on paper, far fewer men in reality, a silent erosion of State power from within. Patron-client bond; King gives Mansab + Jagir, Mansabdar gives loyalty and maintains the army Loyalty is personal; to the King, not to the State or any law (warn) King cannot deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir (bad) Loyalty dissolves; the bond was transactional and conditional (bad) State erodes; hollow armies on paper, fewer men in reality  The Mansabdari weakness: an institutional / organisational / systemic weakness. Teacher: loyalty should be impersonal (non-human), to religion, land or language. On paper a 2 lakh army, in reality a 1 lakh army.  Teacher's board: Mansab plus Jagir given by the King; loyalty and army given back. A patron-client relationship (senior gives, junior takes). After 1707, mansabdars who did not get the desired mansab and jagir became disloyal. Teacher: Institutional / organisational / systemic weakness. Impersonal loyalty (non-human) means loyalty to the State, law, religion, land or language, not to a person. The teacher's reading of the flow: "King cannot deliver" = cannot deliver the *desired* Mansab and Jagir (the teacher crossed out the handout's "land/revenue runs short" line and replaced it with this). The end state: on paper a 2 lakh army, in reality a 1 lakh army. Teacher: Post-1707: if Mansabdars did not get their desired Mansab and Jagir, they became disloyal. The patron-client picture: the patron is senior and gives; the client is junior and takes. Mnemonic: Patron gives, client pledges, ghosts appear. King gives rank + Jagir; Mansabdar gives loyalty + army. If the King cannot deliver the *desired* Mansab and Jagir, loyalty melts, and half the army becomes a ghost. Decode: patron-client bond; loyalty is personal, not institutional (to the King, not the State or law). Teacher's end state: on paper a 2 lakh army, in reality 1 lakh. After 1707, Mansabdars who did not get their desired posts turned disloyal. Why it sticks: "2 on paper, 1 in reality" = half is a ghost army.

items.t: 7 · Mughal land revenue (LR) system
items.x: Usually people think all rights in a property are with the owner. That is not correct. Rights in land belong to four stakeholders:   Stakeholder   Rights    --- ---    The owner (in the Mughal system, ultimately the King)   Right to sell, lease out, rent out, and to get money from these; right to fair tax     The tenant / ryot   Right to occupy and cultivate; right to fair rent     The collector of tax   Right to collect tax; right to be paid for the service     The State   Right to assess / fix tax, enforce the demand and receive tax   LR was the financial backbone of the State: it paid the Mansabdars, maintained the army and kept the treasury alive.  Mughal LR system overview: the King owns all land and the State takes a fixed share as LR. Assessors with record-keepers fix the demand per field. Two systems: Zabti and Ijaradari. Teacher: Assessors fix the demand using past data of production and of LR, and so assess the LR demand. The two systems, Zabti and Ijaradari, are ticked. Who collected revenue, and how was it supervised The State did not collect directly. It relied on Zamindars (non-state actors) in zamindari tracts, who also held police duties. Rule of thumb: State actors get salaries. Non-State actors get a commission or profit for service performed for the State. The revenue hierarchy ran through record-keeping, assessment, settlement, collection and oversight:   Step   Level   Officer   Role    --- --- --- ---    A1 Record keeping   Village   Patwari   Maintains ledgers (Bahi / Bahi khata or Khasra) of individual peasant holdings and crops. A non-state accountant paid by the village community. Like the Kulkarni of Maharashtra, but the Patwari had no watan / vatan (hereditary) right; it was a customary right, not a customary vatan right     A2 Record keeping   Pargana   Qanungo   Consolidated Patwari data; a state official and hereditary custodian of historical tax rates (had vatan right)     B1 Assessment   Pargana   Amil   The State's executive revenue officer at the pargana level; assessed the official demand and audited accounts     B2 Assessment   Sarkar (district)   Amalguzar   Supervisor of the Amil at the sarkar level; assessed the demand and audited accounts     C Settlement   Ryot   Patta and Qabuliyat   See below     D Collection   Village   Muqaddam   Village headman who collected from cultivators     E Oversight   Pargana / sarkar   Amil and Amalguzar   Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system   Mnemonic: Revenue relay: write, file, assess, audit, collect. The Patwari writes (village), the Qanungo files (pargana), the Amil assesses (pargana), the Amalguzar audits (sarkar), the Muqaddam collects (village). Decode: Patwari = village ledger keeper, non-state, no vatan right. Qanungo = pargana, state official, hereditary keeper of old rates (has vatan right). Amil = pargana assessor; Amalguzar = supervises the Amil at sarkar level. Muqaddam = village headman who collects. Why it sticks: P-Q alphabetical (record keepers), then A-A (assessors), and the Muqaddam closes at the bottom with the money. Patta (the title deed) = the official paper given to the individual peasant by the government. The government used the Patwari's ledger / Khasra to create it. It told the peasant exactly how much land he officially held and how much LR he must pay, and so served as a check against over-extraction. Qabuliyat (the acceptance deed) = the document signed by the peasant and given back to the government, promising to pay the LR written on the Patta.  Khudkasht vs Pahikasht. Teacher: a Patta has information on which field or plot is cultivated by which ryot, and how much LR is to be paid. Zamindar = holds the right to collect LR from a land; Jagirdar = holds the right to consume LR from a land. Teacher: A Patta has two pieces of information: which field / plot is cultivated by which ryot and how much LR is to be paid. It is a "safety tool for the Khudkasht / ryot". Teacher: Zamindar = holds the right to *collect* LR from a land. Jagirdar = holds the right to *consume* LR from a land. Mnemonic: Zamindar collects, Jagirdar consumes. "Z Zips it up; J Just eats it." Decode: Zamindar = right to *collect* LR (non-state actor, keeps about 10% Nankar / Malikana). Jagirdar = right to *consume* LR from a land (Mansabdar). Why it sticks: the collector is the middleman; the consumer is the master. Physical collection and the Zabti system Muqaddams collected from cultivators. In zamindari tracts they deposited to Zamindars (who extracted through their own Amlas). Where there were no intermediaries, Muqaddams paid directly to the State. In later periods contractual revenue farmers, the Ijaradars, also collected (covered below). Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system, the State did not trust Zamindars with autonomous authority. State officials (Amil at pargana level, under the Amalguzar at sarkar level) scientifically measured the land and fixed the exact demand. The land records were archived by the Qanungo at pargana level. LR was calculated as a percentage of gross produce (more LR from more fertile areas). Mughal LR demand was a percentage of Gross Produce, not Net Produce. Subtracting the cost of cultivation before taxing was a British reform, much later, and only after the gross-produce method had caused widespread agrarian ruin.  Mansabdari versus Zamindari / Zabti. Mansabdari = the system of Mughal State structure (king and mansabdars; roles, salaries, hierarchy, ranks). Zamindari / Zabti = the system of collection of LR (assessment by the State, collection by the Zamindar). Teacher: Mansabdari = a system of the Mughal *State structure* (king and mansabdars; roles and responsibilities, salaries, hierarchy and ranks). Zamindari / Zabti = a system of *collection of LR*: assessment (how much LR) by the State, collection by the Zamindar. Don't mix the two. The zamindar's position  Teacher's diagram of the LR chain (Zabti): King gets LR from Khalisa lands; Jagirdar Mansabdars from Jagirs; Intermediary Zamindars (1000-3000 villages) and Primary Zamindars (100-300 villages) each keep 10% commission; ryots at the bottom. The Zamindar was an obedient collection agent under strict supervision, making sure the surplus went to the central treasury, not his pocket. His legally fixed commission, about 10%, was called Nankar or Malikana. His own personal lands were Milkiyat, on which he paid LR like any other landholder. Abwabs = customary tributes, extra demands passed from State to Zamindar to peasant. Intermediary Zamindars = big Zamindars who received LR from Primary Zamindars and collected LR themselves where no Primary Zamindar existed in their assigned land. They passed LR from Khalisa lands to the Imperial Treasury and from Jagir lands to Jagirdars. Sometimes Primary Zamindars sent LR straight to the treasury or the Jagirdar.  The Zamindari system. Teacher: the quantum of LR is decided by the State; the Zamindar's earnings are commission (about 10%), Abwab and his hereditary land; he also has police duties; Abwab is a levy from State to Zamindar and a tribute from ryot. Teacher: The quantum of LR is decided by the State, not the zamindar. In the teacher's circle (the rural economy): ryots pay LR up to the Zamindar; he sends LR to K (king) and J (jagirdar); he keeps 10% as commission, Abwab, and has police duties. Teacher: Zamindar roles. He also had police duties (the teacher compares it with an SHO's work) and was the traditional leader of ryots. Abwab from State to Zamindar = levies; Abwab from ryot to Zamindar = tribute.  Teacher's board: the Patta (name of ryot, LR to be paid, details of fields) is the safety tool for the Khudkasht; the Zamindar is a non-state actor, not a govt employee; salary is only for employees; Zamindar's service to the State is LR collection and police duties, for 10% of LR. Teacher: A Zamindar is a non-state actor: a private person, not a govt employee. Salary is used only for employees. His payment for services to the State (LR collection and police duties) is the 10% of LR. Teacher: A classroom ladder of power (vehicle analogy): King = helicopter; Jagirdar = Ferrari; Intermediary Zamindar = Fortuner; Primary Zamindar = Honda City; Khudkasht = cycle / Luna; Pahikasht = on foot. Mnemonic: The power ladder in six vehicles. Sky to ground: Helicopter, Ferrari, Fortuner, Honda City, Luna, Legs. Decode: King = helicopter; Jagirdar = Ferrari; Intermediary Zamindar = Fortuner; Primary Zamindar = Honda City; Khudkasht = cycle / Luna; Pahikasht = on foot. Why it sticks: both Zamindars drive family cars you see on Indian roads; the top two are showpieces and the bottom two have no engine.  The teacher's vehicle analogy for the LR ladder: King (helicopter), Jagirdar (Ferrari), Intermediary Zamindar (Fortuner), Primary Zamindar (Honda City), Khudkasht (cycle/Luna), Pahikasht (on foot).   Level   Collects from   Passes to   Keeps    --- --- --- ---    Ryot (Khudkasht / Pahikasht)   Pays LR   Primary Zamindar (or Muqaddam, or directly to State in non-zamindari areas)   Enough to sustain himself     Primary Zamindar (smaller; 100–300 villages)   Ryots   Intermediary Zamindar   About 10% (Nankar / Malikana)     Intermediary Zamindar (big; 1000–3000 villages)   Primary Zamindars   King (Khalisa) or Jagirdar (Jagir)   About 10% (Nankar / Malikana)     King / Jagirdar   Zamindars   —   King: Khalisa LR. Jagirdar: Jagir LR   Mnemonic: Primary 100-300, Intermediary 1000-3000: add a zero. The Intermediary Zamindar is the Primary Zamindar with one more zero. Decode: Primary Zamindar = smaller, 100 to 300 villages. Intermediary = big, 1000 to 3000 villages. Each keeps about 10% (Nankar / Malikana). Intermediaries pass Khalisa LR to the King and Jagir LR to Jagirdars. Why it sticks: ten times the villages, ten times the status, but the same 10% commission rate. Two kinds of ryot   Axis   Khudkasht   Pahikasht    --- --- ---    Land worked   The same land year after year   Different lands each season (often share-croppers)     Occupancy rights   Customary occupancy: cannot be removed   None; no fixed attachment to land     Standing   Small landowner-cultivator; holds a Patta   Landless and rightless (Vagrant / Banjara)   Khudkasht = occupancy rights of cultivation, NOT ownership. The King owned all land. A Khudkasht could not be arbitrarily removed, but could not sell or mortgage the land either. Mnemonic: Khudkasht = "khud ka khet"; Pahikasht = "paon-paon" wanderer. The Khudkasht stays on his own field (occupancy, not ownership); the Pahikasht goes on foot from field to field. Decode: Khudkasht = same land year after year, cannot be removed, holds a Patta, but cannot sell or mortgage (King owns all land). Pahikasht = different lands each season, no occupancy rights, landless and rightless (vagrant / Banjara). Why it sticks: "khud" = self, and the teacher's own picture gives Khudkasht a cycle and Pahikasht his feet.  Khudkasht vs Pahikasht: the Khudkasht holds a Patta; the Pahikasht is a landless, rightless vagrant or Banjara. Teacher: Pahikasht = cultivates different lands (within a village); landless and rightless. Revenue farming: Muqatai, Ijaradari, Farming System The logic: instead of collecting through the Zamindar network under State supervision, the right to collect all revenues from an area (land, traders, shopkeepers) was auctioned to the highest bidder, called an Ijaradar or Revenue Farmer. A farmer, in the economic sense, works with a profit motive; a peasant works for food security. The Ijaradar was not a cultivator but a merchant or moneylender who bid purely for profit. He farmed revenue, not land. The Ijaradar paid the bid amount, fully or partially in advance, to the Jagirdar (on Jagir land) or to the State (on Khalisa land), then collected his investment plus profit from the peasants and traders. Contracts were typically 3 to 5 years. His incentive was to extract as much as possible within that window, with zero interest in irrigation, peasant welfare or long-term growth. If he failed to deliver, the contract was re-auctioned. Ijaradars were urban bankers and merchants with no roots in the countryside: no long-term stake in the land, no relationship with the peasants.  Teacher's board: the Ijaradari system arises when there is need (war, bad harvest, a State short of LR) or greed (for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise earnings, or a weak Mughal State) for higher LR. Ijaradar = Revenue Farmer. Teacher: Why Ijaradari arises: need or greed, for ↑LR. Need = war, bad harvest, LR collection of the State falling short. Greed = for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise his earnings, and a weak Mughal State. Mnemonic: Why Ijaradari arises: Need or Greed. "Need runs dry, Greed runs wild." Decode: Need = war, bad harvest, State's LR falling short. Greed = a Jagirdar who wants to maximise earnings, or a weak Mughal State. Both want more LR (↑LR). Why it sticks: two words, one reason each: pressure from outside (Need), appetite from inside (Greed).  Teacher's auction analogy: the right to collect revenue from an area is sold like a painting. All bidders are rich; the seller gets the best price through competitive bidding and gets the money in advance; the buyer's motive is profit. Teacher: The painting analogy. Bidders in the auction are all rich. "HK" (the seller) gets the best price, as a result of competitive bidding, and gets the money in advance. "Bhaskar" (the buyer) then gets the painting. Bhaskar and the other bidders have profit as the motive: he plans to sell it at ₹2 crore, so ₹1 crore is the investment and the return he expects is ₹1 crore. In Ijaradari the right to collect revenue is the painting. Mnemonic: The painting auction: 1 crore in, 1 crore profit. The right to collect revenue = the painting; the Ijaradar = Bhaskar, who buys at ₹1 crore to sell at ₹2 crore. Decode: auction, money paid in advance, best price through competitive bidding. Ijaradar's motive is profit: the bid is the investment, and the LR he squeezes must cover bid plus profit. He farms revenue, not land. Why it sticks: seller smiles (advance), buyer smiles (profit), the peasant is the canvas that gets squeezed.  Teacher's board: auctions are held by the Jagirdar (in Jagir areas) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands). Participants are men of money: merchants, moneylenders, bankers (Ijaradars). Motive = profit. Contract 3-4 years. The Zamindar suffers a temporary loss of his Watan right to collect LR. Teacher: Who auctions: the Jagirdar (in a Jagir area) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands). They get money in advance (no wait till harvest) and the best price. Participants are men of money: merchants, moneylenders and bankers = Ijaradars. Motive = profit: collect such LR from ryots as covers the bid/investment plus profits. The teacher writes contract time as 3-4 years (the handout says 3 to 5). The Zamindar suffers a temporary loss of his Watan right to collect LR. Mnemonic: Who auctions, how long: "J or K; 3 to 5, teacher 3-4." The auctioneer is the Jagirdar (on Jagir land) or the King/State (on Khalisa land). Decode: contract length is 3 to 5 years in the handout; the teacher writes 3-4. Learn "3 to 5 (teacher 3-4)": both start at 3. Bidders are merchants, moneylenders, bankers; the Zamindar temporarily loses his Watan right to collect. Why it sticks: Jagir and Khalisa matches the letters J and K, just like the four land types.  The mechanics: the Jagirdar auctions the right to collect LR over an area; merchants and moneylenders participate; the winner pays the bid amount to the Jagirdar in advance and collects LR from the ryots for profit.  Who is happy and who is not under Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar happy (advance, best price); Ijaradar happy (profits); ryots unhappy (no Patta); Zamindar unhappy (lost Watan right and earnings). A revolt needs a leader and followers. Teacher: Who wins and loses in Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar: happy (advance, best ₹). Ijaradar: happy (profits). Ryots: unhappy (no Patta). Zamindar: unhappy (lost Watan right and earnings). Teacher: A revolt needs a leader (L) and followers (Fo). If both (Zamindar as leader, ryots as followers) are unhappy: strong revolt. If the leader is unhappy but followers are happy: no revolt. If the leader is happy but followers unhappy: weak revolt. Mnemonic: Revolt needs a Leader and Followers: L + F. Both unhappy = strong (a general with an army). Only the leader unhappy = none (a general with no army). Only followers unhappy = weak (an army with no general). Decode: under Ijaradari the Zamindar (leader) lost his Watan right and earnings, and the ryots (followers) have no Patta: both are unhappy, so revolt is strongest. King/Jagirdar (advance, best price) and Ijaradar (profit) are the happy ones. Why it sticks: the revolt is the product of two things; set either to zero and it fails.  Example: Churaman Jat, a Zamindar-led peasant revolt (about 1695), the grievance being high LR, led to the Jat Kingdom. Teacher: Example: Churaman 95-21 Jat = Zamindar-led peasant revolt (~1695); grievance = high LR; it led to the Jat Kingdom. (Taken up in Chapter 5.) Mnemonic: Churaman 95-21 Jat: the code starts with 95, the revolt is in 1695. "Ninety-five in his code, sixteen-ninety-five on the calendar." Decode: a Zamindar-led peasant revolt (about 1695) over high LR that led to the Jat Kingdom. Why it sticks: his code's first number is the revolt's year ending. Zamindar vs Ijaradar: why it mattered to the peasant. A Zamindar's right was tied to his bloodline; he and his descendants had to live with the peasants forever, so he rarely squeezed them to starvation. His commission was a state-mandated ~10% (Nankar / Malikana). An Ijaradar promised the State a fixed lump sum (say 1 lakh); if he extracted 3 lakh through torture and extortion, he kept the entire 2 lakh profit. The Zamindar's extraction was capped by law; the Ijaradar's was capped only by the peasant's capacity to endure.  Zamindar versus Ijaradar: basis of right, time horizon, extraction cap, and peasant impact.   Axis   Zamindar   Ijaradar    --- --- ---    Basis of right   Hereditary and traditional leader of rural society   Won an auction; an urban moneylender / merchant     Time horizon   Permanent   Short 3–5 year contract     Extraction cap   Capped (about 10% commission / Nankar / Malikana)   No cap     Peasant impact   Subsistence living possible   Ruined   Mnemonic: Zamindar plants a banyan; Ijaradar sells the timber. The Zamindar's family lives with the peasants forever, so he caps himself at about 10%; the Ijaradar signs a short contract and strips everything. Decode: Zamindar = hereditary, permanent, capped (Nankar / Malikana, about 10%). Ijaradar = auction winner, 3 to 5 years, no cap. Example: pays the State a fixed 1 lakh, extracts 3 lakh, keeps the 2 lakh profit. Why it sticks: "1 in, 3 out, 2 kept" is the Ijaradar's arithmetic.   Parameter   Zabti system   Ijaradari system    --- --- ---    How LR is fixed   Detailed survey   Auction     Settlement with (i.e. LR to be paid agreed with whom)   Ryot (has Patta)   Revenue farmer (Ijaradar), who also has the responsibility to deposit LR to the State     Collection by   Zamindar   Ijaradar     Motive of collector   State-mandated commission   Profit motive     Peasant protection   Patta gives legal right   No protection   Mnemonic: Zabti = Zameen survey; Ijaradari = auction, profit, no Patta. "Zabti: Zameen is measured, Zamindar collects, Patta protects. Ijaradari: bid, bleed, no bill." Decode: Zabti fixes LR by detailed survey, settles with the ryot (Patta), collection by the Zamindar for a State-mandated commission. Ijaradari fixes LR by auction, settles with the revenue farmer, collection by the Ijaradar for profit, and the peasant has no protection. Why it sticks: survey vs auction is the single contrast that explains every other row.  Zabti versus Ijaradari. The Ijaradari story across history: rise and decline Auctioning the right to collect tax is ancient, but it was formally institutionalised in the subcontinent during the Delhi Sultanate as the Muqatai system. It lasted until Akbar 56-05 practically abolished it. Ijaradari maps almost perfectly onto the rise and decline of Mughal authority: abolished when the State was strong, revived when it was weak. (Babur 26-30 had no time for revenue reforms in his four-year reign; the decisive break came under Akbar 56-05.) Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526); Muqatai, the first formal institutionalisation of revenue farming (good) Akbar 56-05; practically abolished it, replaced with the Zabti system Jahangir 05-27; re-emerges marginally as control over Jagirdar-Mansabdars loosens Shahjahan 27-58; reintroduced properly, but only for ruined or devastated lands (warn) Aurangzeb 58-07; expanded it significantly; the Deccan campaigns made quick cash irresistible (bad) Jahandar Shah 12-13; institutionalised in Punjab and Bengal, the richest provinces (bad) Farukhsiyar (1713–19); extended into royal Khalisa lands Successor states; Awadh under Sadat Khan 22-39 and Hyderabad under Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 continue it (bad) Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772); formalised as the EIC's Farming System in Bengal Mnemonic: The door story: strong shuts it, weak opens it. Akbar 56-05 slams it; Jahangir 05-27 leaves it ajar; Shahjahan 27-58 lets in only ruined land (banjar); Aurangzeb 58-07 opens the window (wars); Jahandar Shah 12-13 flings it open in Punjab and Bengal (fertile, richest); Farukhsiyar lets it into the King's Khalisa; Hastings 73-85 gives it a name (1772 Farming System). Decode: before all that, the Delhi Sultanate began it as Muqatai. Rule: abolished when the State was strong, revived when it was weak. Successor states Awadh and Hyderabad continued it. Why it sticks: the door opens a bit wider with each weaker ruler.  Ijaradari rise and decline, with the teacher's notes: notice the pattern; Shah Jahan for ruined lands (banjar); Jahandar Shah in fertile regions; Farukhsiyar's extension to Khalisa lands hurt the Emperor's social power.  Rising land-revenue extraction: Akbar 1/3rd, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb 1/3rd to 1/2, Later Mughals 1/3rd to 2/3rd. Teacher: wars need money, so the LR demand rises. Teacher: Notice the pattern down the chain. Akbar 56-05: Zamindari system (the teacher writes it beside "Zabti"). Shah Jahan: ruined lands = "banjar". Aurangzeb 58-07: wars. Jahandar Shah 12-13: fertile regions. Farukhsiyar: Khalisa lands, the first time (1st), which hurts the Emperor's social power. Warren Hastings 73-85's Farming System = Ijaradari. Teacher: Wars need money, so the LR demand rises.   Emperor   LR as % of produce (tells the story of decline)    --- ---    Akbar 56-05   1/3rd     Shah Jahan (1627–58), Aurangzeb 58-07   High extraction: 1/3rd to 1/2     Later Mughals (1707+)   Extreme extraction: 1/3rd to 2/3rd   Mnemonic: The floor stays at one-third; the ceiling climbs. Akbar 56-05: 1/3. Shahjahan 27-58 and Aurangzeb 58-07: 1/3 to 1/2. Later Mughals: 1/3 to 2/3. Decode: the lower figure never moves; only the top rises: third, half, two-thirds. Wars need money, so the demand rises. Always a share of gross produce (cost of cultivation was subtracted only by a later British reform). Why it sticks: picture a lift: the floor button never changes, the top floor keeps going up. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of Bengal Presidency from 1772 and Governor General of Bengal Presidency from 1773–75 (the Regulating Act of 1773 made him GG, but he formally assumed office as GG in 1774). He formalised revenue farming as the Farming System in 1772. What began as the Muqatai system under the Delhi Sultanate, was abolished by Akbar 56-05 and revived under weaker successors, had become standard practice across large parts of the subcontinent by his time. The ryot at the bottom paid the price at every stage. Mnemonic: Hastings 73-85: 72, 73, 74 on three steps. 1772 Farming System; 1773 Regulating Act makes him GG; 1774 he formally assumes office as GG. Decode: Governor of Bengal Presidency from 1772; the Farming System (formalised revenue farming) = Ijaradari. His code 73-85 starts at the Regulating Act year. Why it sticks: one step per year, 72-73-74.

items.t: 8 · Akbar 56-05's religious vision: Sulh-i-Kul, Ibadat Khana, Mahzar, Din-i-Ilahi
items.x: Akbar 56-05's approach to religion shaped the political character of Mughal rule for generations. He moved in a clear sequence: Ibadat Khana (1575). A House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars from different faiths debated. It exposed him to the diversity of religious thought and to the bitter rivalries among the Ulama. Mahzar, the Infallibility Decree (1579). It gave Akbar 56-05 the authority to adjudicate religious disputes: the Emperor, not the clergy, was the final word on matters of faith. Din-i-Ilahi (1582). A syncretic spiritual order borrowing from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and Christianity. It is best understood as a religio-political experiment, not a movement: not many joined, but its real significance lay in the principle it expressed. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace. The State must treat all religions with equal respect, and no single faith should dominate policy. It became the ideological foundation of Mughal governance under Akbar 56-05 and influenced Mughal politics long after his death. Mnemonic: Akbar 56-05's religion ladder: 75, 79, 82, then peace. "I Must Do Sulh": Ibadat Khana 1575, Mahzar 1579, Din-i-Ilahi 1582, Sulh-i-Kul. Decode: Ibadat Khana (Fatehpur Sikri, debate; goal: mid-path, less conflict) → +4 → Mahzar (Emperor is the final word on faith) → +3 → Din-i-Ilahi (syncretic religio-political order, not a movement) → Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace, equal respect for all faiths). Why it sticks: the gaps are 4 then 3, and the last step has no year because it is the principle that stays.  Akbar's religious vision: Ibadat Khana 1575, Mahzar 1579, Din-i-Ilahi 1582, Sulh-i-Kul. Teacher's goals: mid-path, less conflict; the Emperor is the final word; social peace. Teacher: The goal of each step. Ibadat Khana: a mid-path, to reduce conflict. Mahzar: the Emperor is the *final* word on faith. Din-i-Ilahi: a syncretic religio-political order (a new hybrid religion borrowing from multiple faiths); goal = social peace. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace via equal respect for all faiths; goal = social peace / order.

items.t: 9 · Who actually introduced Jizya in India?
items.x: Jizya is a tax on non-Muslims. It is often associated with the Delhi Sultanate, but it predates the Sultanate by several centuries. Muhammad bin Qasim first imposed Jizya in Sindh during the 8th-century Arab conquest. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and his successors institutionalised it as a formal instrument of revenue and policy across the Delhi Sultanate from the early 13th century. The distinction matters: Jizya arrived in India with the Arabs, but became a pan-subcontinental administrative practice only under the Sultanate. Mnemonic: Jizya: Qasim Started, Aibak Systematised. "Qasim Started it (8th century, Sindh); Aibak made it a System (13th century, Delhi Sultanate)." Decode: Muhammad bin Qasim first imposed Jizya in Sindh during the 8th-century Arab conquest. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and successors institutionalised it from the early 13th century. Why it sticks: "first imposed" and "institutionalised" are the two exam traps; Q is first in the line, A second.  Who introduced Jizya? First imposed by Muhammad bin Qasim in Sindh (8th century); institutionalised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and successors across the Delhi Sultanate.

items.t: 10 · Two maps to fix in memory
items.x: Pre-1526 Indian subcontinent. Teacher's Deccan triangle: Bijapur, Golconda, Goa and Vijayanagara (VN, 1336-1646). Teacher: Pre-1526 subcontinent. In the Deccan, the teacher marks Bijapur and Golconda with Goa on the west coast, and Vijayanagara (VN) 1336–1646 in the south.  Mughal Empire 1530 to 1707: extent of Babur (1530), Akbar (1605) and Aurangzeb (1707). Teacher: Babur had no coastal territory; Akbar added rich coastal trade to the economy; founder and expanders of the State's territory. Teacher: State = organisation that rules a territory and people; territory = the motive of the State. Babur 26-30: no coastal territory. Akbar 56-05: rich coastal trade added to the economy. Babur 26-30 = founder; Akbar 56-05 and Aurangzeb 58-07 = expanders of the territory of the State. Mnemonic: Founder vs expanders, land vs coast. Babur 26-30 = Built the base, Barren of coast. Akbar 56-05 Added coastal trade, Aurangzeb 58-07 Added more territory. Decode: Babur 26-30 = founder with no coastal territory. Akbar 56-05 and Aurangzeb 58-07 = expanders; Akbar 56-05 brought rich coastal trade into the economy (which is why Europeans arriving by sea mattered). Why it sticks: one B for the base, two A's for the additions.  Handout figure: Mughal Empire 1530–1707, with the extent of Babur (1530), Akbar (1605) and Aurangzeb (1707).

items.t: 11 · The teacher's revision boards on the land revenue (LR) system (Lecture 4)
items.x: At the start of Lecture 4 the teacher redrew the whole LR machinery. These four boards are the best one-page revision of Section 7.  Teacher's board: the administrative ladder Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Block (Pargana), Villages; a Jagir with the Zamindar's Milkiyat and the Khudkashts; auction of the right to collect LR in Khalisa or Jagir. Teacher: The ladder: Centre → Provinces (Suba) → Districts (Sarkar) → Blocks (Pargana) → Villages. Inside a Jagir the Zamindar has his Milkiyat (his own holding) and the Khudkashts (cultivating peasants) sit on the rest. Board title: auction of the right to collect LR, in Khalisa (KL) or Jagir. Mnemonic: Admin ladder: Suba, Sarkar, Pargana (S-S-P). "Sab Sarkari Paper": Province = Suba, District = Sarkar, Block = Pargana, then Villages. Decode: Centre → Suba (province) → Sarkar (district) → Pargana (block) → Villages. Inside a Jagir the Zamindar has his Milkiyat and the Khudkashts sit on the rest. Why it sticks: the S-S-P order matches the Amalguzar (sarkar) sitting above the Amil (pargana).  Field survey: past trends of production and LR area-wise, average rainfall, droughts, floods and their frequency, land records (which ryot cultivates which field, size of each field, LR paid in the past). Maintained by the Patwari (village, a non-state actor) and the Qanungo (block level). Used for assessment of LR by the Amil (pargana) and the Amalguzar (district). Settlement through Patta and Qabuliyat. Teacher: Field survey gathers: (1) past trends of production and LR, area-wise; (2) average rainfall, droughts, floods and their frequency; (3) land records: *which ryot cultivates which field, the size of each field, the LR paid in the past.* Maintained by: Patwari (village, non-state actor) and Qanungo (block level). Use of this data: assessment of LR ("how much LR should we demand from which field / ryot") by the Amil (pargana) and the Amalguzar (district). Settlement: a Patta and LR exchanged with the ryot. Mnemonic: Field survey = P-R-L. "Production, Rain, Land records." Decode: (1) past trends of Production and LR, area-wise; (2) average Rainfall, droughts, floods and their frequency; (3) Land records (which ryot cultivates which field, field size, LR paid before). Kept by the Patwari (village) and Qanungo (block); used by the Amil and Amalguzar to assess. Why it sticks: the three P-R-L boxes are what an assessor needs before naming a number.  Any LR / tax system: Assessment → Settlement (2 docs: Patta with the ryot, Qabuliyat with the State, "like a rent contract or any contract with both parties") → Collection (mostly by Zamindars, non-state actors, plus supervision and audit by government officers, Amil and Amalguzar) → Deposit (to the King's Khalisa or to the Jagirdar Mansabdar). Assessment (how much, using the field-survey data) Settlement: two documents, the Patta (with the ryot) and the Qabuliyat (with the State), *like a rent contract with both parties* Collection: mostly by Zamindars (non-state actors), plus supervision / audit by government officers (Amil, Amalguzar) (good) Deposit: to the King (Khalisa) or to the Jagirdar Mansabdar Mnemonic: Any tax system: A-S-C-D. "A Smart Collector Deposits." Decode: Assessment (how much) → Settlement (Patta with the ryot, Qabuliyat with the State, both parties) → Collection (mostly Zamindars, audited by Amil and Amalguzar) → Deposit (King's Khalisa or the Jagirdar Mansabdar). Why it sticks: Settlement (the two documents) sits between the numbers and the cash, so nobody pays what was never agreed.  Amlas are employees of the Zamindar. The Zamindar's Muqaddam (Mukhiya) collects LR from the villages. Teacher: Amlas = employees of the Zamindar. The Muqaddam (Mukhiya) collects LR from the villages for him.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The Mughal story in one breath. Babur 26-30 comes through the Khyber with small bronze guns: Panipat 1526, a kingdom is born. Humayun 30-40 loses at Chausa 39 and Kanauj 40 to Sher Shah 40-45 (Records, Rupiya, Road), flees, returns with Persian troops at Sirhind 55, and falls from his library stairs in Jan 1556. Hemu crowns himself, but Bairam Khan wins Second Panipat 1556 for 13-year-old Akbar 56-05. Akbar 56-05 builds the Mansabdari machine (Zat + Sawar, Jagir, Khalisa, Inam, Mashrut), runs revenue by Zabti (Patwari to Muqaddam, Patta and Qabuliyat, Zamindar 10%), and climbs his religion ladder 75, 79, 82, then Sulh-i-Kul. But loyalty is personal: when the King cannot deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir, loyalty melts, the army turns ghost (2 lakh on paper, 1 lakh real), and weak rulers open the Ijaradari door, ending with Hastings in 1772. Decode: every year and name above is in the chapter's own order: 1526 → 1539 → 1540 → 1555 → 1556 → 1575 → 1579 → 1582 → 1772. Why it sticks: it is one family story: a conqueror, a runaway son, a boy emperor with a guardian, a machine, and its slow rot.

Year and paper   What was asked   The answer or trap   Where in this chapter    --- --- --- ---    Prelims 2003   Assertion-Reason on Shah Alam II 60-06 staying away from Delhi in his early years   He feared his Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk, not a foreign invasion from the North-West.
