items.t: 1 · Framework: how to analyse the decline
items.x: This is where Modern Indian History (MIH) starts. The Mughal State reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07 and began collapsing right after. Within about four decades it was a small area around Delhi–Agra under Maratha protection.  Chapter title slide with the teacher's timeline: Babur 26-30 to Aurangzeb 58-07, then the Later Mughals (weak) from 1707, Bahadur Shah 07-12 to Zafar 37-57 (the 1800s). "MIH starts." "But foundation of decline laid at Aurangzeb 58-07." Power moves down from the Mughal to the Mansabdars. Teacher: MIH starts here. Later Mughals are weak, from Bahadur Shah (1707-12) in the 1700s to Zafar (1837-57) in the 1800s. Power moves from the Mughal down to the Mansabdars. The foundation of decline was laid at Aurangzeb 58-07. After him, the weak emperors either could not revive the State or contributed to its decline.  Teacher: Aurangzeb 58-07 laid foundations, and then weak emperors could not revive or contributed to decline. The five-part equation State power = Political + Economic + Military + Social + Technological. The Mughal decline is a *simultaneous* weakening across all five. Mnemonic: Five parts of State power: P-E-M-S-T. "People Eat Many Sweet Treats." Decode: Political, Economic, Military, Social, Technological. Mughal decline hit all five at once. Why it sticks: if you can taste five sweets at once, you can feel five powers weaken at once.  Framework slide. Teacher: "By 1707 Mughal empire reached its peak" (Aurangzeb's reign), "but" the economic power and social power had not peaked. Travancore never part of the Mughal State; Assam also not. Teacher: By 1707 the Mughal empire reached its peak (territory), but not its economic power peak, and not its social power peak. Travancore was never part of the Mughal State. Assam also not. Two analytical tools (apply to every decline question)   Tool   Meaning   Mughal example    --- --- ---    Vertical power shift = decentralisation   The emperor weakens and power moves downward   After 1707 the emperors were weak personalities, so the Mansabdars under them became the real centre of power     Horizontal power shift = replacement   One entity replaces another at the same level   Delhi Sultanate replaced by the Mughals at Panipat 1526; British super-power replaced by US-USSR at the end of WW2 (1945)   The handout says to apply both lenses to every exam question on decline. Mnemonic: Vertical drops, horizontal swaps. "Vertical = Vacate downward; Horizontal = Hand over sideways." Decode: Vertical = decentralisation: after 1707 power moved from the weak emperors down to the Mansabdars. Horizontal = replacement at the same level: Delhi Sultanate replaced by the Mughals at Panipat 1526; British super-power replaced by US-USSR at the end of WW2 (1945). Why it sticks: use both lenses on every decline question: one for who lost power downward, one for who took the seat. The teacher's components board (what each form of power means)  Teacher's board on the framework: political power is proportional to territory; economic power = treasury (the name of the State's bank account); military power = number of soldiers, army size, technology, no military corruption, strong military leadership. Political power = the emperor's word is rule ("vachan hi hai shasan": decision + rule). Teacher: political power is proportional to the territory of the State. Economic power = the treasury, or public exchequer = the name of the bank account of the State. Military power has four parts: number of soldiers / size of the army; technology; no military corruption; strong military leadership. The teacher's World War examples: 1945, USSR had the largest army; 1945, atomic bomb (USA). Mnemonic: Military power's four parts: S-T-C-C. "Sena, Takneek, Clean hands, Commander." Decode: Size of the army; Technology; no military Corruption; strong military Commander (leadership). Teacher's examples: 1945, USSR had the largest army; 1945, atomic bomb (USA) = technology. Why it sticks: two numbers-and-guns items (Sena, Takneek), two people items (Clean, Commander); the Mughals later failed all four.  Social power: awe and love in people's hearts ("love you emperor"). The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural: religion, language, art). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises; if it rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example 1971, Indira Gandhi, and a film song. Teacher: Social power = awe / love in people's hearts. The common man does not want to be an MP, MLA or minister; he or she wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises; if social power rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the film song of the time. The teacher's list of factors  "Reasons/Factors for decline of Mughals": role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (wars, religious policy); weak emperors post-1707; military weakened (Nadir Shah, rebel states e.g. Marathas); institutional decline (disloyalty of Mansabdars, military corruption); Jagirdari crisis of the 18th century.  Teacher's factors tree, with ticks: Aurangzeb 58-07, institutional line, economic line, military line, weak emperors, lack of reform, all leading to territorial decline. Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: wars, religious policy. Weak emperors post-1707. Military weakened: external (Nadir Shah) and internal (rebel states, e.g. the Marathas). Institutional decline: disloyalty of Mansabdars, military corruption. Jagirdari crisis of the 18th century. Lack of reform (tech and organisation), all ending in territorial decline. Mnemonic: Six factors: "A Weak Mughal Is Just Lost". A = Aurangzeb 58-07 (wars, religious policy); W = Weak emperors post-1707; M = Military weakened (Nadir Shah, Marathas); I = Institutional decline (disloyal Mansabdars, military corruption); J = Jagirdari crisis; L = Lack of reform. Decode: the letters follow the teacher's numbered list 1 to 6. Why it sticks: the sentence tells the whole result: the Mughal was lost. Teacher: "We have covered the concepts of decline of the Mughals. Now let's look at factual data and events to support the concepts." Concepts first, then facts. (L4 slide 27 and L5 slide 2 show this two-layer approach: *org = concept + fact.*)  "Concepts of decline of Mughals": facts = organisation of concept plus fact. Concepts: factionalism (R vs R, R vs N, N vs N), weak personality (Rangila 19-48), military weakness plus shrinking of territory (external: Nadir Shah 1738-40; internal: Marathas). Teacher: Concept summary: Factionalism (Royal vs Royal, Royal vs Noble, Noble vs Noble); Weak personality (Rangila, 1719-48 = Muhammad Shah 19-48); Military weakness plus shrinking of territory (external: Nadir Shah 1738-40; internal: Marathas).

items.t: 2 · Why did Aurangzeb 58-07's wars sow the seeds of decline?
items.x: Aurangzeb 58-07 came to power in 1658 after a brutal succession war (he killed his elder brother Dara Shikoh). He governed as an empire-builder on a mission: to conquer all of India, particularly the Deccan. War helps a State only if ROI (return on investment) is positive and a period of peace follows the conquest. If wars never stop and territory won is eventually lost, it becomes an economic disaster. Mnemonic: War is a sprint to spend, a marathon to earn. Money leaves fast (men, horses, weapons, logistics, attrition); returns arrive slowly (territory, LR, ports, trade, a natural frontier). Decode: war = rapid investment; victory = long, slow ROI. A war helps only if ROI is positive and peace follows. Aurangzeb 58-07's wars never stopped, so territory won was eventually lost: an economic disaster. Why it sticks: sprint out, marathon back, and he never reached the finish line.  Teacher's board: war = rapid investment of money (recruit men and horses, produce weapons, logistics of movement, attrition of soldiers, horses and elephants; the domestic economy suffers if war is fought in the homeland). Victory gives a long, slow ROI: gain of territory (more LR, ports, trade) and geopolitical gains (natural frontier; teacher's example: Hitler wanted territory up to the Urals). Teacher: War = rapid investment of money: recruit more men and horses, produce more weapons, logistics (costs of movement of men, food, weapons), attrition of soldiers, horses and elephants. Domestic economy suffers if the war is fought in the homeland. War victory → ROI is long and slow. The gain of territory brings more LR, ports and more trade, and geopolitical gains such as a natural frontier. Example: Hitler wanted territory up to the Urals. What he won, and what it cost Bijapur (annexed 1686; Adil Shahi dynasty 1489–1686) and Golconda (annexed 1687; Qutb Shahi dynasty 1518–1687). Both were successor kingdoms of the Bahmani Sultanate (1347–1527). In Bijapur it was a three-way fight: Mughals, Bijapur, and the Marathas, who never accepted Mughal authority. By 1705 the Marathas were winning; by the 1750s they had reversed most of Aurangzeb 58-07's gains and some of Akbar 56-05's as well. 40 years of warfare drained the treasury (*the government's bank account*), broke the Mansabdars financially (*they had to maintain armies*), and translated directly into later military corruption (*Mansabdars not maintaining the army as per Sawar*). Mnemonic: Bijapur then Golconda: B before G, 86 before 87. Dynasty ends = annexation year: Adil Shahi 1489–1686 (Bijapur); Qutb Shahi 1518–1687 (Golconda). Decode: Bijapur annexed 1686, Golconda 1687. Adil (A) is older (1489) and Qutb (Q) younger (1518). Both were successors of the Bahmani Sultanate (1347–1527). Bijapur was a three-way fight: Mughals, Bijapur, Marathas. Why it sticks: alphabetical order matches chronological order, both times (A then Q; B then G).  Aurangzeb's wars: war and ROI; the mission; Bijapur (1686, Adil Shahi 1489-1686); Golconda (1687, Qutb Shahi 1518-1687); the Marathas reversed it.  Teacher's board: Role of Aurangzeb (1658-1707, about 50 years, like Akbar's about 50 years). Left: religious orthodoxy (Jizya 1679, temple policy) and executions (GTB 1675, Sambhaji 1689) make social power sad; contribution to the Jagirdari crisis; continuous wars of about 45 years hurt the economy. Right: Akbar = foundation of rise. Teacher: Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (about 50 years), versus Akbar 56-05 (about 50 years). Teacher: Aurangzeb 58-07, four lines. (1) Religious orthodoxy: Jizya (1679), temple policy → social power sad. (2) Execution of leaders: GTB (1675), Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) → social power sad. (3) Contribution to the Jagirdari crisis. (4) Continuous wars of about 45 years → economy sad (high LR demand; military corruption → weak military; wars proved useless ultimately; future emperors inherit a weak treasury). Teacher: Akbar 56-05 = foundation of rise. Universal peace, syncretic policies, religious harmony → social power *happy*. LR system fair, no Ijaradari, economic security. Strong state machinery (Mansabdari system) → military *happy*. Mnemonic: Aurangzeb 58-07 in four lines: R-E-J-W. "Rigid Emperor Jams Wallets." Decode: Religious orthodoxy (Jizya 1679, temple policy); Executions (GTB 1675, Sambhaji 80-89 in 1689); Jagirdari crisis; continuous Wars (about 45 years). First two make social power sad; wars make the economy sad. Why it sticks: four words, four lines of the teacher's board. Mnemonic: Akbar 56-05 = three smiles, Aurangzeb 58-07 = three frowns. Akbar 56-05's three smiles: social (universal peace, religious harmony), economic (fair LR, no Ijaradari), military (Mansabdari machinery). Decode: both ruled about 50 years. Akbar 56-05 = foundation of rise; Aurangzeb 58-07 = foundation of decline (social sad, economy sad, weak military, future emperors inherit a weak treasury). Why it sticks: same length of reign, opposite faces.  Wars table with the teacher's Deccan sketch. Left triangle: Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687, Goa, Vijayanagara 1336-1646. Right triangle: Aurangzeb (external power), Marathas (domestic rebels), Bijapur (existing State). Teacher: The Deccan triangle: Bijapur (1686), Golconda (1687), Goa, and the old Vijayanagara (1336–1646) region below them. The fight triangle = Aurangzeb 58-07 (the external power) + Marathas (domestic rebels) + Bijapur (the existing State).  Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah (r. 1627-56), Adil Shahi dynasty (1489-1686).  Golconda Fort, Hyderabad: seat of the Qutb Shahi dynasty (1518-1687). Gol Gumbaz is the mausoleum (burial building, like the Taj Mahal) of Muhammad Adil Shah (1627–56) of the Adil Shahi dynasty. Mnemonic: Gol Gumbaz is a grave; Golconda is a fort. "Gumbaz holds a body (Bijapur); Golconda is a fort (Hyderabad)." Decode: Gol Gumbaz = mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah (1627–56), Adil Shahi dynasty, Bijapur. Golconda Fort, Hyderabad = seat of the Qutb Shahi dynasty. Why it sticks: both start with "Gol", so pin each to a different dynasty: Gumbaz → Adil, Golconda → Qutb. How 40 years of war drained the State  "40 years of war": endless Deccan campaigns, conquest without a lasting peace ("because Marathas continued rebellion"); treasury drained; Mansabdars suffered economic losses, forced to maintain armies in continuous wars; military corruption post-1707, military weakened, loss of territory for Mughals.  Teacher's sketch: 40-45 years of wars of Aurangzeb, the Mansabdars (rupee sad), post-1707 weak emperors, therefore military corruption, military sad, loss of territory. Endless Deccan campaigns; conquest without lasting peace; Marathas continue rebellion Treasury drained by perpetual warfare (warn) Mansabdars forced to maintain armies in continuous wars; financially crippled (bad) Military corruption post-1707: troops not maintained as per Sawar rank (bad) Military weakened; loss of territory for the Mughals

items.t: 3 · Religious policies and the social foundation
items.x: State power needs social support. Aurangzeb 58-07 followed an orthodox interpretation of Islam in his personal life and his governance, systematically alienating non-Muslim subjects. 3.1 Jizya (1679) and its long history The most damaging measure was the re-introduction of Jizya in 1679 (*abolished in 1564*): an additional tax on non-Muslim adult males. Beyond the money, the manner of collection made people feel religiously discriminated against, and resentment ran deep. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 first introduced Jizya in an institutionalised manner. He was the first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and founder of the Mamluk dynasty (1206–1290; Mamluk = military slave). Babur 26-30 and Humayun 30-40 continued it. Akbar 56-05 abolished it in 1564 as part of his Sulh-i-Kul (Universal Peace) policy. Aurangzeb 58-07 reintroduced it in 1679. Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13 abolished it again in 1712. The handout says Farukhsiyar (1713–19) re-introduced it in 1717. As the empire weakened, Jizya faded with it.  Jizya in India: 712 CE Muhammad bin Qasim imposes it first in Sindh; 13th c. Aibak institutionalises it (1206-10); 1564 Akbar abolishes it; 1679 Aurangzeb re-introduces it (teacher adds Bahadur Shah 07-12); 1712-17 Zulfiqar Khan abolishes in 1712, Farukhsiyar continues the abolition but later re-imposes; 1719 onwards Jizya fades away.  Handout Diagram 1: Jizya in India, Aibak (1206-10) introduces it, Babur and Humayun continue it, Akbar removes it in 1564, Aurangzeb re-introduces it in 1679, Zulfiqar Khan abolishes it in 1712, Farukhsiyar re-introduces it in 1717, it fades with Mughal decline. Who first introduced Jizya? Muhammad bin Qasim introduced it in 712 CE after conquering Sindh. By paying it, the non-Muslim population was granted the status of Zimmis (Dhimmis), "protected people", allowed to practise their religion and exempted from military service. (Handout aside: *is this a gain or a loss of employment opportunity for the masses?*) Who first institutionalised Jizya? Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10. Mnemonic: First vs formal: Qasim is Quick, Aibak is Administrative. "Qasim Quick (712 CE, Sindh); Aibak = Administration (institutionalised)." Decode: Muhammad bin Qasim introduced it first, after conquering Sindh in 712 CE; payers became Zimmis (protected people), allowed their religion and exempt from military service. Aibak 06-10 first institutionalised it. Why it sticks: two different verbs, two different men: "introduced" vs "institutionalised". Discrepancy to check. The handout text says Farukhsiyar *re-introduced* Jizya in 1717. The teacher's slide says Farukhsiyar continued the abolition but later re-imposed Jizya, and that Jizya fades from 1719. Both agree on the direction: abolished 1712, re-imposed by Farukhsiyar, gone by 1719. Mnemonic: Jizya's light switch: ON, ON, OFF, ON, OFF, ON, fade. Qasim 712 ON; Aibak 06-10 ON (institutional); Akbar 56-05 OFF 1564; Aurangzeb 58-07 ON 1679; Zulfiqar Khan OFF 1712; Farukhsiyar 13-19 ON 1717; fades 1719. Decode: Babur 26-30 and Humayun 30-40 continued it. Off 64, on 79, off 12, on 17. Handout says Farukhsiyar re-introduced it in 1717; the teacher's slide says he continued the abolition but later re-imposed it. Both agree: abolished 1712, re-imposed by Farukhsiyar, gone by 1719. Why it sticks: three flips back and forth, then the bulb dies with the empire. 3.2 Temple policy: Kashi Vishwanath (1669) Aurangzeb 58-07 refused temple repairs and reduced their land grants. More significantly he demolished important temples. Best-known case: the Kashi Vishwanath temple at Varanasi, demolished 1669, replaced on the same site by the Gyanvapi Mosque. His own court record, the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, documents his order. The temple's troubled history: razed earlier by Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 (1194, then slave-general of Md Ghori, before he became first Sultan in 1206) and Sikandar Lodi (1490). Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore rebuilt it in 1780 near the original site. Mnemonic: Kashi Vishwanath: three break, one builds (11, 14, 16, 17). "Aibak Sikandar Aurangzeb break; Ahilyabai builds": 1194, 1490, 1669, 1780. Decode: Aibak 06-10 razed it in 1194 (then Ghori's slave-general); Sikandar Lodi in 1490; Aurangzeb 58-07 demolished it in 1669 (Gyanvapi Mosque on the site; court record Maasir-i-Alamgiri); Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore rebuilt it in 1780 near the original site. Why it sticks: the first two digits climb 11 → 14 → 16 → 17, and the builder comes last.  Temple policy table: Aurangzeb refused repairs, cut land grants, demolished key temples; Kashi Vishwanath demolished 1669 with Gyanvapi Mosque on the site; court chronicle Maasir-i-Alamgiri documents the order; earlier razed by Aibak (1194) and Sikandar Lodi (1490); rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore in 1780 near the original site. The teacher underlines the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, Aibak (1194), Sikandar Lodi (1490) and Ahilyabai Holkar.  Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Gyanvapi Mosque, Varanasi (old print). 3.3 Executions that backfired 1675: Guru Tegh Bahadur (GTB), the 9th Sikh Guru. 1689: Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89, elder son of Shivaji 74-80, after weeks of torture. Both were offered convert-or-die; both refused. The executions did not suppress resistance: they created martyrs, hardening anti-Mughal sentiment among Sikhs and Marathas. Mnemonic: Martyr codes: Sambhaji 80-89 ends where he was executed. GTB = 9th Sikh Guru, 1675. Sambhaji 80-89, elder son of Shivaji 74-80, executed 1689: his code ends in 89. Decode: both were offered convert-or-die, both refused; Sambhaji 80-89 after weeks of torture. Executions created martyrs and hardened Sikh and Maratha anti-Mughal feeling. Why it sticks: the end of his code is the year of his death.  Executions that backfired: Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675), Sambhaji 80-89 (1689), both refused to convert; the backfire: martyrs, hardened Sikh and Maratha anti-Mughal sentiment. Teacher: Both GTB (1675) and Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) are boxed on the board as the "execution of leaders" line, under social power sad. Mnemonic: Aurangzeb 58-07's four black dates: 69, 75, 79, 89. "Kashi, Guru, Jizya, Sambhaji" = 1669, 1675, 1679, 1689. Decode: Kashi Vishwanath demolished 1669; Guru Tegh Bahadur executed 1675; Jizya re-introduced 1679; Sambhaji 80-89 executed 1689. All four hit social power. Why it sticks: steps of +6, +4, +10, and the rhythm "sixty-nine, seventy-five, seventy-nine, eighty-nine".

items.t: 4 · Why did the Mansabdari system turn against the empire?
items.x: The Mansabdari system ran on personal loyalty to the emperor as an individual, not impersonal loyalty to the empire as an institution. It was a give-and-take: the emperor granted Mansabs and Jagirs; nobles gave military service and loyalty. Strong emperors made this work; weak emperors could not. After 1707 the Later Mughals could not control powerful Mansabdars. When the emperor could not grant the desired Mansabs and Jagirs, the Mansabdars became disloyal and acted upon that disloyalty (*earlier, either fear or belief in the fairness of a strong emperor kept them in line*): they engaged in court politics for the best Mansabs and Jagirs, or tried replacing the emperor with their favourite from the royal family. Court politics crippled governance. Those who should have led reforms (economic, administrative and military) were consumed by factional rivalry.  Why the Mansabdari system broke: personal loyalty, a give-and-take, weak Later Mughals, disloyalty, factionalism increased and reforms slowed down. Teacher: "busy in court politics and not on work". Teacher: Busy in court politics and not on work. That is the teacher's one-line reason why reform slowed down.  Teacher's scenario board: a Mansabdar didn't get his desired Mansab and Jagir, so a feeling of disloyalty. Under a strong emperor (good strong = faith in future fairness; bad strong = fear) the Mansabdar takes no action. Under a weak emperor the Mansabdar acts on his feeling of disloyalty. Factionalism = group politics = court politics: lobbying the emperor, backbiting, plot/coup (takhtapalat) to bring the favourite as emperor. Mansabdar does not get the desired Mansab and Jagir Feeling of disloyalty Strong emperor: good strong = faith in future fairness; bad strong = fear; so *no action* by the Mansabdar (bad) Weak emperor: the Mansabdar acts on his feeling of disloyalty (bad) Factionalism = group politics = court politics: lobbying the emperor, backbiting, plot/coup (takhtapalat), bringing the favourite as emperor Mnemonic: Strong king = Freeze, weak king = Free-for-all. Strong emperor: Faith (good strong) or Fear (bad strong) makes the unhappy Mansabdar freeze. Weak emperor: the Mansabdar is free to act. Decode: an unhappy Mansabdar (no desired Mansab or Jagir) acts only under a weak emperor: lobbying, backbiting, takhtapalat (coup) to bring his favourite from the royal family. Result: busy in court politics, not on work. Why it sticks: the same feeling of disloyalty exists in both cases; only the king's strength decides whether it acts.

items.t: 5 · Why did the Mughal military weaken?
items.x: Three interconnected problems: 5.1 No technological or organisational reform European powers succeeded with smaller numbers because of better command, tighter discipline, and tactical innovations: File firing: rotating lines for continuous fire. Grapeshot artillery: multiple bullets in one shot; lethal at close range. Bayonet (*a knife*) on the Brown Bess musket (*so a rifle became a sword at close range*). Haider Ali 61-82, Mysore) reorganised his military on the European model and stayed formidable. The Mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reformed nothing. Mnemonic: European tricks: File, Grape, Bayonet. A file of men fire in turns; the shot sprays like grapes; the Brown Bess grows a knife, the bayonet. Decode: file firing = rotating lines for continuous fire; grapeshot = many bullets in one shot, lethal at close range; bayonet on the Brown Bess musket turns a rifle into a sword. Haider Ali 61-82 (Mysore) reorganised on a European model (the slide says the French model, the handout says European) and stayed formidable. Why it sticks: F-G-B runs from long range to close range to hand-to-hand.  "Why the Mughal military collapsed": no reform while Indian rivals upgraded their military with EU help; weak commanders (court politics, not merit); military corruption. Teacher's sketch of shotgun (grapeshot) fire. Teacher: No reform while Indian rivals upgraded the military with European help. Example in the handout: Haider Ali 61-82 reorganised on the French model (the slide says "on the French model"; the handout says "European model"). 5.2 Weak war commanders Under the Later Mughals (1707–1858), court politics, not merit, decided military appointments. 5.3 Military corruption Under weak supervision Mansabdars maintained far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank required, pocketing the difference. Aurangzeb 58-07's war drain and the Jagirdari crisis compounded this. By the early 18th century the army was corrupt, under-equipped, poorly led and technologically frozen. Mnemonic: Three military problems: N-W-C. "No reform, Weak commanders, Corruption." Decode: no technological or organisational reform; weak war commanders (court politics, not merit); military corruption (Mansabdars kept far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank, pocketing the difference). Why it sticks: the paper army and the real army do not match: Sawar on paper, fewer horses in the field. Teacher: The Jagirdari crisis increased the chances of military corruption (written at the bottom of the slide).

items.t: 6 · Factionalism: how it operated in the Mughal court
items.x: Factionalism = Royal vs Royal + Royal vs Noble + Noble vs Noble. It is group politics.  The five court factions: Irani (Shia Persian; Zulfiqar Khan, Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13, who ended Jizya); Turani (Sunni Turkish-Uzbek, like the Mughals; Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, Governor/Subadar/Nawab of Hyderabad Suba 1724-48); Hindustani (converted Indian Muslims; the Sayyid Brothers, who brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power); Hindu (Rajputs and Jats; Sawai Jai Singh); Deccani (nobles absorbed from Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687).   Faction   Identity   Example    --- --- ---    Irani   Shia Persian   Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13; ended Jizya)     Turani   Sunni Turkish-Uzbek (like the Mughals)   Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (1724–48), Governor / Subadar / Nawab of Hyderabad Suba     Hindustani   Converted Indian Muslims   Sayyid Brothers (brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power)     Hindu   Rajputs and Jats   Sawai Jai Singh 99-43     Deccani   Nobles absorbed from Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)   none given   Mnemonic: Five factions: "It's The Hot Hyderabadi Dum". Irani, Turani, Hindustani, Hindu, Deccani. Decode: Irani = Shia Persian, Zulfiqar Khan. Turani = Sunni Turkish-Uzbek (like the Mughals), Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48. Hindustani = converted Indian Muslims, Sayyid Brothers (brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power). Hindu = Rajputs and Jats, Sawai Jai Singh 99-43. Deccani = Bijapur and Golconda nobles (no example given). Why it sticks: "Z-N-S-J" gives the four examples in order: Zulfiqar, Nizam, Sayyids, Jai Singh 99-43. After 1707 weak emperors could not control these groups. Mansabdars competed to dominate the sitting emperor or install their preferred candidate: whoever controlled the emperor controlled Mansabs and Jagirs. No clear succession rule: every emperor's death was potentially a new power struggle. Some Mansabdars who could have stabilised the centre chose not to, and instead used the chaos to carve out their own principalities (the successor states).  Factionalism board: Royal vs Royal (succession dispute, coup d'etat), Royal vs Noble (for better Mansabs), Noble vs Noble (for Jagirs). Right: the "Role of Aurangzeb 58-07" tree (economy and social power down, Jagirdari crisis), institutional failure, military down, tech reforms down, J crisis leading to revolt, factionalism. "We have covered concepts of decline of Mughals. Now let's look at factual data/events to support concepts."

items.t: 7 · The Jagirdari crisis: why did it hit so hard?
items.x: The Jagirdari crisis was a structural mismatch: supply of Jagirs and demand for them fell dangerously out of balance.  Teacher's board "Jagirdari crisis": like a water crisis (number of people up, water down). What? Number of Mansabdars up (over-recruitment) plus land down. Land is the same in the kingdom, but land shrunk because of territory loss in wars (post 1705, Marathas winning). Why over-recruitment? Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (declared most lands of Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 as Khalisa lands, LR to the King, but the Deccani group came in) and post-1707 factionalism (either to be in or to come to power, over-recruitment). Teacher: Water-crisis analogy: number of people up, water down. Jagirdari crisis: number of Mansabdars up + land down. Teacher: What? (1) Over-recruitment (number of Mansabdars rises). (2) Land is the same in the kingdom; land *shrunk* because of loss of territory in wars (post-1705, the Marathas winning). Teacher: Why over-recruitment? (a) Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: he declared most lands of Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 as Khalisa lands (LR to the King), but the Deccani group came in as Mansabdars. (b) Post-1707 factionalism: *either to be in power or to come to power*, the emperors over-recruited.  Teacher: the Mughal emperor depended on Mansabdars for the army (Jagir given, from the Jagir the Mansabdar maintains the army as per Sawar).  The Jagirdari crisis table: the crisis (many Mansabdars, less land, demand-supply mismatch); the origin (after taking Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687, Aurangzeb declared most of their lands Khalisa to be self-sufficient in funding the war against the Marathas); over-recruitment of Mansabdars (later Mughals kept appointing to buy loyalty while land under Mughal control kept shrinking); gross inequality (5 percent of Mansabdars controlled 61 percent of Jagir revenue); luxury inflation (partly from EIC exports).   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    The crisis   High number of Mansabdars but less land for distribution as Jagirs: demand-supply mismatch     The origin   After taking Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), Aurangzeb 58-07 declared most of their lands Khalisa to be self-sufficient in funding the war vs the Marathas. Mansabdars rose, the Jagir lands did not     Over-recruitment   Later Mughals kept appointing Mansabdars to buy the loyalty of Mansdar groups while land under Mughal control kept shrinking     Gross inequality   5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of Jagir revenue     Luxury inflation   Inflation in luxury goods (partly from EIC exports of Indian goods) meant many could not sustain an elite life   Mnemonic: Jagirdari crisis = water crisis. More mouths, less water: more Mansabdars, less land. Decode: demand-supply mismatch. Land shrank through territory loss (post-1705, Marathas winning); over-recruitment came from Aurangzeb 58-07's Deccani nobles and from post-1707 factionalism. The teacher: the impact of the Jagirdari crisis was the most important in the decline of the Mughals. Why it sticks: you know the water crisis already; just swap people for Mansabdars and water for Jagirs. Mnemonic: Four causes: K-O-I-L (the Koel). "Khalisa grab, Over-recruitment, Inequality, Luxury inflation." Decode: after Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) Aurangzeb 58-07 declared most of their lands Khalisa; later Mughals over-recruited to buy loyalty; 5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of Jagir revenue; luxury inflation (partly from EIC exports). Why it sticks: the Koel's nest is crowded and unequal, and "5 and 61" = 5% of Mansabdars hold 61% of the Jagir revenue. The consequences  Teacher: "Impact of J crisis = most imp in decline of Mughals." Factionalism (noble vs noble for Jagirs) leads to political instability (emperor of choice to power). Pressure on the emperor leads to a change in tenure of Jagir given to a Mansabdar (so many Naqdi Mansabdars are waiting), insecurity of tenure (kal ho na ho Jagir), which leads to military corruption and, on the other side, to greater and more frequent application of Ijaradari, over-extraction of LR, peasant revolts under the leadership of Zamindars. Military corruption leads to victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) plus an external power (e.g. Nadir Shah), and to loss of territory (State = organisation = rules + territory). Teacher: Impact of the Jagirdari crisis = most important in the decline of the Mughals. (Written as the slide title and circled.)  The downward spiral: frequent transfers (Jagirs shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars); tenure insecurity (kal ho na ho Jagir); ruthless extraction (maximum in minimum time, no incentive to invest in the land); Ijaradari spreads (revenue-farming strips collection from Zamindars, the rural stabilisers); peasant revolts (Zamindar-led revolts; the Jat Kingdom grew from a 1695 revolt under Churaman Jat). Frequent transfers: Jagirs shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars (warn) Tenure insecurity: no Jagirdar knew how long he would hold the land (kal ho na ho Jagir) (warn) Ruthless extraction: maximum in minimum time; no incentive to invest in the land (bad) Ijaradari spreads: revenue-farming strips collection from Zamindars, the rural stabilisers (bad) Peasant revolts: over-extraction leads to Zamindar-led revolts (Jat Kingdom from the 1695 revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat) Mnemonic: Kal ho na ho Jagir: the tenant who strips the house. A tenant told he may leave tomorrow takes everything today: transfers, insecurity, ruthless extraction, Ijaradari, then revolt. Decode: frequent transfers → tenure insecurity (kal ho na ho Jagir) → maximum in minimum time → Ijaradari spreads (Zamindars, the rural stabilisers, are bypassed) → Zamindar-led revolts. Churaman 95-21 Jat: the Jat Kingdom grew from his 1695 revolt, and the code starts with 95. Why it sticks: five steps, one tenant, and a famous film-style phrase for the insecurity. Effect on the peasantry: over-extraction, stagnation, revolts led by alienated Zamindars. Direct example: the Jat Kingdom emerged from a 1695 peasant revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat, a Zamindar. Meanwhile Mansabdars did not maintain the army as per Sawar, to maximise their earnings, as no one knew when the emperor would transfer the Jagir (*kal ho na ho Jagir*). The teacher ties the military consequences together: military corruption → victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) + an external power (Nadir Shah) → loss of territory.

items.t: 8 · Proof of decline: factionalism in practice
items.x: Succession turmoil (1707-24): Bahadur Shah 07-12 fought brothers to be in power; Jahandar Shah 12-13 (Royal vs Royal), backed by Zulfiqar Khan (Irani), made him Wazir; executed by Farukhsiyar. Farukhsiyar 13-19 (Royal vs Noble), rose with the Sayyid Brothers (Abdullah Wazir, Hussain Ali Mir Bakshi), refused to be their puppet, Sayyids allied with the Marathas and killed him. Muhammad Shah 19-48, installed as puppet ("totally uninterested in ruling"). Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Noble vs Noble): Turani + Irani defeat the Sayyids; Wazir 1722-24, quits Delhi for Hyderabad (1724; leaves for good 1740).  Handout Diagram 2: Factionalism and succession turmoil 1707-1724, Aurangzeb dies 1707 (no succession rule), Jahandar Shah, Farukhsiyar, Sayyid Brothers, Muhammad Shah installed as puppet (1719), Nizam-ul-Mulk with the Irani group defeats the Sayyids and exits to Hyderabad in 1740.   Type   Story   Emperor   Lesson    --- --- --- ---    Royal vs Royal   Bahadur Shah (1707–12) fought his brothers to be in power. Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power backed by Zulfiqar Khan (Irani), but only after executing the father of Farukhsiyar. Reward: Zulfiqar became Wazir. Farukhsiyar (with the Sayyids) removed and executed Jahandar Shah 12-13.   Jahandar Shah 12-13   Back the right claimant, extract the reward     Royal vs Noble   Farukhsiyar rose with the Sayyid Brothers (Abdullah Khan became Wazir; Hussain Ali Khan became Mir Bakshi). He refused to be their puppet and built rival alliances. The Sayyids reached outside the court, allied with the Marathas under Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20; 15,000 Maratha cavalry temporarily took over Delhi in 1719), killed him, and installed Muhammad Shah 19-48 as a puppet   Farukhsiyar (1713–19)   The price of noble support is being a puppet     Noble vs Noble   Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Turani) allied with the Irani group and defeated the Sayyids. He served as Wazir 1722–24, then, seeing the centre was beyond saving, took the Mansab of Governor of Hyderabad Suba in 1724. In 1740 he left Delhi permanently   Md Shah (1719–48)   "Delhi to gayo, at least save my Hyderabad"   Teacher: Bahadur Shah 07-12: fought brothers to be in power. Jahandar Shah 12-13: Royal vs Royal. Farukhsiyar 13-19: Royal vs Noble. Md Shah 19-48: "totally uninterested in ruling." Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48: Noble vs Noble; Wazir 1722-24 (underlined), quits Delhi for Hyderabad (underlined). Mir Bakshi = Chief Military Paymaster / Commander (*defence minister + defence finance authority*, the handout adds). Teacher: On the L5 arc slide the teacher changed "1719-24" to "1707-19" (circled) for the succession turmoil. Turmoil runs from Aurangzeb 58-07's death to Muhammad Shah 19-48's installation. Mnemonic: Succession turmoil = a three-round boxing match: R-R, R-N, N-N. Round 1 Royal vs Royal: Bahadur Shah 07-12 fights his brothers; Jahandar Shah 12-13 wins with Zulfiqar Khan (Irani, made Wazir). Round 2 Royal vs Noble: Farukhsiyar 13-19 with the Sayyids. Round 3 Noble vs Noble: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48. Between 2 and 3: Muhammad Shah 19-48 the puppet. Farukhsiyar removed and executed Jahandar Shah 12-13; the Sayyids, allied with the Marathas, killed Farukhsiyar. Why it sticks: the fighters get bigger each round, and the winner of each round is eventually killed by the next. Mnemonic: Sayyid Brothers: AW! HM! Abdullah = Wazir; Hussain Ali = Mir Bakshi. Mir Bakshi = chief military paymaster/commander. Why it sticks: "15,000 in 1719" repeats the 15 and the 19. Mnemonic: Nizam 24-48: his code starts the year he reaches Hyderabad. "Wazir 22-24, then Hyderabad in 24, and he leaves Delhi for good in 1740."
