His mood: "Delhi to gayo, at least save my Hyderabad." Why it sticks: Wazir ends exactly where the Hyderabad code begins (24).

items.t: 9 · How the Marathas exposed the military collapse
items.x: The military decline is best measured by what the Marathas achieved.  "Marathas expose the military collapse": from 1705 they defeated Mughal forces; by the mid-18th c. they recovered Aurangzeb's Deccan gains and took lands annexed under Akbar (including Gujarat); only Hyderabad held out (Nizam 24-48, a successor State); 1737 Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 marched on Delhi, plundered it, briefly held Md Shah prisoner; Treaty of Bhopal 1738, after defeating Nizam (who led the Mughal army) the Marathas won the Chambal-Narmada lands and the Subah of Malwa. Teacher: military prestige down; 1752, the Mughal came under Maratha protection for fear of Afghan Abdali invasions. From 1705 they systematically defeated Mughal forces. By the mid-18th century they had not only recovered Aurangzeb 58-07's Deccan gains but taken lands annexed under Akbar 56-05, including Gujarat. Only Hyderabad (formerly Golconda) stayed outside Maratha control, held by Nizam as a successor State. 1737: Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 marched to Delhi, plundered the capital, and briefly held Md Shah prisoner. 1738: the Marathas defeated a large Mughal army commanded by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48. Formalised in the Treaty of Bhopal (1738): the Marathas received legal recognition of control over all lands between the Chambal and Narmada and the Subah of Malwa. *Imagine the Mughal emperor became a hostage in his own capital.* Teacher: Next to 1737 the teacher writes "prestige" and "military prestige ↓↓↓". Next to 1738 he sketches the map: Chambal above, Malwa circled in the middle, Narmada below. 1752: the Mughal came under Maratha protection, because of fear of Afghan (Abdali) invasions. Mnemonic: Maratha steps: 05, 37, 38, 52, 54. 1705 winning; 1737 Bajirao 20-40 plunders Delhi; 1738 Bhopal; 1752 protection; 1754 puppet Alamgir II 54-59. Decode: after 1705 the Marathas defeat Mughal forces; 1737 Bajirao 20-40 briefly holds Md Shah prisoner (military prestige down); 1738 they beat Nizam, and the Treaty of Bhopal gives them the lands between Chambal and Narmada plus Malwa. (The handout diagram prints 1739; the text and timeline use 1738, so follow 1738.) Why it sticks: draw a sandwich: Chambal on top, Malwa the filling, Narmada below (the teacher's sketch).

items.t: 10 · Nadir Shah's invasion (1738–40): the five-pillar blow
items.x: Teacher's board "Nadir Shah": Iran to Afghanistan, through the Khyber Pass to Peshawar, then India with Karnal, Panipat, Kurukshetra, Thanesar, Delhi. A State has a territory motive but does a cost-benefit analysis (own resources, economic and military, and geography). Ruling is a cost and maintaining territory is a cost. War aims: annexation, or less than annexation, e.g. plunder (attack and loot). Teacher: A State has a territory motive, *but* does a cost-benefit analysis: (+) own resources (economic, military) and (+) decides on the basis of geography. Example: ruling territory = a cost; maintaining territory = a cost. War aims: annexation, or less than annexation, e.g. plunder (attack and loot). Nadir Shah's aim was plunder. Nadir Shah ruled a Persian empire stretching into Afghanistan (Mughal-claimed territory) and desired India's wealth. His victory was easier because of the weakened Mughal empire plus factionalism.  Map: Persia in the eighteenth century, Nadir Shah's campaigns and his route through Afghanistan (Kabul, Peshawar, Lahore) to Karnal 1739 and Delhi. What happened, step by step  Nadir Shah's invasion 1739: Battle of Karnal, Nizam negotiates (Rs 50 lakh, Nadir does not enter Delhi), Sadat switches sides, Delhi falls.  Teacher's board "Battle of Karnal 1739": recent increase in war expenditure; in 1738 the Marathas took territory (Chambal, Malwa, Narmada: 1738 Treaty of Bhopal). Defeat plus Sadat Khan 22-39 (Nawab Awadh) prisoner leads to negotiations; NS accepted to go back by taking 50 lakh. Nizam 24-48 appointed Mir Bakshi (military intelligence, war paymaster) did negotiations with NS. Factionalism: SK 22-39 convinced NS to attack Delhi because SK wanted to be Mir Bakshi but the post was given to Nizam 24-48. Battle of Karnal: Mughal army routed; Sadat Khan 22-39 taken prisoner; the Mir Bakshi died fighting Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, now Mir Bakshi, negotiates: Rs 50 lakh and Nadir Shah does not enter Delhi (warn) Factionalism: snubbed over the Mir Bakshi post, Sadat Khan 22-39 goads Nadir Shah to attack Delhi for bigger plunder (bad) Delhi falls; Md Shah imprisoned; Nadir Shah rules as emperor of Delhi for 60 days (bad) Sadat Khan 22-39, insulted by Nadir Shah after the victory instead of being rewarded, takes his own life Mnemonic: Karnal 1739: 50 lakh to stay out, a snub to bring him in. Nizam, now Mir Bakshi, buys peace for 50 lakh; Sadat Khan 22-39, passed over for that post, goads Nadir into Delhi; 60 days of Nadir's rule follow. Decode: Karnal defeat, Sadat Khan 22-39 taken prisoner, Nizam negotiates (Nadir does not enter Delhi). Factionalism then breaks the deal: Sadat wanted the Mir Bakshi post that went to Nizam. Nadir's war aim was plunder, not annexation. Sadat's code ends in 39, the year of Karnal. Why it sticks: one snub undoes a 50 lakh treaty. Teacher: Nizam appointed Mir Bakshi = military intelligence + war paymaster. Recent war expenditure had risen (Marathas 1738). Factionalism: Sadat Khan 22-39 wanted to be Mir Bakshi, but the post was given to Nizam.  Teacher's board: NS attacked Delhi. 2 lakh people killed leads to prestige / social power of the Mughals going down. 100 crore looted (gems, gold and silver, horses and elephants, artisans, Shah Jahan 27-58's Peacock Throne): Mansabdars' loss leads to future military corruption; treasury sad leads to military sad (could no longer maintain a strong army). Nadir of Mughal power = lowest point. Military prestige down; encouraged rivals, external and domestic, e.g. Abdali 1748+. The five pillars  Nadir Shah's blow across five pillars: Political, Social, Military, Economic, Technological.   Pillar   The blow    --- ---    Political   Md Shah (1719–48) was publicly humiliated and did not stand up for his own dignity. *For Mansabdars watching, an emperor who could not stand for his dignity wasn't worth defending.*     Social   Nadir Shah's forces massacred roughly two lakh civilians of Delhi. Whatever social legitimacy remained evaporated in the streets of the capital.     Military   A State that can't defend its capital invites more attacks. The defeat directly encouraged the First Afghan Invasion of 1748 by Ahmed Shah Abdali. (The teacher underlines 1748 and writes "attacks".)     Economic   Wealth estimated at about 100 crore rupees of the time (x250-300 for present value) extracted, plus irreplaceable assets, most famously the Peacock Throne with the Kohinoor diamond. Mansabdars were forced to contribute from personal wealth. The empire, already in the Jagirdari crisis, now lacked means to rebuild a strong army.     Technological   Funds that might have bought reform were gone, locking in the existing technology gap, so a weak military.   Mnemonic: Nadir's five blows: P-S-M-E-T. "Please Save My Empire, Thanks." Decode: Political = Md Shah humiliated; Social = about 2 lakh Delhi civilians massacred; Military = invited Abdali's first invasion of 1748; Economic = about 100 crore looted, Peacock Throne with the Kohinoor; Technological = no funds to close the technology gap. Why it sticks: Nadir = the lowest point ("nadir") of Mughal power. Mnemonic: Nadir's numbers: 60, 2, 100, 50. 60 days of rule, 2 lakh killed, 100 crore taken, 50 lakh was the price of staying out. Decode: 1739: Nadir ruled Delhi for 60 days; about two lakh civilians massacred; about 100 crore rupees looted (x250-300 for present value); Nizam negotiated 50 lakh at Karnal, which Nadir accepted to go back. Why it sticks: the offer (50 lakh) is tiny beside the haul (100 crore).  The Peacock Throne, taken by Nadir Shah in 1739, with the Kohinoor diamond. Teacher: Nadir Shah = the lowest point ("Nadir") of Mughal power, the teacher's pun on the name. Loot: gems, gold and silver, horses and elephants, artisans, Shah Jahan 27-58's Peacock Throne. Mansabdars' loss leads to future military corruption; treasury down leads to a military that could no longer maintain a strong army. Student doubt (handout). *If the Marathas plundered Delhi in 1737 and defeated Nizam in 1738, why were they not fighting Nadir Shah in 1739?* Because the Marathas had returned South to their HQ after the Treaty of Bhopal (1738). They had already extracted maximum concessions through the treaty. *Allow the rival State to get weak; why interfere unless there is a deal, like in 1752?* That strategic patience is exactly what gave them the Maratha Protectorate of the Mughal Emperor in 1752. Mnemonic: Let the elephants fight: Marathas wait, then protect. After Bhopal (1738) the Marathas went home to the South while Nadir hit Delhi in 1739; patience gave them the protectorate in 1752. Decode: they had already extracted the maximum through the Treaty of Bhopal; a rival State was allowed to get weak; "why interfere unless there is a deal, like in 1752?" Why it sticks: two elephants fight, the watcher collects the grass.

items.t: 11 · India by the mid-18th century
items.x: Mughal decline arc 1707-54: 1707 Aurangzeb's peak, 1719-24 succession turmoil, 1739 Nadir Shah and Karnal, 1752 Maratha protectorate, 1754 Alamgir II puppet.  The arc with the teacher's ink: 1707 "but foundation of decline (1707+)"; succession turmoil corrected to "1707-19"; 1752 "Ahmed Shah Bahadur 48-54, Mughal came under Maratha protection because of fear of Afghan invasion (Abdali)"; 1754 "Alamgir II 54-59 of Marathas".  Handout Diagram 3: Mughal decline arc (1707-1754): Aurangzeb's peak, Jagirdari crisis plus over-extraction plus peasant revolts, factionalism plus military corruption plus weak commanders, Nadir Shah invades, Karnal 1739, Maratha victory over Nizam 1738, Treaty of Bhopal 1739 (as printed), Maratha protectorate 1752, Alamgir II installed 1754, mid-18th c fragmented polity, Delhi-Agra rump. 1752: the Mughal emperor came under Maratha protection, accepting Maratha military guardianship against further Afghan invasions. *The protector had become the protected.* 1754: the Marathas installed Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet emperor, a Mughal ruler chosen by the very people the Mughals had spent decades trying to suppress. By the mid-18th c the Mughal Empire as a functional State had ceased to exist. What remained was a collection of regional powers, each with its own territory, army and foreign policy. The Maratha State stood at the top. The emperor continued to sit in Delhi, technically retaining symbolic sovereignty until 1858, but his actual authority extended little beyond Delhi and Agra. A ceremonial figurehead kept alive because his symbolic legitimacy was useful to others.  Teacher: by mid-18th c the Mughal emperor's rule is limited to a small area around Delhi and Agra. Symbolically the emperor of Hindustan until 1858. Sovereignty = symbolic power + power on external and domestic affairs (= rule). Rule in different parts by different regional States, in the next chapter.  "India by the mid-18th century" with the teacher's ink: multiple regional powers: Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad; Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand and Farukhabad (Afghans); Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore. "No. 1 power = Marathas". "Factionalism: R vs N" beside the Shah Alam II line. Teacher: Multiple regional powers = Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad (successor states); Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand and Farukhabad (rebel states; the Afghans); Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore (already autonomous). No. 1 power = Marathas. The emperor's symbolic sovereignty and the regional powers are both boxed. Mnemonic: Three kinds of regional power: BAH, JMRF, MRT. Successors BAH: Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad ("Bah!"). Rebels JMRF: Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farukhabad ("Just Make Rotis Fresh"). Already autonomous MRT: Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore. Decode: the teacher's classification of the mid-18th-century map; Rohilkhand and Farukhabad are the Afghans. No. 1 power = Marathas. Why it sticks: three groups of 3, 4, 3: successors, rebels, autonomous. The Prelims 2003 pin: Shah Alam II 60-06 Worth pinning (Prelims 2003). Shah Alam II 60-06 spent the initial years of his reign away from Delhi because of fear of his own Wazir, Imad-ul-Mulk, not fear of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier. Mnemonic: Shah Alam II 60-06: the danger was in the house, not at the gate. "The enemy at home (Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk), not at the border (North-West frontier)." Decode: Assertion A (stayed away from Delhi) is true; Reason R (foreign invasion danger) is false because the cause was his own Wazir, Imad-ul-Mulk. Handout and slides 36 and 37 say (c); the teacher's ticks point to (b) and coaching keys are split; UPSC gave no key. Hold the Wazir fact. Why it sticks: "Imad" starts with "I" for Inside.  Prelims 2003 Assertion-Reason question: A, Shah Alam II spent the initial years as an emperor far away from his capital. R, there was always a lurking danger of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier.  The slide's answer: (c). A is true (Shah Alam II stayed away from Delhi), R is false (the cause was fear of his own Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk, not a frontier invasion). Options (a), (b) and (d) are wrong. The question: *Assertion (A): Shah Alam II 60-06 spent the initial years as an Emperor far away from his capital. Reason (R): There was always a lurking danger of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier.*   Option   Verdict in the handout    --- ---    (a) Both true and R explains A   Wrong: R is false; the threat was internal (Wazir), not external (frontier)     (b) Both true but R does not explain A   Wrong: R is false (same reason)     (c) A is true, R is false   Answer (c)     (d) A false, R true   Wrong: A is true   Teacher's lesson on Assertion-Reason questions  "Assertion-Reason": read as independent statements. (i) Read A and mark T/F. (ii) Read R and mark T/F. (iii) If (i) = T and (ii) = T, then THINK: is R the reason for A?  The teacher marks A = T and R = T ("always" boxed), and ticks (b) while marking (a) wrong.  Teacher's note on the answer key: "UPSC was not bringing any ans key. Coachings have brought out a key: both (c), (b)". Teacher: Method: read as independent statements. (i) Read A and mark T/F. (ii) Read R and mark T/F. (iii) If both are True, THEN THINK: *is R the reason for A?* Teacher: On this PYQ the teacher first marks both A and R as True (boxing the word "always" in R), and ticks (b) ("both true but R is not the correct explanation"). Then he notes: UPSC was not bringing any answer key. Coaching institutes have brought out keys: both (c) and (b) appear. Flag. The handout and slides 36 and 37 give (c) as the answer, reasoning that R is false because the cause was fear of the Wazir. The teacher's own ticks on the L5 slide point to (b), and he says coaching keys are split between (c) and (b). Learn both the facts and the dispute. The fact to hold is that Shah Alam II 60-06's cause was fear of his Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk. Mnemonic: Assertion-Reason method: A-R-T. "Is A true? Is R true? Then Think." Decode: (i) read A alone and mark T/F; (ii) read R alone and mark T/F; (iii) only if both are true, THINK: is R the reason for A? On this PYQ the teacher boxed "always" in R and first ticked (b). Why it sticks: ART is a three-beat routine: A, R, then the Thinking step that most people skip.

items.t: 12 · Exam strategy: how to turn a PYQ into a FYQ
items.x: The key skill is identifying the protagonist of a question, what it is actually centred on. Once you know the protagonist, you know where to put your emphasis.     Question   Protagonist   Weighting    --- --- --- ---    PYQ (Mains 2017)   *"By mid-18th century, India was a spectre of fragmented polity. Elaborate."*   Fragmented polity   30% Mughal decline (cause), 70% rise of regional powers (evidence)     FYQ (illustrative)   *"In the first half of the 18th century, the Mughal Empire was reduced to a figment of imagination. Elaborate."*   The Mughal Empire's own collapse   70% Mughal decline (Maratha victories, Nadir Shah's invasion, Karnal, Bhopal, emperor-as-puppet), 30% regional powers (supporting evidence of Mughal irrelevance)   Same body of knowledge. Two different protagonists. Two very different answers. Mnemonic: Mains 2017: the protagonist gets the 70. PYQ (fragmented polity): 30 Mughal decline, 70 regional powers. FYQ (Mughal Empire's collapse): 70 Mughal decline, 30 regional powers. Decode: ask "who is the question about?" The protagonist (fragmented polity in the PYQ; the Mughal Empire itself in the FYQ) takes 70%; the other side is only 30% support. Why it sticks: 3-7 flips to 7-3 when the hero changes.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The Mughal fall in one breath. Aurangzeb 58-07 wins Bijapur 86 and Golconda 87, but forty years of war drain the treasury and his black dates (69, 75, 79, 89) cost him the people. He dies in 1707 at the peak; the Mansabdars, now unhappy and unpaid in a Jagirdari crisis (5% hold 61%), turn to court politics. Boxing rounds follow: Bahadur Shah 07-12, Jahandar Shah 12-13, Farukhsiyar 13-19 and the Sayyids, then the puppet Muhammad Shah 19-48 in 1719, while Nizam 24-48 slips off to Hyderabad. The Marathas expose the rot: Bajirao 20-40 plunders Delhi 1737, the Treaty of Bhopal follows in 1738. Nadir Shah arrives: Karnal, 60 days, 2 lakh dead, 100 crore gone, 1739; Abdali comes in 1748. The Mughal ends up under Maratha protection in 1752 and gets a puppet, Alamgir II 54-59, in 1754. Decode: 1707 → 1719 → 1737 → 1738 → 1739 → 1748 → 1752 → 1754 is the chapter's own chain. Why it sticks: a rich man's house: he wins big, spends it all, his sons fight, burglars walk in, and the watchman (Marathas) takes charge.

items.t: Exam lens: priority and PYQs
items.x: Teacher: Chapter 3 covers the successor states. Chapters 2 to 7 together are marked less important for Mains (very little) and for Prelims (less).   Year and paper   What was asked   The answer or trap   Where in this chapter    --- --- --- ---    Prelims 2021   The relation between the Carnatic and Hyderabad   Do not treat the Carnatic as a separate independent State. It was the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah   The Carnatic inside Hyderabad   What to prepare: the five-step recipe by which a province became autonomous without declaring independence, and the Carnatic-inside-Hyderabad rule.

items.t: 0 · Control versus rule (the teacher's opening)
items.x: Chapter 3 title slide: Regional States, the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad.  Teacher's board: Control versus Rule. Absentee colonialism (e.g. Angola, Mozambique): raw materials flow out, a few people around the territory; control yes, rule no. Rule = doing L, E, J: making laws and implementing them; governance: local health, education, infrastructure; IAS, IPS. EIC in Bengal: Battle of Plassey 1757 = control / conquest began; Battle of Buxar 1764 = rule began. Teacher: Control ≠ Rule. Control is possible without ruling (absentee colonialism, e.g. Angola, Mozambique: extract raw materials, few people on the ground). Rule = doing L, E, J (making laws, implementing them) plus governance of local health, education, infrastructure, run through IAS, IPS. Teacher: EIC in Bengal: Battle of Plassey 1757 → control / conquest began. Battle of Buxar 1764 → rule began. Mnemonic: Plassey pockets, Buxar bosses. Plassey 1757 = the EIC Pockets Bengal (control); Buxar 1764 = the EIC Bosses it (rule). Seven years from pocket to boss. Decode: Plassey 1757 = control / conquest began; Buxar 1764 = rule began. Control without rule = absentee colonialism (Angola, Mozambique); rule = L, E, J plus governance. Why it sticks: P comes before B, just as 57 comes before 64.

items.t: 1 · Framework: the three classes of regional State
items.x: By the mid-18th century the Mughal State had ceased to function as a single unified polity. What remained was a patchwork of regional powers.  Teacher's board: as the Mughal empire weakened, power decentralised (1707 to 1800) to three kinds of State. Successor States: the Mughal emperor is stabbed in the back by his provincial governors / Subadars, who go on to establish their own rule in B, A, H but never declared independence formally. Rebel States: fought the Mughal State, took some territory of the Mughal State, and established their own State on this territory. Already autonomous States: even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule here: Rajput, Mysore, Travancore.  Three classes of regional States: Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad) arose from powerful Mansabdars who extracted governing authority over a Subah from the emperor (this chapter); Rebel States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Afghans of Farukhabad and Rohilkhand) formed by those who openly rebelled; Already Autonomous (Rajputs, Mysore, Travancore) never under effective Mughal control.   Class   Examples   How they arose    --- --- ---    Successor States   Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad   Powerful Mansabdars who extracted governing authority over a Subah from the emperor (this chapter)     Rebel States   Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Afghans (Farukhabad, Rohilkhand)   Formed by those who openly rebelled against the empire     Already Autonomous   Rajputs, Mysore, Travancore   Never under effective Mughal control to begin with   Teacher: Successor states: "the Mughal emperor is stabbed in the back by his provincial governors / Subadars", who establish their own rule in B, A, H but never declared independence formally. Rebel states: they FOUGHT the Mughal State (boxed), took some territory, and established their own State on it. Already autonomous: "even when the Mughal was powerful, he did not rule here." Mnemonic: Heir, Rebel, Homeowner. The Heir took the house quietly, the Rebel fought for a room, the Homeowner never rented from the emperor at all. Decode: Heir = Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad: governors "stabbed him in the back" but never declared independence); Rebel = Rebel States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Afghans of Farukhabad and Rohilkhand: they FOUGHT the Mughal State); Homeowner = Already Autonomous (Rajputs, Mysore, Travancore: the Mughal never ruled there). Why it sticks: only the Rebel has a fight in the story.  Two maps of the 18th century: the regions of India (Rajputs, Awadh, Bihar, Bengal, Maratha territory, Nizam, Mysore, Northern Circars, Travancore) and a coloured map with the teacher's marks: 1792, 1717, 1724, Malwa, and European settlements.  Handout Map 2: the regional powers of the eighteenth century.  Handout map marked 1700-95. The list of later emperors (teacher's proof of decline)  Teacher's list: BS 07-12, JS 12-13, FS 13-19, Md Shah 19-48, then Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54, Alamgir II 54-59, Shah Alam II 60-06, Akbar II 06-37, Zafar 37-57. The teacher circles "Successor states" against the 1713-48 reigns and writes "Proof of decline of Mughal".   Emperor   Reign    --- ---    Bahadur Shah   1707–12     Jahandar Shah 12-13   1712–13     Farukhsiyar   1713–19     Muhammad Shah 19-48 (Rangila)   1719–48     Ahmad Shah Bahadur   1748–54     Alamgir II 54-59   1754–59     Shah Alam II 60-06   1760–1806     Akbar II 06-37   1806–37     Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57   1837–57   Teacher: The teacher brackets FS 13-19 and Md Shah 19-48 as the reigns in which the Successor States arose, and writes beside the list: "Proof of decline of Mughal." Mnemonic: The queue of nine emperors. Bear, Jaguar, Fox, Monkey, Ant, Alligator, Snake, Ape, Zebra: a zoo queue at the Red Fort gate. Decode (first letters): Bahadur Shah 1707–12, Jahandar Shah 12-13, Farukhsiyar (FS 13-19), Muhammad Shah 19-48, Ahmad Shah Bahadur 1748–54, Alamgir II 54-59, Shah Alam II 60-06, Akbar II 06-37, Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57. Why it sticks: each reign ends where the next begins (12, 13, 19, 48, 54, 59-60, 06, 37), so you only learn the slips. The Fox (13-19) and the Monkey (19-48) are the reigns in which the Successor States arose.

items.t: 2 · Why autonomous but never formally independent?
items.x: Bengal was set up as a successor state by Murshid Quli Khan (MQK, 1717–27) in 1717; Awadh by Sadat Khan 22-39 in 1722; Hyderabad by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 in 1724. Each ruled de facto as sovereign; none declared independence. Mnemonic: BAH! 17-22-24. The emperor sighs "BAH!": Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, in that order, in 17, then 22, then 24 (gaps of 5 and 2). Decode: Bengal 1717 (Murshid Quli Khan, MQK, 1717–27); Awadh 1722 (Sadat Khan 22-39); Hyderabad 1724 (Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48). B-A-H is also alphabetical order. Why it sticks: each founder's code starts with the same two digits as his founding year (17-27, 22-39, 24-48).  Founders of successor states: Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27), 1717 (teacher: Farukhsiyar 13-19); Awadh, Sadat Khan 22-39, 1722 (Md Shah 19-48); Hyderabad, Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, 1724 (Md Shah 19-48). Common thread: each ruled de facto as sovereign, none ever declared independence formally. The teacher adds a column "EIC": 1757, 1764, 1798. De facto = on ground reality; de jure = on paper. All of these are Mansabdars; ministers in the Central Govt; ministers in the Provincial Govt. Teacher: De facto = on-ground reality. De jure = on paper. All of these were Mansabdars, some of them ministers in the Central Govt and some ministers in the Provincial Govt. The State sketch: at the Centre, a Head of State with three branches; in each Province, a similar tree. The teacher's side column "EIC" lists 1757, 1764, 1798 against Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad. The slides and handout do not explain 1798. Check it against your own notes.  Teacher's board: Why did B, A, H not declare independence? Trade: domestic trade is easier, cheaper, lower taxes. Legitimacy. Influence: Hyderabad independent versus Hyderabad with some influence on the rest of the Mughal empire if a minister at the Centre. Examples: 1739, Nizam 24-48 = Mir Bakshi while he is Nawab of Hyderabad; 1738, a large Mughal army led by Nizam 24-48 fought the Marathas.  "Autonomous, but never independent, why": symbolic legitimacy (social power), ambitions at Delhi (political power), military assistance (military power), trade barriers (economic power). Teacher: if declared independence, opponents may unite against you in the name of the emperor; if independence, an attack on Hyderabad is not an attack on the Mughal empire.   Reason   Detail   Teacher's ink    --- --- ---    Symbolic legitimacy (Social power)   A Mughal Subahdar's title commanded the obedience of local nobles   If you declare independence, opponents may unite against you in the name of the emperor     Ambitions at Delhi (Political power)   Prized Mansabs at the Centre: Wazir (PM / Imperial Diwan) and Mir Bakshi (War Paymaster). Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 was Wazir 1722–24 while also Subahdar of Hyderabad, and became Mir Bakshi in 1739–40 while still Subahdar of Hyderabad   Independent Hyderabad has no influence; Hyderabad with a minister at the Centre has some influence on the rest of the Mughal empire     Military assistance (Military power)   Provinces could rely on each other's help in times of war   If independent, an attack on Hyderabad is no longer an attack on the Mughal empire, so the help is gone     Trade barriers (Economic power)   Political independence could hurt trade, because tariffs may then apply. *(Think EU members giving up partial sovereignty for open borders and trade.)*   Domestic trade is easier, cheaper, lower taxes   Mnemonic: Sam Trades safely. S-A-M-T: why B, A, H never declared independence. Decode: Symbolic legitimacy (social power); Ambitions at Delhi (political power: Wazir, Mir Bakshi); Military assistance (military power: an attack on Hyderabad would no longer be an attack on the Mughal empire); Trade barriers (economic power: tariffs, while domestic trade is easier, cheaper, lower taxes). Why it sticks: the four powers run Social, Political, Military, Economic, in the same order as S-A-M-T. Mnemonic: Nizam's two Delhi hats: 22-24 and 39-40. Wazir at "twenty-two to twenty-four", Mir Bakshi in Nadir's time, "thirty-nine, forty". Decode: Wazir 1722–24 (PM / Imperial Diwan) while still Subahdar of Hyderabad; Mir Bakshi 1739–40 (War Paymaster), again while Subahdar of Hyderabad. Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 is the man. Why it sticks: the Wazir hat ends in 24, the very year Hyderabad is set up (1724).

items.t: 3 · Mughal provincial titles and the Bengal Subah's structure
items.x: Provincial offices: Sword, Purse and military audit. Subahdar (Nazim / Nawab): Nizamat, defence, peace, criminal justice, reports to the Emperor. Diwan: Diwani, land revenue and civil justice (the Purse), reports to the Imperial Diwan (Wazir), bypassing the Nazim. Bakshi of the Subah: military audit and intelligence, reports to the Mir Bakshi at the Centre, bypassing the Nazim. The design (Akbar 56-05): checks and balances; every successor State's founder dismantled it. Note: a Nawab need not be a Subahdar; Alivardi Khan 40-56 was Nawab of Patna / Naib Nazim of Bihar before becoming Subahdar of all Bengal in 1740.   Office   Role   Reports to    --- --- ---    Subahdar (Nazim / Nawab)   Nizamat: defence, peace, criminal justice (the Sword)   the Emperor     Diwan   Diwani: land revenue and civil justice (the Purse)   the Imperial Diwan (Wazir), bypassing the Nazim     Bakshi of the Subah   Military audit and intelligence   the Mir Bakshi at the Centre, bypassing the Nazim     The design (Akbar 56-05   Checks and balances. Every successor State's founder dismantled it   none   Mnemonic: Sword, Purse, Eyes. Three officers, three bosses at Delhi: the Sword answers to the Emperor, the Purse to the Wazir, the Eyes to the Mir Bakshi. Decode: Subahdar (Nazim / Nawab) = Sword = Nizamat (defence, peace, criminal justice) reports to the Emperor; Diwan = Purse = Diwani (land revenue, civil justice) reports to the Imperial Diwan (Wazir), bypassing the Nazim; Bakshi of the Subah = Eyes (military audit and intelligence) reports to the Mir Bakshi, bypassing the Nazim. This is Akbar 56-05's checks and balances. Why it sticks: nobody holds Sword, Purse and Eyes together, until a successor-State founder grabs all three.  Teacher's board: Akbar's Mansabdari system, checks and balances. Centre (Delhi): King / Emperor above the Nazim / Subadar (gun power, military head); Wazir / Imperial Diwan above the Diwan (political power + finance power, like CM + FM); Mir Bakshi above the Bakshi (intelligence power). "How to end the authority of the emperor in a province? Ans: end checks and balance, concentrate all power in self or in supporters." Teacher: Akbar 56-05's Mansabdari system = checks and balances, in any province. Nazim / Subadar = gun power (the military head). Diwan = political power + finance power (think CM + FM). Bakshi = intelligence power. Each of the three reports to a *different* officer at Delhi, all under the King. How to end the authority of the emperor in a province? End the checks and balances and concentrate all power in yourself or in your supporters. That is exactly the four-to-five-step recipe in Section 4.  Teacher's vocabulary board: Mansabdar holds posts such as Mir Bakshi, Nazim, Naib Nazim (Naib = Deputy); like "Animal" holding Lion, Tiger, Cheetah. Nazim = Subadar = Nawab of Suba = Governor. E.g. "Nizam" was the title of the Nazim of the Hyderabad Suba. Teacher: Mansabdar is the general term (like "animal"); Mir Bakshi, Nazim, Naib Nazim are particular posts (like lion, tiger, cheetah). Naib = Deputy. Nazim = Subadar = Nawab of Suba = Governor. *Example:* "Nizam" was the title of the Nazim of the Hyderabad Suba. Nawab ≠ Subahdar always. A Nawab could administer a sub-region within a Suba: Alivardi Khan 40-56 was Nawab of Patna (a region inside the Bengal Subah) or Naib Nazim of Bihar before becoming Subahdar of the whole Bengal Subah in 1740. The Naib Nazim = Deputy Subahdar. Mnemonic: Nazim and Nizam are anagrams. Nazim = Subadar = Nawab = Governor; Naib = Deputy; "Nizam" is simply the Nazim's title in Hyderabad (same five letters, shuffled). Decode: Alivardi Khan 40-56 was Nawab of Patna / Naib Nazim of Bihar first, and Subahdar of the whole Bengal Subah only in 1740, so a Nawab need not be a Subahdar. Why it sticks: small seat (Patna) first, big seat (Bengal) later: deputy before boss. The Diwan did not report to the Subahdar. He reported directly to the Imperial Diwan at Delhi. Akbar 56-05 deliberately made the two co-equal. This separation of the Sword (Nizamat) from the Purse (Diwani) is what kept the Mughal Empire stable for over a century. Every successor State founder had to dismantle it. 3.1 Geographical administration of the Bengal Subah (handout tables) Territory: Bengal Subah (West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, East Bengal). Capital: Murshidabad (in West Bengal). Nizamat (Home Minister: law and order, criminal justice, defence / war commander) = Nazim (Subahdar), directly answerable to the Emperor. Diwani (revenue, civil administration, civil justice) = Diwan, directly answerable to the Emperor (under the supervision of the Imperial Diwan, i.e. the Wazir). Parallel audit and intelligence officer = Bakshi of the Subah, reports directly to the Mir Bakshi at Delhi, bypassing the Nazim. The Nazim, the Diwan and the Bakshi were mutually independent. None could overrule the others. All three reported only to their imperial counterparts at Delhi. Chain of command (handout table 3.2)   Branch   Function   Regional level (Patna, Cuttack, Dacca)   Provincial level (Murshidabad)   Imperial level (Delhi)    --- --- --- --- ---    Nizamat   Home Minister (law and order, criminal justice) plus defence (war commander)   Naib Nazim   Nazim (Subahdar)   Emperor (direct reporting; no intermediate minister)     Diwani   Revenue, civil administration, civil justice   Naib Diwan   Diwan   Wazir-i-Mumalik / Imperial Diwan (Diwan-i-Ala), then the Emperor     Bakshi (parallel audit and intelligence line)   Mansabdari records, military payroll, anti-corruption inspection (dagh and chehra), intelligence (waqia-navis)   Subordinate Bakshis (attached to Faujdars and contingents)   Bakshi of Bengal Subah   Mir Bakshi (Bakhshi-ul-Mumalik), then the Emperor   Regional breakdown within the Subah of Bengal (handout table 3.3)   Region within Suba   Headquarters   Nizamat head   Diwani head   Status    --- --- --- --- ---    West Bengal   Murshidabad   Nazim   Diwan   Direct rule     Bihar   Patna   Naib Nazim   Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad)   Delegated rule     Orissa   Cuttack   Naib Nazim   Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad)   Delegated rule     East Bengal   Dacca   Naib Nazim   Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad)   Delegated rule   The Bakshi line operated as a parallel vertical, reporting only to Delhi. Mnemonic: Murshidabad is Mother, three Naib children. Mother rules directly; the three Naib children rule by delegation: Patna-Bihar, Cuttack-Orissa, Dacca-East Bengal. Decode: West Bengal = Murshidabad (Nazim and Diwan, direct rule); Bihar = Patna; Orissa = Cuttack; East Bengal = Dacca (each with a Naib Nazim and a Naib Diwan reporting to Murshidabad: delegated rule). Why it sticks: say the pairs in table order; four seats, one direct, three delegated. The Bakshi's four functions   #   Function   What it meant    --- --- ---    1   Mansabdari records   Who holds what rank, who got promoted, demoted, joined or died; registers updated constantly     2   Military payroll   Calculating each Mansabdar's entitlement, assigning him a Jagir of the right value, transferring Jagirs every 2-3 years to prevent local roots, and in wartime controlling war expenditure     3   Anti-corruption inspection   Two mechanisms by Akbar 56-05: Dagh ("branding": every horse branded with an imperial mark on its flank; at inspection only branded horses counted) and Chehra ("face": each soldier's face, height, complexion and marks recorded in a register)     4   Intelligence (waqia-navis)   Information collectors in every province, district and significant town, sending daily reports to Delhi: court intrigues, market prices, harvest conditions, military movements, suspicious behaviour by the Nazim or Diwan, rebellions brewing, foreign travellers arriving. Reports flowed up through the Bakshi system, the Mir Bakshi being the chief recipient   The Bakshi knew who every noble was (records), what they were paid (payroll), whether they were honest (dagh-chehra) and what they were doing (intelligence). That is why he was the second-highest official in the Empire. Mnemonic: Bakshi: Who, What-paid, Honest, Doing. Four questions the Bakshi could always answer. Decode: Who? = Mansabdari records; What paid? = military payroll (Jagirs transferred every 2-3 years); Honest? = Dagh (branded horse) and Chehra (soldier's face register); Doing? = intelligence (waqia-navis, daily reports to Delhi). Why it sticks: Dagh is the mark on the horse's flank, Chehra is the face of the man.

items.t: 4 · How all three successor States were built: the recipe
items.x: "How a successor State was built": 1 Extract the Subahdari (take the Mansab of Subahdar from the emperor, who was dependent on powerful Mansabdars to be in power; teacher: "army"); 2 End checks and balances (fill Diwan, Naib Nazim and war commander with personal loyalists); 3 Build revenue strength (built a strong revenue administration; teacher: did field survey, efficient LR system); 4 Co-opt the men of money (merchants, bankers and Ijaradars given Mansabs, fusing wealth with political power; teacher: intermediary, Zamindars); 5 Consolidated political and military power by converting Tankha Jagir into Vatan Jagirs to get the loyalty of other powerful Mansabdars in the province. Result: a diffused autonomous polity, the Nawab headed a network of powerful actors, not an absolute concentration of power. 1 Extract the Subahdari: take the Mansab of Subahdar from the emperor, who depended on powerful Mansabdars (their army) to stay in power (warn) 2 End checks and balances: fill the Diwan, Naib Nazim and war commander posts with personal loyalists 3 Build revenue strength: strong revenue administration; field survey, efficient LR system; finance is crucial for everything else 4 Co-opt the men of money: merchants, bankers and Ijaradars get Mansabs, fusing wealth with political power (teacher: *intermediary Zamindars*) 5 Convert Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs: hereditary, for the loyalty of other powerful Mansabdars in the province (good) Result: a diffused autonomous polity: a Nawab on top of a network of powerful actors, with the Mughal link kept as a symbol  Handout Diagram 1: six-step successor State formation: extract Subahdar Mansab, end checks and balances, strong revenue administration, Tankha to Vatan Jagirs, co-opt merchants, bankers and Ijaradars, keep the Mughal symbolic link, leading to a diffused autonomous polity common to Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad. Step 4 in the handout: convert Tankha Jagirs (temporary, transferable) into Vatan Jagirs (hereditary). *Vatan = hereditary.* The emperor's historic tool of control (shifting Jagirs at will) was traded away for local loyalty of provincial Mansabdars to the regional ruler. Step 5 in the handout (co-opting): intermediary Zamindars, revenue farmers, merchants, moneylenders and bankers were promised security of property and reasonable taxes and, most unprecedentedly, given Mansabs. The Mansabdari system was traditionally lineage-based (military / noble bloodlines only). Appointing merchants and bankers to Mansabs was a structural transformation: administrative rank and commercial wealth, historically kept apart, now merged. All the steps were taken while accepting the symbolic sovereignty of the Mughal Emperor. Mnemonic: Tankha moves, Vatan stays. Tankha = Transfer (temporary, shifted at will); Vatan = Vansh (hereditary, stays in the family). Decode: Tankha Jagirs (temporary, transferable) versus Vatan Jagirs (hereditary). Converting Tankha into Vatan traded away the emperor's historic tool of control for the local loyalty of provincial Mansabdars. Why it sticks: T for Transfer, V for Vansh (family line). Count check. The handout heading says "four-step process", its text lists Steps 1 to 5 and the diagram shows six steps (it adds "keep the Mughal symbolic link"). The slide has five steps plus the result. Learn the recipe, not the number. Mnemonic: Every Eager Boss Can Convert. E-E-B-C-C: the five-step recipe for a successor State. Decode: Extract the Subahdari; End checks and balances (loyalists as Diwan, Naib Nazim, war commander); Build revenue strength (field survey, efficient LR system); Co-opt the men of money (merchants, bankers, Ijaradars given Mansabs); Convert Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs. Why it sticks: result = a diffused autonomous polity. Chapter ruling on the count: the slide has five steps plus the result, the handout text says "four-step" and its diagram shows six; learn the recipe, not the number.

items.t: 5 · Bengal: Murshid Quli Khan (MQK, 1717–27)
items.x: Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27): Bengal Subah = Bengal, Orissa and Bihar, vast and commercially rich, capital Murshidabad on the banks of the river Hooghly (the British capital later was Calcutta). MQK's rise: 1717 Nazim of Bengal while still Diwan (finance plus executive power, ended Akbar's checks and balances; teacher adds military power and "justified/right LR demand"). Revenue admin: detailed field surveys; promoted favourite intermediary Zamindars; by 1727 just 15 of them collected 50 percent of Bengal Suba's LR (teacher: co-opting powerful people). Coercion: Mansabdars who opposed had their Tankha Jagirs shifted to Orissa from Bengal. Bengal Subah = Bengal, Orissa and Bihar: vast and commercially rich. Capital: Murshidabad, on the banks of the Hooghly, then the major port (the British later developed Calcutta as an alternative). MQK was the last Bengal Governor appointed as per the wish of the Emperor. His path (handout): Diwan from 1700; under Farukhsiyar (1713–19) he also became Deputy Governor of Bengal Suba and Governor of Orissa. In 1717, when elevated to the Mansab of Nazim of Bengal Subah, he already was Diwan (*combining finance and executive in one man = ending Akbar 56-05's checks and balances*). He still sent tribute to Delhi, but the emperor's approval for appointments in Bengal Suba was now a paper formality. Revenue: brilliant administrator. Collected LR through intermediary Zamindars and got detailed field surveys done for fair assessment. The intermediaries grew powerful: by 1727 just fifteen were collecting 50% of Bengal Suba's LR. Coercion: Mansabdars who resisted had their Tankha Jagirs in Bengal taken and were given Jagirs in Orissa; resisting Zamindars were punished by reducing the land from which they collected LR. Mnemonic: MQK: two hats, fifteen friends. In '17 he wore two hats (Nazim and Diwan, Sword and Purse); fifteen friends (Zamindars) ate half the chapati (50% of LR) by '27. Decode: MQK (Murshid Quli Khan, 1717–27) became Nazim in 1717 while already Diwan; by 1727 just 15 intermediary Zamindars collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR; resisting Mansabdars had Tankha Jagirs shifted from Bengal to Orissa; he was the last Bengal Governor appointed as per the Emperor's wish. Why it sticks: three numbers in a row, 17 (year), 15 (Zamindars), 50 (percent). Teacher: MQK's rise = finance + executive + military power in one man. Field surveys gave a "justified / right LR demand." The LR chain on the board: ryots → intermediary Zamindars (I2) → Diwan of Suba → Imperial Diwan, with the money going either to the King or to a Jagirdar (J). "Co-opting powerful people" is written beside the 15 Zamindars.  Map: Bengal neighbourhood, 1750. Nawab of Bengal; Awadh, Malla, Gorkha, Sikkim, Bhutan, Ahom, Manipur, Burma, Mrauk-U, Borgi Maratha, N. Sarkar, Qing, Bay of Bengal.  Nawab of Murshidabad's boats on the Ganga, by Sita Ram.

items.t: 6 · The Jagat Seths: why Bengal's power was diffused, not centralised
items.x: "Jagat Seth" was a hereditary title, not a personal name, held by successive heads of a banking family: Manikchand under MQK; Mehtab Rai and Swarup Chand under Alivardi Khan 40-56. Already powerful before 1717, under the successor State they rose to what Dutch records called the richest banking house in the world. They loaned to Zamindars (so revenue reached the State on time), loaned to merchants, and ran Hundi services (*pre-modern wire transfer*). Under Shuja-ud-din Md Khan (1727–39) a Jagat Seth was appointed Treasurer of Bengal and Daroga of the Royal Mint: *central bank plus the Nawab's personal banker in one family.*  The House of Jagat Seth, Murshidabad. Power was diffused, not centralised: a network of Nawab + intermediary Zamindars + merchants + bankers, with the Nawab on top but dependent on their cooperation. Proof: the coup of 1740. Alivardi Khan 40-56 (Nawab of Patna) overthrew and killed the sitting Nawab Sarfaraz Khan (1739–40) with the Jagat Seth's backing. He secured formal approval by promising Emperor Md Shah one crore rupees plus Sarfaraz's personal wealth, and approval was duly given. *The emperor had been reduced to a transactional figure.* Mnemonic: Jagat Seth: M-M-S, the bank with three heirs. Manikchand first (under MQK), then the pair Mehtab Rai and Swarup Chand (under Alivardi Khan 40-56). Decode: Jagat Seth = hereditary title, not a name; a Jagat Seth was Treasurer of Bengal and Daroga of the Royal Mint under Shuja-ud-din Md Khan (1727–39). 1740 coup: Alivardi Khan 40-56 overthrew and killed Sarfaraz Khan (1739–40) with their backing and promised Md Shah one crore plus Sarfaraz's wealth. Why it sticks: one bank, one title; Manik alone, then Mehtab-Swarup as a pair.

items.t: 7 · Bengal's virtual break: the Maratha raids and Alivardi Khan 40-56
items.x: Under MQK, Bengal was autonomous but tribute still was sent to Delhi. Under Alivardi the break deepened, triggered by an external shock.  Bengal's virtual break (Alivardi Khan 40-56): 1745-51 Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raided Bengal repeatedly, Alivardi could not defeat him; 1751 settlement: Bhonsle won annual Chauth (one-fourth of revenues) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa; the break: revenue now flowing to Nagpur, Alivardi stopped sending revenue to Delhi and stopped seeking approval for appointments. The teacher sketches Nagpur with arrows to Bihar, Bengal and Orissa. 1745-51: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raids Bengal repeatedly; Alivardi cannot defeat him 1751 settlement: Bhonsle gets annual Chauth (one-fourth of revenues) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa (warn) Part of the revenue now flows to Nagpur (bad) Alivardi stops sending revenue to Delhi and stops seeking the emperor's approval for provincial Mansabdar appointments (good) Virtual break complete, but independence never declared Mnemonic: Raghuji's quarter and the Orissa key. Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raids for six years (45 to 51) and leaves with a quarter of two provinces and the whole third. Decode: 1745-51 raids; 1751 settlement = Chauth (one-fourth) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa; then Alivardi Khan 40-56 stops sending revenue to Delhi and stops seeking approval for appointments. Why it sticks: Bengal and Bihar pay (B-B), Orissa is gone (O). The succession chain after Alivardi  Bengal succession chain 1756-65: Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 (Alivardi's grandson); Mir Jafar 1757-60 (EIC-installed puppet after the Battle of Plassey 1757); Mir Qasim 60-63 (Mir Jafar's son-in-law); Mir Jafar restored 1763-65, then from 1765 Bengal's Diwani passed to the EIC.  Handout Diagram 2: Bengal succession chain: Murshid Quli Khan (founder, 1717-27), Shuja-ud-din (1727-39, son-in-law of MQK), Sarfaraz Khan (1739-40), Alivardi Khan (1740 coup, Jagat Seth backing), Siraj-ud-Daula (1756-57), Mir Jafar (1757-60, war commander), Mir Qasim (1760-63, son-in-law of Mir Jafar), Mir Jafar restored (1763-65). Mnemonic: Musical chairs in Murshidabad. Many Sons-in-law Sit; Alivardi Seizes; Siraj Falls; Jafar, Qasim, Jafar swap the chair until the EIC takes the Diwani. Decode: MQK (1717–27) → Shuja-ud-din (1727–39, son-in-law of MQK) → Sarfaraz Khan (1739–40) → Alivardi Khan 40-56 (coup) → Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 → Mir Jafar 57-60 (1757-60, EIC puppet after Plassey) → Mir Qasim 60-63 (son-in-law of Mir Jafar 57-60) → Mir Jafar 57-60 restored (1763-65) → 1765 Diwani to the EIC. Why it sticks: two sons-in-law bracket the chain (Shuja of MQK at the start, Qasim of Jafar near the end), and Jafar sits twice.

items.t: 8 · Awadh: from Sadat Khan 22-39 to the virtual break of 1753
items.x: Awadh, Sadat Khan 22-39 to the EIC: Sadat Ali Khan 22-39 (= Sadat Khan), Subahdar in 1722 as a reward for crushing revolts; installed nephew Safdar Jung 39-54 as Deputy Subadar (= Naib Nazim) and a loyalist as Diwan. Safdar Jung 39-54: Wazir under Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54 (1748); misused the office to annex Farukhabad; forced to resign in 1753, Awadh's virtual break (no revenue sent to Delhi, though legally still in the empire). Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75: Wazir under Shah Alam II 60-06. Founder: Sadat Ali Khan (1722–39), appointed Subahdar in 1722 as a reward for suppressing local revolts. He installed his nephew and son-in-law Safdar Jung 39-54 as Deputy Governor (Naib Nazim) and his own loyalist as Diwan; tribute to Delhi was reduced. Revenue grew from efficient land assessment and taxes on trade. He created a new loyal class of local elites (Indian Muslims, Afghans, Hindus) by giving them Mansabs and Jagirs. Unlike MQK, Sadat Khan 22-39 kept ambitions at the centre: he wanted a senior Mansab at Delhi (*the Central Government*). He convinced Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739 because the Mir Bakshi post had gone to Chin Qulich Khan (another name of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) instead of him. Nadir Shah ill-treated him after the victory; he committed suicide. Safdar Jung 39-54 was appointed Wazir by Ahmad Shah Bahadur (1748–54) in 1748. He misused the office to annex Farukhabad into Awadh. Other Mansabdars opposed, and in 1753 he was forced to resign. The resignation was Awadh's virtual break: no more revenue to Delhi, no imperial authority inside Awadh, though legally still part of the empire. Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 was appointed Wazir by Shah Alam II 60-06. He fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and was later defeated by the EIC at the Battle of Buxar (1764). Awadh survived nominally until EIC annexation in 1856 from Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. Mnemonic: Three S's of Awadh. Sadat, Safdar, Shuja: one gets the seat, one gets the Wazir's chair and has to quit, one is beaten at Buxar. Decode: Sadat Khan 22-39 (Subahdar 1722, reward for crushing revolts) → nephew and son-in-law Safdar Jung 39-54 (Wazir under Ahmad Shah Bahadur in 1748; annexed Farukhabad; forced to resign 1753 = virtual break) → Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 (Wazir under Shah Alam II 60-06; with Abdali at Panipat 1761; beaten by the EIC at Buxar 1764). Annexed 1856 from Wajid Ali Shah. Why it sticks: the codes link end to start: 22-39, 39-54, 54-75. Mnemonic: Sadat felt "sad at" Delhi. Passed over for Mir Bakshi, Sadat Khan 22-39 got Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739, and ended ill-treated and dead by suicide. Decode: the Mir Bakshi post went to Chin Qulich Khan (another name of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) instead of him. Unlike MQK, Sadat Khan 22-39 kept his ambitions at the centre. Why it sticks: "Sadat" sounds like "sad at" losing the post. Discrepancy to check. The slide calls Safdar Jung 39-54 the nephew of Sadat Khan 22-39; the handout calls him nephew and son-in-law. The handout in Chapter 2 also calls Sadat Khan 22-39 "of Irani group" in the Karnal passage.

items.t: 9 · Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48's path from Delhi to the Deccan
items.x: Hyderabad, Nizam-ul-Mulk's path (Nizam 24-48): set up 1724, Nizam-ul-Mulk aka Asaf Jah I (both underlined), leader of the Turani group, took Hyderabad after defeating Subadar Mubariz Khan. At the centre, 1720: Turani and Irani removed the Sayyid Brothers (who controlled Md Shah 19-48); teacher: "Factionalism: Noble vs Noble". 1740: after serving as Mir Bakshi (1739-40) during Nadir Shah's invasion he gave up on the centre and moved to Hyderabad permanently. Succession: Nazir Jung (1748-50), Muzaffar Jung (1750-51), Salabat Jung 51-62, Nizam-Ali-Khan (1762-1803). Hyderabad was set up within the empire in 1724 by Chin Qulich Khan, aka Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, aka Asaf Jah I (Nizam, 1724–48), after defeating Mubariz Khan, the sitting Nazim of the Deccan. He was the leader of the Turani group. In Aurangzeb 58-07's Deccan wars he and his father built strong roots in the region. 1720: the Turani and Irani groups removed the Sayyid Brothers, kingmakers who controlled Md Shah, and formally restored imperial authority. But the structural problem remained: Md Shah was uninterested in governance. *(Remember: 5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of all Jagir land revenue.)* As Wazir (1722–24) Nizam tried to redistribute Jagirs from big Mansabdars to smaller ones to ease the Jagirdari crisis, but the bigger Mansabdars did not agree. The Marathas defeated him in 1728 and 1738, forcing him to pay Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (*10% hereditary Maratha claim in the Deccan*). He served as Mir Bakshi (1739–40) during Nadir Shah's invasion. By 1740 he gave up on reforming the centre and moved to Hyderabad permanently. Succession after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48: Nazir Jung (1748–50) → Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (1750–51, 3 months) → Salabat Jung 51-62, French dominated under Bussy) → Nizam-Ali-Khan (1762–1803). Mnemonic: Nizam's number trail: 20, 22, 24, then 28, 38, then 39-40. Twenty: Sayyids go. Twenty-two: Wazir. Twenty-four: Hyderabad. Twenty-eight and thirty-eight: Marathas win. Thirty-nine to forty: Mir Bakshi, then home for good. Decode: 1720 Turani and Irani groups removed the Sayyid Brothers; Wazir 1722–24 (his Jagir redistribution failed); 1724 Hyderabad after defeating Mubariz Khan; Marathas defeated him in 1728 and 1738 (Chauth and Sardeshmukhi); Mir Bakshi 1739–40; by 1740 he moved to Hyderabad permanently. One man, three names: Chin Qulich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 = Asaf Jah I. Why it sticks: an even run 20-22-24, a pair 28-38, then 39-40. Mnemonic: Never Make Salabat Nervous. N-M-S-N: the four heirs after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48. Decode: Nazir Jung (1748–50) → Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (1750–51, only 3 months) → Salabat Jung 51-62 (French dominated under Bussy) → Nizam-Ali-Khan (1762–1803). Why it sticks: the dates chain 48-50-51-62, and the shortest reign is the second one (3 months). Mnemonic: A-H = I-T. Alphabet match: Awadh then Hyderabad = Irani then Turani. Decode: Sadat Khan 22-39 of Awadh = "of Irani group" (the handout's Karnal passage, flagged in the chapter's note); Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 of Hyderabad = leader of the Turani group. Why it sticks: A comes before H, and I comes before T.  Charminar, Hyderabad: the civic symbol of Nizam-ul-Mulk's autonomous successor State (old print).

items.t: 10 · How Nizam established Hyderabad as a successor State
items.x: Hyderabad as a successor State: symbolic sovereignty by 1748 (the emperor's name on coins and in the Friday Khutba, but zero influence over war, peace, treaties or appointments); tolerance (the Hindu majority was economically powerful, so Nizam 24-48 followed religious tolerance and punished opponents regardless of community); most aggressive change (of the three States, Hyderabad converted Tankha to Vatan Jagirs most aggressively and made merchants, moneylenders and Ijaradars Mansabdars "upstarts" on the largest scale).   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Symbolic sovereignty (by 1748)   The emperor's name on coins and in the Friday Khutba, but zero influence over war, peace, treaties or appointments     Tolerance   The Hindu majority was economically powerful, so Nizam followed religious tolerance and punished opponents regardless of community     Most aggressive change   Of the three States, Hyderabad converted Tankha to Vatan Jagirs most aggressively and made merchants, moneylenders and Ijaradars Mansabdars ("upstarts") on the largest scale   Merchants and moneylenders got property security and became Mansabdars (*called upstarts*), and in return gave financial support. The most pronounced transformation of the Mansabdari system was in Hyderabad. Result: the same diffused polity: Nawab at top, influential sections under him. Mnemonic: Name, Peace, Upstarts. Hyderabad's three marks: the emperor's Name on coins and Khutba, Peace through tolerance, Upstarts as Mansabdars. Decode: Name = symbolic sovereignty (coins, Friday Khutba, zero influence over war, peace, treaties, appointments); Peace = tolerance (Hindu majority economically powerful; opponents punished regardless of community); Upstarts = merchants, moneylenders and Ijaradars made Mansabdars on the largest scale, with Tankha to Vatan converted most aggressively. Why it sticks: N-P-U, "Nizam's Peaceful Upstarts".

items.t: 11 · The Carnatic: a State within a State
items.x: Hyderabad had a smaller State inside its borders, the Carnatic. By law it was part of the Hyderabad province. But it had its own ruler, the Nawab, and ran its own government.  Teacher's board of parallels: India has Jammu and Kashmir with Art. 370; Assam has Meghalaya as an autonomous State within Assam (Art. 244A); Hyderabad has the Carnatic (part of Hyderabad) "practically autonomous". Teacher: Parallels for the Carnatic: India → J&K with Art. 370; Assam → Meghalaya as an autonomous State within Assam (Art. 244A); Hyderabad → Carnatic (part of Hyderabad), practically autonomous. 11.1 Backstory: the Vijayanagar Empire (1336–1646)  Vijayanagar Empire's structure (1336-1646): Empire (Vijayanagar; the strongest power in South India for about 300 years; the Carnatic was part of it); Provinces (Nayak = CM, Telugu Hindu governors from warrior families); Palayams (Poligar / Palayakkarar, a local chief with his own private army and fort). Teacher's funnel: Bijapur, Golconda (1687), Vijayanagara 1336-1646, Carnatic, Hyderabad Suba, Hyderabad Karnatik. For three hundred years the Vijayanagar Empire was the strongest power in South India, and the Carnatic was part of it. Provinces were ruled by Nayaks (*teacher: Nayak = CM*), Telugu Hindu governors from warrior families. Nayaks divided their provinces into Palayams, each run by a local chief called a Poligar (Palayakkarar) with his own private army and fort. Mnemonic: E-N-P: Empire, Nayak, Poligar. Emperor on top, Nayak (the CM) in the middle, Poligar (a fort-owning local chief) at the bottom. Decode: Empire (Vijayanagar, 1336–1646, strongest in South India for about 300 years) → provinces under Nayaks (Telugu Hindu governors from warrior families; teacher: Nayak = CM) → Palayams under a Poligar (Palayakkarar) with his own private army and fort. Why it sticks: three rungs, E-N-P, read top to bottom.  Hampi / Vijayanagar ruins: the capital whose 1565 sack ended the empire as a major power. 11.2 The long decline (1565–1698) A. Defeat of Vijayanagar at Talikota (1565). A four-state alliance of the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) destroyed the Vijayanagar army. The empire officially continued until 1646, but this defeat was the real end of its power. B. Nayaks independent, then defeated. After 1565 the southern Nayaks of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee ruled autonomously; distance protected them for a while. By 1646 Bijapur and Golconda conquered and divided the Carnatic between themselves. C. Sultanates defeated by the Mughals. Aurangzeb 58-07 conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687). The whole Carnatic now came under Mughal rule. D. Gingee under the Marathas, then lost to the Mughals. Shivaji 74-80 captured Gingee Fort from Bijapur in 1677. After the Mughals executed Sambhaji 80-89 in 1689, the next Chhatrapati, Rajaram 89-00, made Gingee his base against the Mughals. In 1690 Zulfiqar Khan (Nawab of Carnatic) surrounded the fort. The siege lasted eight years (the longest by the Mughals); the Mughals finally captured Gingee in 1698. *(Zulfiqar Khan later became Wazir under Jahandar Shah 12-13, 1712, until his execution in February 1713.)* Mnemonic: Big Aunt Gave Bananas. B-A-G-B: the four Deccan Sultanates that broke Vijayanagar at Talikota in 1565. Decode: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar. Talikota (1565) was the real end of Vijayanagar power, though the empire officially continued until 1646. Why it sticks: four bananas, four Sultanates. Mnemonic: MTG: Mind The Gap. The southern Nayaks of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee ruled autonomously after 1565 because distance protected them, until Bijapur and Golconda divided the Carnatic by 1646. Decode: M = Madurai, T = Tanjore, G = Gingee. Why it sticks: the "gap" is the distance that kept them safe for a while. Mnemonic: Gingee's years: 77, 89-90, 98. Shivaji 74-80 grabs it in 77, Rajaram 89-00 makes it his base in 89, the siege starts in 90 and lasts 8 years, so it falls in 98. Decode: Shivaji 74-80 captured Gingee from Bijapur (1677); after Sambhaji 80-89 was executed (1689), Rajaram 89-00 made it his base; Zulfiqar Khan (Nawab of Carnatic) besieged it from 1690 for eight years, the Mughals' longest siege; captured 1698. Aurangzeb 58-07 had taken Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687). Why it sticks: 1690 + 8 = 1698; and Bijapur (86) falls before Golconda (87), B before G. 11.3 Dividing the region Prelims 2021 trap: the Carnatic and Hyderabad relation. Do not treat the Carnatic as a separate independent State; it was the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah.  The Hyderabad Subah of the Mughals divided into two parts: Hyderabad (north of the Krishna river, ruled directly by the Mughal Governor, the Nizam) and Carnatic, Hyderabad-Karnatic (twelve districts south of the Krishna, capital Gingee, its own Nawab who reported to the Nizam: a "state within a state"). The teacher's sketch shows Hyd Suba with Hyd above the Krishna, Hyd Karnatik below, and TN at the bottom.   Part   Where   Detail    --- --- ---    Hyderabad   North of the Krishna river   Ruled directly by the Mughal Governor (the Nizam)     Carnatic (Hyderabad-Karnatic)   Twelve districts south of the Krishna; capital Gingee *(covered the old Nayak kingdoms of Gingee, Tanjore and Madurai; on 18th-century maps, simply the "Carnatic")*   Had its own Nawab, but he reported to the Nizam: a "state within a state"   Mnemonic: Carnatic = the tenant downstairs. Hyderabad Suba is a two-floor house: the Nizam lives upstairs (north of the Krishna); the Carnatic tenant lives downstairs (south of it) with his own Nawab, but he reports to the Nizam. Decode: Hyderabad = north of the Krishna, ruled directly by the Nizam; Carnatic (Hyderabad-Karnatic) = twelve districts south of the Krishna, capital Gingee, own Nawab, a "state within a state". Prelims 2021 trap: the Carnatic was not a separate independent State; it was the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah. Why it sticks: a tenant lives inside the landlord's building, never in a separate one. Teacher's parallels: J&K (Art. 370), Meghalaya within Assam (Art. 244A). 11.4 and 11.5 Towards autonomy: the Carnatic Nawabs  Carnatic Nawabs towards autonomy: Saadatullah Khan (1710-32), the last Nawab chosen by the emperor (1710), made the post hereditary (adopted Dost Ali) without imperial approval; Dost Ali Khan (1732-40), his adopted heir; Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744), chosen by the Nizam, ending Saadatullah Khan's dynasty, but he also emerged autonomous of the Nizam.   Nawab   What happened    --- ---    Saadatullah Khan (1710–32)   The last Nawab directly chosen by the Mughal Emperor (1710). Two big steps: he moved the capital from Gingee to Arcot and made the Nawab post hereditary in his family without asking the emperor. He was childless and adopted his brother Ghulam Ali's son, Dost Ali. In name the Carnatic was still under the Nizam     Dost Ali Khan (1732–40)   His adopted nephew. Killed in 1740 by the Marathas under Raghuji Bhonsle in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh, close to the Tamil Nadu border     Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744)   Chosen by the Nizam, ending Saadatullah Khan's dynastic rule. But he too emerged autonomous of the Nizam   Mnemonic: S-D-A: Saadat shifts, Dost dies, Anwar is the Nizam's pick. Saadatullah (10-32) shifts the capital to Arcot and makes the post hereditary; Dost (32-40) is killed in Chittoor; Anwar (from 44) comes in on the Nizam's choice but goes autonomous too. Decode: Saadatullah Khan (1710–32): last Nawab chosen by the emperor; moved the capital from Gingee to Arcot; adopted his brother Ghulam Ali's son Dost Ali. Dost Ali Khan (1732–40): killed in 1740 by the Marathas under Raghuji Bhonsle in Chittoor district. Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744): chosen by the Nizam. Why it sticks: each start year equals the previous end year (32, then 40), then 44; and Gingee to Arcot goes G then A.  Handout Carnatic flow: Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646; operational end 1565 Talikota), Nayaks rule provinces, Palayams under Poligars/Palayakkarars, post-1646 Bijapur and Golconda subordinate the Nayaks, Aurangzeb conquers Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 = Mughal Carnatic, 12 districts south of Krishna = Hyderabad-Karnatic under the Nizam post-1724, Saadatullah Khan (1710-32) shifts capital from Gingee to Arcot with dynastic rule, Anwar-ud-din killed at the Battle of Ambur 1749 (2nd Carnatic War, French vs British), Md Ali Wallajah (1752-95) British-backed leading to EIC dependency. The handout's diagram carries the later steps: Anwar-ud-din killed at the Battle of Ambur (1749), 2nd Carnatic War, French versus British; Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (1752–95), British-backed, leading to dependency on the EIC. The text of the handout stops at Anwar-ud-din (1744). Mnemonic: Ambur 49, Wallajah 52. Anwar falls at Ambur in 49; Wallajah rises in 52 with British backing. Decode: Anwar-ud-din killed at the Battle of Ambur (1749), 2nd Carnatic War, French versus British; Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (1752–95), British-backed, leading to dependency on the EIC. Why it sticks: three years from Ambur (49) to Wallajah (52): one Nawab ends, the next begins.

items.t: 12 · Synthesis: the common pattern and what it made possible
items.x: Synthesis, the common pattern: concentration of power (a powerful Mansabdar extracts the Subahdari, dismantles checks and balances, builds revenue strength, converts Tankha to Vatan, co-opts merchants and bankers into the Mansabdari system); no independence (the Mughal umbrella served their interests, but practically independent including decisions of war and peace); unique Carnatic (part of Hyderabad Suba but autonomous: a successor State inside a successor State); Mughal authority (the emperor became a constitutional monarch with no executive power).   Point   Detail    --- ---    Concentration of power   Across Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad (and the Carnatic): a powerful Mansabdar extracts the Subahdari, dismantles checks and balances, builds revenue strength, converts Tankha to Vatan, and co-opts merchants and bankers into the Mansabdari system     No independence   None declared it: the Mughal umbrella served their interests; practically independent, including decisions of war and peace. Each developed its own diplomacy, army and fisc     Unique Carnatic   Part of the Hyderabad Suba but autonomous: a successor State inside a successor State. Fragmentation was not only horizontal (Subahs breaking from the empire) but also vertical (sub-regions within a successor State developing their own semi-autonomous identity)     Mughal authority   The emperor became a constitutional monarch with no executive power: a ceremonial head of State whose legitimacy was still useful to others   The India into which the EIC was stepping: competing, partially autonomous States, each with its own elite coalition and its own fiscal and military interests, and, critically, a world where legitimacy and real power had come apart. That gap between formal authority and actual power is exactly what made the subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration.     Bengal   Awadh   Hyderabad    --- --- --- ---    Founder and year   Murshid Quli Khan, 1717   Sadat Khan 22-39, 1722   Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Asaf Jah I), 1724     Founder's reign   1717–27   1722–39   1724–48     Earlier post   Diwan (from 1700)   Subahdar as reward for crushing revolts   Leader of the Turani group; Wazir 1722–24     Key feature   Field surveys; 15 Zamindars collected 50% of LR; Jagat Seths as bankers   New loyal elite of Indian Muslims, Afghans and Hindus; kept ambitions at the centre   Most aggressive Tankha to Vatan; merchants and moneylenders as Mansabdars; Carnatic inside     Link to Nadir Shah 1739   -   Sadat Khan 22-39 urged the attack on Delhi   Nizam as Mir Bakshi bought Nadir off with Rs 50 lakh (attempt)     Virtual break   Alivardi Khan 40-56, after 1751 settlement with Raghuji Bhonsle   1753, Safdar Jung 39-54 forced to resign   After 1740, Nizam moves to Hyderabad for good     EIC link   Plassey 1757; Diwani 1765   Buxar 1764; annexed 1856   Succession: French-dominated under Bussy (Salabat Jung 51-62)   Mnemonic: 57, 64, 98: the EIC knocks in B-A-H order. Bengal falls at 57, Awadh at 64, Hyderabad's slot says 98. Decode: the teacher's EIC column against Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad = 1757 (Plassey), 1764 (Buxar), 1798. The chapter notes that the slides and handout do not explain 1798, so check it against your own notes. Why it sticks: 57 to 64 is seven years; then the odd one out, 98. Mnemonic: Half to save, full to seize. The Nizam offered Nadir Rs 50 lakh to save Delhi (an attempt); Alivardi offered the emperor a full crore to seize Bengal. Decode: Nizam as Mir Bakshi bought Nadir off with Rs 50 lakh (attempt); Alivardi Khan 40-56 promised Md Shah one crore plus Sarfaraz's personal wealth, and approval was given. Why it sticks: 50 lakh is only half a crore; half saves nothing, full buys a crown. Mnemonic: Break order: 40, 51, 53. Hyderabad drifts away first (after 1740), Bengal breaks after the 1751 settlement, Awadh breaks in 1753. Decode: Hyderabad = after 1740 the Nizam moves there for good; Bengal = Alivardi Khan 40-56 after the settlement with Raghuji Bhonsle (1751); Awadh = 1753, Safdar Jung 39-54 forced to resign. Why it sticks: always ascending, 40, then 51, then 53, in the order H, B, A.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: One breath: from Delhi's decline to the EIC. In '17 MQK (1717–27) wears two hats in Bengal; in '22 Sadat Khan 22-39 is rewarded with Awadh; in '24 Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 takes Hyderabad: "BAH!", yet none says "independent", because the emperor's name still keeps trade easy and enemies divided (S-A-M-T). Five steps (E-E-B-C-C) build each State, and the Sword, Purse and Eyes end up in one hand. Bengal: the Jagat Seths' money helps Alivardi Khan 40-56 win in '40, and Raghuji's quarter plus Orissa in '51 completes the break. Awadh: Sadat, Safdar, Shuja; Safdar Jung 39-54 resigns in '53. Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 goes home for good in '40, with the Carnatic as the tenant downstairs. Then the EIC steps into the gap between paper and power: Plassey 57, Buxar 64, and the teacher's 98.

items.t: 1 · Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80: who he was and why he rose
items.x: Shivaji 74-80, who he was: born 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai; father a Jagirdar of Poona and a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur (Adil Shahi, 1489-1686); training by Dadaji Kondadev; inspiration from his mother Jijabai; first fort at 16 (1646); worked from the Maval region (Sahyadri), hilly and forested, with local warriors and peasants. Teacher's ink: sketch of the Deccan funnel with Golconda, Bijapur, Goa; the two issues (oppressive land revenue, discriminatory religious policy); guerrilla warfare. 1.1 Who he was Shivaji 74-80 Bhonsle was born on 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai. His father was a Jagirdar of Poona and served as a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur (1489-1686), ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty. This dynasty, together with the Qutub Shahi (1518-1687), had replaced the Bahmani Sultanate (1347-1527) in the Deccan. Early training came from his guardian Dadaji Kondadev, who shaped him as a soldier and administrator. The deeper inspiration came from his mother Jijabai and his own fierce ambition. He captured his first fort at the age of 16, in 1646. Working from the Maval region, a hilly, forested terrain in today's Pune district running through the Sahyadri range, he gathered an army of local warriors and peasants. Mnemonic: Sixteen in sixteen-forty-six. He took his first fort at 16, in 16-46: the "16" shows up twice. Decode: born 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle (Jagirdar of Poona, General and Mansabdar in Bijapur) and Jijabai (the deeper inspiration); trained by guardian Dadaji Kondadev ("Dada" = elder guardian); first fort 1646; base = Maval region in the Sahyadri. Why it sticks: 1630 + 16 = 1646, so age and year match. 1.2 Guerrilla warfare: the teacher's boards Teacher: Tactics = guerrilla warfare: hide and seek, attack and withdraw, sabotage. It is not traditional warfare. It uses surprise attacks, speed and geography, and creates shock and awe in the enemy. It is the only way to defeat a much more militarily stronger opponent.  Teacher's board: guerrilla is a tool that can serve positive, neutral or negative goals. Examples written: Naxals in India; Spain (1808-12) against Napoleon; the 1857 Revolt with Kunwar Singh and Tatya Tope; the Ganimi Kava of the Marathas; Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-24, underlined). Teacher: Guerrilla warfare is a tool used for positive, neutral or negative goals. Examples on the board: Naxals in India; Spain (1808-12) against Napoleon; 1857 Revolt (Kunwar Singh and Tatya Tope); Ganimi Kava of the Marathas; Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-24). 1.3 Why he rose against Bijapur and the Mughals  Shivaji versus Bijapur and the Mughals. Bijapur: from 1657 attacks on the oppressive Adil Shahis; in 1659 killed General Afzal Khan with Bagh Nakh and Bichhwa. Mughals: 1663 defeated Shaista Khan and sacked Surat, enraging Aurangzeb 58-07, who sent Jai Singh; his 1665 siege of Fort Purandhar led to a temporary compromise. Teacher's ink: triangle Aurangzeb, Marathas, Bijapur; Marathas' goal Swarajya (boxed); 1674 coronation of C. Shivaji; 1686 Aurangzeb annexes Bijapur; BG Tilak (1890s). From 1657 onwards, Shivaji 74-80 launched systematic attacks on the Kingdom of Bijapur (1489-1686), which followed economically oppressive and religiously discriminatory policies. This was also the period when Aurangzeb 58-07 became Mughal emperor. In 1659, Ali Adil Shah II, Sultan of Bijapur, sent his General Afzal Khan to kill Shivaji 74-80 under the pretext of negotiations. Instead, Shivaji 74-80 killed the seven-feet-tall Afzal Khan using his concealed Bagh Nakh (Tiger Claws) and a Bichhwa (dagger). When Aurangzeb 58-07 launched his campaign for the conquest of the Deccan, Shivaji 74-80 defeated the Mughal General Shaista Khan 64-88 in 1663 and sacked the wealthy port of Surat, which enraged Aurangzeb 58-07. Aurangzeb 58-07 sent General Jai Singh 99-43, who used an encirclement strategy to cut off supplies to Maratha territories. In 1665 Jai Singh 99-43 laid siege to Fort Purandhar (40-50 km southeast of Pune). Teacher: BG Tilak (1890s) used this cultural history (a Maratha against a Mughal general) to arouse nationalism against the British. Teacher: Triangle on the board: Aurangzeb 58-07, the Marathas and Bijapur. The Marathas' goal is Swarajya (boxed). 1674 = coronation of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80; 1686 = Aurangzeb 58-07 annexes Bijapur.  Fort Purandhar (model photo). Teacher's ink: Gherao means starve the enemy; the 1665 siege by Jai Singh, a powerful Hindu Mansabdar of the Mughal State; result: Treaty of Purandhar 1665. Terms: accepts Mughal as emperor, accepts to be Mansabdar (son Sambhaji sent as Mansabdar), alliance against Bijapur (which lasted till 1686). On the left: the standard-book statement that Shivaji never accepted Mughal sovereignty; teacher: Purandhar 1665 was a temporary tactic.  Handout picture for Fort Purandhar, where Jai Singh's 1665 siege forced Shivaji to terms. Teacher: Gherao = starve the enemy. Jai Singh 99-43 was a powerful Mansabdar of the Hindu group of the Mughal State. The standard books say Shivaji 74-80 never accepted Mughal sovereignty; the teacher's correction: the Treaty of Purandhar 1665 was a temporary tactic. Mnemonic: Shivaji 74-80's chain: Fort, Fight, Fangs; Surat, Siege, Sadhu; Crown, Close. 46-57-59 = Fort, Fight, Fangs; 63-65-66 = Surat, Siege, Sadhu; 74-80 = Crown, Close. Decode: 1646 first fort at 16; 1657 systematic attacks on Bijapur begin; 1659 Afzal Khan killed with Bagh Nakh (tiger claws) and Bichhwa; 1663 Shaista Khan 64-88 defeated and Surat sacked; 1665 Jai Singh 99-43 besieges Purandhar; 1666 Agra imprisonment and the Sadhu escape; 1674 coronation at Raigarh; 1680 natural death (Shivaji 74-80). Why it sticks: three triples of alliterating words, then the two ends of his reign. 1.4 Treaty of Purandhar 1665: a tactical pause, not a permanent defeat To prevent the massacre of his soldiers and people, Shivaji 74-80 negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1665). Under its terms: He surrendered 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals. He accepted Aurangzeb 58-07 as Emperor but declined a personal mansab for himself. His son Sambhaji 80-89 was made a Mughal Mansabdar with a rank of 5,000. He agreed to support the Mughals in their war against Bijapur. Mnemonic: Fat Elephants Squash Bananas. F-E-S-B: the four terms of the Treaty of Purandhar (1665). Decode: Forts (23 of 35 surrendered, so 12 kept); Emperor (Aurangzeb 58-07 accepted, but no personal mansab for Shivaji 74-80); Sambhaji 80-89 made a Mughal Mansabdar of 5,000; Bijapur (support the Mughals against it). Jai Singh 99-43 forced it by a gherao (starving siege). Why it sticks: "two-three of three-five" = 23 of 35. Teacher's ruling: a temporary tactic; 1665 bows, 1674 crowns (the coronation was its legal reversal). Treaties are named after the place where signed.  Treaty of Purandhar (1665) and Svarajya. Tactical pause: 23 of 35 forts surrendered; Aurangzeb accepted as emperor but no personal mansab; Sambhaji a Mansabdar of 5,000; help against Bijapur. Agra 1666: Shivaji and Sambhaji insulted and imprisoned; legendary escape disguised as Sadhus smeared in ash via Mathura. Svarajya 1674: coronated Chhatrapati at Raigarh, legally independent of the Mughals; kingdom Svarajya (own rule) covered the Marathi region; died naturally 1680. Teacher's ink: treaties are named after the place where signed; the coronation is a legal reversal of Purandhar; Jat kingdom, Svarajya and the Sikh state share the feature of mass participation. In 1666, Shivaji 74-80 and Sambhaji 80-89 visited the Mughal court at Agra. They were insulted and imprisoned. Their escape became legendary: disguised as Sadhus with bodies smeared in ash, they went to Mathura. Shivaji 74-80 left Sambhaji 80-89 there with a Brahmin family and took a long route back to his capital. Aurangzeb 58-07 marched to the Deccan in 1681, when his own son Prince Akbar 56-05 defected to Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89. Teacher: Treaties are named after the place where they were signed. The coronation = the legal reversal of the Treaty of Purandhar, giving a fully independent kingdom. Common feature of the Jat kingdom, Svarajya and the Sikh state: the result of people / mass participation (the Jat kingdom = the result of peasant revolts).
