Firepower: horse-mounted swivel guns pierced Maratha armour. Leadership and factionalism: Abdali and Najib coordinated well; Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight.  Why Abdali 47-72 won, Lecture 7 version with the teacher's ink. Alliance: Awadh felt encircled and joined the Islamic alliance; Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali in hope of greater political influence under an Afghan emperor (ethnicity = soft power); the Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral because of the Maratha plunders of the past; the Jats offered help to the Marathas, but the alliance failed over tactics (Surajmal wanted guerrilla war, Sadashiv Rao Bhau did not; the Jats still sent supplies); greater military: 60k versus 50k. Logistics (ink: TACTICS), Terrain (ink: TACTICS). Ink: plunders = attack, then loot (boxed) = Chauth, Sardeshmukhi; a sketch of Panipat and Delhi with the supply line cut.   #   Factor   Detail    --- --- ---    1   Strength of his alliance   Awadh felt strategically encircled by the Marathas (Chauth from Bihar and Bengal since 1751 in the east, control of Delhi in the west since 1752, Samrajya to the south) and, when the Marathas sought an alliance with Shuja, he chose the Islamic alliance. The Indian Afghan kingdoms of Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali hoping for greater influence under an Afghan emperor. Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral, a direct consequence of years of Maratha plundering and tribute extraction. 60,000 versus 50,000.     2   Logistics   Abdali cut the supply routes between the Maratha camp at Panipat and Delhi. Famine-like conditions: no food for men, no fodder for horses.     3   Terrain   Panipat's vast open plains gave no advantage to Maratha guerrilla tactics, which depended on hills, forests and narrow passes.     4   Firepower   Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce Maratha armour.     5   Military leadership   Abdali and Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 provided strong, coordinated command.     6   Maratha factionalism   Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight, being opposed to Nana Saheb as Peshwa. In 1765 the Peshwa even plundered Nagpur in retaliation. Bhonsle also did not take part in the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82).   Mnemonic: A Lion Tamer Found Lazy Fighters. A-L-T-F-L-F: the six reasons Abdali won. Decode: Alliance (Awadh encircled and joined; Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali; Sikhs, Rajputs, Jats neutral; 60,000 versus 50,000); Logistics (supply cut between Panipat and Delhi); Terrain (open plains, no hills for guerrilla tactics); Firepower (horse-mounted swivel guns, steadier and better aimed because attached to the seat); Leadership (Abdali and Najib-ud-Daula 57-70); Factionalism (Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight). Why it sticks: the teacher files Logistics and Terrain under TACTICS.  Horse-mounted swivel gun, Abdali's firepower: an engraving of a gun on an ornate saddle.  Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce Maratha armour (a man in a fur cap beside a kneeling camel with a swivel gun mounted on its saddle). Teacher's ink: better stability of the gun; better aiming because it is attached to the seat. Teacher: Why the mounted swivel gun was better: better stability of the gun and better aiming, because it is attached to the seat. Teacher: The alliance factor on the board: Jats offered help to the Marathas, but the alliance failed over tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla war; Sadashiv Rao Bhau did not; the Jats still sent supplies. Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad hoped for greater political influence under an Afghan emperor (ethnicity = soft power). On the Maratha plunder, the teacher's chain: plunder = attack, then loot = Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. Logistics and terrain both fall under TACTICS. 10.3 Impact of the defeat  Panipat 1761, the impact. Maratha losses: Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao died fighting; Nana Saheb 40-61 died within weeks; about 50,000 lost in all. Deeper crisis: factionalism deepened, a run of young or weak Peshwas (Madhav Rao 61-72, Narayan Rao 72-73, infant Madhav Rao II 74-95). Abdali too: heavy losses and a revolt at home; he took his loot but could not consolidate any presence in India. The real result: a power vacuum at the centre; NEITHER the Marathas nor Abdali would rule India; the EIC eventually filled it.  Panipat 1761, the impact, Lecture 7 version. Ink: weak military; arrow under Factionalism. Abdali also suffered: heavy losses plus a revolt at home (a coup attempt) by military commanders, in Afghanistan. The real result: a power vacuum at the centre; it decided that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would rule India; the EIC eventually filled the vacuum. Military losses: Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao died fighting. Nana Saheb had not fought (someone was needed to guard other frontiers in the south); he arrived with reinforcements when the battle was already lost and died within weeks. The Marathas lost 50,000 men in total, combatants and non-combatants. Factionalism deepened: young, inexperienced Peshwas followed one another: the young but brilliant Madhav Rao 61-72, then the incompetent Narayan Rao 72-73, then the infant Madhav Rao II 74-95. Abdali too paid a heavy price: serious losses and an anti-Abdali revolt among his own generals back in Afghanistan. He went home with his loot but could not consolidate any lasting presence in India. The deeper consequence: a power vacuum at the centre. Panipat did not decide who would rule India; it decided that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would. The vacuum was eventually filled by the British EIC, which defeated the regional Indian states one by one. Mnemonic: Two bulls fight, the shopkeeper takes the field. The Marathas and Abdali lock horns at Panipat; neither rules India; the EIC walks in. Decode: Panipat III did not decide who would rule India but that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would (power vacuum). Marathas lost Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao, Nana Saheb died within weeks, about 50,000 lost; Abdali had heavy losses and a revolt among his generals. Next Peshwas: Madhav Rao 61-72, Narayan Rao 72-73, infant Madhav Rao II 74-95. The vacuum was filled by the EIC. Why it sticks: both bulls lose, the shopkeeper gains.

items.t: 11 · After Panipat: decline with moments of strength (1761-1819, about 60 years)
items.x: After Panipat, decline with moments of strength: 1765 Marathas defeated Mysore and extracted tribute; 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad, Northern Sarkars ceded to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year plus protection against both Marathas and Mysore; 1771 Mahadji Scindia recaptured Delhi from the Rohillas; 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War, the Marathas defeated the EIC (its only loss of that period); 1782 Treaty of Salbai, a Maratha-EIC alliance; 1784 Mahadji Shinde hired Benoit de Boigne to raise the Fauj-i-Hind (the Campoo system); 1798 to 1803 Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance (1798) and the EIC took Delhi in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803); 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War, Svarajya annexed by the EIC.  The same table in Lecture 7 with extra notes: 1761-1819 = about 60 years. 1765 (Haider Ali 61-82 strong). 1771: since 1761 Delhi was under the Rohillas; ink: 1752-1803 (minus 1761-71) Delhi with the Marathas. 1782 Treaty of Salbai: a Maratha-EIC alliance that held until the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 (signed by Mahadji Scindhia; Salbai is near Gwalior). 1784: each Campoo was an integrated force having its own infantry, cavalry and artillery, thus self-sufficient units. 1803: EIC took Delhi from Scindhia in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 (sad face). 1817-19: 3rd Anglo-Maratha War, Svarajya annexed (sad face). 1765: the Marathas defeated Mysore and extracted tribute. 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: Hyderabad gave the Northern Sarkars to the EIC for an annual payment of seven lakh rupees and protection against both the Marathas and Mysore. The Northern Sarkars (Northern Circars) were initially four districts: Chicacole (Srikakulam), Rajmandri (Rajahmundry), Ellore (Eluru) and MustafaNagar (Kondapalli), with MurtuzaNagar (Guntur) added later as a fifth. Guntur was not transferred to the EIC in 1766. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans, who had taken it in 1761. 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War: the Marathas defeated the EIC, the only war in this period the EIC lost. 1782 Treaty of Salbai: a Maratha-EIC military alliance. 1784: Mahadji Shinde (Scindia) hired the French military adventurer Benoit de Boigne, who raised and trained the Fauj-i-Hind, also called the Campoo system (each Campoo was an integrated force with its own infantry, own cavalry, own artillery, thus self-sufficient units). It transformed the army from a traditional light-cavalry force into a modern, disciplined European-style infantry-cavalry-artillery machine (similar to Haider Ali 61-82's army (1761-82), also modernised with French help). Other Sardars followed: Holkar hired the Frenchman Dudrenec. 1795 Battle of Kharda: a Maratha victory over Hyderabad. The EIC stayed neutral as the Marathas were still its ally under Salbai 1782. The last battle between Hyderabad and the Marathas. 1798: Hyderabad became the first Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance (also called a subordinate alliance) with the EIC, securing guaranteed protection and ending its vulnerability to Maratha pressure. 1803: the EIC captured Delhi in the Second Anglo-Maratha War. 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War: Svarajya was annexed by the EIC, ending the last Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18's rule. Mnemonic: CREM, with Guntur on top later. Chicacole, Rajmandri, Ellore, MustafaNagar = C-R-E-M; Guntur (MurtuzaNagar) is added later. Decode: 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: the Northern Sarkars go to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year plus protection against the Marathas and Mysore; four districts at first (C-R-E-M); Guntur was not transferred in 1766. Why it sticks: four letters first, the fifth comes later. Mnemonic: After Panipat: a year-rhyme. '65 Mysore pays, '66 Sarkars sold, '71 Mahadji takes Delhi bold, '75 to '82 the EIC loses a war, '82 Salbai seals the score, '84 Campoo drills, '95 Kharda thrills, '98 Hyderabad signs the first Subsidiary line, '03 Delhi goes, '17-'19 Svarajya's last sign. Decode: 1765 Marathas defeat Mysore; 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad (Northern Sarkars); 1771 Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptures Delhi; 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War; 1782 Treaty of Salbai (Maratha-EIC alliance); 1784 de Boigne's Fauj-i-Hind (Campoo); 1795 Battle of Kharda (Marathas beat Hyderabad); 1798 Hyderabad first Subsidiary Alliance; 1803 EIC captures Delhi; 1817-19 Svarajya annexed. Why it sticks: rhyme pairs keep the order; read it out loud once. Mnemonic: Win, lose Delhi, lose all. The three Anglo-Maratha Wars: the Marathas win the first, the EIC takes Delhi in the second, the third ends Svarajya. Decode: First AMW 1775-82 (the only war of that period the EIC lost); Second AMW 1803-05 (EIC captured Delhi in 1803); Third AMW 1817-19 (Svarajya annexed, last Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18 ended). Why it sticks: W-L-L, one win then two losses. Flag on the length of the Salbai alliance. The handout says the Treaty of Salbai (1782) alliance held until 1795; the teacher's note on the Lecture 7 slide says it held until the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Both appear in the class material: the handout's 1795 is tied to the Battle of Kharda (the EIC staying neutral), the teacher's version marks the breakdown at the next Anglo-Maratha war.  Teacher's board: the Campoo system. Left: the Chhatrapati, the Peshwa with M1, M2, M3, M4 and Nana Fadnavis under the Peshwa. Later link: Risala system of Hyder Ali 61-82. King (Scindhia): multiple regiments and every regiment is like a mini army, self-sufficient, with its own transport, own infantry, own cavalry, own supplies, own weapons; all converge on Regiments. Speed (smiley); political stability: chances of a coup by a commander are down (yes). Note: today we are doing this again. Teacher: Campoo = "multiple regiments, and every regiment is like a mini army": self-sufficient, with its own transport, infantry, cavalry, supplies and weapons. Benefits: speed; political stability because the chances of a coup by a commander go down. Later link: the Risala system of Haider Ali 61-82. The teacher adds: "Today, we are doing this again" (the modern parallel to integrated, self-sufficient military units). Mnemonic: Campoo = a camp with everything: I-C-A. Own Infantry, own Cavalry, own Artillery: a mini-army in every regiment. Decode: 1784 Mahadji Shinde (Scindia) hired Benoit de Boigne to raise the Fauj-i-Hind (the Campoo system); each Campoo self-sufficient (own infantry, cavalry, artillery, transport, supplies, weapons); benefits: speed, and a lower chance of a coup by a commander; Holkar hired Dudrenec; later link: the Risala system of Haider Ali 61-82. Why it sticks: Campoo sounds like "camp": a self-contained camp. Mnemonic: Eight treaties: Pandit Wants Bananas, But Sings Beautiful Hindi Songs. P-W-B-B-S-B-H-S in year order. Decode: Purandhar 1665; Warna 1731; Bhopal 1738; Bassein 1739; Sangola 1750; Bhalke 1751; Hyderabad 1766; Salbai 1782. Treaties are named after the place where signed. Why it sticks: the years bunch as 31-38-39, then 50-51, then 66 and 82.

items.t: 12 · Why couldn't the Marathas establish all-India rule?
items.x: Why no all-India Maratha rule? Tribute not annexation; weak centre, strong Sardars; Treaty of Sangola 1750; even Svarajya not centralised (local assemblies of Vatan-holders pressured the Peshwa); much of Samrajya had no government machinery on the ground.  Why no all-India Maratha rule? (Mains). Ink: Admin on the ground, making and implementing of laws by the King (circled) = Centre (circled). Reasons: focused on tribute, not annexation; weak centre, strong Sardars (power never fully centralised in the Maratha Emperor); Treaty of Sangola 1750 (factionalism increased even more after 1761 as now weak Peshwas); even in Svarajya power was not 100% centralised (ink on local assemblies: Democratic spirit, smiley; Strong Centre, sad face); no effective Rule in the whole of Samrajya (much had no government machinery on the ground). Ink bottom right: Control tick, Rule X, not 100%. The Marathas came closer than any other power in the 18th century to an all-India empire, but the reasons they never crossed that threshold are structural: Tribute, not annexation. Often after a victory they limited themselves to Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rather than annexing and establishing direct rule. Extracting tribute is not ruling. Ruling means making and implementing policies through your own administration on the ground; for one central authority to rule effectively, power must be centralised: one country, one ruler, one law, rule of law. Weak centre, strong Sardars. The centre was never strong enough and factionalism weakened it further; the Sardars had always been autonomous. Shivaji 74-80 never gave Jagirs to his officers and Shahu 19-49 never gave Vatan Jagirs to military commanders, so ambitious Sardars seeking their own principalities ventured out on their own to build Samrajya. In territories brought under Maratha control through the Sardars' own efforts, the Chhatrapati's authority would naturally be weak. The Treaty of Sangola 1750. As power shifted down to the Peshwa, the Sardars felt even less constrained and factionalism grew; after 1761 a succession of weak Peshwas accelerated this. Power was not properly centralised even in Svarajya: local assemblies of Vatan right-holders (Deshmukhs and Patils) asserted themselves and pressured the Peshwa. In Samrajya, effective centralised rule did not exist at all in many areas: certain areas were under a Maratha Sardar militarily, but no effective government machinery was present on the ground. Teacher: "Rule" = administration on the ground: making and implementing laws by the King (= the Centre). Control, tick; Rule, cross: not 100%. Even in Svarajya the local assemblies of Vatan-holders show a "democratic spirit" (smiley) but not a "strong centre" (sad face). Mnemonic: The Wise Sardars Stayed Separate. T-W-S-S-S: why there was no all-India Maratha rule. Control tick, Rule cross. Decode: Tribute not annexation; Weak centre, strong Sardars; Sangola 1750; Svarajya itself not centralised (local assemblies of Vatan-holders); Samrajya had no government machinery on the ground in many areas. Why it sticks: the Marathas could collect (control) but not govern (rule): extracting tribute is not ruling. Mains 2014: why so many battles at Panipat?  Why so many battles at Panipat? (Mains 2014). The real reason: not the city but the GATEWAY to Delhi; any power from Central Asia or Afghanistan via the Khyber staged here before the final push, so Delhi rulers chose to stop the enemy at these gates. Practical factors: vast open fields for large armies; weather suited to long campaigns; many warrior communities eased recruitment; farm productivity and proximity to Delhi eased supply. The record: Thanesar (1014 and 1191); Panipat I (1526) and II (1556); Karnal (1739); Panipat III (1761).  The same table in Lecture 7 with ink: the gateway to Delhi (HQ or Capital) for armies marching from the north-west via the Khyber Pass; Delhi's rulers chose to fight the enemy here to keep the capital secure. Geographic factors: vast open fields, weather, many warrior communities, farm productivity and proximity to Delhi easing the supply of food, weapons and transport. Mains 2014: why have so many empire-shaking battles been fought near Panipat? The battles were not fought for the city of Panipat itself. The region is the gateway to Delhi. Any power advancing from Central Asia or Afghanistan had to come through the Khyber Pass, and the natural staging ground before the final push runs through the region of Panipat, Karnal, Kurukshetra and Thanesar. For a ruler in Delhi the sound move was to stop the enemy at these gates. Supporting factors: (1) vast open fields for set-piece battles; (2) weather supporting prolonged campaigns; (3) many warrior communities easing recruitment; (4) agricultural productivity plus proximity to Delhi easing supply. Mnemonic: The gate has a WWF crew. Not the town but the gateway to Delhi from the Khyber, helped by Weather, Warriors, Fields, Farms. Decode: gateway to Delhi for powers from Central Asia or Afghanistan via the Khyber Pass (Panipat, Karnal, Kurukshetra, Thanesar); supporting factors: weather for long campaigns, many warrior communities for recruitment, vast open fields, agricultural productivity plus proximity to Delhi for supply. Why it sticks: W-W-F-F, and "not the town, the gate". Thanesar twice, Panipat thrice, Karnal once. Decode: Thanesar 1014 (Mahmud of Ghazni), Thanesar 1191 (Muhammad Ghori), Panipat I 1526 (Delhi Sultanate shaken), Panipat II 1556 (Hemu's rule ended), Karnal 1739 (Mughals), Panipat III 1761 (Marathas). 2 + 3 + 1 = 6. Why it sticks: the pairs 1526/1556 and 1739/1761 share their first two digits (15 and 17).

items.t: 1 · The middle path between king and rebel
items.x: Teacher's board: in case of rebels establishing their rule in an area. Option 1: continue fighting and end the rebellion. Option 2: lose territory (T, circled) and the rebel establishes an independent kingdom. Mid path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar of the emperor, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute (Z) to Delhi, agrees to maintain an army and help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts: dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, non-interference in the rebel's rule. Teacher: When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor has two options: (1) continue fighting and end the rebellion; (2) lose the territory (T) and let the rebel establish an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar of the emperor, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute to Delhi, agrees to maintain an army / help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts: dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference in the rebel's rule. Mnemonic: The middle-path bargain: MAT and DoWN. The rebel lays the MAT; the emperor gives the DoWN pillow; both sleep in peace. Decode: Rebel gives = Mansabdar status (and accepts the Mughal as emperor), Army (maintains it, helps militarily), Tribute to Delhi. Emperor gives = Dynastic governorship, Watan Jagir, Non-interference. Why it sticks: MAT is what the rebel offers, DWN is what he gets back; the empire does not shrink.  Teacher's board: both sides' core interest is met. Emperor: the empire's territory shall not shrink, and revenue and military come from that territory. Rebel: king of that territory and wants dynastic rule in it.  The middle path, king and rebel. King: the rebel provides an army; the empire does not shrink. Rebel: opportunity as a Mansabdar at the centre (recall: successor states); dynastic governor status; the king accepts the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir. Footer: except for the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once in 1707), this pattern appears among the Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad, Mysore and Rajputs. Teacher's ink: ARTICLE 370 status (boxed); a tree of SS (successor states) to B, A, H (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad); RS (rebel states) to Ma, Ro, Fa (Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad); AAS (already autonomous states) to Rajput, Mysore; also Sikh [RS] and Travancore [AAS], not legally in the Mughal empire.   Side   What it gets on the middle path    --- ---    King (Mughal)   The rebel provides an army; the empire does not shrink     Rebel   Opportunity as a Mansabdar at the centre (recall successor states); dynastic governor status; the king accepts the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir   Teacher: Except for the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), this pattern appears among the Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad, Mysore and Rajputs. The teacher's ink ties this to Article 370 status (a state within a state on special terms) and sorts the regional powers: SS (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad); RS (Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad; plus the Sikhs); AAS (Rajputs, Mysore; plus Travancore). The Sikhs [RS] and Travancore [AAS] were not legally in the Mughal empire. Mnemonic: Sorting the regional powers: BAH! / Ma-Ro-Fa / Raj-My. Successors shout "BAH!"; Rebels chant "Ma-Ro-Fa"; the Autonomous never joined the club. Decode: SS = Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad (BAH). RS = Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad (plus the Sikhs). AAS = Rajputs and Mysore (plus Travancore). Why it sticks: the Sikhs (RS) and Travancore (AAS) are the two "not legally in the Mughal empire" odd ones; the Sikhs never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty, except once in 1707.

items.t: 2 · Framework: three more Rebel States
items.x: Framework, three more Rebel States. Apart from the Marathas the 18th century saw three more: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur (East Rajasthan, south of Delhi); Farrukhabad (est. 1714), the Bangash Pathans of central Uttar Pradesh; Rohilkhand (process began 1721, completed 1737-40), the Rohilla Afghans around Bareilly. All three turned local military power into territorial rule as the Mughal Empire weakened, yet none could build a large, sustainable empire. Ink: establishment years with an arrow to 1737-40. Apart from the Marathas, there were three more Rebel States in the 18th century: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, and the two Afghan kingdoms, Farrukhabad (est. 1714) and Rohilkhand (crystallised 1737-40). All three used the opportunity created by the weakening Mughal Empire to convert local military power into territorial rule, but none could establish a large, sustainable empire. Mnemonic: Three rebel states, three dates: 14, 21, 37-40. F comes before R, in the alphabet and in time: Farrukhabad first, Rohilkhand next. Decode: Farrukhabad = est. 1714 (Bangash Pathans). Rohilkhand = process began 1721, completed 1737-40 (Rohilla Afghans, around Bareilly). The third, the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, sits in East Rajasthan south of Delhi. Why it sticks: the numbers climb 14, 21, then 37-40, just like the alphabet F, R.

items.t: 3 · The Jat Kingdom (1695-1763)
items.x: The Jat Kingdom (1695-1763): the Jats an agrarian community hostile to the Mughals since Jahangir 1605-27; harsh land revenue and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed them into organised resistance under the Zamindars. Chain: Gokla (1669-70), Rajaram (1670-88), Churaman (1695-1721) Bharatpur, Badan Singh (1722-55) consolidates, Surajmal (1756-63) peak, 1763 onwards collapse. Teacher's ink: LR over land revenue; ending over local autonomy; imp with lines to Churaman and Surajmal (both underlined); under Churaman: est of Jat kingdom; under Surajmal: most powerful. 3.1 Who were the Jats and why did they resist? The Jats were primarily an agrarian community of North India, with cultivation as their traditional occupation. Their hostility to the Mughal State stretched back to the reign of Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue policies and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed the Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, toward organised resistance. 3.2 How the resistance developed The first organised Jat revolt came in 1669 (teacher's slide: 1669-70), led by the Zamindar Gokla. The torch passed through Rajaram 89-00 to Churaman 95-21, then Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), then Surajmal 56-63, each pushing resistance further. Their preferred method was guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised and hard for a large Mughal army to counter. The Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, in East Rajasthan, south of Delhi, bordering the Mathura and Agra districts, was formally established by Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721). Like many rebel-state founders (Marathas, Sikhs), Churaman 95-21 turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political and military power. Teacher: Note the two names marked imp: Churaman 95-21 = establishment of the Jat kingdom; Surajmal 56-63 = the most powerful. The hostility is about LR (high land revenue) and ending local autonomy. Mnemonic: The Jat chain: Great Rebels Created Bharatpur's Stronghold. G-R-C-B-S = Gokla, Rajaram 89-00, Churaman 95-21, Badan Singh, Surajmal 56-63. Decode: Gokla 1669-70 (first organised revolt) → Rajaram 89-00 (guerrilla warfare) → Churaman 95-21 (Created the kingdom, Bharatpur) → Badan Singh 1722-55 (Bridge, consolidates) → Surajmal 56-63 (Summit, most powerful). Hostility began with Jahangir 05-27 over LR and local autonomy. Why it sticks: only the two teacher-marked "imp" names carry a job word: C = Created, S = Summit.  Lohagarh Fort, Bharatpur: the Iron Fort, never conquered, even by the British, built by Maharaja Surajmal (1756-63). Aerial photograph of the moated fort with round bastions and a bridge. Mnemonic: Lohagarh = Loha + garh. Loha (iron) + garh (fort) = the Iron Fort, Surajmal 56-63's pride. Decode: Lohagarh Fort, Bharatpur, built by Maharaja Surajmal 56-63; never conquered, even by the British. Why it sticks: the name itself is the fact. 3.3 Surajmal 56-63: the peak  Surajmal's reign (1756-63), the peak. Status: built a strong, centralised State; forced the Mughal emperor to recognise him as an autonomous ruler. Reform 1: recruited European soldiers to modernise the military. Reform 2: introduced a Mughal-style revenue system. Reform 3: removed relatives from court posts to cut factionalism. Extent: from Delhi to Agra, from the Chambal to the Ganga (today's Delhi, Haryana, UP and Rajasthan). Panipat 1761: offered help to the Marathas but the alliance failed over tactics. Teacher's ink: Alamgir II 54-59 = puppet of the Marathas; status: the same thing was accepted during Churaman Jat; Reform 1: Mahadji Scindhia's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind; Reform 3: R vs R (royal family infighting). Under Maharaja Surajmal 56-63 the Jat State reached its peak. He built a strong, centralised State and forced the Mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (within the Mughal Empire). His reforms: He recruited European soldiers to modernise his military. He introduced a Mughal-style revenue system for administrative efficiency. He removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism. At its peak the Jat State stretched from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal River to the Ganga, across present-day Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. After Surajmal 56-63's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Panipat 1761: Surajmal 56-63 offered help to the Marathas before the Third Battle of Panipat, but the alliance could not be established because of differences on war strategy and tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla warfare, but the Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bhau disagreed. The Jats still sent essential supplies to the Marathas during the war. Mnemonic: Jats at Panipat 1761: "No to the plan, yes to the ration." Surajmal 56-63 said no to the plan, but his carts still rolled. Decode: alliance failed over war strategy; Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla warfare, Sadasiv Rao Bhau disagreed; the Jats still sent essential supplies. Contrast: Rohillas and Bangash joined Abdali, the Jats did not. Why it sticks: guerrilla (his plan) versus supplies (his help), two separate facts in one line. Mnemonic: Surajmal 56-63's three reforms: E-R-K. Surajmal 56-63 ran his State like an ERK: Europeans in, Revenue copied, Kin out. Decode: E = recruited European soldiers; R = Mughal-style revenue system; K = removed relatives (kin) from court posts to cut factionalism. Territory: Delhi to Agra, Chambal to Ganga (D-A, C-G). Why it sticks: Reform 1 matches Mahadji Scindia 68-94's Campoo (modern troops); Reform 3 is the contrast with R vs R infighting. Teacher: On the status row: "the same thing was accepted during Churaman 95-21 Jat" (recognition of an autonomous ruler within the Mughal Empire). On the Panipat row, the Maratha link: Alamgir II 54-59 was a puppet of the Marathas. On Reform 1: Mahadji Scindia 68-94's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind is the same kind of modernisation (see Chapter 4). On Reform 3: the Mughal family's infighting (R vs R) is the contrast.  Map: the Jat State at its peak (orange, Delhi in green). Labels include Hariana, Meerut, Delhi, Rewari, Nuh, Ballabhgarh, Narnaul, Alwar, Aligarh, Mathura, Bharatpur, Mahwa, Hindaun, Agra, Gohad, Jalaun, Kalpi, Mastura, Pichhore, Uchad, Datia, Samthar, Narwar, Mahoba. From Delhi to Agra, from the Chambal to the Ganga.  Handout Diagram 1: the Jat Kingdom. Gokla 1669-70 (first organised Jat revolt), Rajaram (1670-88, guerrilla continuation), Churaman (1695-1721, founds Bharatpur Kingdom), Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), Maharaja Surajmal 1756-63 (peak; reforms: European troops, Mughal-style revenue, kin removed from court), peak territory Delhi, Agra, Chambal, Ganga, then 1763 Surajmal dies and the State collapses: not a peasant utopia, the same extractive structure it rose against. 3.4 Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant?  Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant? No peasant utopia. Land revenue stayed high; real power rested with the Zamindars, not the ryots. Though born of peasant revolt, the Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against. After Surajmal's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Teacher's ink: Dreamland (arrow from No peasant utopia); underlines on land revenue, peasant revolt, same extractive structure. Though the kingdom was the result of peasant revolts, it was no peasant utopia. Land revenue remained high, and real power rested with Zamindars, not with the ryots. The Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against. Mnemonic: Jat State: peasant revolt, Zamindar rule. Born in the field, ruled from the haveli: "Kisan ki kranti, zamindar ka raj." Decode: result of peasant revolts, but no peasant utopia: land revenue stayed high, real power with Zamindars not ryots, same extractive structure it rose against; collapse after Surajmal 56-63 died in 1763. Why it sticks: the revolt and the rule have different owners.

items.t: 4 · The Afghans: migration and the rise of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: The Afghans and the rise of Sher Shah Suri. Afghans had migrated into North India since the 15th century (poor economy and instability at home), working its military labour markets as wandering warlords. Steps: the Sur clan migrates from the Sur region of Afghanistan in the Lodi period (late 15th c); a jagir at Sasaram granted to his grandfather under the Lodi Sultans (Bihar); Farid Khan rises, serves many masters including the Mughals after 1526 and studies their administration; 1540 Battle of Kanauj, defeats Humayun and seizes the throne of Delhi. Teacher's ink: a top timeline with 1540-55 SURIS; 1737-40 ROHILKHAND; 1748-61 ABDALI; FARUKHABAD 1714; family = Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate; (Bihar); SHER SHAH SURI with an arrow to Farid Khan; 30-40 under 1540 (Humayun 1530-40). 4.1 Who were the Afghans and what brought them to North India? Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economic conditions and political instability back home. In the military labour markets of North India they functioned largely as wandering warlords, skilled fighters available to whoever could pay. 4.2 Was there ever a moment when Afghans actually ruled Delhi? The story of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 is the story of all these Afghan migrants compressed into one life. His family, the Suris, a clan of the Pashtun tribe, had migrated from the Sur region of Afghanistan to India during the Lodi Sultanate in the late 15th century. His grandfather had received a small jagir in Sasaram (present-day Bihar) in service of the Lodi Sultans. Sher Shah 40-45, born Farid Khan around 1486 in Sasaram, grew up not in Afghanistan but in Bihar, as a second-generation Indian Afghan, a product of the North Indian military labour market. He served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth. He served as an administrator under the Afghan governor of Bihar, then briefly under the Mughals after Babur 26-30 defeated the Lodis in 1526. During this Mughal service he closely studied Mughal administrative methods, knowledge he later turned against them. He built his power base in Bihar and Bengal and by 1540 had defeated Humayun 30-40, first reign) at the Battle of Kanauj, driving him into exile in Persia and seizing the throne of Delhi. Handout comparison: compare Suri with the Bangash Pathans of Farrukhabad (same Afghan migrant background, same military-labour-market entry), but a very different ceiling on what they could achieve, partly because the political window available to them was much narrower. Mnemonic: Sher Shah 40-45's life in one climb: Sur to Sasaram to Sirhind. Farid from Sasaram ruled Delhi for five years (40 to 45); Humayun 30-40 returned at the double-five (55). Decode: Sur clan (Pashtun) migrates in the Lodi period → grandfather's jagir at Sasaram (Bihar) → Farid Khan born c.1486 → serves under Mughals after Babur 26-30 beats the Lodis in 1526 and studies their administration → 1540 Kanauj: beats Humayun 30-40, seizes Delhi → dies 1545 → Suri Interregnum 1540-55 → 1555 Sirhind, Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi (dies 1556). Why it sticks: S-S-S (Sur, Sasaram, Sirhind) bookends the story; 40, 45, 55 climb by 5 and 10. Mnemonic: Afghan markers on the board: S-F-R-A. Sher Found Rohilla Allies. Decode: Suris 1540-55 → Farrukhabad 1714 → Rohilkhand 1737-40 → Abdali 1748-61. Why it sticks: the order is also chronological; each letter is one Afghan marker on the teacher's board timeline. Teacher: The Suri family were Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate (Bihar). The Afghan markers on the board timeline: Suris 1540-55; Farrukhabad 1714; Rohilkhand 1737-40; Abdali 1748-61. 4.3 What Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 achieved in five years  Sher Shah Suri (1540-45), five years that mattered. Administrative hierarchy: Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana), a structure Akbar (56-05) later adopted almost wholesale. Grand Trunk Road: upgraded Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier (ink: ECO and TRADE smileys). Dak Chowki: a reliable postal-relay system (ink: like a relay race, with a sketch of dots in a line). The Rupiya: a standardised silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries (ink: imp, degree of TRUST between buyer and seller, standardisation needs a CENTRAL AUTHORITY). Revenue: land surveys and a fair demand fixed directly with the peasant (ink: in PATTA and QUBULIAT, HEAD and TAIL, one document in 2 copies; Patta with the RYOT, Qubuliat with the GOVT). After 1545: he dies, the Suri Interregnum (1540-55), Humayun retakes Delhi at the Battle of Sirhind (1555).   Reform   What he did   Teacher's note    --- --- ---    Administrative hierarchy   Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana)   Akbar 56-05 later adopted it almost wholesale     Grand Trunk Road   Upgraded the Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier   Boosts economy and trade     Dak Chowki   A reliable postal-relay system   "Like a relay race"     The Rupiya   A standardised (by weight and value) silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries   Important: the degree of trust between buyer and seller; standardisation needs a central authority     Revenue   Land surveys and a fair land revenue demand fixed directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman Zamindar   Recorded in a Patta (with the ryot) and a Qubuliat (with the government): "head and tail," one document in two copies   Mnemonic: Sher Shah 40-45's five reforms: SHE-R-R. Decode: S = Suba-Sarkar-Pargana hierarchy (Centre, Province, District, Sub-district; Akbar 56-05 adopted it); H = Highway, the Grand Trunk Road (upgraded Uttarapath, Bengal to North-West Frontier); E = Express relay post, Dak Chowki ("like a relay race"); R = Rupiya, standard silver coin (trust plus central authority); R = Revenue, surveys and fair demand direct with the peasant. Why it sticks: five letters, five reforms, and he had only five years (1540-45). Mnemonic: Patta and Qubuliat: head and tail. Flip the coin: Patta is the Peasant's page; the other tail belongs to the government. Decode: one document, two copies. Patta = with the ryot (P for Patta, P for Peasant); Qubuliat = with the government. Why it sticks: the teacher's own "head and tail" image plus one shared initial P. Handout: Suri was in a sense the first ruler to seriously attempt "administrative reform": streamlining the State machinery to make it efficient and fair. Unfortunately he had only five years. His successors could not hold together what he built. After his death in 1545 the Afghans fragmented again into competing warlord groups. The period 1540 to 1555, the Suri Interregnum, was a brief Afghan interruption of Mughal rule, ending when Humayun 30-40 recaptured Delhi in 1555 after the Battle of Sirhind and briefly restored Mughal authority before his death in 1556.  Map: Sher Shah Suri's empire (Encyclopaedia Britannica map Mughal Empire 1526-1707; the green line is the boundary of the Suri empire, running from Bengal across north India to the Indus and Sindh and south to Malwa). Teacher's ink: similar to the map of Babur 26-30; similar to the Delhi Sultanate (1208-1526). Legend: extent of the Mughal Empire in 1530; expansion to 1605; expansion to 1707; expansion into Babur's Afghan kingdom; boundary of the Suri empire; routes of Mughal expansion campaigns.  Sher Shah Suri's tomb, Sasaram (Bihar): the red-sandstone mausoleum of the five-year Afghan ruler of Delhi, a domed mausoleum in the middle of a lake.  Handout Diagram 2: Sher Shah Suri. 15th-century Sur clan migration, Sasaram jagir, Farid Khan (born about 1486, rises via the military labour market), 1540 defeats Humayun at Kanauj and seizes Delhi, Suba / Sarkar / Pargana hierarchy (Akbar inherits), Grand Trunk Road, Dak Chowki, standard Rupiya, peasant-direct revenue; 1545 dies, Suri Interregnum 1540-55, 1555 Humayun recaptures Delhi, dies 1556. Teacher: The Suri empire's extent is similar to Babur 26-30's (1526-30) and to the Delhi Sultanate (1208-1526).

items.t: 5 · The 18th century: a new surge of Afghan migration
items.x: The 18th century brought a new surge of Afghan migration as political instability in their homeland intensified. The progressive weakening of the Mughal State created exactly the opportunity these groups had been waiting for. Two Afghan kingdoms emerged: Farrukhabad (today a district in Uttar Pradesh; Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (also called Rampur, with capital Bareilly; Rohilla Afghans).  Map: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand. North India: Gadhwal, Kumaon, Mughals (green, Delhi area), Rampur (purple), Bangash (red), Oudh (large, peach), Bharatpur / Hindu Jats (yellow), Gohad, Karauli. The two Afghan kingdoms, Rohilkhand (Rampur) and the Farrukhabad belt, lie between Awadh and the Marathas. Teacher's ink: Delhi with a line to the green Mughal area; = Rohilkhand [1737-40] to Rampur (Rohilla Afghans); Farukhabad (1714) to Bangash (Bangash Pathans).  Teacher's board: Afghan kingdoms (within the Mughal Empire), with the ink ART 370 plus. Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans): 1714-1743 Md Khan Bangash (underlined); weak Mughal power = opportunity; factionalism, R vs R: Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother; Farrukhsiyar 13-19 killed Jahandar Shah. Third Battle of Panipat (1761): both supported Abdali. Awadh annexed both. Rohilkhand (Rohillas): 1721-1748 Ali Md Khan (underlined). Boxed 1737-1740: Marathas and Nadir Shah weaken the Mughal. Mughal interests: territory does not shrink, military and money. Rebels' interest: dynastic rule over some territory. Teacher: Afghan kingdoms within the Mughal Empire (Article 370-type status): Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans), 1714-43, Md Khan Bangash. Rohilkhand (Rohillas), 1721-48, Ali Md Khan, with 1737-40 boxed as the period when the Marathas and Nadir Shah weakened the Mughals. Mughal interests: territory does not shrink; military and money. Rebels' interest: dynastic rule over some territory. Factionalism (R vs R): Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother; Farrukhsiyar 13-19 killed Jahandar Shah 12-13. Both kingdoms supported Abdali at Panipat (1761); Awadh annexed both.

items.t: 6 · Farrukhabad (est. 1714)
items.x: 6.1 How did a Bangash Pathan warlord found a kingdom near Agra? The founding of Farrukhabad shows how factional Mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit. It was structurally weak from the start, sitting between powerful neighbours, principally Awadh, which preyed on it whenever it could. Its history is best understood as a sequence across three rulers.  Farrukhabad (est. 1714), three rulers. Md Khan Bangash (1714-43): a Pathan warlord who backed Farukhsiyar with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Qaim Khan (1743-49): in 1749 Safdar Jung, Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of Ahmed Shah Bahadur, engineered Qaim Khan's death; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan Bangash (1750-1802): retook it (1750); fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC finally annexed it in 1802; the Bangash Pathans later joined the 1857 Revolt. Teacher's ink: mansabdar over rank of Nawab; JAGIR linked to revenue near the Ganga; Mughal followed mid path; Safdar Jung 39-54; Ahmed Shah Bahadur 48-54; after this other mansabdars accused Safdar of misusing his position, so he was forced to resign, leading to the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire.   Ruler   What happened    --- ---    Md Khan Bangash (1714-43)   A Pathan warlord who backed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue assignments near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Died 1743, succeeded by his son Qaim Khan.     Qaim Khan (1743-49)   In 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 (Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of the emperor) engineered his death in battle; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered.     Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71   Retook it in 1750; driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas and Jats; fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC annexed it in 1802. The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated.   Mnemonic: Farrukhabad's three rulers: Makes, Quits, Avenges. Md Khan Makes it, Qaim Khan Quits (killed), Ahmad Khan Avenges. Decode: Md Khan Bangash 1714-43 makes Farrukhabad (12,000 troops for Farrukhsiyar 13-19, rank of Nawab, revenue near the Ganga) → Qaim Khan 1743-49 quits: 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 engineers his death, Farrukhabad annexed to Awadh and plundered → Ahmad Khan retakes it in 1750. Why it sticks: M-Q-A also runs in time order, with the dates 14, 43, 49, 50. Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19: the handout (section 4.2) says that in 1712-13 Jahandar Shah 12-13 seized power by killing the father of Farrukhsiyar 13-19, and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 avenged this by removing Jahandar Shah 12-13; the teacher's board says Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother. Both are in the class material; the point for answers is Mughal succession violence (R vs R). Mnemonic: J then F: the killer was killed. Jahandar Shah 12-13 struck first, Farrukhsiyar 13-19 struck back; J before F, like the alphabet. Decode: Jahandar Shah 12-13 seized power by killing a relative (the teacher's board: his brother; the handout: Farrukhsiyar 13-19's father); Farrukhsiyar 13-19 then removed Jahandar Shah 12-13. Following the chapter's own ruling, both versions are in the class material; what to write is Mughal succession violence (R vs R). Why it sticks: remember the pattern "killer, then killed", not the victim's relationship. Md Khan Bangash's gesture (handout): he first founded a town called Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Farrukhabad ("the city of Farrukh") was the diplomatic correction: the classic pattern of a rebel State acknowledging Mughal sovereignty in name while building real autonomy on the ground. Mnemonic: Mohammad-abad (me-town) became Farrukh-abad (your-town). "My town" annoyed the king; "Your town" calmed him. Decode: Md Khan Bangash first founded Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed Farrukhsiyar 13-19; Farrukhabad ("city of Farrukh") was the diplomatic correction: sovereignty in name, autonomy on the ground. Why it sticks: one word swap, the name tells the politics. Teacher: Reading the rows: Nawab = a mansabdar rank; the revenue near the Ganga = a Jagir; the Mughal followed the "mid path." After Safdar Jung 39-54's misuse of the Wazir's post, other Mansabdars accused him of misusing his position and he was forced to resign, which was the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire (see Chapter 3). Qaim Khan (handout): the textbook example of the Wazir's loyalty being to his own State, not the Emperor he nominally served; the highest Mughal Mansab had become a tool for personal and regional ambition. 6.2 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750 onwards Ahmad Khan fought back and retook Farrukhabad in 1750. In 1751-52 the Marathas, specifically Malhar Rao Holkar and Jayappaji Rao Scindia sent by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao 40-61, along with Jats under Surajmal 56-63, drove him out. (Note: Awadh had requested the Marathas and Jats in 1751.) As Abdali's invasion progressed, the Marathas signed a treaty in 1752 that allowed him to return and resume rule, at the price of handing half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat. With the Marathas defeated, he recovered his full dominions, including the half ceded in 1752. Once Abdali left India in 1761, Farrukhabad weakened. In 1802 the EIC annexed Farrukhabad. (The "Ceded Provinces" refers to territories Awadh was forced to hand over under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1801; Farrukhabad was merged into the Ceded Provinces after annexation.) The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Mnemonic: Ahmad Khan's see-saw: Win, Lose, Deal, Win, Lose. W-L-D-W-L: five beats, five dates. Decode: 1750 Win (retakes Farrukhabad) → 1751-52 Lose (Marathas under Holkar and Scindia plus Jats under Surajmal 56-63, at Awadh's request) → 1752 Deal (treaty: returns, half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia) → 1761 Win (fights beside Abdali 47-72 at Panipat, recovers full dominions) → 1802 Lose (EIC annexes). Chapter's ruling: the short code for him is inconsistent (50-71 or 50-82), so anchor on 1750 and 1802. Why it sticks: the story alternates, so you cannot lose track of the turn. Flag on Ahmad Khan's dates: the handout's heading reads "Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750-1802", and in the Panipat line-up (Chapter 4) it writes Ahmad Khan 50-82. The slide table reads 1750-1802. The class material is not consistent about the short form (50-71 or 50-82), so remember the anchor dates: retook Farrukhabad 1750; EIC annexed it 1802.

items.t: 7 · Rohilkhand (est. 1737-40)
items.x: Rohilkhand (est. 1737-40), the story. Zamindars of Katehr (Bareilly, Moradabad) hire Afghan mercenaries, the Rohillas, who grow dominant under Daud Khan (ink: UP circled over Katehr). 1721: Ali Md Khan takes over on Daud Khan's death and spends two decades consolidating. 1739: the trigger, Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi; Ali Md Khan stops paying taxes and rules Katehr independently. 1740: co-opted, Emperor Md Shah (19-48) grants him the Subadar title (a Mansabdar); Katehr is renamed Rohilkhand (ink: via mid path). 1761-71: Najib-ud-Daula backs Abdali at Panipat; Delhi falls under Rohilla influence. 1771-74: the end, Mahadji Scindia retakes Delhi (1771); most of Rohilkhand annexed by Awadh with EIC help in 1774 (military alliance since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765); the small remainder became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, under Awadh legally and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance. 7.1 How Afghan mercenaries became rulers The region that became Rohilkhand was originally called Katehr: western Uttar Pradesh, around Bareilly and Moradabad. In the 17th and early 18th century, as Mughal authority weakened, local Zamindars and regional governors in Katehr hired Afghan mercenaries to settle disputes and enforce authority. These Afghan fighters, called Rohillas, became a dominant armed presence. Note: Rohilkhand was formed by settled Afghan mercenaries consolidating power from within the region, already entrenched in Katehr long before Abdali entered India. The word "Rohilla" comes from "Roh," the Afghan homeland, so Rohilkhand means the land of the Rohillas. Mnemonic: Katehr to Rohilkhand: Roh, Rohilla, Rohil-khand. Roh is home; Rohilla is the man from Roh; Rohilkhand is his khand (land). Decode: Roh = the Afghan homeland; Rohillas = the hired Afghan mercenaries of Katehr (around Bareilly and Moradabad, western UP); Katehr was renamed Rohilkhand in 1740. Why it sticks: the word builds itself: Roh + illa + khand. 7.2 1721: the starting point When Daud Khan, the Afghan commander who had consolidated the mercenary groups, died in 1721, his adopted son and protege Ali Md Khan (1721-48) took over leadership. This is the starting point, not yet an independent State, but the moment one man gained control of a significant armed force. After 1721 he moved methodically: for two decades he consolidated, slowly absorbing lands from the very Zamindars his men had been hired to protect and uniting the scattered Afghan groups under his sole command. 7.3 What finally pushed Ali Md Khan to declare independence? Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi in 1739. With the Mughal State paralysed, Ali Md Khan stopped paying taxes to Delhi and began ruling Katehr as an independent power, capturing key districts including Bareilly and Moradabad. Handout comparison with Farrukhabad: both Afghan kingdoms used the same window (Mughal paralysis) to convert military presence into territorial control. Md Khan Bangash did it earlier and more formally through Mughal court politics; Ali Md Khan did it through slow ground-level consolidation followed by outright defiance during the 1739 crisis. 7.4 How the Mughals responded Too weak to crush him, the Mughal State fell back on its standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat. In 1740 Emperor Md Shah (1719-48) formally granted Ali Md Khan the title of Subadar. From 1740 Katehr was officially renamed Rohilkhand and functioned as an autonomous State under nominal Mughal sovereignty. (Ali Md Khan took control in 1721 but was officially recognised as Nawab of Rohilkhand by the Mughals in 1740.) The title gave the rebel legitimacy; it gave the Mughals the illusion of control. Both sides understood the fiction. Mnemonic: Ali Md Khan's three A's: Absorb, Absent, Appointed. 21, 39, 40: Absorb the land, go Absent from Delhi's treasury, get Appointed by the emperor. Decode: Absorb = 1721, after Daud Khan's death his adopted son takes over and spends two decades absorbing lands from the Zamindars; Absent = 1739, Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, so he stops paying taxes; Appointed = 1740, Emperor Md Shah (19-48) grants the Subadar title, Katehr renamed Rohilkhand. Why it sticks: the Mughals' rule was "co-opt what you cannot defeat": the title came only after the defiance. 7.5 How Rohilkhand ended The arc is the same as Farrukhabad: rise on Afghan military power, peak during the Abdali alliance, collapse once that external prop was removed. 1761: under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, Rohilkhand actively supported Abdali at the Third Battle of Panipat. 1761-71: Delhi was effectively under Rohilla influence (the Mughal emperor was in Awadh). 1770: Najib dies; with no Abdali to support since 1761, Rohilkhand weakens. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi and allowed Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 to return home (the Red Fort). 1774: Most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help, because of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which led to a military alliance. The rest, a small part, became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, legally under Awadh, and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance. Mnemonic: Najib-ud-Daula 57-70's slide: 61, 70, 71, 74. Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 backed Abdali 47-72 (61), died (70), Delhi slipped (71), Rohilkhand fell (74), but Rampur survived. Decode: 1761 Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 backs Abdali at Panipat; 1761-71 Delhi under Rohilla influence → 1770 Najib dies → 1771 Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes Delhi, Shah Alam II 60-06 returns → 1774 Awadh plus EIC annex most of Rohilkhand (Treaty of Allahabad 1765 made them allies); the remainder is Rampur (capital Bareilly), under the EIC from 1801. Why it sticks: 70 and 71 are neighbours, then 74 closes the book, with the 1765 treaty as the old pact behind it.  Handout Diagram 3: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand combined. 1714 Md Khan Bangash founds Farrukhabad (Farukhsiyar's backing, Nawab and jagir); Rohilkhand: Afghan mercenaries in Katehr, 1721 Ali Md Khan consolidates; 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, Ali Md Khan declares independence, 1740 Md Shah grants the Nawab title; 1749 Safdar Jung (Awadh Nawab and Wazir) kills Qaim Khan, annexes Farrukhabad; 1752 Marathas (Holkar and Scindia plus Jats) restore Ahmad Khan for half of Farrukhabad; 1761 Panipat, both back Abdali (Ahmad Khan Bangash, Rohilla Najib-ud-Daula); 1761-71 Delhi under Rohilla influence; 1771 Mahadji Scindia retakes Delhi; 1774 Awadh plus EIC (Treaty of Allahabad 1765) annex Rohilkhand, leaving Rampur; 1802 EIC annexes Farrukhabad.

items.t: 8 · Why Abdali came: the immediate trigger
items.x: Why Abdali came, the immediate trigger: to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. March 1758: Raghunath Rao crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir). The Marathas then made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year; on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge. Sabaji Scindia held the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border and defended them fiercely. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was a direct challenge Abdali could not ignore. Teacher's ink: link, practice of auctioning of office, e.g. governorship (read last class); Tribute under Rs 75 lakh a year; famous: ATTOCK se CUTTACK (Orissa); Adina Beg Khan underlined. Prelims 2010. Abdali's immediate reason for the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was to avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. In March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir); the Marathas appointed Adina Beg Khan as Governor of Punjab for an annual tribute of Rs 75 lakh, and on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge. Sabaji Scindia commanded the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar (on the Afghan border) and fiercely defended them against Abdali. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was a direct challenge Abdali could not ignore: that was the immediate trigger. Mnemonic: Prelims 2010: Abdali 47-72 came for his son. Not tribute, not safe passage, not Maratha size: it was the Timur Tears of March 1758. Decode: Raghunath Rao 73-74 drove Timur Shah (Abdali's son, Governor of Punjab and Kashmir) out of Lahore in March 1758; options (b) Maratha expansion, (c) tribute refusal and (d) safe passage are all wrong; answer (a), the expulsion. Why it sticks: the trap options are about politics, the real reason is about a family member. Teacher: Link to the previous lecture: the practice of auctioning an office (e.g. a governorship) is what the Marathas did with Punjab (Adina Beg Khan paid Rs 75 lakh a year as tribute). The famous phrase marking Maratha reach: "Attock se Cuttack" (Orissa). Mnemonic: Punjab under the Marathas: Adina pays, Sabaji guards. A before S: Adina Beg buys the chair, Sabaji stands at the gate. Decode: Adina Beg Khan = Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year (the auctioned office); on his death Sabaji Scindia = in charge, with garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border. "Attock se Cuttack" = Maratha reach (Cuttack = Orissa). Why it sticks: 75 lakh to buy the post; Attock is the western end of the phrase.  Prelims 2010 question slide: What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali to invade India and fight the 3rd Battle of Panipat? (a) To avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore; (b) The fast expansion of the Maratha Empire across the subcontinent; (c) Refusal of the Mughal Emperor to pay annual tribute; (d) Refusal of the Sultan of Punjab to grant safe passage.  Prelims 2010, why. Why (a) is correct: in March 1758 the Marathas drove Abdali's son Timur Shah out of Lahore, the immediate, personal reason that brought Abdali back to India. Why not the others: (b) Maratha expansion was general background, not the immediate trigger; (c) no Mughal tribute dispute caused this invasion; (d) there was no Sultan of Punjab refusing safe passage.

items.t: 9 · Synthesis: three Rebel States, one pattern
items.x: Synthesis, three Rebel States, one pattern. The Jats: from an agrarian base upward, Zamindar-led revolt, territory, a reforming ruler (Surajmal). Farrukhabad: from Mughal court politics downward, 12,000 troops for Farukhsiyar, a Nawab title, a city, a dynasty. Rohilkhand: from the ground up over two decades, hired mercenaries, consolidation, independence in the 1739 Delhi paralysis. The common rule: each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghans, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal) and each collapsed once that support was removed.   State   How it was built    --- ---    The Jats   From an agrarian base upward: Zamindar-led revolt, then territory, then a reforming ruler (Surajmal 56-63)     Farrukhabad   From Mughal court politics downward: 12,000 troops for Farrukhsiyar 13-19, then a Nawab title, then a city, then a dynasty     Rohilkhand   From the ground up over two decades: hired mercenaries, then consolidation, then independence in the 1739 Delhi paralysis     The common rule   Each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63), and each collapsed once that support was removed   Mnemonic: Three states, three directions, one prop. Jats come Up from the soil, Farrukhabad comes Down from the court, Rohilkhand grows from the Roots; all stand on a prop. Decode: Jats = agrarian base upward (Surajmal 56-63); Farrukhabad = Mughal court politics downward (12,000 troops, Nawab title); Rohilkhand = ground up over two decades (mercenaries, 1739). Prop = Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63; remove it and each collapses (1761 Abdali leaves; 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies). Why it sticks: Up, Down, Roots, then "remove the prop, roof falls".

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The Rebel States, one story from soil to Panipat. A rebel lays the MAT, the emperor gives the DoWN: that is the middle path. Soil first: Gokla, Rajaram 89-00, Churaman 95-21 founds Bharatpur, Surajmal 56-63 reaches the summit and dies in 1763. Then the Afghans: Sher Shah 40-45 beats Humayun 30-40 at Kanauj (1540), Humayun 30-40 returns at Sirhind (1555). Court next: Md Khan Makes Farrukhabad (1714), Qaim Quits (1749), Ahmad Avenges (1750); EIC ends it in 1802. Ground-up: Ali Absorbs (1721), goes Absent (1739), is Appointed (1740); Rohilkhand falls in 1774, Rampur remains. Finally the Marathas expel Timur Shah in March 1758, Abdali 47-72 comes for his son, and the props fall away. Decode: MAT/DoWN = the bargain; Jat chain G-R-C-B-S; SHE-R-R reforms; M-Q-A rulers; A-A-A Ali; Timur = trigger for Panipat 1761. Why it sticks: one walk from soil (Jats) to court (Farrukhabad) to ground (Rohilkhand) to Abdali 47-72. Opportunity: the Mughal Empire weakens, factional court politics or paralysis (1739) creates a vacuum Local military power: peasant Zamindars (Jats), Afghan mercenaries (Rohillas), a warlord with troops (Bangash) The middle path: accept Mansabdar status, Mughal sovereignty in name, tribute and troops; get dynastic governorship and a Watan Jagir (warn) Dependence: each needed external support to peak (Abdali; Maratha tactical backing) (bad) Collapse: support removed (1761 Abdali leaves; 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies), neighbours annex (Awadh, then the EIC)   Feature   Jats (Bharatpur)   Farrukhabad   Rohilkhand    --- --- --- ---    Founder and year   Churaman 95-21, 1695   Md Khan Bangash, 1714   Ali Md Khan, 1721 (recognised 1740)     Base   Agrarian Zamindars, peasant discontent over LR   Pathan warlord with 12,000 troops, court politics   Afghan mercenaries hired in Katehr     Peak   Surajmal 56-63, 1756-63   Ahmad Khan with Abdali, 1761   Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, 1761-71 (Delhi influence)     Collapse   1763, Surajmal 56-63 dies   1749 annexed by Awadh; 1802 EIC   1774 Awadh plus EIC; Rampur remains

items.t: 1 · How did Sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?
items.x: How did Sikhism begin and what were its core beliefs? Founder: Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Rise: Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on 4 core principles: one supreme and formless God; direct access to God without rituals or priests; rejection of the caste system; emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Udasis: 4 major spiritual journeys over 30 years, about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. Kartarpur: he finally settled there (present-day Pakistan). Langar: there he established the institution of Langar, a free communal kitchen designed to promote equality. Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539) was a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on four core principles: One supreme and formless God. Direct access to God without rituals or priests. Rejection of the caste system. Emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Guru Nanak undertook four major spiritual journeys (Udasis) over 30 years, covering about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. He finally settled in Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan), where he established the Langar, the free communal kitchen designed to promote equality. Mnemonic: Nanak's four principles: ODRH, "One Direct Road Home". Walk One Direct Road Home. Decode: One supreme formless God; Direct access to God without rituals or priests; Rejection of the caste system; Honest living and selfless service. Founder Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), contemporary of Babur 26-30; rose from 1500 onwards. Why it sticks: the road image gives the order of the four ideas. Mnemonic: Udasis: the three-zero pair. 4 journeys, 30 years, 30,000 km: "four trips, thirty twice." Decode: 4 Udasis; 30 years; about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. Ending: settled at Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan) and set up the Langar, the free communal kitchen for equality. Why it sticks: 30 and 30,000 are the same digits, so you only memorise one number plus the 4.

items.t: 2 · When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State?
items.x: When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State? No conflict at first, but as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba, an area under Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies), religious and political tensions began. 1606, first flashpoint: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, executed by Jahangir 05-27; a turning point, a peaceful spiritual movement began transforming into a martial community. 1675, second flashpoint: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07. Initially there was no conflict. But as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba), an area under the Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies, religious and political tensions built up. First flashpoint, 1606: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, was executed by Jahangir 05-27. A turning point: a peaceful spiritual movement began its transformation into a martial community. Second flashpoint, 1675: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07. Mnemonic: Two flashpoints: 5th in 06, 9th in 75. Five-oh-six, nine-seven-five: Jahangir 05-27's Guru is the 5th, Aurangzeb 58-07's Guru is the 9th. Decode: 1606, 5th Guru Arjan Dev executed by Jahangir 05-27 (first flashpoint; a peaceful movement turns martial). 1675, 9th Guru Teg Bahadur executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07 (second flashpoint). Why it sticks: the Guru's number matches the order of the rulers, early ruler with the earlier Guru. Mnemonic: Anandpur: W of Shimla, S of Chamba. W-Shimla, S-Chamba: the compass letter comes before the town. Decode: Anandpur lies west of Shimla and south of Chamba, in the Shivalik foothills, an area under Shivalik hill chiefs who were Mughal allies; the Sikh demand for a State here started the tension. Why it sticks: "W then S" is the order of the two clues in the sentence.

items.t: 3 · The Khalsa (1699)
items.x: What was the Khalsa and why was it created? When and where: in 1699, in Anandpur. Founder: the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08. What it was: a Sikh military organisation (something like an NSG or STF; its creation marked the formal militarisation of the Sikh community's political ambitions). Why created: to defend the Sikh Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. In 1699, at Anandpur, the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, established the Khalsa, a Sikh military organisation created to defend the Sikh Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. The handout compares it to an NSG/STF: its creation marked the formal militarisation of the Sikh community's political ambitions. Mnemonic: Guru numbers 5, 9, 10 = years 06, 75, 99. Fifth in 1606, ninth in 1675, tenth in 1699: "6, 75, 99." Decode: 5th Guru Arjan Dev, 1606, executed by Jahangir 05-27; 9th Guru Teg Bahadur, 1675, executed by Aurangzeb 58-07; 10th Guru Gobind Singh 76-08, 1699, founds the Khalsa at Anandpur (a military body like NSG/STF, to defend the Panth and struggle for a Sikh State). Why it sticks: the last two digits rise 06, 75, 99; the 10th Guru answers the two executions with an army.

items.t: 4 · December 1704 to October 1708: the Sahibzadas and the Guru's death
items.x: December 1704 to October 1708: Sahibzadas and the Guru's death. Dec 1704, Battle of Chamkaur: the Guru's 2 elder sons, Sahibzada Ajit Singh (aged 18) and Sahibzada Jujhar Singh (aged 14), died in battle. The same month his 2 younger sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh (aged 9) and Sahibzada Fateh Singh (aged 6), were buried alive in a wall on Wazir Khan's orders. 1707: the new emperor Bahadur Shah 07-12, following a pacifist policy (diplomacy more than war), granted the Guru a high Mansab and promised a Sikh State in and around Anandpur, but the promise was never fulfilled. Oct 7, 1708: Wazir Khan sent assassins to attack the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara, Nanded, Maharashtra, where he had accompanied Bahadur Shah. The Guru killed the assassins but later succumbed to his injuries, dying at age 42. No action was taken against Wazir Khan; Anandpur was never given to the Sikhs. Faujdar: district military commander, comparable to a Superintendent of Police today; Wazir Khan was the Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind. Since 2022, 26 December is observed as Veer Bal Divas in memory of the younger Sahibzadas. The same month his two younger sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh (aged 9) and Sahibzada Fateh Singh (aged 6), were buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, the Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind. (A Faujdar = a district military commander, comparable in local authority to a Superintendent of Police today. Since 2022, 26 December is observed as Veer Bal Divas in memory of the younger Sahibzadas.) 1707: the new emperor Bahadur Shah (1707-12), following the pacifist policy (diplomacy more than war), granted the Guru a high Mansab and promised a Sikh State in and around Anandpur. The promise was never fulfilled. 7 October 1708: Wazir Khan arranged assassins to attack the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara in Nanded, Maharashtra, where he had accompanied Bahadur Shah. The Guru killed the assassins himself but later succumbed to his injuries, dying at the age of 42. No action was taken against Wazir Khan; Anandpur was never given to the Sikhs. Mnemonic: Four Sahibzadas: AJ fought, ZF fell. Ages fall 18, 14, 9, 6 as the names go A, J, Z, F. Decode: Dec 1704, Battle of Chamkaur: Ajit Singh (18) and Jujhar Singh (14) died in battle. Same month Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (6) were buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind (a Faujdar is like a Superintendent of Police). 26 December = Veer Bal Divas since 2022. Teacher's board: 1707, Aurangzeb 58-07 dies, leading to the Mughal pacifist policy of 1707 (better relations with rivals). Implementation: Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 given a very high Mansab [Zat] (plus); Anandpur promised [Art 370 like, e.g. Rohilkhand, Jats, Farrukhabad, Ma under Shahu 19-49, Mysore, Rajputs]. 1708: in Nanded [MH] Guru Gobind Singh killed by men sent by Wazir Khan [Faujdar of Sirhind]. Right: responsible for the death of the 4 sons of GGS 76-08; Wazir Khan not punished by the Mughals; Anandpur not given. Teacher: 1707: Aurangzeb 58-07 dies, and the Mughal pacifist policy follows: "better relations with rivals." Implementation for the Guru: a very high Mansab [Zat] and Anandpur promised (an Article 370-like status, like Rohilkhand, Jats, Farrukhabad, the Marathas under Shahu 19-49, Mysore, Rajputs). 1708: in Nanded the Guru is killed by men sent by Wazir Khan [Faujdar of Sirhind], who was also responsible for the death of the Guru's four sons.
