Wazir Khan is not punished; Anandpur is not given. Why it sticks: P-P-P: Promise, Plot, Pledge broken, one letter, one year each.

items.t: 5 · Why the Guru declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru
items.x: Why did Guru Gobind Singh declare the Guru Granth Sahib Ji the final Guru? Declaration: a few days before his death, at Abchal Nagar Sahib, he would be the last living Guru and all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the holy book he had compiled. Why, deliberate: to prevent tensions between the Jat community, which dominated the Khalsa, and the Khatri community of traders, to which all 10 Gurus belonged; vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor permanently closed the question of community dominance. Installed at: the Akal Takht, in the Golden Temple complex, Amritsar. Akal Takht: from here the Gurus issued Hukumnamas (formal orders) and Sikh warriors took blessings before battle against the Mughals. Later exception: the 19th-century sects of Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru, which historically led to serious conflicts within the community.  Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and the Akal Takht, Amritsar: the spiritual and temporal seats of the Sikh community. The gilded shrine in the sarovar (pool) with white buildings behind. A few days before his death, at Abchal Nagar Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 declared that he would be the last living Guru and that all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the holy book he had compiled. The decision was deliberate: to prevent community tensions between the Jat community, which dominated the Khalsa, and the Khatri community of traders, to which all ten Gurus had belonged. By vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor, the question of community dominance was permanently closed. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji was installed at the Akal Takht in the Golden Temple complex, Amritsar. From the Akal Takht the Gurus issued Hukumnamas (formal orders) and Sikh warriors took blessings before going into battle against the Mughals. The 19th-century sects of Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru, which has historically led to serious conflicts within the community. Mnemonic: Jat = Jang, Khatri = Khazana: why the Book became Guru. Jats fought, Khatris funded; the Gurus were Khatris, so the Guru gave the crown to a Book. Decode: Jats dominated the Khalsa (the army); Khatris were traders and moneylenders, and all ten Gurus were Khatris. Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 vested authority in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji (installed at the Akal Takht, where Hukumnamas were issued) to end the rivalry for good. Exception: 19th-century Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru. Why it sticks: J-J (Jat, Jang) versus K-K (Khatri, Khazana); a Book cannot be a Jat or a Khatri.  Teacher's board: Guru Gobind Singh declared himself the last Guru and all (spiritual) authority was vested in the Guru Granth Sahib (two parts: the Holy Book; the Guru itself). Disrespect = Beadbi (very sensitive today also). To prevent disputes or factionalism between Khatris and Jats: Jats dominated the Khalsa; Khatris = men of Z (merchants, Z lenders, ijaradars) [JS 1213 introduced in Punjab, Bengal]; the Gurus were from the Khatri community. Banda Bahadur 08-15: set up a small state in and around Patiala; took revenge, executing Wazir Khan. Teacher: The Guru Granth Sahib has two aspects: the Holy Book and the Guru itself. Disrespect = Beadbi (very sensitive today also). Jats dominated the Khalsa; Khatris were the men of money (merchants, moneylenders, ijaradars) ([*Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal]); all the Gurus were Khatris. The teacher's ink places Banda Bahadur 08-15's small state "in and around Patiala", which takes revenge by executing Wazir Khan.  Handout Diagram 1: the Sikh Guruship lineage. Guru Nanak (1469-1539, formless God, anti-caste, Langar at Kartarpur); 1606 the 5th Guru Arjan Dev executed by Jahangir (1st flashpoint); 1675 the 9th Guru Teg Bahadur executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb (2nd flashpoint); 1699 the 10th Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa at Anandpur (armed body for a Sikh State); Dec 1704 Battle of Chamkaur (2 elder sons die), 2 younger Sahibzadas buried alive by Wazir Khan, Faujdar of Sirhind; 7 Oct 1708 the Guru dies at Nanded, the day before declaring the Guru Granth Sahib Ji the final Guru (ends the Jat-Khatri rift); then Banda Bahadur's State (Ravi to Jamuna) 1708-15, the Misl Confederacy 1715-1801 (12 Misls, Dal Khalsa), and Ranjit Singh unifying the Misls and being coronated in 1801, Sikh State peaking 1801-39.

items.t: 6 · Banda Bahadur 08-15: the first Sikh State, and why it collapsed
items.x: How did Banda Bahadur 08-15 establish the first Sikh State? From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur. May 10, 1710, the Battle of Chappar Chiri: he defeated and killed Wazir Khan, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. The 1st Sikh State was established between the Ravi and the Jamuna, with its own coins, officials and seal (ink: full independence). Mughal response: Farukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress the Sikh State. 1715: defeated as the economic and military support base eroded; Banda Bahadur was captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farukhsiyar. From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur 08-15. He defeated and killed Wazir Khan at the Battle of Chappar Chiri on 10 May 1710, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. He established a Sikh State over territories between the River Ravi and the River Jamuna, with its own coins, its own officials and its own seal for administrative orders (the teacher's ink: full independence). Farrukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress this Sikh State. By 1715 Banda Bahadur 08-15 was defeated; captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Mnemonic: Banda Bahadur 08-15's State: Ravi to Jamuna, COS. Banda Bahadur 08-15's State kept the COS: Coins, Officials, Seal. Decode: From 1708 Banda Bahadur 08-15 carried on; 10 May 1710 Chappar Chiri, kills Wazir Khan, conquers Sirhind; State between the Ravi and the Jamuna with its own Coins, Officials and Seal (full independence). Farrukhsiyar 13-19 sends Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore; 1715 defeated, 1716 executed. Chapter ruling on territory: the handout says Ravi to Jamuna (the answer-writing wording); the teacher's ink says "in and around Patiala". Why it sticks: COS = the three marks of a real State. Mnemonic: Wazir Khan's circle: 04, 08, 10. Oh-four he walled the boys; oh-eight he sent the knives; ten, the circle closed. Decode: Dec 1704 buries the two younger Sahibzadas alive; 7 Oct 1708 arranges assassins against Guru Gobind Singh 76-08; 10 May 1710 killed by Banda Bahadur 08-15 at Chappar Chiri, in revenge. Why it sticks: 04, 08, 10 steps by 4 then 2, and the third event is the revenge. Flag on the territory: the handout places Banda's State between the Ravi and the Jamuna; the teacher's ink on the board says "a small state in and around Patiala." Both appear in the class material; the handout's wording is the answer-writing one.  Why did Banda Bahadur 08-15's Sikh State collapse by 1715? (1) Khatri traders turned against him: constant warfare hurt trade, and the commercial class needs decisive victors and political stability. (2) Divide and Rule: Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari (revenue farming) in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders with business opportunities; both Jahandar Shah and Farukhsiyar offered Mansabs to Khatri traders, who switched sides (this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis discussed earlier). (3) Jat zamindars: Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides; Churaman Jat (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the Mughals after they recognised his Jat Kingdom, conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. Why his State fell (three reasons): Khatri traders turned against him. Constant warfare hurt trade, and the commercial class needs decisive victors and political stability to function. Divide and rule. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari (the revenue-farming system) in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders with business opportunities. Both Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered Mansabs to Khatri traders, who switched sides. (Note: this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis; see Chapter 2.) Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides. Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the Mughals after they recognised his Jat Kingdom, granting him conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. Mnemonic: Why Banda Bahadur 08-15 fell: the K-D-J DJ. The K-D-J DJ changed the tune three times and the crowd walked off the floor. Decode: K = Khatri traders turned (constant war hurt trade; commerce wants a decisive winner); D = Divide and rule: Jahandar Shah 12-13 brought Ijaradari to Punjab to co-opt Khatris, and both he and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered them Mansabs; J = Jat zamindars switched, e.g. Churaman 95-21 went over after the Mughals recognised his Jat Kingdom. Also: Banda Bahadur 08-15 was not a Guru. Why it sticks: three letters, three reasons, in the chapter's own order (1, 2, 3).  Teacher's board: why Banda Bahadur 08-15 lost? Khatris stopped supporting him [Z = money]; Churaman Jat ditto [guns and military], co-opted by accepting a Jat kingdom within the Mughal empire. Right: wanted peace as trade hurt due to constant wars, therefore chose the stronger side; Banda Bahadur was not a Guru; DnR (unclear) by Mughals; (a) Jahandar Shah introduced Ijaradari in Punjab (and Bengal) = business opportunity; (b) Jahandar Shah, Farukhsiyar made Khatris Mansabdars (Rs). Bottom: when personality weakens then power leaves (down or sideways), so factionalism rises (Khatris versus Banda Bahadur). Teacher: Khatris stopped supporting him (money); Churaman 95-21 Jat likewise (guns / military), co-opted by accepting a Jat kingdom within the Mughal empire. The Khatris wanted peace because trade was hurt by constant wars, so they chose the stronger side. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was not a Guru, so he lacked the Gurus' authority. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal (a business opportunity), and Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 made Khatris Mansabdars. The general rule (double-starred): when a personality weakens, power leaves (downward or sideways), and factionalism rises (Khatris against Banda Bahadur 08-15). items.t: 7 · What kept the Sikh State alive: the Misl confederacy
items.x: What kept the Sikh State alive after Banda Bahadur 08-15's defeat? After defeat: the defeat did not end the Sikh State; the Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab and power was decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls: kinship-based clans, united during wars (particularly against Afghan invasions), otherwise independent. Land shares: whenever a Misl conquered territory, lands were distributed among members in proportion to military and monetary contribution; even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share. By 1770: 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs, a confederacy structure (weak centre, strong constituent units). Takeaway: this mirrors the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, a nominal centre holding largely autonomous regional chiefs; decentralisation was both a source of resilience and ultimately a vulnerability. The defeat of Banda Bahadur 08-15 did not end the Sikh State. The Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab, and power became decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls are kinship-based clans. They united during wars, particularly against Afghan invasions, but otherwise operated independently. Whenever a Misl conquered territory, the lands were distributed among its members in proportion to their military and monetary contribution. Even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share of land. By 1770 there were 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs: a confederacy structure with a weak centre and strong constituent units. Takeaway (handout): compare it to the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, where a nominal centre held together largely autonomous regional chiefs. Decentralisation was both a source of resilience and, ultimately, a vulnerability.  Teacher's board: misl confederacy. Death of Banda Bahadur 08-15 = no strong centre, so power decentralised to misl chiefs. Polity structure: a Confederacy (of misls); fragmented. Picture: a big circle Punjab containing about 12 smaller circles (misls), roughly 40-60 misls. Plus the Dal Khalsa = assembly of misl chiefs: e.g. on Abdali's 1748 invasion the Dal Khalsa will meet and a joint defence will be prepared; e.g. Manupur 1748 (written Bomanpur): Abdali defeated by the Sikhs. Teacher: The death of Banda Bahadur 08-15 left no strong centre, so power decentralised to the misl chiefs. Polity structure: a Confederacy (of misls); fragmented. The board's sketch shows one big circle (Punjab) with about a dozen circles inside (misls), "roughly 40-60 misls" (the handout's formal count is 12 major Misls by 1770). The Dal Khalsa = the assembly of misl chiefs: e.g. on Abdali's 1748 invasion the Dal Khalsa will meet and prepare a joint defence, e.g. Manupur 1748, where Abdali was defeated (see Chapter 4). Mnemonic: Misls: a dozen eggs in the Dal Khalsa basket. 12 Misls in one basket; the teacher's 40-60 is only a rough sketch. Decode: Misls = kinship clans; united in wars (esp. against Afghan invasions), otherwise independent; conquered land shared by military and monetary contribution (even the lowest soldier got a share). By 1770: 12 major Misls, with the Dal Khalsa (assembly of Misl chiefs) at the centre. Chapter ruling: the handout's formal count is 12 by 1770; the board's "roughly 40-60" is the sketch. Manupur 1748: Dal Khalsa meets on Abdali 47-72's invasion, Abdali 47-72 defeated. Same shape as the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas. Why it sticks: 12 = a dozen, a basket with a weak centre.  Teacher's board: fragmented polity PYQ. UPSC PYQ Mains: by the mid-18th century India was a spectre of a fragmented polity. [Punjab State PCS FYQ]: by 1715 Punjab was a spectre of a fragmented polity. In today's language = weak centre when there are coalition governments at the centre, leading to factionalism, instability, shorter tenures, a weak PM. items.t: 8 · Ranjit Singh 01-39 unifies the Misls
items.x: Teacher's board: Maharaja Ranjit Singh (RS 01-39, boxed 1801-39). Zaman Shah (Abdali's successor) invasion [crisis = opportunity]. The Sukerchakia misl of RS emerged most powerful. 1801: coronation. 1809: Treaty of Amritsar, the Sutlej River = border with the Company State (Br India); military alliance with the EIC.  Maharaja Ranjit Singh (01-39): a painted portrait of a white-bearded man in a turban with a jewel, yellow coat, seated holding a sword. Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia Misl, coronated Maharaja of the Sikh State in 1801.  How did Ranjit Singh 01-39 unify the Misls and build a powerful Sikh State? 1796-1799, prominence: Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia Misl rose during Zaman Shah's Afghan invasions of Punjab. 1799, Lahore: after Zaman Shah's retreat he captured Lahore from the Bhangi Misl, a platform to establish dominance over the other Misls. 1801, Maharaja: formally coronated Maharaja of the Sikh State. The Misl chiefs were systematically reduced to tribute-paying vassals, with conditional control of lands in return for loyalty and tribute to the Crown. Teacher's ink: bracket [Jagirs] with watan below. Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl played a crucial role in defeating Zaman Shah's third Afghan invasion of 1799 (the slide reads: he rose during Zaman Shah's Afghan invasions of 1796-1799). This gave him the platform to establish dominance over the other Misls, and he was coronated King (Maharaja) of the Sikh State in 1801. The other Misl chiefs were reduced to tribute-paying vassals, retaining conditional control of their lands in return for loyalty and tribute to the King (the teacher's ink: lands held as Jagirs, not Watan). Teacher: Zaman Shah (Abdali's successor) invaded: "crisis = opportunity." The Sukerchakia misl of Ranjit Singh 01-39 emerged the most powerful. 1801: coronation. 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar made the Sutlej the border with the Company State (British India) and brought a military alliance with the EIC. The Misl chiefs' lands: Jagirs, not Watan. Mnemonic: Jagir, not Watan: the chiefs held on conditions. Ranjit Singh 01-39's chiefs got a Jagir with strings; the Watan Jagir of Chapter 5's rebels was a different bargain. Decode: after the 1801 coronation (Ranjit Singh 01-39), Misl chiefs became tribute-paying vassals with conditional control of land in return for loyalty and tribute: Jagirs, not Watan. Why it sticks: "Loyalty and tribute, or no land." 8.1 Territorial expansion: rapid and systematic  Territorial expansion, rapid and systematic. 1799: conquered Lahore. 1808: conquered Jammu from the Dogra Rajputs (Jammu later granted as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820; his son Gulab Singh formally made Raja of Jammu in 1822). 1809: signed the Treaty of Amritsar with the British; it restricted his expansion south of the Sutlej but secured his eastern frontier, allowing him eventually to launch major campaigns into Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819) and Peshawar (1834).  Handout Diagram 3: Ranjit Singh's expansion and administration. Sukerchakia Misl: 1799 Ranjit Singh defeats Zaman Shah's 3rd Afghan invasion, the platform for unification; 1801 coronated King of the Sikh State (Misl chiefs = tribute-paying vassals), 1801 Lahore, 1808 Jammu (Dogras); 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC (Charles Metcalfe): Sutlej = border, the EIC recognises his sovereignty, military alliance; 1818 Multan conquered from the Afghans, Punjab secured; 1819 Kashmir conquered (completes what the Marathas had left unfinished after Abdali's capture); 1834 Peshawar conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa (Haria Ragle), present-day KPK, bordering Afghanistan via the Durand Line; 1838 Tripartite Treaty: Sikhs, EIC and Shah Shuja, Punjab as a buffer against the feared Russian invasion; administration: 40 percent Jagirdari, Kardars collect revenue, village autonomy (feeding Mahalwari in Punjab), secular cabinet (Fakir Azizuddin, Foreign; Dewan Dina Nath, Finance), Sahajdhari Sikhs included. 1801: conquered Lahore (handout list); the slides place the capture of Lahore in 1799 from the Bhangi Misl. 1808: conquered Jammu from the Dogras (the handout adds: in 1819 he returned Jammu to the Dogras but within the Sikh Empire: the Dogras became vassals; the slide adds: Jammu later granted as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820, and his son Gulab Singh formally made Raja of Jammu in 1822). 1809: the handout lists "conquered the whole of Punjab" as the third step; the slide reads: "signed the Treaty of Amritsar ... secured his eastern frontier." Flags on the Ranjit Singh 01-39 dates: the handout gives Lahore 1801 and Jammu returned to the Dogras in 1819; the slides give Lahore 1799 (captured from the Bhangi Misl) and Jammu given as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820 and Gulab Singh made Raja in 1822. Also, the handout says Zaman Shah's third invasion of 1799, the slide says the invasions of 1796-1799. For answers, anchor on: coronation 1801; Treaty of Amritsar 1809; Multan 1818; Kashmir 1819; Peshawar 1834; Tripartite Treaty 1838. Mnemonic: Ranjit Singh 01-39's date rhyme: 01, 09, 18-19, 34, 38. Oh-one: the crown. Oh-nine: the line. Eighteen-nineteen: Multan, Kashmir shine. Thirty-four: Peshawar's gate. Thirty-eight: the pact of fate. Decode: coronation 1801 (Sukerchakia Misl, after Zaman Shah's invasions); Treaty of Amritsar 1809 (Sutlej line); Multan 1818, Kashmir 1819 (back to back); Peshawar 1834; Tripartite Treaty 1838. Chapter ruling: the handout says Lahore 1801 and the slides say Lahore 1799 (from the Bhangi Misl), so anchor on these six dates. Why it sticks: pairs and a rhyme: 01-09, 18-19, 34-38.

items.t: 9 · The Treaty of Amritsar (1809)
items.x: The 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC. Signed in 1809 by Ranjit Singh with the EIC, represented by Charles Metcalfe, the British EIC's Resident in the Delhi court (recall that the Scindias had been removed from Delhi in 1803 and the EIC had established indirect rule there through a British Resident). Outcome 1: the EIC recognised Ranjit Singh as the sovereign ruler of Punjab. Outcome 2: it led to a military alliance (later link to the EIC's Policy of Ring Fence). Outcome 3: the Sutlej River was fixed as the border between the Sikh State and the Company State. Outcome 4: Ranjit Singh was free to expand his State on his side of the Sutlej without British interference. In 1809 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC, represented by Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident in the Delhi court. (Recall that the Scindias had been removed from Delhi in 1803 and the EIC had set up indirect rule there through a British Resident.) Four outcomes: The EIC recognised Ranjit Singh 01-39 as the sovereign ruler of Punjab. It led to a military alliance (later link to the EIC's Policy of Ring Fence). The Sutlej River was fixed as the border between the Sikh State and the Company State. Ranjit Singh 01-39 was free to expand on his side of the Sutlej without British interference. Mnemonic: Treaty of Amritsar 1809: R-M-S-F, "Ranjit Singh 01-39 Met Metcalfe, Shook hands, Freed". Recognised, Military, Sutlej, Free. Decode: 1809, Ranjit Singh 01-39 and the EIC (Charles Metcalfe, Resident at Delhi): Recognised as sovereign of Punjab; Military alliance (link to Ring Fence); Sutlej fixed as border; Free expansion on his side. Map: north of the Sutlej = RJ 01-39, south = EIC. Why it sticks: Metcalfe's name echoes "Met", and R-M-S-F is the order of the four outcomes.  Map of Punjab (districts, rivers Ravi, Beas, Sutlej; Amritsar, Gurdaspur, Hoshiarpur, Jalandhar, Kapurthala, Nawanshahr, Rupnagar, Chandigarh, Firozpur, Moga, Faridkot, Ludhiana, Fatehgarh, Muktsar, Bathinda, Sangrur, Patiala, Mansa). Teacher's ink: yellow lines point to the north side of the Sutlej labelled RJ 01-39 (Ranjit Singh) and to the south side labelled EIC.  Handout map of Punjab with the rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, used to locate the Sutlej border of the Treaty of Amritsar. Teacher: On the Punjab map: north of the Sutlej = Ranjit Singh 01-39 (RJ 01-39); south of the Sutlej = the EIC.

items.t: 10 · How far did Ranjit Singh 01-39 expand after 1809?
items.x: How far did Ranjit Singh expand the Sikh State after 1809? Direction: the eastern border secured by the treaty, he turned west and north. 1818, Multan: removed the Afghans from Multan. 1819, Kashmir: conquered (recall: Abdali captured Punjab and Kashmir during his invasions; the Marathas took Punjab back in 1758, not Kashmir; Ranjit Singh completed what the Marathas left unfinished). 1834, Peshawar: conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, bordering Afghanistan along the Durand Line). Hari Singh Nalwa: his military reputation was so fearsome that, as historical accounts record, Afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children: If you don't stop crying, Haria Ragle will turn up. Ink: Khyber Pass (underlined), Peshawar. With his eastern border secured, Ranjit Singh 01-39 turned west and north: 1818: removed the Afghans from Multan. 1819: conquered Kashmir. (Recall that Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 captured Punjab and Kashmir; Punjab was taken back by the Marathas in 1758 but not Kashmir; Ranjit Singh 01-39 completed what the Marathas left unfinished.) 1834: conquered Peshawar (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, bordering Afghanistan along the Durand Line). Peshawar was conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa, whose reputation was so fearsome that Afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children: "If you don't stop crying, Haria Ragle will turn up." Mnemonic: West and north: Multan, Kashmir, then the long wait for Peshawar. 18, 19 back to back; then 34 and a legend: Haria Ragle. Decode: after 1809, east secured, Ranjit Singh 01-39 turns west and north: 1818 Multan (Afghans removed); 1819 Kashmir (the Marathas retook Punjab in 1758 but not Kashmir; he completed it); 1834 Peshawar, conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Durand Line), whose name Afghan mothers used to quiet children. Why it sticks: Multan and Kashmir are consecutive years; Peshawar needs the one name, Nalwa. 10.1 The 1838 Tripartite Treaty  The 1838 Tripartite Treaty. Signed in 1838 by Ranjit Singh between the Sikh State, the EIC and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan. Design: to establish British indirect rule in Afghanistan through Shah Shuja as a puppet ruler. Aim: to create a buffer of Afghanistan and Punjab against the feared Russian invasion of British India from the north-west. Ink: British Fear of Russia; chain diagram: Russia, AFGH (Afghanistan), KHYBER PASS, SIKH STATE, Company State (Br India). In 1838 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Tripartite Treaty between the Sikh State, the EIC and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan. The design: to establish British indirect rule in Afghanistan through Shah Shuja as a puppet ruler. The aim: to create a buffer of Afghanistan and Punjab against the feared Russian invasion of British India from the north-west. Teacher: British fear of Russia: the chain drawn on the board is Russia, then Afghanistan, then the Khyber Pass, then the Sikh State, then the Company State (British India). Afghanistan and Punjab are the buffer. Mnemonic: Tripartite 1838: Russia Always Knocks; Sikhs Cushion. R-A-K-S-C: the chain from Russia down to the Company. Decode: Russia → Afghanistan → Khyber Pass → Sikh State → Company State. Three parties (Tri): the Sikh State, the EIC and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan; Shah Shuja is the puppet for British indirect rule; Afghanistan and Punjab are the buffer against the feared Russian invasion. Why it sticks: the sentence is the board's chain, top to bottom.

items.t: 11 · What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build?
items.x: What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build? Power built by a skilful combination of coercion, diplomacy and careful balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles like the Dogras (similar to the successor states discussed earlier). Character: militarily strong and economically prosperous. Revenue policy: fair for the masses; trade flourished as a strong State delivered the law-and-order stability commerce requires. Land and King: only 40% of land under the Jagirdari system; from the remaining land revenue went directly to the King, giving considerable monetary power.  What kind of State did Ranjit Singh build (contd.)? Kardar: land revenue, the main income source, collected by Kardars, the chief administrative officer at the Taluqa (district) level, who acted as revenue collector, local magistrate (judge), police chief and customs officer. Ijaradari: Ranjit Singh heavily relied on the Ijaradari system; instead of a fixed cash salary a Kardar often acted as an Ijaradar, but it was ensured the ryot was not oppressed by very high LR. Village autonomy: State authority stopped at the village level; the power of local chiefs and clans was respected (this will connect directly to the Mahalwari Settlement in Punjab, where even the British respected this tradition of village-level autonomy).  What made the Sikh State hold together? Secular administration: key positions held by men from different religious backgrounds, Fakir Azizuddin (a Muslim) as Foreign Minister and Dewan Dina Nath (a Hindu) handling the finances as Finance Minister. Culturally broad: Ranjit Singh was magnanimous; Sikh identity expanded to include non-Khalsa Sikhs, the Sahajdhari Sikhs, who do not maintain the 5 Ks of Khalsa identity (Kesh, Kangha, Kada, Kirpan, Kachhera). The State he built: politically inclusive, respecting village and local autonomy, and culturally broad. The story of the Sikh State after Ranjit Singh (the Anglo-Sikh Wars and eventual annexation by the EIC) continues in a later chapter. The 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, raises the Khalsa in 1699; Wazir Khan walls the boys (1704), plots the Guru's death (1708), and falls at Chappar Chiri (1710) to Banda Bahadur 08-15, who has COS: Coins, Officials, Seal. Then "01, 09, 18-19, 34, 38": Amritsar's Sutlej line, Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar, and the Tripartite chain Russia-Afghanistan-Khyber-Sikhs-Company. items.t: 1 · Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs
items.x: Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs. 16th-c Rajputana: no single central power, roughly 20 major Rajput clans, each controlling its own territory (modern IR: multi-polar world, many power centres, no single dominant one). Akbar's approach: defeating all would be expensive and uncertain, so he co-opted more powerful Rajput chiefs as Mansabdars (ranked nobles with military and administrative responsibilities); home territories recognised as Vatan Jagirs (land remained theirs but within the Mughal framework); obligations: accepted the Mughal Emperor as sovereign, paid tributes, contributed troops; they formed a Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system (about 15% of all Mansabdars); in return Akbar helped them subdue smaller Rajput Chiefs; result: partial consolidation of power. Teacher's ink: (Centralization) under Result; a row of circled numbers 1 2 3 ... 20 (the clans) with an arrow to a block labelled Mewar with a tick for Marwar (a few strong clans swallowing smaller ones); whole Rajputana not under 1 king; a triangle crossed out (no single king or pyramid).   Aspect   What happened    --- ---    16th-century Rajputana   No single central power; roughly 20 major Rajput clans, each controlling its own territory (in modern IR terms a multi-polar world: many power centres, no single dominant one)     Akbar 56-05's approach   Defeating all would be expensive and uncertain, so he co-opted the more powerful Rajput chiefs     Mansabdars   The chosen chiefs became ranked nobles with military and administrative responsibilities     Vatan Jagirs   Their home territories were recognised as Vatan Jagirs: the land remained theirs but within the Mughal framework     Obligations   Accepted the Mughal Emperor as sovereign, paid tributes, contributed troops     Hindu bloc   As a group they formed the Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system (about 15% of all Mansabdars)     In return   Akbar 56-05 helped them subdue the smaller Rajput chiefs     Result   A partial consolidation of power   Mnemonic: Akbar 56-05's Rajput bargain: M-V plus S-T-T. The chief becomes an MVP (Mansabdar with Vatan Jagir) if he gives S-T-T. Decode: Akbar 56-05 co-opts the powerful chiefs: Mansabdar rank + Vatan Jagir (home land stays theirs). In return they give Sovereignty (accept the Mughal Emperor), Tribute, Troops. Bonus: they form the Hindu bloc, about 15% of Mansabdars; roughly 20 clans; Akbar 56-05 helps them subdue smaller chiefs. Why it sticks: MV for what they get, S-T-T for what they pay; 20 clans, 15% share. Teacher: The board's sketch: 20 clans numbered 1 to 20, with a few strong ones (Mewar, Marwar) swallowing the smaller: a partial (Centralization). The whole of Rajputana was never under one king (the crossed-out triangle/pyramid).

items.t: 2 · Rajputs against Aurangzeb 58-07, and the Marathas
items.x: 1680 Rajput revolt, trigger and collapse. Mewar expands: the arrangement held through most of the 17th c, trouble came under Aurangzeb 58-07, with Mewar under Raj Singh expanding aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states. Aurangzeb was uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and become a rival to the Mughal State. 1680, the trigger: a child came to the throne in Marwar, a kingdom astride the trade route connecting Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad; Aurangzeb interfered in the succession. Marwar and Mewar revolted, and collapsed: the other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them if the revolt succeeded; each stood aside, so the rebellion collapsed. Mewar expands: under Raj Singh, aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states Aurangzeb 58-07 is uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and rival the Mughals (warn) 1680, the trigger: a child comes to the throne in Marwar (astride the Delhi/Agra to Ahmedabad trade route); Aurangzeb 58-07 interferes in the succession Marwar and Mewar revolt (bad) The rebellion collapses: the other Rajput chiefs refuse to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them Mnemonic: 1680: three M's, Mewar, Marwar, Mughal. Mewar grows, Marwar gets a child king, the Mughal meddles; the rest sit out. Decode: Mewar under Raj Singh expands, so Aurangzeb 58-07 grows uneasy; 1680 a child comes to the throne of Marwar (astride the Delhi/Agra to Ahmedabad route) and Aurangzeb 58-07 interferes (the trigger); Marwar and Mewar revolt; other chiefs refuse to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them, so it collapses. Why it sticks: the fear of Mewar is the reason in one word.  Handout Diagram 1 (Rajputs): 16th century Rajputana with about 20 major clans and no single centre (multi-polar world); Akbar co-opts powerful Rajput chiefs, who help subdue the smaller; Rajputs = Hindu bloc of Mansabdars (about 15%), accept the Mughal emperor, pay tribute, contribute troops; Aurangzeb uneasy as Mewar under Raj Singh expands; 1680 Marwar and Mewar both revolt, other chiefs refuse to join, rebellion collapses; post-1707 Sawai Jai Singh (1699-1743) of Amber rules Jaipur and remains a Mansabdar in Delhi but on his own terms; 1751 onwards Marathas raid Rajputana (tribute, succession meddling), never conquer the region; post-2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 the EIC signs Subordinate / Subsidiary Alliances with Rajput states.  Rajputana after Aurangzeb 58-07: Marathas, then the EIC. Post-1707: the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms, the most prominent being Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber, who ruled Jaipur and remained a powerful Mansabdar in Delhi but on his own conditions. 1751 onwards: the Marathas begin regular raids into Rajputana, extracting tribute and interfering in succession disputes, never fully conquering the region. After the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05): the EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subordinate Alliances (also called Subsidiary Alliances) with Rajput states. Subordinate Alliance terms: like World History's term Protectorate, the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered control of foreign policy and defence to the EIC, which stationed its own troops, paid for by the Indian ruler; in Suzerainty = loss of external sovereign functions plus loss of symbolic sovereignty. Ink beside the row heading: will do in future. Right ink: a funnel sketch with the labels 200, 1751, 1727-20 (?), 1752 and a boxed GWO (partly illegible). This arrangement held through most of the 17th century. Trouble came under Aurangzeb 58-07. Mewar, under Raj Singh, had been expanding aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states; Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy, not wanting one Rajput power to dominate Rajputana and rival the Mughal State. 1680: a child came to the throne in Marwar, a kingdom astride the important trade route connecting Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad. Aurangzeb 58-07 interfered in the succession: the trigger. Marwar and Mewar both revolted, but the revolt failed. The other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing that if the revolt succeeded Mewar would dominate them. After Aurangzeb 58-07's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms. The most prominent figure was Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber, who ruled Jaipur and remained a powerful Mansabdar in Delhi, but on his own conditions. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids into Rajputana, extracting tribute and interfering in succession disputes, but could never fully conquer the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subordinate Alliances (also called Subsidiary Alliances) with the Rajput states. Mnemonic: Rajputs after Aurangzeb 58-07: 07, 51, 03-05. Seven: own terms. Fifty-one: Maratha raids. Three-to-five: the Company moves in. Why it sticks: three masters in time order, Mughal, Maratha, EIC. Teacher: Subordinate Alliance is like World History's Protectorate: the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered control of foreign policy and defence to the EIC, which stationed its own troops, paid for by the Indian ruler. Under suzerainty = loss of external sovereign functions plus loss of symbolic sovereignty. The teacher's ink: "will do in future" (the Subsidiary Alliance is taken up in Chapter 11). items.t: 4 · Travancore: Marthanda Varma 29-58
items.x: Travancore under Marthanda Varma 29-58. Mughal relation: never part of the Mughal Empire, the Mughal State simply never expanded far enough south to include it. Centralised State: by the 1740s built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region. European-style military: modern weapons, trained soldiers. Takeaway, trade to State capacity: a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast; revenues reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure, a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. Takeaway: Travancore established a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues were reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure: a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. Mnemonic: Travancore's trade income goes to M-I-T. Marthanda Varma 29-58 sends the spice money to MIT: Military, Irrigation, Transport. Decode: never part of the Mughal Empire (Mughals never expanded far enough south); by the 1740s a centralised State by subjugating local chiefs, with a European-style military; State monopoly over Malabar coast trade; revenues reinvested in Military, Irrigation works, Transport infrastructure. Since 1663: the Dutch East India Company's Malabar headquarters at Cochin (central Kerala), captured from the Portuguese. 1741, Battle of Colachel: a landmark in the history of Kerala; Marthanda Varma's army crushed the Dutch East India Company. items.t: 6 · Mysore: from Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82
items.x: Mysore, Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82. The Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646): Mysore was part of it. 1565, Battle of Talikota: a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar forces; the dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 was the operational end as a major power. Wodeyar dynasty: after Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous; under Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar 72-04 it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars were reduced to puppets by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. 1761: Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj: began as a junior military officer (the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts); capable, ambitious and strategic, he seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as the nominal head of State. Pattern alert at the 18th c: the King becomes a puppet as personality weakens (recall Peshwa and Chhatrapati). Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646). The Empire's effective power was shattered at the Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar. The dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 marks the operational end of Vijayanagar as a major power. After Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous under the Wodeyar dynasty. Under Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (1672-1704) it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. Haider Ali 61-82 ended that. He began as a junior military officer, his early career made possible partly because the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts. Capable, ambitious and strategic, in 1761 he overthrew NanjRaj and seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as a nominal head of State. Mnemonic: Vijayanagar: 1336 born, 1565 hit, 1646 gone. Three-three-six birth; fifteen-sixty-five, Talikota blow; sixteen-forty-six, last breath. Decode: Vijayanagar Empire 1336-1646 (Mysore was part of it); 1565 Battle of Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi), a coalition of Deccan Sultanates defeats it, the operational end; the dynasty lingers to 1646. Then Wodeyars gain autonomy; Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar makes Mysore powerful. Why it sticks: start, blow, end: one number each. Mnemonic: Haider Ali 61-82 takes power in 61. The year he seized power is the year his code begins: 61. Decode: by 1761 the Wodeyars were figureheads under corrupt PM NanjRaj; in 1761 Haider Ali 61-82, a junior officer (the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts), overthrew NanjRaj and kept the Wodeyar as nominal head. Pattern: the king becomes a puppet as personality weakens (like Peshwa and Chhatrapati). Why it sticks: the code 61-82 starts exactly in 1761, so the code itself holds the year. Pattern alert at the 18th century: the king becomes a puppet as personality weakens. Recall the Peshwa and Chhatrapati relationship (Chapter 4). 6.1 Haider Ali 61-82's military machine  Haider Ali 61-82's military machine. French assistance: military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. Risalas: the army structured on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments). Each Risala: a commander directly appointed by the King (personal loyalty to the King); a clear chain of command; self-sufficient, with its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindhia). Result: a fast, efficient military, regiments capable of independent action. Poligars subjugated: local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and their own armed men, the real rulers of the rural areas since the Vijayanagar era (1336-1646); a civil war of roughly 20 years spent subjugating them. Deshmukhs subjugated: next slide. Outcome: the power of Non-State Actors was systematically ended. Haider Ali 61-82 took French assistance for military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. The army was now on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments): Each Risala's commander was directly appointed by the King, ensuring personal loyalty upward. Each unit had a clear chain of command. Each was self-sufficient: its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindia, Chapter 4). Result: a fast, efficient military with regiments capable of independent action. He then spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars (local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and had their own armed men, the real rulers of the countryside since the Vijayanagar era) and the Deshmukhs (revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars). Non-State power was systematically dismantled. Mnemonic: Risala = the three C's. Commander (the King's), Chain of command, Complete (self-sufficient). Decode: French-assisted army on a European model; each Risala (regiment) has a commander directly appointed by the King (personal loyalty), a clear chain of command, and is self-sufficient with its own weapons, transport and supplies (like Scindia's Campoo); result is fast, efficient regiments capable of independent action. Why it sticks: three C's, three features, one regiment. Mnemonic: Poligars have Power, Deshmukhs collect Dues. P for Power, D for Dues: Haider Ali 61-82 spent about twenty years breaking both. Decode: Poligars = local chiefs and landlords with land, temple wealth and their own armed men, the real rulers of the countryside since Vijayanagar; Deshmukhs = revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars. Subjugating them ended Non-State power. Why it sticks: one letter each gives the one-line difference. 6.2 How Mysore funded this machine: Military Fiscalism  Military fiscalism of Tipu 82-99 (and Haider Ali 61-82): Mysore's revenue reforms. Khalisa lands expanded: more revenue went to the State treasury. Jagirdari minimised: maximised State income while reducing the independent economic power of nobles. Direct collection: Deshmukhs were removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes directly and received salaries, far smaller than the commissions intermediaries take.  Military fiscalism (contd.). Detailed field surveys: assessed land revenue scientifically (soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends), preventing over-assessment so ryots were not oppressed. Investing in agriculture: 1. old irrigation canals repaired and new ones built; 2. cash crops promoted; 3. sericulture (cultivation of silk via silkworms) introduced. Boosted tax collection: more income for peasants meant more tax revenue for the State; even Tipu's enemies acknowledged that Mysore's population was among the most prosperous. All of this and the last slide = Military Fiscalism: huge generation of State wealth for a stronger military for empire building. (The handout's analogy: replacing a commission-based agent with a salaried employee; the State kept far more of the revenue.) Khalisa land = land whose revenue went directly to the State treasury. Jagirdari land = land whose revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders. Mnemonic: Khalisa = Khazana; Jagir = Jebs of nobles. Khalisa feeds the Khazana (treasury); Jagirdari fills the Jebs (pockets) of nobles. Decode: Khalisa land = revenue goes directly to the State treasury (Mysore expanded it); Jagirdari land = revenue assigned to nobles or commanders (Mysore minimised it). Deshmukhs removed; State officials collect directly on salaries, like replacing a commission agent with a salaried employee. Why it sticks: K-K (Khalisa, Khazana) and J-J (Jagir, Jebs). Mnemonic: Surveys by SCIP; farm help by C-C-S. SCIP: Soil fertility, Crop type, Irrigation access, Past production. CCS: Canals, Cash crops, Silk. Decode: detailed field surveys assessed land revenue by soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends (prevented over-assessment); investment in agriculture = canals repaired and built, cash crops promoted, sericulture introduced. All of this is Military Fiscalism: State wealth as a foundation for military power. Why it sticks: two short codes, one for assessing and one for investing; richer peasants mean a larger tax base.

items.t: 7 · Tipu 82-99 Sultan (1782-99): innovations and why he still lost
items.x: Tipu 82-99's innovations. Modern navy and trading company: a government-owned trading company like the EIC for oceanic trade in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk and cardamom; 30 trading centres inside and outside India, including Muscat, Oman. Why it sticks: "iron = no burst, 2 km"; a cardboard case is just a firework. Mnemonic: 1785: independence, then ask the Khalifa. Eighty-five: Tipu 82-99 cuts both strings (Wodeyars and Mughal) and asks the Khalifa for a sanad. Decode: 1785 Tipu 82-99 formally declared independence from the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor and requested a sanad from the Khalifa recognising him as independent of Mughal authority. Why it sticks: two strings cut, one new authority asked. 7.1 Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France  Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France. 1790s: sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. The 23-year Wars (1792-1815): the French Revolution of 1789 pitted France against the rest of the European monarchies. 1798: Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Alliance with France (did not materialise into military support): exchanged communications with Napoleon; planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution, planted across France and later across Europe); joined the Jacobin Club, the radical political organisation at the heart of the French Revolution. The British were alarmed and this also became a reason for the 4th Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. In the 1790s Tipu 82-99 sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. Since 1789 the French Revolution had set France on a collision course with the monarchies of Europe, including Britain (the 23-year wars, 1792-1815). In 1798 Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Tipu 82-99 exchanged communications with Napoleon and planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution), and joined the Jacobin Club. The alliance did not materialise into military support. The British were alarmed, and it became a reason for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. Mnemonic: Tipu 82-99 Joined, Napoleon Never helped. T-J-N: Tree of Liberty, Jacobin Club, Napoleon's no. Decode: Tipu 82-99 sent an ambassador to France in the 1790s (the French Revolution began 1789; the 23-year wars ran 1792-1815; in 1798 Napoleon attacked Egypt); he exchanged communications with Napoleon, planted a Tree of Liberty and joined the Jacobin Club; No military support came; the British were alarmed, a reason for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. Why it sticks: two things he did, one thing he never got. Prelims 2001: who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? Answer (d): Tipu 82-99 Sultan. He set up modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. The Jacobin membership and Tree of Liberty marked him in British eyes as an ideological adversary, not merely a military one. Mnemonic: Prelims 2001: three fighters, one diplomat. Haider Ali 61-82 hit the field, Mir Qasim 60-63 fought at Buxar, Shah Alam II 60-06 fell; Tipu 82-99 sent envoys: F-T-E. Decode: answer (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan, embassies in France, Turkey, Egypt (plus new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar). Wrong options: (a) Haider Ali 61-82 built the French-model army with Risalas; (b) Mir Qasim 60-63 fought the EIC at Buxar (1764); (c) Shah Alam II 60-06, Mughal Emperor reduced after Buxar. Why it sticks: the other three are all battlefield names; "embassy" belongs to the one who looked abroad. 7.2 Why Mysore lost  Why Mysore lost. Over-ambitious: wanted to dominate all of South India and control its international trade = Vijayanagar 2.0. Drain due to war: constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. 1766, trigger: Haider Ali invaded and annexed Malabar and Calicut [could not successfully invade Travancore], leading to the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. 4 Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. 1799, end: the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War ended with the death of Tipu at Seringapatam, Mysore's power broken. Mysore's long-term ambition was to dominate all of South India and control its international trade (Vijayanagar 2.0). But constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. The ambition was real; the capacity, ultimately, was not enough. 1766: Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, triggering the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. The Fourth (1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam; Mysore's power was broken. Mnemonic: Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 67, 80, 90, 99 and lengths 2-4-2-1. Sixty-seven, eighty, ninety, ninety-nine: two years, four years, two years, one year. Decode: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. The First followed Haider Ali 61-82's 1766 annexation of Malabar and Calicut (the EIC feared losing coastal trade access); the Fourth ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam, Mysore's power broken. Why Mysore lost: ambition to dominate all South India (Vijayanagar 2.0) while constant war drained the State faster than Military Fiscalism refilled it. Why it sticks: the start years climb by 13, 10, 9, and the last war is the shortest, a single year. Flag on Travancore: the handout's section 7 says that in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 "had invaded Travancore and annexed Malabar and Calicut", while the same chapter (section 4) says he annexed Malabar and Calicut, and the teacher's bracket on the slide adds "could not successfully invade Travancore." Use the slide's wording: Malabar and Calicut were annexed; Travancore was not successfully invaded. Mnemonic: Trap-proof: M-C yes, Travancore no. Malabar-Calicut taken, Travancore too tough: follow the slide, not the handout's section 7. Decode: the handout's section 7 says Haider Ali 61-82 "invaded Travancore and annexed Malabar and Calicut"; the teacher's bracket says he "could not successfully invade Travancore". Chapter ruling: use the slide's wording. Why it sticks: two places lost (M and C), one place held (T).  Handout Diagram 3: Mysore's rise and the ambition-versus-capacity collapse. Vijayanagar Empire 1336-1646, 1565 Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi) breaks it; Wodeyar dynasty rises in Mysore, Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (1672-1704) militarily powerful and centrally governed; by 1761 the Wodeyars are figureheads under corrupt PM NanjRaj; 1761 Haider Ali (junior officer whose debts Wodeyars paid) overthrows NanjRaj, Wodeyar kept nominal (pattern: Peshwa-Chhatrapati mirror); French military reform: Risala regiments (personal loyalty to the King, self-sufficient, 20 years subjugating Poligars and Deshmukhs); Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari shrunk, Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries, field surveys, sericulture, cash crops, irrigation; Tipu 82-99: modern navy, government trading company (30 centres including Muscat), iron-cased rockets (Congreve copies), independence from Wodeyars and Mughals (Khalifa sanad); 1790s embassy to France (Prelims 2001 trap: Tipu = modern embassies), Tree of Liberty, Jacobin Club; 1799 Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu dies at Seringapatam.  Prelims 2001 question slide: Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (a) Haider Ali (b) Mir Qasim (c) Shah Alam II (d) Tipu Sultan.  Prelims 2001, answer key. Answer: (d) Tipu Sultan. Why (d) is correct: Tipu set up modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt alongside other administrative innovations such as a new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar; the chapter also covers his iron-cased rocket artillery (later studied by William Congreve), his government-owned trading company (30 trading centres including Muscat, Oman), his sanad request to the Khalifa and his French alliance (Tree of Liberty and Jacobin Club membership). Why the others are wrong: (a) Haider Ali built the Mysore army on a French model (with Risalas) and fought the EIC in the early Anglo-Mysore Wars but did not set up modern embassies; (b) Mir Qasim was a Nawab of Bengal who fought the EIC at Buxar (1764) and did not establish foreign embassies; (c) Shah Alam II 60-06 was a Mughal Emperor whose authority was reduced after Buxar; foreign embassies were not part of his programme.

items.t: 1 · Asia, the economic power of the world
items.x: Sec 1 Asia: Economic Power of the World. Three main attractions: Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) for spices, India for textiles (plus Malabar for spices), China for silk and tea. Routes: China by land (the Silk Route); India and Indonesia a mix of land and sea through the Middle East and the Arabian Sea. Arab traders dominated the Arabian Sea leg; Italian merchants of Genoa and Venice carried goods across the Mediterranean into Europe; both earned enormous profits at each handoff. Teacher's sketch: EU at the top, Mediterranean Sea and Arabian Sea as funnels meeting at a point, a new-route arrow from EU round to the Cape of Good Hope, and a note: the empire of Arabs and Ottoman.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Three main attractions   Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) for spices; India for textiles (plus Malabar for spices); China for silk and tea     Routes   China: land route (the Silk Route). India and Indonesia: a mix of land and sea, through the Middle East and the Arabian Sea     Who controlled trade   Arab traders dominated the Arabian Sea leg. Then Italian merchants of Genoa and Venice carried goods across the Mediterranean into Europe. Both earned enormous profits at each handoff   Mnemonic: Three prizes, three places. "Islands give Spice, India gives Cloth, China gives Silk (and tea)." Decode: Islands = Indonesia (Java, Sumatra) for spices; India = textiles (Malabar also spices); China = silk and tea. Middlemen in order: Arabs on the Arabian Sea leg, then Genoa and Venice across the Mediterranean. Why it sticks: I-I-C is the same order as the sentence; every handoff meant extra profit for a middleman. Teacher: The teacher marked "islands" over Indonesia and sketched the trade as two funnels (the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian Sea) meeting at a point, with the "new route" arrow going round the Cape of Good Hope (CoGH) from Europe (Portugal). Beside the Arabian Sea part he wrote "The empire of Arabs and Ottoman."  Silk and Spice Trade Routes map of Europe, Asia and Africa. Dashed land Silk Route via Constantinople, Antioch, Damascus, Merv to China (Guangzhou); solid sea spice routes via the Red Sea and Aden, Muscat, Cochin, East Africa (Mogadishu, Mombasa) to Java. Labels: Europe, Rome, Constantinople, Antioch, Mediterranean Sea, Damascus, Tyre, Merv, Persia, China, Guangzhou, Egypt, Arabia, Muscat, Aden, India, Cochin, Somalia, Mogadishu, Kenya, Mombasa, Indian Ocean, Java. Teacher's red ink: Traders of Genoa and Venice (dots on Italy), Silk route, Spice route, Constantinople underlined.  Medieval European trade routes map: Hanseatic, Venetian, Genoese, Venetian and Genoese, and overland or river routes (legend). Cities include London, Bruges, Hamburg, Lubeck, Paris, Lyon, Genoa, Venice, Milan, Florence, Rome, Naples, Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria, Lisbon. Teacher's red ink underlines Genoa and Venice. Who gained: the teacher's board on "no political control"  Teacher's board: IF no political control (colonialism or imperialism; note: 1757 colonialism began, Goa an exception). The idea: the presence of Europeans in India was for the purchase of Indian FINISHED GOODS (boxed, "imp"); competition among Europeans for the purchase of Indian finished goods; competition between Arabs and Europeans. Who is FOR this: exports of India, forex for India, strength of Indian kingdoms, India getting a BETTER PRICE (boxed), Indian merchants, Indian artisans. Teacher: If there was no political control (no colonialism or imperialism), the trade was good for India. [1757: colonialism began; Goa is an exception.] The idea (marked imp): Europeans came to India to purchase Indian FINISHED GOODS; there was competition among Europeans for these goods and competition between Arabs and Europeans. So this was good for: exports of India; forex for India; strength of Indian kingdoms; India getting a BETTER PRICE (boxed); Indian merchants; Indian artisans.  Teacher's board: trade flow diagram. A dotted box INDIAN TERRITORY holds Ryots (village) and Artisan (village), with arrows to the Indian merchant (city, town); arrow across the COASTAL AREA to Arabs and Europeans; then OUT OF INDIA (underlined). Europeans pay Export Duty (tax). Below: Domestic TRADE (inside the box) and INTERNATIONAL TRADE (at the coastal boundary). Ryots and artisans (villages) produce Indian merchant (city, town) collects and sells inside Indian territory: domestic trade Coastal area: goods meet Arabs / Europeans: international trade Europeans pay export duty (tax) to the Indian ruler OUT OF INDIA Europe was not wealthy; spices and the 800% profit  Sec 1 continued. Europe not wealthy: eastern goods were luxuries only the rich could afford; profit came from supplying Europe's wealthy classes, and Genoa and Venice guarded this position zealously. Spices held a special place: until the 1600s European food was as spiced as Indian food; spices preserved and made palatable the meat stored through winter (no refrigerator; clove and pepper did the job). Profit was staggering: Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold in Europe at 800% profit; by the 1600s one kilogram of clove cost the equivalent of one kilogram of gold. Teacher's ink: Indonesia did not want anything from the EU (see the triangle trade later); 6 months = average journey time from EU to India; TRADE: a buyer gives Gold or Silver to the seller, but this will deplete the forex reserves of a country.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Europe was not wealthy   Eastern goods were luxuries only the rich could afford. A common European could not afford Indian cotton or Chinese silk. The profit came from supplying Europe's wealthy classes, and Genoa and Venice guarded this position zealously     Spices held a special place   Until the 1600s European food was as spiced as Indian food. Spices preserved and made palatable the meat stored through winter (no industrial refrigerator: clove and pepper did the job)     Profit was staggering   Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold in Europe at 800% profit; by the 1600s, 1 kg of clove cost the equivalent of 1 kg of gold   Mnemonic: Eight-hundred and gold. Picture Da Gama (1498) unloading a ship where every sack sells for 8 times its cost, and a kilo of clove sits on the scale against a kilo of gold. Decode: 1498 cargo = 800% profit; by the 1600s 1 kg clove = 1 kg gold; spices also kept winter meat edible (clove and pepper did the job). Why it sticks: "clove = gold" matches the handout's own joke about "spitting gold" as children. Teacher: Beside the table: "6 months = average journey time from EU to India." And on trade: a buyer gives Gold or Silver to the seller, but this will deplete the forex reserves of a country. A side note in brackets on the slide: [Savings Bank A/c: 4%; 6-7%] (a comparison of rates of return; the handout does not explain it). The handout's aside: *had the present been the 1650s, most of us would have been "spitting gold" as children, with the cloves our mothers tucked into rice that we picked out and pushed to the side of the plate.* (memory hook for clove = gold) Forex versus domestic currency, and the triangle  Teacher's board: Forex versus Domestic Currency. Forex: used in the international market; a country buying from another country; import-export transactions; till 1971 Gold (underlined); 1971 onwards the Dollar (circled) replaced Gold. Domestic currency: within the borders of a state, domestic transactions must be done (ideally) in domestic currency. Triangle diagram Indonesia (top), India (bottom right), EIC (bottom left): (1) EIC buys goods from India; (2) EIC sells Indian goods to Indonesia; (3) Indonesian goods come back to the EIC; (4) EIC sells Indonesian goods to the rest of Europe for profit.   Forex   Domestic currency    --- ---    Used in the international market; a country buying from another country; import-export transactions   Within the borders of a state, domestic transactions must be done (ideally) in domestic currency     Till 1971: Gold. 1971 onwards: the Dollar replaced Gold     (1) Buy goods: the EIC buys goods (cloth) from India (2) Sell Indian goods: the EIC sells Indian goods to Indonesia (3) Sell goods: Indonesian goods (spices) come back to the EIC (4) The EIC sells Indonesian goods to the rest of Europe for profit Mnemonic: Cloth goes, spice comes. "Buy cloth, Sell cloth, Spice back, Sell spice" = B-S-S-S. Decode: (1) EIC buys cloth from India; (2) sells that cloth to Indonesia; (3) Indonesian goods (spices) come back to the EIC; (4) EIC sells them to the rest of Europe for profit. Why it sticks: Indonesia wanted nothing from Europe but accepted Indian cloth, so "to buy spice you first need cloth".  Sec 1 (contd): shift over time. As incomes rose in the 17th and 18th centuries, Indian cotton textiles became the most sought-after commodity, but in the beginning it was spice that started everything. Teacher's ink: as people came out of poverty, as the size of the middle class expanded, demand increased (arrow to incomes rose, underlined). Shift over time: as European incomes rose in the 17th and 18th centuries and spices became more widely available, Indian cotton textiles became the most sought-after commodity from the East. But in the beginning it was spice that started everything. Teacher: "As people came out of poverty / as the size of the middle class expanded, demand increased" (incomes rose: underlined).

items.t: 2 · The Ottoman blockade (1453) and the Age of Discovery
items.x: Sec 2 Ottoman Blockade and Age of Discovery. 1453 interruption: the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia; European traders needed a new way east. Age of Discovery (16th c): this necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points; European powers, led initially by Portugal and Spain, sent ships into the Atlantic searching for a direct sea route to the East. The era gave: 1 better use of the astrolabe for location and the magnetic compass for direction; 2 the system of latitudes and longitudes and the modern world map; 3 geography as a formal discipline; 4 the invention of the Caravel, a ship able to sail at an angle against the wind. Teacher's ink: effectively blockaded; not literally (they demanded a share of profits on trade, making trade unviable for Europeans); a sketch of a ship sailing at an angle to the wind.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    1453: interruption   The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia. European traders needed a new way east     Age of Discovery (16th century)   This necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points. European powers, led initially by Portugal and Spain, sent ships into the Atlantic searching for a direct sea route to the East     What the era gave (1)   Better use of the astrolabe (location) and the magnetic compass (direction)     What the era gave (2)   The system of latitudes and longitudes and the modern world map     What the era gave (3)   Geography as a formal discipline     What the era gave (4)   The invention of the Caravel: a ship able to sail at an angle against the wind   Mnemonic: A Lazy Guide Crosses. "Ahoy! Look, Geography Carries!" = A-L-G-C. Decode: A = Astrolabe (location) and magnetic compass (direction); L = Latitudes and longitudes (modern world map); G = Geography as a formal discipline; C = Caravel (sails at an angle against the wind). Why it sticks: four gifts, four letters; and 1453 is the "why": the Ottomans took Constantinople, so the land routes were effectively blockaded. Teacher: The teacher's correction on the word "blockaded": it is "effectively" blockaded, not literally. The Ottomans demanded a share of the profits on trade, making trade unviable for Europeans. His sketch: a ship with a wind arrow from the upper left, sailing at an angle to it, towards a destination.  The Caravel, sailing at an angle against the wind. Top: silk and spice routes map (red = land, blue = sea) over Europe, Mediterranean, Egypt, Arabia, Persia, Somalia, India, China, Indian Ocean and Java. Bottom: world map Routes after the Age of Discovery, 16th century (Blue = Portugal, White = Spain). Portuguese blue routes from Lisbon, Antwerp and Seville round Africa (Mozambique) to Goa, Cochi, Malacca, Macau, Nagasaki, Tidore and Ternate, and to Brazil (Recife, Salvador, Rio). Spanish white routes across the Americas (Veracruz, Acapulco, Havana, Portobelo, Panama, Cartagena, Callao, Lima) and over the Pacific to Manila.

items.t: 3 · Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494
items.x: Sec 3 Treaty of Tordesillas 1494 (verbatim). Rivalry and mediator: Portugal and Spain competed over who owned the new sea routes and lands; Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. The line: an imaginary line drawn in the Atlantic Ocean, approximately 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands. Division: lands to the EAST of the line went to Portugal; lands to the WEST went to Spain. Why Brazil is Portuguese: Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so it became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas while the rest of the continent became Spanish. Teacher's yellow dotted underlines: 1,185 miles, west of, Cape Verde Islands.   Term   Provision    --- ---    Rivalry and mediator   Portugal and Spain competed over who owned the new sea routes and lands. Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494     The line   An imaginary line in the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands     East   Lands EAST of the line went to Portugal     West   Lands WEST of the line went to Spain     Why Brazil is Portuguese   Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so it became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas; the rest of the continent became Spanish    Map of north-west Africa and the Atlantic with southern Europe (Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania, Senegal, Mali). A red circle marks the Cabo Verde (Cape Verde) islands in the Atlantic, the reference point for the Tordesillas line.  Period map of the Treaty of Tordesillas, anno 1494: a vertical line through the Atlantic, two kings pointing (Spain on the west side, Portugal on the east side), South America and Africa. Teacher's ink: 1492 Columbus reached Central America; arrow Spain (west of the line); a sketch of the Africa funnel, the Cape of Good Hope, and a dotted arrow to East Indies; mid-east circled with India, China, Indonesia and South East Asia all marked as the East; Brazil (only Portugal colony) with a dotted line to the map. Teacher: [1492: Columbus reached Central America] (the Spanish went west). The Portuguese went east round the Cape of Good Hope to the "East Indies", where mid-east, India, China, Indonesia and South East Asia are all "the East." Brazil = the only Portugal colony (in the Americas). The handout defines the East Indies as all lands east of the Cape of Good Hope. Portugal and Spain compete over new sea routes and lands Pope Alexander VI mediates Line ~1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands (good) East of the line: Portugal (warn) West of the line: Spain Brazil's eastern tip falls on the Portuguese side: the only Portuguese colony in the Americas Mnemonic: Spain Sleeps West, Portugal Pushes East. Columbus 1492 sails west; two years later (1494) Pope Alexander VI draws the line. Decode: S-W = Spain gets lands WEST of the line; P-E = Portugal gets lands EAST; line = about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands (1-1-8-5, "one-one-eight-five"); Brazil's eastern tip pokes over the line, so Brazil is the only Portuguese colony in the Americas. Why it sticks: the Portuguese went east round the Cape of Good Hope to the East Indies, so "Portugal = East" feels natural.
