items.t: 4 · The Portuguese in India
items.x: 4.0 · Da Gama at Calicut (1498)  Sec 4 Portuguese Arrive in India. Da Gama at Calicut (1498): armed with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) and backed by the Portuguese Crown, Vasco Da Gama reached Calicut (today's Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, having sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, the southernmost point of Africa. He traded and left: he received permission to trade from the Zamorin of Calicut but faced heavy opposition from Arab traders; no factory or permanent settlement on this voyage. Teacher's ink: NOT COCHIN (beside Calicut); King of Calicut kingdom (over Zamorin). Right-hand board: Primary purpose of Europeans = Trade, not Empire building. But empire building took place in the Americas (weak states) while India had strong states (land powers, i.e. strong armies). Bottom board: resources from mining e.g. gold and silver; if empire building is possible then greater trade profits, and they can get land revenue (LR) and other taxes; with political control, as Government in any territory you can export goods to the home country at low price.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Da Gama at Calicut (1498)   Armed with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) and backed by the Portuguese Crown, Vasco Da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, sailing round the Cape of Good Hope, the southernmost point of Africa     He traded and left   Received permission to trade from the Zamorin of Calicut but faced heavy opposition from Arab traders. No factory or permanent settlement on this voyage   Mnemonic: Gama = Calicut, Cabral = Cochin. "Gama Greets Calicut (98), Cabral Burns it, then Builds in Cochin (00)." Decode: 1498 Da Gama at Calicut, trade permission from the Zamorin, NO factory (teacher: "NOT COCHIN"); 1500 Cabral's first factory at Calicut is destroyed, so he sails south; 1500 first PERMANENT factory at Cochin under the Raja of Cochin. Why it sticks: years go 98 then 00, and "Ga-Ca" (Gama-Calicut) versus "Ca-Co" (Cabral-Cochin) keeps the pairs apart. The handout adds: the Cape was named "Cape of Good Hope" by Portugal's King John II, as it represented hope of finally finding a sea route to India. The teacher wrote "NOT COCHIN" beside Calicut: Da Gama landed at Calicut (1498), and the first permanent factory was at Cochin (1500), not his landing place.  Photo: Vasco da Gama monument at Kappad Beach (Calicut), a stone relief portrait with a ship's wheel and anchor sculpture and the sea behind, where he first landed in India in 1498.  Handout photo: Kappad Beach (Calicut), where Vasco da Gama first landed in India in 1498. Why trade, not empire? (the teacher's board) Teacher: Primary purpose of the Europeans = Trade, not empire building. But empire building did take place in the Americas (weak states), while India had strong states (land powers, i.e. strong armies). And the board adds: resources from mining (gold, silver) are an extra plus; if empire building is possible, there are greater trade profits (+) and they can get land revenue (LR) and other taxes. With political control, as government in any territory you can export goods to the home country at a low price. Why South India was vulnerable (handout): when the Portuguese arrived, the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in India. South India was divided between the Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, without a unified central naval power. This fragmentation let the Portuguese dominate trade and some territory in the 16th century. Character of the Portuguese approach: part commerce, part conquest, part coercion.  Printed map of the west coast of India (Kathiawar to Cape Comorin) with European settlement dates: Diu (1535, Portuguese), Surat (1612, British), Daman (1558, P), Bassein (1533, P), Bombay (1638, B), Goa (1610, P), Cannanore (1501, P), Mahe (1725, French), Calicut (1498, P), Cochin (1500, P) (1669 Dutch), Colombo (1505, P) (1656 Dutch). Caption: Ch 8 Early European arrivals (west coast): Diu, Surat, Goa, Calicut. Teacher's ink: labels Broach/Bharuch, Surat, Diu, Daman, Bassein, Bombay, Goa, Mahe (1725?), Calicut (small kingdom), Cochin (small kingdom on the northern border of Travancore); a north-to-south order sketch: Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, then Goa, Mahe, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. Teacher: Learn the west coast from north to south: Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, Goa, Mahe, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. Calicut = a small kingdom; Cochin = a small kingdom on the northern border of Travancore. Mnemonic: West coast, north to south. "Dear Sir, Do Bring Goa Mangoes; Calicut Cochin Tea." Decode: Dear = Diu; Sir = Surat; Do = Daman; Bring = Bombay; Goa = Goa; Mangoes = Mahe; Calicut = Calicut; Cochin = Cochin; Tea = Travancore. Why it sticks: nine words, nine places, in the teacher's exact order. The dates printed on this map differ from some dates in the handout text (for example Goa 1610 on the map against 1510 in the text; Bombay 1638 on the map against 1668 in the handout). Use the handout text and tables (T1) for exam dates; the map is for locating places and showing who came where. 4.1 · Structure of trade: a State enterprise  4.1 Portuguese Trade Was a State Enterprise. Not a private company: unlike the private companies the British and Dutch would later set up, Portuguese trade was operated as a State enterprise. Estado da India (boxed): directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration, so the Portuguese government itself was the trader. Teacher's ink: English EIC, Dutch VOC/EIC (arrows to British and Dutch); like PSU / Govt; right side: French EIC initially a private company, later taken over by the French Govt. Unlike the private joint-stock companies the British and Dutch later set up, Portuguese trade was a State enterprise called the Estado da India, directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration. The Portuguese government was the trader. Teacher: [Like a PSU / Govt]. The English EIC and the Dutch VOC were private companies. The teacher's side note: the French EIC was initially a private company; later taken over by the French Govt. Mnemonic: Who owns the company? "Portugal = PSU; English and Dutch = Private; French = Private, then PSU." Decode: Estado da India = State enterprise, the Crown was the trader. English EIC and Dutch VOC = private joint-stock companies. French EIC began private and was later nationalised (a PSU). Why it sticks: only the French company changes sides, from private to public. Depot, Factory, Settlement In this period a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. It was a trading post: warehouses for storing goods, offices for trade, homes for company employees, and often a fort for protection. The word comes from "factor," a merchant agent; the factory was where factors worked.  4.1 Depot vs Factory vs Settlement (table). Primary function: Trading Depot (Warehouse) purely storage for goods awaiting ship arrival; Factory (Commercial Hub) administrative and commercial HQ for merchant agents; Settlement (Colonial Enclave) small territorial colony with civil and town administration. Components: basic godowns; offices, warehouses and homes for factors (also called Trading post); factory complex plus surrounding towns and annexed lands. Permanent staff: No; Yes (factors); Yes (factors, soldiers, administrative personnel). Legal status: minimal, simple permission to store goods; factory via formal Imperial or local farmans; Zamindari (revenue) and other sovereign territorial rights. Territorial jurisdiction: No; No; Yes over a defined zone or town. Tax or customs authority: No; No; Yes (taxes can be applied only by a State-like organization). Teacher's ink: think bus depot; Trading post; Don't confuse with LEJ here; for going out of India; Office; multiple factories, warehouses; collect LR and consume LR; L E J (Legislative, Executive, Judicial); Taxes can be charged only by Ruler/Govt.  4.1 Depot vs Factory vs Settlement (State enterprise), continued. Security level: Depot unfortified, low-level guards; Factory often fortified (e.g. Fort Manuel); Settlement heavily fortified military zones with troops. Example: Portuguese warehouses before the Calicut factory (1500); English Factory at Surat (1613); Goa for the Portuguese post-1510, Pondicherry for the French post-1674, Calcutta for the British post-1690. Feature   Trading Depot (Warehouse)   Factory (Commercial Hub)   Settlement (Colonial Enclave) Primary function   Purely storage for goods awaiting ship arrival   Administrative and commercial HQ for merchant agents   Small territorial colony with civil and town administration Core components   Basic godowns and storage rooms   Offices, warehouses, homes for factors (agents); also called Trading post   Factory complex plus surrounding towns and annexed lands Permanent staff   No   Yes: merchant agents known as factors   Yes: factors, soldiers, administrative personnel Legal status   Minimal; simple permission to store goods   Formal Imperial or local farmans   Zamindari (revenue) and other sovereign territorial rights Territorial jurisdiction   No   No   Yes: over a defined zone or town Tax or customs authority   No   No   Yes (taxes only by a State-like body) Security level   Unfortified; low-level guards   Often fortified (e.g. Fort Manuel)   Heavily fortified military zones with troops Example   Portuguese warehouses before Calicut factory (1500)   English factory at Surat (1613)   Goa (Portuguese, post-1510); Pondicherry (French, post-1674); Calcutta (British, post-1690) Mnemonic: Store, Office, State. "Depot stores, Factory trades, Settlement rules." Decode: Depot = godown for goods waiting for the ship (think bus depot; no L-E-J, no tax). Factory = office, factors, farmans, often a fort (e.g. Fort Manuel). Settlement = territory with L-E-J, taxes and troops. Settlement examples climb 10, 74, 90: Goa (post-1510), Pondicherry (post-1674), Calcutta (post-1690). Why it sticks: only the Settlement can collect and consume land revenue, the way a State does. Teacher: [Think bus depot] for a depot ("for going out of India": goods waiting for the ship). A factory is also called a trading post; its function is the "Office." A settlement has multiple factories and warehouses and "collects LR (land revenue) and consumes LR." Don't confuse "LEJ" here: a depot has no (L)egislative, (E)xecutive, (J)udicial jurisdiction; a settlement has sovereign territorial rights: L E J. [Taxes can be charged only by the Ruler / Govt.] Farman, Parwana, Nishan  Teacher's board: Farman (Govt order or notification) branches into three: Imperial or Royal = issued by the King or Emperor; Local or Parwana = by the Governor of a Province; Nishan = by a Prince (son of the King). Left: King, then Governors of Provinces (three branches). Order   Issued by Farman (Imperial or Royal)   King or Emperor Parwana (Local or Provincial)   Governor of a Province Nishan   Prince (son of the King, of the royal blood) Mnemonic: F-P-N goes down the family tree. "Farman = Father-king, Parwana = Province governor, Nishan = Next king (prince)." Decode: Farman = Imperial or Royal order from the King or Emperor; Parwana = Local order from a Provincial Governor; Nishan = order from a Prince of the royal blood. Why it sticks: Top to bottom of power: King, Governor, Prince. The handout defines these when discussing the Danes: Farman (Imperial Decree by the Mughal Emperor), Nishan (Princely Decree by a Prince of the Royal Blood), Parwana (Provincial Decree or Order by a Provincial Governor).  Teacher's board: UPSC Prelims asks (1) where and who set up a factory or fort, (2) a rough idea of the time of setting up of the factory or fort, (3) chronology (1st ORDER, underlined). Teacher: UPSC Prelims: where / who set up a factory or fort; a rough idea of the time; chronology (1st order). 4.2 · Early factories, the first fort and the aggression (1498-1503)  4.2 Early Factories, 1st Fort Manuel (1503) and Aggression (1498-1503). i) Cabral's factories (1500): 1st Portuguese factory in India at Calicut in 1500 by Pedro Cabral, on permission from Samoothiri (Zamorin); short-lived, destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed). Zamorin did not evict Arab traders, so Cabral bombarded Calicut, then sailed south to Cochin where the 1st PERMANENT Portuguese factory was set up (1500) under the Raja of Cochin's protection. ii) Da Gama's 2nd voyage (1502): goal to avenge Cabral's men, force the Zamorin into submission and violently expel Arab competitors; when the Zamorin refused, he bombarded Calicut and massacred innocent fishermen; it disrupted Arab and Venetian domination of the Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea trade. iii) Fort Manuel (1503, Cochin) by Albuquerque: naval commander Afonso de Albuquerque (1509-15) arrived in 1503, defended the Raja of Cochin against the Zamorin and built Fort Manuel before sailing back in 1504; 1st European fort in India. Cochin was the 1st capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530. Teacher's ink: sketch of a slanted line Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore; (1st - 1498) beside Da Gama's 2nd voyage; Notice nature of Portuguese; 1504-15 under Albuquerque; Goa annexed in 1510 (arrow to 1530). 1498: Da Gama at Calicut; trade permission from the Zamorin; no factory 1500, Cabral: first Portuguese factory, Calicut (permission of the Samoothiri/Zamorin); destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed) (bad) Cabral bombards Calicut (the Zamorin would not evict the Arabs) and sails south (good) 1500: first PERMANENT factory, Cochin (protection of the Raja of Cochin) (bad) 1502, Da Gama's 2nd voyage: bombards Calicut, massacres innocent fishermen; aims: avenge Cabral, subdue the Zamorin, expel Arab rivals 1503: Fort Manuel, Cochin (Albuquerque 09-15, then a naval commander): first European fort in India Cochin = first capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530 Mnemonic: Four steps in five years (98, 00, 02, 03). Story: "Gama comes, Cabral burns and builds, Gama avenges, Albuquerque 09-15 walls it." Decode: 1498 Da Gama at Calicut (no factory); 1500 Cabral, first permanent factory at Cochin; 1502 Da Gama's 2nd voyage, bombards Calicut and massacres fishermen to avenge Cabral's men; 1503 Albuquerque 09-15 (then a naval commander) builds Fort Manuel at Cochin, the first European fort in India. Why it sticks: Cochin is both the first factory (1500) and first fort (1503), and stays capital until Goa in 1530. Teacher: The teacher sketched Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore along a slanted line, and marked (1st - 1498) next to Da Gama's second voyage. "Notice the nature of the Portuguese" (the violence). Under Albuquerque 09-15: 1504-15. [Goa annexed in 1510] with an arrow to 1530 (HQ shift). The 2nd voyage disrupted the Arab-Venetian domination of the trade; Europe could now trade directly with India (Portugal a player in the Indian Ocean trade). In the handout, the second voyage marked the forcible integration of Indian Ocean trade into the European mercantilist framework. Albuquerque 09-15's years are written as 09-15 beside his name in the handout, to tell him apart from Almeida 05-09 (05-09); in 1503 he was not yet Governor. 4.3 · Blue Water Policy and the Cartaz System (Almeida 05-09, 1505-09)  4.3 Blue Water Policy and Cartaz System (Almeida 1505-09). Teacher's title note: the decision of the Portuguese to focus on blue waters (oceans or seas); expected also because the primary goal in the 16th c Age of Discovery = Trade; Goa 1510 = exception to this BW policy. 1st Governor: Almeida (1505-09) was the 1st Governor (Viceroy in common usage; legal title Governador, not Viceroy) of the Portuguese Estado da India (ink: CEO of company in India; 1510+ Governor = CEO + CM of Goa). Blue Water Policy: emphasis on NAVAL supremacy rather than territorial conquest; since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. Why South India vulnerable: the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist; South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power. Their approach: focused on commerce, used coercion in trade and engaged in some (boxed) conquest (Goa 1510). Left board: WHY: had a better navy; GOAL = oceanic trade; Indian armies strong; weak since Talikota 1565.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    1st Governor   Francisco de Almeida 05-09 was the 1st Governor of the Portuguese Estado da India (Viceroy in common usage, but the legal title was Governador)     Blue Water Policy   Emphasis on NAVAL supremacy rather than territorial conquest. Since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. The objective: a monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion     Why South India was vulnerable   No Mughal Empire yet (1526-1858); South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power     Their approach   Commerce, coercion in trade, and some (boxed) conquest: Goa 1510   Teacher: Blue Water = oceans and seas. The decision to focus on the blue waters was expected, since the primary goal of the Age of Discovery (16th c) was trade. Goa 1510 = the exception to this Blue Water policy. Almeida 05-09 was the "CEO of the company in India"; from 1510+ the Governor = CEO + CM of Goa. WHY: they had a better navy, the goal was oceanic trade, and Indian armies were strong (so land conquest was hard); the south was also weak since Talikota 1565 (the note is partly unclear on the slide).  Teacher's board: Military, Navy versus Territorial Army. A territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms (plus some had a Navy). Therefore in the 16th c Age of Discovery the Navy of the Europeans was greater than the Navy of Indian powers, usually (why: where Indian navy was good, e.g. Marathas and Travancore, books talk about it). Right: Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain: a state with coastal borders versus a state with only land borders. Land-only: focus on the territorial army. Coastal: focus on territorial army plus Navy, in the budget and technology. Teacher: Territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms. Europe's navy was usually greater than the Indian powers' navy (Marathas and Travancore had good navies, and books talk about it). Land-locked states focus on the territorial army; states with a coast focus on the territorial army plus a Navy, in budget and technology. (Examples on the board: Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain.)  Teacher's board: CARTAZ (circled) analogy. Land: a highway, with a car passing through a TOLL booth. Oceans: a waterway or trade route, with a ship passing through a CARTAZ fees booth. Teacher: Cartaz = a toll booth on the sea. On land a car on a highway pays at a TOLL booth; in the oceans a ship on a trade route pays Cartaz fees.  4.3 (contd). Cartaz System (a naval licensing system, part of the Blue Water Policy): all non-Portuguese ships were forced to buy a pass (a Cartaz) and pay a licence fee to sail safely in the Indian Ocean; pay and get a pass, refuse and face attack. Target Arabs: the Portuguese regularly raided and brutally attacked Arab merchants who controlled the Arabian Sea for generations, and forced local rulers and later Mughal ships to pay for the Cartaz. Battle of Diu (1509): Almeida decisively defeated a massive joint Muslim naval coalition of the Sultanate of Gujarat, the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Zamorin of Calicut, backed by the Ottoman Empire (troops and galleys) and the Republic of Venice; the victory consolidated Portuguese naval supremacy for the next century over the Arabian Sea. Teacher's ink: Indian (beside local rulers); only under Akbar (1556-1605) coastal area added to the Mughal state; Not for Diu itself but for domination of the Arabian Sea; Arabs (over Egypt); all stakeholders of old routes; military ships (beside Ottoman); 1502: defeated Arabs and Zamorin in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. Item   Detail Cartaz System   A naval licensing system, part of the Blue Water Policy: all non-Portuguese ships had to buy a pass (Cartaz) and pay a licence fee. Pay and get a pass; refuse and face attack Target   The Arab traders who controlled the Arabian Sea for generations; also local Indian rulers and, later, Mughal ships Battle of Diu (1509)   Almeida 05-09 decisively defeated a joint Muslim naval coalition: Sultanate of Gujarat, Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, Zamorin of Calicut Backed by   The Ottoman Empire (troops and galleys) and the Republic of Venice (whose spice trade was being destroyed) Result   Portuguese naval supremacy in the Arabian Sea for the next century Mnemonic: Diu 1509: three fight, two back. "G-M-Z fight, O-V back" = "Go Make Zamorin pay; Old Venice backs." Decode: Fighters = Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt, Zamorin of Calicut; backers = Ottoman (troops and galleys) and Venice. Winner = Almeida 05-09, whose last year (09) is also the year of Diu (1509): it was his farewell victory. Why it sticks: the battle was for the Arabian Sea, not for the town of Diu; Cartaz = toll booth on the sea (pay for a pass or be attacked). Teacher: Not a battle for Diu as a territory, but for the domination of the Arabian Sea. The coalition was "all stakeholders of the old routes": Arabs (Egypt), Indian (Gujarat, Zamorin), military ships from the Ottoman. 1502: Arabs and the Zamorin defeated in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. The teacher also notes that only under Akbar 56-05 was the coastal area added to the Mughal state. The handout: the coalition's scale shows how seriously the established trading powers of the Old World viewed the Portuguese threat; Venice's trade was being destroyed by Portuguese dominance of the Indian Ocean. 4.4 · Afonso de Albuquerque 09-15 (2nd Governor, 1509-15)  4.4 Afonso de Albuquerque (2nd Governor, 1509-15). Teacher's title note: set up the 1st fort (Manuel) 1503 in Cochin. Imprisonment and release: Albuquerque brought the King's orders of his appointment as next Governor but was imprisoned as Almeida did not trust him; after the Battle of Diu (1509) a new fleet confirmed the King's orders, so he was released and became 2nd Governor (Governador / Viceroy). Territorial transformation: turned the Portuguese presence from a purely trading enterprise into a territorial colonial State, annexing Goa (1510) from the Sultan of Bijapur for better control of the Arabian Sea (Goa 1510 a notable exception to the Blue Water Policy, a rare land conquest). Teacher's ink: Babur (1526-30) not in India; a sketch of the coast with Goa between north and south. Luso-Indian policy: encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese settlers and Indian women (a substantial share were war widows or captured women, often forced into these marriages without consent); greater political stability via increased numbers; more mansabdars (co-opted). Administrative and religious: integrated local elites into the administration, attempted to regulate practices such as Sati, and promoted Christianity as a tool of political control. Teacher's ink: co-opted; two ways to power: fight all, defeat all, remove all, or co-opt (e.g. B, A, H).   Measure   Detail    --- ---    Imprisonment and release   Albuquerque 09-15 arrived (back in India in 1508) with the King's orders to take over leadership, but Almeida 05-09 did not trust him and arrested him. Goa 1510 = a notable exception to the Blue Water Policy (a rare land conquest)     Luso-Indian policy   Encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese settlers and Indian women (mixed ancestry). A substantial share of the women were war widows or captured women, often forced without consent. Greater political stability     Administrative and religious   Integrated local elites into the administration, attempted to regulate practices such as Sati, and promoted Christianity as a tool of political control   Mnemonic: Almeida 05-09 = Ocean, Albuquerque 09-15 = Annexed. "Almeida 05-09 rules the Ocean; Albuquerque 09-15 Acquires Goa." Decode: Almeida 05-09 = 1st Governor, Blue Water Policy, Cartaz, Diu 1509. Albuquerque 09-15 = 2nd Governor, annexed Goa from Bijapur in 1510 (the exception to Blue Water), Luso-Indian intermarriage. Hand-over year: Almeida 05-09's 09 is Albuquerque 09-15's 09; and 1510 sits right inside his 09-15 span. Why it sticks: A for Albuquerque 09-15, A for Annex. Teacher: The teacher marked [Babur 26-30 not in India] (Babur 26-30 had not yet arrived in 1510). On the Luso-Indian policy: via increased numbers (the Portuguese population grows), like Mughal "more mansabdars" (co-opted). On the elites: "co-opted". Two ways to power: (1) fight all, defeat all, remove all; or (2) co-opt (e.g. Babur 26-30, Akbar 56-05, H...). Co-opt is underlined. The handout says the textbooks often call him "Viceroy," but his legal title was Governador, the formal administrative office that ruled Portuguese territory in India. The same applies to Almeida 05-09.  Teacher's board: Religion = Soft Power. Therefore Conversion leads to a decrease in opposition to the political power of the Christian Portuguese; Conversion leads to a narrative of brotherhood. Example: an increase in Social Power, if success at conversion, leads to an increase in Political Powers.  Teacher's board: Abolition of Sati, or any social reform, can therefore be of 2 intents: (1) Conversion, by weakening the bond of people with their religion, by abolishing, making fun of or targeting the legitimacy of rituals (boxed); (2) Noble intent = reform or women empowerment. Teacher: Religion = Soft Power. Conversion reduces opposition to the political power of the (Christian) Portuguese and gives a narrative of brotherhood: social power (success at conversion) increases political power. Abolition of Sati (or any social reform) can have two intents: (1) Conversion, by weakening the people's bond with their religion (abolishing, making fun of, or targeting the legitimacy of rituals); (2) Noble intent: reform or women's empowerment. 4.5 · Peak under Nuno da Cunha 29-38 (Governor 1529-38)  4.5 Peak under Nuno da Cunha (Governor 1529-38). Capital shifted to Goa (1530): Nuno da Cunha officially shifted the Portuguese HQ from Cochin to Goa in 1530; from here the Portuguese dominated the international trade of the Indian Ocean for nearly a century. Teacher's ink: or capital (over HQ); annexed 1510. Western-coast consolidation: Nuno da Cunha acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, consolidating dominance along the western coast and control over strategic ports and maritime trade routes. Right ink: 1613: Surat factory of EIC after defeating the Portuguese (dotted line to nearly a century).   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Capital shifted to Goa (1530)   Nuno da Cunha 29-38 officially shifted the HQ (capital) from Cochin to Goa in 1530 (Goa annexed 1510). The Portuguese dominated the Indian Ocean trade for nearly a century     Western-coast consolidation   Acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, securing strategic ports and trade routes   Mnemonic: Nuno's 30-34-35. "Thirty: move house. Thirty-four: Bassein. Thirty-five: Diu. Bahadur gave Both." Decode: Nuno da Cunha 29-38 shifted the capital from Cochin to Goa in 1530; acquired Bassein (1534) then Diu (1535), both from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat (B before D, Bassein before Diu). Teacher's extra: Bombay 1534 went with the Bassein deal. Why it sticks: Prelims 2023 asked who surrendered Diu, and the answer is the "B" in the rhyme, Bahadur Shah. Teacher: [1613: the EIC's Surat factory, after defeating the Portuguese] marks the end of the "nearly a century." 4.6 · Religious intolerance: Inquisition and Francis Xavier  4.6 Religious Intolerance. Most aggressive power: the Portuguese were among the most religiously aggressive of all European powers in India; Jesuit missionary activity generated widespread resistance. Slavery and forced conversions: their administration was marked by the slave trade (including in the Hughli settlement in Bengal) and forced conversions. Goa Inquisition (1560-1812): a brutal colonial church court set up to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce Portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy, an era of persecution that caused deep socio-religious backlash. St Francis Xavier (died 1552): in India from 1542, died 1552; spearheaded mass Catholic conversions in coastal India while laying the ideological groundwork for the Goa Inquisition. He died on Shangchuan Island (off China) in 1552, NOT in Goa; his body was later brought to Goa, preserved in the Basilica of Bom Jesus. Teacher's ink: led (arrow from the Xavier row to the Inquisition, a dotted line back from the Inquisition to Xavier).   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Most aggressive power   Among the most religiously aggressive of all European powers in India; Jesuit missionary activity generated widespread resistance     Slavery and forced conversions   The administration was marked by the slave trade (including the Hughli settlement in Bengal) and forced conversions     Goa Inquisition (1560-1812)   A brutal colonial church court to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce Portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy; deep socio-religious backlash     St Francis Xavier   In India from 1542, died 1552; spearheaded mass Catholic conversions in coastal India and laid the ideological groundwork for the Goa Inquisition   Prelims trap (2021): St Francis Xavier did NOT die in Goa. He died on Shangchuan Island (off China) in 1552 while trying to enter mainland China. His body was later brought to Goa and is preserved in the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa. The question tested the place of death, not of burial. Mnemonic: Died in China, resting in Goa. "Shangchuan is where he stopped; Bom Jesus is where he's propped." items.t: 5 · How the Dutch and English broke the Portuguese-Spanish monopoly
items.x: By the second half of the 16th century two new naval powers had emerged: Britain and the Dutch Republic (Netherlands). Both wanted to break the strict monopoly held by Spain and Portugal over European international trade and to achieve freedom of navigation in the oceans. 1588: the British Navy defeated the Spanish Armada ("Invincible Armada") in the Atlantic, severely weakening Spanish-Portuguese naval supremacy. By 1580 Portugal had entered a political union with Spain, so defeating Spain also opened trade routes Portugal had controlled. With the Armada defeated, British and Dutch ships could travel safely to Asia via the Cape of Good Hope. First priority for both: Indonesia (the spice trade of the East Indies). India came later, for a commercial reason: the people of the spice islands had little interest in English or Dutch goods but readily accepted Indian cotton textiles. To buy spices in Indonesia you first needed cloth from India. Mnemonic: Union first, Armada next. "Eighty joins, Eighty-eight sinks": 1580 Portugal joins Spain; 1588 the Armada sinks. Decode: By 1580 Portugal was in a political union with Spain, so when the British Navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588 in the Atlantic, Portuguese routes opened too. British and Dutch ships could now reach Asia via the Cape of Good Hope; first target Indonesia, India came later. Why it sticks: 80 and 88 are 8 years apart, and the same "8" repeats. The handout's clarification: the Netherlands, Holland and "the Dutch Republic" all refer to the same country. "Dutch" is the adjective; "Holland" is technically a region within the Netherlands but is often used as a general name. The trilateral (triangle) trade: England → India → Indonesia → England. This is the commercial logic that shifted the EIC's focus from Indonesia to the Indian subcontinent. (Compare the teacher's triangle in section 1.) Teacher: Board, slide 2: why the monopoly had to be broken. "End the rival's monopoly (e.g. 1502, Da Gama in coastal Malabar) -> a multi-player domain -> establish your own monopoly (requires additional resources), i.e. the Battle of Diu 1509 -> Arabian Sea." Two challenges for the British and the Dutch in trading with the East Indies: (1) How to reach India, China, Indonesia: Spain and Portugal dominate the routes and oceans. (2) How to purchase goods from India: the Portuguese dominate the Indian coastline and the Indian international market. In a small table on the right: "1588: end of monopoly over routes" (the second row was left empty). Teacher: Board, slide 4: who dominated world oceanic trade, by period. 1500s: Portugal vs Spain. 1600s: Dutch vs British. 1700s-1815: British vs French, with the arrow "-> Britain = top naval power." 1870-1945: British + French vs Germany. 1945-91: US vs USSR. 2000s+: US vs China. (The teacher drew smiley faces on the Dutch-British and British-French periods.) Teacher: Slide 5 ink (this section). After "freedom of navigation" he added "in oceans and of TRADE." Underlined: Armada, Atlantic, British and Dutch. Above "Armada": "Naval Fleet." In the trilateral-trade row he struck out both "England" words and wrote "EIC", so the triangle is EIC -> India -> Indonesia -> EIC. Teacher: Board, slide 6 (left): the EIC's triangle. Indonesia at the top, India bottom right, the EIC bottom left. Arrows: the EIC buys goods from India; sells Indian goods to Indonesia; buys Indonesian goods. Teacher: Board, slide 6 (right): CHARTER, State and Company. Charter = founding document, issued by the State (Monarchy or Parliament), granting special powers and rights to a company. State = an organisation with a territorial (circled T) motive (defend, annex), so it has a military and may wage war. A State rules a territory, so coins, currency and taxation are with the State; the circled L, E, J powers are also with the State (my reading: legislative, executive, judicial). Company = an organisation with a profit motive for its shareholders, and it requires property. Mnemonic: State = T, Company = P. "State has T and L-E-J; Company has P." Decode: State = Territory motive (defend, annex), military, may wage war, coins, currency and taxes, and L-E-J (Legislative, Executive, Judicial). Company = Profit motive for shareholders, needs property. Charter = the founding document, issued by the State (Monarchy or Parliament). Why it sticks: later the EIC (a Company) got State-like powers, which is exactly why it could build an empire. items.t: 6 · The Dutch VOC
items.x: 1602: the Dutch East India Company (VOC, Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) was established by a Charter issued by the Dutch Parliament, by merging six smaller Dutch companies that had been competing for eastern trade. Takeaway (handout): the VOC was the world's first multinational company, and the first to issue publicly tradable stocks and shares on a formal exchange: the world's first joint-stock company. An ordinary person could become a part-owner by buying shares, without a say in management: the ancestor of the BSE, NSE, NYSE and the modern shareholder economy. Charter powers: the right to wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts and mint its own currency: powers that ordinarily belong to a State, showing how European powers saw companies as an extension of State power. The first Dutch expedition (1595) went to the East Indies (Indonesia), not India. Dutch settlements in India: Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars) 1605 (first factory), Pulicat (Carnatic) 1610, Surat (Gujarat) 1616, Bimilipatam (Golconda) 1641, Karikal (near Pondicherry) 1645, Chinsura (Bengal) 1653, later Kasimbazar, Baranagore, Patna, Balasore, Nagapatnam, Agra, Cochin (where they captured the Portuguese fort in 1663). At its peak in 1669 the VOC was the richest private company in the world: 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, an army of 10,000 soldiers, 50,000 employees; over its life 5,000 voyages from the Netherlands to the East Indies. 1799: bankrupt and dissolved; possessions taken over by the Dutch government as the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), a Dutch colony until independence in 1945 after World War II. Prelims 2022 trap: the Gajapati dynasty and the Dutch. The claim that the Dutch received land grants from the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha is INCORRECT. The Gajapatis were a 15th-century dynasty centred in Odisha whose power had declined well before the Dutch arrived. Do not confuse later local rulers of the Odisha coast with the Gajapati dynasty itself. items.t: 7 · The English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600
items.x: The English East India Company was formed on 31 December 1600: its founding document was a Royal Charter issued by Queen Elizabeth I 58-03. A Royal Charter is essentially a licence granted by the Monarch. If it was not renewed, the company would legally cease to exist. This shaped the EIC's relationship with the British State for the next two and a half centuries: its survival depended on the goodwill of whoever held power in Britain. The EIC was the 4th joint-stock company in England, formed by pooling money from 215 London merchants ("merchant adventurers") who wanted to challenge Dutch dominance in European trade with the East. The stated goal was trade with the East, not empire-building or colonialism. Britain or England? In 1600 it was England (not Britain) that granted the Charter. England and Scotland united in 1707 to create the Kingdom of Great Britain; in 1801 Ireland was added, creating the United Kingdom. Before 1707 "British" technically means English. What the Royal Charter of 1600 gave the EIC A monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies for 15 years. The right to carry gold (foreign exchange) out of England to purchase eastern goods. Management by a body of private people: a Governor, a Deputy Governor and 24 members, which later evolved into the Board or Court of Directors. Mnemonic: Mo-Go-Man: three gifts of 1600. "Monopoly, Gold, Management." Decode: Mo = Monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies for 15 years (NOT "trade with India"; the teacher corrected this); Go = right to carry Gold (forex) out of England; Man = Management by a Governor, a Deputy Governor and 24 members (later the Court of Directors). Why it sticks: Elizabeth I 58-03 signed on 31 Dec 1600; 215 merchants; the 4th joint-stock company in England. The handout's forex aside: for a State, forex is the currency that matters in international trade; domestic currency works only within a country's borders (like a household's internal reward system for children, valid only inside the home). Until 1971, Gold was forex, until the Dollar took over. (Same idea as the teacher's board in section 1.) Teacher: Ink on the 1600 Charter slides (slides 12 to 16). Board, slide 12: the EIC = joint-stock company; special rights and powers via a Charter (31 Dec 1600); Dutch competition. Slide 13: he underlined founding document, Royal Charter and Elizabeth I 58-03. Teacher: Board, slide 14: why is the VOC (1602) called the first joint-stock company when the English EIC (1600) was also one? "Answer: in 1600 the EIC was not a proper joint-stock company. It operated on a per-VOYAGE system: before each journey to the East Indies the EIC gathered Rs from the public; brought and sold goods in Europe at a profit and shared all the profits; for the next journey, repeated. It is later that the EIC became a proper joint-stock company, i.e. one with permanent capital." Board, slide 15: a proper joint-stock company "does not usually give back all profits; it gives dividends." A pie of the profit: Retain, Re-invest, assets, Dividends. Teacher: Slide 16, what the Charter gave: the teacher's correction. Underlined: England's trade, for 15 years, right to carry gold, out of England, private people, Court (of Directors). "WRONG = monopoly over trade with India with the EIC. CORRECT = monopoly over England's (or British) trade with the East Indies, with the EIC." A line from Grant 2 to "forex is controlled by the State." Under Grant 3: "BoD/CoD = EIC's top decision-making body = not any government organisation." Mnemonic: Per-trip ticket versus permanent pot. "EIC 1600 = pay, sail, share, repeat; VOC 1602 = one pot, dividends." Decode: EIC in 1600 worked per VOYAGE (collect money, sell goods, share all profits, start again). The VOC (1602) had permanent capital and gave dividends (retain, re-invest, assets, dividends). The EIC became a continuous joint-stock fund only in 1657 (Cromwell 51-60). Why it sticks: think of a one-trip cab share versus a company that keeps its shareholders' money. items.t: 8 · Charters until 1793: the EIC's changing legal character
items.x: The EIC's legal existence depended on Charter renewal, and the Charters also tell the shift of power in Britain from the Monarch to Parliament. Year   Event   What it did 1600   Founding Charter (Queen Elizabeth I 58-03, 1558-1603)   15-year monopoly on East Indies trade; carry gold out; Governor, Deputy Governor and 24 members 1601-03   First voyage (James Lancaster)   Sailed not to India but to Indonesia (Java and Sumatra); first EIC factory there; looted the Portuguese ship Sao Tome in the Strait of Malacca 1609   Charter of King James I 03-25   Replaced the 15-year monopoly with a perpetual (indefinite) monopoly 1657   Cromwell 51-60's Charter   Reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company (continuous capital fund) 1661   Charter of King Charles II 60-85   Quasi-State powers: forts, troops, war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction (right to mint money came in 1676) 1793 onwards   Parliament takes over   Parliament begins passing Acts to renew the Charter 1601-03, the first voyage (James Lancaster): the fleet sailed not to India but to Indonesia, consistent with the EIC's original priority of the spice trade. They reached Java and Sumatra, where they set up the very first EIC factory. On the way Lancaster's fleet looted a Portuguese ship, the Sao Tome, in the Strait of Malacca (a cargo of textiles and spices). William Dalrymple and others note that the EIC's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy. Shareholders got substantial dividends; the fleet returned in 1603. 1609, James I 03-25: the original 15-year monopoly became a perpetual monopoly. 1657, Cromwell 51-60's Charter: Context: Charles I 25-49 tried to levy taxes without Parliament's consent, which triggered the English Civil War (1642-51). The Parliamentarians (largely Protestant) defeated the Royalists; Charles I 25-49 was beheaded in 1649; England became a Republic under Oliver Cromwell 51-60 (the handout writes his years as 51-60). After Cromwell 51-60's death in 1658 his son briefly took over, but the experiment proved autocratic and unpopular. In 1660 the Monarchy was restored under Charles II 60-85. Cromwell 51-60 issued a new Charter in 1657, declaring the previous Royal Charter invalid, and reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company. Earlier, money was raised voyage by voyage (pool, voyage, profits, fund dissolved); from 1657 one continuous unified capital fund, giving a stable financial foundation. 1661, Charles II 60-85's Charter (after the Restoration) was arguably the most consequential legally: it turned the EIC from a commercial trading body into a quasi-State power. It gave the right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over settlements in India. (The right to mint its own money came in 1676.) From 1793 Parliament takes over: the British Parliament begins passing Acts for the renewal of the EIC's Charter, mirroring the democratisation of Britain (power moving from Crown to elected representatives). Indian constitutional history and British political history are inseparable threads. Mnemonic: Lancaster loots first. "Lancaster sailed to Spice Islands, not India, and stole his first profit." Decode: First voyage 1601-03 under James Lancaster went to Indonesia (Java and Sumatra), set up the first EIC factory there, and looted the Portuguese ship Sao Tome in the Strait of Malacca; the fleet returned in 1603. Why it sticks: "first profit = piracy" (Dalrymple's point in the chapter). Mnemonic: Charter ladder: E-J-C-C-P. "Every Jolly Child Climbs Parliament." Decode: Elizabeth I 58-03 (1600, 15-year monopoly); James I 03-25 (1609, perpetual); Cromwell 51-60 (1657, permanent joint-stock fund); Charles II 60-85 (1661, quasi-State powers); Parliament (1793 onwards, Acts renew the Charter). Why it sticks: the teacher's "imp" years are 1600, 1661 and 1793 (the first, fourth and last rung); 1609, 1657 and 1676 are "not imp". Mnemonic: Kings out, kings in. "Charles I 25-49 loses his head the year his reign ends (49); Cromwell 51-60's 51-60 ends the year Charles II 60-85's 60-85 begins (60)." Decode: English Civil War 1642-51; Charles I 25-49 beheaded 1649; Republic under Cromwell 51-60; 1660 Restoration; Charles II 60-85. Cromwell 51-60's 1657 Charter ended the per-voyage system. Why it sticks: each reign's last two digits chain into the next: 49, then 51-60, then 60-85. Takeaway (1661): the 1600 EIC was a merchant association with a trade monopoly; the 1661 EIC had the legal powers of a State within its territories. A trading company had, through successive Charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign. Mnemonic: 1661 = FTWC, "Fort, Troops, War, Court". Charles II 60-85 turns merchants into a "semi-State". Decode: F = build Forts; T = command Troops; W = make War and peace; C = civil and criminal jurisdiction (Court). The right to mint money is later (1676, "not imp"). "Any company or citizen of a State must follow (a) the law of the home country and (b) the law of the foreign country where it operates. A State's powers: territorial jurisdiction (circled T) and subject jurisdiction." "The EIC built an empire in India, and the EIC = a Company (empire = 'Company State'). Legally possible because of the 1661 Charter, which gave the EIC State-like powers: war and peace, army, and (a circled letter plus 'er', unclear: possibly 'over') ..." items.t: 9 · The Danish East India Company
items.x: Established 1616, out of envy of Dutch and English profits. Its Charter was issued by King Christian IV 88-48 of Denmark-Norway, granting a 12-year monopoly on trade between Denmark-Norway and the East Indies. The Danes were never in the same league: weaker finance, limited military capacity. The first Danish company ended around 1650; a second Danish EIC was set up in 1670 but wound down gradually, selling all its Indian mainland settlements to the British EIC by 1845. Danish settlements in India 1620: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu: first factory; first fort: Fort Dansborg; official administrative HQ of Danish India from 1620 until 1845. 1624: Pondicherry (brief): under Roland Crappe; a short-lived factory, abandoned for lack of resources, long before the French arrived. 1625: Masulipatnam (Andhra Pradesh); Pipli and Balasore (Odisha). 1755: Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore), Hooghly district, Bengal: a parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan 40-56. Tranquebar remained the HQ, but Serampore became the most commercially successful and culturally significant Danish post. Colonial powers in Tranquebar, Serampore and the Nicobar Islands (the Nicobars were sold separately to the British in 1868; today part of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands UT). 1799-1800: Serampore Mission Press, associated with Baptist missionaries including William Carey: translated the Bible into Indian vernacular languages, ran schools, and made an immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal. Their architectural legacy at Tranquebar and Serampore and their missionary work (not forced conversions) are the most visible Danish traces. Mnemonic: Danes: 20, 24, 25, then 55. "Tranquebar twenty, Pondicherry twenty-four, Pipli twenty-five; Serampore fifty-five." Decode: 1616 Charter of Christian IV 88-48 (12-year monopoly); 1620 Tranquebar (Tamil Nadu, first factory, Fort Dansborg, HQ till 1845); 1624 Pondicherry (Roland Crappe, brief); 1625 Masulipatnam, Pipli, Balasore; 1755 Serampore (parwana from Alivardi Khan 40-56); 1799-1800 Serampore Mission Press (William Carey). Tranquebar = Carnatic, Serampore = Bengal (teacher's labels). Why it sticks: arrival order is "P-E-V-D": Portugal 1500, EIC 1600, VOC 1602, Danes 1616 (order of company founding); the teacher ticked 1616, 1620, 1755 and 1799-1800. Year   Event or settlement   Permission or source 1616   Danish East India Company established   Charter of King Christian IV 88-48, 12-year monopoly 1620   Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) and Fort Dansborg   First factory; admin HQ of Danish India till 1845 1624   Pondicherry (brief)   Under Roland Crappe; abandoned shortly after 1625   Masulipatnam; Pipli and Balasore   None noted 1650   First Danish company ends   None noted 1670   Second Danish EIC established   None noted 1755   Serampore (Frederiksnagore), Bengal   Parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan 40-56 1799-1800   Serampore Mission Press   With William Carey and Baptist missionaries 1845   All mainland settlements sold to the British EIC   None noted 1868   Nicobar Islands sold to the British   None noted Teacher: Ink on the Danes (slides 24 and 25). items.t: 10 · How the EIC broke Portuguese dominance: Hawkins, Swally and Surat
items.x: 1608: the EIC decided to set up a factory at Surat, then the most important port on India's west coast and firmly within Portuguese-dominated territory. It sent Captain William Hawkins to the court of Jahangir 05-27. Jahangir 05-27 first gave Hawkins a Mansab (rank of 400) and a Jagir, but Hawkins was ultimately expelled from the Mughal court due to persistent Portuguese pressure. The lesson: Portugal had to be defeated militarily before the EIC could establish itself on the west coast. 1612, Battle of Swally (Suvali): Captain Thomas Best led a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese. The Mughal State had its own reason to welcome this: Mughal ships traded in the Arabian Sea but were perpetually vulnerable to Portuguese piracy, a source of humiliation for a great land power. Impressed by English sea capability, Jahangir 05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613, giving the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat. 1612 versus 1613: 1612 = the Battle of Swally (military victory) and the local Mughal governor's temporary permission/parwana; 1613 = the legally permanent establishment, when Jahangir 05-27 ratified the local agreement with an imperial farman. 1608: EIC wants a Surat factory; sends Captain William Hawkins to Jahangir 05-27 (bad) Hawkins gets a Mansab (400) and Jagir but is expelled under Portuguese pressure Lesson: defeat Portugal militarily first (good) 1612: Battle of Swally: Captain Thomas Best defeats the Portuguese Mughals welcome it: their ships were vulnerable to Portuguese piracy (good) 1613: Jahangir 05-27's Royal Farman: permanent factory at Surat Mnemonic: Hawkins Hurt, Best Beat, Roe Reaped. "H-B-R: 1608 fail, 1612 fight, 1615-19 rights." Decode: Hawkins (1608, Surat factory bid at Jahangir 05-27's court) got Mansab 400 and a Jagir but was expelled under Portuguese pressure; Thomas Best won the Battle of Swally (1612) against the Portuguese; Roe (1615-19) got the Royal Farman of 1618 with liberal trading rights. Why it sticks: Portugal had to be beaten militarily first, so the fighter (Best) comes between the two diplomats. Mnemonic: 12 is the Sword, 13 is the Seal. "Swally 12 = sword; Surat 13 = signed paper." Decode: 1612 Battle of Swally (Best, military victory, marked "imp") and a temporary local permission; 1613 Jahangir 05-27's Royal Farman making the Surat factory permanent. Prelims 2006 asked the 1613 factory: Surat. Why it sticks: S-S: Swally, Sword; Surat, Seal. Teacher: Ink on Hawkins, Swally and Surat (slides 27 to 29). Slide 27: "Jahangir 05-27" at the top; "imp" above the 1612 Battle of Swally; underlined 1612, Captain Thomas Best, Suvali and rank 400. The 1613 Royal Farman heading is circled. Box 1: "FACTORY" splits into "Warehouse" and "Home, offices for staff." In the lesson box: "Began attacking Mughal ships" (the Portuguese). Box 3: "ESTADO DA INDIA (sad face) vs EIC (happy face)," and "FOR TRADE [not the territory (T) of Surat]": the EIC wanted trade rights, not Surat as territory. Teacher: Board, slide 28: why the EIC's army stayed small until Bengal. "A company = an organisation with a PROFIT motive (of the shareholder), e.g. the EIC had an army of about 500-800 men. If it spent Rupees on an army, it would go against that goal (sad face). If the army came from its own Rupee, it would be small, to meet the core interests of trade." Starred: "1757: free Rupee of Bengal" -> "Large army," "i.e. why Plassey 1757, imp." (Plassey 1757 is marked important.) Teacher: Board, slide 29: Britain's national interest and the EIC. "Britain's national interest = the EIC's interest." Roe = "a government person working for the EIC's benefit." Four points: (1) Britain's trade with the East Indies = the EIC's trade; (2) the EIC has a monopoly over Britain's trade with the East Indies; (3) via the EIC, Britain can dominate WORLD trade. His lesson: "Put companies to act as agents of the State in geopolitics, e.g. the USA's use of companies for implementing sanctions on Russia" (marked "imp").  Lecture 11 slide 27: how the EIC broke Portuguese dominance. Teacher's ink: "imp" over 1612 Battle of Swally; "Factory = warehouse + home/offices"; "Estado da India vs EIC, for trade, not territory of Surat".  Teacher's board (slide 28): a company has a profit motive, so the EIC's army was small (about 500-800 men) until the free Rupee of Bengal after 1757; "Plassey 1757 imp".  Teacher's board (slide 29): Britain's national interest = the EIC's interest; Roe as a government person working for the EIC; companies as agents of the State in geopolitics.

items.t: 11 · The Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)
items.x: England wanted liberal trading rights across the entire Mughal Empire, so King James I 03-25 sent Thomas Roe as formal ambassador to Jahangir 05-27's court. Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 and stayed until 1619. Jahangir 05-27 refused a formal treaty between equals (a trading company was no sovereign equal). Through sustained diplomacy and personal rapport Roe got a series of privileges and a Royal Farman (1618) allowing the EIC to set up factories throughout the Mughal Empire with liberal trading rights: lower customs duties and ease of doing business. 1616-19: new factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach (Bharuch). With Surat they formed the Surat Presidency (1618): the EIC's first administrative Presidency in India, coordinating English trade on the west coast until the later shift to Bombay (1687). Portuguese enraged; naval conflicts continued. 1631-32: Shahjahan 27-58 ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to defeat the Portuguese and eject them from Hugli, because they were misusing their trade privileges with piracy and the slave trade from their Bengal base. Mnemonic: Roe's three: "Aa Aa Bharuch". A-A-B: Agra, Ahmedabad, Broach (Bharuch). Decode: Roe (ambassador, arrived 1615, stayed to 1619) got the Royal Farman of 1618 and new factories in 1616-19 at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach; with Surat these formed the Surat Presidency (1618), the first Presidency. Hugli 1631-32: Shah Jahan 27-58 had Qasim Khan eject the Portuguese for piracy and the slave trade. Why it sticks: Prelims 2015 and 2021 asked first-quarter 17th-century factories: only Broach was right ("bas Bharuch", Hindi bas = only); Chicacole and Trichinopoly had none. Roe's account, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul, is one of the most important primary sources on the Mughal Empire of this period (court administration, wealth, politics, daily life). Teacher: Ink on Roe (slides 30 and 31). Top right: "Ambassador, i.e. British Resident in Jahangir 05-27's court" (starred). Underlined: the title of Roe's memoir, Royal Farman (1618), the right to establish factories across the Empire plus lower duties and ease of business ("= LIBERAL TRADING RIGHTS"), and Surat Presidency (1618). Under Surat Presidency: "HQ (e.g. Cochin 1505-1530, HQ of Portugal; Tranquebar, HQ of the Danes 1620)": a Presidency was the EIC's regional HQ, like those earlier HQs. Slide 31: "27-58" (Shah Jahan's reign code) written above the Hugli row; underlined Hugli action (1631-32) and slave trade.  Lecture 11 slide 30: Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe. Teacher's ink: Ambassador = British Resident at Jahangir's court; "= LIBERAL TRADING RIGHTS"; HQ examples Cochin 1505-30 and Tranquebar 1620.

items.t: 12 · Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661: dowry diplomacy
items.x: The treaty, signed at Whitehall, London, marked the marriage of King Charles II 60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal. 1. Portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash. 2. England received Bombay and Tangier (Morocco). 3. Trade and military cooperation, with England agreeing to protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Result: a continued Portuguese presence in Goa, Daman and Diu under English protection, lasting until 1961, when independent India took over these territories militarily, after a people's movement. 1668: the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at an annual rent of 10 pounds: the start of Bombay's journey from a Portuguese dowry to the commercial capital of British India. Mnemonic: The Bride's Basket: B-T-B. "Bombay, Tangier, Bucks (500,000 pounds)." Decode: Treaty of 1661, signed at Whitehall: Charles II 60-85 marries Catherine of Braganza. Dowry = Bombay + Tangier (Morocco) + 500,000 pounds cash; England protects Portugal's remaining possessions (Goa, Daman, Diu, till 1961). Seven years later, 1668, Bombay goes to the EIC at 10 pounds a year; Bombay Presidency in 1687, about 20 years after 1668 (teacher's "20 yrs" bracket). Why it sticks: 61 wedding, 68 rent, 87 HQ; Bombay is also a cluster of seven islands, and 1687 ends in 7. Teacher: Ink on the 1661 Treaty (slides 32 and 33). Under the title: "Restoration of MONARCHY 1660." Underlined: Whitehall, King Charles II 60-85, Princess Catherine of Braganza, dowry and 500,000 pounds in cash, Bombay and Tangier (in Morocco), military cooperation, protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Beside Term 3: "[Goa, Daman and Diu]." A rough map: EU at the top, Africa below, and Morocco circled (Tangier). Teacher: Board, slide 33: two ways to deal with a rival. (1) "End your rival 100% (destroy)": "Power = 100." (2) (V2) "Thrash the rival and lessen his power permanently; huge anxiety in the rival about survival; instead of (1), convert the rival into your puppet or a junior permanent friend," "non-threatening, never big enough." Result: "Power = 100 + 90" (the second number is partly unclear). The slide follows the 1661 treaty, but the board does not name the countries.  Lecture 11 slide 32: the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661. Teacher's ink: "Restoration of MONARCHY 1660", "[Goa, Daman and Diu]", a sketch of Europe, Africa and Morocco (Tangier), and many underlines.  Teacher's board (slide 33): two strategies against a rival: destroy it 100% (power = 100), or thrash it and make it a puppet or junior permanent friend (power = 100 + 90). Teacher: Board, Lecture 12 slide 2: who beat whom, and why the EIC won. Top row: Portuguese -> "British vs Portuguese" plus "Dutch vs Portuguese" -> the two winners meet in "British vs Dutch" -> "By 1650s" (underlined). Then a grid of South Asia and South East Asia. MAJOR: British in South Asia, Dutch in South East Asia. Minor presence: Dutch in South Asia (a bracket under the Dutch reads Indonesia) and British in South East Asia (bracket: Singapore, Malaya). The brackets sit where the teacher drew them; the grid matches the Treaty of Breda terms in section 13. Teacher: Result: how the EIC won the competition. "For INTERNATIONAL TRADE (boxed) [not T (circled)] of India, i.e. who will BUY Indian GOODS." Then, bracketed and starred: "PRIMARY purpose of empire = TRADE." Why this matters: the rivals were fighting over who would buy Indian goods, not over land (T = territory). The same idea is on the Lecture 10 board for Surat ("for trade, not the territory of Surat").  Lecture 12 slide 2, teacher's board: Portuguese beaten by the British and the Dutch, then British vs Dutch by the 1650s; major and minor presence grid for South Asia and South East Asia; result: the EIC won the competition for international trade (not territory), primary purpose of empire = trade.

items.t: 13 · The Dutch: rise, dominance and fall in Asia
items.x: 1623, the Amboyna Massacre: the Dutch killed English traders in the spice islands, a brutal episode that ended English ambitions in Indonesia; the Dutch had effectively removed both the English and the Portuguese from Indonesia. 1658: the Dutch removed the Portuguese from Ceylon. Anglo-Dutch wars 1654-67, settled in the Treaty of Breda (1667): (1) the British leave Indonesia to the Dutch; (2) the Dutch leave the English alone in India; (3) both keep minor presences in each other's primary domains. Cochin: captured from the Portuguese in 1663, held as HQ of Dutch Malabar (not the overall HQ). Mnemonic: Dutch chain: 23, 58, 63, 67. "Amboyna kills, Ceylon falls, Cochin captured, Breda divides." Decode: 1623 Amboyna Massacre ends English ambitions in Indonesia; 1658 Dutch remove the Portuguese from Ceylon; 1663 Cochin captured; 1667 Treaty of Breda ends the Anglo-Dutch wars (1654-67): the war ends in the treaty year. Why it sticks: Breda is a swap. British leave Indonesia to the Dutch, the Dutch leave the English alone in India, and each keeps only a minor presence in the other's home zone (British: Singapore, Malaya). Teacher: Ink on slide 3. Above the table, "Java, Sumatra" with a tick pointing down: the Dutch zone is Indonesia. Under the 1623 row: "INDONESIAN TRADE" (the label for the Amboyna Massacre row). Underlined: Indonesia, Anglo-Dutch rivalry, "settled" (the Treaty of Breda settled it), Pulicat 1610-1690, Nagapattinam 1690-1795 and 1759 Bedara (Chinsura). Marthanda Varma 29-58 is written 29-58.  Lecture 12 slide 3: Dutch rise, dominance and fall. Teacher's ink: Java, Sumatra with a tick; INDONESIAN TRADE under 1623; Marthanda Varma 29-58; a Cochin, Travancore, Colachel sketch; the Amazon India example (India HQ Bengaluru, regional HQ Gurgaon, North). Teacher: Board, slide 4: the coast zones. A V-shaped peninsula. West side, top to bottom: Gujarat (circle), Konkan, Malabar. East side: Bengal (circle at the top), Coromandel. The next slide places the Dutch locations on this map.  Lecture 12 slide 4, teacher's board: V-shaped peninsula with Gujarat, Konkan and Malabar on the west side and Bengal and Coromandel on the east side. Timeline   Location   Role or status 1605   Masulipatnam   First Dutch factory in India (on a farman from the Sultan of Golconda) 1610-1690   Pulicat (Fort Geldria)   First Dutch fort and main HQ (Coromandel Coast); built on the ruins of an earlier Portuguese structure with Vijayanagara permission 1690-1795   Nagapattinam (Negapatam)   Main HQ (shifted from Pulicat) 1663-1795   Cochin (Fort Kochi)   HQ of Dutch Malabar only, NOT overall HQ 1655-1795   Chinsura   HQ of Dutch Bengal (Fort Gustavus) Teacher: Ink on slide 5 (Dutch locations). Underlined: Masulipatnam, "First Dutch factory," Geldria, "First Dutch fort," "Main HQ" (Pulicat) and Nagapattinam, "Main HQ" (Nagapattinam). A dotted arrow runs from Main HQ at Pulicat down to Main HQ at Nagapattinam: the main HQ moved (1690). Fort Gustavus (Chinsura) has only a dotted underline. Side sketch of the peninsula: top part "N. Overall main HQ: Pulicat (1610-90), then Nagapattinam (1690-1795). (The handout dates Chinsura's Fort Gustavus as 1655-1795, while section 6 and Table T2 list the Chinsura factory as 1653.) items.t: 14 · Napoleon's link: the Kew Letters (1795)
items.x: 1795, during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) leading into the Napoleonic Wars (1804-15): the French army invaded the Netherlands, overthrew the Dutch government and set up a puppet State, the Batavian Republic, controlled by France. Britain declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory. The exiled Dutch leader Prince William V 51-95 had fled to London and issued the "Kew Letters": orders telling Dutch colonial governors to hand over their territories to the British "for safekeeping," so France could not seize them. The British used this as their legal basis to take over the remaining Dutch posts. By 1795 the British occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin (Kerala), Chinsura (Bengal), Pulicat and Tuticorin (Coromandel), and the coastal regions of Ceylon (Trincomalee and Colombo). The teacher marked the Kew Letters "[SYLLABUS X]" (Lecture 11, slide 11): not in the syllabus. Read this section for the story of the Dutch fall, not as an exam topic. Teacher: Ink on slide 6. Under the title: "NOT imp FROM exam - FOR UNDERSTANDING." This is the same call as the Lecture 11 mark "SYLLABUS X" above: read the Kew Letters for the story, do not memorise them. He also inserted "over" so that the line reads "hand over their territories," and wrote "Kew = place near London."

items.t: 15 · Why Ceylon did not become part of British India: the Crown Colony
items.x: 1795-96: the British captured the Dutch areas of Ceylon and gave administration to the EIC, through the Madras Presidency. Treaty of Amiens, 1802: a peace treaty in Europe between Britain and France along with its Dutch ally, the Batavian Republic. The Dutch formally and permanently ceded the coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain. The British government decided Ceylon was too strategically important to be run by a trading company: it removed the EIC's administration entirely and declared Ceylon a British Crown Colony, ruled directly by an appointed British Governor, separate from the EIC's Indian empire. Takeaway: India was a colony ruled by the EIC (a commercial entity with State-like powers); Ceylon was a Crown Colony where the British State itself governed directly. Mnemonic: India Inc. versus Ceylon Crown. "India = Company's colony; Ceylon = Crown's colony." Decode: India was ruled by the EIC (a commercial entity with State powers). Ceylon: captured from the Dutch in 1795-96, ceded in the Treaty of Amiens (1802), then the EIC was removed and the British State ruled it directly through an appointed Governor. Why it sticks: the teacher says the Ceylon story is "not imp", but the meaning of Crown Colony is "imp": ruled directly by the British State. Teacher: Ink on slide 7 (Crown Colony). The words "Crown Colony" in the title are boxed, with "(not imp) BUT concept" and below it "imp: Meaning." So: the Ceylon story is not important for the exam, but the meaning of "Crown Colony" is. Board: British Colonies, RULED BY -> "EIC" = Company's Colony; "Br State" (boxed) = Crown Colony. Under the Amiens panel: "Rule = Doing L, E, J on a T" (L, E, J and T each circled): to rule is to do the Legislative, Executive and Judicial work on a Territory (LEJ as in section 4.1). Underlined in the last panel: "ruled directly" and "by the British State."  Lecture 12 slide 7: why Ceylon became a Crown Colony. Teacher's ink: Crown Colony boxed with (not imp) BUT concept, imp: Meaning; board of British Colonies ruled by the EIC (Company's Colony) or by the British State (Crown Colony); Rule = Doing L, E, J on a T. items.t: 16 · What were Presidencies?
items.x: A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade. A settlement got Presidency status when it had grown large enough with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings and a fort. Initially small coastal towns; as the EIC annexed surrounding territories the towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into provinces of British India (governed directly by the British). The Presidencies were named after the major forts built within them.  Handout diagram: a small EIC factory (trading post), growth in trade and territory, Presidency (regional HQ), expansion into a province of British India. "Surat 1613 Factory" -> "Br: 1st Presidency = Surat (1618)" (Surat underlined); then "shift to Bombay: 1687 (year?)." Right: "Bombay with EIC: since 1668"; "Bombay = Presidency = HQ = 1687" (Western HQ), with a "20 yrs" bracket between 1668 and 1687; "Calcutta settlement 1690" -> "Presidency = 1699" (East India); "Madraspatnam (village): ___" -> "Presidency 1652" (South). The board gives the first year of each pair: 1652 (London order; 1653 implemented) and 1699 (1699/1700 in the handout). Learn both years as in the handout. Mnemonic: Presidency order: S-M-B-C. "Sweet Mangoes Beat Cherries." Under Growth: "To Settlement" -> Settlement splits into Town and Rule/Admin (POLITICAL). Under Presidency: "In Beginning, Presidency = BIG TOWN or CITY"; "Madras, Bombay, Calcutta = TRADE HQs (REGIONAL HQs)." items.t: 17 · How each of the three Presidencies came to be
items.x: 17.1 · Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653) The EIC's first factory in India was a temporary one at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in the Northern Sarkars (Andhra Pradesh) in 1611. (Northern Sarkars = the northern coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh, outside Mughal direct control.) 1639: the EIC, led by Francis Day, purchased land at the village of Madraspatanam from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of the Vijayanagara Empire, 1336-1646) and built Fort St George (1639-44): the first fort built by the EIC in India and the anchor of the first permanent settlement. 1690: the EIC purchased a fort at Cuddalore (south of Madras) from the Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram 89-00 and named it Fort Saint David. Its history: partly built by the Dutch from 1608; construction halted due to Portuguese pressure on the Vijayanagara Empire; a Hindu merchant eventually completed it. In 1677 Shivaji 74-80 conquered the nearby Jinji fort and region including Cuddalore before it passed to the EIC. The Madras Presidency was formally established as the Presidency of Fort St George in 1652, on the orders of the Court of Directors in London; because of the ship travel time, it was implemented in India in 1653. (Both dates appear in sources: the London order versus the on-ground implementation.) Mnemonic: Day in 1639, London 52, ship 53. "Francis Day buys at daybreak, 1639." Decode: First EIC factory in India = Masulipatnam, 1611, temporary. 1639: Francis Day buys Madraspatanam from the Hindu Nayakas (Vijayanagara governors, 1336-1646); Fort St George built 1639-44 (first EIC fort). Presidency: ordered in London 1652, implemented in India 1653 (the ship takes a year). Why it sticks: both 1639 and 1611 sit in the "first" bracket; 52 then 53 is just one step. Teacher: Ink on slide 13 (Madras). Top right: "FACTORY = warehouses + home and office + MAY be a [FORT]" (FORT boxed; "home and office" is hard to read): a factory may or may not have a fort. Underlined: 1st EIC factory, temporary, Masulipatnam, 1611, 1639, Madraspatanam, Hindu Nayakas (Vijayanagara governors), Fort St George (1639-1644) and Presidency of Fort St George (1652). Under Vijayanagara: "1336-1646" (the dynasty's span). Teacher: Ink on slide 15 (Fort St David). Under the 1690 row: "After death of Sambhaji 80-89, Rajaram 89-00 left Svarajya, shifted to e.g. Jinji in Carnatic": the Maratha Chhatrapati who sold the fort had moved to Jinji in the Carnatic. Beside "Layered build": "not imp" (the Dutch, Portuguese and Hindu merchant history of the fort is not needed). Board: a large oval = Madras Presidency, cut by a diagonal with two dots, Madras and Cuddalore: "2 FORTS in Madras Presidency: Madras and Cuddalore." Teacher's ink: FACTORY = warehouses + home and office + may be a FORT (boxed); Vijayanagara 1336-1646; 1st permanent factory = Surat 1613; Presidency 1618; 1534-1661 Portugal; FORT arrow to Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta). Teacher's ink: after the death of Sambhaji 80-89 Rajaram left Svarajya and shifted to Jinji in the Carnatic; Layered build not imp; board of the Madras Presidency with two forts, Madras and Cuddalore. 17.2 · Bombay Presidency (1687) From 1613 to 1687 Surat was the EIC's main trade centre on the west coast. The shift happened because of the growing power of the Marathas in Gujarat, making Surat increasingly risky. Bombay, a cluster of seven islands, offered a more defensible location. Charles II 60-85 received Bombay in 1661 as part of the Portuguese dowry and transferred it to the EIC in 1668 at 10 pounds per annum. The Bombay Presidency was established in 1687, replacing Surat as the western HQ. Bombay Castle (Casa da Orta) was originally built by the Portuguese and expanded by the EIC through the 18th century. Teacher: Ink on slide 13 (Bombay). Right margin: "1st permanent FACTORY = Surat 1613" and, beside "replacing Surat," "PRESIDENCY 1618" (the last digit is slightly unclear; it matches the Surat Presidency of 1618 in Table T5). Also "1534-1661: Portugal" (Portugal held Bombay from the 1534 Bassein deal to the 1661 dowry). Left margin: "FORT" with a line to "Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta)": the fort was originally Portuguese. Underlined: Charles II 60-85, Bombay in 1661, dowry, 1668 at 10 pounds per annum rent, Bombay Presidency, in 1687. 17.3 · Calcutta Presidency (from 1699/1700) The EIC's Bengal presence began with a factory at Hugli in 1651, permitted by a nishan from Shah Shuja, the Mughal governor of Bengal and son of Shahjahan 27-58. 1690: the EIC founded a settlement at the village of Sutanuti: the Calcutta establishment. The Calcutta Presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the Presidency of Fort William, with its own Governor. Through the 18th century the EIC developed Calcutta Port; Calcutta came to account for 60% of all EIC trade from India. 1800: Fort William College was established by Wellesley 98-05 for training EIC civil servants. 1870: the Calcutta Port Act created the Calcutta Port Commissioners and Port Trust, the first formal legal authority governing the port. Covered later (in the chapter on the Battle of Plassey): Child's War, the 1690 pardon and 1691 Farman, and the 1717 Farman. Mnemonic: Su-Go-Ko, "Sudoku" of Calcutta. Sutanuti, Gobindapur, Kolikata = Su-Go-Ko. Bengal = 60% of EIC trade: Rs 100 of goods bought, Rs 60 from Bengal. Why it sticks: the years climb 51, 90, 98, 99; the three village names fit one word. Teacher: Ink on slide 14 (Calcutta). Under Fort William College: "Training of EIC officers"; under Wellesley 98-05 the teacher wrote the full years out as a check. Then a line with the word "annexations" and an arrow down: "Presidency = Province"; "Governor = Ruler / CM / Subadar / Nazim." Reason: before annexations the Governor only managed trade in a region; after annexations he ruled a province like a Mughal Subadar or Nazim (or a modern Chief Minister). items.t: 19 · The French in India and the story of Pondicherry
items.x: The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV 43-15; great-grandfather of Louis XVI, overthrown in the French Revolution of 1789). It started as a private company but was later nationalised, making it in today's terms a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU). Teacher: Ink on slide 19. Beside the title: "# Bengal: Chandernagore" and "# Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674" (Pondicherry, MAJOR HQ and 1674 underlined). So: the French main HQ = Pondicherry (1674); their Bengal base = Chandernagore. Yellow underlines: the 1664 company, King Louis XIV 43-15, "a private company," "later nationalised," Pondicherry (acquired 1674, Sultan of Bijapur, and Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General).  Lecture 12 slide 19: French East India Company and Pondicherry. Teacher's ink: Bengal: Chandernagore; Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674; underlines on 1664, Louis XIV 43-15, private company, later nationalised, Sultan of Bijapur and Francois Martin 01-06. French settlements in India (handout list) 1668, Surat: first factory, on a farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667. 1669, Masulipatnam: farman from the Sultan of Golconda (1518-1687). 1673, Chandarnagar: permission from Shaista Khan 64-88, Mughal governor of Bengal; financial crunch delayed it: a settlement only in 1690-92. 1674, Pondicherry: acquired from Sikandar Adil Shah (1672-86) of Bijapur and his local governor Sher Khan Lodi. Developed as a city by Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General 1701-06, earlier Governor), the real founder of French power in India: centralised French administration with Pondicherry as capital (1701) and built Fort Louis. 1723, Yanam: permission from Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, also called Asaf Jah I. 1724, Mahe (Malabar coast): acquired from the Nair ruler Vazhunnavar in 1721; trade settlement built 1724-25 after overcoming a rebellion; named after Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46, who came with a fleet from Mauritius. 1739, Karaikal: granted by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha ruler of Tanjore, as a reward for French help in a succession dispute. (The Thanjavur Maratha dynasty was founded not by Shivaji 74-80 directly but by his half-brother Venkoji (Ekoji) in 1674, defeating the Nayaka rulers of Madurai.) 1721, Mauritius a French colony, but proper control only by 1735 under Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46 (Governor 1735-46). He came again with a fleet in 1746 and helped Dupleix 42-54 capture Madras in the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48). 1949: a referendum in Chandernagore merged it into India; the rest stayed under French control until 1954. Mnemonic: French pairs: 68-69, 73-74, 23-24. "Soft Mangoes Cost Plenty, Yellow Mangoes Keep." Decode: Surat 1668 (farman of Aurangzeb 58-07, 1667), Masulipatnam 1669 (Golconda), Chandarnagar 1673 (Shaista Khan 64-88), Pondicherry 1674 (Bijapur; the teacher's tick), Yanam 1723 (Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48), Mahe 1724, Karaikal 1739 (Pratap Singh 39-63). Last: 1949 Chandernagore, 1954 the rest. Why it sticks: the years come in pairs, 68-69, 73-74, 23-24; Karaikal's giver Pratap Singh 39-63 starts in 39, the same year as the grant. Mnemonic: Codes that match the year. "Martin 01 makes the capital; La Bourdonnais 35-46 46 helps take Madras." Decode: Francois Martin 01-06 makes Pondicherry capital in 1701 and builds Fort Louis; La Bourdonnais 35-46 (Mauritius, proper control 1735) helps Dupleix 42-54 capture Madras in 1746, 1st Carnatic War (1746-48). Why it sticks: Martin's code starts at his year (01 = 1701); La Bourdonnais 35-46's code ends at his big year (46 = 1746). Teacher: Ink on slide 20 (French acquisitions). Underlined: Surat, "farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667," Chandarnagar, Pondicherry, Sultan of Bijapur, "capital 1701," "Fort Louis built," Yanam, "Mahe on the Malabar coast" and Karaikal. A tick stands beside 1674 (Pondicherry is the key row). The 1721/1735 Mauritius row has a cross beside it (no reason is written; treat it as low priority).  Lecture 12 slide 20: French acquisitions in order. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on Surat, Aurangzeb's 1667 farman, Chandarnagar, Pondicherry, capital 1701, Fort Louis, Yanam, Mahe and Karaikal; a tick beside 1674; a cross beside the Mauritius 1721/1735 row.
