items.t: 1 · How did a trading company become a State?
items.x: How Did a Trading Company Become a State? Company purpose: companies exist to make profit for shareholders, the EIC was no different, but in India it became a Company State. By 1857: EIC controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. 1661 Charter gave EIC: (a) right to build forts, (b) command troops, (c) make war and peace, (d) exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India. 1676: right to mint its own money. Teacher's ink: "controlled" struck through and "RULED" written below; "Charles II" under the 1661 row; forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction underlined; on the right a fork: INDIA into "Br India: 63% (T), 78% pop" and "565 Princely States: 37% (T), 22% pop". Companies exist to make profit for their shareholders. The EIC was no different. But what the EIC became in India went far beyond a trading enterprise. It became a Company State that, by 1857, controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. This chapter deals with Empire Building by the EIC. Teacher: On the slide the teacher struck out "controlled" and wrote "RULED": by 1857 the EIC ruled 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. His fork explains the numbers: India = British India (63% of territory, 78% of population) + 565 Princely States (37% of territory, 22% of population). Mnemonic: Flip to 100. 63 + 37 = 100, and 78 + 22 = 100. Decode: learn only British India's 63% territory, 78% population; the 565 Princely States are whatever completes 100 (37%, 22%). Why it sticks: the company that "RULED" (not just "controlled") took the bigger half of both. 1.1 The 1661 Charter   Year   What the EIC got    --- ---    1661 Charter (teacher's ink: Charles II 60-85)   The right to build forts       The right to command troops       The right to make war and peace       The right to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India     1676   The right to mint its own money   Teacher: The teacher underlined forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction: these are State-like powers in the hands of a company. The same charter sits in the EIC charters table of Chapter 8. Mnemonic: FTWJ: the 1661 Charter of Charles II 60-85. "Fat Tigers Wage Justice." Decode: Forts (build them), Troops (command them), War and peace (make them), Justice (civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India). Then 1676 = the right to mint its own money. Why it sticks: a tiger with forts, troops and courts is already a mini-State; in 1676 it also prints cash. 1.2 Two kinds of wars: for trade and for territory  Teacher's board (no typed text): why the EIC fought wars. Top line: "EIC formed not for (T), GOAL = TRADE with East Indies (not just India)". Heading "WARS by eic" splitting into two branches. Branch 1 "FOR TRADE": "Defensive: protect present trade", under it "Carnatic Wars" (underlined); "Offensive: to expand trade", under it "Battle of Suvali 1612" (underlined). Branch 2 "FOR (T)": (i) "Whenever empire builder GG or Governors, i.e. for personal ambitions": Clive 57-67 [Governor of Bengal Presidency 1757-60, 1765-67], Wellesley 98-05 [1798-1805], Francis Hastings 13-23 [1813-23], Dalhousie 48-56 [1848-56]; (ii) "because of pressure of EIC army, as armies have vested interest in wars", with a small tree: economic power (Def BD), political power (larger army), social power. The wars the EIC fought in India fall into two broad categories. Wars for trade: fought to protect or expand trade. Wars for territory: fought for empire building. These were different in nature and in motivation. Teacher: The board's tree. The EIC was not formed for territory (T). Its goal was trade with the East Indies (not just India). So its wars were of two kinds. (1) For trade: either defensive, to protect present trade (the Carnatic Wars), or offensive, to expand trade (the Battle of Suvali 1612, from Chapter 8). (2) For territory: only in two situations, given below. Note the point for this chapter: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade, even though they ended up laying the base for territory. Mnemonic: Defend at Carnatic, Expand at Suvali. Decode: wars for trade come in two flavours. Defensive (protect present trade) = Carnatic Wars. Offensive (expand trade) = Battle of Suvali 1612. Why it sticks: C = Cover what you have; S = Spread to get more. Wars for territory happened under two specific conditions. When the Governor or Governor-General in India was personally ambitious: an empire builder by temperament. Britain was far away. Communication was slow. These men had enough operational freedom to pursue wars that London might not have formally approved. At times the EIC Army put pressure for wars. Any army has a structural interest in war: war brings a bigger defence budget, prestige, promotions and political relevance to the military. The EIC Army was no different.   Empire builder   Post and years    --- ---    Robert Clive 57-67   Governor of Bengal Presidency, in two stints: 1757-60 and 1765-67     Richard Wellesley 98-05   1798-1805     Francis Hastings 13-23   1813-23     Dalhousie 48-56   1848-56   Overhype threats: the army routinely overhyped threats to the borders; war brings budget, prestige, promotions Pressure to expand: overhyped threats create pressure for territorial expansion New borders: expansion always creates new borders (warn) New threats: new borders bring new neighbours, and so new threats, fictional or real (bad) Back to the start: the new threats are overhyped again; a self-reinforcing cycle Teacher: The board gives the army's vested interest in wars as three kinds of power: economic power (a bigger defence budget, written "Def BD"), political power (a larger army) and social power. The handout's present-day parallel: think of how the Pakistan Army today has eaten Pakistan from within by putting its vested interests above the national interest, while the Indian Army has consistently done the opposite. Mnemonic: GA: the two triggers of wars for territory. "Greedy Governor, Angry Army." Builders: "Clive 57-67 Wanted Fresh Districts." Decode: G = a personally ambitious Governor or Governor-General (Britain far away, communication slow). A = the EIC Army pushing for war (budget, prestige, promotions). Builders: Clive 57-67 (Governor of Bengal Presidency, 1757-60 and 1765-67), Richard Wellesley 98-05, Francis Hastings 13-23, Dalhousie 48-56. Army cycle: overhype threat, expand, new border, new threat, overhype again.

items.t: 2 · Wars for trade: the Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90)
items.x: Wars for Trade: Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90). Also called Child's War, the 1st significant clash between EIC and an Indian power (Josiah Child: Chairman, Court of Directors, London; John Child: Governor of Bombay and "General" of EIC forces in India). Reason 1: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare disrupted EIC trade (hard to source goods from the hinterland). Reason 2: disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties on EIC. Course: EIC seized Hugli and attacked Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea; Aurangzeb 58-07 crushed EIC in Bombay and Bengal; by 1690 the Company surrendered; Feb 1690, Aurangzeb 58-07 pardoned EIC for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation. Why not expel EIC: it was economically useful. Teacher's ink: underlines on economically useful, forex/gold, bankers, merchants, artisans and ryots; a starred yellow box: "1651: 1st EIC factory in Bengal in Hughli"; above it a small unlabelled sketch of a V-shaped line with two circles (a rough river and town sketch). The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686-90 was fought in Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It was the first significant military clash between the EIC and an Indian power. It is also called Child's War, after two men: Josiah Child: Chairman of the Court of Directors of the EIC in London. John Child: Governor of Bombay and the "General" of all EIC forces in India. The reasons were two-fold: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare was disrupting EIC trade (problems in sourcing goods from the hinterland). Ongoing disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties levied on the EIC. The EIC seizes Hugli It escalates: attacks Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea (bad) Aurangzeb 58-07's military crushes the EIC in both Bombay and Bengal By 1690 the Company surrenders February 1690: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC in return for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation (good) 1691 Farman: old privileges restored and duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year Teacher: The starred box on the slide: "1651: the 1st EIC factory in Bengal, in Hughli." That is why Hugli is the place the EIC seizes in this war. Mnemonic: Two Childs, two places. "Josiah sits in London; John fights from Bombay." Decode: Josiah Child = Chairman of the Court of Directors, London (the desk). John Child = Governor of Bombay and "General" of all EIC forces in India (the battlefield). Why it sticks: the war is named after them, so Child's War = the chairman's order plus the general's army. Mnemonic: 86, 90, 91: pay once, then pay small. Decode: the Anglo-Mughal War starts in 1686 (EIC seizes Hugli, where its first Bengal factory stood in 1651). By 1690 the Company surrenders; Feb 1690 Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons it for Rs 1.5 lakh. 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana from the Subahdar of Bengal) = old privileges back plus duty-free Bengal trade for Rs 3,000 a year. Why it sticks: Rs 1.5 lakh once to be forgiven, then Rs 3,000 a year to trade free. 2.1 Why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not abolish the Company and expel the British? Because the EIC was economically useful. Its trade brought forex/gold into India, and Aurangzeb 58-07 needed them for war. With Aurangzeb 58-07's own constant warfare disrupting domestic trade, the EIC's export business was, ironically, even more valuable to the Indian economy. Indian bankers earned interest by lending money to the Company for the purchase of goods. Indian merchants, artisans and ryots all participated in and benefited from this trade ecosystem. Mnemonic: RMEB: why Aurangzeb 58-07 kept the Company. "Ryot makes, Merchant sells, EIC ships, Banker lends." Decode: ryots and artisans produce; Indian merchants sell to the EIC; the EIC exports and brings in forex/gold; bankers earn interest on loans to the Company. Why it sticks: everyone in the chain eats, so nobody cuts the chain. The duty the EIC saves buys more Indian goods, so more exports. 2.2 The 1691 Farman  Anglo-Mughal War (contd.): the 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman), under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval, restored old privileges and gave duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year. Teacher's ink: underlines on "duty-free trade in Bengal" and "for Rs 3,000/year"; a flow diagram: RYOTS and ARTISANS with arrows to "Indian MERCHANT", then an arrow to "EIC" and onward (exports), with "Indian BANKERS" below sending an up-arrow labelled "Loan" to the EIC; on the right: "Rupees saved by EIC will be used to BUY Indian GOODS, so more exports"; a starred box: "TODAY we don't tax exports". The 1691 Farman was technically a Parwana, because it was issued by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman. (For Farman, Parwana and Nishan see Chapter 8.) It was issued under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval. It restored the EIC's old privileges and gave it the right to duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. The Company had been defeated militarily, yet it got this privilege, because of the benefits of European trade with India. Teacher: Why give duty-free trade to a defeated company? The board's flow answers it. Ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant; the Indian merchant sells to the EIC; Indian bankers give loans to the EIC. Everyone in the chain earns. The money the EIC saves on duty will be used to buy more Indian goods, which means more exports. The starred aside: "TODAY we don't tax exports" (the same logic: a State gains more from exports than from taxing them).

items.t: 3 · The Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63): why the French, and why three wars
items.x: Teacher's board (no typed text): the 3 Carnatic Wars. Top: "Who will dominate purchase of goods". "3 Carnatic wars [Reason = international trade of India; main players Br eic vs Fr eic]", with a tree to 1746-48, 1749-54 and 1756-63; from 1756-63 an arrow: "Fr limited to Chandernagore, Pondicherry". Box: "[3 CWs 1746-48, 49-54, 56-63]". "# 1st and 3rd: result or part of some international war, Br vs Fr". "# 2nd: factionalism in Hyd and Carnatic, R vs R", with arrows down to Fr and Br. Right: "# [Br, Fr] ROYAL armies in 3rd CW 1756-63 ONLY" (ONLY underlined). "# Result: 3/2 = 1.5" with a small table: 1st CW and the 1st phase of the 2nd CW marked "French won"; the 2nd phase of the 2nd CW and the 3rd CW marked "British won". To understand why conquest by the EIC began in Bengal, one must first understand what was happening in South India, and why the French were there. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 was the Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742-54. Dupleix 42-54 had personal ambitions of empire building and of dominating the international trade of South India. He would become the template for everything that followed. By 1740, French EIC trade was roughly half the value of British EIC trade. Mnemonic: Dupleix 42-54: "42 to 54, not here in 56." Decode: Dupleix 42-54 = Governor-General of the French EIC, 1742-54, the template for later empire builders. He was recalled in 1754, so he is absent from the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). Why it sticks: his 12 years end two years before the 3rd war begins. Teacher: The board's frame for all three wars. The reason was the international trade of India: "who will dominate the purchase of goods." The main players were the British EIC versus the French EIC. The 1st and 3rd wars were a result or a part of some international war (Britain versus France). The 2nd was caused by factionalism in Hyderabad and Carnatic: "R vs R" (rival against rival), with the French behind one rival and the British behind the other. Royal armies (British and French) took part in the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 ONLY. Result: 3 divided by 2 = 1.5 each: the French won the 1st war and the 1st phase of the 2nd; the British won the 2nd phase of the 2nd and the 3rd. After 1756-63 the French were limited to Chandernagore and Pondicherry (the full list of five posts is in section 6.4). Mnemonic: Odd wars international, even war local; French open, British close. Decode: wars 1 and 3 = IR (Britain vs France, from global wars); war 2 = R vs R (factionalism). Royal armies only in the 3rd. Result "3/2 = 1.5": French won the 1st war and phase 1 of the 2nd; British won phase 2 of the 2nd and the 3rd. Why it sticks: the French win the opening, the British win the ending. 3.1 Reasons for the Carnatic Wars  Reasons for Carnatic Wars. European rivalry: 2 global wars spilled into India, the War of Austrian Succession (1740-48) leading to the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) leading to the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63); as nations fought, their companies fought in India. Succession disputes: disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad drove the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54); the strategy was simple, put your chosen candidate in power to gain strategic influence. Dupleix 42-54's ambition: Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54, Governor-General of French EIC 1742-54, had personal ambitions of empire and of dominating South India's trade, and became the template for all that followed (by 1740 French EIC trade was about half British EIC trade). Teacher's ink: underlines on the two global wars, "Carnatic and Hyderabad", "personal ambitions of empire" and "South India's trade"; under the Dupleix 42-54 row: "42-54", "1742-54" (underlined) and "not in 3CW 1756-63"; on the right: "How a company can build empire: 1st to show, Fr Dupleix 42-54". The EIC-French contest in India had two overlapping reasons. European rivalry. Two global wars spilled into India. As the two nations fought, their respective companies also entered into hostilities in India. Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad contributed to the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54). The strategy was simple: put your chosen candidates in power to gain strategic influence. Mnemonic: Global war first, Indian war follows. Decode: War of Austrian Succession 1740-48 gives the 1st CW 1746-48 (both end in 48). Seven Years' Global War 1756-63 gives the 3rd CW 1756-63 (identical years, 7 years each). Why it sticks: the 3rd war is a carbon copy of the Seven Years' War; the 1st starts 6 years after AWoS begins.   War   Years   Cause   Decisive event   Treaty   Who won (teacher's board)    --- --- --- --- --- ---    1st Carnatic War   1746-48   The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) spilled into India   Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)   Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)   French     2nd Carnatic War   1749-54   Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad (factionalism)   Ambur (1749); Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751)   Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)   Phase 1: French. Phase 2: British     3rd Carnatic War   1756-63   The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) spilled into India   Battle of Wandiwash (1760)   Treaty of Paris (1763)   British   Teacher: Under the Dupleix 42-54 row the teacher wrote "42-54, 1742-54: not in 3CW 1756-63." Remember it as a check: Dupleix 42-54 was recalled in 1754, so he took no part in the 3rd Carnatic War (he comes back in section 6.2 as "Dupleix 42-54 not here"). On the right: "How a company can build an empire: the first to show it was the French, Dupleix 42-54." Mnemonic: 2-5-7 years, and A-P-P treaties. Decode: war lengths grow: 1st 1746-48 (2 years), 2nd 1749-54 (5 years), 3rd 1756-63 (7 years). Treaties in order: Aix-La-Chapelle 1748, Pondicherry 1754, Paris 1763. Why it sticks: each treaty year is the war's last year (48, 54, 63). The handout's heading for this section is printed as "Carnatic Wars (17456-48, 49-54, 56-63)". It is a typing slip for 1746-48.

items.t: 4 · The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)
items.x: 4.1 Reason The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) was the Indian chapter of the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48). In that war Britain and France, along with their respective allies, fought each other across Europe, America and India, each wanting its preferred candidate on the Austrian throne. 4.2 Events during the war  1st Carnatic War (1746-48): Adyar/St Thome. Reason: the Indian chapter of the War of Austrian Succession (1740-48); Britain and France, with their allies, fought across Europe, America and India, each wanting its candidate on the Austrian throne. Events: Dupleix 42-54 captured EIC's Fort St George, Madras; EIC defeated; the Nawab of Carnatic Anwaruddin 44-49 expected the fort handed over as promised; Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry (the slide's wording; it was the Nawab who sent the cavalry). Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746: on the north bank of the River Adyar about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on the key phrases; "Anwar-ud-din 44-49" written under the name; on the right a small circle "Br" and an oval "Eu"; a box "Turning Point" and under it "Indian kings wanted (EU) help in modernizing military". Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George in Madras; the EIC is defeated The Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin 44-49, intervenes: he expected the French to hand over the fort to the Nawab as promised (warn) Dupleix 42-54 refuses Anwaruddin 44-49 sends an army of 10,000 cavalry (bad) Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746): about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroy the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry The battle was fought on the north bank of the River Adyar. The French force was roughly 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers. It completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. What happened here changed the nature of power in India. Who sent the 10,000 cavalry? The slide's compressed wording ("Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry") can be misread. The handout is clear: Anwaruddin 44-49, the Nawab, sent the army of 10,000 cavalry against the French. Mnemonic: 7 + 3 = 1,000 beats 10,000. "Nawab Sent, French Smashed." Decode: about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys + 300 French soldiers = 1,000 men destroyed the Nawab's 10,000 cavalry, on the north bank of the Adyar (1746). The Nawab (Anwaruddin 44-49) sent the cavalry, not Dupleix 42-54; Dupleix 42-54 refused to hand over Fort St George. Why it sticks: odds of 1 to 10, and the Nawab (N) is the one who Needed the fort. The handout's Diagram 1 (section 7) adds one name the text does not give: "La Bourdonnais 35-46 takes Fort St George, Madras." The handout text and the slide credit the capture to Dupleix 42-54 (the Governor-General). La Bourdonnais 35-46 and Madras appear in Chapter 8. 4.3 Why the French won: three advantages of European warfare The French won due to three critical advantages that would define European military superiority in India across all the wars to come.   Advantage   Why it mattered    --- ---    1. Superior artillery   Light, mobile European cannon that could be repositioned rapidly on the battlefield, against which massed cavalry had no answer (link: like the small bronze cannons of Babur 26-30, spelt Babar 26-30 in this handout)     2. Tactical discipline   European-trained infantry fought in coordinated formations, including infantry squares that could hold ground against cavalry charges from any direction     3. Regular cash salaries   Unlike Indian armies, where soldiers were often not paid regularly, European-trained sepoys received regular wages. This created a professional, reliable fighting force with no incentive to desert between campaigns    French-Trained Sepoys: the New Model Force. A black-and-white photograph of a dense body of soldiers in helmets with rifles, kneeling and standing in a tight square (seen from one corner, so it looks like a diamond) on bare rocky ground with hills behind and an officer at the centre. Typed caption: European-trained, regularly-paid Indian sepoys, the disciplined infantry that broke traditional cavalry at Adyar. Teacher's ink: "Infantry Square" written above the picture and two yellow lines tracing the front corner of the square like a roof. Teacher: On the three-advantages slide (Lecture 12, slide 69) the teacher underlined "light, mobile European cannon", "Babur 26-30", "formations", "infantry squares" and "small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery." He labelled the photograph "Infantry Square" and traced its corner: the men face outward on every side, so a cavalry charge from any direction meets a wall of muskets. On the Adyar slide he boxed the words "Turning Point" and wrote under it: "Indian kings wanted European help in modernising their military." Mnemonic: ADC: the French Adyar edge. "The French general's ADC." Decode: Artillery (light, mobile cannon; cf. Babur 26-30's small bronze cannons), Discipline (infantry squares facing every direction), Cash (regular salaries, so no desertion). Why it sticks: an ADC stands beside the commander; these three stood beside every European army. Takeaway (Adyar 1746). This was not just a military victory. For the first time it was proven conclusively that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army. The psychological impact was enormous: it gave Europeans the confidence to start interfering directly in Indian political disputes, which is exactly what Dupleix 42-54 proceeded to do. The Indian royal elites also wanted to use the military service of the Europeans in their internal and external disputes. Teacher: The Wagner Group analogy (handout). Have you heard of the Wagner Group? It is a company which sells military service to the Russian State. In a way the French were now the Wagner Group of India: a company whose army could be hired by Indian rulers. The teacher develops this on the board in section 5.1. 4.4 Consequence: the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)  Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748). Ended: the War of the Austrian Succession. Mutual return: both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras: went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54: deeply frustrating, his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe (North America mattered more to France, where Britain had won). Teacher's ink: at the top "Fr won in India BUT Br won in Americas"; "1740-48" beside the Ended row (last digit hard to read); on the right a small table "MAIN INTEREST: Britain = India; France = Americas, especially N and C Am" with a figure-of-8 sketch labelled NAm, CAm and SAm; at the bottom three points: "# No change in (T)", "# (EU) infantry >>> Indian cavalry", "# Dupleix 42-54 KAT Gaya". However, in North America, which was more strategically important to France, Britain had won. So in the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748), which ended the War of the Austrian Succession, both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54 this was deeply frustrating: his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe. But he was not done. His next opportunity came almost immediately, in the form of succession disputes: one in Hyderabad, one in Carnatic. Teacher: The board's reasoning for the treaty. "The French won in India BUT the British won in the Americas." The two countries valued different places: Britain's main interest = India; France's main interest = the Americas, especially North and Central America. So France gave back Madras to recover what it had lost in America. Three results he lists: (1) no change in territory; (2) European infantry is far greater than Indian cavalry (the lesson of Adyar stays even though Madras is returned); (3) "Dupleix 42-54 KAT gaya" (Hindi: he was cut out, left empty-handed). Mnemonic: BI-FA: who wanted what in 1748. "Britain wants India, France wants the Americas: BI-FA." Decode: France won in India but Britain won in the Americas, so the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) swapped back possessions: Madras returned to the EIC. Results: no change in territory; European infantry far greater than Indian cavalry; Dupleix 42-54 "KAT gaya". Why it sticks: "Aix" sounds like "aches", which is what Dupleix 42-54 felt.

items.t: 5 · The 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): how Dupleix 42-54 invented the blueprint for empire in India
items.x: 5.0 The succession disputes that triggered the war  Teacher's board (no typed text): "2nd CW 1749-54. Reason = FACTIONALISM". Two sections. CARNATIC: Md Ali 52-95 on the left with an up-arrow from "(2) Eng eic"; Chanda Sahib 49-52 on the right with an up-arrow from "(1) Fr eic". HYD: Nasir Jung 48-50 on the left with an up-arrow from "(2) Eic"; Muzaffar Jung 50-51 on the right with an up-arrow from "(1) Fr eic" (the board writes the four names without their years). Mnemonic asides in brackets: "Jinnah Pro Br" (pointing at Md Ali 52-95); "Moon = Romance, Paris = city of [romance]" (pointing at Chanda Sahib 49-52); "Nasir Hussain: Eng Captain, Cricket" (under Nasir Jung 48-50); "MUZAFRANCE" (under Muzaffar Jung 50-51). Right: "Fear of Br = if Fr eic able to put its favorite in power, then LOSS of TRADE for EIC".  2nd Carnatic War: Succession Disputes. Carnatic: Anwaruddin 44-49 was made Nawab of Carnatic by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, then he became autonomous of the Nizam; on his death his son Md Ali Wallajah (Md Ali 52-95) vs Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of the earlier Nawab Dost Ali Khan 32-40). Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 died 1748; son Nasir Jung 48-50 vs Muzaffar Jung 50-51, grandson (from a daughter). French (Dupleix 42-54) interfered in favour of Muzaffar Jung 50-51 in Hyderabad and Chanda Sahib 49-52 in Carnatic, for trade and political influence. EIC backed the opposing sides: Nasir Jung 48-50 in Hyderabad, Md Ali 52-95 in Carnatic. Teacher's ink: "1749-54" under the title; yellow underlines on the four names; in the Carnatic row "Anwar-ud-din 44-49 wanted son Md Ali 52-95 to be Nawab"; right margin "FACTIONALISM", then Md Ali 52-95 vs C Sahib, and Nasir (vs) Muzaffar; in the French row a bracket "Dupleix 42-54 wanted: empire building; monopoly of international trade of South India". In Carnatic: Anwaruddin 44-49 had been appointed Nawab of Carnatic by the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1744. (The slide adds: he then became autonomous of the Nizam.) On his death a succession dispute began between: his son Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (Md Ali 52-95), and Chanda Sahib 49-52, the son-in-law of the earlier Nawab Dost Ali Khan 32-40 (1732-40). In Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 died in 1748. The rivals for the throne were: his son Nasir Jung 48-50, and his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (the slide adds: grandson from a daughter). Dupleix 42-54 backed Muzaffar Jung 50-51 in Hyderabad and Chanda Sahib 49-52 in Carnatic. He wanted his chosen candidates in power for economic/trade and political influence. An anxious EIC backed the opposing sides: Nasir Jung 48-50 in Hyderabad and Md Ali 52-95 in Carnatic.   Place   French EIC's candidate (moved first)   English EIC's candidate (reacted)    --- --- ---    Carnatic   Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40)   Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49)     Hyderabad   Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (grandson of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48)   Nasir Jung 48-50 (son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48)   Teacher: Mnemonics from the handout and the board. French side: "MuzaFFrance" (the board writes MUZAFRANCE) for Muzaffar Jung 50-51; and for Chanda Sahib 49-52: "Paris and the moon (Chanda) are symbols of romance" (board: Moon = Romance, Paris = city of romance). British side: "Nasir Hussain: England captain, cricket" for Nasir Jung 48-50; and "Jinnah, pro-British" written beside Md Ali 52-95 (the same first names as Jinnah's). The circled numbers (1) on the French EIC and (2) on the English EIC show the order: the French interfered first, the EIC only reacted. Mnemonic: CM for France, the other two for Britain. "French picks become CMs." Decode: French candidates = Chanda Sahib 49-52 (Carnatic) and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (Hyderabad). English candidates = Md Ali 52-95 (Carnatic) and Nasir Jung 48-50 (Hyderabad). Order: French = (1) moved first, English = (2) reacted. Why it sticks: the teacher's own hooks (Moon and Paris; MuzaFFrance) cover C and M; whoever is left is British. Teacher: Why did the EIC react at all? The board's reasoning: "Fear of the British = if the French EIC is able to put its favourite in power, then loss of trade for the EIC." On the slide he adds what Dupleix 42-54 wanted: (a) empire building and (b) a monopoly of the international trade of South India. He also notes that Anwaruddin 44-49 wanted his son Md Ali 52-95 to be Nawab.  Teacher's board (no typed text): a sketch map of Carnatic. At the top "HYDERABAD" and below it "R. KRISHNA" (wavy line). A long diagonal coast line running from lower left to upper right, labelled "N SARKARS" along its upper part. A dot "ARCOT" inland on the left with three dotted lines to three dots on the coast: "MADRAS [Hq of eic]", "WANDIWASH [3rd CW 1756-63]" and "PONDICHERRY [Hq of Fr eic]". Bottom left: "MWP" (starred and underlined), "ARCOT = Capital of Carnatic", "Fig. Carnatic". Right: "2nd CW 1749-54: # All gathered in Carnatic; # Nasir and Muzaffar arrived in Carnatic"; a two-column table "Fr eic (smiley): 1st PHASE, till 1751" and "Eng eic (smiley): 2nd PHASE". Teacher: Learn the map by the board's code "MWP": on the coast from north to south come Madras (HQ of the EIC), Wandiwash (the battle of the 3rd Carnatic War) and Pondicherry (HQ of the French EIC). Arcot, inland, is the capital of Carnatic. Hyderabad lies north of the River Krishna, and the Northern Sarkars run along the coast further up. In the 2nd Carnatic War "all gathered in Carnatic": Nasir Jung 48-50 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 also arrived in Carnatic. The war has two phases: the French EIC smiles in the 1st phase (till 1751); the English EIC smiles in the 2nd phase. Mnemonic: MWP: British on top, French at the bottom, battle in the middle. Decode: down the coast, north to south: Madras (HQ of the EIC), Wandiwash (3rd CW battle), Pondicherry (HQ of the French EIC). Arcot sits inland as capital of Carnatic. Why it sticks: the handout's line, "where the French were washed away", puts Wandiwash between the two HQs. 5.1 Phase 1: French victory (1749-51) Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 is killed (good) Chanda Sahib 49-52 is declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot By December 1750: Nasir Jung 48-50 is also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is declared Nizam Muzaffar Jung 50-51 marches toward Hyderabad, accompanied by Bussy's army (bad) February 1751, Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool; the Nawab of Kurnool is also killed (good) Bussy reaches Hyderabad and installs Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 was killed. Chanda Sahib 49-52 was declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot. (The slide notes: Ambur is 190 km west of Chennai; the teacher added "towards Bengaluru.") By December 1750, Nasir Jung 48-50 was also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 was declared Nizam. Bussy was the junior of Dupleix 42-54. Accompanied by Bussy's army, Muzaffar Jung 50-51 began marching toward Hyderabad. But he was killed in February 1751 at the Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool, who felt cheated as he was not given the territory promised to him for his support. The Nawab of Kurnool was also killed. (The slide's aside on the pass: "unlucky lol.") Bussy now reached Hyderabad and installed Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam. He was a son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 and an uncle of the recently killed Muzaffar Jung 50-51. Mnemonic: Three deaths, three years: 49, 50, 51. Decode: 1749 Ambur: Anwaruddin 44-49 killed, Chanda Sahib 49-52 crowned at Arcot. Dec 1750: Nasir Jung 48-50 killed, Muzaffar Jung 50-51 declared Nizam. Feb 1751, Lakkireddipalli Pass: Muzaffar killed by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool (also killed); Bussy installs Salabat Jung 51-62. Why it sticks: one ruler falls each year, and the Hyderabad ladder reads Nasir, Muzaffar, Salabat (N, M, S). Teacher: Beside the Hyderabad row the teacher starred: "Asaf Jahi dynasty, by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 [Asaf Jah I]." All the Hyderabad claimants here (Nasir Jung 48-50, Muzaffar Jung 50-51, Salabat Jung 51-62) belong to this one family; see Chapter 3.  Teacher's board (no typed text): the Wagner Group analogy. "# Death of MJ is BLOT on MILITARY reputation of Fr eic", with a line "= Like WAGNER GROUP". In a large bracket: "MJ and C Sahib HIRED Wagner Group / Fr eic TO BE Nawab". On the left: "so BUSSY CREATED TERROR for general msg that Don't mess with Fr eic [on way to Hyd]", with an arrow to "made Salabat Jung 51-62 Nizam". On the right under "WAGNER GROUP": "# a company; # sells service for rupees = MILITARY SERVICE". Teacher: The Wagner Group board. The Wagner Group is a company that sells a service for money, and the service is military service. In the same way Muzaffar Jung 50-51 ("MJ") and Chanda Sahib 49-52 hired the French EIC, like a Wagner Group, to become rulers. So the death of MJ was a blot on the military reputation of the French EIC: a firm that sells protection cannot let its client be killed. That is why Bussy created terror on the way to Hyderabad, as a general message: "don't mess with the French EIC," and then made Salabat Jung 51-62 the Nizam. The gains from Phase 1  Dupleix 42-54's Gains from Phase 1. Hyderabad: Bussy was made French agent/resident at the Nizam's court; a French army stationed for protection of the Nizam; this army was to be paid for by Hyderabad, thus the French EIC was given the Northern Sarkars (present-day Andhra), Bussy administered it and kept its revenues (brutal methods of LR extraction: terror and massacre); 2,00,000 pounds for the French EIC from the Nizam; Bussy got personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam. Carnatic: Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of all lands between the River Krishna and Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as Deputy Nawab of Arcot; personal jagir of Rs 1 lakh a year in Villianallur near Pondicherry. Teacher's ink: "Fr eic's" above the title; left margin "HYD UNDER French MILITARY Domination" with an arrow to the army bullet, and "THINK: Fr selling a MILITARY SERVICE" with an arrow to the payment bullet; "[NXT PAGE]" after the jagirs bullet; top right "in a way Salabat 51-62 = puppet of Fr eic" and "(+) Fr can counter any anti-Fr DECISION via supervision"; bottom right a triangle sketch with "R. KRISHNA" along the top, "Carnatic" inside and "Kanya Kumari or Cape Comorin" at the bottom tip.   Where   Gain    --- ---    Hyderabad: the resident   Bussy was made the French resident and agent at the Nizam's court, wielding real political influence     Hyderabad: the army   A French army was stationed for the Nizam's protection, and Hyderabad was to pay for it     Hyderabad: the payment   The payment was the Northern Sarkars region (present-day Andhra Pradesh): Bussy administered it on behalf of the Nizam and kept its revenues as payment for the French army     Hyderabad: cash   2,00,000 pounds for the French EIC from the Nizam     Hyderabad: personal   Bussy extracted personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam     Carnatic: title   Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of all lands between the River Krishna and Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as his Deputy Nawab of Arcot     Carnatic: personal   Dupleix 42-54 extracted a personal jagir of Rs 1 lakh per annum in Villianallur near Pondicherry   In the Northern Sarkars Bussy's methods were brutal: terror and massacre of civilians for land revenue extraction. In Andhra folklore this terror is preserved in the word "boochi" (meaning ghost, or the feared), derived from Bussy's name. Teacher: The teacher's notes on the gains slide. He wrote "Fr eic's" above the title: these are the French EIC's gains, not only Dupleix 42-54's. (1) "Hyderabad under French military domination" (the army stationed there). (2) "THINK: the French are selling a military service" (Hyderabad pays for the army, the Wagner idea again). (3) "In a way Salabat Jung 51-62 = a puppet of the French EIC." (4) Plus: "the French can counter any anti-French decision via supervision" (that is what a resident sitting in the court is for). His triangle sketch fixes the geography: Carnatic = the land from the River Krishna (top) down to Kanya Kumari or Cape Comorin (the tip). Mnemonic: Bussy's hand: five Hyderabad gains. Decode: Thumb = Resident (Bussy at the Nizam's court). Index finger = a French army (Hyderabad pays). Middle finger (the tall one) = Northern Sarkars as payment, revenues kept by Bussy. Ring finger = cash, 2,00,000 pounds. Little finger = personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam. Why it sticks: the ring finger is the money finger. Bonus: Bussy's terror gave Andhra the word "boochi" (ghost).  Handout figure (a photographed notebook page, also shown as Lecture 13 slide 8): "FR GAINS post War of Succession (@ 2nd Carnatic War 1750-54)". Notes: money gain of 200,000 pounds; Dupleix 42-54 got 80 villages, the Jagirdari of Villianallur in present day Pondicherry, worth 1 lakh rupees; Bussy as Fr agent in Hyd court along with a French army; Dupleix 42-54 was declared Nawab of all lands between River Krishna and Cape Comorin, with Chanda Sahib 49-52 under Dupleix 42-54 as Nawab of Arcot. On the left a printed map of South India with European settlements and their years, such as Yanam (1725 F) and Masulipatnam (1615 Du) both circled in blue, Madras (1639 B), Pondicherry (1674 F), Karaikal (1739 F), Hyderabad, Kurnool, Mysore and Cape Comorin; two pink lines run from the Krishna near Hyderabad and from Cape Comorin to the note, marking the extent of Carnatic. The slide version adds in red: "[TODAY x 300% for inflation = 3 cr rupees p.a.]". Teacher: The notebook page adds two things. (1) Dupleix 42-54 got 80 villages as the Jagirdari of Villianallur, worth Rs 1 lakh. (2) In red: "today, for inflation, = 3 crore rupees per annum," to show how large a personal income this was. The two circled places on the map, Yanam and Masulipatnam, are Bussy's personal jagirs. Two things to check on the notebook page. (1) Its title dates the 2nd Carnatic War "1750-54"; the handout and every slide give 1749-54. (2) The red bracket is written "x 300%", but Rs 1 lakh becomes Rs 3 crore only when multiplied by 300 times; take the point (a very large income), not the arithmetic. Mnemonic: Krishna to Kumari; 80 villages, 1 lakh. Decode: Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of everything from the River Krishna down to Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as Deputy Nawab of Arcot. His personal jagir: Villianallur near Pondicherry, 80 villages, Rs 1 lakh a year (about 300 times that today = 3 crore). Why it sticks: picture a map triangle, Krishna at the top, Kanya Kumari at the tip; "80 gaon, ek lakh".  Teacher's board (no typed text). Left: "THINK: as employee of Fr eic: # SALARY, (BUT) now PERSONAL # JAGIRS + CASH" (BUT circled, jagirs and cash underlined). A vertical divider. Right: "interest of these empire BUILDER (employees)" with employees circled, and lines from it to "Fr eic", "Eng eic" (underlined), "Estado da India" and "Dutch VOC". Teacher: THINK: why do Company men build empires? As an employee of the French EIC a man gets only a salary. BUT empire building now brings him personal jagirs plus cash. So the personal interest of these empire-builder employees drives the wars. And this holds for every company: the French EIC, the English EIC, the Estado da India and the Dutch VOC. (This is condition 1 of section 1.2: the personally ambitious Governor.) Takeaway: Dupleix 42-54 had just invented the model of empire building in India. Put your candidate in power, station your army at his expense, extract territory as payment, and sit in the court as the real power behind the throne. This is exactly the model the British EIC would refine and use with devastating effect for the next century. (The handout's aside: "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54" would be the thoughts of the EIC.) 1. Succession dispute = opportunity: interfere and bring your favourite claimant into power 2. Extract gains, military domination: station your army in the Indian State and make the State pay for this army 3. Extract gains, territory as payment: take land as payment for the army (bad) 4. Puppet State: station your Resident in the Indian King's court, who establishes his indirect rule Teacher: On the model slide (Lecture 13, slide 10) the teacher wrote "FACTIONALISM (R vs R)" above step 1: the opening is always a quarrel between two rivals. Beside step 2 he wrote "Free of cost domination": the Indian State itself pays for the army that dominates it. He underlined "Resident in the Indian King's court" and "Indirect Rule" in step 4. Mnemonic: SART: Dupleix 42-54's four-step model. "Smart Armies Take Rule." Decode: Succession dispute = the opening (R vs R). Army stationed, and the State pays ("free of cost domination"). Territory taken as payment. Resident in the king's court = puppet State, indirect rule. Why it sticks: each step needs the one before it, like a ladder to the throne.  Teacher's board (no typed text), headed "FYQ-M" (underlined; the first letter is unclear, probably PYQ-M). The question in white ink: "MODEL of empire BUILDING (in India) by TRADING Companies was FOUNDED [by FRENCH] and [implemented by BRITISH]. Analyse". "by French" is boxed with a line below to "CW2" (the 2nd Carnatic War); "implemented by British" is in a larger rounded box with a line below to "future topics". Teacher: The Mains question on the board: "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." The teacher split the answer into two parts: "founded by French" = the 2nd Carnatic War (this section: the four steps above, with Hyderabad and Carnatic as the examples); "implemented by British" = future topics (Plassey and Buxar in Chapter 10, the Subsidiary Alliance in Chapter 11). Mnemonic: F then B: Founded, then Built. Decode: the Mains question splits in two. French Founded the model = 2nd Carnatic War (the four steps). British Built (implemented) it = future topics (Plassey, Buxar, Subsidiary Alliance). Why it sticks: the alphabet does it, F before B.  PYQ 2, Prelims 1996, on Dupleix 42-54: Who among the following were the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories? (a) Clive 57-67 (b) Dupleix 42-54 (c) Albuquerque 09-15 (d) Warren Hastings 73-85. The typed options carry no years. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on "first European", "quarrels of Indian princes" and "to acquire territories"; years written in yellow beside the four options in order: "57-60, 65-67 [1700s, Governor Bengal Presidency]"; "42-54 [1742-54]"; "09-15 [1509-1615]" as written; "73-85 [1700s]". Prelims 1996: the first European to take part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories = (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model: back a candidate, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment, sit in court as the real power. It was first used in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 came later: he used and refined the model in Bengal (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764) but did not invent it. Albuquerque 09-15 was a 16th-century Portuguese conqueror (took Goa 1510): an earlier era of direct conquest, not the "back-a-claimant" model. Warren Hastings 73-85 was a later EIC Governor-General: a refiner, not the originator. Mnemonic: D-C-H: Dupleix 42-54 Did it, Clive 57-67 Copied, Hastings Honed. Decode: Prelims 1996 asks the first European to meddle in Indian princes' quarrels for territory: Dupleix 42-54. Then Clive 57-67, then Warren Hastings 73-85. Albuquerque 09-15 (Goa 1510) = direct conquest, an earlier era. Why it sticks: the codes themselves rise, 42, 57, 73, so the smallest is the first. 5.2 Phase 2: the EIC bounces back The EIC decided to fight back by supporting Md Ali 52-95 (Carnatic), who was holding out in Trichinopoly. Dupleix 42-54 got obsessed with eliminating any future challenge to his power. Hence he made the critical mistake of leaving the capital Arcot unguarded and focusing on Trichinopoly. Robert Clive 57-67, operating from Madras with a small force of roughly 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys, took over Arcot (the slide dates it: Arcot 1751). He then defended it against a massive counter-siege for 53 days. The capital was now with the British! Clive 57-67 became a celebrated figure back in Britain. The French government in Paris, anxious to honour the 1748 treaty and preserve its more lucrative American possessions, refused to help Dupleix 42-54. By 1754 the French had lost the 2nd Carnatic War. Md Ali 52-95 holds out in Trichinopoly, backed by the EIC (warn) Dupleix 42-54's critical mistake: he focuses on Trichinopoly and leaves the capital Arcot unguarded Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (1751) from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys He defends it through a 53-day counter-siege (warn) Paris refuses to help Dupleix 42-54: it wants to honour the 1748 treaty and keep its American possessions (bad) By 1754 the French have lost the 2nd Carnatic War Teacher: On the slide the teacher underlined only two phrases: "1748 treaty" and "refused to help Dupleix 42-54." That is the real reason for the defeat: France chose America over India again, exactly as in 1748. Mnemonic: Arcot 1751: 200 + 300 = 500 men, 53 days. Decode: Dupleix 42-54 obsessed over Trichinopoly and left Arcot unguarded. Clive 57-67 took it from Madras with about 200 Europeans + 300 sepoys = 500, then held it through a 53-day counter-siege. Paris refused help (to honour the 1748 treaty and keep America); by 1754 France had lost the 2nd CW. Why it sticks: "five hundred men, fifty-three days": 5-0-0 then 5-3. 5.3 The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)  Treaty of Pondicherry (1754). Recall: Dupleix 42-54 recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of high war expenditure (he died in poverty in France, 1763). 1. Hyderabad: French influence remained in Hyderabad via Bussy as agent; French army in Hyderabad and Northern Sarkars with the French. 2. Factories: French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained. 3. Carnatic: Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic, hence EIC influence in Carnatic. Chanda Sahib 49-52: escaped to Tanjore, beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha Raja of Thanjavur, an old rival (Maratha rule in Tanjore began 1674 when Venkoji / Ekoji, half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region). Teacher's ink: "42-54" written above the recall row; underlines on high war expenditure, French influence, Bussy as agent, French army, Northern Sarkars and EIC influence in Carnatic, with small numerals 1, 2, 3 over the three French retentions; "[Fr (smiley)]" beside the Hyderabad row and "[Br (smiley)]" beside the Carnatic row; "[Company = ORG with PROFIT MOTIVE]" beside the recall row; "[FACTORY: warehouses + homes + offices + maybe fort]" beside the Factories row. Dupleix 42-54 was recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of the high war expenditure. He died in poverty in France in 1763, abandoned by the State he had served. The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) was a middle path:   Clause   Terms   Who smiles (teacher's ink)    --- --- ---    1. Hyderabad   French influence remained in Hyderabad: (1) Bussy as agent, (2) the French army in Hyderabad, (3) the Northern Sarkars with the French   French     2. Factories   French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained       3. Carnatic   Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic: hence EIC influence in Carnatic   British   Chanda Sahib 49-52, having escaped to Tanjore (present-day Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu), was beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, the Maratha Raja of Thanjavur: an old rival. Maratha rule in Tanjore had begun in 1674 when Venkoji (also known as Ekoji), half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region. Teacher: Why was a winning Governor-General recalled? The teacher's bracket: "Company = an organisation with a profit motive." High war expenditure eats profit, so the company removes the man who causes it. Beside the Factories row he repeats the definition from Chapter 8: "Factory = warehouses + homes + offices + maybe a fort." His two smileys read the treaty as a split: the French smile in Hyderabad, the British smile in Carnatic. Mnemonic: BAN: what France kept in Hyderabad (Treaty of Pondicherry 1754). "French influence stays, French clauses BAN the British from Hyderabad." Decode: Bussy as agent, Army (French army in Hyderabad), Northern Sarkars with the French. Clause 2: French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic retained. Clause 3: Md Ali 52-95 becomes Nawab of Carnatic = EIC influence there. Why it sticks: France smiles in clause 1, Britain smiles in clause 3, a middle path. Also: Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu, and died poor in 1763. Mnemonic: Chanda Sahib 49-52 fled to Tanjore and lost his head; 74 = 74. Decode: Chanda Sahib 49-52 escaped to Tanjore and was beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, the Maratha Raja of Thanjavur (an old rival). Maratha rule there began in 1674 when Venkoji (Ekoji), half-brother of Shivaji 74-80, conquered it. Why it sticks: the 74 in 1674 is the same 74 that starts Shivaji 74-80's code.  Teacher's board (no typed text): how wars end. "# WAR is expensive for BOTH: losing party, victorious party". "# So BOTH want end of war". "# VICTOR would go for end of war if achieved [WAR AIMS] (boxed), i.e. core goal of war". In yellow: a bracket at the top right "1740-48: AWoS; 1st CW 1746-48", and under the war aims line "[EIC = core motive: TRADE]" with two branches "HYD (smiley)" and "CARNATIC (smiley)". "# When TREATY is negotiated, then power differential between both sides and ability (economic, military etc.) = imp factors" (imp factors underlined). Teacher: The board's theory of treaties (marked "imp factors"). War is expensive for both, the losing party and the victorious party, so both want an end to the war. The victor will agree to end the war if it has achieved its war aims, that is, the core goal of the war. For the EIC the core motive was trade, so it could settle once its trade was safe (the two branches read Hyderabad and Carnatic, each with a smiley, matching the treaty slide's split). When a treaty is negotiated, the important factors are the power differential between the two sides and their ability, economic and military. Apply this to all three treaties: 1748 (the bracket recalls the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 and the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48), 1754 and 1763.

items.t: 6 · The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)
items.x: 6.1 Reason  Teacher's board (no typed text). "3 CW 1746-63" (the three Carnatic Wars) with a tree: on the left the circled numbers 1 and 3 with a circled "IR" below; on the right a circled 2 with "Factionalism" below. Then "(3): ROYAL MILITARIES (Fr, Br) joined armies of Fr eic, Eng eic". Bottom left: "3rd CW: [EIC + Br] vs [Fr eic + Fr]". The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) was once again a European conflict brought to Indian shores: the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), fought across Europe, the Americas, Africa and India. French side: Count de Lally (of the French State, not the French EIC) arrived from France with the Royal military and led the French alongside Bussy of the French EIC. British side: Eyre Coote (of the British State, not the EIC) arrived from Britain with the Royal military and led the British alongside Robert Clive 57-67 of the EIC. Teacher: The board's recap before the 3rd war. Of the three Carnatic Wars (1746-63), wars 1 and 3 come from "IR" (international relations: Britain against France), war 2 from factionalism. What is new in war 3: the Royal militaries (French and British) joined the armies of the French EIC and the English EIC. So the line-up is [EIC + Britain] versus [French EIC + France]. On the typed slide he wrote "had impacts" above "a European conflict on Indian shores" and underlined Count de Lally, Eyre Coote and royal military on both sides. Mnemonic: Royals only in the 3rd: "Lally vs Coote, Bussy vs Clive 57-67". Decode: Royal (State) leaders: Count de Lally (France) vs Eyre Coote (Britain). Company leaders: Bussy (French EIC) vs Clive 57-67 (EIC). The line-up is [EIC + Britain] vs [French EIC + France]. Why it sticks: royal armies joined in the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 ONLY; the two L and C pairs run crossed, Lally-Coote, Bussy-Clive. 6.2 Why did France lose the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)?  Handout map (also Lecture 13, slide 16): a close-up of the Coromandel Coast from an old printed map. Labels from north to south: Masulipatam 175? (year cut off), Coromandel Coast, Madras 1639, Chingleput 1780, Wandiwash 1760, Pondicherry (Fr.), Karikal (Fr.), then Trincomali 1782 and Ceylon (Dutch) at the bottom; "Circars" and "Fr. 1718: Br. 178?" are partly cut off at the top. Caption strip: Ch 9, Carnatic Wars: Madras (Br.) vs Pondicherry (Fr.); Wandiwash 1760. On the slide version the teacher drew three yellow pointer lines from Madras 1639, Wandiwash 1760 and Pondicherry (Fr.). The most decisive battle was the Battle of Wandiwash (1760). (The handout's memory line: "where the French were washed away.") After that the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry itself, their headquarters officially since 1701, with Fort Louis. The chain slides add: Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760, and the Siege of Pondicherry came in 1761. Teacher: The three pointer lines on the map mark the same three coastal places as the board's "MWP": Madras (the British base), Wandiwash (between the two) and Pondicherry (the French base). Wandiwash lies between the two headquarters, which is why the decisive battle was there.  PYQ 1, Prelims 1995, Battle of Wandiwash: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched? (a) Battle of Buxar: Mir Jafar vs. Clive 57-67 (b) Battle of Wandiwash: French vs. East India Company (c) Battle of Chilianwala: Dalhousie 48-56 vs Marathas (d) Battle of Kharda: Nizam vs. East India Company. Teacher's ink: a circled F beside (a); a tick beside (b); in (c) "Marathas" struck through, "SIKH" written beside it, circled F; in (d) "East India Company" struck through, "MARATHAS 1795" written below, circled F. Prelims 1995: UPSC asked "match the battle to who fought it" by jumbling correct pairs. The correct pairs are: Battle of Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06); Battle of Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Battle of Kharda (1795) = Nizam of Hyderabad vs the Marathas; Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the East India Company. The answer was (b). The trap in (a): Mir Jafar 57-60 was the EIC's man at Plassey 1757, not its enemy at Buxar. Mnemonic: 60, 61, 63: Wandiwash washes, Pondicherry falls, Paris signs. Decode: 22 January 1760 Wandiwash (Eyre Coote beats Lally, decisive); 1761 Siege of Pondicherry (HQ since 1701, Fort Louis); 1763 Treaty of Paris. Why it sticks: 60, 61, then a gap year, 63; "where the French were washed away". Mnemonic: B-C-K-W: match the battle to its two sides (Prelims 1995). "Q for Buxar, Sikh for Chilli, Khadda for Kharda, W for French." Decode: Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63, not Mir Jafar 57-60. Chilianwala (1849) = Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs. Kharda (1795) = Nizam vs the Marathas. Wandiwash (1760) = French vs EIC, the correct pair. Why it sticks: Chilli is hot like a Sikh; Kharda (kharaa, "standing") = the Nizam stands against the Marathas. France lost for four reasons.  Wandiwash (1760): Why France Lost the 3rd War. Battle of Wandiwash 1760: the most decisive battle; after it the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry, their headquarters since 1701 with Fort Louis. 1. Tactical mistake: Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic; Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took the Northern Sarkars in 1759. 2. Poor leadership: Lally, despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, demoralised his army. Teacher's ink: underlines on Fort Louis, Lally and rude conduct; under row 2 "# DUPLEIX 42-54 not HERE"; top right a sketch: a line from "CARNATIC" up to "N. SARKARS" with "Bussy" at its end, a curve marked (1) "LALLY" with an arrow "TO HELP" back to Carnatic, and (2) "BENGAL" with an arrow down into the N. Sarkars.  Why France Lost the 3rd War (contd.). 3. Financial weakness: French soldiers went unpaid for months; the French EIC had spent heavily in earlier wars without gains; Britain had profited from eastern trade since 1600; British capitalism was mature (Industrial Revolution 1750-1850) while French feudalism ended only after the French Revolution of 1789. 4. Superior British navy: Britain dominated the Coromandel coast, decisive in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Teacher's ink: "Financial weakness", "soldiers" and "unpaid for months" underlined; on the right, arrows from "earlier wars" to "1740-48 AWoS [1st CW 1746-48]" and "2nd CW 1749-54: Hyd gains BUT STILL higher war expenditure" (BUT and STILL underlined); at the bottom left, written along a diagonal line, "CARNATIC" above and "COROMANDEL COAST" below.   Reason   Detail    --- ---    1. Tactical mistake   Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic. Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took over the Northern Sarkars in 1759     2. Poor leadership   Lally was despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, which demoralised the army     3. Financial weakness   French soldiers went unpaid for months. The French EIC had spent heavily in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) and the first two Carnatic Wars without commensurate gains. In contrast, Britain had been profiting from eastern trade since 1600. British capitalism was mature; feudalism in France ended only after the French Revolution of 1789, while the Industrial Revolution had begun in Britain (1750-1850)     4. Superior British navy   This gave Britain decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Britain's navy was able to dominate the Coromandel coast   Teacher: The sketch for the tactical mistake. Step (1): Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars and goes down to Carnatic to help Lally. Step (2): from Bengal, Clive 57-67 comes down into the now unguarded Northern Sarkars (1759). Under "Poor leadership" the teacher wrote "Dupleix 42-54 not here": the one able French leader had been recalled in 1754, so France fought this war with Lally. Teacher: On financial weakness. The "earlier wars" that drained the French EIC are the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 [the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48] and the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54. His note on the second: "Hyderabad gains, BUT STILL higher war expenditure": even the winning phase cost more than it earned. For the navy point he wrote Carnatic over Coromandel Coast: Carnatic is the land along the Coromandel coast, so whoever commands the sea commands the war there. Mnemonic: LMNT: why France lost the 3rd war ("Lally's missing element"). Decode: Leadership (Lally, rude, despised by officers and sepoys; Dupleix 42-54 not here). Money (soldiers unpaid for months; British capitalism mature, French feudalism ended only in 1789). Navy (Britain dominated the Coromandel coast). Tactical mistake (Bussy left the Northern Sarkars for Lally; Clive 57-67 took them in 1759). Why it sticks: four letters for four reasons, and the "element" that is missing is a good commander.  Teacher's board (no typed text): "if you want to see [CAPITALISM] in SOCIETY" (Capitalism boxed), with three bullets: "wake up at 4am and sit in BALCONY (facing a main road)"; "[PPL] at mass level have a belief [can be RICH by WORKING HARD]"; "BOMBAY never sleeps [so CITY provides money opportunities 24x7]". On the left: "FR 1789 ended Feudalism, then Capitalism in France" and "[BUT merchants existed PRE 1789]" (BUT underlined). Teacher: What does "British capitalism was mature" mean? The board's picture. If you want to see capitalism in a society: wake up at 4 am and sit in a balcony facing a main road. People are already at work. In a capitalist society people at the mass level have a belief that they can become rich by working hard. Bombay never sleeps, because the city provides opportunities to earn 24x7. The French Revolution of 1789 ended feudalism, and only then did capitalism come to France (but note: merchants existed in France before 1789 too). Britain had this money-making society earlier, so it could pay for its wars. 6.3 Why did the EIC win the Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)?   Factor   Detail    --- ---    1. France starved Dupleix 42-54 of reinforcements   To preserve its gains from the 1748 Treaty (Aix-La-Chapelle)     2. Leadership   French: the recall of Dupleix 42-54 after the 2nd Carnatic War hurt the chances of French victory; Lally displayed poor leadership in the 3rd Carnatic War. British: Robert Clive 57-67 and Eyre Coote displayed good leadership     3. Superior British navy   British naval dominance of the coast     4. Finances   The EIC was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital; it had accumulated wealth, along with huge monetary gains after Plassey 1757. The French EIC was a State PSU with weak finances. The French economy was weak compared to Britain, which was the world's top economy of the time. Past war expenditure without any formidable gains hurt French capabilities, e.g. Lally's troops went unpaid (the slide adds: unpaid for months, so low morale)     5. Tactical mistakes   Leaving Arcot (the capital of Carnatic) unguarded in the 2nd Carnatic War and leaving the Northern Sarkars unguarded in the 3rd Carnatic War   Teacher: Above the slide's title the teacher wrote "all (3)": this table answers "Why the EIC won all 3 Carnatic Wars," while section 6.2 answers only the 3rd war. For a Mains answer, use 6.3 for the whole contest and 6.2 for Wandiwash. Mnemonic: LMNT plus one = the five reasons the EIC won all 3 wars. Decode: the four LMNT reasons (Leadership, Money, Navy, Tactical mistakes) plus the extra one: France starved Dupleix 42-54 of reinforcements to preserve its 1748 gains. Finance contrast: the EIC = private joint-stock firm with deep capital (and Plassey 1757 wealth); the French EIC = a State PSU with weak finances. Why it sticks: 6.2 has 4 (Wandiwash, 3rd war), 6.3 has 5 (all 3 wars); private beats PSU. The handout numbers these factors 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 (the number 2 is printed twice). There are five factors; they are renumbered 1 to 5 here. 6.4 The Treaty of Paris (1763)  Treaty of Paris (1763). France lost all gains since 1749, under "PM KYC (Yojana)": restricted to its pre-1749 position; France retained only 5 small trading posts: Pondicherry (E), Mahe (west coast), Karaikal (E), Yanam (E), Chandernagore (E). Barred: France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases. 1769: French EIC abolished by France = the French State gave up ambitions of dominating India's international trade. British monopoly: having countered the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now held monopoly over India's international trade. Teacher's ink: at the top "[1748: T of Aix La Chapelle, T of Pondicherry 1754]"; "PM KYC (Yojana)" underlined; "CENTRES" written over "posts", which is struck through; "Malabar" under Mahe (west coast) and "BENGAL" under Chandernagore; underlines on strong army or fortifying its bases, French EIC abolished by France, British EIC, monopoly and India's international trade; a word above "1650s" [unclear: ROYALTY or RIVALRY]; below the last row "NOT (T)"; on the right "Who will BUY INDIAN GOODS; Who will DOMINATE exports from India". Under the Treaty of Paris (1763): France lost all gains made in India since 1749 and was restricted to its pre-1749 position. France retained only five small trading posts: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam and Chandernagore. France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases.   Letter   Post   Where (slide and teacher's ink)    --- --- ---    P   Pondicherry   East coast     M   Mahe   West coast (teacher: Malabar)     K   Karaikal   East coast     Y   Yanam   East coast     C   Chandernagore   East (teacher: Bengal)   Teacher: The slide's mnemonic "PM KYC (Yojana)" is underlined by the teacher: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore. Only Mahe is on the west coast (Malabar); Chandernagore is in Bengal. He replaced "trading posts" with "trading CENTRES." At the top he lined up the three treaties to learn in order: 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle, 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry, 1763 Treaty of Paris. Mnemonic: PM KYC: 3 east, 1 west, 1 Bengal. Decode: Pondicherry, Karaikal, Yanam = east coast (3). Mahe = the only west coast post (Malabar). Chandernagore = Bengal. Five posts in all. Why it sticks: "M for Malabar", "C for Chandernagore, the Bengal one"; the three east-coast letters P, K, Y are what is left. France was also barred from a strong army or fortified bases. In 1769 the French EIC was abolished by France. This signifies that the French government had given up on its ambitions of dominating the international trade of India. The abolition of the French EIC does not mean other French traders could not trade in India, just that the French State was not interested in running a government company for it. After successfully countering the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by the 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now had a monopoly over India's international trade. Teacher: Under the British monopoly row the teacher wrote "NOT (T)": in 1763 the EIC has a monopoly over trade, not territory. What was decided was only "who will buy Indian goods, who will dominate exports from India." This fits the board in section 1.2: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade. Mnemonic: P-D-F: "Please Don't Forget" the order the EIC beat its rivals. Decode: Portuguese by 1612, Dutch by the 1650s, French by 1763, leaving the British EIC the monopoly over India's international trade. Also: the French EIC was abolished by France in 1769, six years after Paris. Why it sticks: the dates climb 12, 50s, 63 in the same order as the letters. A handwritten word above "1650s" on this slide is [unclear: it reads ROYALTY or RIVALRY]. Check your own notebook. 6.5 Link with Plassey, and what came later  Carnatic Wars: Legacy and After. Link with Plassey 1757: the 3rd Carnatic War brought large British royal military to India; that strength and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey possible; without Carnatic, perhaps no Plassey would have happened, which led to empire building by EIC. Treaty of Hyderabad 1766: Hyderabad ceded the Northern Sarkars to EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year and protection against Marathas and Mysore. Domination of South India by EIC: the Carnatic Wars, though fought for India's international trade, laid the foundation of British domination of South India; Subsidiary Alliance: Hyderabad = 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with EIC (1798); Mysore 1799; Travancore 1805; Carnatic was annexed 1801. Teacher's ink: on the right a flow "7yr GLOBAL WAR, then 3rd CW, then Br ROYAL MILITARY in INDIA, then confidence of CLIVE for accepting Jafar's offer"; under the Domination row "3rd CW + 3.5 Decades"; underlines on Northern Sarkars to EIC, Hyderabad, Subsidiary Alliance, (1798), Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic and annexed 1801. Takeaway: link with the Battle of Plassey (1757). The 3rd Carnatic War brought large numbers of British Royal military troops to India, and it was this military strength, and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy, that made Plassey possible. Without Carnatic there may not have been a Plassey, which led to Empire Building by the EIC. Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) 3rd Carnatic War British Royal military in India (good) Confidence of Clive 57-67 for accepting Jafar's offer: Plassey 1757 Later: In the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766), Hyderabad formally ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually and protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Hyderabad became the 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC, in 1798. Mysore signed in 1799 and Travancore in 1805, while Carnatic was annexed in 1801. Thus the Carnatic Wars, though fought for the international trade of India, laid the foundation of British domination of South India. Teacher: Under "Domination of South India" the teacher wrote "3rd CW + 3.5 decades": that is, from the end of the 3rd Carnatic War (1763) it took about three and a half decades to reach the first Subsidiary Alliance (Hyderabad, 1798). He underlined each item of that row: Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic annexed 1801. "Jafar's offer" in his flow is Mir Jafar 57-60's deal with Clive 57-67, the story of Chapter 10. Mnemonic: 98, 99, 01, 05: the South's Subsidiary Alliance order. "Hyderabad Made Calls to Travancore": H-M-C-T. Decode: Hyderabad 1798 (1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance), Mysore 1799, Carnatic annexed 1801, Travancore 1805. Earlier, the Treaty of Hyderabad 1766: the Northern Sarkars ceded to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year and protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Why it sticks: "3rd CW + 3.5 decades": 1763 plus about 35 years is 1798.

items.t: 7 · Diagram 1: the Carnatic Wars in one chain
items.x: Handout Diagram 1, Carnatic Wars, nine boxes joined by arrows. Row 1: Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 (Anglo-French rivalry spills into India); 1st Carnatic War 1746-48 (Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746; La Bourdonnais takes Fort St George Madras); Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle 1748 (Madras returned; Dupleix 42-54 sees a small sepoy force can crush 10,000 cavalry). Row 2: 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54 (Battle of Ambur 1749; Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Dupleix 42-54 invents the empire-building model); Robert Clive 57-67, Siege of Arcot 1751 (53-day defence; Muhammad Ali Wallajah prevails); Treaty of Pondicherry 1754 (Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu; French momentum broken). Row 3: 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 (Seven Years Global War; Count de Lally vs Sir Eyre Coote); Battle of Wandiwash 22 Jan 1760 (Sir Eyre Coote, decisive EIC victory, Prelims 1995 warning mark); Siege of Pondicherry 1761 leading to the Treaty of Paris 1763 (French power in India permanently broken). How to read Diagram 1. In the printed figure the arrows of the middle row run from the Treaty of Pondicherry box to Arcot and then to the 2nd Carnatic War box, which is the reverse of the time order. Read the middle row from left to right instead: 2nd Carnatic War (Ambur 1749), then Arcot 1751, then the Treaty of Pondicherry 1754. The class slides (Lecture 12, slides 66 and 67) show the same chain in the correct order, as below. Austrian War of Succession (1740-48): Anglo-French rivalry in Europe spills into India 1st Carnatic War (1746-48): Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746; the French crush the Nawab's cavalry Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748): ends the Austrian War; Madras returned to the EIC 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): Ambur 1749; Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Dupleix 42-54 invents the empire model (good) Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751): 53-day defence; Md Ali 52-95 (Wallajah) prevails (warn) Treaty of Pondicherry (1754): Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu; French momentum broken 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63): Seven Years' Global War; de Lally versus Eyre Coote (good) Wandiwash (22 January 1760): decisive EIC victory over the French (bad) Siege of Pondicherry (1761), then Treaty of Paris (1763): French power in India permanently broken

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The Carnatic story of "Dupleix 42-54 and the Five Hundred". A quarrel in Austria (1740-48) lights India: at Adyar 1746, 1,000 French-trained men crush 10,000 cavalry. Aix 1748 hands Madras back, and Dupleix 42-54 "aches". So he plays kingmaker (SART): Ambur 1749, three deaths in 49, 50, 51, and Bussy's five-finger gains. Then 500 men under Clive 57-67 take unguarded Arcot (1751) and hold 53 days; Paris will not help, and Pondicherry 1754 ends the 2nd war with Dupleix 42-54 recalled. Seven Years' War 1756-63: Lally vs Coote; Wandiwash 22 Jan 1760 washes the French away, Pondicherry falls 1761, Paris 1763 leaves only PM KYC. 1769: the French EIC is abolished. 1798: Hyderabad signs the first Subsidiary Alliance. Decode: Adyar 1746, Aix 1748, Ambur 1749, Arcot 1751, Pondicherry 1754, Wandiwash 1760, Paris 1763: A-A-A-A-P-W-P in order.

items.t: Exam lens: priority and PYQs
items.x: Teacher: No overall priority label is written on the Chapter 10 title slide, but the board marks inside the chapter show what the teacher wants. "imp Reason" (Lecture 14, slide 3): the EIC could build an empire because India had multiple States and not one State ruling the whole of India. A circled "PYQ (M)" (Lecture 14, slide 15): "Why there were recurrent famines in British ruled India", with the note "one para from this topic" (the Great Bengal Famine 1770). "In Prelims: match the following. Correct: PoRF = W. Hastings 73-85" (Lecture 14, slide 16). Ticks on the three policies of Clive 57-67's toolkit (Indirect Rule, Ring Fence, mini Subsidiary Alliance) and on private trade and domestic trade after Plassey. Boxed: the word DRAIN, the annual tribute of Rs 26 lakh, and Awadh versus EIC + Bengal at Buxar. (Plassey 1757 was already marked "imp" in Lecture 11: see Chapter 8.)   Year and paper   What was asked   The answer or trap   Where in this chapter    --- --- --- ---    Prelims 2004   Three statements: (1) in the Third Battle of Panipat, Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated Ibrahim Lodi; (2) Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War; (3) Mir Jafar 57-60 entered into a conspiracy with the English for the defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 in the Battle of Plassey. Which is/are correct? Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) Only 3 (c) 2 and 3 (d) None of these   (b) Only 3. Statement 1 is false: in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Abdali defeated the Marathas; Ibrahim Lodi lost the First Panipat (1526) to Babur 26-30. Statement 2 is false: Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99) at Srirangapatna, not the Third (1789-92). The teacher's ink: [1st BoP 1526] F, [4th 1799] F, T, and (b) circled. Only statement 3 is from this chapter, but the answer can still be reached from it   Section 5 (the conspiracy and the battle)     Prelims 2005   The correct chronological order of the battles fought in India in the 18th century: (a) Wandiwash, Buxar, Ambur, Plassey (b) Ambur, Plassey, Wandiwash, Buxar (c) Wandiwash, Plassey, Ambur, Buxar (d) Ambur, Buxar, Wandiwash, Plassey   (b): Ambur (1749), Plassey (1757), Wandiwash (1760), Buxar (1764). The teacher wrote the years over option (a) (1760, 1764, 1749, 1757) and ticked (b). (a) puts Wandiwash and Buxar before Ambur; (c) puts Wandiwash before Plassey; (d) puts Buxar before Wandiwash. Ambur and Wandiwash are Carnatic Wars battles (Chapter 9)   Section 9 (chronology box)     Mains (the year is not written on the slide)   Why were there recurrent famines in British-ruled India?   The teacher: one paragraph of that answer comes from this topic: the Great Bengal Famine 1770 under the Dual Government (high revenue demand, harsh collection, hoarding unchecked, nobody responsible for relief) and his "Famine = Nature factor AND Human factor" board   Section 8.2.2 (Indirect Rule, the 1770 famine and Direct Rule)   What to prepare: Prelims hooks: the four Farmans (1613, 1618, 1691, 1717) and what each gave; Dr William Hamilton and "Magna Carta of the Company"; what MQK 17-27 allowed and refused; Dastak, Gomasta, interloper, free merchant; Black Hole numbers (146 and 123, against 30 to 40) and the Holwell monument dates (1760, 1821, 1901, 1940); Treaty of Alinagar; Plassey 23 June 1757 and Mir Jafar 57-60 as Bakshi; Hector Munroe at Buxar 1764 (Clive 57-67 was in London); the Treaty of Allahabad figures (Rs 26 lakh, Rs 50 lakh, Kora and Allahabad, Benaras annexed 1775); Diwani versus Nizamat; Md Reza Khan; Dual Government 1765-72; Ring Fence = Warren Hastings 73-85 in a match-the-following; first Subsidiary Alliance = Hyderabad 1798, not Awadh; the battle order Ambur, Plassey, Wandiwash, Buxar. Mains hooks: "conquest without rule" (Plassey) against "legal right to rule" (Buxar); how Plassey began the Drain of Wealth and changed the trade structure; why the EIC did not annex Bengal outright; how the Dual Government produced the 1770 famine (one para for the recurrent-famines question); Clive 57-67 as the father of the empire-building toolkit; why the EIC could build an empire (many States, resources not united).

items.t: 0 · The chapter on one board
