items.t: 0 · What the name means: Subsidiary, or Subordinate, Alliance
items.x: Chapter 11 title slide: Subsidiary Alliance of Wellesley 98-05 (1798–1805), Modern Indian History, Chapter 11. Teacher's ink: "Richard" written above the name Wellesley 98-05; "Subordinate [SA]" written below the word Subsidiary; a large bracket on the right reading "BRO: ARTHUR (Br Royal Military), HENRY (eic)". Teacher: Three things are added to the title by hand. (1) "Richard" above the surname: the Governor General is Richard Wellesley 98-05. (2) "Subordinate [SA]" under the word Subsidiary: read Subsidiary Alliance as Subordinate Alliance. (3) "[BRO: ARTHUR (Br Royal Military), HENRY (eic)]": his two brothers, Arthur in the British Royal Military and Henry with the EIC. The whole chapter turns on these two ideas: an unequal alliance, and three brothers working together.  Teacher's board: the meaning of Subordinate Alliance. Two touching ovals: the right oval "Alliance" (circled 1) with the note "between equals i.e. equal rights of both parties"; the left oval "Subordinate" (circled 2) with the note "one party's rights are less respected". Below: "# alliance:" a level yellow line between two dots, with the example "Treaty of Amritsar 1809" and a level line between dots marked Sikh and eic. Then "# SA" (circled): a yellow line sloping down from a dot marked eic to a dot marked Indian State, with the example "1798:" a sloping line from eic down to HYD.   Word (the teacher's order)   Meaning on the board   Picture on the board   Example on the board    --- --- --- ---    1. Alliance   Between equals, that is, equal rights of both parties   A level line between two dots   Treaty of Amritsar 1809: Sikh and EIC on the same level     2. Subordinate   One party's rights are less respected   A line sloping down from the EIC to the Indian State   1798: EIC above, Hyderabad (HYD) below   Teacher: Read the two words in the teacher's order: first "Alliance", then "Subordinate". An alliance by itself is a treaty between equals. The word "Subordinate" then cancels that equality: one party's rights are less respected. So a Subordinate (Subsidiary) Alliance looks like an alliance on paper, but the two dots are not on the same level: the EIC is on top. The teacher draws the same sloping line again on slide 43 under the word "Imbalance." Mnemonic: Amritsar is flat, Hyderabad is a slide. Alliance = LEVEL line. Subordinate = SLOPE. Decode: Alliance = between equals, equal rights (Treaty of Amritsar 1809, Sikh and EIC, on one level). Subordinate = one party's rights less respected (1798, EIC on top, Hyderabad below). Subsidiary = Subordinate. Why it sticks: you can picture a flat table (Amritsar) and a playground slide (Hyderabad).

items.t: 1 · Who were the Wellesleys?
items.x: Who Were the Wellesleys? Table of two rows. Richard Wellesley 98-05: Governor General of Bengal 1798–1805; empire builder who saw that expanding the empire raised his profile with a nationalistic British public; founded Fort William College, Calcutta 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to districts. Henry WELLESLEYPROT: handled administration and diplomacy of the EIC. Teacher's yellow underlines: "empire builder", "Fort William College, Calcutta 1800", "train British civil servants", "Indian languages, laws". No handwriting.   Brother   Role    --- ---    Richard Wellesley 98-05   Governor General of Bengal from 1798 to 1805. He was joined in India by both his brothers, Arthur and Henry Wellesley. An empire builder     Henry Wellesley   Handled the administration and diplomacy of the EIC     Arthur Wellesley   A military commander, but NOT an EIC officer: a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army   Wellesley 98-05 was an empire builder. He understood that expanding the empire raised his profile among a nationalistic British public, which was useful for his political ambitions back home. He established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to the districts. Mnemonic: RAH! The three brothers. Richard Rules, Arthur Army, Henry Handles (R-A-H). Decode: Richard Wellesley 98-05 = Governor General of Bengal, the empire builder. Arthur = military commander, but Royal Army (33rd Regiment of Foot), NOT an EIC officer. Henry = administration and diplomacy of the EIC. Why it sticks: the cheer "RAH!" lists them in order of rank. Teacher: The yellow underlines on this slide are "empire builder", "Fort William College, Calcutta 1800", "train British civil servants" and "Indian languages, laws". These are exactly the words UPSC has used: the founder pair and the purpose. Fort William College has been tested in UPSC Prelims three times. Prelims 2018: the institution and founder pair (alongside Sanskrit College Banaras and Calcutta Madarsa). Prelims 2020 and Prelims 2021: the purpose of establishment. Learn: Wellesley 98-05, Calcutta, 1800, to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs. Mnemonic: Fort William teaches the "3 L-C" subjects. Eighteen-hundred, Calcutta, Wellesley 98-05's school: Languages, Laws, Customs for the new civil servants. Decode: Fort William College = Calcutta, 1800, founder Wellesley 98-05. Purpose (Prelims 2020 and 2021) = train British civil servants in Indian Languages, Laws and Customs before district postings. Founder pair asked in Prelims 2018. Why it sticks: "Languages, Laws, Customs" is the purpose; no mention of sepoys or English-teaching. 1.1 Arthur Wellesley: a Royal Army officer, not an EIC officer  Who Were the Wellesleys? (contd.) Arthur WELLESLEYPROT: military commander but NOT an EIC officer; a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (infantry); led his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99) including the Siege of Seringapatam (1799), and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) including the Battle of Assaye (1803); also fought Napoleon's army 1808–15. Yellow underlines: "NOT an EIC officer", "Royal Army", "4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99)", "2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) incl. Battle of Assaye (1803)", "fought", "Napoleon's army 1808–15". Teacher's handwriting on the right: "Br State helped eic in INDIA, e.g. 3rd CW 1756-63, therefore eic GOT HELP of Br State in Empire BUILDING in INDIA". Arthur Wellesley was a military commander, but he was NOT an EIC officer. He was a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army, commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (that is, infantry). He led his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99), including the Siege of Seringapatam (1799), and in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05), including the Battle of Assaye (1803). He also fought Napoleon's army between 1808 and 1815. Mnemonic: Arthur's three marches. "Ninety-nine, Tipu 82-99's town; Oh-three, Assaye's crown; Oh-eight, the Frenchman's frown." Decode: 1799 = Siege of Seringapatam (4th Anglo-Mysore War 1798-99, Tipu 82-99 falls). 1803 = Battle of Assaye (2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05). 1808 to 1815 = fights Napoleon's army. Regiment: 33rd Foot, a Royal (not EIC) unit. Teacher: Written beside the Arthur row: "Br State helped EIC in India, e.g. 3rd CW 1756-63; therefore the EIC GOT HELP of the Br State in Empire BUILDING in India." The reasoning: Arthur is proof that the British State's own army fought the EIC's wars. This was not new in 1798: Royal help goes back to the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). So the empire was built by the Company and the British State together, not by a private company alone. 1.2 Two European armies in India (3rd Carnatic War 1756–63 till 1858)  Two European Armies in India (3rd Carnatic War 1756–63 till 1858). Company's Army: the EIC's own private military, paid for by the EIC; majorly Indian sepoys but also European sepoys; senior officers always European i.e. British. King's Army (Royal Military): official British State's regiments sent to India to support the EIC; the EIC had to reimburse the British State for the cost of Royal troops deployed in India. Legally distinct: both forces fought together but were legally and institutionally distinct; the Company State received direct military support from the British Crown, hence the British State cannot escape responsibility for empire building in India. Teacher's yellow underline: "EIC had to reimburse the British State". No handwriting. From the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) till 1858, two separate European military forces operated in India side by side:   Force   What it was   Who paid    --- --- ---    Company's Army   The EIC's own private military. Majorly Indian sepoys, but it also had European sepoys. Senior officers were always European, that is, British   Paid for by the EIC     King's Army (Royal Military)   The official British State's regiments sent to India to support the EIC   The EIC had to reimburse the British State for the cost of Royal troops deployed in India   Both forces fought together, but they were legally and institutionally distinct. Mnemonic: Company pays its own; the King lends and sends the bill. Decode: Company's Army = the EIC's own private military, paid by the EIC, mostly Indian sepoys, always British senior officers. King's Army (Royal Military) = British State regiments sent to support the EIC; the EIC has to reimburse the British State. Both side by side from the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 till 1858. Why it sticks: "King lends, Company pays" also reminds you the British State shares responsibility. The handout's note: the Company State in India received direct military support from the British Crown. Hence the British State cannot escape responsibility for empire building in India. (The teacher underlined "EIC had to reimburse the British State" in yellow: the Crown lent its regiments, and the Company paid the bill.) 1.3 Arthur's own verdict on the Marathas  Two European Armies in India (contd.). Arthur's own verdict: on record, the Marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced, and the Battle of Assaye (1803) the toughest fight of his career. Had India been one State ruling the whole, not a fragmented polity, it would not have been colonised. No handwriting on this slide. Arthur Wellesley on record stated that the Marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced, and that the Battle of Assaye (1803) against them was the toughest fight of his entire military career. The Marathas were harder to defeat militarily. The handout's conclusion: had India not been a fragmented polity, that is, had there been one State ruling the whole of India, India would not have been colonised. This is a ready Mains line on why the EIC won.

items.t: 2 · Pitt's India Act 1784 banned conquest: how Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated it
items.x: 2.1 Context of Pitt's India Act 1784 (the teacher's board)  Teacher's board: "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]". A left-to-right chain: GBF 1770, then by 1772 eic bankrupt, then sought help of Br State, then Br State gave money or a loan to eic BUT (circled) brought eic under Br State's supervision via the boxed "Regulating Act 1773". Under the box: "CORE GOAL: Eic shall NOT waste Br taxpayer money on WARS and again go bankrupt". Right column: "1st A-Ma war 1775-8[last digit unclear]" plus (circled +) "2nd A-My war 1780-84" equals "HIGH WAR expenditure", "therefore Br State anxious", "therefore passed PIA 1784 which banned conquest i.e. eic can DEFEND but Cannot START WARS on its own" (the last phrase underlined in yellow). GBF 1770 (as written on the board) (warn) By 1772 the EIC is bankrupt; it seeks the help of the British State The British State gives money (a loan) to the EIC, BUT brings the EIC under its supervision via the Regulating Act 1773 Core goal of 1773: the EIC shall not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again (warn) 1st Anglo-Maratha War plus 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): high war expenditure; the British State is anxious (bad) Pitt's India Act 1784 bans conquest: the EIC can defend but cannot start wars on its own Teacher: The heading reads "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]": the Act was passed by the British Parliament (the circled P) when William Pitt was Prime Minister. The logic of the chain is money: the British State had already rescued a bankrupt Company once (the loan, with supervision through the Regulating Act 1773). Its core goal was that the EIC should not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again. When two more wars again produced high war expenditure, the State grew anxious and wrote the ban into law. The teacher underlined in yellow: "Cannot START WARS." Unclear handwriting on slide 34. The years of the "1st A-Ma war" on the board read "1775-8[unclear]": the last digit is not legible. The handout and slide 35 print 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82). Use 1775–82, and check your class notebook. The board's abbreviation "GBF 1770" is not expanded on this slide; it is from the Chapter 10 boards of the same lecture, see Chapter 10. Mnemonic: Seventy, seventy-two, seventy-three, eighty-four. "Seventy GBF, seventy-two broke, seventy-three leash, eighty-four lock." Decode: GBF 1770 starts the board chain. 1772 = EIC bankrupt, seeks British State help. 1773 = loan, but supervision via the Regulating Act. Then more wars (1st Anglo-Maratha 1775-82 plus 2nd Anglo-Mysore 1780-84, high war expenditure). 1784 = Pitt's India Act locks conquest. Why it sticks: the rhyme "broke, leash, lock" tells the whole money story. 2.2 The ban and the reason for it  Pitt's India Act 1784 Banned Conquest: How Wellesley 98-05 Re-initiated It. Ban: the Governor-General could not start an offensive war without express command of the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State; he had the right to enter war only on grounds of defence. Reason: high war expenditure; the Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), Battle of Buxar (1764), two Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84) and the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) had drained company finances; Parliament mandated diplomacy over war: Policy of Indirect Rule plus a balance of power among Indian States instead of direct conquest. Teacher's yellow underlines: "could not start an offensive war", "High war expenditure", "drained company finances". No handwriting.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    The ban   Pitt's India Act of 1784 had banned conquest. The Governor-General (GG) could not start an offensive war without the express command and authority of either the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State (discussed in a later chapter)     The exception   The GG had the right to enter war on grounds of defence     The reason   High war expenditure     The wars that drained Company finances   The Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), the Battle of Buxar (1764), two Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84) and the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82)     What Parliament mandated instead   Diplomacy rather than war, in the form of the Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) and maintaining a balance of power among Indian States, instead of pursuing direct conquest   The handout's recall: the pacifist policy of the Mughals after 1707 was also for the same reason (the cost of war). And the handout's note: Wellesley 98-05 could not legally start an offensive war without prior authorisation. Mnemonic: Defend yes, declare no: ask "CD or BC". Decode: Under Pitt's India Act 1784 the GG could start an offensive war only with the express command of the Court of Directors (CD) or the Board of Control (BC). Defence needed no permission. Reason for the ban = high war expenditure. Why it sticks: "CD or BC" is the two-door permission slip. Mnemonic: Three, one, two, one: the war-bill count. "Car-Bux-My-Ma" = 3-1-2-1. Decode: 3 Carnatic Wars (1746-63); 1 Buxar (1764); 2 Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-69 and 1780-84); 1 First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). These drained Company finances, so Parliament chose diplomacy: Policy of Indirect Rule plus balance of power. 2.3 The Napoleon threat: there, but not real  Teacher's board headed "WORLD HISTORY" (underlined in yellow). A rough map in yellow outline: "France" at top left; a yellow dotted line from France through "1798" to "Egypt"; "M. east" with another dotted line; a pink dotted line running on from France towards the V-shaped sea on the right; three yellow arrows pointing down to "Br TRADE of ARABIAN Sea"; a curved line from the right-hand V to "DIPLOMATIC CONTACT WITH TIPU 82-99". A pink arrow leads to "THREAT of Napoleon-Mysore alliance / Napoleon ATTACKING Br India". Below, "PRELIMS" (pink underline), then "# THREAT Was THERE BUT not Real", with a tree: "Real [High Chance]" and "un Real [Less Chance]", and the reason "because Br NAVY = SUPERIOR [Wont have been able to Reach India]". 1798: France (Napoleon) attacks Egypt; the dotted line on the board runs France to Egypt, marked 1798 Aim: the Middle East; to hurt the British trade of the Arabian Sea (three arrows on the board) Diplomatic contact with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore (warn) Threat: a Napoleon and Mysore alliance, or Napoleon attacking British India (good) But the threat was "there, not real"; the British Navy was superior, so the French would not have been able to reach India Teacher: This is the board marked PRELIMS. The teacher splits the word "threat" into two kinds: Real = high chance; Unreal = less chance. His verdict: "THREAT was THERE BUT not Real", that is, a threat existed, but with a low chance. The reason he writes beside it: "because Br NAVY = SUPERIOR [would not have been able to reach India]." So in an exam statement, "Napoleonic danger" is a correct feature of the Subsidiary Alliance (the danger was there), even though the danger was not a real, high-chance one. Mnemonic: Egypt knocks, the Navy blocks. "Ninety-eight: Napoleon at Egypt's gate, Tipu 82-99 waves; the Navy bars the sea. THERE, not REAL." Decode: 1798 = Napoleon attacks Egypt (aim: Middle East, hurt British trade of the Arabian Sea); contact with Tipu 82-99; fear = Napoleon-Mysore alliance or attack on British India. Reality: British Navy superior, so the French could not reach India. Teacher's PRELIMS line: "Threat was THERE but not REAL."  Pitt's India Act 1784 Banned Conquest: How Wellesley 98-05 Re-initiated It (contd.). Wellesley's trick: re-initiated conquest by overhyping a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance; Napoleon attacked Egypt in 1798 to control the Middle East and hurt British trade, and was in contact with Tipu 82-99; a threat existed but not a real one, as Britain's superior navy would have destroyed a French fleet in the Arabian Sea before it arrived. Middle path: the British State agreed anyway, since protecting India from European rivals was the primary goal of British foreign policy; Wellesley 98-05 offered the Subsidiary Alliance: political domination without the cost, administrative burden and symbolism of full annexation. Teacher's ink: beside "Middle path" he wrote "= SA = CONTROL w/o annexation"; a handwritten "w/o" after "administrative burden &". Yellow underline: "Re-initiated conquest". Pink underlines: "overhyping", "A threat existed but not a real one", and the whole Subsidiary Alliance phrase. Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated conquest by overhyping the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance. Napoleon had attacked Egypt in 1798 with the goal of controlling the Middle East and hurting British trade, and he was in communication with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore. A threat existed, but not a real one. Britain's navy was superior to France's, and a French fleet heading for India through the Arabian Sea would have been destroyed before arriving. The handout's note: the British had already burnt French ships in the Mediterranean once Napoleon landed in Egypt, leaving his army stranded with no way home. But the British State agreed anyway, because protecting India from European rivals was the primary goal of British foreign policy and it did not want to take any risks. Wellesley 98-05 also offered a middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance. It gave political domination without the cost, the administrative burden and the symbolism of full annexation. Teacher: Beside "Middle path" the teacher wrote "= SA = CONTROL w/o annexation." He also added a handwritten "w/o" before "symbolism", so the phrase reads: without the cost, without the administrative burden and without the symbolism of full annexation. This is the one-line definition to carry: the Subsidiary Alliance is control without annexation. It suited a State that had banned conquest because conquest was costly: the SA promised the gains of conquest without its bill. Mnemonic: CBS: control with no Cost, Burden or Symbol. Decode: SA = "control without annexation" = political domination without (C) the cost, (B) the administrative burden and (S) the symbolism of full annexation. The teacher's handwritten "w/o" sits before each. Why it sticks: CBS is a TV channel; Wellesley 98-05 got control "on air" without paying the bill. Pitt's India Act 1784: no offensive war without the Court of Directors or the Board of Control; war only in defence 1798: Napoleon attacks Egypt and is in communication with Tipu 82-99 (warn) Wellesley 98-05 overhypes the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance The British State agrees anyway: protecting India from European rivals is its primary foreign-policy goal; it will not take risks (good) Middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance; control without annexation Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: option (b) was a TRUE statement: "Napoleonic danger was a feature of the SA." The danger was not real (less chance of a Napoleonic attack on India), but the danger was there (a chance existed). Do not mark it false. Prelims 1999: "At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag flying high in India?" Options: (a) Warren Hastings 73-85, (b) Lord Cornwallis 86-93, (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 (correct), (d) Lord Hastings. The trap: two different Governors General share the surname Hastings. Warren Hastings 73-85 is the pre-Napoleon era: wrong. Francis Hastings 13-23 (also called Lord Hastings) is the post-Napoleon era: wrong. Why (c): the tenure of Wellesley 98-05 (1798–1805) overlaps with Napoleon's offensive phase (1796–1812). Students sometimes pick (d) Lord Hastings because the name sounds Napoleon-era. It is NOT. Mnemonic: Warren Way-before, Francis Following, Wellesley 98-05 in the middle. Decode: Warren Hastings 73-85 = pre-Napoleon (wrong). Francis Hastings 13-23 (Lord Hastings) = post-Napoleon (wrong). Wellesley 98-05 overlaps Napoleon's offensive phase (1796-1812) = Prelims 1999 answer (c). Why it sticks: W for Way-before and Wellesley 98-05 is the one who stands W-ithin the war years; both Hastings are off the clock. Mnemonic: "Danger there" is TRUE. Decode: Prelims 2018 and 2021 option (b) "Napoleonic danger was a feature of the SA" is TRUE: the danger was not real, but it was there. Do not tick it as false.

items.t: 3 · Two roots of the SA: Dupleix 42-54 and ToA 1765
items.x: The Policy of Subsidiary Alliance did not appear from nowhere. It has two roots: one French and one British.  Two Roots of SA: Dupleix 42-54 (French) plus ToA 1765 (British). French root, Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad, 1751: as GG of French Establishments in India he installed the first proto-form of SA; when Salabat Jung 51-62 became Nizam of Hyderabad with French backing, a French force under Bussy was permanently stationed, paid via Northern Sarkars revenues; the template: an external army at the Indian State's cost plus a foreign adviser at court who established indirect rule. British root, Clive 57-67's ToA 1765: Robert Clive 57-67 planted a mini SA at Awadh via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765): EIC army in Awadh paid by subsidy from Awadh, the Nawab's own army reduced, a British Resident stationed; very close to the French template. No handwriting on this slide.   Feature   French root: Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad, 1751   British root: Clive 57-67's ToA 1765 at Awadh    --- --- ---    Who   Dupleix 42-54, as Governor General of French Establishments in India (GG of the French EIC)   Robert Clive 57-67     What he set up   The first mini or proto-form of the Subsidiary Alliance, at Hyderabad in 1751   The mini Subsidiary Alliance planted at Awadh via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765)     The occasion   Salabat Jung 51-62 became Nizam of Hyderabad with French backing   The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) with Awadh     The army   A French force under Bussy was permanently stationed   An EIC army in Awadh     Who paid   Paid out in the form of Northern Sarkars revenues (and control)   Paid by subsidy from Awadh     The ruler's own army   Not stated in the handout   Size of the Nawab's controlled army reduced (not disbanded)     The man at court   A foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule   A British Resident stationed   Dupleix 42-54 had discovered the template: an external army at the Indian State's cost, with a foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule. Clive 57-67's mini SA at Awadh was the British version, very close to the French template that Dupleix 42-54 had pioneered. Mnemonic: D-B-H versus C-A-A: French first, British second. Decode: French root = Dupleix 42-54, Bussy, Hyderabad, 1751 (Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam; French force paid from the Northern Sarkars). British root = Clive 57-67, Allahabad (ToA 1765), Awadh (EIC army paid by Awadh subsidy, Nawab's army reduced, Resident). Years: 51 comes before 65. Why it sticks: "DBH" = Dupleix-Bussy-Hyderabad; "CAA" = Clive-Allahabad-Awadh, two three-letter tags. 3.1 Wellesley 98-05's step: from a device to a policy  Two Roots of SA (contd.). Wellesley's step: formalised the relationship in a written treaty, took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy explicitly, and disbanded its army. The SA was NOT his invention, but he initiated it as a policy: a pre-meditated formalised plan implemented State by State across India. No handwriting on this slide. Wellesley 98-05 took the next step. He formalised the relationship in a written treaty, took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy explicitly, and disbanded its army. The Subsidiary Alliance was NOT a Wellesley 98-05 invention. BUT the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance was initiated by him. Why "policy": a policy means a pre-meditated, formalised plan of action with a pre-decided intent, which is reflected in a series of events executed in line with that policy. Wellesley 98-05 formalised the SA into a policy, added the takeover of Foreign Policy and the disbanding of the Indian State's army, and implemented this policy State by State across India. Invention versus policy. The idea is older: Dupleix 42-54 (Hyderabad, 1751) and Clive 57-67 (Awadh, ToA 1765). The policy is Wellesley 98-05's: a written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over, the army disbanded, applied State by State. If a statement says "Wellesley 98-05 invented the Subsidiary Alliance", it is wrong; if it says he "initiated the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance", it is right. Mnemonic: Idea: Dupleix 42-54 and Clive 57-67. Policy: Wellesley 98-05. "W-F-A". Decode: Wellesley 98-05 did not invent the SA but initiated it as a policy through W-F-A: (W)ritten treaty, (F)oreign Policy taken over, (A)rmy disbanded, applied State by State. Statement "invented" = wrong; "initiated the Policy" = right. Why it sticks: "Invented" has no W-F-A, "initiated" does. 1751, Hyderabad (Dupleix 42-54): French force under Bussy stationed, paid from the Northern Sarkars; a foreign adviser at court 1765, Awadh (Clive 57-67, ToA 1765); EIC army paid by Awadh's subsidy, Nawab's army reduced, British Resident stationed (warn) Wellesley 98-05: written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over explicitly, the State's army disbanded (bad) A policy, not a one-off: implemented State by State across India

items.t: 4 · The model treaty of the Subsidiary Alliance and its legal logic
items.x: The standard terms of any Subsidiary Alliance fell into two groups, though the actual terms varied a little from State to State, depending on context. 4.0 The teacher's board: how the SA splits sovereignty  Teacher's board headed "SA" (circled, underlined in yellow). "Sovereignty:" on the left; in the centre "Symbolic Sovereignty (Indian king)". Below, underlined in yellow: "Power to Do" and the circled letters L, E, J. Left half, tagged "[Taken By eic]": "External Sovereign Fns" with three branches marked "D, C, FA": Def, Communications, Foreign Affairs. Under Def: "eic will maintain Army BUT (circled) TAKES money (circled rupee sign)" and "= SUBSIDY: Def BD [Decided By eic]". Right half, tagged "[Indian king]": "Domestic Sovereign Functions" with branches Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.   Part of sovereignty   What it contains   Who holds it under the SA    --- --- ---    Symbolic Sovereignty   The throne and the title   The Indian king     External Sovereign Functions: D, C, FA   Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs   Taken by the EIC     Domestic Sovereign Functions   Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.   The Indian king   Teacher: The teacher starts from the word Sovereignty and separates Symbolic Sovereignty (who is called king) from the "power to do" (the three circled letters L, E, J; the board does not expand them here). The power to do is then cut in two. External Sovereign Functions (D, C, FA: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) are "[Taken by EIC]". Domestic Sovereign Functions (Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.) stay with the "[Indian king]". Under Def he writes the heart of the SA: "EIC will maintain the Army BUT TAKES money = SUBSIDY: Def BD [Decided by EIC]." That is: the subsidy is simply the Indian State's defence budget (Def BD), but the size of that budget is decided by the EIC, not by the ruler who pays it. Mnemonic: EIC keeps the "DC-FA" cupboard; the king keeps the home shelf. Decode: External functions taken by the EIC = D-C-FA = Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs. Domestic functions with the Indian king = Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health (and symbolic sovereignty). Subsidy = Def BD, size decided by the EIC. Why it sticks: "outside the house" (external) goes to the foreigner; "inside the house" (domestic) stays with the king.  Teacher's board: "Symbolic Sovereignty" with a line splitting into two branches. Left branch: "Nizamat [minus Domestic L&O]" in a bracket. Right branch: "Nizamat (minus MILITARY) + Diwani (civil admin + Finance)", with "= Criminal Jurisdiction" written beside "Nizamat (minus MILITARY)". Bottom line: "# simple: MILITARY, Foreign Policy with eic; Rest of Nizamat and Diwani and Symbolic Sovereignty with Indian King". Teacher: The same split, now in the Mughal vocabulary of Nizamat and Diwani. Diwani = civil administration plus Finance. Nizamat (minus Military) = Criminal Jurisdiction. The teacher's own summary line: "Simple: MILITARY and Foreign Policy with the EIC; the rest of Nizamat, and Diwani, and Symbolic Sovereignty with the Indian King." This is why the handout writes the ruler's promise as non-interference in "succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military)". Unclear on slide 41. The left branch of the diagram reads "Nizamat [minus Domestic L&O]" and the board does not label whose share it is. Going by the summary line at the bottom, it appears to be the part of Nizamat that went to the EIC (Nizamat without domestic law and order, that is, the military), set against the right branch that stayed with the king. Treat this reading as [unclear] and check your class notebook. 4.0b The same board, redrawn at the start of Lecture 15 (Treaty of SA)  Lecture 15 opens with the teacher's board "Treaty of SA". Left list: "# Br Resident" (underlined); "# Military alliance b/w EIC and Indian State". Top centre: "Symbolic Sovereignty (Indian King)". A split line "Power to (L) | (E) (J)" with L, E and J circled. Left branch: "External Sovereign Fns" with the box "EIC" and three sub-branches D, C, FA. Right branch: "Domestic Sovereign Fns" with the box "Indian King" and five sub-branches: Fin, Home, Admin, Health etc, infra. Bottom left: a rounded box "Def BD" pointing to "+ annual subsidy by Indian king to EIC [has to be used for military therefore not (a surplus) income]".   Part of sovereignty (L15 slide 1)   Holder   Branches the teacher writes    --- --- ---    Symbolic Sovereignty   The Indian king   The title and throne     External Sovereign Functions   The EIC   D (Defence), C (Communications), FA (Foreign Affairs)     Domestic Sovereign Functions   The Indian king   Fin (Finance), Home, Admin, Health etc, infra   Teacher: Lecture 15 begins by redrawing the Lecture 14 board (slide 40) so that the model treaty can be revised in one picture. The two terms he writes at the left are the first two of the five EIC terms: "Br Resident" (underlined) and "Military alliance between the EIC and the Indian State". The "Def BD" (defence budget) box carries the third and fourth: the Indian king pays an annual subsidy, and it "has to be used for military", so it is not income for the Company. That is exactly why option (c) "secure a fixed income for the Company" is false in the Prelims 2018 and 2021 question (Section 8). Two small differences from the Lecture 14 board. (1) The domestic list is written Fin, Home, Admin, Health etc, infra here, against Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc on slide 40. Same idea (domestic functions stay with the king); learn the idea, not the exact list. (2) The circled L, E, J after "Power to" are not expanded on the slide (the same as on slide 40). Reading them as Legislature, Executive, Judiciary is a natural guess but is not written: [unclear: check your notebook]. The symbol before "income" in the bottom note is also slightly unclear; the sense is "used for military, so not income". Mnemonic: Resident, Alliance, then the cupboard split: R-A + "DC-FA vs home". Decode: Board order = (R) Br Resident, (A) military Alliance, then sovereignty: symbolic sovereignty with the Indian king; external functions D-C-FA with the EIC; domestic functions (Fin, Home, Admin, Health, infra) with the king; the subsidy is the Def BD and is "for military, not income". Why it sticks: you can redraw the whole treaty from the first two letters R-A plus the "DC-FA" cupboard you already know. 4.1 What the EIC got (5 terms)  Model Treaty: What the EIC Got (5 terms). 1: British Resident permanently in the Indian ruler's court, with the ruler as a puppet (elements 1 and 2 of PoIR). 2: Formal military alliance between EIC and Indian State. 3: Indian State's army DISBANDED, replaced by an EIC army stationed in the State. 4: Indian State pays ANNUAL SUBSIDY to fund that EIC army. 5: EIC takes over FOREIGN POLICY: war and peace, diplomacy, defence budget, foreign trade; the GG's consent needed before any European could be stationed at the court, and the ruler had to consult the GG before negotiating with any other Indian State or foreign power. Note: the subsidy was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. Teacher's ink: term 1 joined to "(1) Puppet Nawab (2) Br Resident", two arrows meeting in a V at a circled 3 "CONTROL" crossed by yellow dotted lines, "= promise in SA TREATY"; beside term 2: "So MILITARY maintained for Indian State, can be used FOR Br India as well"; beside term 4: "= Def BD"; from term 5 a curved arrow to "money will GO TO Indian State BUT Decisions of eic". Yellow underlines on the key words of each term.   #   Term   Fine print from the handout    --- --- ---    1   A British Resident stationed permanently in the Indian ruler's court, with the ruler as a puppet   Elements 1 and 2 of PoIR, but not yet element 3: the British promised non-interference in internal affairs by the British Resident. This promise was seldom kept, and the British breached the treaty in many cases     2   A formal military alliance between the EIC and the Indian State       3   The Indian State's own army was disbanded and replaced by an EIC-maintained army permanently stationed in the State       4   The Indian State paid an annual subsidy to fund this EIC army   So technically this army is owned by the Indian State; the EIC only maintains it. But because of the 5th point, this ownership of the Indian State was lost     5   The EIC took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy   Decisions on war and peace, diplomacy, the defence budget and foreign trade. The GG's consent was needed before any European could be stationed at the court. The ruler had to consult the GG before negotiating with any other Indian State or foreign power. The subsidy, that is, the defence budget of the Indian State, was decided by the EIC   Teacher: Ink on the five terms (slide 42), with the reasoning. Term 1: the teacher writes "(1) Puppet Nawab (2) Br Resident" and draws both into a circled "(3) CONTROL", which he crosses with dotted lines and labels "= promise in SA TREATY". Meaning: the three elements of indirect rule are a puppet ruler, a Resident, and control through the Resident. The SA treaty openly had the first two; the third (control) was promised away on paper by the non-interference clause. Term 2: "So the MILITARY maintained for the Indian State can be used FOR Br India as well." An alliance cuts both ways: the army paid for by the ruler is now also the EIC's army for British India's needs. Term 4: "= Def BD". The annual subsidy is nothing but the State's defence budget. Term 5: "The money will GO TO the Indian State BUT the Decisions are the EIC's." The State keeps earning and paying; the EIC decides. Mnemonic: P-R-C: two shown, one hidden. Decode: Indirect rule = (1) Puppet Nawab, (2) British Resident, (3) Control. The SA treaty shows P and R openly; control is "promised away" by the non-interference clause (the teacher's crossed-out circled 3). Term 2: the ruler's army can serve British India too. Term 4 = Def BD. Term 5: money goes to the State, decisions to the EIC. The handout's note: the annual subsidy money was NOT surplus income that the EIC could use for anything. The subsidy was to be spent only for maintaining the army. The slide adds: the subsidy was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. Mnemonic: "Raj Always Disarms, Squeezes, Fixes-foreign". Decode: What the EIC got, in order: (R) Resident at court, (A) military Alliance, (D) State army Disbanded and replaced, (S) annual Subsidy, (F) Foreign Policy taken over. Count = 5. The subsidy was earmarked for the army, not surplus income. Why it sticks: R-A-D-S-F reads in the table's 1-2-3-4-5 order. 4.2 What the Indian ruler got (2 terms)  Model Treaty: What the Indian Ruler Got (2 terms). 1: EIC protection against neighbours and domestic threats. 2: Formal promise of NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs: succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military). Imbalance: the ruler gets 2 promises, the EIC takes 5 operational levers; the non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: creeping PoIR through the back door. Teacher's ink: "Indian" written above "Ruler gets 2 promises"; under "Imbalance" a dot marked eic joined by a thick sloping line down to a dot marked Indian state; on the right "[Compare with DUAL GOVT (1765-72) in Bengal]" and "From 1772 everything in Bengal with eic [symbolically Nawabs contd into 19th c]". Yellow underlines: "Indian Ruler Got", "EIC protection", "neighbours", "domestic threats", "NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs", "succession", "Diwani", "Nizamat", "non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident".   #   Term    --- ---    1   EIC protection against neighbours and domestic threats     2   A formal promise of non-interference in internal affairs: succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military)   Teacher: The imbalance. The slide's own line: the ruler gets 2 promises; the EIC takes 5 operational levers. The non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: "creeping PoIR through the back door". Under the word Imbalance the teacher redraws the sloping line: EIC on top, Indian State below (the same picture as on slide 29). His comparison: "[Compare with DUAL GOVT (1765-72) in Bengal]". Then: "From 1772 everything in Bengal with the EIC [symbolically the Nawabs continued into the 19th century]." The point of the comparison: in both cases an Indian ruler keeps the name and the responsibility while the Company holds real power. In Bengal the split ended in 1772 with everything going to the EIC; the SA sets up a similar split in State after State. Mnemonic: Two crumbs for the ruler, five keys for the EIC. Decode: Ruler got 2 = (P) Protection against neighbours and domestic threats, (N) Non-interference in succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military). EIC took 5 levers. The non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: creeping PoIR through the back door. Why it sticks: "P-N" sounds like "pen": the promise lived only on paper. 4.3 Why the EIC took Foreign Policy: the legal logic  Model Treaty: Why the EIC Took Foreign Policy (Legal Logic). Legal logic of Term 5: the EIC's army was paid by the Indian State's subsidy, so legally the right to deploy it could still rest with the ruler; taking over Foreign Policy closed that loophole: war and peace (and thus the right to deploy the army) now legally rested with the EIC. Note: ToA 1765 was a mini SA: EIC army stationed at Awadh's expense, BUT Awadh's own army was NOT disbanded and Foreign Policy NOT taken over; the full package came only in 1801. Formula: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC military replacing the Indian State's military + Annual Subsidy + Loss of Foreign Policy. No handwriting on this slide. The EIC maintains the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money (warn) Loophole: one could argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belong to the Indian ruler The EIC takes Foreign Policy: the decision of war and peace (bad) Loophole closed: the right to deploy the army now legally rests with the EIC There is a legal logic to why the EIC specifically demanded Foreign Policy. The EIC maintained the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money. One could therefore argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belonged to the Indian ruler. The EIC closed this loophole by taking Foreign Policy. The decision of war and peace, and therefore the right to deploy the army, now legally rested with the EIC. Mnemonic: The Nizam pays the guard; the Company holds the whistle. Decode: The army was paid from the State's subsidy, so the ruler could claim the right to deploy it (the loophole). Taking Foreign Policy = holding war and peace, so the right to deploy legally rested with the EIC (loophole closed). Why it sticks: whoever holds the whistle sends the guard out, whoever pays only pays. Why ToA 1765 was only a "mini" Subsidiary Alliance: an EIC army was stationed there at Awadh's expense, BUT Awadh's own army was not disbanded and Foreign Policy was not taken over. The proper SA (the full package) came only in 1801. Mnemonic: Mini = two Missing items. Decode: ToA 1765 at Awadh had the EIC army at Awadh's cost but was missing (1) disbanding of Awadh's own army and (2) takeover of Foreign Policy. So it was only a "mini" SA; the full package came in 1801. The formula: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing the Indian State's Military + annual subsidy + loss of Foreign Policy. (PoSA = Policy of Subsidiary Alliance; PoIR = Policy of Indirect Rule; PoRF = Policy of Ring Fence, from Chapter 10. "Informally" because the treaty itself promised non-interference.) Mnemonic: I-R-E-A-L: "I REALly lost control". Decode: PoSA = (I) PoIR informally + (R) PoRF (Ring Fence) + (E) EIC military replacing the State's military + (A) Annual subsidy + (L) Loss of Foreign Policy. Why it sticks: the five letters spell REAL with an I in front, the ruler's lament.  Handout diagram: MODEL TREATY OF SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE, "What each side gave and got, plus the legal logic of why EIC demanded Foreign Policy". Left column, What the EIC GOT (5 terms): 1. British Resident permanently in the Indian ruler's court (elements 1 and 2 of PoIR); 2. formal military alliance between EIC and Indian State; 3. Indian State's army DISBANDED, replaced by an EIC army stationed in the State; 4. Indian State pays ANNUAL SUBSIDY to fund this EIC army; 5. EIC takes over FOREIGN POLICY (war and peace, diplomacy, defence, foreign trade); note: the annual subsidy was NOT surplus income for the EIC, it was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. Right column, What the INDIAN RULER GOT (2 terms): 1. EIC PROTECTION against neighbours and domestic threats; 2. formal promise of NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs (succession, Diwani, Nizamat); Imbalance: the ruler gets 2 promises, the EIC takes 5 operational levers; the non-interference promise was ROUTINELY broken via the British Resident's interference (creeping PoIR through the back door). Red box: LEGAL LOGIC of Term 5: the EIC's army was paid for by the Indian State's subsidy, so legally the right to deploy it could still belong to the ruler; taking over Foreign Policy CLOSED this loophole. Note: the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 with Awadh was a mini SA (Awadh's own army NOT disbanded, Foreign Policy NOT taken over; the full package came only in 1801). Bottom line: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing Indian State's Military + Annual Subsidy + Loss of Foreign Policy. 4.4 The PYQ on SA features (Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021) UPSC asked the same question in both Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: "Which statement does NOT apply to the Subsidiary Alliance?" The four options tested the features of the SA. The false option was (c) "Secure a fixed income for the Company." The SA's annual subsidy was earmarked for maintaining the EIC army stationed in the host State. It was NOT surplus income for the EIC. The other three options were true: to maintain a large standing army, to defend against Napoleonic danger, and to establish British paramountcy. Mnemonic: A-N-P true, F for False. Decode: Prelims 2018 and 2021 "NOT apply to SA": (A) large standing Army, (N) Napoleonic danger, (P) British Paramountcy are true. (F) Fixed income for the Company is the false one, because the subsidy was earmarked for the army.

items.t: 5 · The vicious chain: consequences of the Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States
items.x: Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance. Link 1, disbanded armies to mass unemployment: disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men: Mansabdars lost their positions, sepoys lost their livelihoods (the EIC also recruited sepoys from outside the host State to cut any loyalty to the Nawab: a classic Divide and Rule). Link 2, EIC's compounded military power: since the EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, operational control was entirely with the EIC; having taken Foreign Policy it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere, so the EIC now maintained a large army at the expense of Indian States. Teacher's ink: "positions" struck through and "MILITARY ROLE" written above it; a yellow line to a circled "DnR: Eic will NOT (Less) keep sepoys FROM Bengal in Bengal ARMY"; lower left "WHO PAYS for eic ARMY in Indian State (SA)? Indian State / King, therefore Free of ARMY" (underlined); at the bottom a bracket: "every SA LEADS (Free of Cost, circled) EIC ARMY increases".   #   Link   How it worked    --- --- ---    1   Disbanded armies, so mass unemployment   Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men: Mansabdars lost their positions (the teacher corrects this to "military role"), sepoys lost their livelihoods     2   The EIC's compounded military power at the host State's expense   The EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, so operational control was entirely with the EIC. Having taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. The EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States     3   High and rising subsidy, so Drain of Wealth   Subsidy payments were high to begin with and the EIC gradually increased its demands. The same money could have been used by the ruler for his own State's development. Instead there was Drain of Wealth     4   Tax hikes, so unrest   To pay the ever-rising subsidy, rulers had to raise taxes. High taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest     5   Maladministration accusations, so grounds for annexation   The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left     6   Territory in lieu of cash   When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment     7   Permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity   By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC   Mnemonic: Unlucky Farmers Dread Tax Men Taking Land. Decode, in link order: (U) Unemployment of disbanded soldiers, (F) Free army for the EIC, (D) Drain of Wealth through high rising subsidy, (T) Tax hikes, (M) Maladministration charge, (T) Territory in lieu of cash, (L) Lost alliance-forming capacity. Count = 7. Why it sticks: a farmer's story, and the sentence has exactly seven words. 5.1 Links 1 and 2: unemployment and the EIC's free army Link 1. Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men. Mansabdars lost their positions; sepoys lost their livelihoods. The handout's note: the EIC also recruited sepoys from outside the host State, to reduce any chance of loyalty to the Nawab in case he revolted: a classic Divide and Rule strategy. Link 2. Since the EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, operational control was entirely with the EIC. Since it had also taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. Hence the EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States. The handout's note: EIC Armies = the army of the Indian State maintained by the EIC using the Indian State's subsidy + the EIC's own army maintained from its own money. Both were available to the EIC for its own wars. Teacher's correction on slide 45. In the line "Mansabdars lost their positions", the teacher struck out "positions" and wrote "MILITARY ROLE" above it. The handout prints "positions". Use the teacher's wording: Mansabdars lost their military role. Mnemonic: Mansabdar = Military ROLE, not "positions". Decode: The handout says "positions"; the teacher struck it out and wrote "MILITARY ROLE". Use the teacher's wording. Same two M's: Mansabdar, Military. Teacher: Divide and Rule (the circled "DnR"). Beside the note on recruiting outsiders the teacher wrote: "DnR: the EIC will NOT keep sepoys from Bengal in the Bengal Army", with "(Less)" written above "NOT". So read it as: the EIC would keep few or no local men in the army of their own region. The reasoning is in the handout's note: a sepoy from outside has no loyalty to the local Nawab if he revolts. Who pays? The teacher asks: "WHO PAYS for the EIC army in an Indian State (SA)?" Answer: "the Indian State / King", therefore a "FREE army" for the Company (his written phrase is "Free of ARMY"). The boxed conclusion: "[Every SA leads to a free-of-cost increase in the EIC army]". Each new treaty adds a paid-for army to the Company's strength without adding a rupee to its costs. Mnemonic: King pays the sepoys, Company plays the war. Decode: Who pays for the EIC army in an Indian State? The Indian State/king, so the army is free of cost to the EIC and every SA increases it. Sepoys are recruited from outside the host State (the teacher's DnR) so they have no loyalty to the local Nawab.  Teacher's board, the analogy: "SA Concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (the word LIKE underlined, BALI inside a large circle, "Concept" written small under SA). Below: "SA (circled) LED TO MILITARY Power SHIFT". Teacher: The Bali analogy. The board reads: "SA concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (BALI in a big circle), and under it "SA LED TO MILITARY POWER SHIFT." Read it together with the previous board: under every SA the Indian State's military strength moves across to the EIC. The State pays, its own army is disbanded, and the army it pays for fights for the Company. So with each alliance the ally grows weaker and the EIC grows stronger: a shift of military power. The board gives only the name of the analogy ("like Bali of Ramayana") and its conclusion ("military power shift"). The story behind the analogy was explained orally and is not written on the slide. Check your class notebook for the spoken explanation before using it in an answer. 5.2 Links 3 and 4: Drain of Wealth and tax hikes  Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance (contd.). High and rising subsidy to Drain of Wealth: subsidy payments were high to begin with and the EIC gradually raised its demands; the same money could have funded the Indian ruler's own State development; instead there was Drain of Wealth. Tax hikes to unrest: to pay the ever-rising subsidy, rulers had to raise taxes; high taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest. Teacher's ink: "Peasant Revolts" written after "for unrest". Yellow underlines: "same money could have funded", "State development", "Tax hikes to unrest", "rulers had to raise taxes", "peasant resentment", "for unrest". Link 3. Subsidy payments were high to begin with, and the EIC gradually increased its demands. The same money could have been used by the Indian ruler for his own State's development. Instead there was Drain of Wealth. Link 4. To pay the ever-rising subsidy, Indian rulers had to raise taxes. High taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest. Teacher: After the words "for unrest" the teacher wrote "Peasant Revolts". That is where this link ends: rising subsidy, then higher taxes, then peasant resentment, then peasant revolts. His underlines pick out the cause ("rulers had to raise taxes") and the cost (the "same money could have funded" the "State development"). Mnemonic: S-T-A-R of unrest. Decode: (S) Subsidy rises, (T) Taxes raised, (A) Anger (peasant resentment, rulers unpopular), (R) Revolts (the teacher's "Peasant Revolts"). Drain of Wealth is the leak at the start: the same money could have built the State. Why it sticks: each letter is one step up the staircase to unrest. 5.3 Links 5 and 6: maladministration and territory in lieu of cash  Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance (contd.). Maladministration accusations to annexation grounds: the EIC then accused rulers of maladministration; in reality the ruler had no real power left: the Resident had in many cases established Indirect Rule illegally, breaching the treaty's own non-interference promise; the ruler had no power but all the responsibility (starkest: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, State annexed 1856). Territory in lieu of cash: when the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment; in 1801 half of Awadh was annexed as permanent subsidy payment; in 1853 Hyderabad was made to give Berar. Teacher's ink under "Territory in lieu of cash": "Subsidy = TOOL of empire building". Yellow underlines: "1801 half of Awadh", "in 1853 Hyderabad was made to give Berar". Link 5. The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left. The British Resident had in many cases established Indirect Rule illegally, in direct breach of the treaty's own promise of non-interference. The ruler had no power, but all the responsibility. The most stark example was Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh: accused of maladministration, his State annexed in 1856. Link 6. When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment. In 1801, half of Awadh was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. In 1853, Hyderabad was made to give Berar. The handout's aside: the EIC can say "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54". He gave this idea when he took the Northern Sarkars from Hyderabad in 1751. Teacher: Under "Territory in lieu of cash" the teacher wrote: "Subsidy = TOOL of empire building." The subsidy was not only a payment. It was set high, it kept rising, and when the ruler defaulted the EIC took land. So the subsidy itself was the instrument that turned an "alliance" into annexation. He underlined the two examples to memorise: 1801, half of Awadh; 1853, Berar from Hyderabad. Mnemonic: Awadh: 01 half, 56 whole. Hyderabad: 53 Berar. Decode: 1801 = half of Awadh taken as permanent subsidy payment; 1856 = Awadh annexed entirely, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah accused of maladministration (the starkest example). 1853 = Hyderabad made to give Berar. Teacher: "Subsidy = TOOL of empire building." Why it sticks: "01" looks like "one half", and half becomes whole by 56. 5.4 Link 7 and the takeaway  Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance (contd.). Permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity: by losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC; so the SA was, in effect, a sophisticated Divide and Rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. Takeaway: the EIC via SA got all military and diplomatic powers with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances; the seven links explain why every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent. No handwriting on this slide. Link 7. By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC. Hence the Subsidiary Alliance was, in effect, a sophisticated Divide and Rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. Takeaway: the EIC via the SA got all military and diplomatic powers, with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances. The seven vicious-chain links explain why every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent. The State's army is disbanded: Mansabdars lose their military role, sepoys their livelihood The EIC's army grows free of cost and can be used for the EIC's own wars (warn) Subsidy high and rising: Drain of Wealth (warn) Taxes raised: rulers unpopular, peasant resentment, peasant revolts (bad) "Maladministration": the ruler has no power but all the responsibility (Awadh annexed 1856) (bad) Territory in lieu of cash: half of Awadh 1801, Berar 1853 (bad) No alliances possible against the EIC: annexed or permanently dependent

items.t: 6 · Which States signed, and under what circumstances
items.x: Sections 6 and 7 combine the handout with the teacher's ink from Lecture 15 (slides 2 to 10). The Lecture 14 slides stop at the vicious chain (slide 49); Lecture 15 picks the chapter up with the five arguments, the signatories (his corrected count is ten), the annexations and the recall, and then ends the chapter with the PYQ slides (11 to 23), which are in Section 8. Where the slide's typed text disagrees with the teacher's pen or with the handout, an alert says which to use. 6.1 Why some rulers walked in willingly The SA was not forced on every signatory at sword-point. In several cases the Indian ruler walked in willingly, persuaded by five arguments:   #   Argument   What it meant    --- --- ---    1   Protection against internal revolts   A guaranteed EIC army inside the palace walls was attractive insurance against rival claimants or mutinous nobles     2   Protection against external threats   Small States feared Maratha Chauth raids, Mysorean expansion or Rohilla incursions far more than the distant British     3   Better than annexation   The subsidy was, on paper, cheaper than annexation or a losing war against the EIC     4   Preservation of royal dignity   The ruler's title, court and ceremonial status were formally preserved. The flag of sovereignty flew, even after its substance had been handed over     5   For winning succession disputes and for protection from neighbours   In many cases rulers sought EIC help in succession disputes and for protection from other Indian States. The EIC used this as an opportunity by making military help conditional upon the Indian ruler signing the SA   Mnemonic: I Eat Banana Daily, Sir. Decode: Five reasons rulers walked in: (I) Internal revolts protection, (E) External threats protection, (B) Better than annexation, (D) royal Dignity preserved, (S) Succession disputes and neighbours (the EIC made help conditional on signing). Why it sticks: five words, five arguments, in table order.  Why Some Rulers Walked In Willingly, 5 Arguments (contd.). The fifth row: "Winning succession disputes: rulers often sought EIC help in succession disputes and protection from other Indian States; EIC made military help conditional on the ruler signing SA." Teacher's ink in the Argument cell, under the words "Winning succession disputes": "FACTIONALISM". (Slide 2, the first four arguments, is typed text with no ink.) Teacher: Under the fifth argument, "Winning succession disputes", the teacher writes one word: "FACTIONALISM". That is the label for argument 5: the rulers did not sign only out of fear of outsiders; they signed because groups inside the ruling family or court fought over the throne or the regency, and the side that wanted the EIC's help had to sign the SA to get it. He returns to the word on slide 7 (Nagpur regency) and draws a five-way tag for the Marathas (see 6.2). The first four arguments (slide 2) carry no ink. Mnemonic: Fifth reason = Factions. The last SA signed under Wellesley 98-05 before his recall   Wellesley 98-05     9   1816   Bhonsle of Nagpur (Treaty of Nagpur)   Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent   Francis Hastings 13-23     10   1818   Holkar of Indore (Treaty of Mandsaur)   Forced to sign after decisive defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19)   Francis Hastings 13-23    Signatories (1798-1818): Hyderabad and Mysore.
