Awadh, 1798 to 1801, step by step: 1798: Sadat Ali Khan II offers the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy; in exchange John Shore 93-98 is to remove his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship Shore 93-98 obliges (warn) By 1801 Sadat Ali Khan II defaults Wellesley 98-05 sends his brother Henry Wellesley to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance (bad) Half of Awadh annexed as permanent subsidy payment: the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand 1801, Awadh. In 1798, Sadat Ali Khan II had offered the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy in exchange for John Shore 93-98 removing his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship. Shore 93-98 obliged. By 1801, Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted. Wellesley 98-05 sent his brother Henry Wellesley to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance. Half of Awadh (the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand) was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. The handout's note: this was unfair. The revenue from this territory was twice the Rs 76 lakh annual subsidy it was meant to cover. These territories became the Ceded Districts, and in 1836 were given full province status as the North-West Provinces (NWP 1836) of British India. Recall on Rohilkhand: most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help in 1774. The EIC had helped because of the ToA 1765 military alliance. The remaining small part of Rohilkhand became the autonomous State of Rampur, but under Awadh legally, and from 1801 under the EIC legally. Mnemonic: Uncle pays 76, nephew goes; Henry takes D-G-R. Decode: 1798 = Sadat Ali Khan II offers Rs 76 lakh annual subsidy so that John Shore 93-98 removes his nephew Wazir Ali from the Nawabship (Shore obliges). 1801 = default; Wellesley 98-05 sends his brother Henry, who imposes the full SA. Half of Awadh annexed = D-G-R: Doab, Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand (revenue twice Rs 76 lakh; later Ceded Districts, NWP 1836). Why it sticks: one family quarrel, one price tag, three places. Mnemonic: 74 gave, 01 took: R for Rohilkhand's Remnant = Rampur. Decode: 1774 = most of Rohilkhand annexed by Awadh with EIC help (ToA 1765 alliance). The remaining small part became the autonomous State of Rampur, under Awadh legally and from 1801 under the EIC.  Signatories (contd.): the Peshwa, Scindia, and Jats-Rajputs-Bundelas. "Treaty of Bassein/Vasai" is underlined. Under "1803 - Scindia of Gwalior" the teacher writes "or 1804" (a small "or" above "1804"). Above the third row, over the words "the war", he writes "2nd A-Ma" (2nd Anglo-Maratha). Teacher: Three small inks on this slide. (1) "Treaty of Bassein/Vasai" is underlined: know both names, Bassein and Vasai. (2) Under Scindia: "or 1804". The slide and handout print 1803; the teacher adds that the date may also be given as 1804. (3) "2nd A-Ma" over "the war" in the Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas row: the war in which they were forced to sign is the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Scindia's date: 1803 (handout and slide) or 1804 (teacher's ink). Both are inside the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Learn 1803 as the base date and know that 1804 is also acceptable. If an exam option shows only one of them, check the other options before deciding; the safe anchor is "during the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War". The Peshwa and the Treaty of Bassein, 1802: Yashwantrao Holkar defeats Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18; he was avenging his brother's death Bajirao II 96-18 flees (warn) December 1802, Treaty of Bassein (Vasai): he signs the SA to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British (bad) The 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) follows Mnemonic: Hit, Bolt, Sign, Scream, War. Decode: Yashwantrao Holkar defeats (Hit) Bajirao II 96-18, avenging his brother's death; Bajirao II 96-18 flees (Bolt) and signs (Sign) the Treaty of Bassein, December 1802, to regain the Peshwaship; Scindia and Bhonsle scream "sold the Confederacy"; the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) follows. Why it sticks: five short verbs run in time order. December 1802, Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. He had been defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar (avenging his brother's death). He fled, and signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802) to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support. The handout's note: Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British, and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) followed. The full treatment of Bassein 1802 and the war is in the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter (Chapter 13). Recall: the Marathas captured Bassein from the Portuguese via the Treaty of Bassein (1739), and brought it under Peshwa control along with Salsette. So there are two Treaties of Bassein: 1739 (Marathas and the Portuguese) and 1802 (Peshwa and the EIC). 1816, Bhonsle of Nagpur. After defeat in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the Bhonsles had resisted signing a full Subsidiary Alliance for over a decade. In 1816 Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur. (The story belongs to the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter, Chapter 13.)  Signatories (contd.): Travancore 1805, Bhonsle of Nagpur 1816, Holkar of Indore 1818. Underlines: "Appa Sahib" and "Nagpur regency". Right margin: "FACTIONALISM = N vs N, i.e. Who will Regent". Bottom tree headed "Post 1761 Pes in Factionalism?" (the second word is unclear) with five branches: "Peshwa [FACTIONALISM]", "Scindhia [WAR]", "Holkar [WAR]", "Bhonsle [factionalism]", "Gaikwad [Factionalism]". Teacher: The Nagpur row defines the word. Beside the Bhonsle entry (Appa Sahib, Nagpur regency underlined) he writes "FACTIONALISM = N vs N, i.e. who will Regent." So factionalism means rival groups fighting over who rules, here over the regency of Nagpur. (The two "N"s are not expanded on the slide: [unclear: check your notebook]; the handout only says Appa Sahib used EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent.) Teacher: The five-way tree: what happened to each Maratha power after 1761. The heading reads "Post 1761 ... in Factionalism?" (the second word looks like "Pes", perhaps Peshwa; [unclear: check your notebook]). His five tags: Peshwa = FACTIONALISM; Scindia = WAR; Holkar = WAR; Bhonsle = factionalism; Gaikwad = factionalism. Match them to the signatories above:   Maratha power   Teacher's tag   The signatory entry that proves it    --- --- ---    Peshwa (Bajirao II 96-18)   Factionalism   Defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar, fled and signed Bassein (Dec 1802) to regain the Peshwaship     Scindia (Gwalior)   War   Forced to sign during the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05)     Holkar (Indore)   War   Forced to sign after decisive defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19): Mandsaur 1818     Bhonsle (Nagpur)   Factionalism   Appa Sahib won the Nagpur regency fight with EIC backing: Nagpur 1816     Gaikwad (Baroda)   Factionalism   Signed for EIC help in a Gaikwad succession dispute: Cambay, June 1802   Mnemonic: Three quarrel at home, two fight in the field: P-B-G versus S-H. Decode: Factionalism = Peshwa, Bhonsle, Gaikwad (P-B-G: Bassein, Nagpur, Cambay). War = Scindia (2nd Anglo-Maratha War) and Holkar (3rd Anglo-Maratha War, Mandsaur 1818). Why it sticks: "Please Bring Gifts" settles a family quarrel; "Shoot, Hit" is war. Mnemonic: Cab, Bus, Snake, Mandi: match the treaty. Decode: Gaikwad took a Cab = Cambay (June 1802). Peshwa took a Bus = Bassein (December 1802). Bhonsle met a Nag(snake) = Nagpur (1816, Appa Sahib). Holkar went to the Mandi = Mandsaur (1818). Why it sticks: four letters C, B, N, M match four rulers G, P, B, H in signing order. Mnemonic: Bassein twice: 1739 and 1802. Decode: Treaty of Bassein (1739) = Marathas and the Portuguese (Bassein plus Salsette under Peshwa control). Treaty of Bassein (1802) = Peshwa and the EIC (an SA). Why it sticks: same bus stop, two journeys: first Marathas win, then Peshwa signs away. Two wordings to notice in the handout. (1) The date of the 4th Anglo-Mysore War: Section 1, Section 6 and slide 31 print "4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99)", while Section 7 and the index of the next chapter print "4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799" (as does Chapter 7). The fall of Seringapatam and the death of Tipu 82-99 are 1799 in every version. (2) Seringapatam: Section 1 and slide 31 call it the "Siege of Seringapatam (1799)"; Section 6 calls it the "Battle of Seringapatam (1799)". It is the same event. Mnemonic: Tipu 82-99's code ends where the war ends: 99. Decode: 4th Anglo-Mysore War is printed "1798-99" in some places and "1799" in others, but the fall of Seringapatam and the death of Tipu 82-99 are 1799 in every version. "Siege" and "Battle" of Seringapatam are the same event.

items.t: 7 · Direct annexations and the recall of Wellesley 98-05
items.x: What territory did Wellesley 98-05 directly annex, and why was he eventually recalled? Beyond Subsidiary Alliances, Wellesley 98-05 also directly annexed territory:   When   Territory   Detail    --- --- ---    1799   Mysore territory   Significant territory taken from Mysore after the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799     Early 1801   Half of Awadh (the Ceded Districts)   Annexed as permanent subsidy payment (the NWP 1836 territories, covered in section 6)     1801   Carnatic   Annexed on grounds of maladministration, six years after the death of Md Ali 52-95 (1752–1795), who had been the EIC's loyal ally since the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54     1803–05   2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Bhonsle   Bhonsle of Nagpur lost significant territory, including Orissa (which Bhonsle had himself taken from Bengal in 1751)     1803–05   2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Scindia   Scindia lost territory in Gujarat and all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi    Direct Annexations + Wellesley 98-05's Recall. Top right, bracketed: "FYQ on Wellesley 98-05" (first letter unclear). Mysore row: "To MADRAS PRESIDENCY" beside "Mysore territory". Awadh row: "SUBSIDY, as TOOL or, empire BUILDING". Carnatic row: "(not on RECORD REASON)" with a line to the Carnatic detail, and a vertical line down to "BUT an imp context" (underlined); to the right of the row: "Nawab HAD Taken MANY Loans from EIC and its officers [sad face] / [bracket] Financial maladmin". 2nd Anglo-Maratha row: underlines under Bhonsle, Orissa, Scindia, in Gujarat, and a long underline under "all territory north of River Yamuna, including Delhi"; a bracket "[Now PoIR in Delhi]" (the letters PoIR are unclear) and a line down to "[1771 - 1803]". Teacher: Ink beside each annexation, row by row (slide 9). Mysore 1799: "To MADRAS PRESIDENCY". The territory taken from Mysore after the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 went to the EIC's Madras Presidency. Half of Awadh, early 1801: "SUBSIDY as TOOL or empire BUILDING". The same sentence as on slide 48 of Lecture 14 ("Subsidy = TOOL of empire building"): the subsidy was the tool through which an alliance became territory. Carnatic 1801: "(not on RECORD REASON)" ... "BUT an imp context". The reason on record is maladministration (the handout's wording). The teacher says the important context behind it is that "the Nawab HAD taken MANY loans from the EIC and its officers", which he labels "Financial maladmin". So "maladministration" here means financial mismanagement and debt to the Company and its officers. 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05: he underlines the five things to remember: Bhonsle, Orissa, Scindia, Gujarat, and "all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi". Beside the Delhi line: "[Now PoIR in Delhi]" and, below it, a bracketed "[1771 - 1803]". The slide does not explain either note, and the letters "PoIR" are themselves hard to read. [unclear: check your notebook] for his spoken reason. All that is certain from the text is that Scindia lost Delhi and everything north of the Yamuna in 1803-05.   Annexation   Reason on record   Teacher's added context    --- --- ---    Mysore territory 1799   4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799   Went to the Madras Presidency     Half of Awadh 1801   Permanent subsidy payment (default)   Subsidy as tool of empire building     Carnatic 1801   Maladministration, six years after Md Ali 52-95 died   Not the real record reason: the Nawab's many loans from the EIC and its officers (financial maladministration)     Orissa, Gujarat, Delhi side 1803-05   2nd Anglo-Maratha War   "Now PoIR in Delhi"; "[1771 - 1803]" (unclear)   Carnatic: use "maladministration" as the recorded ground, and add the teacher's context. The handout gives only "annexed on grounds of maladministration". The teacher's two additions ("not on record reason", "Nawab had taken many loans from the EIC and its officers") do not contradict it; they explain what the word covered. In a Mains answer write: annexed on the ground of maladministration, in the background of the Nawab's heavy debts to the Company and its officers. Mnemonic: Carnatic: Record says "mal-admin", ledger says "loans". Decode: Carnatic 1801: recorded reason = maladministration (six years after Md Ali 52-95 died in 1795); teacher's context = the Nawab owed many loans to the EIC and its officers (financial maladmin). Why it sticks: a ledger is the book that explains the record. Wellesley 98-05 was eventually recalled to London due to high war expenditure. Empire building was profitable only if wars were short and cheap. His were neither.  Direct Annexations + Wellesley 98-05's Recall (contd.): why recalled. Top right bracket: "IR: Wars HURT Eco of Both Sides", with a white line to the typed Detail cell. Middle chain: "GBF 1770, then 1772 BANKRUPTCY, then Loan FROM Br STATE, then RAct 1773, then (BUT STILL) Wars [sad face circled], then PIA 1784, then (down arrow) BUT STILL, then (circled) Wars". Bottom left: "Wellesley 98-05" (underlined) with two branches "4th A-My 1799" and "2nd A-Ma 1803-05". A bracketed box: "* Wars are expensive for Both" with branches "Winner" and "Loser". GBF 1770; 1772 bankruptcy of the EIC Loan from the British State, with supervision through the Regulating Act 1773 (warn) BUT STILL wars (sad face): the EIC keeps fighting Pitt's India Act 1784 bans offensive war (bad) BUT STILL wars (circled): under Wellesley 98-05 the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 (bad) Wars are expensive for both, winner and loser: high war expenditure, so he is recalled Teacher: The board repeats the money chain of slide 34 (GBF 1770, bankruptcy 1772, loan from the British State, Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784) and adds the punch line: "BUT STILL wars", twice. Two laws, one rescue loan, and the wars did not stop. Under Wellesley 98-05 (underlined) he lists the two wars that cost him his post: 4th A-My 1799 and 2nd A-Ma 1803-05. In the box: "Wars are expensive for both," with the branches Winner and Loser. The point: even the winner pays, so a Governor General who wins two big wars can still be recalled for the bill. The (IR) note at the top says the same: "Wars HURT the economy of both sides." Mnemonic: "But still, wars": the refrain of the board. Decode: Loan (Regulating Act 1773) but still wars; Pitt's India Act 1784 but still wars; Wellesley 98-05's two wars (Mysore 1799, 2nd Anglo-Maratha 1803-05) end in recall for high war expenditure. Winner and loser both pay. Why it sticks: two "but still"s, two wars, one recall. Mnemonic: Wellesley 98-05's MAC, then B-O and S-G-D. Decode: Direct annexations: (M) Mysore territory 1799, (A) half of Awadh 1801, (C) Carnatic 1801 (maladministration, six years after Md Ali 52-95 died in 1795). 1803-05 war: Bhonsle loses Orissa (B-O); Scindia loses Gujarat and all north of the Yamuna including Delhi (S-G-D). Why it sticks: "MAC" is one gadget, and 95 + 6 = 01. The chapter comes full circle on money. High war expenditure produced the ban on conquest in Pitt's India Act 1784. Wellesley 98-05 got round the ban with the Napoleon threat and the Subsidiary Alliance. And high war expenditure is what finally got Wellesley 98-05 recalled. Mnemonic: The money circle: Bill, Ban, Trick, Bill, Boot. Decode: High war expenditure (Bill) leads to Pitt's India Act 1784 (Ban); Wellesley 98-05 gets round it with the Napoleon threat and the SA (Trick); his wars again run up high war expenditure (Bill); he is recalled to London (Boot). Why it sticks: the chapter starts and ends on the same word, money. The handout page for this chapter ends with an index of the next chapter (Mysore's four wars, Dhondia Wagh, Tipu 82-99's religious policy, the Carnatic annexed in 1801, Travancore and Velu Thampi Dalawa). That material belongs to Chapter 12, not here.

items.t: 8 · The PYQ slides of Lecture 15 (slides 11 to 23)
items.x: Lecture 15 closes Chapter 11 with five PYQs, each shown as question, answer and (for three of them) a written explanation. Slide 11 is a typed alert card (the Hastings-Hastings trap) that repeats the handout alert in Section 2.3. Slide 24 is the Chapter 12 title slide and is not in this chapter. The teacher's ink appears only on slides 12, 15, 16 and 19; slides 13, 14, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22 and 23 are typed answers and explanations with no handwriting. Each answer below was checked against the question bank for this chapter (`bank/ch11.json`). 8.1 PYQ 1: Prelims 1999, the Governor General who kept the flag flying (slides 11 to 14)  PYQ 1, Prelims 1999: "At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag flying high in India?" Teacher's ink: "1799-1815" underlined at top left with a curved line to the word "Napoleon"; "high" underlined; beside the options (a) Warren Hastings 73-85 and (b) Lord Cornwallis 86-93 a bracket "1700s"; beside (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 and (d) Lord Hastings 13-23 (as written, "13-93") a bracket "1800s" with "1798" above it; a tick through the (c). On the right: "SA" with a bracket over "My" and "Ma", and a short line to "high". Teacher: How he solves it. (1) Napoleon is dated "1799-1815" (underlined and joined to the word "Napoleon" in the question). (2) He writes the code beside each option and sorts them by century: (a) Warren Hastings 73-85 and (b) Cornwallis 86-93 = the "1700s"; (c) Wellesley 98-05 and (d) Hastings 13-23 = the "1800s", with "1798" written over the second bracket because Wellesley 98-05 starts in 1798. (3) He underlines "high" and writes "SA" over "My" and "Ma". The slide does not spell it out; my reading is that keeping the flag high meant expanding, and Wellesley 98-05's expansion ran through the Subsidiary Alliance and the dealings with Mysore (My) and the Marathas (Ma). [Reading, not written: check your notebook.] (4) Tick on (c). Two ink differences from the handout; the handout and slide answer still win. (1) Napoleon's dates: the teacher writes 1799-1815; the handout alert says Wellesley 98-05's tenure overlaps Napoleon's offensive phase (1796-1812). The two ranges frame the same era and give the same answer, (c). Learn 1796-1812 (handout) if a question gives dates, and treat 1799-1815 as the teacher's quick bracket for the same era. (2) The code beside (d): the ink reads "13-93", which looks like a slip; Francis Hastings 13-23 is the right code (handout, slide 14 and Section 2.3). Use 13-23. Answer: (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 (slide 13). Slide 14's explanation: (a) wrong, Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor General 1773-85, well before the Napoleonic era; (b) wrong, Cornwallis 86-93 was "a quiet phase, not a Napoleonic-era expansionist"; (d) wrong, Francis Hastings 13-23 fought after Napoleon's defeat in 1815. Bank check: the bank's answer key reads (a), which is a key error (its own explanation says (c)); use (c). Mnemonic: Seventy-three, eighty-six | ninety-eight, thirteen. Decode: The teacher's two brackets: 1700s = Warren Hastings 73-85 and Cornwallis 86-93 (both wrong); 1800s = Wellesley 98-05 (correct, starts 1798) and Francis Hastings 13-23 (wrong, after 1815). Why it sticks: two pairs of two-digit starts: 73, 86, 98, 13. 8.2 PYQ 2 and PYQ 3: "Which does NOT apply to the Subsidiary Alliance" (Prelims 2018, Prelims 2021; slides 15 to 18)  PYQ 2, Prelims 2018, answer slide with the teacher's marks. Options: (a) Maintain standing army, (b) Keep India safe from Napoleon, (c) Secure fixed income for Company, (d) Establish British paramountcy. Circled letters before each option: (a) T, (b) T, (c) F, (d) T. Beside (a): "(* BALI) (* FREE of ARMY)". Beside (b): "(* THREAT" with a split "REAL | UNREAL". Beside (d): "[LOSS of D, C, FA]". Typed answer: (c); the subsidy was earmarked for the EIC army's maintenance, not the Company's general revenue; the other three DO apply. On the question slide (15) he had written "[SUPREMACY]" under "paramountcy".   Option (2018 wording)   Teacher's mark   His margin tag   What it points back to    --- --- --- ---    (a) Maintain standing army   T   "BALI", "FREE of ARMY"   Bali analogy and the free army at the State's cost (5.1)     (b) Keep India safe from Napoleon   T   "THREAT", split REAL or UNREAL   The threat was there but not real (2.3)     (c) Secure fixed income for Company   F   none   Subsidy is the Def BD, earmarked for the army, not income (4.0b, 4.4)     (d) Establish British paramountcy   T   "LOSS of D, C, FA"; on slide 15 "[SUPREMACY]"   Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs lost to the EIC (4.0): paramountcy = supremacy   Teacher: The T-T-F-T drill. He circles T on (a), (b) and (d), and F on (c), and gives each true option a tag to recall the reason: (a) "BALI" and "FREE of ARMY" (the Indian State pays for an EIC army: every SA adds a free army and shifts military power); (b) "THREAT" split into REAL and UNREAL (the Napoleonic danger was a feature of the SA even though it was not a real, high-chance one); (d) "LOSS of D, C, FA" (the State loses Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs, which is what paramountcy means; on slide 15 he glosses paramountcy as "SUPREMACY"). The one false option is the one that says the Company gets income. Answer: (c) in both years. Prelims 2018 (slides 15 and 16) and Prelims 2021 (slides 17 and 18) are the same four-option set; the 2021 wording is slightly more polished ("to maintain a large standing army at others' expense"; "to keep India safe from Napoleonic danger"; "to establish British paramountcy over the Indian states"). Slide 18: "Subsidy is not surplus income", and the other three options DO apply by the same reasoning as 2018. The 2021 slide (17) carries no ink. Bank check: both entries are keyed (c) and match. Mnemonic: Three T's from the Bali board, one F for the fixed income: B-T-L-F. Decode: (a) T with Bali and Free-of-army; (b) T with Threat (real or unreal); (d) T with Loss of D, C, FA; (c) F = fixed income for the Company, which the earmarked subsidy is not. Why it sticks: Bali, Threat, Loss are the three true tags; "F" is the odd one out. 8.3 PYQ 4: Prelims 2018, institution and founder pairs (slides 19 to 21)  PYQ 4, Prelims 2018: "With reference to educational institutions during colonial rule in India, consider the pairs (Institution, Founder): 1. Sanskrit College at Banaras, William Jones; 2. Calcutta Madarsa, Warren Hastings; 3. Fort William College, Arthur WELLESLEYPROT. Which pairs are correctly matched? (a) 1 and 2 (b) Only 2 (c) 1 and 3 (d) Only 3." Teacher's ink: a circled F after pair 1 (William Jones) and a circled F after pair 3 (Arthur WELLESLEYPROT); a small tick at "(b) Only 2".  PYQ 4, Prelims 2018, answer explanation (typed, no ink): (b) Only 2 is correct. Fort William College was founded by Richard Wellesley 98-05 in 1800, not Arthur WELLESLEYPROT, his military-commander brother. Pair 1 is wrong: Sanskrit College at Banaras was founded by Jonathan Duncan (1791), not William Jones. Pair 3 is wrong for the same reason. Partial match: Fort William College is the home anchor of this chapter; the other institutions belong to Education Reforms.   Pair   Teacher's mark   Why    --- --- ---    1. Sanskrit College at Banaras, William Jones   F   Founded by Jonathan Duncan (1791) (slide 21); not in this chapter's handout     2. Calcutta Madarsa, Warren Hastings 73-85   (no mark; true)   The tick sits on (b) Only 2     3. Fort William College, Arthur Wellesley   F   Founded by Richard Wellesley 98-05, in 1800; Arthur was the Royal Army brother (1.1)   Answer: (b) Only 2 (slide 20). Bank check: keyed (b) and matches. The trap is the swap of Richard for Arthur: the question tests whether you know the founder by his full name, which is why the teacher stressed "Richard" on the title slide of Section 0. Mnemonic: Two F's, one true: Jones F, Arthur F, Madarsa-Hastings T. Decode: Pair 1 (Sanskrit College Banaras, Jones) is F: Jonathan Duncan 1791. Pair 3 (Fort William, Arthur) is F: Richard Wellesley 98-05, 1800. Only pair 2 (Calcutta Madarsa, Warren Hastings 73-85) is right, so (b) Only 2. Why it sticks: the two circled F's are the two wrong names, Jones and Arthur. Mnemonic: Duncan in Banaras, Richard in Calcutta. Decode: Jonathan Duncan = Sanskrit College Banaras (1791); Richard Wellesley 98-05 = Fort William College, Calcutta (1800). Why it sticks: two founders, two cities, two dates: 1791 and 1800. 8.4 PYQ 5: Prelims 2020, why Wellesley 98-05 established Fort William College (slides 22 and 23)  PYQ 5, Prelims 2020: "Wellesley established the Fort William College at Calcutta because (a) he was asked by the Board of Directors at London to do so (b) he wanted to revive interest in oriental learning in India (c) he wanted to provide William Carey and his associates with employment (d) he wanted to train British civilians for administrative purpose in India." Typed answer: (d). No handwriting. Answer: (d) (slide 22). Slide 23's explanation: the purpose was administrative: Wellesley 98-05 wanted his EIC officers linguistically and legally competent before they began ruling Indian districts. (a) wrong: the Board did not ask; it was Wellesley 98-05's own initiative. (b) wrong: reviving oriental learning was the Asiatic Society's mandate (William Jones from 1784), not this College's. (c) wrong: William Carey joined later as a linguist-teacher; employment for him was not the founding purpose. Bank check: the Prelims 2020 entry is keyed (d) and matches; the bank also holds a Prelims 2021 repeat of this question, also keyed (d), which is not shown on the class slides. Mnemonic: Fort William = Furnish administrators: (d), not (a), (b) or (c). Decode: (a) the Board asked = no, Wellesley 98-05's own idea; (b) oriental learning = the Asiatic Society (William Jones from 1784); (c) jobs for William Carey = no, he joined later; (d) train British civilians for administration = yes. Why it sticks: "F-W-F-A": Fort William Furnishes Administrators. No conflict between slides and handout on any of the five answers. The slide answers, the handout alerts in Sections 1, 2.3 and 4.4, and the bank agree on (c), (c), (c), (b), (d) for Prelims 1999, 2018 (SA), 2021 (SA), 2018 (pairs) and 2020. The only mismatch is the bank's wrong key (a) on Prelims 1999 (see the Exam lens).

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The Wellesley 98-05 story in ten beats. Seventy-two the Company broke, seventy-three the leash, eighty-four Pitt locked the war-gate. Ninety-eight: Richard Wellesley 98-05 shouts "Napoleon at Egypt, Tipu 82-99 beside!" The threat was there, not real, but the gate swings open. Hyderabad signs first (98), Mysore falls (99), Awadh gives half (01), Cambay and Bassein follow (02), Scindia (03), Travancore the last of his own (05). Raj Always Disarms, Squeezes, Fixes-foreign: the king pays, the Company plays. The bill climbs again, Wellesley 98-05 is recalled, and Bhonsle (1816) and Holkar (1818) finish the ten under Francis Hastings 13-23. Decode: 1772 bankrupt, 1773 Regulating Act, 1784 Pitt's India Act ban; 1798 Napoleon in Egypt; ten SAs in order (Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Awadh 1801, Gaikwad/Cambay 1802, Peshwa/Bassein 1802, Scindia 1803, Jats-Rajputs-Bundelas 1803-05, Travancore 1805, Bhonsle/Nagpur 1816, Holkar/Mandsaur 1818); recall for high war expenditure.

items.t: Exam lens: priority and PYQs

Root cause: multiple States, motive = Territory, so rivalry; the EIC's edge = better leadership and a better army. Why it sticks: "F-W-I" sounds like "FWI, for what?" items.t: 1 · Why was Mysore such a serious threat?
items.x: Why Mysore a Serious Threat. Table: Rulers Hyder Ali 61-82 then Tipu 82-99 wanted to dominate the trade and politics of South India; 1.1 Military Fiscalism. Teacher's ink: "GOALS of [TRADE + (T)] & efficient TOOLS to achieve goals"; Military Fiscalism boxed with "GOAL" under Military and "TOOL" (underlined) under Fiscalism; "(1) Eicompany: INTERNATIONAL TRADE (Indian exports)" with "[Tipu 82-99 - Govt Company]"; "(2) Br vs Fr: GLOBAL Geopolitical RIVALRY" with "[HA 61-82, Tipu 82-99: Good Relation alliance with Fr]"; "(3) Mysore wanted VN 2.0" with a sketched wedge in a circle, "Dream of Tipu 82-99"; "Anxiety/RIVALRY @" four circled neighbours Ma, Hyd, Tr, Ca. Hyder Ali 61-82 and then Tipu 82-99 made Mysore more than a State trying to survive: it tried to dominate the trade, the coastline and the politics of South India. That made it a threat to every neighbouring power, and to the EIC in two special ways. 1.1 Military Fiscalism Mysore followed Military Fiscalism: the primary goal of maximising State revenue was to fund an ever-stronger military. (The EIC had followed the same model since 1765 to build its own strong military.) Under Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99, Mysore built a centralised State with a modern military and a navy, with French assistance. France gave arms and technical support in exchange for trade concessions, to counter EIC trade. The French connection made both the EIC and the neighbouring Indian States even more anxious. Teacher: Military Fiscalism is read as two words: Military = GOAL, Fiscalism = TOOL (he underlined TOOL). The teacher's frame for the whole chapter: each player has goals (the box: TRADE + T for territory) and efficient tools to achieve them. For Mysore the goal is military strength; the tool is revenue maximisation. He then listed three reasons for the threat: (1) the EIC is a company, its business is international trade (Indian exports), and Tipu 82-99 ran a government company that competed for it; (2) a British versus French global geopolitical rivalry, with Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99 in a good-relation alliance with France; (3) "Mysore wanted VN 2.0" and a sketch of a wedge in a circle, labelled "Dream of Tipu 82-99." The sketch is unclear: check your notebook. Chapter 7's board links Mysore to the Vijayanagar empire (1336-1646), so "VN" most likely means Vijayanagar, but that is a reading, not his words (Chapter 7). Under all three he wrote "Anxiety/RIVALRY @ Ma, Hyd, Tr, Ca" (Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore, Carnatic): the four neighbours who feared Mysore. Mnemonic: Military is the Mission, Fiscalism is the Fuel. Decode: Military = GOAL (a stronger army), Fiscalism = TOOL (maximise State revenue to pay for it). Same model the EIC used from 1765. Mysore added a navy and French arms for trade concessions. Why it sticks: M-M and F-F: Mission and Military, Fuel and Fiscalism. Mnemonic: T-F-D: the teacher's three threats, and "Ma-Hy-Tr-Ca" the four anxious neighbours. Decode: Trade (Tipu 82-99's government company versus the EIC), France (Br vs Fr rivalry; Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99 allied with France), Dream (VN 2.0, unclear). Neighbours who feared Mysore: Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore, Carnatic. Why it sticks: say it as "Ma, Hi, Tra, Ca": Ma says "Hi" to Tra-Ca. 1.2 Mercantilist trading State  Why Mysore a Serious Threat (contd.). 1.2 Mercantilist State: Tipu set up a State-owned trading company that entered international trade directly. Trade embargo: in the late 1780s Tipu barred exports of pepper, cardamom and sandalwood from Mysore ports and barred local merchants from engaging with British traders; Malabar (under Mysore since 1766) was the critical pepper source for the EIC. Teacher's ink: "Trade" underlined with an arrow down to "3RD A-My 1790-92"; "France" underlined in the Other aspects row. Tipu 82-99 set up a State-owned trading company that entered international trade directly. Mysore was acting as a rival Mercantilist State, exactly as the EIC did. Two mercantilist powers competing over the same trade routes and coastal markets cannot coexist easily. In the late 1780s he put a trade embargo on exports of pepper, cardamom and sandalwood from ports under Mysore's control, and barred local merchants from dealing with British traders entirely. Malabar was a critical source of pepper for the EIC and had been under Mysore's control since 1766. He brought in his own Mauludi calendar: a new lunisolar calendar based on the Prophet's birth era, introduced to replace the Islamic Hijri calendar. He sent delegations to France, Turkey (the Ottoman Empire) and Egypt to seek anti-British alliances. Takeaway: the EIC-Mysore rivalry was not just a military conflict. It was a clash between two entities following the same model (Military Fiscalism plus Mercantilism) in the same geography. Only one could win. The EIC's diplomatic advantage: Mysore's ambitions also threatened every neighbouring State, so coalitions against Mysore were easy to build. Teacher: He underlined "Trade" in "Trade embargo" and drew an arrow to "3rd A-My 1790-92": the embargo (late 1780s) is the economic background that leads to the 3rd war. He also underlined France in "Other aspects" (the delegations): a Prelims hook, see Prelims 2001 below. Mnemonic: PCS embargo; FTE embassies. Decode: Tipu 82-99's embargo covered Pepper, Cardamom, Sandalwood (late 1780s). His delegations went to France, Turkey, Egypt. He also made the Mauludi lunisolar calendar (Prophet's birth era) to replace the Hijri. Why it sticks: an aspirant's "PCS" for goods, "FTE" for faraway friends.  PYQ 1, Prelims 2001: Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (a) Haider Ali (b) Mir Qasim (c) Shah Alam II (d) Tipu Sultan. Teacher's ink, in yellow, beside each option: 61-82, 60-63, 60-06, 82-99. There is no tick on this slide; the next slide gives the answer (d). Prelims 2001: answer (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan 82-99. The teacher added the reign codes to each option so you can place each ruler: Haider Ali 61-82 (built the French-model army but set up no modern embassies), Mir Qasim 60-63 (Nawab of Bengal, Buxar 1764), Shah Alam II 60-06 (the Mughal Emperor). Tipu 82-99's delegations to France, Turkey and Egypt are the "embassies on modern lines." Mnemonic: Prelims 2001: "T for Tipu 82-99, T for Turkey, T for Trade company." Decode: the ruler who sent embassies on modern lines is Tipu 82-99; the codes on the options: Haider Ali 61-82, Mir Qasim 60-63, Shah Alam II 60-06. Why it sticks: the only option with a code that ends in 99 is the one that looked furthest ahead. Mnemonic: Hyder 61-82, Tipu 82-99: the baton passes at 82. Decode: Hyder Ali 61-82 died of cancer in December 1782; Tipu 82-99 took over and continued the 2nd war. Tipu 82-99's code ends in 99, the year of the 4th war. Why it sticks: both codes share the number 82, one ends where the other begins.  Map of South India with the teacher's labels. White labels with lines into the map: Guntur (yellow), Kanara, SRI Rangapatnam, Mangalore, Coorg, "Malabar (LOST @ 3RD war)", Coimbatore (yellow), "Bara Mahal (Lost in 3RD war)", "Dundigul (Lost in 3RD war)". Top right: "To HYD 1766" underlined, then "N. Sarkars Given By Hyd to eic [4/5 districts given]"; bullets: "eic to give 7 lakh Rs p.a." and "eic to militarily help HYD vs My [& vs (Ma) in future if need]". Blue, pink and green lines mark the Peshwa, Nizam and Tippoo dominions and the Carnatic. Teacher: A working map for the whole chapter. Guntur sits inside the Northern Sarkars: under the 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad, Hyderabad gave the Northern Sarkars to the EIC (4 of the 5 districts were given, Guntur was not) and the EIC promised 7 lakh rupees a year plus military help to Hyderabad against Mysore (and, in the line as he wrote it, against the Marathas, circled Ma, in future if needed). Lost in the 3rd war: Malabar, Bara Mahal (Baramahal), Dindigul. Lost in the 4th: Kanara, Coimbatore. Seringapatam is Mysore's capital; Mangalore is its coastal port; Coorg lies between them (section 8).

items.t: 2 · 1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69): the EIC lost?
items.x: 1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), the reason. Hyder Ali 61-82 modernised his army with the French (at Mahe on the Malabar coast), e.g. a 1755 arsenal at Dindigul Fort; 1766 he annexed Malabar and Calicut (spice trade); 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: the EIC promised to help Hyderabad invade Mysore to get the Northern Sarkars; Marathas joined, giving a triple alliance of EIC + Hyderabad + Marathas (formed twice, the 2nd time in 1790). Teacher's ink: underlines under Malabar and Calicut, "1766 Treaty of Hyderabad", the triple alliance and "1790"; a bracket "[not Part of TRAVANCORE]" beside Malabar and Calicut; "+ 7 Lakh Rs p.a. To HYD"; "1st (1767-69)" and "3RD A-My [1790-92]"; a sketch: a line from MADRAS up through ANDHRA to Bengal. 2.1 Reason Even before Hyder Ali 61-82 came to power, he had begun modernising his army with French help (the French were present in Mahe). In 1755 he set up a modern arsenal (arms factory) at Dindigul Fort. This continued friendship threatened the EIC. 1766: Hyder Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar (the slide adds Calicut), important for the spice trade. The same year, the EIC promised to help Hyderabad invade Mysore, so that the EIC would get the Northern Sarkars (important to connect Bengal with Madras). (Recall: in 1766 Hyderabad gave the EIC the Northern Sarkars in return for protection against Mysore and the Marathas.) The Marathas also saw Mysore as a rival and joined. So the EIC crafted a triple alliance of EIC, Hyderabad and Marathas against Mysore. (It was formed twice; the 2nd time in 1790.) Teacher: Beside Malabar and Calicut: "[not Part of Travancore]." The 1766 annexation took Malabar and Calicut, not Travancore (Chapter 7 says the same: Travancore itself was not taken). His map line from Madras through Andhra to Bengal shows why the EIC wanted the Northern Sarkars: a land link between its two Presidencies. He added "+ 7 lakh Rs p.a. to HYD": what the EIC promised to pay Hyderabad for the Sarkars. The arrow "3rd A-My [1790-92]" under the triple-alliance line marks the second time it was formed. Mnemonic: 1766: four given, Guntur kept, seven lakh promised. Decode: 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: the Northern Sarkars go to the EIC (4 of 5 districts handed over; Guntur was not), the EIC promises 7 lakh rupees a year and military help to Hyderabad against Mysore. The EIC wanted Andhra to join Bengal and Madras. Why it sticks: Guntur is the fifth finger held back; it comes back to bite in 1780. Mnemonic: "Confederacy = Conspiracy against the Company; Alliance = Allies of the Company." Decode: Triple Alliance = EIC + Hyderabad + Marathas against Mysore, formed 1766-67 and again 1790. Triple Confederacy (1780-82) = Marathas + Mysore + Hyderabad against the EIC, built by Nana Fadnis. Same three Indian powers, opposite sides. Why it sticks: C for Confederacy and Company-opponent, A for Alliance and Allied-with-Company. 2.2 Events  1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69) (contd.). Events: Hyder broke the coalition by diplomacy: 1767 paid the Marathas 35 lakh rupees to exit; allied with Hyderabad by giving the Nizam 20 lakh rupees plus a promise to help make the Nizam's son Nawab of Carnatic plus a joint future attack on Carnatic (under Md Ali 52-95, an EIC ally). 1768: Hyderabad feared a counter-invasion and made peace with the EIC. 1769: Hyder 61-82 marched to the gates of Madras while the EIC's Bombay navy took coastal Mysore, e.g. Mangalore. Treaty of Madras (1769): the EIC, fearing Madras's destruction, was forced to sign; both sides returned each other's territories and agreed to a defensive military alliance. Teacher's ink: "BY eic" under "made peace"; underlines under Madras, EIC's Bombay, e.g. Mangalore, Treaty of Madras (1769), returned each other's territories, defensive military alliance; a bracket on the right: "IR: No permanent friends/enemies in Foreign Policy". Hyder Ali 61-82 broke the coalition through skilled diplomacy: 1767: he paid the Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit the war. Then he allied with Hyderabad: he gave the Nizam Rs 20 lakh, promised to make the Nizam's son Nawab of Carnatic, and agreed to a joint future attack on Carnatic (it was under Md Ali 52-95, an ally of the EIC). 1768: Hyderabad feared a counter-invasion of Hyderabad itself by the EIC and exited by making peace with the EIC. 1769: Hyder Ali 61-82 had outmanoeuvred the EIC forces and marched to the gates of Madras. Meanwhile the EIC navy from Bombay captured coastal areas of Mysore, e.g. Mangalore. Teacher: "IR: No permanent friends or enemies in foreign policy" (International Relations): the Marathas and Hyderabad were EIC allies in 1766 and Hyder 61-82's partners (or paid-off neutrals) in 1767-68. The teacher inserted "BY eic" under "made peace" with a caret mark beside the 1768 line, so the Hyderabad peace seems to be one made with the EIC's initiative; the caret is hard to read: check your notebook. He underlined Madras, "EIC's Bombay" navy and Mangalore: the war had a land front at Madras and a sea front on the west coast. Mnemonic: 35 for the Marathas, 20 for the Nizam: the bigger power, the bigger bribe. Decode: 1767 Hyder 61-82 pays the Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit; he gives the Nizam Rs 20 lakh plus the promise of making his son Nawab of Carnatic and a joint attack on Carnatic (Md Ali 52-95's State). 1768 Hyderabad, fearing an EIC counter-invasion, makes peace with the EIC. Why it sticks: M is bigger than N in the alphabet's second half, and 35 is bigger than 20. 2.3 Result: the Treaty of Madras (1769) The EIC, fearing the destruction of Madras, was forced to sign the Treaty of Madras (1769). Both sides returned conquered territories and agreed to a defensive military alliance: each promised to help the other if attacked by a third party. This was a PoRF arrangement only on paper (PoRF = Policy of Ring Fence, Chapter 10): a fake alliance in practice, as the very next war showed.  Teacher's board: the concept of a military alliance. Offensive: an alliance valid even when one member is the aggressor; example PACT of STEEL 1939 between Germany and Italy. Defensive: valid only when a member is the victim of aggression; examples NATO 1949, SEATO 1954, Baghdad Pact 1955 [CENTO 1958]; an arrow from the list to "Pak was member; 1965 war, 1971 war; Pak = Aggressor". A small sketch of three circles at top right is unclear. Teacher: Why the teacher stopped to teach "military alliance". The 1769 treaty was a defensive alliance, so he separated the two kinds. Offensive alliance: valid even when one member is the aggressor (Pact of Steel 1939, Germany and Italy). Defensive alliance: valid only when a member is the victim of aggression (NATO 1949, SEATO 1954, Baghdad Pact 1955, later CENTO 1958). His example: Pakistan was a member of these defensive blocs, but in the 1965 and 1971 wars Pakistan was the aggressor, so the pacts did not bind the others. Keep the rule: a defensive clause is only as good as the question "who attacked whom". (The next slide, 33, is a small board with "wp" and "ep" and a circled 1971, crossed out: a side sketch with no new facts.) Mnemonic: Offensive = Steel 39; Defensive = NATO 49, SEATO 54, Baghdad 55, CENTO 58. Decode: Offensive alliance (valid even if a member is the aggressor): Pact of Steel 1939, Germany and Italy. Defensive alliance (valid only if a member is the victim): NATO 1949, SEATO 1954, Baghdad Pact 1955 [CENTO 1958]. Pakistan was a member but the aggressor in 1965 and 1971. Why it sticks: after 49 the years climb 54, 55, 58: steps of 5, 1, 3. Mnemonic: Madras: gates, give back, guard. Decode: Treaty of Madras 1769: Hyder 61-82 at the gates of Madras; both sides give back territory; a defensive alliance to guard each other against a third party. It was a farce, as 1771 and 1780 showed. Why it sticks: three G words, in order of events.

items.t: 3 · 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): how the EIC broke the Mysore-Marathas-Hyderabad alliance
items.x: 3.1 Reason for war  2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84), the reason. Marathas attacked Mysore in 1771 and the EIC refused its 1769 treaty duty to defend Mysore. Final trigger: France entered the American War of Independence (1776-83) in 1778, so the EIC seized the French Mahe port in Malabar (1779), under Mysore's protection and Hyder's French-arms route. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "French Mahe port in Malabar (1779)", "under Mysore's protection" and "Hyder's French-arms route"; a sketch "Fr -> Mahe" with "French used to supply arms to Mysore from Mahe". Right: "USA independence via American Revolution (AR 65-83), 1765-83", splitting into "violent PROTEST (1765-76)" and "Am WAR of Independence [1776-83]". 1771: the Marathas attacked Mysore, and the EIC refused to honour its 1769 treaty obligation to come to Mysore's defence. The final trigger: France entered the American War of Independence (1776-83) against Britain in 1778, and the EIC seized the French port of Mahe in Malabar in 1779. Mahe was under Mysore's military protection, and through it Hyder Ali 61-82 was importing French arms and ammunition. Teacher: He drew Mahe as the supply route: France to Mahe to Mysore. Seizing Mahe cut the arms line, so Hyder 61-82 attacked. The teacher also gave the world frame: the American Revolution runs 1765-83, in two phases: violent protest 1765-76 and the American War of Independence 1776-83. France joined that war in 1778; so a war in America opens a war in India (the teacher tags the 2nd war "Fr FACTOR"). Mnemonic: 71 refused, 78 France, 79 Mahe, 80 war. Decode: 1771 Marathas attack Mysore, the EIC refuses its 1769 duty. 1778 France enters the American War (1776-83). 1779 the EIC seizes French Mahe (under Mysore's protection; Hyder 61-82's arms route). 1780 Hyder Ali 61-82 invades Carnatic. The American Revolution: protest 1765-76, war 1776-83. Why it sticks: four steps up the years 71, 78, 79, 80, the last three almost consecutive. 3.2 Events  2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84) (contd.). Events: Hyder 61-82 invaded Carnatic (EIC ally) and took Arcot (capital). Battle of Pollilur (Sep 1780): Colonel Baillie's infantry annihilated, Hyder 61-82 using iron-cased rockets, a shock to the EIC; alert: Pollilur (Sep 1780) is tested in UPSC Prelims (rocket-warfare innovation). Triple Confederacy 1780-82: Marathas-Mysore-Hyderabad vs the EIC, built by Nana Fadnis (de-facto ruler and top minister in the Peshwa's council; the 1st Indian statesman to grasp the EIC's empire ambitions). Hyderabad joined as the EIC had illegally occupied Guntur and stopped the annual 7 lakh Rs. Teacher's ink: circled "PRE" beside Nana Fadnis; underlines under "Hyder 61-82 using iron-cased rockets", "Triple Confederacy", "Nana Fadnis", "1st Indian" and "grasp the EIC's empire ambitions"; board: "1780-82 alliance of My, MA, Hyd", with an arrow from MA to "1st A-Ma 1775-82" and "Guntur Taken By eic". Hyder Ali 61-82 invaded Carnatic (an EIC ally) and captured Arcot (the capital). He then inflicted one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India at the Battle of Pollilur (September 1780): Colonel Baillie's disciplined infantry formations were annihilated, Hyder Ali 61-82's troops using iron-cased rockets to devastating effect. Pollilur was a shock to the EIC. Battle of Pollilur (September 1780) has been tested in UPSC Prelims (the rocket-warfare innovation of Mysore). Keep the four tags: Sep 1780, Colonel Baillie, iron-cased rockets, Hyder Ali 61-82. Mnemonic: Baillie's ranks burn at Pollilur: Sep 1780, iron rockets. Decode: Pollilur, September 1780: Colonel Baillie's infantry is annihilated by Hyder 61-82's iron-cased rockets; Arcot, the Carnatic capital, had been taken just before. One of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India. Why it sticks: "rocket" and "Pollilur" both have an "o" and an "l": the rocket lit up the line. The Triple Confederacy (1780-82): an alliance of Marathas, Mysore and Hyderabad against the EIC, established by Nana Fadnis, the de-facto ruler and most important minister in the Peshwa's council. Nana Fadnis (Fadnavis) was the first Indian statesman to understand that the EIC was in India not just for trade but had ambitions of empire building. Hyderabad joined because the EIC had illegally occupied Guntur (one of the 5 districts of the Northern Sarkars, not handed over in 1766) and had stopped paying the annual 7 lakh rupees agreed for ceding the Northern Sarkars. Teacher: He circled "PRE" beside Nana Fadnis and underlined "1st Indian": this is a Prelims line. On the board he wrote the three members (My, Ma, Hyd) with the dates 1780-82, drew an arrow from the Marathas to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) (the Marathas were already at war with the EIC) and noted "Guntur taken by EIC" under Hyderabad (their grievance). A confederacy, he stresses, is an alliance against the EIC: the reverse of the triple alliance of 1766 and 1790. Mnemonic: Nana's three: My-Ma-Hy, and Hyderabad's two grievances: Guntur and 7 lakh. Decode: Triple Confederacy 1780-82: Mysore + Marathas + Hyderabad against the EIC, built by Nana Fadnis (the first Indian statesman to see the EIC's empire ambitions: PRE). Hyderabad joined because the EIC illegally held Guntur and stopped the 7 lakh a year. Why it sticks: "My Ma Hy": My Ma says Hi to the Nana. 3.3 How the EIC broke it, and the result  2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84) (contd.). The EIC breaks it: Warren Hastings 73-85 returned Guntur to Hyderabad and signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas (ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82). Marathas and Hyderabad withdrew, leaving Mysore isolated; Nana Fadnis kept the Marathas from aiding Britain. Hyder 61-82 died of cancer, Dec 1782; Tipu 82-99 took over and continued the war. Result: Treaty of Mangalore (1784): stalemate; both sides returned each other's territories; status quo maintained. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines only (Hastings 73-85, Guntur to Hyderabad, Treaty of Salbai (May 1782), ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War, Stalemate). Warren Hastings 73-85 broke the coalition through careful diplomacy: He returned Guntur to Hyderabad, removing their grievance. He signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas, which ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). The Marathas and Hyderabad withdrew their support, leaving Mysore isolated to fight the EIC alone. Nana Fadnis ensured the Marathas did not send an army in favour of the British (the handout's note: Chanakya Neeti, let both rivals destroy each other). Hyder Ali 61-82 died of cancer in December 1782. Tipu 82-99 took over and continued the war. Result: the Treaty of Mangalore (1784). The war ended in a stalemate. Both sides returned each other's territories; the status quo was maintained. Teacher: He underlined both of Hastings 73-85's moves and tagged the war "(Tie)" on the board of slide 29. Remember what each partner got: Hyderabad = Guntur back; the Marathas = the Treaty of Salbai (which also closed their own war with the EIC). That is why the coalition collapsed: each partner's grievance was settled separately. Mnemonic: G-S: Guntur back, Salbai signed; then Hyder dies, Mangalore ties. Decode: Warren Hastings 73-85 returns Guntur to Hyderabad and signs Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas (it ends the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82). Hyder 61-82 dies, Dec 1782; Tipu 82-99 fights on; Mangalore 1784 returns territories (stalemate). Why it sticks: 82 for Salbai and for Hyder's death, 84 for the stalemate: "82, 82, 84".  Two maps. Left: Anglo-Mysore Wars I (1767-69) and II (1780-84): Peshwa's territories, Nizam's territories, Hyderabad, Northern Sarkars, Goa, Mysore (green), Mangalore, Mahe, Madras, Conjevaram, Pondicherry, Travancore. Teacher's red ink: beside the Peshwa's coast "1750 Tofangala" (unclear, underlined); "1766" beside the Northern Sarkars; "1652 presidency" beside Madras. Right: Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-1792 with territories relinquished (to the Peshwa, to the Nizam, to the British). Red ink: "Malabar" with "[imp for spices]", pink lines to the hatched areas, "Baramahal", "Dundigul", two small arrows up at the areas given to the Peshwa and the Nizam, and "# Notice: encirclement by EIC". Unclear ink on slide 37 (left map). The words "1750 Tofangala" beside the Peshwa's coast cannot be read with confidence: check your notebook. The other two notes are clear: "1766" marks the Northern Sarkars (the Treaty of Hyderabad) and "1652 presidency" marks Madras (it was already an EIC Presidency long before these wars). items.t: 4 · 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92): when the tide turned
items.x: 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92). Reason: Tipu 82-99 attacked Travancore, a formal EIC ally, giving Cornwallis 86-93 his justification for war; the EIC formed a Triple Alliance with the Marathas and Hyderabad in 1790 (in 1782-84 the Marathas had not fought Mysore). Events: combined EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad forces put Mysore under severe pressure from multiple directions; Tipu 82-99 fought hard but could not hold against a coordinated three-front campaign. Treaty of Seringapatam / Srirangapatnam (1792): Mysore lost half its Kingdom, including the rich Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal; a war fine of 3 crore rupees; two of Tipu's own sons surrendered as hostages to guarantee compliance. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "attacked Travancore", "Cornwallis 86-93", "Triple Alliance", "Treaty of Seringapatam /", "(1792)", "half its Kingdom", "3 crore rupees", "Two of Tipu's own sons" and "hostages". 4.1 Reason and events Tipu 82-99 attacked Travancore, a formal ally of the EIC. This gave Cornwallis 86-93 the justification to declare war. The EIC formed a Triple Alliance with the Marathas and Hyderabad in 1790 (in 1782-84 the Marathas did not fight Mysore). The combined forces of EIC, Marathas and Hyderabad put Mysore under severe military pressure from multiple directions. Tipu 82-99 fought hard but could not hold against a coordinated three-front campaign. (The handout's Travancore section dates Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore to 1789 and calls it the pretext for this war: see section 10.1.) Teacher: Underlined: "attacked Travancore", "Cornwallis 86-93", "Triple Alliance". The three words tell the story: a trigger (Travancore), a Governor General who uses it (Cornwallis 86-93), and the coalition that Mysore had broken in 1767 and 1782 now rebuilt against it. His earlier arrow (slide 30) said the same: the triple alliance of 1766-67 is formed twice, the second time in 1790 (3rd A-My). Mnemonic: Travancore trigger, Cornwallis 86-93 chooses, three fronts close. Decode: 1789 Tipu 82-99 attacks Travancore (a formal EIC ally) → Cornwallis 86-93 declares war → Triple Alliance 1790 (EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad; in 1782-84 the Marathas had stayed out) → three-front pressure → Seringapatam 1792. Why it sticks: every stage hands the baton to the next: trigger, chooser, closer. 4.2 Result: the Treaty of Seringapatam / Srirangapatnam (1792)   Term   Detail    --- ---    Territory   Mysore lost half its Kingdom, including the rich Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal     War fine   3 crore rupees     Hostages   Two of Tipu 82-99's own sons surrendered to guarantee compliance   Teacher: He underlined every term: half its Kingdom, 3 crore rupees, Two of Tipu 82-99's own sons, hostages. On the map (slide 37) he marked Malabar [important for spices], Baramahal and Dindigul with pink lines to the hatched British areas, and two small arrows to the Peshwa's and the Nizam's shares, with the comment "Notice: encirclement by EIC": the EIC now held land on Mysore's west (Malabar), south-east (Baramahal) and far south (Dindigul), with allies to its north. Source mismatch on the war's dates. The title and the teacher's board say the 3rd war is 1790-92. The handout text in section 6 and slide 45 write "1789-92" (counting from Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789) and the handout's flow chart (section 5) writes "1789-92" too. Teacher's marked map of South India (dominions of the Peishwa, the Nizam and Tippoo; Carnatic, Malabar, Travancore, Baramahal, Mahe, Calicut, Pondicherry, Karikal, Guntur). Pink line along the borders of Tippoo's dominions; blue line along the Carnatic coast; a blue circle around Guntur; green underlines under the Peishwa, Nizam and Tippoo names; BIDAR in blue with a dot; Mahe and Calicut highlighted in blue with a yellow blob; Pondicherry and Karikal highlighted. items.t: 5 · 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): how Mysore finally fell
items.x: 5.1 Reason  4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799), the reason. Tipu 82-99's ongoing negotiations with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his pretext in London (Britain was already at war with France). An empire-builder, Wellesley 98-05 used Tipu 82-99's secret letters to the French as proof of a threat and got British approval for war. Teacher's ink: underlines under "Napoleon" and "Wellesley 98-05"; a yellow note "(* Recall PIA 1784)". Tipu 82-99's ongoing negotiations with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his political pretext in London. Britain was already at war with France. Wellesley 98-05, an empire builder by nature, used Tipu 82-99's secret letters to the French as proof of a threat and got British approval for war. Teacher: "(* Recall PIA 1784)": Pitt's India Act 1784 banned offensive wars without the Court's command, so Wellesley 98-05 needed an excuse. The Napoleon letters were the excuse; the full story is in Chapter 11 (the teacher's verdict there: the threat was there but not real). The teacher tagged this war "Reason: Fr FACTOR" on the board (slide 29). 5.2 Events and result  4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799) (contd.). Events: the EIC and Hyderabad fought Mysore (Hyderabad had to, under the SA of 1798); Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18 sent no army, on Nana Fadnis's advice; Arthur WELLESLEYPROT, commanding his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces, was among the key commanders at the Siege of Srirangapatnam; Tipu 82-99 died defending his capital. Result: the best remaining parts (Kanara, Coimbatore and others) were divided between the EIC and Hyderabad; Mysore's central core went back to the old Wodeyar dynasty, with five-year-old Krishnaraja III on the throne under a Subsidiary Alliance (1799); the last major military threat in the south was over; territory offered to the Peshwa on condition of signing an SA was refused (Nana Fadnis's advice). Teacher's ink, top right: "D, C, FA of HYD with eic - MILITARY alliance, therefore No choice", with a line to "SA of 1798"; underlines under EIC and Hyderabad, Arthur WELLESLEYPROT, Royal regiment, Tipu died defending his capital, Kanara, Coimbatore, Wodeyar dynasty, five-year-old Krishnaraja III, Subsidiary Alliance and (1799). The EIC and Hyderabad fought Mysore (Hyderabad had to, because of the SA of 1798). Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18 did not send an army, on the advice of Nana Fadnis, despite EIC requests. Arthur Wellesley, commanding his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces, was among the key military commanders in the Siege of Srirangapatnam. Tipu 82-99 died defending his capital. Teacher: "D, C, FA of HYD with EIC: military alliance, therefore no choice." Since the 1798 SA, Hyderabad's Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs were in the EIC's hands (the three external functions from Chapter 11), so Hyderabad could not refuse to fight. He underlined "Arthur Wellesley" and "Royal regiment": Arthur Wellesley was a Royal Army officer, not an EIC officer, commanding his regiment alongside the EIC forces (and carries no reign code: only Richard Wellesley 98-05, the Governor General, is Wellesley 98-05). Result: The best parts of Mysore's remaining territory (Kanara, Coimbatore and others) were divided between the EIC and Hyderabad. The central core of Mysore went back to the old Wodeyar dynasty, with five-year-old Krishnaraja III placed on the throne under a Subsidiary Alliance (1799). The last major military threat to the EIC in the south was over. Some territory was offered to the Peshwa on condition of signing an SA; the Marathas refused, on Nana Fadnis's advice. Teacher: Underlined: Kanara, Coimbatore, Wodeyar dynasty, five-year-old Krishnaraja III, Subsidiary Alliance (1799). On the map (slide 42) he marked Kanara (the west coast near Mangalore) and Coimbatore (to the south-east of Mysore): the 4th war's gains to the EIC. The 1792 gains were Malabar, Dindigul, Baramahal; the 1799 gains were Kanara, Coimbatore. Do not mix the two lists.  Map: Anglo-Mysore War IV (1799). Mysore (1792) in green; hatched areas to the Peshwa, to the Nizam and to the British; Hyderabad, Northern Sarkars, Goa, Mangalore, Mahe, Madras, Pondicherry, Travancore. Teacher's red ink: "Kanara" with a line to the hatched British area on the west coast near Mangalore, and "Coimbatore" with a line to the hatched area south-east of Mysore.  Handout figure: Anglo-Mysore War IV (1799), the same map as slide 42 without ink. Mysore (1792) is the pale green core; the territories taken in 1799 are hatched, to the Peshwa (a strip near Goa), to the Nizam (north) and to the British (the west coast around Mangalore and the area south-east of Mysore); Travancore lies at the southern tip.  PYQ 2, Prelims 2004 (marked Partial). Statements: 1. In the Third Battle of Panipat, Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated Ibrahim Lodi. 2. Tipu Sultan was killed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War. 3. Mir Jafar entered in conspiracy with the English for the defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-daula in the Battle of Plassey. Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) Only 3 (c) 2 and 3 (d) None of these. Teacher's ink: top right a list "ABDALI, FARUKHABAD, ROHILKHAND, AWADH" then a circled "vs" and a circled "Ma"; a circled F beside statement 1; "4th" and a circled F beside statement 2; a circled T beside statement 3; a tick on option (b).  PYQ 2, answer. (b) Only 3. Statement 1 wrong: at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Abdali defeated the Marathas, not Ibrahim Lodi (Lodi lost at the First Panipat, 1526, to Babur 26-30). Statement 2 wrong: Tipu 82-99 was killed in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799) at the Siege of Seringapatam, not the 3rd. Statement 3 correct: Mir Jafar 57-60 conspired with the English against Siraj-ud-daula at Plassey 1757. Hook: Panipat 1761 = Abdali vs Marathas (not Lodi); Tipu died in the 4th war 1799 (not 3rd); Plassey plot = Mir Jafar. Prelims 2004: answer (b) Only 3. For this chapter, the line to carry is "Tipu 82-99 died in the 4th war (1799), at Seringapatam, not in the 3rd." The teacher's side list Abdali, Farrukhabad, Rohilkhand, Awadh against Ma (Marathas) names the Third Panipat sides as he drew them (see Chapter 4); do not add to it from outside the board. The slide and the handout agree; no conflict. Mnemonic: Prelims 2004: "Lodi 26, Marathas 61, Tipu 82-99 dies in 4th, 99." Decode: Ibrahim Lodi lost the First Panipat (1526) to Babur 26-30. At the Third Panipat (1761) Abdali beat the Marathas. Tipu 82-99 died in the 4th war (1799), not the 3rd. Only statement 3 (Mir Jafar 57-60's conspiracy at Plassey 1757) is true: (b). Why it sticks: Tipu 82-99's code ends in 99, and 99 is the 4th war. Mnemonic: Five-year-old king, ninety-nine, SA. Decode: 1799: the Wodeyars return in Mysore's central core, Krishnaraja III, age 5, under a Subsidiary Alliance (1799); Kanara and Coimbatore go to the EIC (with Hyderabad). Hyderabad fought because of its SA of 1798. The Peshwa (Baji Rao II 96-18) sent no army and refused the SA offer, on Nana Fadnis's advice. Why it sticks: "5 on the throne, 99 on the calendar". Mnemonic: Tipu 82-99's death chain: Napoleon, Wellesley 98-05, Hyderabad, Arthur, Wodeyar. items.t: 6 · Why did Mysore lose?
items.x: Why Did Mysore Lose? 1. No stable alliance: Mysore's aggressive expansion and the EIC's diplomacy prevented it from building stable alliances. 2. French naval gap: Mysore was strategically dependent on French arms; France was tied up in the American War of Independence (1776-83) then the Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804), and its navy was no match for Britain's, so no French fleet ever resupplied Mysore at scale. Teacher's ink: underlines under "No stable alliance" and "French naval gap"; yellow notes top right: "External ally weak and could not help" and "Domestic - Rivalry".  Why Did Mysore Lose? (contd.). 3. Military Fiscalism, over-extension: revenue-maximisation funded a strong army, but war fines (3 crore rupees after the 3rd war) drained the treasury needed for a long campaign; the EIC was relatively rich. 4. Seringapatam open to siege: once a three-way coalition (EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad) could surround Mysore from many directions, as in 1789-92 and 1799, its geography became a vulnerability, not a stronghold. Verdict: Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 judged Mysore too strong and ambitious for Indirect Rule; it had to be defeated militarily then subordinated; Mysore fought well and modernised seriously; it lost because it fought largely alone. Teacher's ink: a circled "BUT" with a comma above "Military Fiscalism, over-extension"; underline under "war fines (3 crore rupees".   #   Reason   Explanation   Teacher's ink    --- --- --- ---    1   No stable alliance   Mysore's aggressive expansion and the EIC's diplomacy prevented stable alliances   "External ally weak and could not help"; "Domestic - Rivalry" (Indian neighbours were rivals)     2   French naval gap   Mysore depended on French arms and ammunition. France was busy with the American War of Independence (1776-83) and then the Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804), and its navy was no match for Britain's. A French fleet able to resupply Mysore at scale never reached the Indian coast   Underlined     3   Military Fiscalism over-extension   Revenue-maximisation funded a strong army, but war fines (3 crore rupees after the 3rd war) drained the treasury needed for a long campaign; the EIC was relatively rich   Circled "BUT" (the strength became the weakness); underlined 3 crore rupees     4   Seringapatam open to siege   A three-way coalition (EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad) could surround Mysore from many directions, as in 1789-92 and 1799; the capital's geography became a vulnerability, not a stronghold   none   Teacher: The two yellow notes beside reason 1 explain it: an external ally (France) was weak and could not help, and the domestic Indian neighbours were rivals (the "multiple States, motive T, rivalry" logic of the title board). On reason 3 he wrote a circled "BUT": the same Military Fiscalism that made Mysore strong also emptied its treasury: strength and weakness from one source. Verdict: Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 concluded that Mysore was too strong and too ambitious for Indirect Rule to work: it had to be defeated militarily and then subordinated. Mysore fought well and modernised seriously. It lost because it fought largely alone. Mnemonic: Four NOs: no ally, no fleet, no funds, no fortress-safety. Decode: No stable alliance (and weak outside ally, domestic rivals). No French fleet (France busy in the American War 1776-83, then the Revolutionary Wars 1792-1804; Britain's navy stronger). No money (Military Fiscalism over-extended; 3 crore fine; "BUT"). No safe Seringapatam (surrounded by a three-way coalition in 1789-92 and 1799). Why it sticks: say "A, F, M, S" as "A Fort Made Sad"; the verdict, "fought well, fought alone". How the teacher's "Why Indian States lost" skeleton uses this chapter (150 or 250 words): Intro (about 25 words): Indian States lost to the EIC because they were many, not one: each pursued territory, so they were rivals and could not form a stable alliance; the EIC had better leadership and a better army and used diplomacy and war. Body (three branches from the title board): (1) Factionalism: Mysore's expansion made Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore and Carnatic anxious, so the EIC built the triple alliances of 1766-67 and 1790; Hastings 73-85 broke the Triple Confederacy (1780-82) by settling each partner separately (Guntur to Hyderabad, Salbai with the Marathas). (2) War defeats and fear of neighbours: Mysore lost Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal in 1792 and Kanara and Coimbatore in 1799; Hyderabad, fearing neighbours, signed the first SA (1798) and had no choice but to fight Mysore. (3) Internal revolts: Travancore signed the SA in 1805 to crush a Nair mutiny, and the Kundara Proclamation of 1809 followed; demobilised Mysore soldiers fed Dhondia Wagh (1799-1800). Closing: Mysore fought well and modernised, but fought largely alone; by 1809 the EIC was paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari. items.t: 8 · A note on Tipu 82-99's religious policy
items.x: *(No class notes beyond the slides' typed text: slides 47 and 48 carry no ink.)* Tipu 82-99's religious approach was syncretic yet contradictory, often a source of confusion.   Facet   Detail    --- ---    8.1 Patronage in the Mysore heartland   He patronised the Sringeri Sharada Math, wrote letters to its Shankaracharya seeking blessings, got yajnas conducted before wars and made generous grants to several Hindu temples in Mysore     8.2 Coercion in conquered Malabar and Coorg   Forced conversions of Nairs and Christians in Malabar; destroyed churches and temples during his campaigns there. The same brutalities in 1785 in Coorg against the Kodavas (the handout's note: mountain warriors who still do not need a licence for certain arms; earlier under the Hindu Nayakas) who were resisting occupation by Mysore     Geography   North to south: Mysore, Coorg (in the Western Ghats), Malabar. Coorg connected the capital (Seringapatam) to the wealthy coastal ports of Malabar     Conclusion   Secularism was not a value for Tipu 82-99 but a tactic for domestic stability of his Kingdom, since values (as per the discipline of Psychology) are hardest to change in one's personality     Note   The King of Coorg allied with the EIC in 1790 and helped Cornwallis 86-93's army navigate the mountains in the 3rd war (1790-92)   Mnemonic: Heart gets gifts, edges get force; Coorg is the corridor. Decode: Heartland (Mysore): Sringeri Sharada Math, the Shankaracharya's blessings, yajnas before wars, temple grants. Conquered lands: Malabar (Nairs and Christians converted; churches and temples destroyed) and Coorg 1785 (Kodavas). Order north to south: Mysore, Coorg, Malabar; Coorg links capital to coast. The King of Coorg joined the EIC in 1790. Why it sticks: M-C-M from top to bottom, with the middle one as the road between the other two. Mnemonic: Tipu 82-99: two faces, one tactic. Decode: patronage at home (the heartland) and coercion in conquered Malabar and Coorg lead to the handout's conclusion: secularism was a tactic for domestic stability, not a value. A practice statement that calls his policy "uniformly tolerant" is the wrong one. Why it sticks: statements that say "uniformly tolerant" are the wrong ones (FYQ statement 3).

items.t: 9 · The Carnatic annexed (1801)
items.x: Carnatic Annexed (1801) (contd.). 9.1 Carnatic Debts: wealth was quietly extracted before annexation; successive Nawabs borrowed massive sums from private EIC officials at high interest, using the Jagirs of Carnatic as collateral; EIC officials collected land revenue from these fertile lands directly as interest. 9.2 Carnatic Treaty (1801), Wellesley 98-05's justifications: (i) maladministration by the Nawab; (ii) the accusation that the Nawab had been secretly communicating with Tipu 82-99. Wellesley held that a Nawab so financially compromised was not worth preserving even as a puppet. Teacher's ink: the word "Financial" written above "Maladministration"; underlines under "secretly communicating with" and "Tipu 82-99." The EIC had influence over Carnatic indirectly since the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54), keeping its ally Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah 52-95 on the throne. Its grip tightened after establishing domination over South India's trade after the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). Six years after Md Ali 52-95's death in 1795, the EIC annexed Carnatic in 1801. (Wars and treaties: Chapter 9.) 9.1 The Carnatic Debts Even before formal annexation, much of Carnatic's wealth had been quietly extracted through the Carnatic Debts. Successive Nawabs borrowed massive sums from private EIC officials at high interest rates, using the Jagirs of Carnatic as collateral. EIC officials collected land revenue from those fertile lands directly as payment of interest. 9.2 Carnatic Treaty (1801): annexation under Wellesley 98-05 Wellesley 98-05 used two justifications: Maladministration by the Nawab (the teacher inserted "Financial": so, financial maladministration). The accusation that the Nawab had been secretly communicating with Tipu 82-99. Wellesley 98-05 held that a Nawab so financially compromised was not worth preserving even as a puppet. Teacher: Two small ink marks carry the point. He added "Financial" before "Maladministration": the charge was about money (the Carnatic Debts), not law and order. He underlined "secretly communicating with Tipu 82-99": the same Tipu 82-99 who had been the 4th war's target was used as the second excuse. Carnatic was annexed outright: it became direct EIC territory, not an SA State (the contrast with Mysore, Hyderabad and Travancore). Mnemonic: Loan, Collateral, Interest: how the Carnatic Debts worked. Money and Mole: the two charges. Decode: Loan from private EIC officials at high interest → Jagirs as collateral → the officials collect the land revenue as interest. Charges in 1801: financial maladministration ("Money") and secret contact with Tipu 82-99 ("Mole"). Md Ali 52-95 died 1795; 95 + 6 = 01. Why it sticks: L-C-I are three steps of a trap; Money and Mole are the two accusations.

items.t: 10 · Travancore: what happens when the SA breaks its own promises?
items.x: *(No class ink on slides 51, 52 or 53: handout and typed slides only.)* 10.1 Travancore before the SA Travancore's modern State was built in the 18th century by Marthanda Varma 29-58, who decisively defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel (1741) and reorganised the kingdom into a centralised revenue-based State. His successor Rama Varma 58-98 maintained the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore, relevant during Tipu 82-99's late-1780s expansion and embargo on Travancore's pepper exports (section 1). Rama Varma 58-98's EIC alliance was the trigger for Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789, which Cornwallis 86-93 used as the pretext for the 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (section 4). After Rama Varma 58-98's death in 1798, the kingdom entered fiscal and political strain. 10.2 British Resident stationed (1800), Subsidiary Alliance signed (1805) Travancore signed a "Treaty of Perpetual Friendship" with the EIC in 1795 (in Rama Varma 58-98's reign): they agreed to pay for a British force to protect against Tipu 82-99. In 1800 a British Resident was stationed in Travancore's court (the handout's note: can you see the imprint of ToA 1765, Chapter 10?). In 1805 Travancore signed a proper Subsidiary Alliance with Wellesley 98-05. The EIC extracted it in exchange for helping the king crush a revolt by his own Nair troops, who had mutinied over non-payment of salary. The State lost sovereignty on the standard SA template (see the SA terms in Chapter 11). Takeaway: Travancore is the chapter's clearest worked example of how the SA gets extracted: not at sword-point, but in exchange for internal-security help that the EIC Resident has often had a hand in destabilising in the first place. The Nair troops' salary mutiny gave the king an immediate problem; Wellesley 98-05 priced the help at full sovereign concession. Within four years the consequences exploded in the Velu Thampi Dalawa revolt and the Kundara Proclamation (1809). Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 cover the same State from other angles. Chapter 7 gives Marthanda Varma 29-58's trade monopoly and the Colachel victory and tells the Malabar 1766 story; Chapter 11 lists Travancore as the 8th SA signatory (1805), the last under Wellesley 98-05 before his recall. This chapter adds the 1795 Treaty, the 1800 Resident, the mechanism of extraction and the 1809 revolt (Chapter 7, Chapter 11). Mnemonic: Travancore's ladder: 95 Friend, 00 Watcher, 05 Master, 09 Rebel. Decode: 1795 Treaty of Perpetual Friendship (pay for a British force against Tipu 82-99); 1800 a British Resident in the court (the imprint of ToA 1765); 1805 the proper SA, in exchange for crushing the Nair mutiny; 1809 Kundara. Before it: Marthanda Varma 29-58 (Colachel 1741), Rama Varma 58-98 (died 1798); the 1789 attack. Why it sticks: steps of five (95, 00, 05), then a jump of four to 09. Mnemonic: Pay the army, pay the price. Decode: the Nair troops mutinied over unpaid salary; the EIC helped crush them; the king paid with sovereignty under the standard SA template: the SA was extracted not at sword-point but for internal-security help. Why it sticks: the king could not pay his soldiers, so he paid the EIC more. Mnemonic: Marthanda 29-58 builds, Rama 58-98 hedges. Decode: Marthanda Varma 29-58 built the centralised revenue-based State and beat the Dutch at Colachel (1741); Rama Varma 58-98 kept the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore, which triggered Tipu 82-99's 1789 attack. The baton passes at 58. Why it sticks: the code numbers join: 58 ends one and begins the other.

items.t: 11 · Velu Thampi Dalawa and the Kundara Proclamation (1809)
items.x: *(No class ink on slide 54.)* By 1809 the SA's consequences were unbearable. Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister of Travancore (1802-09), led a major armed revolt against the EIC, supported by soldiers and peasants angered by heavy subsidy demands and constant British interference in internal affairs, a direct breach of the SA treaty's own promise of non-interference. In January 1809, from the town of Kundara, he issued the Kundara Proclamation (1809): a public call to all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy. The revolt was crushed within months. Velu Thampi died later the same year. Travancore was reduced to a subservient SA State. (The handout's note: every consequence of the SA from Chapter 11 (loss of military jobs, high taxes from subsidy pressure, PoIR creeping in illegally) played out here within four years of signing.) The Kundara Proclamation (January 1809) is one of the most significant early revolts against the British in South India. Use that wording. (The handout's flow chart in section 12 says "first organised revolt in south India"; the text and slide 54 say "one of the most significant early revolts": the safer claim in an answer.) Mnemonic: Dalawa 02-09, Kundara January 09. Decode: Velu Thampi Dalawa was PM 1802-09, rose against subsidy demands and interference (a breach of the SA's own promise of non-interference), issued the Kundara Proclamation in January 1809 from Kundara; crushed within months; he died that year. Why it sticks: his tenure ends the same year he rebels, 09.
