The two underlines are the two commercial reasons; the Malabar coast point is the third.  Handout map for Chapter 13: the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwa (Poona). Labelled areas: RAJPUTANA, SIND, MALWA, Gaikwar (Baroda), Holkar (Indore), Sindhia (Gwalior), Bhonsle (Nagpur, at the right edge), KHANDESH, BERAR, Nizam's Dominions (Hyderabad), the Peshwa's territory around Poona and Bombay, and the Arabian Sea. Crosses mark the 1803 battles at Assaye, Argaon and Gawilgarh. Small years are printed along the chiefs' names. The small years on the map (for example 1802 along the Peshwa's territory, 1804 along Sindhia, 1805 along Gaikwar, 1803 near Agra and Surat) are not explained in the handout text. The Gaikwar "1805" does not match the text, which says the Gaikwad signed in June 1802 (Treaty of Cambay). Use the map for where things are, and the text for the years. Mnemonic: C-C-M: coast, cotton, Malabar. Decode: the Deccan mattered for its large coastline, the Gujarat-China cotton trade, and Maratha control over parts of the Malabar coast. The Marathas and Mysore were the last two powers to check the EIC: 3 + 4 = 7 wars (three Maratha, four Mysore). Why it sticks: "CCM" is one seaside shop; seven wars is a week.

items.t: 2 · First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82)
items.x: 2.1 What triggered the war?  1st War, Trigger (1775). Root cause: factionalism within the Maratha Confederacy, a pattern that repeats across all 3 wars. 1773: Raghunath Rao 73-74 became Peshwa after the murder of his nephew Narayan Rao 72-73. Baarbhai Conspiracy 1774: Nana Fadnis and 11 other ministers of the Peshwa's council removed Raghunath Rao 73-74. Treaty of Surat (1775): Raghunath Rao 73-74 approached the EIC Bombay Governor William Hornby and signed it; the EIC would help him regain the Peshwaship in return for Salsette and Bassein (Vasai, near Mumbai) plus some revenue from Bharuch and Surat. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under Factionalism, the Peshwa names and years, Baarbhai Conspiracy 1774, William Hornby, "EIC to help him", "in return for", Salsette and Bassein, and the Bharuch and Surat revenue. The cause was factionalism within the Maratha Confederacy itself, a pattern that repeats across all three wars. In 1773 Raghunath Rao 73-74 became Peshwa after the murder of his nephew Narayan Rao 72-73. In the Baarbhai Conspiracy (1774), Nana Fadnis and eleven other ministers of the Peshwa's council removed Raghunath Rao 73-74 from power. Raghunath Rao 73-74 then approached the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby, and signed the Treaty of Surat (1775). Under it the EIC agreed to help him regain the Peshwaship in return for Salsette and Bassein (Vasai, near Mumbai) along with some revenue from Bharuch and Surat. Teacher: Everything is underlined: factionalism (the root cause), the names and years of the Peshwas, the Baarbhai Conspiracy 1774, the Governor of Bombay (William Hornby), and the deal itself: "EIC to help him" in return for "Salsette and Bassein" and revenue. The deal is the thing to learn: help for land and money. The pattern, in the handout's words: this is exactly what happened in the Carnatic and Hyderabad during the Carnatic Wars: a succession dispute, a losing claimant, and the Europeans offering military help in exchange for territory and influence. Factionalism of Indian States was the Europeans' most reliable ally. See Chapter 9. 1773: Narayan Rao 72-73 is murdered; Raghunath Rao 73-74 becomes Peshwa (warn) 1774, Baarbhai Conspiracy: Nana Fadnis + 11 ministers remove Raghunath Rao 73-74 Raghunath Rao 73-74 goes to the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby (bad) 1775, Treaty of Surat: EIC help for him in return for Salsette, Bassein and revenue from Bharuch, Surat (bad) 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) begins Mnemonic: Murder, Mutiny, Mortgage: 1773, 1774, 1775. Decode: 1773 Narayan Rao 72-73 murdered, Raghunath Rao 73-74 becomes Peshwa; 1774 the Baarbhai Conspiracy (Nana Fadnis + eleven ministers = twelve, a dozen) removes him; 1775 he mortgages Salsette, Bassein and revenue to the EIC (Treaty of Surat). Why it sticks: three years, three steps, and the "12" in Baarbhai (Nana plus eleven) is one dozen. Mnemonic: Surat pays in land and money: SB for land, BS for money. Decode: Treaty of Surat 1775 = Salsette and Bassein (land) + Bharuch and Surat (revenue). Salsette and Bassein are the "S-B" pair; the revenue towns are the "B-S" pair, flipped. Why it sticks: the second pair is the first pair reversed. 2.2 Warren Hastings 73-85 overturns Surat: the Treaty of Purandhar (1776)  Treaty of Purandhar (1776), negotiated by Warren Hastings 73-85 with Nana Fadnis. 1. The EIC would recognise Madhav Rao II 74-95 as the legitimate Peshwa and Raghunath Rao 73-74 would be pensioned off. 2. The EIC would receive Salsette and Bharuch. 3. Marathas would not allow any French presence in their domain. Teacher's ink: a bracketed note beside the title "[1665: To PURANDHAR]"; top right "GBF 1770 -> 1772 -> Loan by BANKRUPTCY" with a circled word that cannot be read; yellow underlines under "recognise Madhav Rao II 74-95", "Raghunath", "pensioned off", "Salsette & Bharuch" and "French presence". Warren Hastings 73-85, the Governor General in Calcutta, overturned the Treaty of Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure. He negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) with Nana Fadnis:   Clause   Term    --- ---    1   The EIC would recognise Madhav Rao II 74-95 as the legitimate Peshwa, and Raghunath Rao 73-74 would be pensioned off     2   The EIC would receive Salsette and Bharuch     3   The Marathas would not allow any French presence in their domain   Teacher: On the Purandhar slide he wrote "[1665: To PURANDHAR]" (do not confuse the two Purandhars: the first was in 1665, the chapter on the rise of the Marathas, see Chapter 4). At the top right he wrote "GBF 1770 -> 1772 -> Loan by BANKRUPTCY" with a circled word that is [unclear: check your notebook]. Read it with Chapter 10: the Great Bengal Famine 1770 led to the EIC's bankruptcy in 1772, which is the money trouble behind Warren Hastings 73-85's wish to avoid war expenditure. The handout adds: this fits the Policy of Relative Isolation discussed in a later chapter. Mnemonic: Purandhar 1776, three P-S-F clauses: Peshwa, Salsette, French. Decode: Peshwa (Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised, Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned off), Salsette and Bharuch to the EIC, French kept out. Negotiated by Warren Hastings 73-85 with Nana Fadnis. Why it sticks: "PSF" like a bank deposit scheme; Hastings pays off the old claimant. Mnemonic: Two Purandhars: 1665 and 1776. Decode: the teacher's bracket warns of two treaties at one fort: 1665 (Chapter 4) and 1776 (this chapter, Warren Hastings 73-85 with Nana Fadnis). Both years contain a 6. Why it sticks: 16-65 and 17-76, the 6 sits in both, so "6 means Purandhar".  Treaty of Purandhar, Aftermath. Warren Hastings 73-85 (GG, Calcutta) overturned the Treaty of Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure, then negotiated Purandhar. But Bombay kept sheltering Raghunath Rao 73-74; Nana Fadnis retaliated by offering a port to the French, talks collapsed and war resumed. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Bombay kept sheltering Raghunath Rao 73-74", "Fadnis", "port to the French" and "talks collapsed & war resumed"; in white: "eg of FACTIONALISM within EIC" with "eg" and "EIC" circled. However, the EIC in Bombay continued sheltering Raghunath Rao 73-74. Nana Fadnis retaliated by offering a port to the French. Talks collapsed and war resumed. Teacher: The teacher's white note: "eg of FACTIONALISM within EIC" (both "eg" and "EIC" circled). So the Bombay EIC and the Calcutta EIC (Warren Hastings 73-85) were pulling in two directions. Factionalism was not only a Maratha disease. Mnemonic: Calcutta signs, Bombay hides, Poona flirts with France. Decode: Warren Hastings 73-85 (Calcutta) signs Purandhar; Bombay keeps sheltering Raghunath Rao 73-74 (factionalism within the EIC); Nana Fadnis (Poona) offers a port to the French; war resumes. Why it sticks: three cities, three moves, and each one breaks the treaty. 2.3 Events and the Treaty of Salbai (1782)  1st War, Events. Battle of Wadgaon 1779, near Pune: Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. Stalemate by 1782: the war continued inconclusively; the EIC was in difficulty but so were the Marathas, also engaged in the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Battle of Wadgaon 1779", "defeated" and "the EIC & Raghunath Rao 73-74". In 1779, at the Battle of Wadgaon (near Pune), Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. But the war continued inconclusively. By 1782 the EIC was in a difficult position, but so were the Marathas, who were also engaged in the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Mnemonic: Wadgaon 79: N-M-T won. Decode: Battle of Wadgaon (1779), near Pune: Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar beat the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. The war then stalled until 1782 while the Marathas were also busy with the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Why it sticks: N-M-T is "NMT", a three-man team; 79 then 82, three years of stalemate.  Treaty of Salbai (1782), negotiated and signed at Gwalior by Mahadji Scindhia for the Marathas. 1. Military alliance between the EIC and the Marathas: the Marathas broke their anti-British alliance (the Triple Confederacy) and agreed to fight on the side of the EIC if Hyder Ali 61-82 did not restore the territories he had taken from the British and the Nawab of Arcot (PoRF established by the EIC with the Marathas). 2. EIC got Salsette and Bharuch. 3. No French settlements in Maratha domain. 4. The EIC returned all Maratha territory it had captured, recognised Madhav Rao II 74-95 as Peshwa and pensioned off Raghunath Rao 73-74. Teacher's ink: "alliance WITH neighbours" beside clause 1; a boxed "TRIPLE CONFEDERACY (alliance of Ma, My, HYD) 1780-82" with lines down to "1st A-Ma 1775-82" and "2nd A-My 1780-84"; yellow underlines under the title, "Military alliance", "agreed to fight on the side of the EIC", "Salsette & Bharuch", "No French settlements", "recognised Madhav Rao II 74-95" and "pensioned off Raghunath Rao 73-74". The Treaty of Salbai (1782) was negotiated and signed at Gwalior by Mahadji Scindhia on behalf of the Marathas. It ended the war. Its terms:   Clause   Term    --- ---    1   Military alliance between the EIC and the Marathas. The Marathas broke their anti-British alliance (the Triple Confederacy) and agreed to fight on the side of the EIC if Hyder Ali 61-82 did not restore the territories he had taken from the British and the Nawab of Arcot. (The handout: PoRF established by the EIC with the Marathas.)     2   The EIC got Salsette and Bharuch     3   No French settlements in Maratha domain     4   The EIC returned all Maratha territory it had captured, recognised Madhav Rao II 74-95 as Peshwa and pensioned off Raghunath Rao 73-74   Teacher: Beside clause 1 the teacher wrote "alliance WITH neighbours": that is the meaning of the Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) (a buffer of allied neighbours around the EIC, see Chapter 10). His box explains the Triple Confederacy: an alliance of Marathas (Ma), Mysore (My) and Hyderabad (HYD), 1780-82. From it two lines run down: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). He underlined military alliance, salsette and Bharuch, no French settlements, Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised and Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned off. Why pension a rival? The handout: giving pensions was deliberate EIC diplomatic practice; this way the EIC could use this person in future succession disputes. The same device returns in 1818 with Bajirao II 96-18 at Bithur (Section 7). Mnemonic: Salbai = A-S-F-R: Alliance, Salsette, French, Return. Decode: Salbai 1782, signed at Gwalior by Mahadji Scindhia: Alliance (Marathas fight for the EIC against Hyder Ali 61-82 if he keeps the territories), Salsette and Bharuch to the EIC, French excluded, Return of all Maratha territory (plus Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised, Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned). Why it sticks: "ASFR" sounds like "as fair": the Marathas got their land back and the EIC got an ally. Mnemonic: Triple Confederacy: M-M-H, 1780-82. Decode: Marathas + Mysore + Hyderabad, an anti-British alliance of 1780-82. It gave two wars: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Salbai broke the confederacy by buying the Marathas out. Why it sticks: M-M-H is a humming sound: three voices, then Salbai silences one.  Handout flow chart of the Maratha chain of events, from 1773 to 1819: 1773 Narayan Rao 72-73 murdered, Raghunath Rao 73-74 usurps the Peshwaship; 1774 Baarbhai Conspiracy, Nana Fadnis and eleven ministers depose Raghunath Rao; 1775 Raghunath Rao signs the Treaty of Surat with the EIC at Bombay, the 1st Anglo-Maratha War; 1782 Treaty of Salbai via Mahadji Scindhia, Raghunath Rao pensioned (bloodline kept alive, a pattern); 1795 Madhav Rao II 74-95 suicide, Bajirao II 96-18 becomes Peshwa, Nana Fadnis dies 1800 (glue gone); 1802 Yashwantrao Holkar defeats the Peshwa and Scindhia, Bajirao II flees, Treaty of Bassein (SA) leads to the 2nd War; 1817 Bajirao II, Bhonsle and Holkar unite under Francis Hastings 13-23's pressure, the 3rd War; 1819 Peshwa pensioned to Bithur, adopted son Nana Sahib leads to the Kanpur revolt 1857 (the bloodline tactic backfires). The handout figure above is a one-page summary of the whole story; it dates the Peshwa's pension to 1819 and Bajirao 20-40's surrender in the text to June 1818 (Section 6). Both belong to the same settlement (the text's 3rd war is 1817-19).

items.t: 3 · The inter-war period (1782-1803)
items.x: Inter-War Period (1782-1803): a period of Maratha decline, not strength. 21-year gap between the Treaty of Salbai 1782 and the Treaty of Bassein 1802. Mahadji Scindhia dominated Maratha politics until his death in 1794. Madhav Rao II 74-95 committed suicide in 1795. Bajirao II 96-18 became Peshwa in 1796 (formally tenured 1796-1818). Nana Fadnis died 1800: the one man who held the Confederacy together for 2 decades; his death accelerated factionalism, an opportunity for Wellesley 98-05. No ink. The 21-year gap between the Treaty of Salbai (1782) and the Treaty of Bassein (1802) was not a period of Maratha strength: it was a period of Maratha decline.   Year   What happened    --- ---    1794   Mahadji Scindhia, who had dominated Maratha politics, dies     1795   Madhav Rao II 74-95 commits suicide     1796   Bajirao II 96-18 becomes Peshwa (the handout: Peshwa from 1796, formally tenured 1796-1818)     1800   Nana Fadnis dies: the one man who had consistently held the Confederacy together for two decades; factionalism accelerates sharply   The Maratha capital, Shaniwar Wada at Pune, and the whole Confederacy were engulfed in factionalism. The empire-builder Wellesley 98-05 was waiting for exactly this opportunity. Mnemonic: 94 dies, 95 suicides, 96 crowned, 1800 the glue goes. Decode: 1794 Mahadji Scindhia dies; 1795 Madhav Rao II 74-95 commits suicide; 1796 Bajirao II 96-18 becomes Peshwa; 1800 Nana Fadnis dies, the Confederacy's glue. The gap from Salbai (1782) to Bassein (1802) is 21 years. Why it sticks: four consecutive-ish years, four verbs: dies, suicides, crowned, gone; and 82 plus 21 is 1803, one year after Bassein.

items.t: 4 · Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05): Wellesley 98-05's war
items.x: 4.1 The trigger: Bassein (December 1802)  2nd War, Trigger: Bassein (Dec 1802). 1801: Vithoji Rao Holkar plundered Peshwa territory; captured and brutally executed on the orders of Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. Oct 1802: to avenge his stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar attacked and defeated both the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia (who backed the Peshwa). Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802): Bajirao II 96-18 fled and signed it, a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC for help to regain the Peshwaship; the Army of Svarajya was to be disbanded once the EIC restored its now-puppet Peshwa; it also triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Treaty of Cambay (June 1802): Gaikwad had already signed an SA to get EIC help in a succession dispute. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Yashwantrao Holkar attacked & defeated", "Peshwa", "Scindhia", "Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802)", "Bajirao II 96-18 fled", "Subsidiary Alliance", "2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05)" and "Gaikwad". In 1801 Vithoji Rao Holkar had been plundering the Peshwa's territories. He was captured and brutally executed on the orders of Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. To avenge the death of his stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar attacked and defeated both the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia (who had supported the Peshwa) in October 1802. Bajirao II 96-18 fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802): he agreed to a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC in exchange for EIC help to regain the Peshwaship. The great army of Svarajya was to be disbanded once the EIC put its now-puppet Bajirao II 96-18 back as Peshwa. The Treaty of Bassein also triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Ironically, it made Scindhia, Holkar and Bhonsle, who had been rivals, unite against the EIC. The Gaikwad had already signed an SA in June 1802 (Treaty of Cambay) to get EIC help in a succession dispute. Teacher: He underlined Yashwantrao Holkar attacked and defeated, Peshwa, Scindhia, Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802), Bajirao II 96-18 fled, Subsidiary Alliance, 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) and Gaikwad. The sequence of the SAs matters for the exam (slide 72, section 4.3): Gaikwad (June 1802) came before the Peshwa (December 1802). Mnemonic: V-Y-B: Vithoji's Vengeance Brings Bassein. Decode: Vithoji Rao Holkar executed on the Peshwa's orders (1801) -> Yashwantrao Holkar defeats the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia (October 1802) -> Bajirao II 96-18 flees and signs Bassein (December 1802): SA, army of Svarajya to be disbanded. Why it sticks: Vengeance chain: a stepbrother's blood leads to a Peshwa's flight. Mnemonic: Cambay before Bassein: June, then December. Decode: the Gaikwad signed the Treaty of Cambay (June 1802) for EIC help in a succession dispute; the Peshwa signed Bassein (December 1802). The Gaikwad is the first signatory of the 1802 pair. Why it sticks: June comes before December, and Cambay (a small place) signs before Bassein. 4.2 The battlefield: Assaye (1803)  2nd War, Battle of Assaye (1803). The EIC deployed significant military force. Arthur WELLESLEYPROT, commanding his Royal regiment alongside the EIC army, fought key engagements, including the Battle of Assaye (1803) against the Marathas, which he later described as the toughest fight of his entire military career, harder, in his view, than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Assaye" (title), "Arthur WELLESLEYPROT", "Royal regiment" and "alongside the EIC army". The EIC deployed significant military force. Arthur Wellesley, commanding his Royal regiment alongside the EIC army, fought key engagements, including the Battle of Assaye (1803) against the Marathas. He later described it as the toughest fight of his entire military career, harder, in his view, than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe. Teacher: He underlined Assaye, Arthur Wellesley, Royal regiment and alongside the EIC army. Note the two forces again: the Royal regiment (the King's army) fought alongside the EIC army (the Company's army), as at Plassey in Chapter 10. Arthur Wellesley is not the Governor General: the Governor General is Wellesley 98-05. (See Chapter 11 on the three Wellesley 98-05 brothers.) Mnemonic: Assaye 1803: Arthur's "toughest", tougher than Napoleon. Decode: Assaye (1803): Arthur Wellesley's Royal regiment fought with the EIC army against the Marathas. His own verdict: the toughest fight of his career, harder than anything against Napoleon. Arthur is the soldier; Wellesley 98-05 is the Governor General. Why it sticks: "Arthur at Assaye" starts with A twice; the brother with the code (98-05) sits in Calcutta. 4.3 Consequences  2nd War, Consequences 1 to 3. The war was lost by the Marathas. 1. Bajirao II 96-18 regained the Peshwaship but now a puppet of the EIC. 2. Scindhia lost all territory north of the River Yamuna including Delhi and Agra and all his territory in Gujarat, and was forced to sign an SA; a British Resident in Delhi established the Policy of Indirect Rule, so the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 was now effectively under EIC indirect control. 3. Bhonsle of Nagpur lost Orissa but refused the full SA; forced into a mini-alliance (like the ToA with Awadh), ceding territory and accepting an EIC army paid for by Bhonsle. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Bajirao II 96-18 regained", "Peshwaship", "Scindhia lost", "Gujarat", "SA", "British Resident in Delhi", "Policy of Indirect Rule", "Shah Alam II 60-06", "Bhonsle of Nagpur" (with a small tick above "Nagpur"), "Orissa", "ceding territory", "accepting an EIC" and "army paid for by Bhonsle". The war was lost by the Marathas. The consequences were far-reaching: Bajirao II 96-18 regained the Peshwaship but was now a puppet of the EIC. Scindhia lost all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi and Agra, and all his territory in Gujarat. He was forced to sign a Subsidiary Alliance. In Delhi a British Resident was stationed, who established the Policy of Indirect Rule: the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 was now effectively under the EIC's indirect control. Bhonsle of Nagpur lost Orissa but stubbornly refused to accept the Subsidiary Alliance. He was forced to sign a mini alliance (similar in structure to the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 with Awadh): he ceded territory and accepted an EIC army to be paid for by Bhonsle, but not yet the full Subsidiary Alliance. Recall (the handout's bracket): Bhonsle had raided the Bengal Suba from 1745-51 and had extracted the Chauth of Bengal and Bihar and control of Orissa from Alivardi Khan 40-56. So Orissa now returns to the EIC, the inheritor of Bengal (Chapter 10). The handout prints the Awadh treaty year as "17765"; it is 1765. The Emperor's masters, in order (handout bracket): the Emperor was earlier a puppet of Zulfikar Khan, then the Sayyid Brothers, then the Irani and Turani group, then Safdar Jung 39-54, then the Marathas, and now the EIC. See Chapter 2. Mnemonic: Six masters of the Emperor: Z-S-I-S-M-E. Decode: Zulfikar Khan, Sayyid Brothers, Irani and Turani group, Safdar Jung 39-54, Marathas, EIC. The sixth master after 1803 is the EIC, through the Resident in Delhi (Policy of Indirect Rule) and Shah Alam II 60-06. Why it sticks: "ZSISME" reads as "Zis is me": each new master says "this is me" and takes the Emperor.  2nd War, Consequences (contd.). 4. Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas, who had previously paid Chauth and Sardeshmukhi tributes to the Marathas, were now forced to sign an SA with the EIC, as the EIC replaced the Marathas as the dominant regional power of north and central India. 5. Wellesley 98-05 was recalled to London over the high war expenditure in his tenure; Cornwallis 86-93 was despatched with clear orders to follow a policy of non-interference (arrived July 1805 and died October 1805). Non-Intervention: after Wellesley 98-05 the EIC followed a Policy of Non-Intervention to prevent war expenditure, giving Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild strength and confidence. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Jats, Rajputs & Bundelas", "Wellesley 98-05 was recalled", "high war expenditure", "Cornwallis 86-93 was despatched", "policy of non-interference", the July-October note, "prevent war expenditure" and "Bhonsle & Holkar time to rebuild strength & confidence"; two small ticks near "followed" and "Bhonsle". In white on the right: a bracket "SA" with arrows to "1802: Gaikwad", "1802: Peshwa", "1803/04: Sandhia". The Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas, who had earlier paid Chauth and Sardeshmukhi tributes to the Marathas, were now forced to sign an SA with the EIC, as the EIC replaced the Marathas as the dominant regional power of north and central India. Wellesley 98-05 was recalled to London because of the high war expenditure in his tenure. Cornwallis 86-93 was despatched with clear orders to follow a policy of non-interference (he arrived in July 1805 and died in October 1805). Teacher: His white list shows the order in which the Subsidiary Alliances were signed: 1802: Gaikwad, 1802: Peshwa, 1803/04: Scindhia. (The 1816 tick on the overview board adds Bhonsle and 1818 adds Holkar, see Section 7.) He underlined "high war expenditure" and "policy of non-interference" and ticked Bhonsle and followed in the last row: the Policy of Non-Intervention was meant to prevent war expenditure, but it gave Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild their military strength and confidence. Cornwallis 86-93: the handout and slide use the teacher's code 86-93 for the name Cornwallis 86-93, even though the 1805 visit is a later and very short one (July to October 1805, ending in his death). The code belongs to the man, not to the 1805 episode; it is kept as written. Mnemonic: GPS-BH: the order of the Subsidiary Alliances. Decode: Gaikwad (June 1802, Cambay), Peshwa (Dec 1802, Bassein), Scindhia (1803/04), then Bhonsle (1816, Treaty of Nagpur; a mini alliance after the 2nd war) and Holkar (1818, Treaty of Mandsaur). Why it sticks: like a GPS giving directions: five turns, in order, one per Maratha power. Mnemonic: P-S-B-J-W: the five results of the 2nd war. Decode: Peshwa puppet; Scindhia loses all north of the Yamuna (Delhi, Agra, Gujarat) and signs SA; Bhonsle loses Orissa and accepts a mini alliance; Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas sign SA; Wellesley 98-05 recalled (high war expenditure), Cornwallis 86-93 sent for non-interference. Why it sticks: "PSBJW" = "Please Send Back Just Wellesley 98-05": the story ends with Wellesley 98-05 recalled. 4.4 The Vellore Mutiny (1806)  Vellore Mutiny (1806), under George Barlow (Acting GG, 1805-07). Cause: new dress codes forbade sepoys from wearing religious marks (tilaks and turbans) and mandated leather cockades (ribbons shaped like a Christian cross on the hat, made of cow or pig skin). Result: an uprising in the Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu), often called the "Prelude to 1857". Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "New dress codes", "leather cockades", "made of cow / pig skin" and "Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu)". The handout's bracketed note on the Vellore Mutiny (1806), during George Barlow (Acting GG, 1805-07). Cause: new dress codes forbade sepoys from wearing religious marks (tilaks and turbans) and mandated leather cockades (ribbons shaped like a Christian cross on the hat, made of cow or pig skin). Result: an uprising in the Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu). It is often called the "Prelude to 1857." Teacher: He underlined new dress codes, leather cockades, "made of cow / pig skin" and Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu). These are the four exam handles: dress, cockade, cow or pig, Vellore. Mnemonic: Vellore 1806: Barlow's bad dress code. Decode: under George Barlow (Acting GG, 1805-07): no tilak, no turban; a leather cockade (cross-shaped, cow or pig skin) instead; sepoys rise in Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu) in 1806: the "Prelude to 1857". Why it sticks: the fort, the cockade and the cow; and 1806 comes before 1857.

items.t: 5 · The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 and the Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)
items.x: Pindaris and Policy of Paramountcy. Pindaris: disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar; raided EIC territory in the Northern Sarkars and parts of the Madras Presidency. PoP (1813-58): GG Francis Hastings 13-23 defeated them and re-initiated imperial expansion via the Policy of Paramountcy; the EIC to be the paramount or supreme power in India, doing anything, even annexation, to protect its interests. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Disbanded soldiers of Scindhia & Holkar" and "raided EIC territory". After Wellesley 98-05 the EIC followed a Policy of Non-Intervention to prevent war expenditure. This gave Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild their military strength and confidence. Meanwhile the Pindaris, disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar, began raiding EIC territory in the Northern Sarkars and parts of the Madras Presidency. They were defeated by the next empire-builder, Governor General Francis Hastings 13-23, whose Policy of Paramountcy (PoP, 1813-58) re-initiated imperial expansion. Under PoP the EIC was to be the paramount or supreme power in India and it would do anything, even annexation, if needed to protect its interests. Teacher: He underlined "disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar" and "raided EIC territory" (the who and the what of the Pindaris). Two Hastings appear in this chapter: Warren Hastings 73-85 (1st war, Surat to Purandhar to Salbai) and Francis Hastings 13-23 (3rd war, Pindaris, Paramountcy). Do not mix them up. The Hastings trap. A question that says only "Lord Hastings" or "Hastings" can mean either. Fix it by the war: 1775-82 = Warren Hastings 73-85; 1817-19 = Francis Hastings 13-23. The codes are the quickest tell: 73-85 against 13-23. Mnemonic: Warren = the first War, Francis = the Final one. Decode: Warren Hastings 73-85 handled the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (Purandhar 1776, Salbai 1782); Francis Hastings 13-23 handled the 3rd (Pindaris, Paramountcy 1813-58, the Peshwaship abolished). Why it sticks: W for Warren and War, F for Francis and Final. Mnemonic: Pindaris = sacked soldiers raiding the Sarkars. Decode: disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar, raiders of the Northern Sarkars and parts of Madras Presidency; crushed by Francis Hastings 13-23, who then ran the Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58). Why it sticks: "pink slips" turned into pirates on land. Mnemonic: Paramountcy runs 13 to 58, like the Company State. Decode: PoP starts 1813 (Francis Hastings 13-23) and runs to 1858. The aim: the EIC supreme; do anything, even annex, to protect its interests. Why it sticks: 13 is the start year and also the first two digits of the code 13-23; 58 matches the end of Company rule (Chapter 10's "Company 65, Crown 58").  Treaty of Nagpur (1816), Appa Sahib. Appa Sahib signed an SA for help in a succession dispute (who will be regent). Loophole: the treaty required disbanding the official state army but rulers could keep retainers and police for internal security; Appa Sahib exploited this by secretly recruiting fierce Arab and Rohilla mercenaries. PoP (teacher's white ink "1813-58"): the British Resident began treating Appa Sahib as a puppet. PoP: the British Resident began treating Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "signed SA", "succession dispute @ who will be regent", "secretly recruiting fierce", "Arab & Rohilla mercenaries", "British Resident", "Appa Sahib" and "as a puppet" (both rows), and "Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet". The British Resident began treating Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet, in a way that left him with no real authority. In Nagpur, Appa Sahib signed an SA under the Treaty of Nagpur (1816) for EIC help in a factionalism dispute over who would be regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur (Maharaja Parsoji Bhonsle suffered from paralysis and was unable to rule). The treaty required disbanding the official state army, but rulers were allowed to keep retainers and police for internal security. Appa Sahib exploited this loophole by secretly recruiting fierce Arab and Rohilla mercenaries. Once his power was secure, and having Parsoji secretly murdered to become the actual Maharaja, Appa Sahib now wanted to rule independently and not as a puppet of the British Resident. Teacher: Beside the Nagpur slide he wrote "1813-58" next to PoP (slide 75). On the overview board he wrote that the 3rd war's reason was "PoIR as part of PoP": the Policy of Indirect Rule (Residents controlling puppets) now ran inside the Policy of Paramountcy. Teacher: He underlined "signed SA", the succession dispute over the regent, "secretly recruiting fierce Arab and Rohilla mercenaries" and, in the PoP rows, "British Resident" and "as a puppet" (for both Appa Sahib and Bajirao II 96-18). This is the same pattern as Surat 1775 and Bassein 1802: a succession or power dispute, the ruler asks the EIC for help, the EIC takes control. The loophole is the SA template's weak point and the reason the 3rd war broke out. Mnemonic: Nagpur 1816: R-A-R, retainers allowed, Arabs and Rohillas recruited. Decode: Treaty of Nagpur (1816): Appa Sahib signs SA for help over who will be regent; state army to be disbanded, but retainers and police allowed; he secretly hires Arab and Rohilla mercenaries; murders Parsoji; wants to rule independently. Why it sticks: "RAR" is a roar: the loophole that roars back in 1817. Mnemonic: Same script, third time: Surat, Bassein, Nagpur. Decode: Raghunath Rao 73-74 (1775, Surat), Bajirao II 96-18 (1802, Bassein), Appa Sahib (1816, Nagpur): each rulers' succession or power dispute made him ask the EIC for help, and each time the EIC gained a foothold. Why it sticks: three actors, one script: "Help me, EIC!"

items.t: 6 · Third Anglo-Maratha War and the Pindari War (1817-19)
items.x: 6.1 The Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817)  3rd War, Sitabuldi (Nov 1817). Revolt: late 1817, Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib and Yashwantrao Holkar united against the EIC; this led to the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19). Bajirao II 96-18 and Appa Sahib fought with men they personally recruited outside EIC supervision. Battle of Sitabuldi (hills): Appa Sahib acted as Senapati (Commander-in-Chief); was defeated. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Bajirao II 96-18", "Appa Sahib", "Holkar", "vs EIC", "personally recruited", "Battle of Sitabuldi" and "was defeated". In late 1817 Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib (regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur) and Yashwantrao Holkar united in revolt, determined to end the EIC's political domination. (The handout's bracket: this is a violation of SA treaties.) This led to the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19). Bajirao II 96-18 had signed a Subsidiary Alliance under which the EIC army had replaced the Svarajya's own army, so technically he had no State army. He fought with men he personally recruited outside the EIC's supervision. Appa Sahib acted as Senapati (Commander-in-Chief). He used his Arab mercenaries to launch a surprise, close-quarters attack directly on the British Residency and the adjacent Sitabuldi hills. Despite heavily outnumbering the garrison, his forces were defeated at the Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817). The handout's tested-in-Prelims note on Sitabuldi: (i) Appa Sahib signed the SA in 1816 but fought the British in 1817: the SA did not prevent the war, its terms caused it. (ii) The "disbanded army" requirement was bypassed through Arab and Rohilla mercenaries hired as "internal security retainers": the SA template's loophole exposed. Naming slip to watch. The handout and the typed slide (76) name "Yashwantrao Holkar" among the rebels of 1817, while the teacher's board (61) and the later battle slides (77, 79) write only "Holkar". Learn "Holkar of Indore" for the 3rd war and "Yashwantrao Holkar" for the 1802 revenge on the Peshwa; if a question gives a specific first name for 1817, follow the handout's wording. Mnemonic: BAH! The three who revolted in 1817: Bajirao 20-40, Appa, Holkar. Decode: Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib (Bhonsle of Nagpur) and Holkar united against the EIC in late 1817. Bajirao II 96-18 and Appa Sahib fought with men they recruited themselves (the SA had disbanded the state army); Holkar alone had a proper army (teacher's board). Why it sticks: "Bah!" is how a rebel spits at the Resident. Mnemonic: Sitabuldi 1817: hills, Residency, Arabs, still lost. Decode: Appa Sahib as Senapati sent his Arab mercenaries in a surprise, close-quarters attack on the British Residency and the Sitabuldi hills (November 1817); heavily outnumbering the garrison, he still lost. Prelims twist: SA signed in 1816, war in 1817. Why it sticks: "Sita-buldi", sits on the hills; the Nagpur hills hold, and the SA's loophole is exposed. 6.2 Battles and surrender  3rd War, Battles and Surrender. Force size: the EIC deployed its largest military force ever in India, about 1.2 lakh troops. Battle of Mahidpur (Dec 1817): Holkar was defeated. Battle of Koregaon (1 Jan 1818): Peshwa was defeated; a small EIC force of Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army; later commemorated as the Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar. Surrender: Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 surrendered in June 1818. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Mahidpur", "Holkar", "Koregaon", "Peshwa", "Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army" and "Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar". items.t: 7 · Consequences of the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)
items.x: 3rd War, Consequences 1 to 3. 1. The Peshwaship was abolished. Bajirao II 96-18 was pensioned off to Bithur, near Kanpur (his adopted son was Nana Sahib, who would later lead the Kanpur revolt in 1857). 2. Svarajya annexed into the Bombay Presidency: the original Maratha homeland became a province of the Company State; the regional HQ of EIC trade evolved into a province of British India. 3. Appa Sahib deposed; replaced by a puppet; Bhonsle lost huge territory. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Peshwaship was abolished", a long underline from "Bajirao II 96-18 was pensioned off to Bithur" through the Nana Sahib line, "Svarajya annexed", "Appa Sahib deposed" and "Bhonsle lost huge territory". The Peshwaship was abolished. Bajirao II 96-18 was pensioned off to Bithur, near Kanpur. (His adopted son was Nana Sahib, who would later lead the Kanpur revolt in 1857.) Svarajya was annexed into the Bombay Presidency. The original Maratha homeland became a province of the Company State; the regional headquarters of EIC trade evolved into a province of British India. Appa Sahib was deposed and replaced by a puppet. Bhonsle lost huge territory.  3rd War, Consequences (contd.). 4. Holkar's Subsidiary Alliance via the Treaty of Mandsaur (1818); Holkar of Indore was forced to sign after being decisively defeated at Mahidpur. 5. Sambhaji 80-89's line goes through Shahu 19-49 (Satara) to Ram Raja (1749-77), with the note "(To SANGOLA)". The board digit here is [unclear: check your notebook]. Learn Sangola 1750 from Chapter 4. The last digit of "Shahu 19-49 19-4?" on the board is also unclear; the handout notes use Shahu 19-49. The handout's figure says "the bloodline tactic backfires" (compare Raghunath Rao 73-74's pension in 1782). Why it sticks: Bithur and Kanpur both start where a B and a K meet; the pensioner's son returns to the same city. Mnemonic: Satara fell in 1848: Dalhousie 48-56's first year. Satara and Kolhapur had been spared in 1818 as the Chhatrapati's symbolic line. Why it sticks: "48 and 48": the day he arrived, the Chhatrapati's Satara lapsed. Peshwaship abolished 1819, Bajirao II 96-18 pensioned to Bithur, near Kanpur; Svarajya (Maharashtra) annexed into the Bombay Presidency, trade HQ becomes a Company province; Satara and Kolhapur not annexed yet, the Chhatrapati kept as a symbolic figurehead; Appa Sahib Bhonsle deposed 1818, a pliant successor installed, Nagpur loses huge territory; Holkar signs the Treaty of Mandsaur 1818 (SA), Scindhia and Bhonsle reduced to Subsidiary-Alliance rulers; 1848, Dalhousie 48-56 annexes Satara under the Doctrine of Lapse (Ch 14); residual Maratha presence ends. Bhonsle's treaty status: three readings. The text says after the 2nd war Bhonsle refused the full SA and signed only a mini alliance (territory ceded, an EIC army he paid for). items.t: 8 · Why did the Marathas lose?
items.x: Why Did the Marathas Lose? Four structural reasons. 1. Factionalism (teacher's white tick). 2. Absence of unified command: Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle and Gaikwad of Baroda never coordinated effectively ("unified command" underlined in white; a white tick near "effectively"). 3. EIC's superior finances. 4. Naval and logistics advantage: the Konkan coast could be blockaded by EIC ships; the EIC moved troops faster across India via sea and better roads than the Marathas (yellow dotted underline under "Naval & logistics advantage"). Four structural reasons explain the Maratha defeat: Factionalism. Absence of unified command. Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle and the Gaikwad of Baroda never coordinated effectively. The EIC's superior finances. Naval and logistics advantage. The Konkan coast could be blockaded by EIC ships; the EIC could move troops faster across India via sea and better road infrastructure than the Marathas. Takeaway (slide 81): the Confederacy fell less from EIC military superiority than from its own structure: factionalism and no unified command, against the EIC's deeper finances and naval-logistics reach. The pattern repeats across all three wars: a divided Maratha house was the EIC's most reliable ally. Teacher: He ticked "Factionalism" (the first and the repeating cause), underlined "unified command" in white, put a tick near "effectively" and a dotted underline under "Naval & logistics advantage". On the overview board (slide 61) the same lesson shows: factionalism is the reason in two wars out of three, and a disbanded army is the weak point in the third. Reading the four reasons: the first two are internal (the Marathas' own structure), the last two are external (the EIC's edge). Mnemonic: F-U-F-N: Factions, Unity, Funds, Navy. Decode: four reasons the Marathas lost: Factionalism, no Unified command (Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad of Baroda), the EIC's Finances, the EIC's Naval and logistics edge (Konkan coast blockaded; sea and roads). Why it sticks: "Fun!" with a missing "N": two internal, two external; the Marathas had no fun.

items.t: 9 · Wars due to the EIC army over-hyping the threat to borders
items.x: Teacher's board: "WARS BY eic". Two branches: "FOR TRADE" and "FOR (T)" (the T circled, for territory). Under "FOR T": "empire BUILDER GGs" and a boxed "VESTED INTEREST of eic ARMY", with a line down from the box to "OVERHYPE THREAT TO BORDERS". Teacher: A new tree for all the EIC's wars. Wars by the EIC are of two kinds: for trade, and for T (territory). Wars for territory again have two drivers: (1) empire-builder Governor Generals, and (2) the vested interest of the EIC army (the army benefits from a big threat), which overhypes the threat to the borders. The wars in this section are the second kind: the army's overhyping.  Mnemonic: Trade, then T: two branches, two drivers. Decode: Wars by the EIC = for trade or for T (territory). For territory: empire-builder GGs (Wellesley 98-05, Francis Hastings 13-23) or the army's vested interest (it overhypes the threat to the borders). Why it sticks: a tree has one trunk and one fork: the army branch is the one that overhypes.  Teacher's board: "Concep (WM) . PROTECTORATE". "Symbolic Sovereignty (not Taken)" splits into two branches: "EXT" with "(Br)" below, and "Dom" with "(not Taken)" below. Teacher: The concept of a protectorate. Symbolic sovereignty is not taken. Of the two kinds of sovereign function: external ("EXT") goes to Britain ("Br"); domestic ("Dom") is not taken. The word in brackets after "Concep" is [unclear: check your notebook]. The handout's bracket gives the same idea: a protectorate is like a Subsidiary Alliance: the State loses external sovereign functions but retains symbolic sovereignty and domestic sovereign functions. Mnemonic: Protectorate: Sign kept, Home kept, Foreign lost. Decode: protectorate = symbolic sovereignty kept, domestic functions kept, external functions go to Britain. (Same logic as a Subsidiary Alliance.) Why it sticks: you keep your signboard and your house, but someone else answers the doorbell for foreign visitors. 9.1 Nepal, Burma and Coorg  Wars from EIC Border Over-Hyping. Anglo-Nepal 1814-16, Francis Hastings 13-23: Treaty of Sugauli (1816): Nepal a British Protectorate; lost Kumaon, Garhwal and the Terai (Protectorate = like an SA: loses external sovereignty, keeps symbolic + domestic). 1st Anglo-Burmese 1824-26, Amherst 23-28: Burma was expanding, giving the EIC a border-threat pretext; Treaty of Yandabo (1826) annexed Assam, Nagaland and parts of lower Burma (Arakan and Tenasserim); Cachar annexed 1830 (Ahom Assam had backed the EIC, a stab in the back). Coorg 1834, William Bentinck 28-35: on grounds of maladministration by Vira Raja (massive coffee plantations set up after annexation). items.t: 10 · The Prelims PYQs on the class slides (slides 88 to 94)
items.x: Slide 88 (typed, "Alert: Prelims PYQs"): three real Prelims PYQs sit under this chapter, all chronology traps. PYQ 1 (Prelims 1999): match the year to the war; use the year of outbreak, not the end year. PYQ 2 (Prelims 2004): match the AD range to the war; 1767-69 is Mysore, not Maratha. PYQ 3 (Prelims 2010): the immediate reason Abdali invaded and fought the Third Battle of Panipat. The slide only announces the PYQs.  PYQ 1, Prelims 1999 (marked "Partial"). Match List I (Years) with List II (Events). A. 1775, B. 1780, C. 1824, D. 1838; 1. First Anglo-Burmese War, 2. First Anglo-Afghan War, 3. First Anglo-Maratha War, 4. Second Anglo-Mysore War. Teacher's ink: circled matches A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2; year ranges written beside the events (1824-26, 1838-42, 1775-82, 1780-84); a tick against option (c) A-3 B-4 C-1 D-2 and a cross against option (d). Options: (a) A-3 B-2 C-1 D-4, (b) A-4 B-3 C-1 D-2, (c) A-3 B-4 C-1 D-2, (d) A-2 B-3 C-4 D-1. Prelims 1999: answer (c) A-3 B-4 C-1 D-2. The anchor is the year the war broke out. 1775 = 1st Anglo-Maratha War (Treaty of Surat); 1780 = 2nd Anglo-Mysore War; 1824 = 1st Anglo-Burmese War; 1838 = 1st Anglo-Afghan War. The trap: memorising wars by their end year (1782, 1784, 1826, 1842) gives a wrong code. The teacher's method: write the full range beside each war and match the first number. Mnemonic: Prelims 1999: 75, 80, 24, 38 = 3, 4, 1, 2. Decode: 1775 First Anglo-Maratha (3), 1780 Second Anglo-Mysore (4), 1824 First Anglo-Burmese (1), 1838 First Anglo-Afghan (2). Answer (c). Use the start year. Why it sticks: the matching digits read 3-4-1-2, "three-four, one-two", a counting rhyme.  PYQ 2, Prelims 2004 (marked "Partial"). Which of the following pairs are correctly matched? List I (AD ranges): A. AD 1767-69, B. AD 1790-92, C. AD 1824-26, D. AD 1845-46. List II (Wars): 1. First Anglo-Maratha War, 2. Third Mysore War, 3. First Anglo-Burmese War, 4. Second Sikh War. Options: (a) 2 and 4, (b) 3 and 4, (c) 1 and 2, (d) 2 and 3. No ink on the slide. Prelims 2004: answer (d) 2 and 3. B (1790-92 = 3rd Anglo-Mysore War) and C (1824-26 = 1st Anglo-Burmese War) are correct. A is wrong: 1767-69 is the 1st Anglo-Mysore War, not the 1st Anglo-Maratha (that began in 1775). D is wrong: 1845-46 is the 1st Anglo-Sikh War; the 2nd was 1848-49. The teacher left no ink here; the typed answer slide (92) marks the question "Partial" because these wars sit in several chapters. Mnemonic: Prelims 2004: only the middle two are true. Decode: A 1767-69 = Mysore I, not Maratha I (that is 1775); B 1790-92 = Mysore III (true); C 1824-26 = Burmese I (true); D 1845-46 = Sikh I, not Sikh II (1848-49). Answer (d) 2 and 3. Why it sticks: the two ends lie, the middle two (B, C = 2, 3) are honest.  PYQ 3, Prelims 2010. What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat? (a) He wanted to avenge the expulsion by Marathas of his Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore. (b) The frustrated Governor of Jullandhar Adina Beg Khan invited him to invade India. (c) He wanted to punish Mughal administration for non-payment of agreed annual tribute. (d) He wanted to annex all the fertile plains of Punjab up to the borders of Delhi to his kingdom. Teacher's ink: "1761" at the top right; no other marks. Prelims 2010: answer (a). The immediate provocation was the Maratha thrust into the north-west: they had seized Lahore and driven out Abdali's son and viceroy Timur Shah from the Punjab, so Abdali invaded to recover it and avenge the expulsion, ending in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761). (b) is wrong: Adina Beg Khan invited the Marathas, not Abdali. (c) tribute was not the trigger; (d) annexing Punjab is a general ambition, not the immediate reason. Full story in Chapter 4. Mnemonic: Prelims 2010: Lahore, Timur Shah, 1761. Decode: Abdali's immediate reason for the Third Panipat (1761): the Marathas expelled his viceroy (his son) Timur Shah from Lahore. Not Adina Beg's invitation (he invited the Marathas), not tribute, not a general annexation plan. Why it sticks: "Timur's Tale ends at Lahore": one trigger, one year on the board.

items.t: 1 · Peak of Expansion: how far and by what means
items.x: Peak of Expansion table. Extent by 1856: Company State ruled 63% of India, home to 78% of its population; after Dalhousie 48-56, no further annexation of the Indian mainland. PoP 1813-58, three instruments: Doctrine of Lapse, Wars, Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy. Teacher's ink: after "no further annexation of Indian mainland" a dash and "into Br ruled India" and a box "i.e. Br India"; under Doctrine of Lapse "Succession Disputes (R v R) -> Instability -> Hurt Br Business Interests" with a bracket "Br interests = Paramount"; a circle "BERAR" above "HYD"; boxed "MMP" over the Also row. By the end of Dalhousie 48-56's tenure the Company State controlled 63% of India, home to 78% of its population. After Dalhousie 48-56 there were no further annexations. He used the Policy of Paramountcy (PoP 1813-58) in three ways: Doctrine of Lapse: annexation by refusing to recognise adopted heirs. Wars: the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War 1848-49 (Punjab annexed) and the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 (Pegu annexed). Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar 1853 from Hyderabad. Besides these: the Maritime Ring Fence, the modernisation infrastructure and the five-policy framework. Teacher: "Annexation of the Indian mainland" means annexation "into British-ruled India, that is British India." He writes "i.e. Br India" and underlines British India. On the Lapse row he supplies the logic of why the British cared about succession: succession disputes (R v R, read as ruler against ruler) → instability → hurt British business interests; and "British interests = Paramount." So the Doctrine of Lapse is not just a legal trick: instability in an Indian State threatens British trade, and British interests are supreme. The small BERAR / HYD circle is the picture for the third instrument: Berar sits at the top of the Hyderabad circle. Mnemonic: "Lapse, War, Lieu": the three roads of Paramountcy. Decode: Lapse (refuse adopted heirs), Wars (Punjab 1848-49 and Pegu 1852-53), Lieu of subsidy (Berar 1853). Result: 63% of territory, 78% of population, and no more annexations after Dalhousie 48-56. Why it sticks: Lapse and Lieu both start with L; the war sits between them. Mnemonic: 63 and 78: "six-three of land, seven-eight of people". Decode: 63% of India's territory, 78% of its population were under the Company State by 1856. Why it sticks: the two numbers are the same digits reversed and moved (63, 78: 6+3 = 9, 7+8 = 15).

items.t: 2 · The Doctrine of Lapse: legal principle against pretext
items.x: Doctrine of Lapse: Principle vs Pretext. Origin: formulated by the Court of Directors of the EIC in 1847, implemented systematically by Dalhousie 48-56. The rule: if an Indian ruler died without a biological heir, his rights lapsed and the State was annexed into British India. The override: under Hindu law adoption was a legitimate succession mechanism; the Doctrine refused to recognise this. Teacher's ink: above the table "Top Decision Making Body of EIC [not a Govt body] = Board of Directors"; "PRELIMS" under Origin; "e.g. R2 Rule, R2 Pension" under the rule row; "DoL overrides Hindu Law"; right side "(Dalhousie 48-56 # Author of DoL)". The Doctrine of Lapse was formulated by the Court of Directors of the EIC in 1847 but implemented systematically by Dalhousie 48-56. The rule was simple: if an Indian ruler died without a biological heir, his rights lapsed and the State was annexed into British India. Under Hindu law, adoption was a legitimate mechanism for succession: adopted sons inherited with full legitimacy. The Doctrine of Lapse refused to recognise this. Teacher: The Court of Directors is the "top decision-making body of the EIC," that is the Board of Directors, "not a Government body." He writes "PRELIMS" beside it, so the Prelims trap is: who formulated the doctrine (the Court of Directors, 1847) against who implemented it (Dalhousie 48-56). His bracket: "Dalhousie 48-56 # Author of DoL" (he is credited as author in common speech because he applied it). "Rights lapsed" means e.g. R2 Rule, R2 Pension: the right to rule and the right to the pension both lapsed (read R2 as "right to"). And "DoL overrides Hindu Law." "Author of the Doctrine" is not the same as "formulator." The handout and slide say formulated by the Court of Directors in 1847, implemented systematically by Dalhousie 48-56. The teacher's bracket lets you call Dalhousie 48-56 its author in a loose sense. In a Prelims statement, choose by the verb: formulated = Court of Directors; implemented = Dalhousie 48-56. Mnemonic: "Court Formulates 47, Dalhousie 48-56 Does 48". Decode: Court of Directors formulates in 1847; Dalhousie 48-56 implements from 1848 (Satara is the first Lapse State, 1848). Rule: no biological heir = rights lapse; adoption under Hindu law is overridden. Why it sticks: the court writes the law, the Governor General does the deed, one year apart (47, 48).

items.t: 4 · The Inam Commission (1852)
items.x: Inam Commission (1852). Target: Dalhousie 48-56 also targeted privileged landholdings. Set-up: 1852, Bombay Presidency set up the Inam Commission to investigate tax-free grants (inams) made by earlier Indian rulers to Brahmins, temples and others. Method: the Commission demanded proof of title; insufficient-proof grants were confiscated; about 20,000 estates seized in the Bombay Presidency alone. Logic: Doctrine of Lapse applied to land titles instead of thrones. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on Bombay Presidency, tax-free grants (inams), proof of title and 20,000 estates; white "ignore" (underlined) beside the Logic row label. Dalhousie 48-56 also targeted privileged landholdings. In 1852 the Bombay Presidency set up the Inam Commission to investigate inams (tax-free grants) made by earlier Indian rulers to Brahmins, temples and others. The Commission demanded proof of title; grants with insufficient proof were confiscated. Around 20,000 estates were seized in the Bombay Presidency alone. The logic: the Inam Commission was the Doctrine of Lapse applied to land titles instead of thrones. If you cannot prove your claim to the Company's satisfaction, the Company takes it. The logic was identical. Teacher: He underlines Bombay Presidency, tax-free grants (inams), proof of title and about 20,000 estates as the four facts to hold. Beside the Logic row label he writes "ignore" (underlined): the comparison with Lapse is a handout aid, not something he wants memorised for the exam. items.t: 5 · The Doctrine of Lapse applied to pensions: Nana Sahib
items.x: Lapse Applied to Pensions: Nana Sahib. Dalhousie 48-56 extended the Doctrine of Lapse to pensions. Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 died in 1851; Dalhousie 48-56 refused to continue the State pension of Rs 8 lakh per annum to his adopted son Nana Sahib. The argument: adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or State pensions. 1857 link: the refusal made Nana Sahib a key 1857 leader from Bithur, where Bajirao II 96-18 had been pensioned off in 1819 after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines only. Dalhousie 48-56 extended the Doctrine of Lapse to pensions. Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 died in 1851. Dalhousie 48-56 refused to continue the State pension of Rs 8 lakh per annum to his adopted son Nana Sahib. The argument: adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or State pensions. The refusal made Nana Sahib a key 1857 leader from Bithur, where Bajirao II 96-18 had been pensioned off in 1819 after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War. Mnemonic: "Eight lakh, fifty-one, Bithur": the Nana Sahib chain. Decode: pension Rs 8 lakh a year; Bajirao II 96-18 died 1851; pensioned at Bithur in 1819; adopted son Nana Sahib refused, so he became an 1857 leader. Why it sticks: 8 lakh, 51, 19, 57: four numbers around one town, Bithur.

items.t: 6 · Annexation in lieu of subsidy: Berar (1853)
items.x: Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar (1853). Dalhousie 48-56's second instrument. Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 and had been paying ever-rising subsidy ever since. By 1853 Hyderabad could not pay; Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar as permanent payment of the subsidy. Recall: 1801, half of Awadh annexed as subsidy. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on Berar and "1801: half of Awadh". Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy is the second instrument (the slide's order) of Dalhousie 48-56. Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 and had been paying ever-rising subsidy ever since. By 1853 Hyderabad could not pay. Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar as permanent payment of the subsidy. Recall: in 1801 half of Awadh was annexed as subsidy (Section 7). The pattern is the same: unpaid subsidy becomes territory. Mnemonic: "98 signs, 53 pays in land": Hyderabad's subsidy line. Decode: Hyderabad signs the first Subsidiary Alliance (1798), cannot pay by 1853, so Berar is taken as permanent payment. Same trick as Awadh 1801. Why it sticks: 98 to 53 is a 55-year slide from signature to seizure.

items.t: 7 · The annexation of Awadh (1856)
items.x: Teacher's board: Clive, Wellesley 98-05, Dalhousie 48-56 on Awadh. The six steps of Awadh's fall: 1765: Treaty of Allahabad (by Robert Clive 57-67) established PoIR + PoRF + a mini Subsidiary Alliance in Awadh. The EIC gradually increased its subsidy demands on Awadh. 1798: John Shore 93-98 replaced Wazir Ali 97-98 as Nawab with his uncle Sadat Ali Khan II, in return for an annual subsidy of Rs 76 lakh and the cession of Allahabad fort. 1801: Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted. Wellesley 98-05 imposed the full Subsidiary Alliance by sending Henry Wellesley. Half of Awadh (Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand and the Doab) was annexed as permanent payment of the subsidy, called the Ceded Districts; it was unjust, as the revenue was twice the subsidy. The EIC kept demanding more subsidy despite the permanent payment. The Nawab had to raise taxes and by 1855 there was a threat of peasant revolts. 1856: Dalhousie 48-56 annexed the rest of Awadh on grounds of maladministration. By 1855 the British Resident had established Indirect Rule and Nawab Wajid Ali Shah had no real power, hence no power but all responsibility. The handout also describes the 1765 treaty as "PoIR + PoRF + mini SA"; that is the Clive 57-67 chain taught in Chapter 10 and Chapter 11. items.t: 8 · The Sikh State: from ideal buffer to annexation target
items.x: 8.1 Buffer to target  Sikh State: From Buffer to Target. PoRF aim: stable, strong, friendly border States as a protective buffer around British India. If unstable: either Indirect Rule (Nepal 1814-16, Afghanistan 1839, Punjab 1845) or direct annexation (Assam and parts of lower Burma 1824-26, Punjab 1849, Burma 1852-53). Ideal buffer: the Sikh State under Ranjit Singh 01-39; after his death in 1839 factionalism tore it apart. Teacher's ink: "imp" over "stable, strong, friendly"; "Great Game" with Russia pointing down through bands "Afghanistan" and "Punjab" to "Br India", "Sutlej"; "PoRF" circled, "this fear to 1809: ToA Amritsar"; "1838 Tripartite Treaty" with Shah Shuja and "for PoIR in AFGH via installing Puppet Shah Shuja vs Dost Md"; bottom: "It is nature of Power to centralize itself in strong personality BUT if personality weakens then Power leaves either vertically downward [R v N, R v R, N v N] or via Horizontal Replacement [annexed by Br 1849]". Under the Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) the EIC wanted stable, strong, friendly border States as a protective buffer around British India. If stability could not be achieved, the EIC either: established Indirect Rule: Nepal 1814-16, Afghanistan 1839, Punjab 1845; or directly annexed: Assam and parts of lower Burma 1824-26, Punjab 1849, Burma 1852-53. The Sikh State had been that ideal buffer under Maharaja Ranjit Singh 01-39. After his death in 1839, factionalism tore the State apart: Royal family members fought for succession. The Sindhanwaliyas, a Jat clan or misl. Dogra Rajputs who served as Wazirs at different times. The Khalsa Army itself. Succession disputes and political murders followed; the PoRF was now useless as the State weakened from within. Teacher: "Imp" is written over "stable, strong, friendly": the three qualities the EIC wanted in a buffer State. His Great Game sketch: Russia → Afghanistan → Punjab (with the Sutlej) → British India. "This fear led to 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar" (the EIC's PoRF with the Sikhs). 1838 Tripartite Treaty: the EIC aimed PoIR in Afghanistan via installing a puppet, Shah Shuja, against Dost Md (a cryptic scribble beside it reads like "R30139 EIC Shah Shuja" [unclear: check your notebook]). His general law of power: power centralises in a strong personality, BUT if the personality weakens, power leaves either "vertically downward" [R v N, R v R, N v N: read as ruler against noble, ruler against ruler, noble against noble] or by "horizontal replacement" [annexed by the British, 1849]. Ranjit Singh 01-39's strength held the Sikh State; after 1839 power leaked down into factions, then sideways to the British.  Sikh State: From Buffer to Target (contd.). Four factions: royal family members fought for succession; the Sindhanwaliyas (a Jat clan or misl); Dogra Rajputs who served as Wazirs at different times; the Khalsa Army itself. Collapse: succession disputes and political murders; PoRF now useless as the State weakened from within. The Khalsa Army's democratic spirit (governance by Panchayats) was harder for the EIC to manage than a feudal-loyal army. Teacher's ink: yellow ticks at items 1, 2 and 4; "Dogra Rajputs" underlined; a white bracket beside item 3: "[also Rulers of Jammu (part of Sikh empire)]". Teacher: Beside the Dogra Rajputs he notes they were also "Rulers of Jammu (part of the Sikh empire)." This sets up Gulab Singh in the Treaty of Amritsar 1846 (Section 8.2). The Khalsa Army's democratic spirit: the handout adds that it wanted governance by Panchayats, a form of collective military and civil self-governance, and was harder for the EIC to manage than a feudal-loyal army. Mnemonic: "Four factions fell the Sikh State": R-S-D-K. Decode: Royal family (succession fights), Sindhanwaliyas (a Jat clan or misl), Dogra Rajputs (Wazirs), Khalsa Army. After Ranjit Singh 01-39's death in 1839. Why it sticks: four initials, R-S-D-K, one per faction. Mnemonic: Indirect rule list "N-A-P" (1814-16, 1839, 1845) against annexation list "A-P-B" (1824-26, 1849, 1852-53). Decode: Indirect Rule = Nepal 1814-16, Afghanistan 1839, Punjab 1845. Direct annexation = Assam and parts of lower Burma 1824-26, Punjab 1849, Burma 1852-53. Punjab appears on both lists: first Indirect Rule, then annexed. Why it sticks: Punjab is the only name on both lists: first Indirect Rule, then annexed. 8.2 The First Anglo-Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846)  Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846). Teacher's ink: "Signed after 1st war"; top right "[* connect ToA 1765 @ Awadh] = quasi/mini (SA)". Clauses: 1 Military Restraint (Khalsa Army size reduced, an EIC army stationed, not fully disbanded out of respect for Sikh religious sentiment) with the white bracket "[Khalsa by GGS 76-08 in 1699]"; 2 Territorial Cession (the fertile Jalandhar Doab annexed); 3 The Kashmir Mechanism (could not pay the 1.5 crore war indemnity, ceded hills between the Beas and Indus, Kashmir and Hazara; the EIC sold them to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees; formalised by the Treaty of Amritsar 16 March 1846) with "Took from Punjab and sold to Dogras"; 4 Administrative Oversight (PoIR initiated, a Resident, Henry Lawrence, as effective Regent). Result of the 1st Anglo-Sikh War: the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846). Military restraint: the Khalsa Army was reduced in size and an EIC army was stationed. The Khalsa was not fully disbanded out of respect for Sikh religious sentiment. Territorial cession: the fertile Jalandhar Doab (the land between the Beas and Sutlej) was annexed by the EIC. The Kashmir mechanism: the Lahore Darbar could not pay the full war indemnity of Rs 1.5 crore, so it ceded the hills between the Beas and Indus (Kashmir and Hazara) to the EIC. The EIC then transferred (sold) these territories to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees. Gulab Singh was recognised as Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, subordinate to the British. This was formalised by the Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846). Administrative oversight: PoIR was initiated in Punjab: a British Resident (Henry Lawrence) was stationed as the effective Regent. Teacher: "Signed after the 1st war." He links it to ToA 1765 at Awadh: both are "quasi / mini SA": a defeated State keeps its ruler but its army is cut, an EIC army is stationed, and a Resident is placed. Beside clause 1 he writes "[Khalsa by GGS 76-08 in 1699]": the Khalsa was founded by Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 (GGS) 76-08 in 1699 (so "Khalsa Army" ties to the religious sentiment the handout mentions). Under the Kashmir mechanism: "Took from Punjab and sold to Dogras." (Dogras: Gulab Singh, ruler of Jammu, see slide 20.) Strategic Note. Kashmir, of enormous strategic importance, was sold to reward Gulab Singh's neutrality. The "Kashmir Question" has its legal origin here, creating a Hindu monarchy over a Muslim-majority population. Two Treaties of Amritsar must be distinguished. (1) Treaty of Amritsar 1809: between Ranjit Singh 01-39 and the EIC; it established the Sutlej as the Sikh-EIC boundary (PoRF with the Sikhs). (2) Treaty of Amritsar 1846 (16 March): formalised the Kashmir sale to Gulab Singh; the legal foundation of the Princely State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) is a third document, signed seven days earlier. Mnemonic: Lahore 9, Amritsar 16: "nine-sixteen" in March 1846. Decode: 9 March 1846 Treaty of Lahore (army cut, Jalandhar Doab, Kashmir ceded, Resident Henry Lawrence). 16 March 1846 Treaty of Amritsar (Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees). Not to be confused with Amritsar 1809 (Sutlej boundary). Why it sticks: Lahore is first (9), Amritsar one week later (16); 1809 is the old one. Mnemonic: "MJKR": the four clauses of the Treaty of Lahore. Decode: Military restraint (Khalsa reduced, EIC army stationed), Jalandhar Doab annexed, Kashmir mechanism (indemnity Rs 1.5 crore unpaid, Kashmir and Hazara ceded then sold for 75 lakh to Gulab Singh), Resident (Henry Lawrence, PoIR in Punjab). Why it sticks: M-J-K-R follows the clause order 1 to 4. Mnemonic: Indemnity 1.5 crore, sale 75 lakh: "half price". Decode: war indemnity Rs 1.5 crore; Kashmir and Hazara sold to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees, exactly half. Why it sticks: Kashmir is sold at half the bill. 8.3 The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49)  2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49). Reason: the Sikh Governors of Multan (Mulraj) and Haripur (Chattar Singh) revolted, giving empire-builder Dalhousie 48-56 the opportunity he needed. Results: Punjab annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 (a child of 5 at accession); the Koh-i-Noor surrendered to the British Crown; Punjab initially governed by a Board of Administration (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel). Conclusion: the last major independent State outside the Company State was gone; the EIC's frontier now touched the Afghan foothills. Teacher's ink: yellow lines to "Br interest paramount" beside the Reason row; "[Khyber Pass: entry point]" beside the Conclusion. Reason. The Sikh Governors of Multan (Mulraj) and Haripur (Chattar Singh) revolted, giving empire-builder Dalhousie 48-56 the opportunity he needed. Result. Annexation: Punjab was annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 (a child of 5 at accession). The Koh-i-Noor: as part of the terms of surrender, the diamond was taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 and surrendered to the British Crown. Administrative shift: Punjab was initially governed by a "Board of Administration" (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel). Conclusion. The last major independent State outside the Company State was gone. The EIC's frontier now touched the natural boundaries of the Afghan foothills. Teacher: "British interest paramount" is written at the end of the Reason row: the revolt of two governors was an opportunity, and the real reason is the same as for Lapse: PoP means British interests come first. For the Conclusion he adds "Khyber Pass: entry point" (underlined): the frontier now reached the pass through which invaders came into India. Chilianwala (1849) was a battle of the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War between the EIC and the Sikhs, not "Dalhousie 48-56 against the Marathas." This is the Prelims 1995 trap (slide 63). The slide answer names Chilianwala only through this PYQ; no other detail of the war's battles is given in the notes. Mnemonic: "Mulraj and Chattar rebel: Dalhousie 48-56 smiles." Decode: Mulraj (Multan) and Chattar Singh (Haripur) revolted; result 1849: Punjab annexed from Duleep Singh 43-49 (child of 5), Koh-i-Noor to the Crown, Board of Administration (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel). The Khyber Pass frontier is now British. Why it sticks: "M and C" are the two rebels; "D" (Dalhousie 48-56) delights. Mnemonic: Duleep 43-49: five years old, six years on the throne. Decode: Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 was a child of 5 at accession; his code runs 43 to 49, and 1849 is the year Punjab was annexed and the Koh-i-Noor went to the British Crown. Why it sticks: the code's end year (49) is the annexation year, so his reign and his State end together.

items.t: 9 · The Second Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53): Lower Burma and Pegu
items.x: 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53), Pegu. Logic: fought on the PoRF logic of securing the eastern frontier from an expansionist Burma. Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Lower Burma / Pegu. Combined with Arakan and Tenasserim (annexed 1824-26 under the 1st Anglo-Burmese War and the Treaty of Yandabo 1826), this brought the eastern shore of the Bay of Bengal under British control, effectively a British lake. Note: Sindh was annexed in 1843 by Charles Napier under Ellenborough 42-44, NOT Dalhousie 48-56; Dalhousie 48-56's annexations were Lower Burma 1852-53, Berar 1853, Punjab 1849 and the seven Lapse States. The war was fought on the PoRF logic of securing the eastern frontier from an expansionist Burma. Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Lower Burma / Pegu. Combined with Arakan and Tenasserim (annexed 1824-26 under the 1st Anglo-Burmese War and the Treaty of Yandabo 1826), this brought the eastern shore of the Bay of Bengal under British control: the Bay was now effectively a British lake.
