items.t: 10 · Britain's maritime Ring Fence
items.x: A land empire is visible on a map. A maritime empire is harder to see but just as deliberate. While the EIC was annexing territories inland, it was simultaneously, piece by piece, bringing every coastline touching the Indian Ocean under British control. By the time Dalhousie 48-56 left in 1856, the picture was complete. PoRF logic did not stop at India's coastline: every sea approach had to be controlled, through whichever instrument was cheapest and most effective (not always annexation). 10.1 The Indian Ocean coastline (Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, 1668-1853)  The three-column timeline of the maritime Ring Fence (handout figure). Beyond India (strategic frontier): 1854 Treaty of Kalat; 1876 Treaty of Jacobabad; 1856-57 Anglo-Persian War; 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention; 1909 Anglo-Persian Oil Co. Arabian Sea (anticlockwise sweep): 1668 Bombay; 1789-99 Mysore / Malabar; 1802 Gaikwad-Baroda and Peshwa SA; 1805 Travancore; 1818 Svarajya annexed; 1843 Sindh. Bay of Bengal (clockwise sweep): 1757 Bengal; 1766 Northern Sarkars; 1801 Carnatic; 1803-05 Orissa; 1824-26 and 1852-53 Burma. Teacher's ink: a yellow zigzag line on the right with circled numbers 3, 2 and 3 [unclear: check your notebook].   Sweep   Coastal steps in order    --- ---    Bay of Bengal (clockwise sweep)   1757 Bengal, 1766 Northern Sarkars, 1801 Carnatic, 1803-05 Orissa, 1824-26 and 1852-53 Burma     Arabian Sea (anticlockwise sweep)   1668 Bombay, 1789-99 Mysore / Malabar, 1802 Gaikwad-Baroda and Peshwa SA, 1805 Travancore, 1818 Svarajya annexed, 1843 Sindh     Beyond India (strategic frontier)   1854 Treaty of Kalat, 1876 Treaty of Jacobabad, 1856-57 Anglo-Persian War, 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention, 1909 Anglo-Persian Oil Co.   The teacher's yellow zigzag on slide 32 and its three circled numbers (3, 2, 3) cannot be read with confidence. It seems to retell the three panels in a different order from the printed red 1, 2, 3. Check your notebook for what he said. Mnemonic: Two sweeps and one beyond: "Bay clockwise from Bengal, Sea anticlockwise from Bombay". Decode: Bay of Bengal clockwise: Bengal 1757, Northern Sarkars 1766, Carnatic 1801, Orissa 1803-05, Burma 1824-26 and 1852-53. Arabian Sea anticlockwise: Bombay 1668, Mysore/Malabar 1789-99, Gaikwad-Baroda and Peshwa SA 1802, Travancore 1805, Svarajya 1818, Sindh 1843. Beyond India: Kalat 1854, Jacobabad 1876, Persia 1856-57, 1907, 1909. Why it sticks: the two coasts meet at the tip, as if a hand closes around the peninsula; the third panel is what lies outside the fist. 10.2 Sea approaches beyond India: Balochistan and the Persian Gulf (self read) Teacher: Slides 28 to 31 (Balochistan, Treaty of Kalat, Treaty of Jacobabad, Gwadar, Persian Gulf) are marked "Self Read, not MIH syllabus" (MIH is Modern Indian History). They are in the handout and slides, so they are covered here fully, but he does not expect them to be taught or tested as core. Balochistan coast and Gwadar. The Makran coast (today's Balochistan coastline) belonged to the State of Makran, itself a vassal of the Khan of Kalat. The British brought this region under control through two treaties that fall on opposite sides of 1857 and the Government of India Act 1858:   Treaty   Signed by   Negotiated by   Terms    --- --- --- ---    Treaty of Kalat (1854)   The EIC, under Dalhousie 48-56   Major John Jacob   The Khan of Kalat surrendered foreign policy and allowed EIC military outposts inside Kalat; in exchange the EIC paid the Khan an annual subsidy of Rs 50,000. A reverse-SA pattern: the imperial power pays the local ruler for special rights to an external power     Treaty of Jacobabad (1876)   The British State (the Crown)   Robert Sandeman, under Viceroy Lytton 76-80   By 1876 the Government of India Act 1858 had abolished the EIC. This treaty ran under the Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1947), not the EIC's PoP. It went further: the British State could station troops permanently in Kalat, build railways and telegraphs through it and act as supreme arbitrator between the Khan and his tribal chiefs (Sardars)   PoIR had fully arrived in Kalat in 1876: the Resident was not just in the court, he was now the court. The shift from 1854 to 1876 in Kalat mirrors what happened to all 565 Indian princely States overnight in 1858: from subordinates of a trading company to legal subjects of the British Crown. The same geography and subordination, with a different legal authority above them. (The handout leaves the detail to the chapters on 1857 and the constitutional Acts: Chapter 17, Chapter 21.) Gwadar: a unique 170-year Omani enclave inside Balochistan. In 1783 the Khan of Kalat gifted the port of Gwadar to a prince of Oman, so Gwadar became an overseas territory of the Sultanate of Oman for over 170 years. The British Empire controlled everything around Gwadar but never owned it. Pakistan purchased Gwadar from Oman in 1958, eleven years after Independence. Today Gwadar is at the heart of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The Persian Gulf and Iran (Persia). Persia stayed a formally independent sovereign State; the British never annexed it. But formal independence did not mean freedom from foreign control. Three mechanisms: Temporary military force (1856-57). The Anglo-Persian War (1856-57) captured coastal cities including Bushehr and Kharg Island. Under the Treaty of Paris (1857) the British withdrew in exchange for Iran giving up its claims to Herat in Afghanistan (PoRF logic: protect the western land approach to India, not for Iran's sake). Formal diplomatic partition (1907). Under the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence. The southern coastal region along the Persian Gulf was recognised as the British sphere: naval dominance without a single annexation. Economic control (1909). The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (1909), later the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (today's BP), gave Britain economic control of the Iranian coastline; oil was extracted and shipped under British naval protection. The handout's closing remark: economic imperialism at its most efficient: control the resource, control the coast, without the cost of running a colony. The British learnt that formal annexation was expensive; a sphere of influence and an oil company could do the same more cheaply. Mnemonic: Kalat 54 pays, Jacobabad 76 rules: "Pay then Pack". Decode: Treaty of Kalat 1854 (EIC, Major John Jacob, Dalhousie 48-56): the EIC pays the Khan Rs 50,000 a year; he gives up foreign policy and allows outposts. Treaty of Jacobabad 1876 (British State, Robert Sandeman, Lytton 76-80): troops, railways, telegraphs, arbitration over the Sardars: the Resident is the court. Why it sticks: 1854 is the EIC era (company pays), 1876 is the Crown era (crown commands); 22 years apart. Mnemonic: Gwadar: gifted 83, sold 58, held by Oman between. Decode: 1783 Khan of Kalat gifts Gwadar to a prince of Oman; 1958 Pakistan buys it from Oman, 11 years after Independence; over 170 years an Omani enclave, never owned by the British. Why it sticks: 83 and 58 are the same digits flipped, like Company 65, Crown 58 in Chapter 10. Mnemonic: Persia in three steps: "Force 56-57, Split 07, Oil 09". Decode: 1856-57 Anglo-Persian War (Bushehr, Kharg Island), Treaty of Paris 1857 (Herat given up); 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention (southern coast in the British sphere); 1909 Anglo-Persian Oil Company (BP). Why it sticks: force, then paper, then money: each cheaper than the last.

items.t: 11 · Dalhousie 48-56 as moderniser
items.x: Not just an annexationist: the most transformative Governor General in physical and institutional infrastructure. A follower of Utilitarianism (James Mill: reform through laws by a strong State), he built the skeleton of modern India's communication and administrative framework. Teacher: Slide 33 (Moderniser 1/3) has "MMP" circled beside the title. This section is where his "future syllabus" fan (title slide) lands: Railways, Post and Telegraph, Canals, Wood's Despatch.  Dalhousie 48-56 as Moderniser (1/3). Framing: not just an annexationist; the most transformative GG in physical and institutional infrastructure; follower of Utilitarianism (James Mill). 1 Railways (1853): primarily for army movement, secondarily for administration, raw-material extraction and market creation; first line Bombay-Thane 1853; by 1856 Calcutta-Raniganj (coal-rich) and Madras-Arakkonam. 2 Telegraph (1853): Telegraph Department, about 4,000 miles across major cities. 3 Post Office Act (1854): uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate, Peshawar to Calcutta. 4 PWD: removed from military control, made civilian; GT Road (Peshawar to Calcutta) restored; canals and bridges. Teacher's ink: "MMP" circled; many yellow underlines; right side "West (1853)", "East (By 1856)", "South (By 1856)" and a small tilted "Peshawar" at the top.  Handout flowchart summarising the moderniser list: Railway 1853 (Bombay-Thane, 21 miles, first rail line in India), then Telegraph 1854 (4,000 miles of network, Telegraph Department established), then Post Office Act 1854 (uniform half-anna rate, Peshawar to Calcutta), then Public Works Department (removed from the military, a separate civilian arm, GT Road), then Ganges Canal (irrigation and transport in North India), then Wood's Despatch 1854 ("Magna Carta of Indian Education"; the figure says cross-ref Ch 19), then Port reform (Calcutta, Bombay and Madras upgraded for steamship traffic). The same figure is slide 36 of Lecture 16, with no ink.   #   Item   What to remember    --- --- ---    1   Railways (1853)   Built primarily for army movement, secondarily for administration, raw-material extraction and market creation. First line: Bombay to Thane, opened 1853. By 1856: Calcutta-Raniganj (coal-rich) and Madras-Arakkonam. The teacher's board: West (1853), East (by 1856), South (by 1856)     2   Telegraph (1853)   Telegraph Department established; about 4,000 miles laid across major cities     3   Post Office Act (1854)   A network with a uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate from Peshawar to Calcutta     4   Public Works Department (PWD)   Removed from military control, made civilian. GT Road (Peshawar to Calcutta) restored to functionality. Canals and bridges built across India     5   Wood's Despatch (1854)   Sometimes called the "Magna Carta of Indian Education": a blueprint for mass education: vernacular elementary schools, universities, structured education administration. Dalhousie 48-56 supported and implemented it     6   Vernacular push   Favoured vernacular elementary schools for their utilitarian value, expanding them in Bengal and Bihar. Backed technical education: the goal was efficient labour, good consumers and cheaper administration     7   Female education   J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie 48-56's Council) opened a girls' school in Calcutta in 1849: the Bethune School, India's first successful secular school for girls. (Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule's Pune school, 1 January 1848, predates it as India's first girls' school overall; secular = completely free from religious instruction)     8   Widow remarriage   Dalhousie 48-56 supported Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's work on girls' education and the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856. Vidyasagar became Principal of Sanskrit College in 1851 and Inspector of Schools in 1856, both under Dalhousie 48-56's tenure     9   Universities   Groundwork through Wood's Despatch, but Dalhousie 48-56 left India in 1856. The three universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta) were officially established in 1857 under Canning 56-62. Also the Engineering College at Roorkee; a Director of Education at the Provincial level with an Inspector at the District level    Dalhousie 48-56 as Moderniser (2/3). 5 Wood's Despatch (1854): "Magna Carta of Indian Education", blueprint for mass education; vernacular elementary schools, universities, structured education administration. 6 Vernacular push: favoured vernacular elementary schools for utilitarian value in Bengal and Bihar; backed technical education. 7 Female Education: J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie's Council) opened the Bethune School in Calcutta in 1849; the Phules' Pune school (1 Jan 1848) predates it. Teacher's ink: "Woods Despatch" in yellow above the vernacular row; yellow underlines on "Magna Carta of Indian Education", "mass education", "universities", "vernacular elementary schools", "technical education" and "J.E. Drinkwater Bethune". Teacher: The teacher writes "Woods Despatch" above the vernacular-schools row: the vernacular push comes from Wood's Despatch. On the title slide he lists "implement Wood's Despatch 1854" and the Hindu Widow Remarriages Act 1856 with a bracket: "Though passed during Canning 56-62." Dalhousie 48-56 supported the reform; it was passed after he left in 1856 (Canning 56-62 took over in 1856). Source note on dates. The slide 33 table and the handout write Telegraph (1853); the flowchart (slide 36, handout figure) writes Telegraph 1854. The teacher underlines (1853) beside the Telegraph row on slide 33, so use 1853. The flowchart also gives Bombay-Thane = 21 miles, and adds Ganges Canal and Port reform (Calcutta, Bombay and Madras upgraded for steamships), which are in the handout figure but not in its text. Universities and Wood's Despatch belong to Chapter 19. The handout says the three universities were established in 1857 under Canning 56-62 and that Dalhousie 48-56's part was groundwork. For the details of Wood's Despatch (grants-in-aid, universities, aims) see Chapter 19. The question bank lists Prelims PYQs on it for that chapter.  Dalhousie 48-56 as Moderniser (3/3). 8 Widow Remarriage: Dalhousie 48-56 supported Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's work on girls' education and the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856; Vidyasagar became Principal of Sanskrit College in 1851 and Inspector of Schools in 1856. 9 Universities: groundwork via Wood's Despatch, but he left in 1856; the three universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta) officially established 1857 under Canning 56-62; Engineering College at Roorkee; Director of Education (Provincial) and Inspector (District). Teacher's ink: yellow underlines only. Why the infrastructure was built, in the handout's own words: easier troop movement, cheaper administration, raw-material extraction and market creation. The infrastructure outlasted its purpose: India inherited it and built a nation on it. The Mains 2013 skeleton Mains 2013 (10 marks, 200 words): "In many ways, Lord Dalhousie 48-56 was the founder of modern India." Elaborate. The directive "Elaborate" asks for examples and reasoning, not a yes-or-no debate. The phrase "in many ways" accepts a qualified yes: list the ways and say why they were foundational.  Intro (about 25 words): Dalhousie 48-56 was in many ways the founder of modern India: the physical and institutional infrastructure he built for colonial purposes outlasted them, and India inherited it.  Body (pick 4 to 5): (1) Railways 1853 (Bombay-Thane; by 1856 Calcutta-Raniganj and Madras-Arakkonam). (2) Telegraph 1853, about 4,000 miles. (3) Post Office Act 1854, half-anna uniform rate, Peshawar to Calcutta. (4) PWD made civilian, GT Road, canals and bridges. (5) Wood's Despatch 1854, "Magna Carta of Indian Education": vernacular schools, universities, an education administration. (6) Three universities (established 1857 under Canning 56-62; groundwork his). Add the colonial purpose (troops, cheaper administration, raw materials, markets).  Closing (about 25 words): What he built for empire became the skeleton of an independent nation: the infrastructure outlasted its colonial purpose. The strongest single anchor is Wood's Despatch. Mnemonic: "RTPP-WU": Dalhousie 48-56's moderniser list. Decode: Railways (Bombay-Thane 1853), Telegraph (1853, 4,000 miles), Post Office Act (1854, half-anna), PWD (civilian; GT Road, canals), Wood's Despatch (1854), Universities (groundwork; set up 1857 under Canning 56-62). Why it sticks: "R-T-P-P-W-U" as "Rail, Tar, Post, Pay, Wood, Uni" in the order of the slide. Mnemonic: Three rails: "West 53, East 56, South 56". Decode: West: Bombay-Thane (1853). East: Calcutta-Raniganj (by 1856, coal-rich). South: Madras-Arakkonam (by 1856). The teacher drew exactly this West, East, South board. Why it sticks: the first is the odd one out in time: 53 first, then both others in 56. Mnemonic: Half-anna, two paise, Peshawar to Calcutta: the GT Road's twin. Decode: Post Office Act 1854: a uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate over the same line as the GT Road (Peshawar to Calcutta), which the PWD (now civilian) restored. Why it sticks: the letter and the road run the same line, west to east. Mnemonic: Girls' school ladder: Phule 1848, Bethune 1849, Vidyasagar 1851, 1856. Decode: 1 Jan 1848 Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule's Pune school (first girls' school overall); 1849 Bethune School, Calcutta (J.E. Drinkwater Bethune, Law Member): first successful secular school for girls; 1851 Vidyasagar Principal of Sanskrit College; 1856 Inspector of Schools and the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act. Why it sticks: four years in ascending order from 48 to 56, each one step later.

items.t: 12 · The five-policy arc (1600-1858) and the Policies towards Indian Kings
items.x: Teacher: This section is the teacher's "Next Topic: Policies of British towards Indian Kings." His board splits it in two: "EIC till 1858" and "Br State 1858+". It is the handout's Sec 12 (Five-Policy Arc) and so belongs to this chapter, not to Chapter 15 (which starts on slide 64 with "British Imperial Ideology"). Slide 44, the first of the arc's table slides, has "MMP" boxed with "1 Q" under it.  Teacher's board: "Next Topic": a yellow box "Policies of British Towards Indian Kings" with a branching line to "EIC Till 1858" ("Till 1858" underlined) and "Br State 1858+". A time written in a circle at top left and a scribble beside it.  Flowchart of the policy phases (handout figure) with the teacher's ink. Boxes from earlier to later: Relative Isolation (pre-1757); PoIR + PoRF (1757-1813); PoSA, Subsidiary Alliance (1798-1818), Wellesley 98-05's annexation tool; Policy of Paramountcy (1813-1857), Hastings: EIC = supreme power; Subordinate Union (post-1857). Red ink: "(next page)"; "PoRI +"; a long arrow "Level of Aggression by EIC" rising, with "up army -> up confidence" at Paramountcy. Yellow ink: "PoIR: Puppet 1 Nawab, 2 Br Resident, 3 controls"; "Notice: Relative isolation. How? not annexing because a company, here for business not for ruling, e.g. didn't annex Awadh after BoBuxar 1764"; "Plassey: Plunder, SA, LR income" joined to "army"; "Post annexation" with arrows to "army". Teacher: The rising-aggression arrow: the level of aggression by the EIC rises from the top box to the bottom: more army, then more confidence. The army grew from three sources: Plassey plunder, subsidy (SA) and land-revenue income (and, after annexation, the revenue of annexed land: his last arrows read "post annexation → army"). PoIR in his sketch: ① a puppet Nawab, ② a British Resident, ③ the Resident controls the puppet. Relative isolation in one line: the EIC did not annex because it was a company, "here for business, not for ruling," e.g. it did not annex Awadh after Buxar 1764 (Chapter 10's ToA 1765). This is the reason the first policy is called "relative". The slide flowchart and the handout give different dates for the phases. Teacher and handout win. Flowchart: Relative Isolation pre-1757; PoIR + PoRF 1757-1813; PoSA 1798-1818; Paramountcy 1813-1857; Subordinate Union post-1857. Handout: Relative Isolation until 1813 (the "arc" starts at 1600); PoIR and PoRF run alongside, with military alliances from 1765; PoSA 1798-1858; Paramountcy 1813-58; Subordinate Union 1858-1947. The teacher's own board for Paramountcy says (1813-58) and for isolation includes ToA 1765 inside it (slide 39). For answers use the handout's dates, and know the flowchart's version exists. 12.1 Relative Isolation (until 1813)  Teacher's board: Policy of Relative Isolation. "PRIMARY motive = TRADE and not Indian Politics"; circled 1: "initially EIC army = small [Child's war 1686-90: A2S807 THRASHED EIC]" and "therefore STAYED ISOLATED FROM Indian Politics"; circled 2: "Relative = NOT 100% = not absolute", "if OPPORTUNITY PRESENTED itself then TEMPORARILY interfered -> EXTRACTED TRADE/Rs Benefits -> Reverted BACK TO Isolation"; "E.g.: 1st A-Ma war 1775-82 [Reason: RR 73-74 promised Salsette and Vasai/Bassein if made Peshwa, therefore To Surat 1775 -> war]"; "# Shuja, Shah Alam II 60-06, Qasim 60-63 attacked EIC -> VICTORY = opportunity -> ToA 1765". The EIC was militarily not confident in its early decades; its primary interest was international trade. It stayed out of Indian politics as far as possible but not absolutely. It defended and expanded its trading interests through diplomacy and selective warfare, signed military alliances (Treaty of Allahabad 1765, Treaty of Salbai 1782) and interfered in succession disputes (Treaty of Surat 1775) to extract territories for trade expansion. (The Treaty of Purandhar 1776 shows the isolation pull: Hastings 73-85 wanted to settle commercially and avoid full war.) Teacher: Relative isolation, point by point. (1) Primary motive = trade, not Indian politics. The EIC's army was initially small: his proof is the "Child's war 1686-90" in which "[a Mughal ruler, written A2S807 and not readable with confidence] thrashed the EIC" [unclear: check your notebook; the scribble resembles Aurangzeb 58-07's code]. Therefore the EIC stayed isolated from Indian politics. (2) "Relative" = not 100% = not absolute: if an opportunity presented itself, the EIC "temporarily" interfered (the word is boxed), extracted trade or rupee benefits, then reverted back to isolation. Two examples he gives: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 (the reason: RR 73-74 promised Salsette and Vasai/Bassein if made Peshwa, therefore the Treaty of Surat 1775 and then war: see Chapter 13) and Shuja 54-75, Shah Alam II 60-06 and Qasim 60-63 attacking the EIC (Buxar): victory was an opportunity, giving ToA 1765 (underlined: see Chapter 10). Mnemonic: Isolation "rules of thumb": Trade, Temporary, Treaty. Decode: Trade is the primary motive; interference is Temporary (when an opportunity arises, then revert); the tools are Treaties (Allahabad 1765, Surat 1775, Purandhar 1776, Salbai 1782). Proofs: small army (Child's War 1686-90); 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 and Buxar 1764 as the "opportunities". Why it sticks: three T's, one per hand-written circled point. Mnemonic: Treaty dates of the isolation era in a row: 65, 75, 76, 82. Decode: Allahabad 1765 (alliance), Surat 1775 (succession dispute), Purandhar 1776 (Hastings 73-85 settle commercially), Salbai 1782 (alliance; also PoRF with the Marathas). Why it sticks: 65, 75, 76, 82: two twenty-fives then six, then seven more.  Teacher's board: "No interference" with a long curved arrow to "PoParamountcy". A yellow timeline from "1757": "rising Power of EIC [Company State]", therefore "rising interference / Aggression", "By 1813", then "PoParamountcy". Teacher: From no interference to Paramountcy: after 1757 the power of the EIC (the Company State) kept rising; therefore interference and aggression kept rising; by 1813 this became the Policy of Paramountcy. The curved arrow from "No interference" to "PoParamountcy" is the whole story of the arc in one line. Slide 42, a board on geopolitics. The teacher uses a general rule to explain why policies change: "In geopolitics, States behave in line with their power" (political, military, economic, intellectual/tech, social and soft power). When power is very low, States invoke ethics; when it is very high, they choose national interest first and then develop a language of ethics in line with it. He applies it to India's own rise: yesterday NAM, today NAM partially, tomorrow "we will/should interfere in others' affairs." He gives no more detail; it is an analogy for the EIC's rising aggression. 12.2 Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) and Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF)  Five-Policy Arc (1600-1858): Isolation and PoIR/PoRF. Relative Isolation (until 1813): trade first, alliances (ToA 1765, Salbai 1782), Treaty of Surat 1775, Purandhar 1776 (Hastings 73-85). PoIR: a British Resident in court controlling administration without formal annexation; examples Bengal by 1772, Delhi 1803, Travancore by 1809, Satara by 1818, Punjab 1846, Awadh by 1855. PoRF: a military alliance with a frontier State as buffer against external threats; examples Awadh (ToA 1765), Hyderabad (Treaty of Hyderabad 1766), Mysore (Treaty of Madras 1769), Marathas (Treaty of Salbai 1782), Sikh (Treaty of Amritsar 1809). Teacher's ink: "MMP" boxed with "1 Q" beneath it.   Policy   Definition   Examples    --- --- ---    PoIR (Indirect Rule)   A British Resident in the court controlling administration without formal annexation   Bengal by 1772, Delhi 1803, Travancore by 1809, Satara by 1818, Punjab 1846, Awadh by 1855     PoRF (Ring Fence)   A military alliance with a frontier State as a buffer against external threats   Awadh (ToA 1765), Hyderabad (Treaty of Hyderabad 1766), Mysore (Treaty of Madras 1769), Marathas (Treaty of Salbai 1782), Sikh (Treaty of Amritsar 1809)   Teacher: Beside the title he boxes "MMP" and writes "1 Q" (one question is expected from this part; the notes do not say more). Mnemonic: PoIR places in order: "Ben-Del-Tra-Sat-Pun-Awa": 72, 03, 09, 18, 46, 55. Decode: Bengal by 1772, Delhi 1803, Travancore by 1809, Satara by 1818, Punjab 1846, Awadh by 1855. A British Resident in court; no formal annexation. Why it sticks: the years climb 72, 03, 09, 18, 46, 55 with gaps of 31, 6, 9, 28, 9; Satara and Punjab and Awadh all end up annexed later. Mnemonic: PoRF buffer chain: "Awadh 65, Hyderabad 66, Mysore 69, Marathas 82, Sikhs 1809". Decode: Awadh (ToA 1765), Hyderabad (Treaty of Hyderabad 1766), Mysore (Treaty of Madras 1769), Marathas (Treaty of Salbai 1782), Sikh (Treaty of Amritsar 1809). Each is a buffer around British India against an outside threat. Why it sticks: "65, 66, 69, 82, 09" spoken like jersey numbers walking around the border clockwise. 12.3 Policy of Subsidiary Alliance (PoSA, 1798-1858)  Five-Policy Arc: PoSA (1798-1858). Definition: the EIC subordinated Indian rulers as junior alliance partners by taking over Foreign Policy and Military, both funded by an annual subsidy from the Indian State, while formally promising non-interference in internal affairs. Broken in practice: the promise was routinely broken through illegal PoIR; Bajirao II 96-18 signed the SA via the Treaty of Bassein 1802 to regain his throne; the Resident Mountstuart Elphinstone soon bypassed the Peshwa. 3rd Maratha War: Bajirao II 96-18's 1817 war was a ruler trying to shake off interference. No powers, but all the blame: same pattern as Awadh 1856. No ink. PoSA (1798-1858): the EIC subordinated Indian rulers as junior alliance partners by taking over their foreign policy and military, both funded by an annual subsidy from the Indian State, while formally promising non-interference in internal affairs. The promise was routinely broken through illegal PoIR. Bajirao II 96-18 signed the SA via the Treaty of Bassein 1802 to regain his throne; the treaty promised non-interference, but British Resident Mountstuart Elphinstone soon bypassed the Peshwa and interfered directly: creeping PoIR through the back door. When Bajirao II 96-18 launched the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817), it was not aggression: it was a ruler trying to shake off interference the treaty had explicitly promised would never happen. No powers, but all the blame: the same pattern as Awadh 1856 (Section 7). Mnemonic: SA: "Promise Non-interference, Practice Interference". Decode: PoSA takes foreign policy and military, paid by subsidy, promises non-interference; broken by illegal PoIR. Bajirao II 96-18: Bassein 1802 (to regain his throne), Elphinstone bypasses him, 1817 the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War. "No powers, all blame" = Awadh 1856. Why it sticks: the same two words twice (non-interference then interference): the promise and the break. 12.4 Policy of Paramountcy / Subordinate Isolation (1813-58)  Five-Policy Arc: Paramountcy (1813-58). Initiated by Francis Hastings 13-23. From 1813 the EIC formally declared itself paramount, the supreme power among all States in India, interfering in internal affairs and annexing if needed. Diplomatic isolation: after 1813 the EIC dropped the fiction of equal-sovereign alliance; every Indian State was locked in a sealed bubble with no communication, negotiation or alliance with any other State without the EIC as absolute gatekeeper. Conceptually: PoP = PoSA minus the rights of the Indian State. No ink. Initiated by Francis Hastings 13-23. From 1813 the EIC formally declared itself paramount: the supreme power among all States in India. To protect British interests it would interfere in internal affairs and annex if needed. (Earlier this happened in practice; from 1813 the EIC shed the pretence. Indian States were to have no rights if British interests demanded otherwise.) Diplomatic isolation (cutting off a State's right to deal with other States independently) had existed since early SA treaties. After 1813 every Indian State, large or small, was locked in a sealed bubble: no communication, negotiation or alliance with any other State without the EIC as absolute gatekeeper. Conceptually: Policy of Paramountcy = Policy of SA minus the rights of the Indian State. Mnemonic: "PoP = SA minus rights"; Francis Hastings 13-23 starts it in 1813. Decode: Paramountcy = Subsidiary Alliance minus the Indian State's rights; sealed bubble: no talk, treaty or alliance without the EIC as gatekeeper; started by Francis Hastings 13-23 in 1813; the teacher: it contributed to the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19. Why it sticks: subtraction sign: SA is the full price, take away the rights and you get PoP. 12.5 Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1947)  Teacher's board: Policy of Subordinate Union. "SUBORDINATE => Indian Kings will be Junior to Br State"; "Union => Br CROWN = MONARCH of Indian Kings" with an arrow to a rounded box "MUGHAL" marked "not"; "i.e. WHY FROM 1858 Indian Kings (Kings circled) called Indian PRINCES (Princes circled)"; "Princes = Son of King (King circled) = Br MONARCH"; "therefore WHOLE INDIA = PART OF Br empire", branching into "Br India: Ruled by British" and "565 Ps (Pr States): Ruled by Indian Prince".  Teacher's board: Subordinate Union and symbolic sovereignty. "SUBORDINATE UNION: Symbolic Sovereignty (Br)" splits into "EXT (D, C, FA) [Br]" and "Domestic Sovereign Fns [Indian PRINCE]". Below, "SA: Sym Sov (Indian King)" splits into "ext (D, C, FA) (EIC)" and "Domestic Affairs [Indian King]". After 1857 the EIC was abolished and the British State took direct control. Indian rulers were now not just subordinate but legally part of the British Empire, hence "union." Paramountcy became the formal legal relationship between the British Monarch and the Indian Prince. (Prince, not King: Indian rulers were now legally junior members of the British imperial family.) Sovereignty and the external sovereign functions (Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) were with the British Crown; domestic sovereign functions remained with the Indian Prince. Conceptually: Policy of Subordinate Union = Policy of Paramountcy + sovereignty formally with the British Crown. Teacher: Two words, two circled numbers: ① SUBORDINATE: Indian kings will be junior to the British State. ② UNION: the British Crown = the monarch of Indian kings (and he draws "not Mughal": the monarch is the British Crown, not the Mughal emperor). That is why from 1858 Indian "Kings" were called Indian "Princes": a Prince is the son of a King, and the King is the British monarch. Therefore the whole of India is part of the British empire, and it splits into British India (ruled by the British) and 565 princely States (ruled by an Indian Prince). Symbolic sovereignty: under Subordinate Union the British hold external sovereignty (D, C, FA: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) and the Indian Prince holds domestic sovereign functions; under SA the same split existed but the Indian king held symbolic sovereignty and the EIC held the external functions (D, C, FA). Do not use "Prince" and "King" loosely in answers about 1858 onwards. The handout and the teacher both say: after 1858 the correct word is Indian Prince; "King" is the pre-1858 word. Paramountcy of the EIC (1813-58) and Paramountcy of the Crown (1858-1947) are two different legal relationships. Mnemonic: Prince = son of the King, and the King is in London. Decode: from 1858 Indian "Kings" become Indian Princes because the British Crown is the monarch of Indian kings (not the Mughal). 565 princely States are ruled by Indian Princes; British India is ruled by the British. External functions D-C-FA go to the Crown. Why it sticks: "Prince" literally means junior to a King; the King is the Crown. Mnemonic: "D-C-FA": what Subordinate Union takes (Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs). Decode: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs = external functions with the British Crown; domestic sovereign functions stay with the Indian Prince. Subordinate Union = Paramountcy + sovereignty with the Crown. Why it sticks: "D-C-FA" reads like a three-letter department: "DC and FA".  The arc's last stage (typed slide, no ink): Subordinate Union 1858-1947: after 1857 the EIC abolished, the British State takes direct control; Indian rulers legally part of the British Empire (Prince, not King); sovereignty and external functions (D, C, FA) with the British Crown; domestic sovereign functions with the Indian Prince; formula: Subordinate Union = Paramountcy + sovereignty formally with the British Crown. 12.6 The arc in five steps 1600: a trading company that wanted to be left alone (Relative Isolation) 1765: a military alliance partner (PoIR and PoRF; ToA 1765) 1798: a dominant power controlling neighbours' armies and foreign policies (PoSA) 1813: a State openly declaring all others subservient to its interests (Paramountcy, Francis Hastings 13-23) (bad) 1858: a Crown that absorbed 565 Indian princes as legal subordinates (Subordinate Union) Each stage built legally and institutionally on the previous. This logical unfolding is exactly why 1857 happened when it did. (Handout, Sec 12.) Mnemonic: "Alone, Ally, Army, All-ruler, Absorber": the five steps. Decode: 1600 Alone (left alone, isolation); 1765 Ally (military alliance partner); 1798 Army (controls neighbours' armies and foreign policy); 1813 All-ruler (Paramountcy: supreme); 1858 Absorber (the Crown absorbs 565 princes). Why it sticks: five A-words, one per step: Alone, Ally, Army, All, Absorb. Mnemonic: 1600, 1765, 1798, 1813, 1858: "Sixteen hundred, then 65, 98, 13, 58". Decode: the five dates of the policy arc: 1600, 1765, 1798, 1813, 1858. Gaps: 165, 33, 15, 45. Why it sticks: listen to the rhythm: the middle two (98 and 13) are the quickest steps, only 15 years apart.

items.t: 13 · Critique: consolidation at the cost of legitimacy
items.x: Consolidation at the Cost of Legitimacy (typed slide, no ink). Thesis: Dalhousie 48-56 consolidated the Company State but destroyed its legitimacy; almost every major 1857 leader was annexation-aggrieved: 1 Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi, Lapse 1854); 2 Nana Sahib (Bajirao II 96-18's pension refused 1851); 3 Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, the last Mughal, whose titular dignity Dalhousie 48-56 sought to end. Coalition: the court of Awadh, disbanded Sikh soldiery, dispossessed talukdars and inam-holders stripped by the Inam Commission 1852. 13.1 Consolidation at the cost of legitimacy Dalhousie 48-56 consolidated the Company State but destroyed its legitimacy. Almost every major leader of the 1857 revolt was annexation-aggrieved:   Leader   Grievance    --- ---    Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi   Lapse 1854 (Section 3)     Nana Sahib   Bajirao II 96-18's pension refused, 1851 (Section 5)     Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57   The last Mughal, whose titular dignity Dalhousie 48-56 sought to end   The court of Awadh (Section 7), the disbanded Sikh soldiery (Section 8), the dispossessed talukdars and the inam-holders stripped by the Inam Commission 1852 (Section 4) all joined or supported the revolt. (Recall: the Inam Commission was Lapse applied to land titles: the same legitimacy-override logic.) See Chapter 21. Mnemonic: "Lakshmibai, Nana, Zafar": the three annexation-aggrieved names (Lapse 1854, Pension 1851, Dignity). Decode: Lakshmibai (Jhansi Lapse 1854), Nana Sahib (Bajirao II 96-18's pension of Rs 8 lakh refused 1851), Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 (the last Mughal's titular dignity). Plus the Awadh court, disbanded Sikh soldiers, talukdars and inam-holders. Why it sticks: the three grievances are Throne, Pension, Title: L-N-Z = Land, Name, Zafar. 13.2 Post-Dalhousie: Canning 56-62 inherits and the Queen ends Lapse  Post-Dalhousie: Queen Victoria Ends Lapse (typed slide, no ink). Handover: Dalhousie 48-56 handed power to Canning 56-62 in 1856, who inherited the empire and the revolt his annexations had sown. 1858: after the suppression of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the Company State and transferred power to the Crown. Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged respect for the treaties and rights of Indian rulers: an explicit reversal. No further annexations followed, even where Paramountcy-era instruments were tightened (Treaty of Jacobabad 1876). The empire was complete; it only needed managing. Dalhousie 48-56 handed power to Canning 56-62 in 1856, who inherited the empire Dalhousie 48-56 built and the revolt his annexations had sown the seeds of. After the suppression of the 1857 revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the Company State and transferred power to the British Crown. Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged that the treaties and rights of Indian rulers would be respected: an explicit reversal of Dalhousie 48-56's core policy. Paramountcy became Subordinate Union (Section 12.5). No further annexations followed, a line Dalhousie 48-56's successors (including Viceroy Lytton 76-80) did not cross, even where Paramountcy-era instruments were tightened (the Treaty of Jacobabad 1876 with Kalat). The empire was complete; it only needed managing. Mnemonic: 58 is the reversal: Act, Proclamation, Union. Decode: 1858: the Government of India Act abolishes the Company State; Queen Victoria's Proclamation ends Lapse and respects treaties; Paramountcy gives way to Subordinate Union. After Dalhousie 48-56 (Canning 56-62 inherits) there are no further annexations. Why it sticks: three things in one year, each undoing what Dalhousie 48-56 built.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The story of "Dalhousie 48-56's three roads, two coasts, one crack": from Paramountcy to 1857. A trading company wanted to be left Alone (1600), became an Ally (1765), then an Army that ran its neighbours (SA 1798), then the All-ruler (Paramountcy 1813, Francis Hastings 13-23): by 1856 it held 63% of land and 78% of people. Then Dalhousie 48-56 went down his three roads: Lapse (Court of Directors 1847: Satara 48, 49 twins, Baghat 50, Udaipur 52, Jhansi and Nagpur 54), War (Lahore 9 March 1846 and Amritsar 16 March, then Punjab 1849 and the Koh-i-Noor; Pegu 1852-53), and Lieu (Berar 1853). Awadh fell by misgovernance, not Lapse: Clive 57-67's 1765, Shore's Rs 76 lakh 1798, Wellesley 98-05's half in 1801, then the rest in 1856. Round the coast the maritime fence closed (Bay clockwise, Sea anticlockwise, Kalat 1854 then Jacobabad 1876), and Dalhousie 48-56 laid rail, wire, post and Wood's Despatch. But Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib and Zafar carried the grievance into 1857, and in 1858 the Crown reversed Lapse and became the Absorber of 565 princes. Decode: 1847, 1848-54, 1856, 1857, 1858.

The handout's three-bucket answer, see the skeleton below. The slide sends you to a separate MMP deck (Fable_MMP_Ch_15) for the answer map; that deck is not in this notebook   Section 12   What to prepare. Prelims hooks: the champion-to-ideology pairs (Warren Hastings 73-85 = Orientalism; Cornwallis 86-93 = Authoritarianism; Macaulay = Liberalism; Bentham and James Mill = Utilitarianism; Charles Grant = Evangelicalism; Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05 = post-1857); the four Orientalist institutions with year, founder and role (1781, 1784, 1791, 1800); Fort William College = train British civilians; the Cornwallis 86-93 four-point shift; Sleeman = Thugs; Lytton 76-80 = Forward Policy; Dufferin 84-88 = Upper Burma 1886; Imperial Preference = tariff, Ottawa 1932; Charter Act 1833 did not give an Indian the law member's seat (slide 104). Mains hooks: why ideology came before policy (belief and narrative together); the Orientalism to Authoritarianism to Liberal-Utilitarian-Evangelical to Racism arc; the post-1857 six-front shift; world events that fed Indian nationalism (Mains 2014). Closing idea: every ideology was a different answer to one question, "how exactly should we civilise India?", and every one served British power. Mains PYQ skeleton (Mains 2014, from the handout and slide 101 only)   Part   What to write    --- ---    Intro   Colonial rule was challenged by ideas as much as by arms; the White Man's Burden produced its own opposite, anti-colonial currents that travelled into India through newspapers, returning students and political exiles     Body 1: political and ideological   Enlightenment, American Revolution (movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83), French Revolution 1789 (liberty, equality, fraternity), European revolutions of 1830 and 1848, Irish Home Rule (1870-1914) and Irish armed struggle (1916-21)     Body 2: economic   The Industrial Revolution's destruction of Indian handloom (deindustrialisation) fed the Drain Theory of Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt     Body 3: social and ideological   Russian Revolution 1917 (peasant-worker mobilisation model, anti-imperial vocabulary); self-determination (Wilson's Fourteen Points 1918) and rising anti-racism     Body 4: the carriers   Gandhi from South Africa (1893-1915 diaspora struggles); Nehru from Cambridge (western liberal-democratic theory)     Closing   The ideas arrived through people; the empire's own moral claim became its weak point   The question bank page for this chapter holds the full list: 14 Prelims PYQs, 1 Mains PYQ, 15 practice Prelims questions and 2 practice Mains questions. Use the Question bank button on the chapter page; it is not copied here. Several of the 14 are cross-listed items (education chronology, Charter Act 1833, Press Regulation 1799, Factory Act, economic critics of colonialism) that belong mainly to other chapters.
