items.t: 1 · Why ideology comes before policy
items.x: British Imperial Ideologies are the ideas that shaped colonial policy. They were not one fixed set. They changed over time and sometimes competed. They shared one function: they gave the British a way to tell themselves and the world that what they were doing in India was not just profitable but morally right. Every ideology was both a genuine belief held by some Englishmen and a convenient narrative to make imperialism look ethical. Both layers operate at once. For Mains: always show both layers. Sincere belief and convenient cover story together. Many Englishmen were sincere (Section 5.5), and the ideas still served British power.

items.t: 2 · Foundation: the White Man's Burden (WMB)
items.x: No class notes beyond the board. The typed slides 69-71 repeat the handout; the board on slide 65 is the only ink (below).  Teacher's board: WMB (circled). "# Civilize Rest of WORLD"; "# We are Superior". A bracket with four bullets: "(IR) 1750-1850 : 1st"; "7YR GLOBAL WAR 1756-63 : WON"; "EARLIEST of Democracies"; "empire". All other ideologies rested on one belief: Western European civilisation was superior, so the British had a responsibility to civilise the rest of the world. This is the White Man's Burden (WMB). Teacher: WMB = "Civilize the rest of the world" and "We are superior". His bracket gives the reasons for the confidence: the Industrial Revolution 1750-1850: first (Britain was first); the Seven Years' Global War 1756-63: won; the earliest of democracies; and empire. (After "1st" the line trails off, and slide 70 of the handout carries the rest.) 2.1 The roots of British civilisational confidence The British had genuine reasons to believe in their superiority: World's first modern democracy: the English Civil War + Glorious Revolution (17th century). Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850). Won the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63): the top global power. Financially backed the coalition that defeated Napoleon at Leipzig (1813); led the allied armies to final victory with Prussia at Waterloo (1815). Capitalism and science transforming British society at an unprecedented pace. A nation that achieves all this within 150 years can convince itself that it is destined to lead the world. Every major imperial power had its own version of WMB. Mnemonic: "Democracy, Machines, War, Napoleon, Science": D-M-W-N-S. Decode: first modern Democracy (Civil War + Glorious Revolution, 17th century); Machines = Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850); Won the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63); Napoleon beaten (Leipzig 1813, Waterloo 1815); Science and capitalism. Why it sticks: five proud steps in time order, the 17th century to 1815. Mnemonic: Leipzig 13, Waterloo 15. Decode: Britain financed the coalition that won at Leipzig (1813) and led the allied armies with Prussia to final victory at Waterloo (1815). Why it sticks: the two years are two steps apart, 13 then 15: money first, sword second. 2.2 WMB as roof, and the counter-ideologies as reaction WMB was the roof over everything else. The specific ideologies below were different answers to the same question: how exactly should we civilise India? WMB also generated its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies worldwide: American Revolution: a political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. French Revolution (1789): liberty, equality, fraternity. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848. Irish Home Rule movement (1870-1914) and the Irish armed struggle for independence (1916-21). These challenged imperial-superiority assumptions and inspired colonised peoples, including Indian nationalists. (Section 12 develops this: Mains 2014.) Slide 71 shows only two of the four counter-ideologies (the American Revolution and the Irish struggle). The handout lists all four; Section 12 repeats the four. Use the handout's four. Mnemonic: "A-F-E-I": the four counter-currents. Decode: American Revolution (from 1765; war 1776-83), French Revolution (1789), European revolutions (1830 and 1848), Irish Home Rule (1870-1914; armed struggle 1916-21). Why it sticks: "AFEI" is simply the order in time.

items.t: 3 · Orientalism (1765-1813): Rule India, the India Way
items.x: 3.1 Orientalism defined In the 18th century the British used language and literature as the measure of civilisation. Scholars like William Jones studied Sanskrit and found it older and grammatically more sophisticated than ancient Greek and Latin. The conclusion: India had been a great ancient civilisation, and European and Indian languages belonged to the same family (today's Indo-European family: genuine scholarship, not propaganda). So Orientalism said: India's ancient past was glorious even if its present was degenerate, so the British should study Indian tradition and rule India by its own customs and laws. In short: Rule India, the India Way. A date slip on slide 72. The typed slide writes William Jones as "(late 19th c)"; the handout places this scholarship in the 18th century, and the Asiatic Society that Jones founded is dated 1784. Use the handout: 18th century. Teacher: On his board the teacher glosses "Oriental" as "related to east" and writes "Rule India the INDIA WAY" with four bullets: Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages, Indian syllabus in schools and colleges. These four bullets are the practical content of Orientalism. Mnemonic: "HILL": the four things Orientalism ruled by. Decode: Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian Languages, Indian syllabus (Learning in schools and colleges). Why it sticks: the teacher's four bullets fit the word HILL; Orientalism = "go up the hill of Indian tradition". 3.2 Why the EIC adopted Orientalism Two practical reasons: The EIC was militarily not yet confident before 1813. Victory in the Carnatic, Mysore and Maratha Wars was never guaranteed, and one badly handled cultural insult could trigger mass resistance. Ruling through Indian customs reduced that risk. Some Englishmen believed India was not ready for British modernity. Imposing alien systems would do more damage than good. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Orientalism's most prominent champion. He argued that the more the British understood Indian traditions, the lighter the chains of colonialism would feel. Mnemonic: "Scared and Spared": two reasons for Orientalism. Decode: the EIC was scared (not militarily confident before 1813; one insult could spark mass resistance) and wanted to spare India from alien systems (some Englishmen thought India not ready for British modernity). Champion: Warren Hastings 73-85, "lighter chains". Why it sticks: scared for self, sparing the Indian. 3.2.1 The four Orientalist institutions  Typed slide: Four Orientalist Institutions: 1781 Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings 73-85); 1784 Asiatic Society of Bengal (Sir William Jones); 1791 Sanskrit College in Banaras (Jonathan Duncan); 1800 Fort William College (Wellesley 98-05). No ink.   #   Year   Institution   Founder and capacity    --- --- --- ---    1   1781   Calcutta Madrasa   Warren Hastings 73-85, as Governor-General of Bengal; mainly for the study of Islamic law and customs     2   1784   Asiatic Society of Bengal   Sir William Jones, as Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court at Calcutta; to study Asian history, antiquities and culture     3   1791   Sanskrit College, Banaras   Jonathan Duncan, as British Resident at Benares; for the study of Hindu law and philosophy     4   1800   Fort William College, Calcutta   Wellesley 98-05, as Governor-General of Bengal; to train newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages and administration    Handout flow chart of the Orientalist institutions: Calcutta Madrasa 1781 (Warren Hastings 73-85 as GG of Bengal; Islamic law and customs) to Asiatic Society of Bengal 1784 (Sir William Jones, Puisne Judge; Sanskrit-Greek-Latin kinship) to Sanskrit College Banaras 1791 (Jonathan Duncan, Resident at Benares; Hindu law and philosophy) to the Prelims 2020 box (Fort William College Calcutta 1800, Wellesley 98-05: TRAIN BRITISH CIVILIANS). It continues with H.T. Colebrooke, H.H. Wilson and James Prinsep (Brahmi decipherment; Orientalist scholarship), then "ASI founded 1861, Alexander Cunningham", then the Prelims 2023 box. The figure holds names the handout text does not: Colebrooke, Wilson and Prinsep (Brahmi decipherment) and the ASI founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham. The handout's summary table (Section 13) also lists Colebrooke and Wilson as Orientalism's champions. They are figure-only items; learn them lightly. Mnemonic: "1781-84-91-1800: Mad, Asia, Sanskrit, Fort." Decode: 1781 Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings 73-85); 1784 Asiatic Society (William Jones); 1791 Sanskrit College Banaras (Jonathan Duncan); 1800 Fort William College (Wellesley 98-05). Why it sticks: the years climb 81, 84, 91 and then jump to the century mark, 1800. Mnemonic: Who wore which hat. Decode: Hastings 73-85 = Governor-General; Jones = Puisne Judge; Duncan = Resident at Benares; Wellesley 98-05 = Governor-General. Two GGs, one judge, one Resident. Why it sticks: the "capacity" column is a favourite trap, and two of the four are GGs. Wellesley 98-05's second motive for Fort William College: to keep French republican ideas away from his officers. The French Revolution 1789 had overthrown the monarchy by 1792, and Wellesley 98-05 did not want anti-monarchy ideas infecting his men. 3.3 Orientalism's political angle The British supported the Aryan Invasion Theory: ancient India's cultural greatness was actually brought by Europeans who migrated to India in ancient times. Even while praising India, the British claimed credit. The argument of kinship: Europeans and Indians were separated kin connected through language. It was used to reduce Indian opposition: "we are not foreigners, we are cousins who have come home." This was a rhetoric of love to disguise the reality of exploitation. Mnemonic: "Cousins come home." Decode: Aryan Invasion Theory = Europeans brought India's greatness; kinship through language = "we are cousins who have come home". Real purpose: a rhetoric of love to disguise exploitation. Why it sticks: an exploiter who calls himself family.  PYQ 3, Prelims 2020, answer slide: Wellesley and Fort William College. Answer (d), train British civilians; (a) Board of Directors wrong, Wellesley's own initiative; (b) revive oriental learning wrong, the Asiatic Society 1784 and Sanskrit College 1791 did that; (c) employment for Carey wrong. Hook: Fort William College = train EIC civilians in Indian languages. No ink. Prelims 2020 trap: answer (d) train British civilians. The three wrong options each sound plausible. (a) the Board of Directors asked: wrong, it was Wellesley 98-05's own initiative. (b) revive oriental learning: wrong, that was the Asiatic Society 1784 and Sanskrit College 1791. (c) employment for William Carey: wrong, Carey was an employee, not the founding purpose. The slide and the handout agree. Mnemonic: Fort William = Fitness for Work: train civilians. Decode: Fort William College (1800, Wellesley 98-05) trains newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages and administration. Not Board orders, not oriental revival, not Carey's job. Why it sticks: a college for new recruits = a training camp, not a museum.

items.t: 4 · Authoritarianism: Cornwallis 86-93 and Conservatism
items.x: 4.1 The Cornwallis 86-93 shift  Typed slide: Authoritarianism, the Cornwallis 86-93 Shift (critics of Orientalism; first systematic GG; 1 All-British senior administration). No ink; the ink for this idea is on the master board, slide 66. Orientalism had critics from the beginning. The study of ancient India had only confirmed that India's past was glorious and its present degenerate. That made restoring the past pointless and called for imposing the British system instead. Cornwallis 86-93 was the first Governor-General to implement this vision systematically. He ruled India, the English Way. Four specific measures: All-British senior administration. He replaced all Indians in senior administrative positions with British officials. His argument: Indian administrators were corrupt and incompetent; only British authority could deliver rule of law. (Deeper argument: only by removing Indians from power can the British civilise India. This "corrupt-native-needs-the-honest-foreigner" story was used through 1947 to justify exclusion.) Rule of Law through codification. The Charter Act 1793, influenced by Cornwallis 86-93, established civil law and protection of individual rights and private property. It reintroduced separation of powers at the district level: the District Collector would no longer also be the District Judge. Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal, converting zamindars into large landlords on the English model. (Full treatment in the Land Revenue Systems chapter, Chapter 16.) Aloof Elite. EIC officials were discouraged from mixing with Indians. Indian wives were discouraged. Eurasians were barred from EIC service. Officials having Indian wives were barred from purchasing land in India.  Typed slide: The Cornwallis 86-93 Shift (contd.): 2 Rule of Law (Charter Act 1793; Collector no longer also Judge); 3 Permanent Settlement 1793; 4 Aloof Elite. No ink. Teacher: Authoritarianism = "MY WAY OR HIGHWAY" and "Removed Indians from all senior positions." About the Permanent Settlement he wrote: "PS 1793 based on English way of agriculture = OUTLIER to Orientalism." That is the reasoning: Orientalism meant ruling the Indian way, but the Permanent Settlement copied the English landlord model, so it breaks the Orientalist pattern and belongs with Authoritarianism. Mnemonic: "A-R-P-A": Cornwallis 86-93's four steps. Decode: All-British senior posts (Indians removed); Rule of law by codification (Charter Act 1793; Collector is no longer Judge); Permanent Settlement 1793 (zamindars as English-style landlords); Aloof Elite (no mixing, no Indian wives, Eurasians barred, no land purchase for officers with Indian wives). Why it sticks: "ARPA" like "Arpa", one tidy list of four. Mnemonic: Collector or Judge, not both. Decode: Charter Act 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93's influence) separated powers at the district level: the District Collector no longer also functions as the District Judge. Why it sticks: one chair, one job. 4.2 The Aloof-Elite doctrine Cornwallis 86-93 had personally commanded the British army's defeat in the American War of Independence (1776-83). He had watched British settlers in the 13 American colonies develop deep roots (family, property, identity) and then fight for independence as their homeland. He was determined not to let the same happen in India. The rule: keep the rulers separate from the ruled. Never let India become home. Wellesley 98-05 shared this authoritarian instinct. Both administrations were control-oriented, centralised and mistrustful of Indian agency.  Typed slide: Cornwallis 86-93's Aloof-Elite Doctrine (why: the American War of Independence 1776-83; the rule: keep rulers separate; Wellesley 98-05 too). No ink. Mnemonic: "Lost America, so no roots in India." Decode: Cornwallis 86-93 lost in the American War of Independence (1776-83); British settlers in the 13 colonies grew roots and fought for their homeland; so in India: no mixing, no marriage, no land, never let India become home. Why it sticks: a lost war turned into a rule. 4.3 Conservatism: Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras 1820-27) was a hybrid of Orientalism and Authoritarianism. India should be governed through its own traditions, but the British would govern, with no leadership role for Indians. Total power centralised in EIC hands, but exercised through Indian forms (Indian laws and customs). His Ryotwari Settlement (1801-07, 1820+) in the Madras Presidency was inspired by the ancient Indian model of the State collecting revenue directly from the peasant, without intermediaries. But all collection was done by EIC officials, with no Indians in senior roles. The formula: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. Mountstuart Elphinstone, John Malcolm and Charles Metcalfe followed the same school. Elphinstone, a disciple of Munro, later implemented the Ryotwari Settlement in Bombay. Mnemonic: "Indian coat, British hand." Decode: Munro's Conservatism = Orientalist in form (Indian traditions, Ryotwari's direct State-peasant model) and Authoritarian in substance (all collection by EIC officials; no Indians in senior roles). School: Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe (Elphinstone took Ryotwari to Bombay). Why it sticks: the coat is Indian, the hand inside it is British. No class notes beyond the typed slide for Conservatism. The master board (slide 66) has no column for it.

items.t: 5 · Three new ideologies (post 1813): Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism
items.x: 5.1 The post-1813 sharp turn By 1813 the landscape had changed dramatically: The EIC had defeated all major Indian powers; only Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State remained as potential rivals. The Company's army had grown huge. Britain had defeated Napoleon. The Industrial Revolution was in full swing. The EIC was now confident enough to rule India the British way: openly, aggressively, without apology. There was also a new economic motive: an India with western tastes and western education would become a market for British manufactured goods. Three ideologies filled the space Orientalism had occupied: Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism. Mnemonic: "Four wins, one market": why 1813 turned. Decode: four changes (Indian powers beaten except Holkar, Bhonsle, Sikh State; a huge army; Napoleon beaten; Industrial Revolution in full swing) plus one motive: a market for British goods through western tastes and education. Why it sticks: strength first, then shopkeeping. Mnemonic: Three left standing: H-B-S. Decode: Holkar, Bhonsle, Sikh State were the only potential rivals left by 1813. Why it sticks: "HBS" like a station code, three stops left. 5.2 Liberalism  Typed slide: Liberalism (argument: the Great Bengal Famine 1770; goal: liberate India from feudalism; champion Macaulay). No ink. Liberals argued that the EIC had governed India badly under Orientalism. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (one crore Indians perished while the EIC doubled land revenue) was cited as proof. India needed to be modernised through the best ideas of the age (best meaning western). Goal: liberate India from feudalism: feudal polity (no democracy), feudal economy (agrarian, closed, unequal), feudal society (birth-based discrimination, no women's rights), and replace it with modern British institutions. Thomas Macaulay, legal member of the GG's council under the Charter Act 1833, was the most prominent Liberal. His three signature interventions:  Typed slide: Liberalism (contd.), Macaulay's 3 Interventions: Law Commission 1834; Minute on Education 1835 (Brown Sahibs); Charter Act 1813 (ended the EIC's trade monopoly); social reform: Bentinck 28-35's Sati Abolition Act 1829. No ink. Law Commission (1834): codified western-style laws for British India by 1837. Minute on Indian Education (1835): proposed western education in English to create Brown Sahibs (brown on the outside, British on the inside): a class of Indians as cultural intermediaries between British rulers and the Indian masses. Charter Act 1813 (a Liberal-influenced reform): ended the EIC's monopoly over Indian trade and let non-EIC British businesses enter India freely. This was economic liberalism for British businesses, not for Indian ones. Social reform followed too: Bentinck 28-35 brought the Sati Abolition Act 1829 under Liberal influence (full treatment in Chapter 19). A date wrinkle. The slide and the handout list the Charter Act 1813 among Macaulay's "interventions", yet his seat on the GG's council came under the Charter Act 1833. The handout itself calls the 1813 Act a "Liberal-influenced reform", so read it as a Liberal-era measure that opened trade, not as Macaulay's own act. Learn the pair: Law Commission 1834, Minute 1835 are his. Mnemonic: "Law, Learn, Lift the monopoly": Macaulay's three. Decode: Law Commission (1834; codified western-style laws by 1837); Learn = Minute on Education (1835; English; Brown Sahibs); Lift the monopoly = Charter Act 1813 (non-EIC British businesses allowed in). Why it sticks: three L-words in a row. Mnemonic: Brown skin, British mind: "Brown Sahib". Decode: Macaulay's Minute on Education 1835: western education in English to create Indians who are brown outside and British inside, cultural go-betweens for the rulers and the masses. Why it sticks: the phrase itself is the picture. Mnemonic: Three feudals: P-E-S. Decode: Liberals wanted to end feudal Polity (no democracy), Economy (agrarian, closed, unequal) and Society (birth-based discrimination, no women's rights). Why it sticks: "PES" = polity, economy, society, the old triple. Mnemonic: 1770 and "doubled". Decode: Liberals' proof that Orientalism governed badly: the Great Bengal Famine 1770, one crore perished while the EIC doubled land revenue. Why it sticks: crore dead, revenue doubled: the two numbers sit in one line. 5.3 Utilitarianism  Typed slide: Utilitarianism (Bentham and James Mill; History of British India 1818; push for the Law Commission; inherent authoritarian streak). No ink. Associated with Jeremy Bentham and James Mill. India needed not culture change but good policy and a strong rule of law. The State's job: design laws that maximise benefit for the largest number of people. James Mill's History of British India (1818) declared India's great past a myth and argued India needed an effective schoolmaster: someone to impose good governance from above. Mill joined the Court of Directors of the EIC in London and pushed for the Law Commission in 1834 under Macaulay. Utilitarianism contains an inherent authoritarian streak. Teacher: Utilitarianism = "civil servant mind" with four words: effectiveness, max results, implementable, practical. Then: "Bring good laws and a strong State for rule of law." The reasoning: a utilitarian cares about what works, not what is traditional or Christian, so the answer is laws and a strong State. Mnemonic: "Mill, the Schoolmaster": History 1818. Decode: James Mill's History of British India (1818) called India's great past a myth and said India needed an effective schoolmaster imposing good governance from above; as a Director in London he pushed the Law Commission 1834 under Macaulay. Why it sticks: one teacher, one cane, one book in 1818. 5.4 Evangelicalism  Typed slide: Evangelicalism (India's problem = its religion; model Protestant Christianity; Charles Grant and the Charter Act 1813; Lex Loci Act 1850). No ink. Evangelists argued India's fundamental problem was its religion, which promoted superstition, ignorance, idolatry and tyranny of priests and blocked scientific thinking. Religion shapes values; values shape society. Change the religion, change everything. Their model was Protestant Christianity in western Europe, where Protestant ethics supported the rise of capitalism and modernity. Charles Grant, a member of the Court of Directors and later an MP, influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise the entry of Christian missionaries into India. The Lex Loci Act / Removal of Religious-Caste Disabilities Act (1850) allowed a convert to retain inheritance rights in family property, removing one practical obstacle to conversion (full treatment in Chapter 19). Teacher: "Evangelicalism: CHRISTIANIZE India to MODERNIZE India." Mnemonic: Charter 1813: Grant opens the gate; Lex Loci 1850 clears the road. Decode: Charles Grant (Director, later MP) influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise missionary entry; the Lex Loci Act 1850 let a convert keep inheritance rights in family property. Why it sticks: gate first (1813), then the road (1850). Charter Act 1813 appears under two ideologies. Liberal side: ended the EIC's trade monopoly (section 5.2). Evangelical side: allowed missionaries (this section). Both are in the handout. Keep the two effects apart. Mnemonic: Three ideas, three verbs after 1813: L-U-E. Decode: Liberalism = give the best (= west) ideas; Utilitarianism = good laws and a strong State; Evangelicalism = Christianize to modernize. Why it sticks: "LUE" = clue; the clue is one verb each. 5.5 Common ground across the three All three pushed for reform of the colonial State and together built the narrative of Benevolent Colonialism: "we are here to help you." Many Englishmen who believed in these ideologies were sincere. And yet all three together contributed to the conditions that produced the Revolt of 1857: cultural, economic and political resistance to a colonial project that had touched almost every aspect of Indian life.

items.t: 6 · The Liberalism shift 1828-35
items.x: The short window from Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's 1835 Minute is the high-water mark of Liberal confidence in India. Four headline interventions: Sati Abolition Act 1829: criminalised widow-burning (full treatment in Chapter 19). Thuggee Suppression (1830s-40s): under Captain William Sleeman; restored police order on the Grand Trunk roads (Section 8; Prelims 1997). Macaulay's Education Minute 1835: made English the medium of higher instruction, displacing Persian. Cornwallis 86-93 Code progressively revised into a uniform criminal procedure: the foundation Macaulay's 1834 Law Commission would build on. Charter Act 1833: the trap (slide 104). The slide warns: the Charter Act 1833 did NOT make the provision that an Indian be appointed as a law member in the GG's council (Prelims 2003, answer (d) in the bank). Macaulay, the law member, was a Briton. Mnemonic: "Sati, Thugs, English, Code": the 1828-35 four. Decode: Sati Abolition 1829; Thugs suppressed (Sleeman); English replaces Persian in higher instruction (Minute 1835); Code: Cornwallis 86-93 Code revised into uniform criminal procedure (base for the 1834 Law Commission). Why it sticks: S-T-E-C, in the order of the handout list.

items.t: 7 · Racism + Authoritarianism (post 1857)
items.x: The Revolt of 1857 shook the British not just militarily but psychologically. The scale of Indian violence against British rule (soldiers, civilians, women, children) broke the paternalistic narrative. The British had told themselves they were trustees and reformers. 1857 told them that a very large number of Indians did not see it that way. Teacher: Column 4 of the board: "1857 Revolt = SHOCK for British." "Indians are beyond Reform." "Ideology = DOGS & Indians not allowed." "Up-up Authoritarianism (+) up-up RACISM." (The teacher underlined "Dogs", "Indians" and "not allowed" in green.) 7.1 The six-front sharp shift after 1857 Reformist impulse retreated sharply. Liberalism, Utilitarianism and Evangelicalism (Section 5) collapsed. Many concluded that Indians were beyond redemption through reform. Racial sciences shift. European racial classification in the second half of the 19th century shifted from language (the Orientalist criterion) to physical features. Indians were now classed as an inferior and fundamentally different race: not separated kin (Section 3) but a lower order of humanity. Aryan Invasion Theory kept but twisted. Europeans had founded the Vedic civilisation, but by intermarrying with indigenous Indians over millennia they lost their racial superiority and degraded. Even India's ancient greatness was now used as evidence of Indian inferiority. "Dogs and Indians not allowed": seen on signs at clubs and parks in colonial India; it captures the spirit of post-1857 attitudes. Authoritarianism increased. The British became distrustful of sharing power with Indians in any meaningful way. Social reforms slowed sharply. Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 explicitly promised religious tolerance and non-interference in Indian customs: a direct acknowledgement that missionary and reformer interference had been a major grievance of 1857. From here, social and political reforms came mainly in response to pressure from Indian leaders, not British initiative.  Typed slide: Six-Front Shift (contd.): 4 "Dogs and Indians not allowed"; 5 Authoritarianism up; 6 reforms slowed (Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858). No ink. The table below contrasts the two uses of the Aryan idea and of race.   Aspect   Orientalism (before 1857)   After 1857    --- --- ---    Criterion of race   Language   Physical features     Indians seen as   Separated kin, cousins   Inferior, different race, a lower order     Aryan Invasion Theory   Europeans brought India's greatness: "cousins come home"   Europeans founded Vedic civilisation but intermarried and degraded     Policy mood   Rule India the India Way   Reform retreated; more Authoritarianism   Mnemonic: "R-R-A-D-A-S": the six fronts. Decode: Reform retreated; Racial sciences (language to physical features); Aryan theory twisted; Dogs and Indians not allowed; Authoritarianism up; Social reforms slowed (Queen's Proclamation 1858). Why it sticks: the six initials follow the handout order exactly. Mnemonic: 1858: the Queen promises not to meddle. Decode: Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858: religious tolerance and non-interference in Indian customs, because missionary and reformer interference was a major grievance of 1857. Why it sticks: after the fire, the promise of "hands off". 7.2 Post-1857 architects: Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05  Typed slide: Post-1857 Architects: Lytton 76-80 (Vernacular Press Act 1878 and Arms Act 1878) and Curzon 99-05 (Partition of Bengal 1905). No ink. The architects of this harder imperialism were Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05: men for whom empire was a project of prestige, paramountcy and racial hierarchy. Lytton 76-80: the Vernacular Press Act 1878 and Arms Act 1878 reinstated racial privilege (VPA in Chapter 19). Curzon 99-05: the Partition of Bengal (1905) was the same mindset applied administratively (in Chapter 29). Mnemonic: "L78, C05": two Viceroys, two marks. Decode: Lytton 76-80 = Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act, both 1878; Curzon 99-05 = Partition of Bengal 1905. Both = prestige, paramountcy, racial hierarchy. Why it sticks: the initials and the last two digits: L-78, C-05.

items.t: 8 · Law and order paternalism: Sleeman and the Thugs
items.x: Typed slide: Law and Order Paternalism, Sleeman (a parallel track; the Thuggee and Dacoity Department set up 1835; three tools; over 3,000 Thugs convicted 1831-41). No ink. Between Orientalism and Liberalism the EIC also ran a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism: reclaiming the roads, the courts and rural policing in the name of the peasant's physical safety. The flagship was the Thuggee and Dacoity Suppression campaign of the 1830s-40s, built around Captain (later Major-General Sir) William Sleeman, under Bentinck 28-35. His Thuggee and Dacoity Department (set up 1835) used three tools: Informant networks infiltrating Thug bands. Approver testimony: captured Thugs gave evidence against their associates in exchange for lighter sentences. Swift judicial commissions: dedicated tribunals delivering rapid trials. Together these dismantled organised highway murder cults that had made long-distance trade on the Grand Trunk Road a life-and-death gamble. Over 3,000 Thugs were convicted between 1831 and 1841. Mnemonic: "I-A-S" for Sleeman: Informant, Approver, Swift commission. Decode: Informant networks; Approver testimony (lighter sentence for evidence); Swift judicial commissions. Department set up 1835; over 3,000 convicted 1831-41. Why it sticks: Sleeman's tools spell IAS.  PYQ 1, Prelims 1997, answer slide: Suppression of Thugs. Answer (b) Captain Sleeman; (a) Prendergast = Upper Burma 1885-86; (c) Burnes = Afghan-frontier agent killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841; (d) Pemberton = Assam/Burma frontier officer. Hook: Sleeman = Thugs; Prendergast = Burma; Burnes = Afghanistan. No ink. Prelims 1997 trap: answer (b) Captain Sleeman. Prendergast = Upper Burma 1885-86 (Section 10). Burnes = Afghan frontier, killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841 (Section 9). Pemberton = Assam/Burma frontier officer. The slide and the handout agree. Mnemonic: Sleeman = Thugs, Prendergast = Burma, Burnes = Afghanistan. Decode: S-T, P-B, B-A: the three names and their three places. Handout hook, copied as written. Why it sticks: say it as one line, S-P-B, and the places follow: Thugs, Burma, Afghanistan.

items.t: 9 · The Forward Policy in Afghanistan: from Auckland 36-42 to Lytton 76-80
items.x: Typed slide: Forward Policy in Afghanistan, Auckland 36-42 to Lytton 76-80. What it was; 1 Auckland 36-42 launched the disastrous 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42; 2 Ellenborough 42-44: "Ended Forward Policy (*Correct this in notes) - re-established British dominance of Kabul in 1842". No ink. The Forward Policy was the militarised face of post-1840s British imperialism on the north-west frontier: Britain should actively push its effective frontier into Afghanistan to pre-empt Tsarist Russian influence, rather than defend a fixed line at the Indus. Its arc ran through multiple Governors-General and is a classic PYQ trap: Auckland 36-42 launched the disastrous 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42) to reinstall Shah Shuja against Dost Mohammad. The retreat from Kabul (January 1842) wiped out almost an entire British-Indian army. Ellenborough 42-44 initiated what later came to be called the Forward Policy: a punitive return to Kabul in 1842 to restore British prestige, followed by a doctrine of pushing the frontier outward. Lytton 76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80), forcing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879. The war continued into its 2nd phase after the massacre of British Resident Louis Cavagnari at Kabul. Ripon 80-84 reversed the Forward Policy and withdrew British forces from Afghanistan: the pendulum swing that Liberal governments in London demanded. Slide versus handout on Ellenborough 42-44. The handout says he initiated the Forward Policy (a punitive return to Kabul 1842 to restore prestige; the handout's flow chart says the same). Slide 91 says he "Ended Forward Policy (*Correct this in notes)", and the slide itself carries the typed reminder to correct it, so the slide is flagged by its own author as unsettled. This notebook follows the handout: Ellenborough 42-44 = punitive return to Kabul 1842, then the frontier-outward doctrine. For the exam the safe core is the same either way: Auckland 36-42 = 1st war 1839-42; Lytton 76-80 = carried forward the Forward Policy (2nd war 1878-80); Ripon 80-84 = reversed it. Check your notebook for what the teacher said aloud. The slide also spells the name "Aukland"; the handout spells "Auckland 36-42". 9.1 The Treaty of Gandamak 1879  Typed slide: Forward Policy in Afghanistan (contd.), Lytton 76-80 to Ripon 80-84: the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80; the Treaty of Gandamak 1879 as a mini subsidiary alliance; the massacre of Cavagnari; Ripon 80-84 reversed the policy. No ink. The handout calls Gandamak 1879 a mini subsidiary alliance, with five terms:   Term   Detail    --- ---    British Resident stationed   At the Amir's court     Army stationed   British forces     Foreign policy taken   By the British     Territory   Khyber Pass and some other lands to the British     In return   The British pay 6 lakh annually to the Amir   Mnemonic: Gandamak 1879: "R-A-F-K-6". Decode: Resident stationed; Army stationed; Foreign policy taken; Khyber Pass (and some other lands) to the British; 6 lakh a year paid to the Amir. A mini subsidiary alliance, 1879, in the 2nd war (1878-80). Why it sticks: "RAF-K-6": the RAF flies over the Khyber, the cheque is six lakh. Mnemonic: 1839-42 and 1878-80: "39 and 78 are 39 years apart." Decode: 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42 (Auckland 36-42: Shah Shuja against Dost Mohammad; January 1842 retreat from Kabul) and the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80 (Lytton 76-80; Gandamak 1879; Cavagnari killed). Why it sticks: 1839 plus 39 = 1878, close enough to place both wars. Mnemonic: Lytton 76-80 = Forward; Ripon 80-84 = Retreat. Decode: Lytton 76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy (2nd Anglo-Afghan War); Ripon 80-84 reversed it and withdrew. Why it sticks: handout hook, copied as written; the two terms are consecutive (76-80, 80-84).  PYQ 14, Prelims 1999, answer slide: Forward Policy in Afghanistan. Answer (d) Lytton 76-80, who carried forward the Forward Policy begun by Ellenborough 42-44 and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80; (a) Minto II 1905-10 post-Curzon; (b) Dufferin 84-88 Upper Burma 1886; (c) Elgin I or II, different eras. Hook: Lytton = Forward; Ripon = Retreat. No ink. Prelims 1999 trap: answer (d) Lytton 76-80. (a) Minto (Minto II 1905-10) belongs to a different era, after Curzon 99-05. (b) Dufferin 84-88 is famous for Upper Burma 1886, not Afghanistan. (c) Elgin (I 1862-63 or II 1894-99) is a different era. This slide's answer text says Lytton 76-80 carried forward the policy "initiated by Ellenborough 42-44", which supports the handout over slide 91. 9.2 Revision: Russophobia and the Great Game  Typed slide: Revision, Russophobia and the Great Game (Russophobia; the Great Game; the offensive answer = Forward Policy; the defensive twin = Policy of Ring Fence; the Persian flank: Anglo-Persian War 1856-57 and Anglo-Russian Convention 1907). No ink. Russophobia: the British fear that Czarist Russia, expanding through Central Asia, would one day reach the north-west land approach to India. The Great Game: this Anglo-Russian rivalry over Central Asia. It shaped British frontier and foreign policy far more than trade. Offensive answer: the Forward Policy, pushing the effective frontier outward through the two Anglo-Afghan Wars (1839-42 and 1878-80). Defensive twin: the Policy of Ring Fence: keeping strong, friendly border States as a buffer around British India, with Afghanistan and Punjab as the buffer in the north-west. The 1838 Tripartite Treaty (Sikh State, EIC and Shah Shuja) was built on this buffer logic (see Chapter 6, Chapter 14). The Persian flank: the same logic produced the Anglo-Persian War 1856-57 and finally the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, which split Iran into three: a Russian sphere in the north, a neutral buffer in the middle and a British sphere in the south (see Chapter 14). This is a "Revision" box with no ink. It belongs with the policies chapter: the Ring Fence idea began with Clive 57-67 in 1765 (Chapter 10) and the Five-Policy Arc is in Chapter 14. Mnemonic: Offence and defence: Forward vs Ring Fence. Decode: Russophobia / Great Game. Offence = Forward Policy (push the frontier out, two Afghan wars 1839-42 and 1878-80). Defence = Ring Fence (friendly buffer States: Afghanistan and Punjab; the 1838 Tripartite Treaty). Persia: Anglo-Persian War 1856-57 and the 1907 Convention. Why it sticks: one team, a striker and a goalkeeper. Mnemonic: Iran cut in three, 1907: "Russia up, Neutral mid, British down". Decode: Anglo-Russian Convention 1907: north = Russian sphere; middle = neutral buffer; south = British sphere. Why it sticks: top to bottom: R, N, B.

items.t: 10 · Dufferin 84-88 and Upper Burma (1886)
items.x: Typed slide: Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886): the last major territorial extension; Viceroy Dufferin 84-88; King Thibaw deposed; General Henry Prendergast; merged with Lower Burma. No ink. The last major territorial extension of British India was Upper Burma, annexed in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86. The Viceroy was Dufferin 84-88. King Thibaw was deposed and exiled to Ratnagiri. The field commander was General Henry Prendergast, the same man who appeared as a distractor in the Prelims 1997 Thuggee question. Upper Burma was merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) and governed as a province of British India until the 1937 separation. "Lower Burma, British from 1852" is the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53) of Dalhousie 48-56 (Chapter 14). The handout's Ch 14 section on it is the home for that war.  Typed slide: Alert, Last Major Extension (Prelims 2000): the discussion of Dalhousie 48-56 (Punjab 1849, Awadh 1856), Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05, and the hook "Dufferin = 1886 = Upper Burma = last major extension". No ink.  PYQ 2, Prelims 2000, answer slide: Answer (a) Dufferin 84-88. The slide ends with a nuance: Burma is not traditionally part of India; if "India" is meant, the answer is Dalhousie 48-56; if the political territory of the British State is meant, Dufferin 84-88; the PYQ says British India, so legally Dufferin 84-88, but the famous answer is Dalhousie 48-56, so the UPSC key may say Dalhousie 48-56. No ink. Prelims 2000: Dufferin 84-88 (a), with a slide nuance. Handout: Dufferin 84-88 added Upper Burma in January 1886: (a). Traps: Dalhousie 48-56 (Punjab 1849, Awadh 1856, Doctrine of Lapse) was the big annexation GG, but his last major extension was Awadh 1856; Lytton 76-80 made no territorial extension (he tightened Paramountcy-era instruments, such as the Treaty of Jacobabad 1876, without annexing); Curzon 99-05's Partition of Bengal 1905 was administrative, not territorial. Slide 108 adds a real-exam wrinkle: because Burma was not traditionally part of India, the "famous" answer is Dalhousie 48-56 and the official key might say that, but the question says "British Indian territory", so (a) Dufferin 84-88 is the legally correct answer. Use (a), as the handout and bank do, and keep the Dalhousie 48-56 possibility in mind as the slide's warning. Mnemonic: Dufferin 84-88 = 1886 = Upper Burma = the last. Decode: Dufferin 84-88 added Upper Burma in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86; Thibaw to Ratnagiri; Prendergast commanded; merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) until the 1937 separation. Why it sticks: handout hook, copied as written; "Dufferin 84-88 ends, Dalhousie 48-56 began" for the order. Mnemonic: Burma in three dates: 1852, 1886, 1937. Decode: 1852 Lower Burma British; 1886 Upper Burma annexed (Dufferin 84-88); 1937 Burma separated from British India. Why it sticks: first half, second half, then the split.

items.t: 11 · Imperial Preference
items.x: Typed slide: Imperial Preference (definition; formalised at the Ottawa Conference 1932; effect on India). No ink. "Imperial Preference" was a commercial tariff arrangement: the constituent units of the British Empire (Britain, the Dominions and India) granted one another preferential (lower) tariff rates denied to non-Empire competitors. Formalised at the Ottawa Conference of 1932, locking India's trade into an Empire-first structure that subordinated Indian industrial interests to British manufacturing needs. (Full treatment in the Drain Theory chapter, Chapter 27.) Effect on India: British goods entered Indian ports at a lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors. India's tariff regime systematically advantaged the very British manufacturing economy that Indian industries were trying to compete with.  Typed slide: Alert, Imperial Preference (Prelims 1999): (b) racial discrimination wrong, a separate phenomenon; (c) subordination of Indian interest too vague; (d) preference to British political agents over Indian Princes wrong, Political Department protocol. Correct (a) special privileges on British imports in India. No ink. Prelims 1999 trap: answer (a) special privileges on British imports in India. (b) racial discrimination is a different phenomenon (Section 7). (c) subordination of Indian interest is too vague, a general description of colonialism and not the specific definition. (d) preference to British political agents over Princes is Political Department protocol. The key word is tariff. Mnemonic: Imperial Preference = tariff = British imports first. Decode: Britain, Dominions and India gave each other lower tariffs than non-Empire rivals; formalised at Ottawa 1932; British goods paid less than German, Japanese or American goods at Indian ports. Why it sticks: handout hook, copied as written; "Ottawa 32" = a trade fence in the year 1932. 11.1 The stray table of five antiquarians (Prelims 2023)  Typed slide: Five Antiquarians: Alexander Rea (Amaravati, Bhattiprolu); A.H. Longhurst (Nagarjunakonda, Hampi); Robert Sewell (A Forgotten Empire, on Vijayanagara); James Burgess (first Director of the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India); Walter Elliot (Madras Civil Service; catalogued Andhra Buddhist sites and coins). No ink.   #   Name   Notable work    --- --- ---    1   Alexander Rea   Excavated at Amaravati and Bhattiprolu     2   A.H. Longhurst   Excavated at Nagarjunakonda and Hampi     3   Robert Sewell   Wrote "A Forgotten Empire" (Vijayanagara)     4   James Burgess   First Director of the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India     5   Walter Elliot   Of the Madras Civil Service; catalogued Andhra Buddhist sites and coins   This table is out of place in the handout and slide. It sits between Imperial Preference (Section 11) and the foreign ideologies (Section 12) with no heading or link to the ideology story; it answers Prelims 2023: all five were associated with archaeological excavations (a). The handout's flow chart ties it to Orientalist scholarship through the ASI (founded 1861, Alexander Cunningham) (see section 3.2.1). The rest of the 2023 bank item mentions the ASI reorganisation in its explanation; the full story is not in this chapter. Mnemonic: "Rea, Long, Sew, Bur, El": Rea digs, Long digs, Sewell writes, Burgess heads, Elliot catalogues. Handout timeline of the ideologies on a time line 1757, 1765, 1813, 1857, 1947: Orientalism 1765-1813 (Jones, Wilkins, Asiatic Society); Authoritarianism, Cornwallis 86-93 (racial bar, Permanent Settlement); Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism post 1813 (Bentinck, Macaulay, Trevelyan); Racism + Authoritarianism post 1857 (post-Mutiny mistrust; racial categories institutionalised). Under all, a bar: "White Man's Burden, foundation throughout (moral pretext)". Names only in the figure: Wilkins (Orientalism) and Trevelyan (Liberal-era) are not in the handout text. Use the figure as a picture of the sequence, and the text for facts.

items.t: 12 · Foreign ideologies motivating India's anti-colonial struggle
items.x: Handout numbering glitch. Section 12's sub-points are numbered 13.1 to 13.3 in the handout (and the heading before the summary is "Sec. 13"). Here they are called 12.1 to 12.3. WMB (Section 2) produced its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies across the globe that travelled back into India through newspapers, returning students and political exiles. 12.1 Pre-1900 political and ideological currents  Typed slide: Foreign Ideologies, Pre-1900 Currents (American Revolution 1765-83; French Revolution 1789; European revolutions of 1830 and 1848; Irish struggle). No ink. American Revolution (1765-83): political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. French Revolution of 1789: liberty, equality, fraternity. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848: democratic uprisings across the continent. Irish Home Rule (1870-1914) and Irish armed struggle (1916-21) against Britain: direct anti-British inspiration. All challenged imperial superiority and inspired colonised peoples worldwide. 12.2 Three 20th-century shocks that radicalised Indian nationalism  Typed slide: Three 20th-Century Shocks That Radicalised Nationalism (deindustrialisation and the Drain Theory; the Russian Revolution 1917; self-determination). No ink. Industrial Revolution's destructive impact on Indian handloom: deindustrialisation fed the Drain Theory of Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. Russian Revolution of 1917: gave the Indian left a peasant-worker mobilisation model and an anti-imperial vocabulary. Post-WWI principle of self-determination (Wilson's Fourteen Points, 1918) and rising anti-racism: made continued British rule increasingly indefensible in international forums. 12.3 Returning Indian leaders brought these currents home  Typed slide: Returning Indian Leaders Brought These Currents Home (Gandhi from South Africa; Nehru from Cambridge; Mains 2014 with a pointer to the separate MMP deck Fable_MMP_Ch_15). No ink. The world-developments travelled through people, not ideas alone: Gandhi from South Africa: anti-colonial training from Indian-diaspora struggles in South Africa (1893-1915). Nehru from Cambridge: Western liberal-democratic political theory absorbed during his Cambridge studies, applied in Indian Congress politics. Mains 2014 (10M, 150 words): *"What were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti-colonial struggle in India?"* The handout's three-bucket answer: Enlightenment + American + French + Irish revolutions (political and ideological) then Industrial Revolution deindustrialisation (economic) then Russian Revolution 1917 + Wilson's self-determination + anti-racism (social and ideological) then returning leaders (Gandhi from South Africa, Nehru from Cambridge). The handout points to a companion Appendix FYQ_Mains with the full five-part treatment; that appendix is not in this notebook. The skeleton is in the Exam lens. Mnemonic: "P-E-S then People": the Mains 2014 answer frame. Decode: Political (American, French, 1830 and 1848, Irish); Economic (Industrial Revolution's handloom destruction, Drain Theory of Naoroji and Dutt); Social and ideological (Russia 1917, Wilson 1918, anti-racism); then People (Gandhi from South Africa, Nehru from Cambridge). Why it sticks: the three buckets are the same P-E-S as the feudal triple in Section 5.2, now turned against the British. Mnemonic: Gandhi 93-15, Nehru Cambridge. Decode: Gandhi's South African struggles ran 1893-1915; Nehru absorbed western liberal-democratic theory at Cambridge. Why it sticks: 93 to 15 is the 22-year apprenticeship, the same range as in Chapter 35.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The story of "The Burden that Changed its Coat". The British pick up the White Man's Burden (Britain first in the Industrial Revolution 1750-1850, won 1756-63, beat Napoleon at Leipzig 1813 and Waterloo 1815) and ask "how should we civilise India?" At first they are scared: Orientalism (1765-1813), Warren Hastings 73-85 and Jones: Madrasa 1781, Asiatic Society 1784, Sanskrit College 1791, Fort William 1800. Rule India the India Way. Cornwallis 86-93 says My way or highway: no Indians in senior posts, Collector is not Judge, Permanent Settlement 1793, an Aloof Elite, because he lost America. After 1813 the EIC is confident: Liberalism (Macaulay: Law 1834, Minute 1835), Utilitarianism (Mill's schoolmaster 1818) and Evangelicalism (Grant 1813, Lex Loci 1850), and the Sleeman police net chases the Thugs. Then 1857 shocks them: "Dogs and Indians not allowed", the Queen's 1858 promise, Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05; the Forward Policy runs from Auckland 36-42 to Ripon 80-84's retreat; Dufferin 84-88 ends the land-grab at Upper Burma 1886; Ottawa 1932 locks in Imperial Preference. And the world's revolutions come home with Gandhi and Nehru. Decode: 1765, 1781-1800, 1793, 1813, 1829-35, 1857-58, 1878, 1886, 1905, 1932.

Teacher ticked all three   Section 3.2     Prelims 2017   Who was associated with introducing Ryotwari: 1 Lord Cornwallis 86-93, 2 Alexander Read, 3 Thomas Munro   (c) 2 and 3 only. Teacher wrote the years: 86-93, 1792, 1801-07, 1820. Cornwallis 86-93 = Permanent Settlement   Section 3.1     Prelims 2021   One result of British rule in the 19th century: handicraft exports up / Indian factories up / commercialisation of agriculture / rapid urban growth   (c) commercialisation of Indian agriculture. Teacher: (a) F, (b) F, (c) T, (d) F   Section 5     Prelims 2024   Cornwallis 86-93's revenue collection: (1) Ryotwari: peasants exempted in bad harvest; (2) Permanent: Zamindar removed if failed to pay   (b) 2 only. Statement 1 fails twice: Ryotwari was not Cornwallis 86-93's, and relief was remission (reduction), not exemption (zero). Statement 2 = the Sunset Clause   Section 2.4 (Pillar 4)     Prelims 1995 (class slide, revision)   Correctly matched pair of battle and combatants   (b) Wandiwash (1760): French against the EIC. Buxar (1764) was Mir Qasim 60-63, Shuja 54-75 and Shah Alam II 60-06, not Mir Jafar 57-60; Chilianwala (1849) was the Sikhs, not Marathas; Kharda (1795) was Marathas against the Nizam   Section 7     Prelims 2011 (Kheda, class slide)   Why did Gandhi organise the Kheda Satyagraha: (1) no suspension of revenue in a drought; (2) a proposed permanent settlement in Gujarat   Answer slide says (a) Only 1; the teacher's pen on the question slide reads differently. Read the alert in Section 7   Section 7     Mains FYQ (class slide)   "British empire in India was BUILT and SUSTAINED by policies and tactics of DnR. Analyse."   Teacher: PS 1793 belongs under "Sustained". Skeleton below   Section 2.4     Mains (teacher's starred prompt)   "Why so many famines in British India?"   Cash-revenue demand, commercialisation, less food reserve, plus the 1770 famine (see Chapter 10)   Sections 2.1 and 5   What to prepare: Prelims hooks: the five-question frame; Mughal chain (Khudkasht, Primary Zamindar, Intermediary Zamindar, Jagirdar or State) and the Zamindar as a commission collector; Ijaradari; Dual Government 1765-72 with Muhammad Reza Khan; 1770 famine; Rs 1.4 million loan at 4% leading to the Regulating Act 1773; Farming System 1772; the four pillars of PS 1793 (owner, settlement, 10/11 fixed with 1789-90 base year, Sunset Clause); BOB places; Regulation VII of 1799; Cornwallis 86-93 Code litigation; Rent Act 1859 (12 years); Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 (Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission 1880); Read and Munro, not Cornwallis 86-93; Wingate 1835; Pringle 1830 (55%); Madras Torture Commission 1855; Mirasidars; Bombay Deccan Riots 1875; Regulation VII of 1822 (Holt Mackenzie); R.M. Bird 1833 (66%, 30 years); summary settlement of Awadh 1856; cash crops list. Mains hooks: compare the three systems on the five questions; why ryots suffered everywhere; why three systems; PS 1793 as Divide and Rule; the cash-revenue to famine chain; the 1859 and 1885 corrections. The Question bank button on this chapter's page holds the book's own PYQ set for this chapter (9 Prelims PYQs, 15 Prelims practice questions, 2 Mains practice questions). It is not copied here. This chapter's exam table carries only what the teacher put on slides or what the handout quotes. Prelims 2000, the first two rows. The class slide (Lecture 18, slides 26 and 27) lists the options as (b) A-1 B-4 C-2 D-3 and the teacher circled A = 1 (Jagirdari), B = 4 (Zamindari), C = 2 (Ryotwari), D = 3 (Mahalwari); his reason: the jagir was land allotted to a feudal noble, and the Zamindar was a revenue collector on commission. The handout's alert writes the same letter (b) but reads it as A-4 B-1 C-2 D-3 (A = Zamindari because PS 1793 made Zamindars big landlords; B = Jagirdari). Both give (b), and both agree that C = Ryotwari and D = Mahalwari. If the exam prints the codes as in the class slide, use the teacher's circles (A = Jagirdari, B = Zamindari), which also fits Section 1 of the handout (the Zamindar was never an owner before 1793). If it prints the handout's codes, follow the codes in front of you. Either way, tie C and D first, then pick the option. Mains skeletons (from the class notes only). (1) "Why so many famines in British India?" Intro: the teacher's idea that famine is a function of nature and of human factors (see Chapter 10). Body: high LR demand in cash (Mughals took much in kind); ryots pushed or induced by moneylenders and traders into cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane); land that grew rice, wheat and millets now fed British factories and global markets; less food grain in reserve when drought or flood hit; indebtedness and land loss. Closing: cash revenue demand to cash crops to collapse of food security to the late-19th-century famines; the 1770 Bengal famine as the early case. (2) "British empire built and sustained by DnR. Analyse." Intro: DnR means setting leaders against leaders, followers against followers. Body on the board: BUILT = Triple Alliance and Treaty of Amritsar 1809, Subsidiary Alliance (takes over external affairs), and used factionalism as opportunity (Treaty of Bassein 1802 with Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18); SUSTAINED = PS 1793: loyal Zamindars at the top, ryots with no rights below (Zamindars largely stayed on the British side in 1857). Closing: Zamindar loyalty bought political stability for a cheap price. (3) Practice Mains (bank): Compare PS and Ryotwari on the cultivating class. Body: PS: Zamindar owner, ryot "tenant at will", Patta ignored, abwabs, absentee landlords, corrected by the 1859 Act and 1885 Act. Ryotwari: ryot owner, direct settlement, but over-assessment, debt, Mirasidars. Closing: neither matched the Mughal Patta protection.

items.t: 0 · The chapter on one board
items.x: Chapter 16 title slide. Ink: UPSC branches to States and People (boxed), People leads to economic security in the Agrarian economy; circles AGRI (GDP) and RYOTS (work profile). Under the title a yellow line and five headings: Landowner? | Assessment of LR | Settlement with WHO? | WHO collects LR | Rights of Tenants. Teacher: Why this chapter matters for UPSC: the State's duty to its people is economic security, and in a pre-industrial country that means the agrarian economy: agriculture is the big share of GDP, and ryots are the big share of the work profile. Then he gives the five-question frame he repeats for the Mughal system, Ijaradari, PS 1793, Ryotwari and Mahalwari: who is the landowner, how is the revenue assessed, with whom is the settlement made, who collects, and what rights do tenants have. Learn every system as a row of those five answers. Mnemonic: Lazy Aunts Sip Chai Together: the five questions. Decode: Landowner, Assessment, Settlement (with whom), Collection (by whom), Tenants' rights. Why it sticks: the same five questions fit every system in the chapter, so the sentence is your answer-skeleton.

items.t: 1 · The Mughal blueprint for land revenue
items.x: Teacher's board: State, intermediaries and ryots. State (King) holds the right to receive LR, decide and revise LR. Two arrows from the State: from khalisa lands straight to Zamindars; from jagirs to Jagirdars (who get the right to receive LR, given by the State). Zamindars hold the Vatan right to collect LR and keep commission (10%). Ryots send LR upward and hold Occupancy Rights (customary) and the right to fair LR (Patta system). A circle of State, Intermediaries and Ryots is labelled "multiple right holders". The Khudkasht was the actual cultivator. He held customary occupancy rights over his land (he could not simply be thrown off). He paid land revenue by the Patta system: a document (patta) recorded the amount he owed, a legal safeguard against arbitrary over-extraction. He also paid abwabs (informal tributes) to his Primary Zamindar. Khudkasht (cultivator): customary occupancy rights; pays LR per his patta; pays abwabs to the Primary Zamindar Primary Zamindar: keeps his commission, passes the rest up Intermediary Zamindar: collects, keeps his cut, passes the rest up (good) Jagirdar if the land was a jagir; the State if it was khalisa land  Handout figure of the Mughal chain: Khudkasht (cultivator), Primary Zamindar (village or local), Intermediary Zamindar (regional), Jagirdar or State (top of chain), with a dotted line of supervision from a box at the bottom. The figure's bottom box says "Amlas" (state-appointed, audit chain). The handout's text names the supervising State officers as Amils and Amalguzars. The teacher and the Mahalwari section stress that Amlas are different: private employees of Zamindars, not State officers (Section 4.1). Treat "Amlas" in the figure as a label slip and use Amils and Amalguzars for the State's supervisors. Amils and Amalguzars (government officers) supervised the chain so that Zamindars did not under-report collections. Critical point: the Zamindar was not the owner of land. He was a revenue collector on commission (the teacher's board: Vatan right to collect LR and keep a 10% commission). He also had police duties alongside revenue work. Legal private ownership of property was not a Mughal idea; it was British, imported from English law. Ijaradari: when the State needed money in a hurry it auctioned the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder. The British would replicate this (Section 2.2).  Teacher's board, pre-British era. Only the King was legal owner of land; individual LEGAL rights (boxed; "think of property ownership papers") did not exist. Khudkashts had customary occupancy rights in a Patta, which records who cultivates, details of plot and crop, and the LR demand. Land was not a commodity (it came by conquest or gift); sale, purchase, lease, mortgage did not exist, so a land market did not exist. "This dev with British [1793+]". Teacher: Legal against customary. In the Mughal era only the King was the legal owner and no individual legal property rights existed. The Khudkasht's right was customary (from custom, not from a law made by the State), recorded in his patta. Land was not a commodity: it changed hands only by conquest or gift, so there was no land market. The market in land develops with the British, from 1793. (The ink "Ded" beside "This" reads like "dev(elops)"; check your notebook.)  Mughal LR system on the five-question frame. Landowner: Khudkasht, milkiyat [practical]. Assessment: detailed survey, plus % of gross produce (e.g. one-third), plus revisable. Settlement with: Ryot [Qubuliyat by the ryot to the State; Patta given by the State to the ryot]. Collection: non-State actor, i.e. Zamindar. Tenants: rightless landless Pahikashts.   The five questions   Mughal system   Ijaradari (Mughal fallback)    --- --- ---    Landowner   Khudkasht (practically his milkiyat; legally only the King owned)   Ryot or Khudkasht (practical)     Assessment   Detailed survey; % of gross produce (e.g. one-third); revisable   Summary, by auction; an amount     Settlement with   The ryot (he gives a Qubuliyat to the State; the State gives him a patta)   The Ijaradar, via auction     Collection by   A non-State actor: the Zamindar   The Ijaradar     Tenants   Rightless, landless Pahikashts   (not written)   Mnemonic: K-P-I-J: the chain climbs "Kisan, Primary, Intermediary, Jagirdar". Decode: Khudkasht pays to Primary Zamindar (plus abwabs), who keeps a commission and passes up to the Intermediary Zamindar, who keeps a cut and passes up to the Jagirdar (jagir land) or the State (khalisa land). Amils and Amalguzars check that nobody under-reports. Why it sticks: every step takes a bite except the last, which is the receiver. Mnemonic: Mughal = Survey, Gross, Revisable; Ijaradari = Auction. Decode: Mughal assessment = detailed survey, % of gross produce (one-third), revisable; collected by Zamindars. Ijaradari = summary assessment by auction, settlement and collection with the Ijaradar. The British used the second for 1772. Why it sticks: survey versus auction, careful versus hasty.

items.t: 2 · Bengal: three experiments
items.x: 2.1 Experiment 1: Dual Government (1765-72)  Bengal Experiment 1: Dual Government (1765-72). 1765 Diwani via Treaty of Allahabad; Reza Khan appointed Diwan (Orientalism); Patta ignored, then back-to-back droughts; 1770 famine, 50 lakh to 1 crore dead, revenue doubled in 1770 and brutality; British whistleblowers; Reza Khan imprisoned 1772-74. Ink: Pre-British era, Rent and Revenue were used interchangeably. In 1765 the EIC received the Diwani (right to collect land revenue) of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar through the Treaty of Allahabad (ToA 1765) (the treaty itself is in Chapter 10). It did not administer directly. It appointed Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as its Diwan. The Mughal collection system continued: the EIC followed Orientalism (Indian traditions are best administered on their own terms). Ideology did not stop greed. In five years: frantic experiments to squeeze more revenue; the Patta system was ignored; rents were extracted far beyond what pattas recorded. Then back-to-back droughts. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed between 50 lakh and 1 crore. The EIC doubled the revenue demand in 1770 and used brutality to collect. For the first time some British men acted as whistleblowers, writing to London newspapers. Reza Khan was made a scapegoat: imprisoned without trial on corruption charges, 1772-74. Teacher: In the Pre-British era the words "rent" and "revenue" were used interchangeably (his note beside the slide). Underlines: Deputy Subadar, Orientalism, Patta ignored, back-to-back droughts, doubled in 1770, brutality, imprisoned without trial, 1772-74. The famine fits his nature factor and human factor idea from Chapter 10: droughts were nature; the doubled demand, ignored pattas and brutality were human. The handout here gives the famine toll as 50 lakh to 1 crore. Chapter 10's handout says about 1 crore, one-third of Bengal. Quote the range in this chapter's answers; "about one crore" is the upper end. Mnemonic: Greed, Drought, Double: why 1770 happened. Decode: Greed (patta ignored, rents beyond the record) + Drought (back-to-back) + Double (revenue demand doubled in 1770, with brutality) = Great Bengal Famine 1770, 50 lakh to 1 crore. Reza Khan jailed 1772-74 as the scapegoat. Why it sticks: three Ds, one death toll.  Why the EIC went bankrupt by 1772. From 1757 the EIC used India's own land revenue to buy Indian goods instead of bringing gold. By 1772: corruption (Nabobs), 1770 famine, army and Dual System expenses. Bailout: Parliament granted 1.4 million pounds at 4% interest on condition of parliamentary oversight. Result: the Regulating Act of 1773. Underlines on "1.4 million at 4% interest", "parliamentary oversight", "Regulating Act of 1773". Since 1757 the EIC had bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue rather than gold from England, so a famine hit its income directly (the Drain logic of Chapter 10). Famine destroyed the agrarian economy and land revenue collapsed. By 1772 the EIC was on the verge of bankruptcy: rampant corruption by its officials (the "Nabobs"), the 1770 famine, and heavy expenses of the army and the Dual System. The EIC asked the British Government for an emergency bailout. Parliament granted 1.4 million pounds at 4% interest, on the strict condition of parliamentary oversight, which led directly to the Regulating Act of 1773 (Chapter 17). Mnemonic: N-F-E, then 1.4 at 4: the bankruptcy of 1772. Decode: Nabobs' corruption + Famine of 1770 + Expenses (army and Dual System) = bankrupt by 1772. Bailout: 1.4 million pounds at 4%, condition: parliamentary oversight, so the Regulating Act 1773. Why it sticks: "one-four at four" repeats the 4; the condition is the lock on the loan. 2.2 Experiment 2: the Farming System of Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772)  Bengal Experiment 2: Hastings's Farming System (1772). Ink: "english name for IJARADARI"; Warren Hastings = Governor of Bengal Presidency; Revenue Farmer = Ijaradar. Right-hand list: To Purandhar 1776 @ Ma; To Salbai 1782; HA 61-82 military alliance 1769; 2nd A-My 1780-84. Bottom: Ryot (sad face) with 1757+ high LR, 1770 GBF, 1772 Ijaradari; DC over Ijaradar, with supervision. Teacher: Farming System = the English name for Ijaradari; Revenue Farmer = Ijaradar. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of the Bengal Presidency. The ryot's sad face carries three blows in a row: 1757+ high LR, 1770 Great Bengal Famine, 1772 Ijaradari. On the right he lists events of Hastings's years (as written: "To Purandhar 1776 @ Ma", "To Salbai 1782", "HA 61-82: military alliance 1769", "2nd A-My 1780-84"); "To" reads as his shorthand for Treaty, "Ma" for Marathas, "HA" for Haidar Ali 61-82 ([unclear: check your notebook]). They belong to Chapter 12 and Chapter 13.  Teacher's board: Till 1813, Orientalist ideology: Rule India the India way. Teacher: Till 1813 the ideology was Orientalism: "Rule India the India way." That is why the EIC kept Mughal collection after 1765 and revived Ijaradari in 1772 (and why Hastings 73-85 is called an Orientalist). The turn away from it follows the Charter Act of 1813 (Chapter 17). Warren Hastings 73-85, himself an Orientalist, revived the Mughal Ijaradari system. The right to collect LR in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder: the Revenue Farmer (so named because, like a farmer, he aimed to extract profit through a contract; not a farmer who tills soil). The Revenue Farmer worked under a European District Collector (DC) (European = English, Scottish or Irish, not English alone). Outcome: farmers squeezed the maximum from ryots to recover their bids and make profit. The demand was often so high that peasants paid nothing: self-defeating. Revenue did not improve; the rural population was ruined. Mnemonic: Bid, Bleed, Bust: the Farming System. Decode: Revenue Farmers bid at auction (assessment = auction, settlement = Revenue Farmer); they bled the ryots to recover the bid and profit; demand so high peasants paid nothing, so the system went bust. Supervisor: a European DC. Why it sticks: three verbs, same order as the outcome. 2.3 Primer: tax, property, settlement (taught first in the lecture) The lecture teaches these concepts before the Mughal system (Lecture 17, slides 5 to 12, 21, 22); the handout puts them here as Section 2.3. Read them before the pillars of PS 1793.  Handout figure: three columns. Rights in Land, five layers (cultivate or occupy; fair rent or revenue; sell, lease, mortgage; collect taxes; receive proceeds and revise rates). Assessment types (field-survey vs summary; absolute vs percentage; permanent vs revisable). Settlement types (with cultivator, Ryotwari-style; with intermediary, Zamindari or Mahalwari).  Teacher's board: rights. Of cultivator: occupancy rights (right to cultivate a plot), tenant or small landowner. Of tenant: right to fair rent, occupancy rights. Of owner: right to sell, rent out, lease out, mortgage; right to fair LR. Right to collect LR: with the State today, or with Zamindars or Deshmukhs (Vatan right holders, non-State actors). Right to assess: State. Right to receive: State today, or Jagirdars (given by the State). Rights in land have five layers:   Layer   Right    --- ---    a)   The ryot's right to cultivate and occupy his plot     b)   The right to fair rents (tenant ryot) or fair land revenue (owner)     c)   The landowner's right to sell, lease, rent and mortgage land and receive those proceeds     d)   The right to collect taxes (State, or Vatan right holders such as Zamindars)     e)   The right to receive tax proceeds and revise tax rates (State; Jagirdars receive but by the State's grant)   Teacher: Two kinds of rights on his board (Lecture 17, slide 3): rights given by law (made by the State, an organisation, through rules) and customary or traditional rights (from the conventions of a society), e.g. the Vatan rights of Zamindars. (The star note "MIH" and the small "7 ... PPT" beside the law branch are [unclear: check your notebook].)  Teacher's board: taxes and rents. Taxes (e.g. LR) are always borne by the owner of land or property and always go to the State. Rents are always borne by tenants and always go to the property owner (private or State). "Lease = long-term rent". Salary only for employees. Mnemonic: Rent climbs one step, Tax climbs the next. Decode: Tenant pays rent to the property owner; the owner pays tax to the State. Rent is borne by the tenant; tax is always borne by the owner. A salary is only for employees. Why it sticks: a two-rung ladder: Tenant, Owner, State.  Teacher's board: the word "Zamindar" changes meaning. Before 1793: collector of LR and not owner of the land from which he collected. From 1793: legal landowner [conditional ownership]. From 1947: "Zamindari abolition" meant abolishing big landownership. Teacher: Meaning of words changes, the word stays the same. Zamindar before 1793 = collector of LR, not owner; after 1793 = legal landowner (he stars "conditional ownership": the Sunset Clause can take the land); after 1947 "Zamindari abolition" meant abolishing big landownership. Mnemonic: Zamindar's three lives: Collector, Owner, Abolished. Decode: before 1793 collector (10% commission), 1793+ legal landowner (conditional), 1947+ the big-landownership class abolished. Why it sticks: C, O, A in order, with 1793 as the hinge. Assessment = deciding how much tax is owed, by detailed field survey (soil quality, irrigation, crop type, plot size, rainfall; the board adds frequency of drought or flood and past LR trends) or summarily (a rough estimate). The demand is a fixed absolute amount or a percentage of produce; it is permanent or revisable. Settlement = with whom the State negotiates the tax demand, and who is responsible for depositing it.  Teacher's board: settlement with Mr XYZ. Agreement on LR done by the State with XYZ, plus the responsibility to deposit LR in his bank account is XYZ's. Tax borne by someone else but deposited with the State by someone else = indirect taxes, e.g. GST [XYZ = shopkeeper]. Settlement may or may not be with the landowner: PS 1793 and Ryotwari 1801, 1820: XYZ = landowner; Mahalwari 1822: XYZ is not the landowner. Teacher: Settlement = agreement on LR plus the duty to deposit it. His analogy: in GST the shopkeeper deposits a tax that the buyer bears, so the depositor need not be the one who bears the tax. In the land systems the owner always bears the tax, but the settlement may or may not be with the owner: PS 1793: with the landowner (Zamindar); Ryotwari: with the landowner (ryot); Mahalwari 1822: not the landowner (the Mahal, via its Lambardar). Rent is always paid by a tenant to a property owner. Taxes are always borne by the property owner. The State is always the ultimate recipient but may collect through its own officers or non-State intermediaries. In the Farming System of 1772, assessment was by auction and settlement was with the Revenue Farmer. Mnemonic: SAP: three assessment forks. Decode: Survey or summary; Absolute amount or percentage; Permanent or revisable. Every system in this chapter picks one side of each fork. Why it sticks: SAP is what the ryot lost. 2.4 Experiment 3: the Permanent Settlement Act, 1793  Permanent Settlement Act, 1793. Applied in Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras, Benaras (BOB migrated from North Madras to Benaras and Settled Permanently). Cornwallis: GG of Bengal 1786-93, one primary assignment: fix the LR problem; passed the Act through the GG(Bengal)'s Council; extended to Madras. 1801 rollback: Munro convinced the Court of Directors; PS survived in North Madras. Ink: AUTHORITARIANISM under Cornwallis; inspired by the way agri was done in England; CW 86-93: from landlord family, from England [agrarian capitalism], "my way or highway"; CW 86-93 = Believer. Applied in: Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras, Benaras. Mnemonic: BOB migrated from North Madras to Benaras and Settled Permanently. Decode: Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras, Benaras (the handout's own line; the first letters BOB lead the list). Why it sticks: BOB is a person walking from the south to Benaras and settling. Cornwallis 86-93 (GG of Bengal 1786-93) was sent with one primary assignment: fix the land revenue problem. After several experiments he passed the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 through the GG(Bengal)'s Council and extended it to Madras on his instructions. By 1801 Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras, though it survived in North Madras. Teacher: AUTHORITARIANISM under Cornwallis 86-93: "my way or highway." He came from a landlord family and was inspired by how agriculture was done in England (agrarian capitalism); his own words: CW 86-93 = Believer (a believer in English landlordism). The belief explains the model: see Pillar 1 below.  Teacher's board: PS 1793 on the five questions. Landowner = Z. Assessment: no field survey, summarily decided, in absolute amount (Z not in %), not revisable. Settlement with Z. Collection by DC. Tenant = Khudkasht, Pahikasht: NO RIGHTS (boxed); Z can charge whatever rent and remove them from the plot as per his wishes.   The five questions   Permanent Settlement 1793    --- ---    Landowner   The Zamindar     Assessment   No field survey; summary; an absolute amount (not %); not revisable     Settlement with   The Zamindar     Collection by   The District Collector (DC)     Tenants   No rights: the Zamindar can charge whatever rent and remove them from the plot   Pillar 1: landownership went to the Zamindar.  PS 1793, Pillar 1: Landownership to the Zamindar. Zamindars given full proprietary rights for the first time; land became a commodity; hereditary, transferable within the family. Three reasons: English-style landlordism (agrarian capitalists, security of property induces investment); agrarian capitalism improves food security, trade and EIC LR income; loyalty of Zamindars buys political stability. Revenue Farmers not made owners. Ink: HEREDITARY LANDOWNERSHIP; "PS 1793 (ACT): legal ownership, security of property, and only then anyone invests Rs in property". Zamindars got full proprietary rights for the first time, making them legal owners. Land became a commodity: sold, purchased, leased, rented, mortgaged. Hereditary, transferable within the family. Why? (a) Ideology: belief in English-style landlordism; convert Zamindars into agrarian capitalists like England's landed gentry; security of property would induce investment. (b) Agrarian capitalism would improve food security, boost agricultural trade and grow the EIC's LR income. (c) Loyalty of Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, would buy political stability. Revenue Farmers, though wealthy, were not made landowners: they were not part of the traditional agrarian economy and lacked agricultural expertise.  Teacher's board: landowner criteria = a big landowner. A rich man will invest in productivity (irrigation, better equipment and machines [Industrial Revolution 1750-1850 in England], hire huge labour); production for profit motive rises; food security and govt LR income rise. Who to make big landowner? An already rich person: the Zamindar (ticked) [by 1727, 15 Intermediary Zamindars collected 50% of the LR of Bengal Suba]; moneylender; merchants [urban areas].  Teacher's board: why Zamindar chosen. Part of rural economy; traditional leader of rural society (King, Jagirdar, Zamindar, Ryots). He thinks 24x7 about agri (his commission rises with production). Merchants and moneylenders [Ijaradars] think 24x7 about margin and interest: outsiders to the rural economy. Below: PS 1793 = DnR (Divide and Rule): leaders or seniors against followers or juniors (masses); apply to company, country, society, political, family, geopolitics. Four patterns: L1 vs L2; F1 vs F2; L happy and F sad; L sad and F happy [Bangladesh, Nepal]. Teacher: Why a big landowner? A rich man invests (irrigation, better equipment and machines as in England's Industrial Revolution of 1750-1850, hired labour), produces for profit, so production rises: food security and government LR income rise. Whom to make big landowner? An already rich person: the Zamindar (ticked; by 1727, 15 Intermediary Zamindars collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR, the group Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) had built), a moneylender, or a merchant of urban areas. Why the Zamindar over the rest? He is part of the rural economy and the traditional leader of rural society, and thinks about agriculture 24x7 because his commission depends on production; merchants and moneylenders (Ijaradars) think about margin and interest and are outsiders to the rural economy. Teacher: "PS 1793 = DnR" (Divide and Rule).
