His general picture: in any setting (company, country, society, politics, family, geopolitics) there are leaders and followers; DnR can pit leader against leader, follower against follower, or favour one tier over the other (L happy, F sad or L sad, F happy, the last with "Bangladesh, Nepal" as examples). The slide does not write which pattern PS 1793 is. Read from Section 2.5, it is leaders (Zamindars) rewarded, masses (ryots) stripped of rights; that is a reading, not his ink. Mnemonic: I-A-L: three reasons for the Zamindar owner. Decode: Ideology (English landlordism, security induces investment), Agrarian capitalism (food security, trade, EIC revenue), Loyalty (traditional leaders buy political stability). Revenue Farmers were rich but outsiders. Why it sticks: "I AL" is the name of someone who gave the land and kept the loyalty. Pillar 2: settlement with the Zamindar. Fewer, bigger counterparties (the teacher writes "LR payers" above "counterparties") made collection simpler. The State negotiated with Zamindars; the Zamindar was responsible for depositing LR. Pillar 3: assessment was permanent.  Teacher's worked example. Pre-1793: ryot produces Rs 100; LR = 2/3 x 100 = 66 (66%); Zamindar collects 66 from ryot = Z's revenue; ryot keeps 34; Zamindar keeps 10% of 66 = 6.6; Govt gets 59.4. 1793+: from the books, 10/11 x old LR (Z's revenue) = 10/11 x 66 = 60, fixed forever = permanently; Govt gets 60 [figure, not %] = new LR; the rest is the Zamindar's wish. e.g. Zamindar 13, ryot 40-13 = 27. LR was fixed at 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue (what he had collected from ryots before deducting his commission), with 1789-90 as the base year. Fixed forever, as an absolute annual amount, not a percentage. Teacher: The arithmetic (Lecture 17, slide 30). Before 1793: ryot's produce Rs 100; LR = two-thirds = 66% = Rs 66, which the Zamindar collects (Z's revenue); ryot keeps Rs 34; Zamindar keeps 10% of 66 = Rs 6.6; the State gets Rs 59.4. After 1793: 10/11 x 66 = Rs 60, and Rs 60 is fixed forever (boxed FOREVER = Permanent-ly, "FIG not %"). Anything above Rs 60 the Zamindar can keep: in his example the Zamindar takes Rs 13 and the ryot keeps 40 - 13 = Rs 27 (the ink does not explain where the 40 comes from; [unclear: check your notebook]).  Teacher's board: why LR fixed so high. (1) Inflation reduces the value of the rupee; every passing year the value received by Govt falls, practically nothing in 100 years, so LR was initially fixed very high to compensate for the loss in the long term. Formula: 10/11 of Z's revenue, result fixed forever. (2) If in 1794 ryots produce Rs 120 [Rs 120 = boss = Z], LR = 60: in rupees and not % to incentivise Z to invest in the land's productivity. (3) If in 1795 ryots produce Rs 0, LR = 60. Teacher: Why so high and why in rupees: inflation shrinks what the State receives each year (practically nothing in 100 years), so the initial demand was fixed very high to compensate the State for the long-term loss. And because it is a fixed amount, not a percentage: if the ryots produce Rs 120 in 1794 the State still gets Rs 60, so the Zamindar keeps the gain and is incentivised to invest; if they produce Rs 0 in 1795 the State still gets Rs 60 (the Zamindar carries the risk). Why permanent and absolute? (a) To incentivise the Zamindar: revenue would not rise however profits grew, so he had every reason to invest and produce more. (b) Certainty for the State: even in a drought year the State knew what it would receive. (c) Less administration: no repeat assessment surveys (the teacher adds: corruption would fall, since no officer could reduce the demand). (d) Trade-off: since the State gave up future increases, it set the initial demand very high. Estimates vary: some historians say double the 1765 level; others, 20% above 1757 levels. Mnemonic: 66 to 60, then forever: the PS arithmetic. Decode: ryot's Rs 100, LR 2/3 = 66; Permanent Settlement takes 10/11 of 66 = 60 (base year 1789-90) and freezes it as a figure, not a %. Inflation is why it was set high; the Zamindar keeps every rupee above 60. Why it sticks: sixty-six, sixty, then the clock stops. Mnemonic: I-C-A-T: why permanent and absolute. Decode: Incentivise the Zamindar, Certainty for the State, less Administration, Trade-off (so demand set very high: double 1765 or 20% above 1757). Why it sticks: "I CAT" waits at the Zamindar's door for the tax. Pillar 4: the Sunset Clause.  Teacher's board: settlement with Z means the responsibility to deposit LR with Govt. Sunset Clause: must pay LR by the evening of the pre-decided date, else the Zamindari will be auctioned (put on auction).  PS 1793, Pillar 4: The Sunset Clause. If a Zamindar failed to pay LR by the evening of a pre-set deadline, his land was auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required LR. The new buyer only needed to agree to pay, not pay at once. Collection by the District Collector. Ink: [in our e.g. Rs 60]; "not value of land": who can pay the value of the land of 300 villages? No one. If a Zamindar did not pay LR by the evening of a pre-set deadline, his land was auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required land revenue. The buyer only had to agree to pay (not pay in full at once), given the large amounts. Collection was by State officers: the District Collector. Teacher: The buyer bids for the LR, not the land's value. In his example the buyer agrees to pay Rs 60 a year; the board asks "who can pay the value of the land of 300 villages?" and answers "No one." That is why the Sunset Clause is workable. Mnemonic: Sun sets, land sells. Decode: Zamindar misses the evening deadline, so the land is auctioned to anyone who agrees to pay the fixed LR (not the land's value). The District Collector collects. Why it sticks: sunset is a deadline you can see. Mnemonic: Z-Z-P-S: the four pillars. Decode: Zamindar owns (Pillar 1), settlement with Zamindar (2), Permanent assessment, 10/11, base year 1789-90, absolute (3), Sunset Clause (4). Why it sticks: two Zs, a P and an S: Zamindar, Zamindar, Permanent, Sunset.  PYQ 7, Prelims 2024: revenue collection by Cornwallis. Ink: "8643" above Cornwallis (reads as 86-93 run together); (1) Ryotwari, peasants exempted in bad harvest: circled F, with a line to "ZERO LR", then "Remit" ticked and "Exempt" crossed; (2) Permanent, Zamindar removed if failed to pay: circled T, with a line down to "Sunset Clause". Prelims 2024: answer (b) 2 only. Statement 1 (F): Ryotwari is not Cornwallis 86-93's, and a bad harvest earned remission (a reduction of LR), not exemption (zero LR): the teacher ticks "Remit" and crosses "Exempt = zero LR." Statement 2 (T): a Zamindar who failed to pay lost his land at auction: the Sunset Clause. Mnemonic: Remit is a trim, exempt is a zero; Sunset is a sale. Decode: Prelims 2024: Ryotwari remission = reduced LR (not zero), and not Cornwallis 86-93's; the Permanent Settlement punished default by auction (Sunset Clause). Answer (b). Why it sticks: a haircut, not a shave. 2.5 Impact of PS 1793  Impact of PS 1793: results diverged from intentions. 1 Short term: frequent auctions, buyers Jotedars and the Zamindar's own family; later stabilised, Zamindars loyal (largely British side in 1857). 2 Long term: certainty and regularity of LR achieved. 3 Vision failed: Zamindars did not invest. 4 Absentee landlordism. 5 Ryot ruined: tenant at will, Patta ignored, abwabs (now illegal) still collected. Underlines on auctions, Jotedars, family, loyal, absentee, moved to cities, tenant at will. The results diverged sharply from Cornwallis 86-93's intentions. Short term: frequent land auctions; the demand was so high that many Zamindars defaulted. Buyers: Jotedars (rich farmers, less wealthy than Zamindars) and the Zamindar's own family members, who bid to keep land in the family. Over time it stabilised and Zamindars became loyal (in 1857 Bengal's Zamindars largely stayed on the British side). Long term: the British got certainty and regularity of LR income. That objective was achieved. But the core economic vision failed: Zamindars did not invest. The demand left little surplus, and they would not risk old family wealth in an uncertain colonial environment (the teacher writes "therefore LR" above "the demand"). Absentee landlordism: Zamindars leased lands to intermediaries for a lease amount and moved to cities. The hands-on agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned. The ryot's situation became catastrophic. PS gave legal rights to Zamindars but did not recognise the ryot's customary rights. The ryot became a "tenant at will," evicted without legal protection; Patta ignored; high rents; abwabs, now illegal for lack of legal basis, still collected. Teacher: Underlines: Auctions, frequent, Buyers, Jotedars, the Zamindar's own family, later stabilised, Zamindars became loyal; certainty and regularity; Zamindars did not invest; absentee landlordism, moved to cities, the agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned; "tenant at will," Patta ignored, high rents, abwabs still collected. The loyalty is exactly the "Sustained" half of his DnR Mains question (Section 0). Mnemonic: A Clever Visitor Always Takes Rent Legally: the seven impacts in order. Decode: Auctions (Jotedars and family buy; later loyal), Certainty (LR regular, long term), Vision failed (no investment), Absentee landlords, Tenant at will (patta ignored, abwabs), Regulation VII 1799 (Zamindars regain coercion), Litigation (Cornwallis 86-93 Code). Why it sticks: seven words, seven points, in the handout's order.  Zamindars regain coercive powers: Regulation VII of 1799. Cornwallis removed Zamindars' police powers (a Zamindar was a businessman, not law enforcement). Wellesley reversed this: Zamindar may seize a tenant's property (crops, cattle) without a court order if rent defaulted; imprison tenants; increase rents at will. Result: a wave of peasant revolts after 1793. Ink: "7th Law of 1799". Zamindars regained coercive powers in 1799. Cornwallis 86-93 had removed their police powers (a Zamindar is a businessman, not law enforcement). Wellesley 98-05 reversed this through Regulation VII of 1799. The Zamindar could now: (a) seize a tenant's property (crops, cattle) without a court order on rent default; (b) imprison tenants; (c) increase rents at will. (Class slide: the result was a wave of peasant revolts after 1793.) Mnemonic: Seize, Imprison, Increase: Regulation VII of 1799. Decode: Wellesley 98-05 undid Cornwallis 86-93's removal of police powers; the teacher writes "7th Law of 1799". Seize property without court order, Imprison, Increase rent at will. Why it sticks: "SII": the Zamindar's three new verbs; 7th law, 1799.  Increased litigation: the Cornwallis Code of 1793 (a). The District Collector was stripped of all judicial and magisterial powers, so revenue disputes once settled swiftly and informally on the spot now had to be filed formally in the Diwani Adalats. Ink: "not of THIS CHAPTER. BUT HERE So STUDENT Knows". Increased litigation after 1793 came from the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judicial changes that made the system inefficient in practice): (a) the District Collector was stripped of all judicial and magisterial powers, so revenue disputes once settled swiftly and informally on the spot had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats; (b) court fees were abolished to make justice "accessible," which flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits (fees reimposed in 1795); (c) formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) with a rigid hierarchy of appeals let cases be deliberately prolonged. Teacher: "Not of this chapter, but here so the student knows" (his words on slide 36). The judicial reforms themselves belong to Chapter 18; here you only need the three points because of Prelims 2011. Mnemonic: C-F-V: why courts clogged after 1793. Decode: Collector stripped of judicial and magisterial power (disputes go to Diwani Adalats), Fees abolished (reimposed 1795, but the flood had come), Vakils with a rigid appeal ladder (cases prolonged). Why it sticks: Collector, Fees, Vakils, "CFV" like a court-fee voucher.  PYQ 3, Prelims 2011: litigation surge after 1793. Options: Zamindar's position stronger; EIC an overlord of Zamindars; judicial system more efficient; none.  Answer slide: (d) None of (a), (b), (c). Teacher underlines "Cornwallis Code of 1793". Why the others fail: (a) impoverished ryots could not drag powerful landlords to court; (b) the EIC became overlord decades earlier, in 1765; (c) the Cornwallis courts were slow, costly, procedure-heavy. Prelims 2011: answer (d). The three options on offer are not the cause; the cause is the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (point 7). (a) strong Zamindars did not mean more suits: ryots had no means to sue. (b) the EIC was already the overlord of the Zamindars' region since 1765 (the Diwani). (c) the courts became less efficient.  PYQ 2, Prelims 2001: why Zamindars did not issue pattas under PS 1793. Ink: "Rent AGREEMENT" above "pattas". Options: trusted by farmers; no official check upon the Zamindar; responsibility of the British Government; farmers not interested. Prelims 2001: answer (b) "no official check upon the Zamindar." The slide adds: Bengal Regulation VIII of 1793 required Zamindars to issue pattas (specifying rent and tenancy terms, so a patta is a rent agreement); the ryot could demand a patta. The gap was enforcement: the government cared about punctual payment of its fixed revenue. (a) trust does not explain it; (c) issuing pattas was the Zamindar's duty; (d) pattas protected cultivators. Mnemonic: Patta needs a policeman: Prelims 2001. Decode: the Zamindar owed the ryot a patta (a rent agreement) but nobody checked him: option (b), no official check. Same chain as "Patta ignored" in the impact list. Why it sticks: a promise without a checker is just a wish. Mnemonic: Prelims 2011: "Code, not Calm" (answer d). Decode: litigation rose because of the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793, not because Zamindars grew stronger, not because the EIC was overlord (that was 1765), not because courts were efficient. Why it sticks: Code = the cause; the other three are decoys.  Mains FYQ on the board: "British empire in India was BUILT (1) and SUSTAINED (2) by policies and tactics of DnR. Analyse." PS 1793 points to Sustained. Under BUILT: Triple Alliance, Treaty of Amritsar 1809; SA (Subsidiary Alliance) takes over external affairs (both CREATED division); USED division: factionalism = opportunity, e.g. Bassein 1802 [SA with Peshwa BR II 96-18]. Teacher: FYQ-M: built and sustained by DnR. Built = created division (the Triple Alliance and the Treaty of Amritsar 1809; the Subsidiary Alliance, which takes over external affairs) and used division (factionalism as opportunity, e.g. the Treaty of Bassein 1802, an SA with Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18). Sustained = PS 1793 (his arrow). Treaties belong to Chapter 11, Chapter 13 and Chapter 6; here you only need to hang PS 1793 on the "Sustained" hook. Mnemonic: Built by dividing, sustained by buying. Decode: BUILT: Triple Alliance and Amritsar 1809, SA (takes external affairs), Bassein 1802 (Baji Rao II 96-18, factionalism used). SUSTAINED: PS 1793, loyal Zamindars. Why it sticks: two verbs, two halves of the question. 2.6 The Rent Act of 1859 and the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885  The Rent Act of 1859: tenant protections (Bengal Presidency). Ink: "No more Tenant at will of Z". (a) more than 12 years on the same plot gives occupancy rights; (b) fewer than 12 years, no frequent rent rises; (c) Patta revived; (d) no imprisonment by Zamindars. In practice poorly implemented; loophole: evict just before 12 years; private armed men. Ink: "Z contd to keep [LATHIYALS]". Revolts: Indigo 1859-63, Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873. After decades of peasant revolts the British were compelled to act. The Rent Act of 1859 (Bengal Presidency):   Provision   Content    --- ---    a)   A tenant who cultivated the same plot continuously for more than 12 years gained occupancy rights: no eviction without a court order; rent not raised without the Zamindar showing just cause     b)   With fewer than 12 years on a plot, rents could not be increased frequently     c)   The Patta system was revived: Zamindars had to collect rents at recorded rates     d)   Zamindars lost the power to imprison tenants   Teacher: "No more tenant at will of the Zamindar" (top right of slide 38). In practice it was poorly implemented: the loophole was to evict the tenant just before he completed 12 years, permanently denying him occupancy rights; Zamindars kept private armed men ("Z contd to keep LATHIYALS," the Zamindar's club-men, paid through bribery) and officials turned a blind eye. The failure drove the Indigo Revolt (1859-63) and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), where ryots fought specifically for occupancy rights (the revolts themselves: Chapter 20, Chapter 22).  The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885). Ink: "Tenancy" boxed and ticked; the Act ticked; "only for" beside it; a three-circle sketch at right (S, Z and a third circle with arrows). Origin: after Ripon 80-84 set up the Rent Commission in 1880; passed under Dufferin 84-88's tenure by the Bengal Legislative Council. (a) rights of Zamindars and ryots defined; (b) Zamindars' powers reduced; (c) occupancy rights for more than 12 years total across plots in the same village, over the last plot cultivated, closing the loophole; (d) implemented sincerely. The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) followed Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880 (passed under Dufferin 84-88's tenure, enacted by the Bengal Legislative Council): Rights of all stakeholders, Zamindars and ryots, clearly defined in law. Powers of Zamindars significantly reduced. Occupancy rights strengthened: even tenants who cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years now got occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated, closing the loophole. The government implemented it sincerely this time. Teacher: He boxes "Tenancy" and ticks both "Tenancy" and "Act" with a note "only for ..." and sketches three circles joined by arrows (State, Zamindar and a third, unclear) ([unclear: check your notebook]). Underlines: Rent Commission in 1880, dufferin's tenure, Bengal Legislative Council, "even tenants who cultivated different plots ... more than 12 years", "got occupancy rights", "sincerely". Mnemonic: Twelve years: same plot (1859), any plots (1885). Decode: 1859 Rent Act: more than 12 years on the same plot = occupancy rights (loophole: evict at year 11). 1885 Tenancy Act (Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission 1880, enacted under Dufferin 84-88): 12 years in total across plots in the village = rights on the last plot, loophole shut, sincerely implemented. Why it sticks: the dozen stays; the "where" widens from plot to village. Mnemonic: 59 Rent, 59-63 Indigo, 73 Pabna, 80 Commission, 85 Act. Decode: Rent Act 1859 (poorly implemented) → Indigo Revolt 1859-63 → Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 → Rent Commission 1880 (Ripon 80-84) → Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 (Dufferin 84-88's tenure). Why it sticks: the numbers go up in sensible steps: 59, 73, 80, 85.

items.t: 3 · Ryotwari settlement
items.x: Ryotwari: where applied. Applied in Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras and Bombay (SCAM-B, and indeed a B-grade scam). Teacher's board "Annexations": Sind 1843 (Charles Napier); Coorg 1834 (famous coffee plantations); Assam (1824-26, 1st Anglo-Burmese War, Yandabo 1826); Bombay (1817-19, 3rd Anglo-Maratha War); Madras: 1766 N. Sarkars, 3rd and 4th Anglo-Mysore War, 1801 Carnatic. Right: Malabar, Kanara (4th), 3rd A-My, Baramahal, Dindigul. Applied in: Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras and Bombay. Mnemonic: SCAM-B: it was a B-grade scam. Decode: Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras, Bombay (the handout's own line). The teacher's annexation years: Sind 1843, Coorg 1834, Assam 1824-26, Bombay 1817-19. Why it sticks: a scam that needs a B-grade ticket: SCAM-B. Teacher: Ryotwari followed annexations. Sind 1843 (Charles Napier), Coorg 1834 (famous for coffee plantations), Assam 1824-26 (First Anglo-Burmese War; Yandabo 1826, written "Toyandobo 1826"), Bombay 1817-19 (Third Anglo-Maratha War). Madras came in pieces: 1766 Northern Sarkars; the Third and Fourth Anglo-Mysore Wars (Malabar and Baramahal from the 3rd, Kanara from the 4th, Dindigul too, as drawn); 1801 the Carnatic (see Chapter 12). Circled 1 and 2 above the table: [unclear: check your notebook]. The class map (Lecture 18, slide 24) lists Berar under Ryotwari as well; the handout's list does not. Both agree on the five places above. 3.1 Ryotwari in Madras (1801 onward, firmly from 1820)  Ryotwari in Madras: from the PS 1793 attempt to Munro. Cornwallis and Wellesley tried to create big landlords in Madras by recognising the Poligars as Zamindars (Poligar = local chief with private armies, autonomous since the Vijayanagar Empire 1336-1646). The experiment failed; Munro convinced the Court of Directors in 1801. 1792 Alexander Read; 1801-07 Munro; 1820 Munro. Munro first experimented in Baramahal (annexed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-92); diluted after he left in 1807; re-established as Governor of Madras 1820-27; he died in India. Ink: basic premise of PS 1793: big landlords very rich, pay LR (10/11), invest huge Rs in land; in Bengal MQK 17-27 created big Zs; by 1727 15 Zs collected 50% of LR of Bengal Suba. The first attempt in Madras was the same as Bengal: extend PS. Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars by recognising the Poligars (landed magnates with private armies, autonomous since the Vijayanagar Empire of 1336-1646) as landowners. The experiment failed. Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London in 1801 to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras. He had first experimented in parts of Madras in 1792 under Alexander Read (the slide: in Baramahal, annexed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-92). 1801-07 Ryotwari applied in Madras. It was diluted after he left for Britain in 1807; he re-established it firmly as Governor of Madras (1820-27). He died in India.  PYQ 5, Prelims 2017: architects of Ryotwari. Ink: 86-93 above Lord Cornwallis; 1792 above Alexander Read; 1801-07 and 1820 beside Thomas Munro. Prelims 2017: answer (c) 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is wrong: Lord Cornwallis 86-93 was the PS 1793 architect and even tried PS in Madras through the Poligars. Read (1792) and Munro (1801-07, and 1820) are the Ryotwari pair. The teacher's years on the slide are the answer key. Handout hook: Read and Munro = Ryotwari (Scottish, yeoman); Cornwallis 86-93 = Permanent (English landlordism). Mnemonic: Read 92, Munro 01 to 07, Munro 20: Ryotwari's three dates. Decode: Alexander Read 1792 (Baramahal; Munro under him), Munro 1801-07 (Court of Directors convinced; diluted when he left in 1807), Munro 1820 (Governor of Madras 1820-27). Cornwallis 86-93 = PS. Why it sticks: Read starts it, Munro twice, Cornwallis 86-93 not at all. Why Munro pushed Ryotwari over PS: five reasons.  Why Munro chose Ryotwari over PS: 5 reasons. a) Scottish ideology (ticked; yeoman farmer; Orientalist); b) no big Zamindars (MQK 17-27, 15 Zamindars collected 50%); c) State finances (3 Carnatic Wars 1746-63, 4 Anglo-Mysore Wars 1767-99; PS fixes LR forever in amount terms, not %); d) eliminate middlemen (Deshmukhs and Poligars); e) political stability. Ink: PS 1793 written under "PS"; "To Bar POLITICAL AUTHORITY" beside row e.   Reason   What it says    --- ---    a) Scottish ideology   Munro was from Scotland, where the hero of agrarian society was the Yeoman farmer (a landowner who also cultivates his own land, a more prosperous Khudkasht). As an Orientalist he argued ancient India had no intermediaries between the State and the cultivator     b) No big Zamindars   In Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) created super-rich Intermediary Zamindars: by 1727, 15 of them collected 50% of Bengal's LR, which made PS viable. Madras had no such class     c) State finances   Madras was under stress from low productivity and past wars: three Carnatic Wars (1746-63) and four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-99). PS fixes LR forever in amount, not %, so there is no room to grow State income     d) Eliminate intermediaries   Poligars' profits came at the State's expense (the slide adds Deshmukhs). Remove them: the share can go partly to the State, partly to lighter burden on ryots     e) Political stability   Removing Poligars as a class of powerful non-State actors reduces resistance; loyalty of the masses comes from giving them land (the teacher: "To bar political authority")   Teacher: He ticks (a) Scottish ideology and writes beside (e) "To bar POLITICAL AUTHORITY" (the Poligars' private armies and autonomy are what he means). On slide 2 he restates the logic of PS: big landlords must be very rich, so they can pay the LR (10/11) and invest huge sums in land; Bengal had them (15 Zs, 50%), Madras did not. Mnemonic: Sam Never Forgets Every Poligar: Munro's five reasons. Decode: Scottish yeoman ideology (ticked), No big Zamindars in Madras, Finances stressed (3 Carnatic + 4 Mysore wars; PS fixes in amount), Eliminate intermediaries (Poligars), Political stability (non-State actors removed). Why it sticks: S-N-F-E-P in handout order; Sam = Scotsman. Mnemonic: Fifteen Zamindars, half of Bengal, by 1727. Decode: MQK 17-27 built super-rich Intermediary Zamindars; by 1727, 15 collected 50% of Bengal's LR; that wealth base made PS viable in Bengal and its absence made Madras different. Why it sticks: 15 and 50, 1727 echoes the end of MQK 17-27's term. 3.2 Under Ryotwari  Under Ryotwari. Landowner: the ryot held legal title. Settlement: directly with the ryot. Assessment: detailed field surveys with revision and remission of LR in bad harvests; two phases, from % of gross produce to % of net rental value. Ink: in %, revisable (circled plusses); "Remit = yes, not 0"; Collection by DC and his juniors (Indians); Net produce = Gross minus costs; Ricardian Theory of Rent.   The five questions   Ryotwari    --- ---    Landowner   The ryot, who held legal title     Settlement   Directly with the ryot: the State dealt with each cultivator individually     Assessment   Detailed field surveys (soil productivity, irrigation, acreage, crops, past trends), in %, revisable, with revision and remission in bad harvests     Collection   By State officers: the DC and his juniors (Indians)     Tenants   (not stated on the slides)    Teacher's board: the field survey is the most crucial thing in Ryotwari, and very tough. Improper survey leads to unjust LR demand, a sad face, landlessness (boxed). Proper survey leads to a justified demand and success of the system. Left: very high LR so people abandon land; higher LR means default on LR, government auction; higher LR means higher loan interest from the moneylender, default, loss of mortgaged land. Right: the names of the officers who designed and implemented surveys = imp; Bombay: Wingate Settlement = Ryotwari. Teacher: The field survey is the crux of Ryotwari (very tough). Improper survey → unjust LR demand → landlessness. Three roads to loss of land from high LR: people abandon the land; default on LR → government auction; higher interest on a moneylender's loan → default → loss of the mortgaged land. And: "name of officers who designed and implemented the survey = imp" (underlined imp), with "Bombay: Wingate Settlement = Ryotwari." Learn the surveyors' names. Assessment evolved in two phases.     Phase 1: gross produce   Phase 2: rental value or net produce    --- --- ---    Where and when   Madras, by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro (1792-1820)   Bombay (Pringle 1830, Wingate 1835) and Madras (1855, 1864)     Demand   33% to 50% of estimated gross produce   Based on net produce (gross crop value minus cost of cultivation: seeds, manure, bullocks, labour, implements): the Ricardian theory of Economic Rent     Flaw or fix   Surveys often improper; method arbitrary and ignored the cost of cultivation   Reformed after the ruin of the agrarian economy     Result   Severe over-assessment: poverty, land abandonment ("Kheti hi chhod diye"); crop failure → borrow from moneylenders at high interest → default → lose mortgaged land or lose it in government auctions   Bombay: Wingate fixes it; Madras: capped at 50%   Mnemonic: Gross is greedy (33-50), Net is neat (Ricardo). Decode: Phase 1 (Read and Munro, 1792-1820) = 33% to 50% of gross produce, ignoring the cost of cultivation: ruin. Phase 2 = net produce (gross minus costs), the Ricardian theory of Economic Rent. Why it sticks: gross grabs, net leaves the cultivator his costs. Mnemonic: Crop fails, Money-lender, Default, Land gone: C-M-D-L. Decode: crop failure → borrow from the moneylender at high interest → default → lose the mortgaged land (or default on LR and lose land at government auction). The teacher's end: landlessness. Why it sticks: the four-step slide down the same slope. Phase 2 in Bombay.  Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Bombay. Bombay (1819): Elphinstone brought Ryotwari (no fresh survey, used existing Maratha records and assessments). R.K. Pringle (1830) first applied Economic Rent theory but faulty calculations led to excessive demand (LR = 55%). Wingate Settlement of 1835 (Bombay Survey System by Wingate and Goldsmid, across Bombay Deccan by 1847): fixed the flaw, assessed LR fairly, reasonable annual amount for 30 years. Ink: "Check it was %"; sketch of the Deccan split into Bombay Deccan and HYD Deccan. Elphinstone brought Ryotwari to Bombay (the slide dates it 1819 and says he did no fresh survey and used existing Maratha revenue records and assessments). R.K. Pringle (1830) first applied the Economic Rent theory but faulty calculations gave an excessive 55% demand. The Wingate Settlement of 1835 (Bombay Survey System, by Wingate and Goldsmid, implemented across the Bombay Deccan by 1847) fixed the flaw: it assessed LR fairly and fixed a reasonable annual amount for 30 years. Teacher: Beside "reasonable annual amount for 30 years" he writes "Check it was %" (is the Wingate demand a percentage? [unclear: check your notebook]; the handout says annual amount). His sketch splits the Deccan into the Bombay Deccan and the Hyderabad Deccan: Wingate applied to the Bombay part. Pringle's date. The handout says R.K. Pringle (1830); the teacher's ink on the comparison slide (Lecture 18, slide 23) reads "PRINGLE 1830" (next to a partly unclear "Bomb 44", [unclear: check your notebook]); the milestone slide (slide 22) places "Pringle's revenue survey" at 1824-1828. Use 1830 for the Economic Rent application, and treat 1824-28 as the survey years on that card. Phase 2 in Madras.  Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Madras. Lower bureaucracy relied on Mirasidars (rich landowner-cultivators as village revenue officers); the DC and his officers held judicial, police and revenue powers; Mirasidars oppressed ryots, forced defaults and bought the best lands in auctions. Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed coercion; Court of Directors ordered 30-year settlements in 1855 with lower LR; in 1864 SoS Charles Wood capped LR at half the net produce. Result: Mirasidars became big landowners. Ink: "his DC and juniors" arrow to Mirasidars; powers: Admin (LR collection), J, Police; "Over Concentration of Powers". Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed severe oppression in revenue collection. The Madras Rules (1855/1864) capped LR at 50% of net produce or rental value for 30 years (the slide: the Court of Directors ordered 30-year settlements with lower LR in 1855; in 1864 SoS Charles Wood directed the half-of-net-produce cap). The handout adds that addressing these grievances kept Madras relatively quiet during the 1857 revolt. Corruption: the lower bureaucracy relied on Mirasidars (rich landowner-cultivators acting as village-level revenue officers). Because the DC and his officers held concentrated judicial, police and revenue powers, Mirasidars oppressed ryots, forced defaults and bought the best lands in auctions. The goal of removing big intermediaries failed: Mirasidars became big landowners themselves. Teacher: "Over concentration of powers": the DC and his juniors (the Mirasidars) held admin (LR collection), judicial and police powers together, so a village official could squeeze the ryot, force default and then buy the land. Mnemonic: Pringle Pushed 55, Wingate Won 35, Madras Capped 50. Decode: Pringle (1830): Economic Rent but faulty, 55% of net produce. Wingate Settlement 1835: fair, annual amount for 30 years, Bombay Deccan by 1847. Madras: Torture Commission 1855, Rules 1855/1864 cap at 50% of net produce for 30 years (SoS Charles Wood, 1864). Why it sticks: 55 too high, 35 the fix, 50 the ceiling. Mnemonic: A-J-P: the Mirasidar's three hats. Decode: Admin (LR collection), Judicial, Police: concentrated powers with the DC's lower staff, so Mirasidars oppressed ryots, forced defaults and bought the best lands; the aim to remove big intermediaries failed. Why it sticks: one man wearing three hats takes the whole village.  PYQ 4, Prelims 2012: Ryotwari, three statements. Ink: a tick-like mark beside each statement.  Answer slide: (c) 1, 2 and 3. Rent reached the State directly (settlement with the ryot); the ryot held title and a patta (the Patta system PS 1793 had killed in Bengal was preserved); lands were surveyed and assessed first. Prelims 2012 (handout and class agree): answer (c) 1, 2 and 3. (1) Rent paid directly by peasants to the government: settlement is with the ryot. (2) Pattas given to ryots: the patta system was preserved. (3) Surveyed and assessed before taxed: detailed field surveys. Mnemonic: Ryotwari: Pays direct, gets a Patta, after the Survey: P-P-S. Decode: Prelims 2012 answer (c): ryot pays the State directly (settlement), receives a patta, land surveyed and assessed first. Why it sticks: all three tick, so (c). 3.3 Impact in Bombay  Collection at Ryotwari (Bombay). After annexing the Maratha Svarajya (3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19) the EIC initially used Patils and Deshmukhs to collect revenue, in line with Orientalism; later by officers (Patil was now an ordinary government officer collecting taxes for a salary). Ink: "earlier Commission"; Maratha: Deshmukh above village Patils P1...Pn, ryots paying LR upward.  Impact of Ryotwari in Bombay. a) Patils demoted (earlier executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and a commission; now a salaried officer); b) massive indebtedness to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders in the central Deccan in the 1850s; c) not solely Ryotwari: crop failures and the collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65). Combined result: the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Collection: after annexing the Maratha Svarajya (3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19) the EIC first used Patils (village headmen) and Deshmukhs to collect revenue, a nod to Orientalism; later it used officers. a) Patils lost their historic status. Earlier a Patil held executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and earned a commission (the teacher: "earlier commission"); now he was an ordinary salaried officer. b) Massive indebtedness to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders swept the central Deccan in the 1850s. c) Not solely Ryotwari: crop failures and the collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65). Indian cotton boomed in 1861-65 because the Union naval blockade cut off Confederate cotton; when the war ended, US cotton flooded markets again and the premium vanished. Combined result: the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Mnemonic: Boom 61, bust 65, riot 75. Decode: US Civil War 1861-65: Union blockade cuts Confederate cotton, Indian cotton booms; war ends 1865, US cotton floods back, prices collapse; debts (Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders) plus crop failures give the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875; Patils lost status under Ryotwari. Why it sticks: three two-digit beats: 61, 65, 75. Teacher: Underlines: Patils demoted, executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and a commission, indebtedness, Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders, "crop failures played a role", "collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65)", Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875.

items.t: 4 · Mahalwari settlement
items.x: Mahalwari: where applied. Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab (Mahal, Taj Mahal, Tea in a CUP, Mahalwari in CUP). UP = United Provinces of Agra and Oudh created 1902. Ink: 1801 and 1856 annexed (pointing at United Provinces); Punjab annexed in 1849; "UP = Awadh = 1801 | 1856, undivided"; ceded districts, 1822 Mahalwari, NWP 1836; names: 1877 "NWP and Oudh", 1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh", 1937 UP, 1950 Uttar Pradesh. Applied in: Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab. Mnemonic: Mahal, Taj Mahal, Tea in a CUP: Mahalwari in CUP. Decode: Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab (the handout's chain). Teacher's dates: Punjab annexed 1849; United Provinces = Awadh, taken in two bites (1801, 1856). Why it sticks: Taj Mahal sounds like Mahal; tea in a CUP is the picture. Teacher: UP = Awadh, undivided, taken in two parts: 1801 and 1856. The 1801 ceded districts were the first part; they got Mahalwari in 1822 and were organised as the North-Western Provinces (NWP) in 1836; Awadh was annexed in 1856; Punjab was annexed in 1849. The name changed in four steps: 1877 "NWP and Oudh;" 1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh;" 1937 "UP;" 1950 "Uttar Pradesh." (The handout's note says the "UP of 1937 = United Provinces of Agra and Oudh created in 1902": the board untangles it: 1902 is when it was named so; 1937 the short form UP; 1950 the modern name.) Mnemonic: Names climb: 77, 02, 37, 50. Decode: 1877 North-Western Provinces and Oudh → 1902 United Provinces of Agra and Oudh → 1937 UP → 1950 Uttar Pradesh. NWP itself dates from 1836. Why it sticks: four numbers, each shorter than the name before. 4.1 Origin in Awadh  The Mahalwari Settlement: origin in Awadh. Before: Taluqdars (Intermediary Zamindars) and Primary Zamindars dominated. 1801-22: half of Awadh under the British (1801); severe over-extraction; Taluqdars who resisted lost their milkiyats (landed estates), an entire class of magnates was crushed. Change via auctions: Amils/Amalguzars and Tehsildars grew powerful buying the best lands; (Amlas are distinct: private employees of Zamindars); moneylenders, bankers, merchants also acquired milkiyat lands. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations implemented through Regulation VII of 1822. Ink: Taluqdars = traditional leaders of rural society; milkiyat = personal lands; "7th Law of 1822". Before the British, Taluqdars (Intermediary Zamindars) and Primary Zamindars dominated Awadh's agrarian economy. Half of Awadh came under British administration in 1801 (the nucleus of the North-Western Provinces). 1801-22: severe over-extraction. Taluqdars who resisted lost their milkiyats (landed estates): an entire class of landed magnates was crushed. In Mahalwari areas the Mughal-era revenue officers (Amils and Amalguzars at the district level, Tehsildars at the sub-district level) grew powerful and bought the best lands in auctions (note: Amlas are different, private employees of Zamindars, not State officers). Moneylenders, bankers and merchants also acquired milkiyat lands. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through Regulation VII of 1822, creating the Mahalwari Settlement. Mahal = a community of people at the village, estate or district level. Teacher: Taluqdar = a traditional leader of rural society; milkiyat = personal lands (so milkiyat holders = big landowners). He writes "7th Law of 1822" against Regulation VII of 1822 (as he did "7th Law of 1799" in Section 2.5): two Regulation VIIs, 1799 for Zamindar powers, 1822 for Mahalwari. Mnemonic: Two Seventh Laws: 1799 empowers, 1822 creates. Decode: Regulation VII of 1799 (Wellesley 98-05): Zamindars get coercion back. Regulation VII of 1822 (Holt Mackenzie): Mahalwari. The teacher calls both "7th Law". Why it sticks: same number, two Acts, 23 years apart.  Teacher's board: Mahal = community of people at village level, or district level, or estate level [some other size]. Why Mahalwari (1822): settlement done with the Mahal, represented by the village headman or Lambardar. 4.2 The hybrid structure  Teacher's board: a circle split in two. Majority areas: landowner = ryot; settlement = Mahal. Other part: landowner = Z = IZ = Taluqdar; settlement = Z = IZ. Left: 1822-33 assessment done at per field, plot, ryot level; 1833: LR assessed at Mahal level to respect village autonomy. Bottom: Mahalwari = HYBRID of Ryotwari and Zamindari [landownership].  Mahalwari: the final hybrid structure. A) ryot as landowner (most areas): settlement with the Mahal; Lambardar is the interface; the Mahal decides how the demand is divided; similar to Ryotwari minus settlement with the ryot. B) Taluqdar as landowner (some areas): settlement with the Taluqdar; law recognised ryots' occupancy rights and mandated recording of rents, so the Patta had legal backing; similar to PS 1793 minus permanent assessment. Collection by State officers.   The five questions   Mahalwari (a hybrid)    --- ---    Landowner   Most areas: the ryot. Some areas: the Taluqdar     Settlement   Most areas: with the Mahal, through the Lambardar (its representative; he is the interface between State and community, preserving village autonomy; the Mahal decides internally how to spread the total demand). Some areas: with the Taluqdar     Assessment   Mahal-level after 1833 (before: per field or ryot); 66% of rental value for 30 years, revisable     Collection   State officers (the teacher: DC)     Tenants   Where the Taluqdar was owner, the law recognised ryots' occupancy rights and required recording of rents: the Patta had legal backing   Teacher: Mahalwari = a HYBRID of Ryotwari and Zamindari (on landownership). The slide's rule of thumb: type A = Ryotwari minus settlement with the ryot (it is with the Mahal); type B = PS 1793 minus permanent assessment. Mnemonic: Mahalwari = Ryotwari minus one, PS minus one. Decode: ryot-as-owner areas: like Ryotwari but the settlement is with the Mahal (via the Lambardar). Taluqdar-as-owner areas: like PS 1793 but assessment is not permanent, and ryots' patta rights have legal backing. Why it sticks: each parent is missing exactly one part. 4.3 The Revised Mahalwari System (R.M. Bird, 1833)  1833 Revised Mahalwari System: R.M. Bird, 1833 (in NWP 1836). LR was first assessed at individual field/ryot level, but improper surveys led to excessive demands. (a) assessment at the Mahal level; (b) the community decides each member's contribution; (c) if the Mahal fell short, the State could auction individual ryots' lands; (d) LR fixed at 66% of Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years, subject to revision. Dalhousie extended Mahalwari to Punjab and Central India. Ink: 1822-33; Net produce above Net Assets. Initially LR was assessed at the individual field or ryot level, but improper surveys led to excessive demands. In 1833, R.M. Bird introduced the Revised Mahalwari System in the NWP: (a) assessment at the Mahal level, not plot level, respecting the community's collective character; (b) individual contributions decided by the community; (c) if the Mahal's collective LR fell short, the State could auction individual ryots' lands; (d) LR fixed at 66% of the Rental Value (Net Assets, the teacher: net produce) for 30 years, subject to State revision. Dalhousie 48-56 extended Mahalwari to Punjab and Central India. Mnemonic: M-C-A-6: Bird's four rules. Decode: Mahal-level assessment, Community splits the share, Auction of individual ryot lands if the Mahal falls short, 66% of net assets for 30 years, revisable. Dalhousie 48-56 carried it to Punjab and Central India. Why it sticks: Bird says "MCA 6": 66 is the number to keep (against Madras's 50). Mnemonic: Mackenzie 22, Bird 33: two-two, three-three. Decode: Holt Mackenzie, Regulation VII of 1822; R.M. Bird, Revised Mahalwari 1833 (NWP 1836 follows); 66% against Madras's 50%. Why it sticks: repeated digits, in the teacher's order of the two architects. 4.4 Why Mahalwari failed  Why Mahalwari failed. Mechanism: improper field surveys, unjust LR, ryots lose land in State auctions or fall into debt to moneylenders and lose mortgaged land. 1856 summary settlement in Awadh (no field surveys, simply because surveys take time): unjust LR, landlessness. Fed 1857: crushing of Taluqdars 1801-22, unjust LR demand, summary settlement of 1856, ryot landlessness fed directly into the 1857 revolt in the NWP (1836) and Awadh. Ink: 1801, NWP 1836, 1856; "Landlessness in LTM"; Taluqdars sad (leaders), ryot short term smiley and long term sad; both arrows to the boxed 1857 Revolt. Improper field surveys → unjust land revenue → ryots lose land in State auctions or fall into debt and lose mortgaged land. When Awadh was finally annexed in 1856 a summary settlement was made (revenue without field surveys, because surveys take time): unjust demands and landlessness. Crushing of Taluqdars (1801-22), unjust demands, the summary settlement of 1856 and landlessness of ryots fed directly into the 1857 revolt in the NWP and Awadh (see Chapter 21). Teacher: Two sad groups, both heading to 1857. Taluqdars (the leaders) were crushed; the ryot may have gained in the short term (smiley) but suffered in the long term (sad: landlessness in the long term). Both arrows end at the boxed "1857 REVOLT." Mnemonic: Crush, Summary, Landless: the road to 1857 in Awadh. Decode: Crushed Taluqdars (1801-22), Summary settlement 1856 (no survey, unjust LR), Landlessness of ryots; together they fed the 1857 revolt in the NWP and Awadh. Why it sticks: three words, one fire.

items.t: 5 · Commercialisation of agriculture
items.x: Teacher's board. Pre-IR (Industrial Revolution) 1750-1850: India = source of finished goods, e.g. finished cotton. Post-IR: India = export market (buying British machine-made goods) plus raw materials (RM, EM), e.g. raw cotton to a factory in Britain. Crops: (A) Food for food security; (B) Cash for commerce, trade, profit. Britain wanted Indians to produce more B and less A = commercialisation of agri, so a higher chance of famine. Starred: PYQ: Why so many famines in British India?  Commercialisation of agriculture: the cash-revenue chain. (1) Cash revenue demand (Mughals took much in kind; the British demanded cash); (2) shift to cash crops (compelled or induced by moneylenders and traders): indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane; (3) structural transformation (rice, wheat, millets land turned to crops for British factories and global markets); (4) food security collapse and famines. Ink: "More ROLE of Rs Lenders" with an arrow from box 1; "AND" circled between boxes 1 and 2.  Handout figure of the same chain: British land revenue demanded in cash (not kind); ryots pressured to generate cash and shift from food to cash crops; moneylenders and traders induce the shift (interest-driven debt trap); tea, coffee, indigo (plantation cash crops, export orientation); cotton, jute, opium for British factories and global markets; oilseeds and sugarcane added to the mix; food grain reserves shrink; rural indebtedness, land auctions, peasant dispossession; famines of the late 19th century and peasant revolts (1857, Pabna, Deccan 1875). Under the Mughals much of the demand could be met in kind (grain for grain). The British demanded revenue in cash. To get cash, ryots were compelled, or induced by moneylenders and traders, to shift from food crops (feed the family, low market price) to cash crops: indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane. The higher the demand, the greater the pressure to grow cash crops: a structural transformation. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets now served British factories or global commodity markets. Food security declined: less food grain in reserve when drought or flood struck. This is one of the most important long-term legacies of British land policy and fed directly into the famines of the late 19th century. Teacher: Two Indias. Before the Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) India was a source of finished goods (e.g. finished cotton); after it, India became an export market for British machine-made goods and a source of raw materials (raw cotton to British factories). Britain wanted Indians to grow more cash crops (B) and fewer food crops (A) = commercialisation of agriculture, so a higher chance of famine. His starred Mains prompt: "Why so many famines in British India?" And on slide 20 he adds that the moneylender's role rises along with cash demand ("More role of Rs Lenders", and a circled AND joining cash demand and the shift). The handout figure also names tea and coffee (plantation crops), oilseeds and a debt trap, and ends with peasant revolts (1857, Pabna, Deccan 1875). The handout's text lists indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane; use the text's list for Prelims, and the figure's extras only as colour in a Mains answer. Mnemonic: Cash Calls, Crops Change, Larders Fall: C-C-L-F. Decode: Cash revenue demand → Cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane) → Less food grain in reserve → Famines of the late 19th century. (The handout's hook: "Cash revenue demand → cash crops → food security collapse → late-19th-century famines".) Why it sticks: each C or L or F is a link you can say aloud. Mnemonic: I Cook Only Juicy Sweets: the five cash crops. Decode: Indigo, Cotton, Opium, Jute, Sugarcane (the handout's text list). Rice, wheat and millets lost land to them. Why it sticks: a cook who picks only juicy, sweet things, not staples.  PYQ 6, Prelims 2021: economic result of British rule. Ink: 19th century underlined; (a) handicraft exports "= FG therefore F"; (b) Indian factories F; (c) commercialisation "RM therefore T"; (d) urban population F with "when IR of India" and a sad face. Right: 1800s, IR 1750-1850 boxed, "mature stage"; India = RM, EM source. Prelims 2021: answer (c) commercialisation of Indian agriculture. Teacher: (a) F (before the IR India exported finished goods; in the 19th century, the mature IR stage, India became a source of raw materials and an export market, so handicraft exports fell: deindustrialisation); (b) F (no conclusive evidence of growing Indian-owned factories); (c) T ("RM": raw materials need cash crops); (d) F (no conclusive evidence of rapid urbanisation). Mnemonic: FG out, RM in: Prelims 2021 (c). Decode: before the IR, India sold Finished Goods; in the 19th century India supplied Raw Materials, so cash crops (commercialisation) is true; handicraft exports, Indian factories and rapid urbanisation are false. Why it sticks: the exit of FG and the entry of RM tell the whole story.

items.t: 6 · Reading the three systems together
items.x: Why three different systems? Cornwallis (an Englishman who believed in landlordism) created Permanent Settlement; Munro (a Scotsman who believed in the yeoman farmer) created Ryotwari; Mahalwari was a practical compromise where neither clean model fit. Ideology, geography and fiscal pressure. Ink: ticks above "landlordism" and "yeoman". Why three systems? Ideology, geography and fiscal pressure pulled in different directions. Cornwallis 86-93, an Englishman who believed in landlordism, made the Permanent Settlement. Munro, a Scotsman who believed in the yeoman farmer, made Ryotwari. Mahalwari was a practical compromise where neither clean model fit. 6.1 Permanent Settlement against Ryotwari against Mahalwari  Comparison: Permanent Settlement (1793) / Ryotwari (1801, 1820+) / Mahalwari (1822, rev. 1833) on landowner, settlement with, assessment, collection by, where applied, architect, key failure. Ink: "/ DC" after "State officers" in the Ryotwari and Mahalwari columns; in the Ryotwari "where applied" cell "PRINGLE 1830" and "Bomb 44" (unclear); "Wingate and Goldsmid 1835" under it; underlines on Read and Munro, Elphinstone, Holt Mackenzie, R.M. Bird.   Dimension   Permanent Settlement (1793)   Ryotwari (1801, 1820+)   Mahalwari (1822, revised 1833)    --- --- --- ---    Landowner   Zamindar   Ryot   Mostly ryot; sometimes Taluqdar (hybrid)     Settlement with   Zamindar   Ryot directly   Mahal (via the Lambardar) or Taluqdar     Assessment   Permanent: fixed forever (10/11 of pre-existing revenue)   Detailed field surveys; 50% of net rental value (Madras Rules 1855/1864) for 30 years   Mahal-level; 66% of Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years     Collection by   District Collector   State officers (teacher: / DC)   State officers (teacher: / DC)     Where applied   Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, Benaras, North Madras (BOB + Benaras + N. Madras)   Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras, Bombay (SCAM-B)   Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab (CUP)     Architect or driver   Cornwallis 86-93 (English landlordism)   Alexander Read + Thomas Munro (Scottish yeoman); slide adds Elphinstone (Bombay)   Holt Mackenzie + R.M. Bird (hybrid, practical)     Key failure   Absentee landlordism; ryot a "tenant at will"; Patta collapses   Over-assessment; Mirasidar abuse; Bombay Deccan Riots 1875   Improper surveys; summary settlement 1856; 1857 NWP and Awadh epicentre    Class map: Land Revenue Systems under the British (1793-1858). Permanent Settlement (blue): the east (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; north coastal Andhra and Benaras (E. UP) were also PS). Ryotwari (green): Madras and Bombay Presidencies, Sindh, Coorg, Assam Province, Berar. Mahalwari (orange): Central Provinces, United Provinces (NWP), Punjab. Grey: princely states with their own systems. Footnote: shaded by present-day state, dominant system only. No ink. Reading the map. It shades by today's state and shows the dominant system only. Princely states (grey) had their own revenue arrangements and are not among the three. The north coastal Andhra and Benaras pockets belong to PS (the handout's "North Madras" and "Benaras"). Berar appears under Ryotwari on the map but not in the handout's list. Mnemonic: Z-Z, R-R, M-M: who owns, who settles. Decode: PS: Zamindar owns and settles. Ryotwari: Ryot owns and settles. Mahalwari: Mostly ryot owns, Mahal settles (or Taluqdar both). Assessment: PS permanent; Ryotwari 50% net (Madras Rules); Mahalwari 66% net, 30 years. Why it sticks: pairs repeat, only the last one splits. Mnemonic: 66, 50, 10/11: the three assessments. Decode: Mahalwari 66% of rental value (30 years); Ryotwari 50% of net rental value in Madras (30 years); PS 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue, forever. Why it sticks: sixty-six is the biggest slice, 50 the middle, 10/11 the odd one, frozen. Mnemonic: Three men, three maps: Cornwallis 86-93 East, Munro South-West, Mackenzie and Bird North. Decode: Cornwallis 86-93 (English landlordism) = Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, Benaras, North Madras. Read and Munro (Scottish yeoman) = Madras, Bombay, Sind, Coorg, Assam. Holt Mackenzie and R.M. Bird (practical hybrid) = Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab. Why it sticks: compass directions follow the three men. 6.2 Common causes of ryot suffering  Common causes of ryot suffering across all three systems. What united all three was a common outcome: ryots suffered. Whether the landowner was a Zamindar, the ryot himself or a Taluqdar, high land revenue demands, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the imperfect but customary protections of the Mughal system. No ink. What united all three was a common outcome: ryots suffered. Whoever the landowner was (Zamindar, ryot, Taluqdar), the mix of high land revenue demands, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the imperfect but customary protections of the Mughal system. Mnemonic: H-F-L-P: why the ryot lost everywhere. Decode: High demand, Faulty surveys, Legal vulnerability (no rights, "tenant at will"), Predatory moneylending. Worse off than under the Mughal patta. Why it sticks: "HFLP" sounds like "help": the ryot got none.  PYQ 1, Prelims 2000: match list on four land revenue systems. Ink: circles beside List I: A = 1, B = 4, C = 2, D = 3; ticks beside Ryotwari and Mahalwari; (b) A-1 B-4 C-2 D-3 ticked.  Answer slide: (b). A big feudal landlords = Jagirdari (jagir allotted to a Mughal noble); B revenue farmers or rent collectors = Zamindari (a commission collector, not owner); C peasant with sublet, mortgage, transfer rights = Ryotwari; D village-level settlements = Mahalwari, post Bird 1833. Hook: Mughal jagir = land allotted to the feudal noble; Zamindar = revenue collector with a commission; peasant with title = Ryotwari; village Mahal = Mahalwari. Prelims 2000, the handout and the class slide disagree on the first two rows (see the alert in the Exam lens). Handout: A = Zamindari, B = Jagirdari, code A-4 B-1 C-2 D-3 = (b); class slide and teacher's circles: A = Jagirdari, B = Zamindari, code A-1 B-4 C-2 D-3 = (b). The letter (b) is common. C = Ryotwari and D = Mahalwari are common. If you remember only one rule: peasant with the right to sell = Ryotwari; village level = Mahalwari. Mnemonic: Title with the ryot, village with the Mahal. Decode: Prelims 2000: land to each peasant with sublet, mortgage, transfer, gift or sale rights = Ryotwari; settlements at village level = Mahalwari (after Bird 1833). The landlord rows (Jagirdari and Zamindari) are where the handout and slide differ; answer letter (b). Why it sticks: the two sure rows are the ones you can say in a sentence.

items.t: 7 · Revision PYQs on the class slides (not in the handout)
items.x: Lecture 18, slides 40 to 43 are two revision PYQs from other chapters that the teacher placed at the end of this block. No handout coverage in this chapter.  PYQ 8, Prelims 1995: correctly matched pair. Ink: Buxar 1764, Wandiwash 1760, Chilianwala 1849, Kharda 1795; above "Combatants": 54-75 and 60-63 with "Shuja, Qasim, Shah Alam II 60-06"; (a) circled F; (b) ticked; "Sikh" above Marathas in (c); circled "MA" under the Nizam row in (d). Prelims 1995: answer (b) Battle of Wandiwash (1760): French against the EIC (3rd Carnatic War 1756-63, which ended French ambitions). Munro counters with Ryotwari (SCAM-B; Read 92, Munro 01-07, Munro 20): survey, gross to net, Pringle 55, Wingate 35, Madras 50; Mirasidars wear three hats; boom 61, bust 65, riot 75. Mackenzie 22 and Bird 33 build Mahalwari in CUP (66% for 30 years), and 1856's summary settlement lights 1857. Cash revenue calls for cash crops, and the larder empties (C-C-L-F). Mains hooks: how each Act moved power from the EIC to the Br State; why the State chose regulation, not abolition, in 1773; centralisation in the GG (peak 1833) and the start of a separate legislature; Dual Government versus Dual Control; Sub-Imperialism and State responsibility for conquest; why 1857 was "the final nail". Closing idea: the sovereignty moved to the Crown by 1793 and the Company's body was left in place until the Crown could take it over in 1858. Mains question on the slides and the skeleton (from the notes only). Teacher: FYQ (Lecture 18, slide 47): "1857 Revolt was only a final nail in the coffin of EIC's empire in India. Discuss." His answer line on the slide: each Charter or Regulating Act stripped EIC powers and transferred them to the Br State. Introduction: the revolt is often seen as the end of Company rule, but the decline of the EIC's autonomy began nearly a century earlier; 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound. Body: (1) 1773: Parliament's right to regulate political affairs recognised; Directors must report; Crown-chosen Supreme Court. (2) 1784: Board of Control; Double Government and Dual Control; Principal Servants can be recalled. (3) 1793: Crown sovereignty, Principal Servants only after Crown approval, Parliament renews the Charter. (4) 1813: India trade monopoly ended; Crown sovereignty re-stated. (5) 1833: commercial function ended; BoC supervises all administration. (6) 1853: no fixed term, patronage lost to the Civil Services exam, Budget under Parliament. (7) 1858: the revolt, the public, free traders and the educated middle class demanded direct rule. Closing: the revolt gave the occasion, the Acts had already done the work; the Crown took the Company's body after taking its head in 1793.

items.t: 1 · Why the Br State wanted to regulate the EIC
items.x: The 1857 revolt is often seen as the reason EIC rule ended. But if one reads the laws Parliament passed from 1773 onwards, the story is clear: the decline of the EIC's autonomy began nearly a century before 1857. Each Charter Act and Regulating Act slowly stripped the EIC of powers and transferred them to the British State. 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound. 1.1 The five drivers  Why the Br State Wanted to Regulate EIC. Drivers: Money (State wanted its share from the loot of Bengal; in 1767 it demanded 400,000 pounds a year, underlined); Fear due to American Revolution (1765-83, 13 colonies to USA); Protecting the Br taxpayer (1772 bankruptcy, 1.4 million pounds loan); White Man's Burden betrayed (Great Bengal Famine 1770 and the Nabobs). Ink: beside the American Revolution row "EIC shall never do AR65-83 in India"; a sketch with "13 colonies", a small circle "Br", a loop and a cone with a zigzag arrow "ToA 1765"; "AR65-83" underlined.   Driver   Detail    --- ---    1. Money   After Plassey (1757) and the ToA 1765, the EIC got both plunder and Bengal's land revenue. In 1767 the Br State demanded 400,000 pounds a year from the EIC, arguing the State had helped the EIC in conquest. The State wanted its share     2. Fear of another America   The American Revolution began in 1765 (the Stamp Act crisis marks the start of the political revolution) and by 1783 the USA was created. The armed War of Independence began in 1775. What if EIC officials, growing rich and powerful in India, did the same?     3. Protecting the taxpayer   In 1772 the EIC went bankrupt and was bailed out with a 1.4 million pound loan from the State ("too big to fail"). The State wanted oversight to prevent reckless war expenditure     4. White Man's Burden betrayed   The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 and the "Nabobs" (corrupt EIC officers who returned to Britain filthy rich) embarrassed the State and went against the civilising mission narrative     5. Career ambitions of EIC men   Senior officials such as Robert Clive 57-67 and Warren Hastings 73-85 also wanted a formal relationship with the State: the Crown gave legitimacy and career advancement   Teacher: "EIC shall never do AR65-83 in India" (the American Revolution, 1765-83). The sketch shows 13 colonies on one side with Br (Britain) tied by a line, and the cone with an upward arrow marked ToA 1765: the Company's Bengal income rising just as the colonies were slipping away. The 400,000 pounds a year (1767) is underlined. Mnemonic: MAPCA: "Money, America, Pocket, Conscience, Ambition". Decode: Money (1767: 400,000 pounds a year); America (revolution 1765-83, fear of an Indian USA); Pocket of the taxpayer (1772 bankrupt, 1.4 million pounds loan); Conscience, the White Man's Burden betrayed (famine 1770, Nabobs); Ambition of Clive 57-67 and Hastings 73-85 for a Crown link. Why it sticks: five letters, five drivers, in the order of the table. Mnemonic: Two 7s and a 2: 1767, 1772. Decode: 1767 the State asks for 400,000 pounds a year. 1772 the EIC is bankrupt and borrows 1.4 million pounds from the State. The 1767 demand comes first, the bailout comes five years later. Why it sticks: the State first asks, then has to pay. Mnemonic: AR 65-83 beside ToA 1765. Decode: the American Revolution runs 1765 to 1783 (armed war from 1775, USA in 1783); the ToA 1765 (Diwani for the EIC) starts the same year. The teacher's sketch puts them side by side. Why it sticks: both begin in 65. 1.2 Select Committee of Parliament (1772) Parliament set up a Select Committee to study the EIC's affairs in India and to advise on the relationship between the British State and the EIC with regard to the EIC's territorial possessions. Only political functions were examined (in capitalism the State does not interfere in a company's business). Result: the EIC kept its monopoly over trade with India. But the Court of Directors (CoD) in London was now made accountable for the EIC's political functions in India. This led directly to the Regulating Act of 1773. 1765 ToA: the EIC becomes a Company State, with two incomes, trade and land revenue (warn) 1767: the State demands 400,000 pounds a year; 1765-83: the American Revolution; 1770: famine and Nabobs (bad) 1772: the EIC goes bankrupt; the State lends 1.4 million pounds; Select Committee of Parliament Result: trade monopoly kept; the CoD made accountable for political functions (good) Regulating Act 1773: the State regulates the EIC's CMR matters, not its trade

items.t: 2 · Regulating Act of 1773
items.x: 2.1 @GG: provisions shaping the Company State in India  Board only, "RA 1773". Left, India side: GG(Be) with arrows to G(Bo) and G(Ma) marked "war & peace" ("W & P"), curved "all info" arrows back up to GG(Be). A long arrow from GG(Be) labelled "all info (6 months)" splits into "Commerce" and "CMR" and ends at a box "CoD of EIC", which sends "CMR info" to a small circled "E", which has an arrow to a large circled "P"; both sit in a box "Br STATE". Bottom: GG(Be) with four branches C1 to C4 = "Supreme Council of Bengal" = "GG(Be)'s Council", boxed "4 Councillors". Labels "INDIA" at the left and "Britain" at the right. [The circled E and P are not explained on the slide: unclear, probably the Executive and Parliament; check your notebook.]  Regulating Act 1773 @GG (India structure): 1. GG of Bengal created. 2. Bombay and Madras subordinated in war and peace, except emergency circumstances; could be suspended if they disobeyed. 3. Commerce untouched. 4. Supreme Council of Bengal, GG + 4C, majority vote of the 4C, GG only a casting vote (a check on an empire-builder GG causing war expenditure). 5. Legislative function to GG's Council. Ink: underlines under "in war & peace, except emergency circumstances", "suspended", "(GG + 4C)", "casting vote" and the law-making clause; row 3 margin "GG is not Boss in commerce matters"; row 5 "[TREATY = LAW]". The Governor of the Bengal Presidency was elevated to Governor-General of the Bengal Presidency (GG/Bengal). He stayed Governor of Bengal but was now a General over the Governors of Bombay and Madras in specific matters. The Governors of Bombay and Madras were subordinated to GG(Bengal) in matters of war and peace, except in emergency circumstances. They could be suspended if they disobeyed. The logic: high war expenditure caused the 1772 bankruptcy, so the GG was made accountable; and accountability without power is meaningless. Commercial affairs were untouched. In commerce the Governors stayed independent regional managers. A Supreme Council of Bengal was created with four councillors (GG + 4). All decisions were by majority vote of the four councillors. The GG had only a casting vote, a tiebreaker. This was a check on any empire-building ambitions of the GG. Legislative function was given to the GG's Council: it could make laws governing Bengal and on matters of war and peace. Teacher: "GG is not boss in commerce matters" (row 3): in commerce the Governors stayed independent. "[Treaty = Law]" (row 5): in the teacher's reading, a treaty on war and peace is made by law of the GG's Council. The Governor in "Governor-General" = ruler of the Bengal Presidency, in charge of making laws and implementing them; the General = he is senior to G(Bo) and G(Ma) (Lecture 19, slide 27, below).  Board only, "Decision making" with "[* Check vs Empire BUILDER GG]". (1) GG proposes a decision. (2) Vote by ONLY C1, C2, C3, C4. (3) If tie, then the tie-breaker vote by GG, boxed, with "casting vote" below. Right of a vertical line: "GG needs support of at least 2C to get his decision passed". Teacher: Decision making in the Supreme Council. The council is a check against the empire-builder GG. (1) The GG proposes. (2) Only the four councillors C1 to C4 vote. (3) If it is a tie, the tie-breaker (casting) vote is the GG's. So the GG needs the support of at least 2 councillors to get his decision passed (2 for and 2 against is a tie, which he then breaks).  Handout flow chart: GG (Bengal), Supreme Council of 4 Councillors, majority vote decides, GG = casting vote (only on tie). Mnemonic: 4 votes, 4 Cs, GG waits for a tie. Decode: RA 1773 council = GG + 4C. Only C1 to C4 vote. GG votes only on a tie (casting vote), so he needs at least 2 councillors with him. Why it sticks: the GG is the referee, not a player. 2.2 @Br State: provisions shaping the EIC-State relationship  Regulating Act 1773 @Br State (EIC-State): 1. Parliament's right to regulate political affairs recognised, for the first time. 2. Information to London (GG to CoD, CoD to the Br State on political matters). 3. Supreme Court, Calcutta: 1 Chief Justice + 3 puisne judges, all chosen by Crown, 1st CJ Elijah Impey (1774); Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823, "Thus 3 SCs". 4. No gifts. 5. Tenures. Ink: "[not today's SC]" beside row 3; "(not BY EIC)" after "all chosen by Crown"; beside row 5 "Hastings 73-85 [GG's TERMS]"; underlines under "first time", "all chosen by Crown", "Thus 3 SCs", "barred from accepting gifts from Indians", "GG(Bengal) 5 yrs, re-appointable", "future ones by CoD". For the first time Parliament's right to regulate the EIC's political affairs was legally recognised. Commercial affairs stayed outside supervision. (Since 1600 the EIC had commercial functions; since 1765 also political functions, civil, military and revenue.) The GG collects information on commercial and political matters and sends it to the Court of Directors (CoD) in London. The CoD submits information on political matters to the British State. A Supreme Court in Calcutta: one Chief Justice and three puisne judges ("puny", junior judges), all chosen by the Crown. The first Chief Justice was Sir Elijah Impey (1774). It heard cases involving British-born subjects and their Indian servants in the Bengal Presidency, under British law. Similar courts followed at Madras in 1800 and Bombay in 1823 (earlier cases involving British subjects went to Mayor's Courts): thus 3 Supreme Courts. To curb corruption, EIC officials were barred from accepting gifts from Indians. Tenures: Directors of the EIC 4 years, not immediately re-eligible; GG(Bengal) 5 years, re-appointable; Councillors 4 years; all first appointees were named in the Act itself, future ones by the CoD. Teacher: "[not today's SC]": this Supreme Court is not today's Supreme Court of India; it is a British-law court at Calcutta. "(not BY EIC)": the judges were chosen by the Crown, not by the EIC, so the court was the State's own instrument. "Hastings 73-85 [GG's terms]": the first GG's 5 years is the tenure on the slide. Slide typeset detail: "Sir" is struck through before Elijah Impey on slide 52 (the first Chief Justice is simply Elijah Impey, 1774). The handout writes "Sir Elijah Impey". Either is fine for the exam. Source note on the code: slide 53 types "Warren Hastings 73-85" and the teacher's ink on slide 52 is also 73-85 (the last digit is hard to read, it could look like 86). Use 73-85, as the handout, the typed slide and the PYQ ink (Lecture 19, slide 52) all write.   Post   Term   Remark    --- --- ---    Directors of the EIC   4 years   Not immediately re-eligible     GG(Bengal)   5 years   Re-appointable (Warren Hastings 73-85 the first)     Councillors   4 years   First ones named in the Act; later ones by the CoD   Mnemonic: "4-5-4": Directors, GG, Councillors. Decode: Directors 4 years (not immediately re-eligible), GG 5 years (re-appointable), Councillors 4 years. First names in the Act, later names by the CoD. Why it sticks: the GG is the middle number and the longest term. Mnemonic: Crown chooses the court: 1+3, then 1774, 1800, 1823. Decode: Supreme Court Calcutta = 1 Chief Justice + 3 puisne judges, all by the Crown; first CJ Elijah Impey 1774; copies at Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823 = 3 Supreme Courts. Why it sticks: after Calcutta, a gap of 26 years to Madras and then 23 to Bombay. 2.3 Impact of the 1773 Act  Regulating Act 1773 Impact: 1. SC vs GG's Council (SC set up 1774, Hastings 73-85 took office as first GG 1774, conflict over cases from EIC officials' official acts). 2. Poor supervision (distance, no modern communication). 3. Centralisation began. 4. Bombay and Madras still acted independent ("emergency circumstances", the Treaty of Surat 1775 signed by G(Bo) without GG's approval, then the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82). 5. GG had no veto, then factionalism, then the indecision problem. Ink: Impact underlined; "distance" underlined; a sketch of three equal G's changing into one GG above two G's; "indecision problem" underlined. The Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta in 1774. (The Act was passed in 1773; Warren Hastings 73-85 assumed office as the first GG of Bengal in 1774.) Conflict arose between the Supreme Court and the GG's Council over cases arising from acts done by EIC officials in their official capacity. Poor supervision: the huge distance between India and London and no modern communication. Centralisation of power in the GG began: the journey of India's central executive and central legislature starts here. (The teacher's sketch: three equal G's become one GG with two G's below.) Bombay and Madras still acted independently because of the vague phrase "emergency circumstances." Example: the Treaty of Surat (1775) was signed by the Governor of Bombay without the GG's approval, leading directly to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). The GG had no veto over his council. With factional politics this led to paralysis, the indecision problem. Philip Francis, a councillor who wanted to replace Hastings 73-85, kept opposing the GG and wrote complaint letters to London. This contributed to Edmund Burke leading an impeachment trial against Hastings 73-85 in Parliament on corruption charges; he spent his life savings and was acquitted. (Robert Clive 57-67 was likewise tried in Parliament in 1773 and acquitted.) Mnemonic: "Distance, Surat, Francis": three failures of 1773. Decode: Distance (poor supervision from London); Surat (Treaty of Surat 1775 by Bombay without the GG, then the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82, the "emergency circumstances" gap); Francis (Philip Francis blocks Hastings 73-85, Burke's impeachment, Hastings 73-85 acquitted). Why it sticks: three words, three headaches. Mnemonic: Clive 57-67 73 and Hastings: both tried, both acquitted. Decode: Robert Clive 57-67 was tried in Parliament in 1773 and acquitted; Warren Hastings 73-85 was impeached (Burke led it) and was acquitted after spending his life savings. Why it sticks: both walked free but lost their peace. 2.4 Amending Act of 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act)  Amending Act 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act). Purpose: resolved the SC versus GG's Council jurisdictional conflict. No ink. The Amending Act of 1781 (also called the Bengal Judicature Act or Declaratory Act) resolved the jurisdiction conflict. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction was now: All cases within Calcutta's territory. All cases of British subjects in the Bengal Presidency (excluding cases arising from official acts of EIC officials, which went to the GG's Council). All cases related to EIC property in Fort William. Mnemonic: "Calcutta, Britons, Fort": the 1781 three. Decode: Calcutta territory; British subjects in Bengal (official acts of EIC officials go to the GG's Council); EIC property in Fort William. Why it sticks: place, people, property. Prelims 2005 trap (full question in the Exam lens). (1) Warren Hastings 73-85 and the regular police force on the British pattern: WRONG, it is Cornwallis 86-93's reform under the Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 (Chapter 18). (2) Supreme Court at Calcutta by the Regulating Act 1773: CORRECT. (3) IPC in 1860: CORRECT (Macaulay's draft from the 1834 Law Commission). Answer (b) 2 and 3. The teacher also inked, beside statement 1, "Till 1813 orientalism. Rule India, the India way": until 1813 the policy was to rule India by its own ways (orientalism), which is why a British-pattern police is out of place under Hastings 73-85.  PYQ 5, Prelims 2005: Hastings, Calcutta SC and IPC. Ink: "73-85" over Hastings in statement 1, F; beside statement 1 "Till 1813 orientalism. Rule India, the India way"; T beside statements 2 and 3; option (b) ticked. Mnemonic: Hastings No police, Cornwallis 86-93 police. Decode: Prelims 2005: Hastings 73-85 did not set up the British-pattern regular police (F); Cornwallis 86-93 did, in the Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793. SC Calcutta 1773 (T), IPC 1860 (T), answer (b). Why it sticks: the officer who won the case file also wrote the police rulebook.
