The section below uses both.

items.t: 3 · Pitt's India Act, also the East India Company Act (1784)
items.x: Teacher: Named after the British PM William Pitt. Context: Britain lost its 13 North American colonies in 1783 (American War of Independence 1776-83, USA created). The Br State became anxious about India, so it shifted from supervision to direct control of the EIC.  Board: context of Pitt's India Act. Top: "AR65-83 → USA (1783)" then "up-up Anxiety in Br STATE @ EIC in INDIA", with "EIC declaring independence" circled. A yellow line runs to "SHIFT TO CONTROL of PIA 1784". Bottom chain: "GBF 1770 → 1772 (1.4 mn pounds LOAN) → RACT 1773 → WARS", branching into "1775-82 1st A-Ma → Ma (smiley, circled)" and "1780-84 2nd A-My → Tie". [Some letters are unclear: "GBF1770" and the year after the loan.] Teacher: Two roads lead to the 1784 shift to control. Road 1 (top): the American Revolution 1765-83 produced the USA in 1783, so anxiety in the Br State that the EIC in India might declare independence (circled). Road 2 (bottom): GBF 1770, then the 1772 bankruptcy and the 1.4 million pound loan, then the Regulating Act 1773, then the Wars: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 (he writes "Ma" with a smiley beside it) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War 1780-84 (he writes "Tie"). Both roads end at "shift to control of PIA 1784." The smiley and the "Tie" are the teacher's own result notes on the two wars (the 1st Anglo-Maratha War marked "Ma" with a smile, the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War marked "Tie"). The handout does not give these outcomes; they are covered in Chapter 13 and Chapter 12. Check your notebook for what he said aloud.  Board: "* Who chose Directors in CoD", boxed answer "Ans: SHAREHOLDERS of EIC". Star before the question. Teacher: Starred question: who chose the Directors in the CoD? Answer, boxed: the SHAREHOLDERS of the EIC. (The CoD is the EIC's own body; the BoC is the State's body.) 3.1 The concept of Double Government (1784-1833)  Board diagram. White heading with a green bracket: "ENGLISH / Br EIC, Pvt PEOPLE". India side: GG(Be) with a fork of three ticks, arrows "War, Peace" to G(Bo) and G(Ma), yellow "Revenue" on the Bo arrow, curved "info" arrows back up. A long arrow "all info" from GG(Be) to the box "CoD of EIC", with "Commerce" and "CMR / POLITICAL" below. From the CoD, "all incoming & outgoing letters" to a yellow box "BoC" inside a big box "Br STATE", with a circled E and "pm" below and an arrow to a circled P. Beside BoC: three tick lines "ministries" and "= ministry for Indian Affairs". Yellow arrow "Binding ORDERS" from BoC to CoD and a long yellow line "Binding ORDERS (Bypassing CoD)" from BoC to GG(Be). Bottom left: GG(Be) with four ticks C1 to C4 (white) → three ticks C1 to C3 (yellow) "#RA 1773". Bottom right: "SHIFT FROM REGULATION/SUPERVISION TO CONTROL, #PIA 1784 → CONTROL". Teacher: The whole 1784 structure on one board. The CoD of the EIC sits with the English EIC and private people; the BoC sits in the Br State box (the teacher marks "pm" beside it and the circled E leading to P: [unclear: probably Executive led by the PM, and Parliament; check your notebook]). The BoC = "ministry for Indian Affairs." From the CoD, all incoming and outgoing letters go to the BoC. BoC to CoD = binding orders; BoC to GG(Be) = binding orders, bypassing the CoD. Bottom: the council shrinks from C1 to C4 (RA 1773) to C1 to C3 (PIA 1784). The summary: "Shift from regulation / supervision to CONTROL: PIA 1784."  Board: "Concept: DOUBLE GOVT of EIC AFFAIRS", 1784-1833 above it, and a bracket "not the same as Dual Govt in Bengal Suba, not the same as SA". "Work of EIC categorised into 2 parts and put under 2 TOP bosses/AUTH". Table with columns "Commerce" and "C, M, R". Row 1 "Top AUTHORITY (Final) [Govt]", with "Top" circled and "no one above": Commerce = CoD of EIC; CMR = BoC of Br State. Row 2 "Hierarchy": Commerce: CoD of EIC over GG(Bo), GG(Be), G(Ma); CMR: BoC of Br State, then CoD of EIC, then GG(Be), then G(Bo) and G(Ma). Right: "1833: Commercial fn of EIC ended, therefore only 1 WORK, therefore only one TOP AUTH i.e. BoC".  Board: "DUAL GOVT: Bengal 1765-72: Diwani → EIC, Nizamat → Nawab". "SA: Ext → EIC, Dom → Indian King". "UT with L: Public Order, LAO, Land → Union Govt via LG; rest SUBJECTS → CM & State LA". "MERA GHAR: abc → Papa meri Jaan; PQR → Mumma meri maa" (an analogy). [LAO as written, the letters are not certain.] Teacher: Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833) is not the same as the Dual Government in Bengal (1765-72), and is not the same as the Subsidiary Alliance (SA). The EIC's work is split into two parts and put under two top bosses. Top authority (final) = the one with no one above: commerce: the CoD of the EIC; CMR (political): the BoC of the Br State. 1833: the commercial function of the EIC ended, so only one work, so only one top authority, the BoC. To keep them apart he lists three look-alike splits: Dual Government Bengal 1765-72 (Diwani with the EIC, Nizamat with the Nawab); SA (external affairs with the EIC, domestic with the Indian king); the UT with Legislature split (public order, police, land with the Union Government through the LG; the rest with the CM and State Legislative Assembly), and a family joke, "Mera Ghar": ABC = Papa, PQR = Mumma.   Arrangement   Who holds what   Years    --- --- ---    Double Government of EIC affairs   Commerce: CoD of the EIC. CMR (political): BoC of the Br State   1784-1833     Dual Government in Bengal   Diwani: the EIC. Nizamat: the Nawab   1765-72 (Chapter 10)     Subsidiary Alliance   External affairs: the EIC. Domestic affairs: the Indian king   From 1798 (Chapter 11)   Mnemonic: "CoD for coins, BoC for the crown": Double Government 1784-1833. Decode: Commerce = CoD (the EIC's own body, chosen by the shareholders); Civil, Military, Revenue = BoC (the State's body). It ends in 1833 when commerce ends. Not to be confused with Bengal's Dual Government (Diwani to the EIC, Nizamat to the Nawab, 1765-72). Why it sticks: coins are trade, crown is rule; 84 to 33 is the span.  Handout diagram: PRE-1784 Parliament supervises EIC (informal) versus POST-1784 Double Government (1784-1833): Board of Control (British State) and Court of Directors (EIC) together = Double Government of EIC affairs. 3.2 @Br State: provisions shaping the EIC-State relationship  Pitt's India Act 1784 @Br State (EIC-State): Name and context; 1. "Br territorial possessions" used for the first time (still unclear whether Br meant the Br State or the EIC); 2. Double Government 1784-1833 (BoC 1784 in London, a ministry for Indian affairs; commerce stays under the CoD); 3. BoC composition and role (6 members, a Secretary of State as President; superintend, direct and control Civil, Military and Revenue government); 4. Secret Committee; 5. Letters to BoC. Ink: yellow underlines under "@Br State", "PM William Pitt" and the start of row 5. The Act used the phrase "British territorial possessions in India" (for the first time) but left it ambiguous whether British India belonged to the EIC or the British State. Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833): political affairs went under the supreme control of the Br State through a new Board of Control (BoC) in London, effectively a ministry for Indian affairs. On commercial affairs the top authority remained the CoD of the EIC; on political affairs it was now the BoC. The BoC had six members: one Secretary of State (a Cabinet minister) as President of the BoC, the Chancellor of the Exchequer (the Finance Minister) and four members of the Privy Council. (The Privy Council is the Crown's advisory body; earlier it worked like the Mughal Darbar or the Chhatrapati's Ashtapradhan.) Its role: to superintend, direct and control all acts relating to Civil, Military and Revenue government of the British territorial possessions in the East Indies. "East Indies" was deliberate: territories annexed outside India (for example Burma later) also came under the BoC. A Secret Committee of three directors within the CoD, through which the BoC could send confidential orders directly to India, bypassing the full CoD, for sensitive military and diplomatic matters. The CoD now had to send all incoming and outgoing letters on India to the BoC. (In 1773 it was information; now original letters: the State's anxiety had grown after 1776-83.) Mnemonic: BoC = SC-4: "Secretary, Chancellor, four Privy". Decode: 6 members of the BoC: one Secretary of State (President), the Chancellor of the Exchequer, four Privy Councillors. 1 + 1 + 4 = 6. Why it sticks: S, C, then a quartet of Privy members. Mnemonic: 1773 = info, 1784 = original letters. Decode: RA 1773: the CoD sends information on political matters to the State. PIA 1784: the CoD sends all incoming and outgoing original letters to the BoC (the Secret Committee of 3 lets the BoC bypass the full CoD). Prelims 2002: the 1773 link = B-4, the 1784 link = D-1 (BoC). Why it sticks: a summary becomes the real letter.  Pitt's India Act 1784 @Br State (contd.): 6. Patronage retained (EIC kept the right to appoint officials, but the Crown got a unilateral power to recall or remove Principal Servants). 7. Dual Control over GG (1784-1858). Ink: "= Br STATE" near the header with a line to the Detail column; under row 6 "Power to give JOB"; "L = imp = GG, Governors, Councillors, C-in-C of EIC ARMY". The EIC retained commerce and patronage in 1784: the right to independently appoint EIC officials, including the Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors). The CoD kept the exclusive power to nominate them; the Crown's prior approval was not required (a doubt on this was settled by the Amending Act of 1786). The Crown's control ran through the BoC (policy) and the Crown's power to recall or remove officers. Dual Control over GG (1784-1858): the BoC could pass binding orders both to the CoD and directly to the GG, bypassing the CoD. So the GG had two bosses in political, civil, military and revenue matters, the CoD and the BoC. In commerce only one boss, the CoD. Teacher: "Power to give job" = patronage. "= imp = GG, Governors, Councillors, C-in-C of EIC army" = the Principal Servants, marked imp. "= Br STATE" is the teacher's bracket for Crown (the one who got the power to recall or remove). Source conflict inside the handout on the Principal Servants. Section 3.1 #6 says the CoD appointed them without Crown approval in 1784; Section 3.3 #6 and the slide "System that lasted to 1858" say they were appointed only after Crown approval. The teacher resolves it by inking "Done in [1793]" (Lecture 19, slide 15): Crown approval comes with the Charter Act 1793 (see Section 4). In 1784 the Crown only gets the power to recall or remove.  Board: "next concept" "1 DUAL CONTROL, 2 OVER GG in C,M,R matters", with "1784-1858" above and "= Two Bosses of GG in C,M,R [Political matters / Company State]", a note "a person who can give DIRECT ORDER". Hierarchy: "BoC of Br State" over "CoD of EIC", bracket "LONDON"; arrow 1 from CoD down to a box GG and curved arrow 2 from BoC to GG; below GG three G's. Left box: "* SINGLE CONTROL??" BoC → CoD → GG → G G G. Right box: "* In DUAL CONTROL of GG THR is Breach of (Chain of Command): everyone has only one Boss". Teacher: Dual Control over the GG (1784-1858) = two bosses of the GG in C, M, R matters (political matters, the Company State). A boss = a person who can give a direct order. In single control the chain would be BoC → CoD → GG → Governors. In dual control the BoC also orders the GG directly (arrow 2), so there is a breach of the chain of command: "everyone has only one boss" is the rule it breaks.   Feature   Double Government of EIC affairs   Dual Control over GG    --- --- ---    Years   1784-1833   1784-1858     What is split   The EIC's work: commerce (CoD) and CMR (BoC)   The GG's bosses: CoD and BoC in CMR matters     Who is the top authority   Commerce: CoD; CMR: BoC   In CMR: both, each can give direct orders     When it ended   1833, when the commercial function ended (one work, one top authority = BoC)   1858, when the India Council and the SoS replaced the BoC and CoD (the GG reports only to the SoS)   Mnemonic: "Double splits the work (84-33), Dual splits the boss (84-58)." Decode: Double Government 1784-1833 divides the work (commerce to CoD, CMR to BoC). Dual Control 1784-1858 gives the GG two bosses in CMR matters. Both start in 1784; 33 ends the first, 58 ends the second. Why it sticks: "Double work, Dual boss"; the end years match the Acts that end the trading (1833) and the Company (1858). 3.3 @GG: provisions shaping the Company State in India  Pitt's India Act 1784 @GG (India structure). Aim: resolve the indecision problem of RA 1773. 1. Council reduced to 3, one seat mandated for the CIC as ex-officio ordinary member. 2. Regular + casting vote. 3. Bombay/Madras Governors subordinated in war, peace AND revenue (so PS 1793 could extend to parts of Madras, the Northern Sarkars). 4. Roles clarified. 5. Councils under Governors. Ink: "C3 = C-in-C" beside a circled GG with C1, C2, C3; "ONLY, 1784-93, when C-in-C = ORDINARY member of EIC army"; underlines under "from 4 to 3 councillors", "ex-officio ordinary member", "war, peace AND revenue" and the "emergency circumstances" phrase. Aim: resolve the indecision problem of 1773. GG(Bengal)'s council cut from 4 councillors to 3. One seat was mandated for the Commander-in-Chief (CIC) of the EIC army as an ex-officio ordinary member. (Ordinary = mandated in the Act; ex-officio = member because he is the CIC; extra-ordinary = the CoD chooses whether to appoint him.) Council of 1784 = GG + 2 councillors + CIC. The GG was given both a regular vote and a casting vote. With just one councillor's support the GG could create a tie and break it in his favour. (Earlier he needed at least two. In effect one councillor was removed and his vote was given to the GG.) Bombay and Madras Governors were now subordinated to GG(Bengal) in war, peace and revenue (earlier only war and peace). This is how the Permanent Settlement of 1793 could extend to parts of Madras (the Northern Sarkars; see Chapter 16). Responsibilities of the GG and the Governors were more clearly defined, removing the vagueness of "except in emergency circumstances" (RA 1773). A Council of 3 was created under each of the Governors of Bombay and Madras (the beginning of today's State assemblies and Council of Ministers, without separation of powers). "Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." The Act thus banned imperial expansion, a response to the heavy war expenditure of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). (The handout's aside: in reality only fiscal decline was repugnant, not empire-building.)  Board: casting vote with 4 councillors (before) versus 3 councillors + GG vote (after 1784). Left: GG with C1 to C4; (1) GG proposes; (2) vote: C1 Y, C2 Y, C3 N, C4 N, so a tie; (3) GG uses the casting vote; (4) Y = 3, N = 2. Right: GG with C1 to C3 and "C4's normal vote given to GG"; (2) vote C1 N, C2 N, C3 Y, GG Y, tie; (3) GG uses the casting vote; Y = 3, N = 2. Slanted at the right edge: "GOAL = yes factional, yes indecision, help GG more powerful" [reading uncertain]. Teacher: Why the 1784 council helps the GG. Before (1773): the GG proposes and the votes are 2 for, 2 against, a tie, he uses the casting vote: 3 against 2. After (1784): the council is C1, C2, C3, and the GG now also votes: with only C3 for him and C1, C2 against, the votes are 2-2 (C3 + GG against C1 + C2), a tie, he casts: 3 against 2. So C4's normal vote is given to the GG. The aim, as he writes: to end factionalism and indecision and make the GG more powerful.  Board: "Concept" (circled). ORDINARY member: the law says a person will be a member of a council. EXTRA-ORDINARY member: the law does not say so, but gives power to someone (e.g. CoD) to appoint that person as a member. "in 1784 PIA: C-in-C of EIC army was made ordinary member of GG council". "1793: C-in-C can be extra-ordinary member if CoD wants." Teacher: Ordinary versus extra-ordinary member. Ordinary: the law itself says that a person will be a member of the council. Extra-ordinary: the law does not say so, but gives someone, for example the CoD, the power to appoint that person. 1784 (PIA): the C-in-C was made an ordinary member of the GG's council; 1793: the C-in-C can be an extra-ordinary member if the CoD wants. Mnemonic: ORDinary = ORDered by law; EXTRA = Extra choice. Decode: Ordinary member = the law orders the person to sit (the CIC in 1784). Extra-ordinary member = the law only gives the CoD a choice to appoint him (the CIC in 1793, "if CoD wants"). Why it sticks: Ordered versus Optional.  Board: the GG's council compared, 1773, 1784, 1793. 1773: GG with C1 to C4, "(civilian members i.e. NOT SOLDIERS)". 1784: GG with C1, C2, C3 [C-in-C] and a line to "SOLDIER". 1793: GG with C1, C2, C3 plus a dotted line to "C-in-C", "(all civilians)" under C1 to C3 and "EXTRA ORDINARY MEMBERS" under the C-in-C. Mnemonic: 4, then 2 + soldier, then 3 + soldier extra. Decode: 1773 = GG + 4 civilians. 1784 = GG + 2 civilians + CIC (a soldier, ordinary). 1793 = GG + 3 civilians + CIC (extra-ordinary). Both later forms have a soldier, but 1784's is compulsory and 1793's is optional. Why it sticks: the soldier moves from a chair that is reserved to a chair that is offered. Mnemonic: Conquest "repugnant" = after two wars: 75-82 and 80-84. Decode: PIA 1784 says "Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." Reaction to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). The teacher's results: Ma (smiley) and Tie. Why it sticks: two wars, two dates, one ban.  Pitt's 1784 @GG #6: Conquest Banned (verbatim). "Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." It thus banned imperial expansion; (in reality only fiscal decline was repugnant and not empire building). No ink. 3.4 Impact of the 1784 Act and the Amending Act of 1786  Pitt's India Act 1784 Impact: 1. Dual control = no control. 2. Indecision continued (if all 3C vote No the GG cannot get his proposal passed). 3. GG versus C-in-C friction. 4. Amending Act 1786 (veto in extraordinary circumstances; same person may hold both GG and C-in-C; Cornwallis 86-93's insistence). Ink: under row 2, "continued BUT" with a curved arrow to the detail [exact form unclear]; yellow underlines under the Amending Act 1786, the veto, "same person to both GG & C-in-C" and "Cornwallis 86-93's insistence". Dual control in practice meant no effective control: the GG could play his two masters (CoD and BoC) against each other, given the distance and no modern communication. The GG still had no veto over his council: if all three councillors opposed him, the indecision problem continued. (The teacher's note: "indecision continued, BUT" the position improved because he needed only one councillor.) Conflict between the GG and the C-in-C: the decision of war and peace rested with the GG, but the right to use the army rested with the C-in-C. The Amending Act of 1786 amended Pitt's Act by: (i) giving the GG a veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances; (ii) letting the EIC appoint the same person to both posts, GG and C-in-C, to avoid the rift (the posts were not merged, and it was not compulsory, just permitted). This was done on the insistence of Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-93), who became the first person to hold both posts. Mnemonic: "No veto, then veto 86": Cornwallis 86-93 wears two hats. Decode: RA 1773 and PIA 1784 give the GG no veto. Amending Act 1786 gives a veto in extraordinary circumstances and allows GG + C-in-C in one person (not merged, not compulsory). Cornwallis 86-93 insisted and was the first to do it. Why it sticks: the code 86-93 starts with the Act's year, 86.  Pitt's 1784: The Firsts (one place): 1st GG(Bengal) 1773 Warren Hastings 73-85; 1st GG(India) 1833 William Bentinck 28-35; 1st "Viceroy & GG" 1858 Charles Canning 56-62; 1st GG of partitioned India Louis Mountbatten from 15 Aug 1947 (now a symbolic head); 1st Indian GG C. Rajagopalachari (June 1948 to 26 Jan 1950); 1st President of the Republic Rajendra Prasad. Ink: "To understand: * GG = PM of Br India" and "(Powerless) GG = PRESIDENT of INDIA".   First   Holder   When    --- --- ---    1st GG (Bengal)   Warren Hastings 73-85   1773 (RA 1773; he took office 1774)     1st GG (India)   William Bentinck 28-35   1833 (Charter Act 1833)     1st "Viceroy and GG"   Charles Canning 56-62   1858 (GOI Act 1858)     1st GG of partitioned India   Louis Mountbatten   From 15 Aug 1947 (a now symbolic head)     1st Indian GG   C. Rajagopalachari   June 1948 to 26 Jan 1950     1st President of the Republic   Rajendra Prasad   After 26 Jan 1950   Teacher: "To understand: GG = PM of Br India" (starred): before 1858 the GG ran British India as a Prime Minister would. "(Powerless) GG = President of India": after 1947 the GG is only a symbolic head, like the President. The same line appears on the 1853 slide: since 1833 the GG was effectively the PM of Br India and the CM of Bengal. Mnemonic: "H-B-C-M-R-R": the six firsts in order. Decode: Hastings 73-85 (GG Bengal 1773), Bentinck 28-35 (GG India 1833), Canning 56-62 (Viceroy 1858), Mountbatten (partitioned India, 15 Aug 1947), Rajagopalachari (first Indian GG, June 1948 to 26 Jan 1950), Rajendra Prasad (first President). Why it sticks: H to B to C is the Company ladder, M to R to R is the free India ladder.  Pitt's 1784, System That Lasted to 1858: binding orders by BoC to CoD and to GG; Principal Servants appointed only after Crown approval; original letters to BoC; GG as the main authority in India. Ink: yellow underlines under "binding orders", "Principal Servants" and "original letters"; beside the Principal Servants line, "Done in [1793]". The system of controlling the EIC's political affairs built in 1773-1786 continued till 1858 with very little structural change: binding orders by the BoC to the CoD and to the GG; Principal Servants appointed only after Crown approval (done in 1793); original letters to the BoC; the GG as the main authority in India. Prelims 2002 and 2004 trap cluster. Prelims 2002 (match): A-2 Charter Act 1813 (trade monopoly ended), B-4 Regulating Act 1773 (Directors report to the State), C-3 Act of 1858 (power to the Crown), D-1 Pitt's India Act 1784 (BoC). Correct option (a). The teacher wrote "BoC 1784", "1813", "1858". Prelims 2004 (pair NOT matched): (a) Pitt's India Act : Warren Hastings 73-85 is loose (Hastings 73-85 was GG of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773); (c) Vernacular Press Act : Curzon 99-05 is the flagrant error (1878, Lytton 76-80). UPSC's key: (c). The teacher marked F on (c) and T under (d) (Ilbert Bill : Ripon 80-84).  PYQ 2, Prelims 2002: Acts to Provisions. Ink: circled 2 beside A (Charter Act 1813), circled 4 beside B (Regulating Act 1773), circled 3 beside C (Act of 1858), "1784" and circled 1 beside D (Pitt's India Act); "BoC 1784" beside provision 1; "1813" beside provision 2; "1858" beside provision 3.  PYQ 4, Prelims 2004: pair NOT correctly matched. Ink: circled F beside (c) Vernacular Press Act : Curzon; circled T below (d) Ilbert Bill : Ripon. Mnemonic: Prelims 2004: "Hastings 73, Pitt 84; Lytton 76-80 press, Curzon 99-05 partition". Decode: Pitt's India Act is 1784, Hastings 73-85 sits under the 1773 Act (loose pair). The Vernacular Press Act 1878 is Lytton 76-80's; Curzon 99-05 = Partition of Bengal 1905. The true error UPSC wants: (c). Why it sticks: the press law goes with the poet-viceroy Lytton 76-80, not the partitioner. Mnemonic: Prelims 2002: "B-4 info, D-1 BoC, A-2 trade, C-3 Crown". Decode: B Regulating 1773 = 4 (Directors present documents); D Pitt's 1784 = 1 (Board of Control); A Charter 1813 = 2 (India trade ended); C Act of 1858 = 3 (Crown takes over). Option (a). Why it sticks: the list reads 2-4-3-1 in the order of the option letters A-B-C-D.

items.t: 4 · Charter Act of 1793
items.x: 4.1 @Br State  Charter Act 1793 @Br State (EIC-State): 1. Crown sovereignty (verbatim): "Subjects of the Crown cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on behalf of the Crown"; EIC now only a manager/agent of the Br State. 2. BoC size decreased. 3. BoC salary by EIC. 4. 20-year renewal, by Parliament. 5. Principal Servants + Crown approval. 6. Patronage retained. Ink: yellow underlines under "cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on", "manager/agent of the Br State", "(GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors)" and "independently appoint"; right side a diagram "MUGHAL + SIKH" (with "Tipu, Nizam" above it, partly cut off [unclear]) forking into "INDIAN STATES" and "Br INDIA [of EIC struck out, of Br CROWN]". "Subjects of the Crown cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on behalf of the Crown." So the EIC was now only a manager or agent of the British State. Sovereignty over British India was with the British State, not the EIC. (However, Mughal sovereignty over the whole of India was accepted until 1858.) The size of the BoC was decreased: the President was retained with only two junior members under him, who need not be Privy Councillors. This concentrated real authority in the President and reduced factionalism. The salary of BoC members was now paid by the EIC. (This later connects to the Home Charges under the Drain of Wealth theory of the Moderates, Chapter 27.) The EIC's charter was renewed for 20 years, and for the first time by Parliament, not the Monarch. Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors) were appointed by the EIC but only after the approval of the Crown. The State took hold of the head of the Company State in India while its body stayed under the EIC, making a declaration of independence impossible. The EIC retained commerce and patronage: it independently appointed officials other than the Principal Servants. Teacher: The diagram on the right shows who owned what. India = Mughal + Sikh (and, the teacher adds, names such as Tipu 82-99 and the Nizam [unclear: check your notebook]) on one side, Indian States, and British India [of the EIC → of the Br Crown] on the other: after 1793 British India belongs to the Br Crown, not the EIC, while the Mughal claim over the whole of India is still allowed to stand until 1858. The right-hand margin of the 1813 slide gives the three-step chain: 1784 "Br (T) possessions" (circled T, territorial), 1793 "sovereign powers only on behalf of Crown", 1813 (blank, then "undoubted sovereignty of Crown").  Board: boxed "PRINCIPAL SERVANTS", "now = more LOYAL to Br STATE than EIC". Fork of three ticks: left "appointed by EIC", right "only after CROWN APPROVAL"; under "appointed by EIC" a fork "Salary" and "appointment LETTER", "By EIC". Teacher: Principal Servants: now more loyal to the Br State than the EIC, because they are appointed by the EIC (the appointment letter and the salary are the EIC's) but only after Crown approval. That is the head taken by the State while the body stays with the EIC. Mnemonic: "Sovereignty 84-93-13": possessions, behalf, undoubted. Decode: 1784 "Br territorial possessions" (ambiguous), 1793 "sovereign powers only on behalf of the Crown" (EIC = agent), 1813 "undoubted sovereignty of the Crown". Prelims 2019 ink: "(1784, 1793, 1813)". Why it sticks: the claim grows from "possessions" to "behalf" to "undoubted". Mnemonic: Head to Crown, body to Company (1793). Decode: Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors) are appointed by the EIC after Crown approval: the State owns the head, the EIC keeps the body (appointment letter, salary, patronage for lesser posts). So no declaration of independence. Why it sticks: you cannot rebel with a head that belongs to someone else. 4.2 @GG  Charter Act 1793 @GG (India structure): 1. GG's power increased (over his council and the Bombay/Madras Governors; can supersede them when present; can issue directives without his council when absent from Bengal). 2. CIC to extraordinary member (seat to a civilian). 3. Hallmark: Civil Law (a code of regulations for Bengal; courts bound; laws printed in the vernacular; Cornwallis 86-93's rule-of-law belief; Hindu and Islamic laws + Permanent Settlement Act 1793). Ink: "Not imp" under row 1; "# WRITTEN Law, WRITTEN JUDGEMENT" under row 3; yellow underlines under "Hindu & Islamic laws + Permanent" and "Settlement Act 1793". GG(Bengal)'s power over his council and over the Governors of Bombay and Madras increased further. When present in Madras or Bombay, the GG could supersede their Governors; even when absent from Bengal he could issue directives to the presidencies without consulting his own council. (Teacher: "Not imp.") The CIC's seat was given to a civilian. The CIC could be appointed an extraordinary member by the CoD (and was). GG's council 1793 = GG + CIC (extraordinary) + 3 ordinary councillors. Hallmark: Civil Law. A code of all regulations governing Bengal was to be framed, dealing with rights of persons and property; courts were bound to follow them; all laws were printed in the vernacular so people knew their rights. (This is Cornwallis 86-93's belief in the rule of law and anti-corruption; the laws included Hindu and Islamic laws and the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 for land revenue and property.) Teacher: "Written law, written judgement": the hallmark of 1793 is that law becomes written, and so do court judgements. He underlines "Hindu and Islamic laws + Permanent Settlement Act 1793" (the Cornwallis 86-93 Code, Chapter 18).  Board: Law [Code = WRITTEN law] is on Civil matters or Criminal matters. Civil: Personal (inheritance; marriage and divorce; parent-child relations), "handled by customs of that community i.e. Customary Law i.e. Personal Law of that Religion", "State can make LAW FOR Social Reforms"; Non-Personal (secular): property, contracts, "handled by Civil Law made by State". Criminal: "always non-personal (secular)", "not Accused vs Victim: State vs Accused", "therefore L&O = State's Responsibility". Bottom right list: Sati Abolition Act 1829; Removal of Religious Disabilities Act 1850; Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856; Hindu Succession Act; Triple Talaq; UCC; Abolition of Untouchability by COI 1950. Teacher: What "code" means. A code = written law. Law is on civil matters or criminal matters. Civil, personal (inheritance, marriage and divorce, parent-child relations) is handled by the customs of that community, i.e. the personal law of that religion; the State can make law for social reforms (his list: Sati Abolition Act 1829, Removal of Religious Disabilities Act 1850, Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856, Hindu Succession Act, Triple Talaq, UCC, abolition of untouchability by the COI 1950). Civil, non-personal (secular) (property, contracts) is handled by civil law made by the State. Criminal is always non-personal: State versus the accused, not accused versus victim, therefore law and order is the State's responsibility.   Year   Act   Council   The CIC's seat    --- --- --- ---    1773   Regulating Act   GG + 4 councillors (all civilians)   None     1784   Pitt's India Act   GG + 2 councillors + CIC (GG's regular and casting vote)   Ordinary, ex-officio (mandated by the Act)     1793   Charter Act   GG + CIC + 3 councillors (3 civilians)   Extra-ordinary (CoD may appoint; he was)

items.t: 5 · Charter Act of 1813: Westernisation begins
items.x: 5.1 Context  Charter Act 1813 Context (Westernisation Begins). 1. Narrative to end monopoly (Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations 1776, Free Market / Laissez Faire; Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists say British manufacturers would industrialise India via technology transfer + FDI, fulfilling WMB; heavy lobbying by manufacturers + non-EIC traders). 2. Br national interest (Industrial Revolution 1750-1850; raw-material source + export market; a trading company's monopoly no longer in the national interest). 3. Push to westernisation (the "Great Ancient India" idea a myth). Ink: yellow underlines through the table; after the lobbying bullet "[RECALL: INTERLOPERS]"; "ORIENTALISM" beside row 3. The narrative for ending the monopoly. Adam Smith's "Wealth of Nations" (1776) argued for a free market (laissez faire), so the monopoly was under intellectual attack since 1776. Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists argued that British manufacturers would industrialise India through technology transfer and FDI, fulfilling the White Man's Burden (WMB). There was also heavy lobbying by manufacturers and non-EIC traders. (Teacher: "[Recall: interlopers]", the non-EIC British traders of Chapter 10.) British national interest. The Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) was progressing; British manufacturers wanted India as a source of raw materials and an export market. It was no longer in the British national interest for a trading company to hold the monopoly over British business with India. The push to westernisation. Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists argued that the idea of a Great Ancient India was a myth and that westernising India fulfilled the White Man's Burden.  Board: "Br National interest 1813". Left, till the IR (1750-1850) matured: want finished goods (FGs) from India to sell at profit to the rest of the world, therefore want a Big MNC i.e. EIC to buy Indian FG in BULK, therefore monopoly to TRADER EIC. Right, once the IR matured: want RM (raw material) from India (not FGs); India as an export market [sell Br FG], MACHINE MADE; therefore monopoly of a TRADER not in Br National Interest. Teacher: Br national interest in 1813: before and after the Industrial Revolution matured. Till the IR (1750-1850) matured: Britain wanted finished goods (FGs) from India to sell at a profit to the rest of the world, so it wanted a big MNC, the EIC, to buy Indian FG in bulk, therefore monopoly to the trader EIC. Once the IR matured: Britain wanted raw material (RM) from India, not FGs, and India as an export market to sell British machine-made FG, therefore the monopoly of a trader is not in the British national interest. Mnemonic: FG out, RM out, FG in: why 1813 killed the monopoly. Decode: Before the Industrial Revolution matured: India's finished goods are bought in bulk by the EIC (monopoly makes sense). After: Britain wants India's raw material and sells its own machine-made goods into India (monopoly of a trader does not). Why it sticks: goods go from India first, then goods go into India.  Board: "WESTERNIZATION" in three branches. Polity and Administration (west like). Economy (west like): machines, factories of manufacturers, industry (machine based). Society: Education and Customs/Religion, with "Social Reforms" under customs/religion. Teacher: Westernisation has three arms: polity and administration (west like), economy (west like: machines, factories of manufacturers, machine-based industry) and society (education, and customs and religion, which leads to social reforms).  Board: "Economic Nationalism". Left: when a weak economy or sector compared to the rest of the world, protectionism, e.g. MAGA (underlined). Right: when an economy or sector is STRONG vs the rest of the world, globalization and neo-liberalism, e.g. USA [1945-2020]. Slide 24 is a teaching aside on economic nationalism (weak economy turns protectionist, strong economy turns globalist). It explains why Britain, now strong, wanted free trade in 1813. Nothing in the handout text matches it. 5.2 @Br State  Charter Act 1813 @Br State (EIC-State): 1. Crown sovereignty (verbatim) "undoubted sovereignty of Crown over Indian territorial possessions" (the Crown not yet challenging Mughal sovereignty over India as a whole). 2. India-trade monopoly ended, but Tea, Opium and China trade kept. 3. Cultural Colonialism began (missionaries with a CoD or BoC licence; Rs 1 lakh a year on education; the western-versus-Indian debate till 1835). 4. Contributed to 1857. 5. 20-year renewal. Ink: a small "Br" inserted above "trade" in row 2; underlines under "retained monopoly over Tea," and "Opium trade and trade with China", "conversions", "Rs 1 lakh/yr on education"; right margin: "1784: Br (T) possessions; 1793: Sovereign Powers only on Behalf of Crown; 1813". "Undoubted sovereignty of the Crown over Indian territorial possessions." Sovereignty was of the British State, not the EIC. (At this stage the Crown was not challenging Mughal sovereignty over India as a whole.) The EIC's monopoly over (British) trade with India was ended, but the EIC retained the monopoly over Tea, Opium and trade with China. (The teacher inserted "Br": the monopoly was over British trade with India.) Cultural Colonialism began. Christian missionaries could enter India for conversions with a licence from the CoD or the BoC. A push to education and social reforms was mandated: the EIC was to spend Rs 1 lakh a year on education. The debate on western versus Indian education and medium continued till 1835, when it was settled in favour of western education in English. The 1813 Act contributed to the 1857 revolt by enabling cultural colonialism and undermining Indian institutions and social structures. The Charter was renewed for 20 years. Mnemonic: 1813: "Tea, Opium, China stay; Missions, Money (1 lakh) enter". Decode: Trade monopoly with India ended, but Tea, Opium and China stay with the EIC. Missionaries may enter (licence from CoD or BoC); Rs 1 lakh a year on education; Crown sovereignty re-stated; 20-year renewal. Why it sticks: three things stay, two things arrive. Prelims 2019 trap (full question in the Exam lens). (1) Ended the trade monopoly except tea and China: CORRECT. (2) Asserted the sovereignty of the Crown over Indian territories: CORRECT. (3) Revenues of India controlled by Parliament: WRONG for 1813 (see the source-conflict alert in the Exam lens: BoC revenue supervision 1784; Budget under Parliament 1853; the teacher inked 1858). Answer (a) 1 and 2.  PYQ 9, Prelims 2019: Charter Act of 1813. Ink: circled T after statement 1; "(1784, 1793, 1813)" and circled T after statement 2; "1858" and circled F after statement 3. Mnemonic: Prelims 2019: "Two truths, one future". Decode: Statements 1 and 2 are true (trade monopoly ended except tea/China; Crown sovereignty, 1784-93-13 chain). Statement 3 (revenue under Parliament) is not an 1813 provision. Answer (a). Why it sticks: the third claim belongs to a later Act, not this one.

items.t: 6 · Charter Act of 1833, also the St. Helena Act
items.x: Mnemonic: Napoleon's island changed hands in 1833. Decode: St. Helena (South Atlantic, remote, a refuelling and repair port) was taken over from the EIC by the Br State. Napoleon was exiled there after 1815 and died there in 1821. The Act is also called the St. Helena Act. Why it sticks: the same isolated rock that held Napoleon is dropped from the Company's assets. 6.1 @Br State  Charter Act 1833 / St. Helena Act @Br State. St. Helena: taken over from the EIC by the Br State; Napoleon exiled 1815, died 1821. 1. Commercial function fully ended (Tea, Opium and China monopolies lost; the EIC would no longer do business; only a political function remained, as an agent of the Br State; Double Government 1784-1833 thus ended). 2. BoC power extended to all administrative affairs (implementation, officers, transfers and postings; link: the 2023 SC case on Delhi administration). 3. President of BoC renamed Minister for Indian Affairs in 1833. Ink: underlines under "Commercial function", "fully ended", "St. Helena Act" and "to all administrative affairs in India"; at right a large "8" with a dot and a tick-like mark [unclear: check your notebook]. The EIC lost its monopoly over Tea, Opium and China trade. Its commercial function was fully ended: the EIC would no longer conduct business and had only a political function, and that only as an agent of the British State. (The Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833) thus ended: no more dual identity of trader and ruler. The slide adds that books still use the phrase till 1858.) The BoC's supervisory power was extended to all administrative affairs in India: not just policy and laws, but supervision over implementation, officers, their transfers and postings. (The handout links this to the 2023 Supreme Court case on administrative control between the Centre and Delhi's elected executive.) The President of the BoC was renamed Minister for Indian Affairs in 1833. The "8 ✓" in the right margin of slide 26 cannot be read with confidence (it could be the teacher marking the 8 numbered points of the Act or a shorthand). [unclear: check your notebook.] Mnemonic: "3-3-3": commerce gone, control wide, minister named (1833). Decode: three @Br State points of 1833: commercial function fully ended (Tea, Opium, China gone; Double Government ends), BoC power extended to all administrative affairs (officers, transfers, postings), President of BoC renamed Minister for Indian Affairs. Why it sticks: three Acts of trading, supervising and naming. 6.2 @GG  Board: "GG(Be) vs GG(I)". Left: "Governor General of Bengal Presidency [1773]", Governor = ruler of Bengal Presidency, in charge of making laws and implementing them; General = it signifies that he is senior to G(Bo), G(Ma); yellow "Ruler of Bombay: G(Bo), Madras: G(Ma)". Right: "Governor General of India (1833)", "= Br India", General "same as before", Governor = ruler of Br India (Bengal, Bombay, Madras), "therefore now a TRUE PM of Br India", "Law making powers of G(Bo), G(Madras) taken away". Teacher: GG(Bengal) versus GG(India) in one word-play. 1773: "Governor" = ruler of the Bengal Presidency, in charge of making laws and implementing them; "General" = senior to the Governors of Bombay and Madras. 1833: "General" is the same as before; "Governor" is now the ruler of all British India (Bengal, Bombay, Madras), therefore he is now a true PM of British India, and the law-making powers of the Governors of Bombay and Madras are taken away.  Charter Act 1833 @GG (India structure): 1. GG(India)-in-Council (landmark; one country, one law, one executive). 2. Executive and Legislative head of Br India (laws equally for Indians and Britishers). 3. Bombay/Madras legislative powers taken (restored by the Indian Councils Act 1861). 4. Centralisation peaked 1833, decentralisation began 1861, peaked 1935. Ink: underlines under "GG(India)-in-Council" and "one country, one law, one executive"; a note at top right "implementation of law". A landmark: GG(Bengal)-in-Council was elevated to GG(India)-in-Council. As the EIC's territory expanded and Britishers entered India in larger numbers after 1813, uniform laws and administration across British India became necessary: one country, one law, one executive (like GST today or the Napoleonic Code of 1804). (Teacher: "implementation of law.") The GG(India) was made Executive and Legislative head of British India: empowered to make and administer laws for the whole of British India, equally applicable to Indians and Britishers. The legislative powers of the Governors of Bombay and Madras were taken away (restored by the Indian Councils Act 1861, Chapter 25). Centralisation in the GG peaked in 1833; decentralisation to the provinces began in 1861 and peaked in 1935 (the journey of federalism and Centre-State relations).  Charter Act 1833 @GG (contd.): 5. Law Member added (Macaulay), the grain of separation of executive and legislative functions at council level. 6. Law Commission 1834 under Macaulay; work completed 1837; CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam). 7. Racial equality (verbatim), UCS + subordinate judicial posts opened to Indians. 8. 20-year renewal. Ink: underlines under "One Law Member (Thomas Macaulay)" and "grain of separation..."; "IPC | CrPC | Indian evidence Act"; "not imp" beside row 7; right side "open to Indians 1853" with "CCS (Grp A)" and a triangle "Br" at the top, "Indians" at the base, "UCS 1833". One Law Member (Thomas Macaulay) was added to the GG(India)'s council to draft uniform laws. This introduced the grain of separation of the executive and legislative functions at the council level (not at the GG's level, he still headed both). The journey of a separate legislature begins here. In 1834 a Law Commission was set up under Macaulay for codification of laws. Work was completed by 1837, but deliberation went on. Full implementation post-1857: Civil Procedure Code (1859), Indian Penal Code (1860), Criminal Procedure Code (1861). (In 2024 India replaced these with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.) The teacher adds the Indian Evidence Act to the list. Racial equality promised: "No person to be deprived of chance to enter EIC service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour." The Uncovenanted Civil Services (UCS, roughly today's Group B) and subordinate judicial positions below the district judge (e.g. Munsifs) were opened to Indians to reduce the cost of administration. (Teacher: "not imp.") The Charter was renewed for 20 years. Teacher: A triangle for the services: Br at the top, Indians at the base: UCS opened to Indians in 1833; the CCS (Group A) opened to Indians in 1853. Mnemonic: Macaulay's trio: IPC 60, CPC 59, CrPC 61. Decode: Law Commission 1834 under Macaulay, work done 1837, codes after 1857: CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (the teacher adds the Indian Evidence Act). Replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. Why it sticks: 59, 60, 61 in a row, C-I-C in order. Mnemonic: UCS 33, CCS 53: lower door first, upper door twenty years later. Decode: Uncovenanted Civil Services (Group B, Munsifs) opened to Indians in 1833; Covenanted Civil Services (Group A) opened to Indians in 1853. Why it sticks: the same two digits, 33 then 53, with a gap of 20. Mnemonic: 1833: one country, one law, one boss, one Law Member. Decode: GG(Bengal) becomes GG(India), executive + legislative head of all British India, the Governors of Bombay and Madras lose legislative power, and one Law Member (Macaulay) is added to the council for legislative work. Centralisation peaks in 1833; decentralisation begins 1861 and peaks 1935. Why it sticks: four "ones" for the top of the centralisation arc.   Feature   1833   1853    --- --- ---    GG's title   GG(India)-in-Council   Same     Law-making   Only the GG's council for all British India; Governors of Bombay and Madras lose it   Same, but 4 provincial members can draft province laws     Added to council   1 Law Member (Macaulay), for legislative sittings only   The Law Member is promoted to the 4th ordinary member; 6 Legal Members added     Executive meetings   GG + CIC + 3 ordinary   GG + CIC + 4 ordinary     Legislative meetings   Executive + Law Member   [GG + CIC + 4] + 6 = 12 persons    Handout flow of the council: 1773 GG + 4 (Regulating Act); 1784 GG + 2 councillors + CIC (Pitt's India Act, CIC = ordinary member); 1793 GG + CIC (ex-officio) + 3 councillors (Charter Act; CIC seat to civilian); 1833 GG + CIC + 3 (Exec) + 1 Law Member (Leg); 1853 GG + CIC + 4 (Exec) + 6 Legal Members = 12 (Leg). The handout figure above calls the 1793 CIC "ex-officio." The text and the teacher say extra-ordinary (see the source-conflict alert in the Exam lens). Use the text and the teacher. Prelims 2003, 2007 and 2023 trap cluster. Prelims 2003 (NOT in 1833): (a) trading abolished: in 1833; (b) GG of India in Council: in 1833; (c) all law-making to the GG in Council: in 1833; (d) an Indian as law member: NOT in 1833 (Macaulay was an Englishman; an Indian Law Member came much later). Answer (d). Prelims 2007: (1) Clive 57-67 first GG of Bengal: WRONG (Hastings 73-85, under RA 1773; the teacher: "RA 1773: G → GG"); (2) Bentinck 28-35 first GG of India: CORRECT (Charter 1833). Answer (b). Prelims 2023: the Act that redesignated GG of Bengal as GG of India: Charter Act 1833 (d). RA 1773 only created GG/Bengal; PIA 1784 created the BoC and Double Government; Charter 1793 raised the GG's power but did not rename him.  PYQ 3, Prelims 2003: provision NOT made in the Charter Act 1833. Ink: "not" underlined; T beside (a), (b), (c); F beside (d).  PYQ 7, Prelims 2007: first GG of Bengal versus first GG of India. Ink: "first Governor-General" underlined in statement 1 with an arrow to "W. Hastings 73-85 (RA 1773: G → GG)"; F after statement 1; circled T after statement 2; "28-35" and "Charter 1833" below. Mnemonic: Prelims 2003: "Macaulay was an Englishman". Decode: (d) an Indian law member is the odd one out. The first Law Member was Macaulay (English). Trading ended, GG of India in Council, all law-making to the GG: all 1833. Why it sticks: the exception is the only thing that did not happen. Mnemonic: Prelims 2007: "Clive 57-67 is Governor, Hastings 73-85 is General, Bentinck 28-35 is India". Decode: Clive 57-67 = Governor of Bengal only; Hastings 73-85 = first GG (Bengal), RA 1773 ("G → GG"); Bentinck 28-35 = first GG (India), Charter 1833. Answer (b). Why it sticks: Governor, then General, then India: the order of the ranks. Mnemonic: Prelims 2006: "1833 trimmed Tea, Opium, China; 1813 cut India." Decode: 1813 ended the India-trade monopoly (Tea, Opium, China kept); 1833 ended those three and the commercial function; 1858 ended the Company. Ink: Tea + Opium to China, "1813", F. Statement 1 (1833 ended India trade) is false; statement 2 (1858 abolished the EIC) is true. Answer (b). Why it sticks: the three ends are three Acts: 1813, 1833, 1858.  PYQ 6, Prelims 2006: Charter 1833 + GOI 1858. Ink: "Tea, opium" joined to "China" above statement 1; "1813" and circled F after statement 1; circled T after statement 2.

items.t: 7 · Charter Act of 1853
items.x: 7.1 @Br State  Charter Act 1853 @Br State (EIC-State): 1. No fixed renewal ("till Parliament specifies otherwise", a sword hanging over the EIC's founding document). 2. Patronage lost, CCS exam (the first exam held in 1855 in London; from 1853 the EIC hardly controlled policies in India). 3. CCS opened to Indians (UCS had been opened in 1833). 4. Budget to Parliament. Ink: underlines under "Charter", the "till Parliament specifies otherwise" phrase, "sword permanently hanging over the EIC's founding document" and "1st exam held 1855 in London"; "[* UPSC exam]" beside row 2. The Charter was valid only "till Parliament specifies otherwise": no fixed renewal period. (A sword permanently hanging over the EIC's neck, since the Charter was its founding document.) The EIC lost patronage (the power to independently appoint its officials) because a Civil Services Examination was introduced. The first exam was held in 1855 in London. From this point the EIC hardly controlled policies in India. (Teacher: "[* UPSC exam]".) The Covenanted Civil Services (CCS) were opened to Indians (the UCS had been opened in 1833). The revenues of British India (the Budget) were placed under the control of the British Parliament. Mnemonic: "No term, no patronage, no budget": 1853 strips three things. Decode: no fixed Charter term ("till Parliament specifies otherwise"), patronage lost to the Civil Services Examination (first held 1855 in London) and the Budget under Parliament. CCS opened to Indians. Why it sticks: the Company loses its calendar, its jobs and its purse. 7.2 @GG  Charter Act 1853 @GG (India structure): 1. Deeper separation of powers (6 more Legal Members). 2. Provincial law-making (4 provincial reps; the Rent Act of 1859 for Bengal). 3. Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal (since 1833 the GG was effectively PM of Br India + CM of Bengal; in 1854 Dalhousie 48-56 appointed Frederick James Halliday as the first LG of Bengal). Ink: underlines under "adding 6 more Legal Members", "Rent Act of 1859 for Bengal", "since 1833 GG" and "PM of Br India + CM of Bengal".  Board: "2 KIND of LAWS": all country level, and at province level "because of unique problems, context of each province", "e.g.: PS 1793 → Bengal; Ryotwari 1801-07, 1820 → [SCAM-B, unclear]". Right of a divider: "Since 1833, only GG(I)'s council can make Law." Deeper separation of the executive and legislative functions within the GG(India)'s council by adding 6 more Legal Members. Provincial law-making. Since 1833 only the GG's council could make laws for all British India, but every country has issues that need province-specific laws. The four provincial representatives in the council would draft such laws (for example the Rent Act of 1859 for Bengal by the Bengal member). A Lieutenant-Governor (LG) for Bengal. The GG was empowered to appoint an LG to reduce his workload (since 1833 the GG was effectively PM of British India and CM of Bengal, an impossible dual burden). In 1854 Dalhousie 48-56 appointed Frederick James Halliday as the first LG of Bengal. Teacher: Two kinds of laws: all-country-level and province-level (because of the unique problems and context of each province). Examples of province-level subjects: the Permanent Settlement 1793 for Bengal; the Ryotwari system 1801-07 and 1820 (the slide reads "SCAM-B" beside it [unclear: check your notebook]). Solution: since 1833 only the GG(I)'s council can make law, so 1853 adds 6 more legal members: Bengal, Bombay, Madras and NWP (the North-Western Provinces, "NWP 1836") = the 4 provincial representatives. items.t: 8 · Government of India Act 1858, also the Act for Better Government of India
items.x: 8.1 Background  GOI Act 1858 Background: 1. EIC blamed for 1857. 2. Public demand (replace Absentee Sovereignty with direct rule). 3. Free traders. 4. Indian Western-Educated Middle Class (WEMC). 5. Stronger control. No ink.   Driver   Detail    --- ---    1. EIC blamed for 1857   The EIC was blamed for mismanagement of Indian affairs and for the 1857 revolt, in which many British were killed and the EIC's monopoly on violence was broken     2. Public demand   The British public demanded an end to EIC rule, replacing Absentee Sovereignty with direct rule of the British State (since Charter 1793 sovereignty was with the State, but it was absent and ruled through its agent, the EIC)     3. Free traders   Non-EIC merchants wanted direct British rule, claiming the EIC ignored their business interests     4. WEMC   The Indian Western-Educated Middle Class wanted direct British rule for accountability and modernisation (the Industrial Revolution and democracy came under State rule in Britain, not under a company)     5. Stronger control   Britain wanted stronger control over India after 1857   8.2 @Br State  GOI Act 1858 @Br State (EIC-State): 1. Crown direct rule (irony: in 1856 the EIC annexed Awadh for maladministration, now the EIC removed on the same grounds; EIC formally dissolved 1874). 2. Subordinate Union / Paramountcy (Mughal sovereignty legally ended, 1526-40 and 1556-1858; Crown sovereign over the whole of India; Br India ~63% territory, 78% population ruled directly by the GG; Princely States under Paramountcy: Sov, D, C, FA with the Crown, domestic affairs with the Prince). 3. Zafar 37-57 to Rangoon. 4. Secretary of State for India. Ink: a diagram "India [Sym Sov: Br Monarch]" forking into "Br India" (Ext (Br), Dom (Br)) and "565 PS" (Ext (Br), Dom (Prince)), a bracket "Paramountcy" under the 565 PS side. EIC rule was replaced by the direct rule of the British State in British India. (Irony: in 1856 the EIC annexed Awadh on grounds of maladministration; now the EIC was removed on the same grounds. The EIC was formally dissolved in 1874.) Policy of Subordinate Union towards Indian rulers. Mughal sovereignty over Indian territory was legally ended (Mughal State 1526-40 and 1556-1858). Note: Mughal sovereignty was not over the whole of India (Travancore was never part of the Mughal State and the Sikh State was legally independent). The British Crown was now sovereign over the whole of India: (i) British India (about 63% of the territory and 78% of the population) was ruled directly by the GG; (ii) Princely States were ruled by Indian princes under Paramountcy, a legal relationship in which Sovereignty, Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs (Sov, D, C, FA) rested with the Crown and domestic affairs with the Prince (the handout's analogy: "Article 370 without democracy"). Zafar 37-57 (Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, the last Mughal Emperor) was pensioned off to Rangoon in Burma. The Secretary of State for India (SoS) replaced the President of the BoC / Minister for Indian Affairs as the main authority and director of policy in India. Teacher: The board for Paramountcy. India = [symbolic sovereign: the Br Monarch], split into British India (external and domestic both with the British) and the 565 Princely States (external with the British, domestic with the Prince). The bracket "Paramountcy" sits under the 565 PS side. Beside the Proclamation (slide 39) he writes "Rule of Indian Princes in 565 PS" and "Rule of Br State in Br India" (Section 8.3).  GOI Act 1858 @Br State (contd.): 5. Council of India (replaced the BoC 1784 in London, headed by the SoS with 15 members). 6. Dual Control over GG (1784-1858) ended: "Viceroy & GG" now reported only to the SoS (as GG = ruler of Br India; as Viceroy = Crown's representative). 7. Powers unchanged. 8. Canning 56-62 = first Viceroy. 9. CCS exam continued, still held only in London. Ink: "Board of Control (BoC 1784)" underlined; "Viceroy & GG" and "As GG = ruler of Br India" underlined; a long underline with "[*vice captain]" below; a diagram of BoC to CoD (crossed out "x x /") to GG on the left and SoS for India to GG on the right. The Council of India (India Council) replaced the Board of Control (BoC 1784) in London, headed by the SoS with 15 members. (Seven members of the EIC's CoD were absorbed into the India Council for continuity and experience.) Dual Control over the GG (1784-1858) ended: as "Viceroy and GG" he now reported only to the SoS. (As GG he is the ruler of British India; as Viceroy he is the representative of the Crown in India, like a Vice-Captain representing the Captain when the Captain is not on the field.) No change in the actual powers of the GG(India) as "Viceroy and GG." In 1858 Charles Canning 56-62 became the first Viceroy. The same Civil Services examination continued and was still held only in London. Teacher: "[*vice captain]": Viceroy = the Crown's vice-captain. The diagram: before (left) the BoC orders the GG and the CoD orders the GG (the CoD is crossed out "xx/" with the BoC): dual control. After (right): the SoS for India orders the GG, one boss.   Feature   Before 1858   After 1858    --- --- ---    Body in London   BoC (1784) and CoD (EIC)   Council of India (15 members) headed by the Secretary of State (SoS)     Policy head   President of the BoC / Minister for Indian Affairs (1833)   Secretary of State for India     Bosses of the GG   Two: CoD and BoC (Dual Control 1784-1858)   One: the SoS     GG's title   GG(India)   Viceroy and GG (Canning 56-62 first)     Civil Services exam   Held in London   Still only in London   Mnemonic: "SoS 15, seven from CoD": the India Council. Decode: India Council = 15 members, headed by the SoS, with 7 members of the EIC's CoD absorbed for continuity. It replaces the BoC (1784). The GG reports to the SoS only (Dual Control ended). Why it sticks: fifteen chairs, seven of them still warm from the CoD. Mnemonic: GG rules, Viceroy represents: "Vice-Captain". Decode: As GG = ruler of British India; as Viceroy = the Crown's representative (the teacher: vice captain). Canning 56-62 = first Viceroy 1858 (same man, two titles). Powers unchanged. Why it sticks: the captain is the Crown, the vice-captain walks on to the field. Mnemonic: "Sov, D, C, FA": what Paramountcy keeps for the Crown. Decode: Sovereignty, Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs rest with the Crown; domestic affairs with the Prince (565 Princely States). British India = 63% of the territory, 78% of the population. Why it sticks: "Sov-D-C-FA" sounds like a short cheer; the prince cheers only on the home ground. Mnemonic: "Awadh 56, EIC 58": the irony. Decode: the EIC annexed Awadh in 1856 on grounds of maladministration; the GOI Act 1858 removed the EIC on the same grounds. EIC formally dissolved 1874. Zafar 37-57 sent to Rangoon. Why it sticks: the judge ends up in the dock two years later. 8.3 Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)  Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) [the word "Queen" struck through in the title]. Announcement: transfer of governance from the EIC to the Br Crown. a) No annexation (no intention to annex more Indian States). b) Crown administration (Br India under the Br Crown). c) Non-discrimination (religious non-interference, fair treatment, opportunity in public service without discrimination of race or creed, re-affirming the Charter 1833 clause). d) Amnesty (those who took part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions). Ink: beside (a) "Rule of Indian Princes in 565 PS"; beside (b) "Rule of Br State in Br India"; "religious non-interference" underlined. The Proclamation announced the transfer of governance from the East India Company to the British Crown. It specifically: (a) Disclaimed any intention to annex Indian States (a walk-back from Dalhousie 48-56's Doctrine of Lapse and the Awadh annexation 1856). Teacher: "Rule of Indian Princes in 565 PS." (b) Placed the Indian administration (British India) under the British Crown. Teacher: "Rule of Br State in Br India." (c) Promised religious non-interference, fair treatment of all subjects and opportunity in public service without discrimination of race or creed (re-affirming the Charter Act 1833 racial-equality clause). Religious non-interference is underlined. (d) Granted amnesty to those who took part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions. The word "Queen" is struck through in the slide title (the teacher's ink). The handout uses "Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)" throughout and the Prelims 2014 question says "Queen Victoria's Proclamation". No fact changes. Mnemonic: "No-A, Crown, Faith, Free": the four lines of the Proclamation. Decode: (a) No Annexation (princes rule the 565 PS); (b) Crown administration (Br State rules Br India); (c) Faith: religious non-interference, fair treatment, public service open to race and creed; (d) Free: amnesty to the 1857 rebels (with limited exceptions). Why it sticks: four clauses a, b, c, d = No-A, Crown, Faith, Free. Prelims 2014 and 2006 trap cluster. Prelims 2014: objects of the Proclamation: (1) disclaim annexation: CORRECT; (2) administration under the Crown: CORRECT; (3) regulate the EIC's trade with India: WRONG (the teacher: "ended 1813"; the EIC's commercial function was over by 1833 and the Company was being dissolved). Answer (a) 1 and 2. Prelims 2006: (1) Charter 1833 abolished the EIC's monopoly of Indian trade: WRONG (1813 did that; 1833 ended Tea, Opium, China); (2) under GOI 1858 Parliament abolished the EIC altogether and took over direct rule: CORRECT. Answer (b).  PYQ 8, Prelims 2014: Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 objects. Ink: T beside statement 1; T beside statement 2; F beside statement 3 with "ended 1813" below; a tick before option (a). Mnemonic: Prelims 2014: "Crown, no annexation; trade ended 13". Decode: statements 1 (no annexation) and 2 (Crown administration) are true; statement 3 (regulate trade) is false because trade monopoly ended in 1813 (1833 finished the commercial function). Option (a). Why it sticks: the Proclamation is about land and rule, not trade. 8.4 Royal Titles Act (1876)  Royal Titles Act (1876). 1. Kaesar-i-Hind: Royal Titles Act (1876) by the Br Parliament empowered Victoria to take the title of Kaesar-i-Hind / Empress of India. 2. Delhi Darbar 1877: in 1877 Lytton 76-80 organised the Imperial / Delhi Darbar where Victoria got coronated. Ink: "Imperial / Delhi Darbar" and "Victoria got" underlined; "corona" with the handwritten "TED". The Royal Titles Act (1876) by the British Parliament empowered Queen Victoria to take the title of Kaesar-i-Hind (Empress of India). In 1877 Lytton 76-80 organised the Imperial (Delhi) Darbar where Victoria was coronated as Kaesar-i-Hind. (She had been unofficially using the title since 1858.) Teacher: He completes the slide's word "corona" + "TED" with underlines under Imperial / Delhi Darbar and Victoria got: the point is the ceremony (coronation) at the 1877 Delhi Darbar under Lytton 76-80. Mnemonic: 76 title, 77 Darbar, Lytton 76-80 hosts. Decode: 1876 Royal Titles Act (Parliament lets Victoria become Kaesar-i-Hind); 1877 Delhi Darbar organised by Lytton 76-80; she had used the title unofficially since 1858. Why it sticks: Lytton 76-80's code starts with 76, the year of the Act.

items.t: 9 · Conquest in India: policy versus drift
items.x: No class slides on this section until Lecture 19, slides 41 to 43 (typed "MMP" slides without ink); the handout gives the same points. It is the "Br State responsibility for conquest" Mains angle. 9.1 No official policy of conquest  MMP: Conquest in India: No Official Policy. Surface view: Britain had no official policy of conquest; expansion was driven by Sub-Imperialism, the policies, actions and personal ambitions of senior EIC officials in India (many built political careers back home). The ban: Pitt's India Act (1784) explicitly banned conquest, a response to the heavy expenditure of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). No ink. On the surface, Britain had no official policy of conquest. Imperial expansion was largely driven by Sub-Imperialism: the policies, actions and personal ambitions of senior EIC officials in India, many of whom built political careers back home after their India tenures. Pitt's India Act (1784) explicitly banned conquest in India, a response to the heavy expenditure of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). 9.2 British State responsibility  MMP: Br State Responsibility for Conquest: a) Tools of conquest (the Charter gave the right to wage war, acquire and administer territory, issued by the Crown and later by Parliament). b) Military aid (Plassey 1757 won with the Royal Br Military; the arrival of Royal Military in October 1857 turned the tide). c) Financed the Company (trade monopoly 1600-1813; Charles II rented Bombay for 10 pounds a year in 1668; Thomas Roe; the 1.4 million pound loan of 1772). No ink.  MMP continued: d) Follow the money (over 1,50,000 pounds to the Monarch for Charter renewals in the 17th century; 1698 New Company offered 2 million pounds against the EIC's 7,00,000; 1767 EIC to pay 4,00,000 pounds a year; many Parliamentarians and Queen Elizabeth I were shareholders). e) Controlled the empire builders (Principal Servants only after Crown approval, binding orders to the GG). f) EIC as a foreign policy tool (like MNCs today; the 1st Afghan War 1838-42, part of the Great Game). No ink. However, the British State was responsible for conquest, for these reasons: a) Tools of conquest given by the State: the EIC's Charter gave it the right to wage war, acquire and administer territory; the Charter was issued first by the Crown and later by Parliament. b) Military aid at critical junctures: Plassey (1757) was won with the help of the Royal British Military (Chapter 10); when the 1857 revolt nearly overthrew Company rule, the arrival of the Royal Military in October 1857 turned the tide. The State helped both the initiation and the survival of conquest. c) The State financed the Company: trade monopoly over Britain's East Indies trade (1600-1813). King Charles II 60-85 rented Bombay (received as a dowry from the Portuguese in 1661) to the EIC for just 10 pounds a year in 1668. Thomas Roe was sent as a State representative to Jahangir 05-27's court to lobby. The State bailed out the EIC with a 1.4 million pound loan in 1772. d) Follow the money trail: over 1,50,000 pounds to the Monarch in the 17th century for Charter renewals; in 1698 Parliament gave the monopoly to a "New Company" because it offered a 2 million pound loan against the EIC's 7,00,000; in 1767 the EIC had to pay 4,00,000 pounds a year; many Parliamentarians and even Queen Elizabeth I 58-03 were shareholders receiving dividends. e) The State controlled the empire-builders: after 1784 Principal Servants (the sub-imperialists themselves) could be appointed only after Crown approval, and binding orders could go directly to the GG (empire-builders were, in effect, favourites of the State). f) The EIC as a foreign-policy tool: Britain dominated world trade through the EIC, as large MNCs today serve a State's foreign policy (the handout's examples: Google or private banks for sanctions on Russia, Airtel in Africa). The 1st Afghan War (1838-42) fought by the EIC was part of the Great Game between Britain and Russia. Mnemonic: TMFFEF: six reasons the State owns the conquest. Decode: Tools (Charter: war and territory), Military aid (Plassey 1757, Royal Military Oct 1857), Financed (monopoly 1600-1813, Bombay for 10 pounds 1668, 1.4 million loan 1772), Follow the money (1,50,000 pounds; 1698 New Company 2 million vs 7,00,000; 1767 4,00,000 a year; shareholders), Empire-builders controlled (Crown approval, binding orders), Foreign-policy tool (1st Afghan War 1838-42, Great Game). Why it sticks: six letters in the order a to f. Mnemonic: Bombay for a tenner: 1661 dowry, 1668 rent. Decode: Charles II 60-85 got Bombay from the Portuguese as a dowry in 1661 and rented it to the EIC for 10 pounds a year in 1668. Why it sticks: seven years from gift to rent, and the rent is a ten-pound note. Mnemonic: 1698: 2 million beats 7 lakh. Decode: In 1698 Parliament gave the monopoly to a New Company because it offered a 2 million pound loan against the EIC's 7,00,000. In 1767 the EIC had to pay 4,00,000 pounds a year. Why it sticks: the bigger loan wins the licence.

Write 1857 over the question and put each option's years beside it: Canning 56-62 covers 1857; Bentinck 28-35 is earlier; Hardinge 10-16 is in the 1900s; Lytton 76-80 is later. Answer: Canning 56-62 (who also became the first Viceroy in 1858). Mnemonic: Mutiny 57 sits inside Canning 56-62. Decode: 1857 falls between 56 and 62, so Canning 56-62 was GG during the Sepoy Mutiny (and the first Viceroy in 1858). Bentinck 28-35 earlier; Lytton 76-80 later; Hardinge 10-16 in the 1900s. Why it sticks: the revolt is the year in the middle of his code.

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The story of "The Company That Lost Its Head, Body and Name". The trader becomes a ruler after ToA 1765, and the State grows nervous: money (1767), America (1765-83), bankruptcy (1772), famine, Nabobs. 1773: Hastings 73-85 becomes GG with four councillors and a casting vote, Calcutta gets a Crown-chosen Supreme Court, and the Directors must report. 1784: Pitt's Board of Control takes the political side (Double Government 1784-1833, Dual Control 1784-1858), the council shrinks to GG + 2 + CIC, and conquest is "repugnant". 1793: the Crown takes the head (sovereignty, Principal Servants after approval) and Cornwallis 86-93 writes the code; 1813 ends the India trade (Tea, Opium, China stay) and brings missionaries; 1833 makes the GG of India, adds Macaulay, ends all trade and opens the UCS; 1853 gives no term, an exam in 1855, the Budget to Parliament, 6 Legal Members and Halliday as LG. 1857 is the final nail: the GOI Act 1858 hands the body to the Crown (SoS, 15-member India Council, Canning 56-62 the first Viceroy, Paramountcy over 565 princes), the Proclamation promises no annexation, and the Royal Titles Act 1876 makes Victoria Empress at Lytton 76-80's 1877 Darbar. Decode: 1765, 1773, 1784, 1793, 1813, 1833, 1853, 1858, 1874, 1876-77.

From this chapter you can build the administrative skeleton: the three pillars changed only when a crisis (the 1770 famine, the 1857 revolt) or Indian pressure forced it, and the British Indianised only as far as cost or politics demanded. Closing idea: codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police are the institutions independent India inherited. Nothing direct   As the handout says, Sepoy Army composition and grievances are in Chapter 21: The Revolt of 1857     Mains 2017, 15 marks   Examine how the decline of traditional artisanal industry crippled the rural economy   Nothing direct   Chapter 15, Chapter 16     Mains 2014, 10 marks   Examine critically the various facets of the British economic policies in India   Nothing direct   Chapter 27 (Drain of Wealth) and Chapter 16   Teacher versus bank. The teacher writes "No Qs in MAINS" on the title slide, and the handout says the same thing in other words: Mains PYQs "mapped" to administration are really economic-impact questions that other chapters answer. There is no direct Mains question on the judiciary, civil services or police in these sources. Use the cross-chapter table above and do not spend Mains time on this chapter. A practice skeleton for the nearest Mains-style question, "Trace how the EIC moved from patronage to an exam-based civil service" (built only from this chapter's notes, not a past question). Intro: the EIC began as a trading company with recruitment by nomination and patronage, which bred corruption. Body: (1) Cornwallis 86-93 (1793): two tiers, CCS and UCS, higher salaries, private trade curbed, strict seniority, but entry still by nomination until 1853; (2) training: Fort William College 1800, Haileybury 1806 to 1858, universities from 1858; (3) Charter Act 1853, exam in London, first held 1855, Satyendranath Tagore 1864, with a low age limit and English Literature to keep Indians out; (4) Indianisation demands from 1860, answered by the Statutory Civil Services Act (Lytton 76-80), Aitchison 1887, Islington 1912, GOI Act 1919 (exam in India 1922), Lee 1923, GOI Act 1935 and the PSC. Closing: reform came only under pressure; by 1947 more than 50% of posts were Indianised and the UPSC (Article 378) inherited the structure.
