items.x: Chapter 18 title slide: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police. Teacher's ink top right, each line marked with #: "No Qs in MAINS", "Few Qs in PRELIMS (RARE)", "STILL TROUBLES aspirants :. in every Book" and "BEST IN OUR BOOK/NOTES". Under the title: "= HISTORY of PubAd in Br INDIA" ("Br" written small above "in" as an insertion). Teacher: Four verdicts on this chapter: no questions in Mains, few and rare questions in Prelims, it still troubles aspirants in every book, and this handout is the best version. He calls the whole subject the history of Public Administration (PubAd) in British India. That is how to read it: not as a list of Acts but as how a Company State built its working machinery.  Administration: Machinery of the State. Typeset: Administration = the machinery of the State used to implement its policies, laws and schemes on the ground; EIC transition = trading company to Company State (1765-1858, and the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function); 3 pillars = Judiciary, Civil Services, Police. Teacher's ink beside the title: a circled "ORG" with three arrows pointing up at it, then "WORK = RULE" which splits into a circled T and a circled Ppl.

items.t: 1 · Administration as the machinery of the State
items.x: Administration is the machinery of the State: how the State implements its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC changed from a trading company into a Company State (the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function; the slide dates the Company State 1765-1858), it had to build this machinery from scratch. More accurately, it had to decide how much of the existing Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. The chapter covers three pillars: Judiciary, Civil Services and Police. Teacher: ORG with three arrows up: the organisation (the State) is made of its three machines. "WORK = RULE", and rule splits into T (territory) and Ppl (people). The State's work is to rule a territory and its people, and administration is how it does that work every day. This links to his L, E, J shorthand (legislative, executive, judicial power) from Chapter 8 and Chapter 10: the Company State had taken the territory; this chapter is about how it handled the people. Note for Mains (the handout's own warning). UPSC Mains PYQs mapped to administration overwhelmingly ask about the economic impact of British rule: Drain of Wealth, de-industrialisation and the Sepoy Army as an imperial tool. They cannot be answered from this chapter alone: Drain of Wealth and the economic critique are in the Moderates / Drain Theory chapter; de-industrialisation and the destruction of handicrafts are in the British Imperial Ideology and Land Revenue Systems chapters; Sepoy Army composition and grievances are in the 1857 Revolt chapter. This chapter provides the administrative skeleton; those chapters supply the economic and military flesh. Mnemonic: Judge, Collector, Constable: the three pillars. Decode: Judiciary, Civil Services (the Collector is the face of it), Police (the Constable). Territory plus people is what they rule. Why it sticks: you meet them in that order in an Indian town: court, collectorate, thana.

items.t: 2 · Judiciary
items.x: 2.1 Why judicial reform was so complicated  Judicial Administration issues: six questions. Q1 Which law (Hindu, Islamic or British)? Q2 Written down, or left to the judges' discretion? Q3 What hierarchy of courts? Q4 Should lawyers be allowed to represent parties? Q5 Judges: Indians or British? Q6 In which language should courts function? Final row: each carried political, social and financial implications, and the answers changed as British confidence, ambition and administrative needs evolved. No ink on this slide. The EIC was not walking into a blank slate. It entered a society with established legal traditions, different religious communities and a functioning (though imperfect) court system. It had to answer six questions:   No.   Question   Where the chapter answers it    --- --- ---    1   Which law should apply: Hindu, Islamic or British?   Personal laws kept; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Supreme Court on British law     2   Should laws be written down or left to the judges' discretion?   Codification: Gentoo Code, Hedaya, Code of 1781, Cornwallis 86-93 Code     3   What hierarchy of courts?   1772, 1773, 1793, Bentinck 28-35     4   Should lawyers be allowed to represent parties?   Yes, from 1793     5   Should judges be Indians or British?   All senior posts European under Cornwallis 86-93; lower posts opened from 1833     6   In which language should courts function?   Persian replaced in 1835   Each question carried political, social and financial implications, and the answers changed as British confidence, ambition and administrative needs evolved. Mnemonic: Wise Writers Hear Lawyers In Languages: the six questions. Decode: Which law, Written or discretion, Hierarchy of courts, Lawyers allowed, Indians or British judges, Language of courts. Why it sticks: W-W-H-L-I-L is the order on the slide, and the sentence reads like a court scene. 2.2 The Mughal judicial system in Bengal (before 1772)  Teacher's board: Traditional Mughal (J) system in Provinces. Levels down the left: Province or SUBA, DISTRICT/SARKAR, LOCAL. Two columns split by yellow lines: CIVIL [Diwani, which splits into LR and Civil] and CRIMINAL [Nizamat]. Civil: Sadar Diwani Adalat [CJ = Diwan] at the top, with arrows up from the district Diwani Adalat [J = Pandits and Maulvis] (personal law) and from "J = AMALGUZAR = Rev officer at DISTRICT level" (LR, non-personal), which in turn has an arrow up from the KACHARI [J = Zamindar]. Criminal: Sadar Nizamat Adalat [CJ = Nazim/Subadar], arrow up from Faujdari/Nizamat Adalat [J = Kazi (Mufti), "2 People Bench"], which has an arrow up from the Kachari [only for petty crimes] [J = Z]. Bottom: "Law = ISLAMIC LAW". The Mughal system in Bengal had two separate hierarchies, one for civil and one for criminal matters. Civil matters (Diwani = finance, land revenue and civil justice): Courts ran from the local level up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA) at the suba (provincial) level. In inter-personal matters (marriage, inheritance) the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims applied. Pandits judged Hindu cases and Maulvis judged Muslim cases. At the top the Diwan served as Chief Justice of the SDA. For land revenue and non-personal civil disputes, the original jurisdiction lay with the Zamindar at the local level, in his revenue court, the Kachari. Appeals went up: Zamindar, then Amil (the provincial revenue officer at district level), then the SDA at the provincial capital (Murshidabad), presided over by the Diwan or Naib Diwan. Around this time Muhammad Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held the posts of Chief Justice of both the SDA and the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. "Amil" versus "Amalguzar." The handout uses Amil only because it is a snapshot of the corrupted, mutated system of 18th-century Bengal; the canonical Mughal-administrative term is Amalguzar. The teacher's general board (slide 5) writes Amalguzar = revenue officer at district level; his Bengal board (slide 6) writes Amil (Rev officer). Same post. Criminal matters: Nizamat Adalats (commonly called Faujdari Adalats) sat at the district level, with the Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA) at the top. The Mughal State was an Islamic state, so Islamic law governed criminal proceedings, applied uniformly regardless of religion. At the village level the Zamindar held petty criminal jurisdiction alongside his police duties. Major crimes bypassed the Zamindar and went straight to the district Faujdari Adalat. Strict division of labour: the Kazis were the actual judges who pronounced verdicts (the board calls it a "2 People Bench," Kazi with Mufti), the Muftis gave expert interpretation of Islamic law, and the district Faujdar (executive police chief) secured the accused and physically executed the sentence. The Naib Nazim headed the SNA. Teacher: Civil courts were religion-specific (your judge depended on your faith); criminal courts were State-uniform (the law of the ruling State applied to everyone). On the board: civil has two tracks under the SDA: the personal-law track (Diwani Adalat, Pandits and Maulvis) and the LR / non-personal track (Amalguzar, then the Zamindar's Kachari). Criminal has one track, with "Law = Islamic Law."  Teacher's board: 18th c BENGAL at the SUBA level. Left notes: "(* 1765: EIC made Md Reza Khan EIC's Diwan)" and "(* Reza = Naib Nazim)". CIVIL: SDA [CJ = Subadar's Deputy / Naib Nazim]; at the DISTRICT: DA [J = Pundits / Maulvis] and Amil (Rev officer), under which the Zamindar's KACHARI at LOCAL level. CRIMINAL: SNA [CJ = Naib Nazim]; FA/NA [J = Kazi and Mufti]; the Zamindar's KACHARI for petty crimes. Bottom: "H and M Law for personal matters" and "Muslim Law for CRIMINAL matters". Who is Chief Justice of the SNA? Two boards, two answers, one reason. The teacher's general Mughal board (slide 5) writes SNA [CJ = Nazim / Subadar]; his 18th-century Bengal boards (slides 6, 7, 12) and the handout write CJ = Naib Nazim. The difference is the date: by the 18th century the real Subadar had become a distant authority and the Naib Nazim (Muhammad Reza Khan) ran the courts. For Bengal before 1772, use Naib Nazim for the SNA, and for the SDA the handout says Diwan (the board adds that Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held both chief justiceships, having been made the EIC's Diwan in 1765).  Teacher's board: "Standard Books focus = Personal matters in Civil AND Criminal matters", with a circled "Remember". 18th c Bengal (Mughal system). At the SUBA: SDA (CJ = Naib Nazim) with "Law: for H = Hindu Law, for M = Muslim Law"; SNA with "Law = Islamic". At the DISTRICT: DA (J = Pundits and Maulvis) and FA/NA (J = Kazi and Mufti). Teacher: Most standard books stop at "personal law in civil matters AND criminal law in criminal matters," and the teacher tells you to remember exactly that pair. Civil = Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims. Criminal = Islamic law for everyone.  Teacher's board: "FAUJDAR = Like SP at DISTRICT", with a brace giving two functions: "LEO" and "execute Judgement of NA/FA". Teacher: The Faujdar is like today's SP (Superintendent of Police) at the district, and he did two jobs, which the board lists as LEO (as written on the board; the handout describes the Faujdar as the executive police chief who secured the accused) and executing the judgement of the Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat. He does not judge; the Kazi judges.  Teacher's board: PRE 1772. CIVIL and CRIMINAL columns. At the SUBA: SDA (CJ = Naib Nazim) and SNA joined by a brace, with "Law = H and M" under the SDA and "Law = Islamic" under the SNA. At the DISTRICT: DA (J = PUNDITS / MAULVIS) and NA/FA (J = Kazi and MUFTI).   Level   Civil (Diwani)   Criminal (Nizamat)    --- --- ---    Suba (province)   Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA), CJ the Diwan (Reza Khan held both chief justiceships)   Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA), headed by the Naib Nazim     District   Diwani Adalat: Pandits (Hindu cases) and Maulvis (Muslim cases); revenue side: Amil (Amalguzar)   Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat: Kazi judges, Mufti interprets, Faujdar executes     Local   Zamindar's Kachari: land revenue and non-personal disputes   Zamindar: petty crimes only; major crimes go straight to the district court     Law applied   Personal law (Hindu law, Muslim law)   Islamic law for all   Mnemonic: Z-A-D: the revenue ladder, bottom to top. Decode: Zamindar's Kachari (original jurisdiction), then Amil (the Amalguzar, district revenue officer), then Diwan (chief justice of the SDA at Murshidabad). Personal matters go along a separate rung: Pandit or Maulvi in the Diwani Adalat. Why it sticks: Z to A to D is the alphabet backwards, going up. Mnemonic: Kazi decides, Mufti guides, Faujdar finishes. Decode: the Kazi pronounces the verdict; the Mufti gives the expert reading of Islamic law; the Faujdar (like today's SP) secures the accused and executes the sentence. Civil courts follow your faith; criminal courts follow the State. Why it sticks: three jobs, three K-M-F verbs, in the order of a trial. 2.3 The Dual Government period (1765-1772) After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC gained the Diwani rights over Bengal: revenue administration, Treasury and control of property / civil courts. (Modern welfare duties such as health and education were not included: they were traditionally handled by private or religious patronage, not by the Mughal government.) The Nawab retained the Nizamat (law and order). This created the Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism ("rule India the Indian way"), the EIC did not rush to impose its own system. Muhammad Reza Khan continued to head both the Diwani (on the EIC's behalf) and the Nizamat (on the Nawab's behalf). Indian officials remained the effective decision-makers on the ground. The EIC was mainly concerned with collecting land revenue. Outcome: revenue collection was poor; law and order deteriorated, made catastrophic by the Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which killed roughly one-third of Bengal's population. There is no ink on slide 11, but its typed outcome row carries a starred note: "Poverty leads to Crimes". Hunger pushed people into crime, so law and order failed because of the famine, and the famine was worsened by a hands-off administration. (For the Dual Government itself, Diwani versus Nizamat and Reza Khan as the EIC's Diwan, see Chapter 10.) Mnemonic: One man, two hats, two masters. Decode: Reza Khan headed the Diwani (for the EIC) and the Nizamat (for the Nawab) during 1765-72; Orientalism meant Indian officials stayed in charge; the EIC only wanted revenue; the result was poor revenue and a collapse of law and order, then the 1770 famine (one-third of Bengal). Why it sticks: one Indian official was carrying both the Company's and the Nawab's bag. 2.4 Direct Government (1772) and the judicial plan of Hastings 73-85  Teacher's board: 1772 CHANGES. At the SUBA: SDA and SNA joined by a brace "CJ: Governor / GG from 1773". At the DISTRICT, civil: DA [J = European DC] assisted by Pundits and Maulvis. Criminal: NA [J = K and M] with "European DC | Supervision" written above. Reason (circled "J" at the end): "L and O = sensitive, so Br continue with K and M as J". In 1772 Hastings 73-85 (Governor from 1772, GG of Bengal 1773-1785) ended the Dual Government and took direct administration of both the Diwani and the Nizamat. Rationale: EIC administration, based on rule of law and equality before law, would be fairer and more efficient and would firmly establish British authority. (The ideology shifts slightly from pure Orientalism to a hybrid: rule more directly, but still use Indian legal frameworks.)   Court   Judge   Law and detail    --- --- ---    Diwani (civil) courts at the district   The British DC is the judge, assisted by Pandits and Maulvis   Personal laws continued in marriage and inheritance     Nizamat (criminal) courts at the district   Kazis and Muftis continue as judges, now supervised by the European DC   The British thought law and order too sensitive to replace fully     Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat   Headed by the Governor (from 1773, the GG of Bengal) and his Council members   The top of both ladders passes to the Company   Muhammad Reza Khan (Naib Nazim) was imprisoned without trial from 1772 to 1774, accused of corruption and poor law-and-order maintenance. Conditions did not improve, so he was released in 1774 and reinstated as head of the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Teacher: Why Kazis and Muftis stayed in the criminal courts: "Law and order (L and O) = sensitive, therefore the British continue with K and M as J." Taking over civil justice was safe; taking over criminal justice from the Muslim judges was too risky, so the DC only supervises there. Civil: the DC sits as judge. Criminal: the DC watches. Mnemonic: Civil: DC sits. Criminal: DC watches. Top: Governor presides. Decode: 1772 Diwani court = British DC is the judge (with Pandits and Maulvis); Nizamat court = Kazi and Mufti judge, DC supervises; SDA and SNA = Governor (GG from 1773) and Council. Reza Khan jailed 72 to 74, then back as head of the SNA. Why it sticks: sit, watch, preside: three verbs, three levels. #### 2.4.1 The changes of 1773  Teacher's board: 1773 Act. At the SUBA: SDA. Civil DISTRICT: "DA" crossed out with a yellow X; a long arrow curves up from "Mofussil COURTS [J = (eu) Judge i.e. EIC officer, assisted by Pundits and Maulvis]" (Mofussil: "closer to village") to the SDA. Criminal: SNA and NA. Far right, "Britishers": "SC at Calcutta [as per RA 1773, implemented in 1774]" (1774 underlined). Bottom right: "* Mofussil = Rural Areas". Two further adjustments: A proper attempt at separation of revenue and judicial powers: an officer serving as DC was not to serve as judge too. In practice the overlap remained, but the principle was established. To bring justice physically closer to the people, the district-level Diwani Adalats were replaced by 18 Mofussil courts, each headed by a European judge. (Mofussil = rural areas and countryside districts below the district headquarters.)  Changes of 1773 and Supreme Court (1774). Typeset table: (1) separation attempt (1773), (2) 18 Mofussil courts, Supreme Court Calcutta (1774) under the Regulating Act 1773 for British subjects under British law, later Supreme Courts Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823. Teacher's ink in the first row: "[* PROPER SoP @ DC / By CW 86-93)", with "PROPER" and "SoP" underlined. Teacher: "PROPER SoP @ DC by CW 86-93." The handout calls 1773 a "proper attempt" at separation; the teacher corrects the weight of the word: the real, proper Separation of Powers at the level of the DC was done by Cornwallis 86-93 in 1793. In 1773 it was only the principle. Expect the exam to attach the DC's loss of judicial power to 1793 and Cornwallis 86-93 (this is Prelims 2010). 1773 versus 1793, do not mix. 1773 (Hastings 73-85): separation attempted, overlap remained, 18 Mofussil courts. 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): the DC is stripped of all judicial powers, the 18 Mofussil courts are abolished and the district Diwani Adalats come back (the teacher's slide 19 note: "Mofussil courts ended, DA back"). #### 2.4.2 The Supreme Court (1774)  Teacher's board: 1774, in yellow circle. SDA (CJ = GG). SNA (CJ = Naib Nazim, Md Reza Khan). Under the SDA: "MCs [J = (eu) Judge, assisted by P and m]" (Mofussil courts). Under the SNA: "NA (J = K and m)" with "eu DC | supervision" above it. The Regulating Act 1773 led to a Supreme Court in Calcutta in 1774, specifically to hear cases involving British subjects in Bengal, under British law. (British people, British judges, British law: a completely separate judicial track.) Supreme Courts followed in Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823). The Supreme Court was entirely separate from the Indian court hierarchy. Teacher: The 1774 picture on one board: SDA headed by the GG; SNA headed by Naib Nazim Md Reza Khan (reinstated 1774); Mofussil courts with a European judge assisted by Pandits and Maulvis; Nizamat courts with Kazi and Mufti under the European DC's supervision. The Supreme Court sits outside this ladder, only for Britishers. Mnemonic: C-M-B: the Supreme Courts, 74, 00, 23. Decode: Calcutta 1774 (Regulating Act 1773, only for British subjects under British law), Madras 1800, Bombay 1823. A separate track from the Indian courts. Why it sticks: C, M, B is the order of the three Presidencies; the years climb 74, 00, 23. #### 2.4.3 Codification of laws  Codification of Laws. Hindu law 1775: committee of 11 Pandits; English translation Gentoo Code (1776); "Gentoo" from Portuguese "Gentios". Islamic law 1778: Al-Hidayah translated first into Persian by Indian scholars and then into English as The Hedaya (1791). Code of 1781: written orders compulsory, rules for court functioning. Teacher's ink: "WRITTEN LAW" with an arrow to the Hindu law row; yellow underlines under Gentoo Code (1776) and The Hedaya (1791) joined by yellow lines to "ENGLISH WRITTEN"; a boxed "in Bengal" beside the Code of 1781. 1775: a committee of 11 Pandits compiled Hindu law into a single coherent code so courts could interpret it uniformly. The English translation was published as the Gentoo Code (1776). ("Gentoo" comes from the Portuguese "Gentios," a derogatory term for Hindus, used because Hindus worshipped multiple Gods unlike monotheistic Christians.) 1778: a similar effort for Islamic law. Because of Mughal rule, Islamic law was already well organised, so the EIC simply translated the most authoritative existing Arabic legal manual, the Al-Hidayah, first into Persian by Indian scholars and then into English as The Hedaya (1791). The Code of 1781 made written orders compulsory and prescribed rules for court functioning. Teacher: "WRITTEN LAW": this answers question 2 of slide 4 (written or discretion?). "ENGLISH WRITTEN": the Gentoo Code and the Hedaya are both the English written versions of Indian law, so British judges could use them. The Code of 1781 is boxed "in Bengal": it applied only in Bengal (see slide 22 below). Mnemonic: 75-76, 78-91, 81: the three codes. Decode: 1775 11 Pandits compile Hindu law, 1776 English Gentoo Code; 1778 Islamic law effort, Arabic Al-Hidayah to Persian to English, 1791 The Hedaya; 1781 Code: written orders compulsory (in Bengal). Path of the Hedaya: Arabic, Persian, English: A-P-E. Why it sticks: the years climb 75, 76, 78, 81, and only the Hedaya (91) comes late. 2.5 The Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judiciary)  Teacher's board: why Cornwallis separated powers. Left: "1793 Act by CW 8693: Mofussil COURTS ended, DA back"; in yellow, a circled + and "CW 8693 = AUTHORITARIAN :. Removed Indians from all senior positions". Centre: a circled "imagine" with a brace to: "PS 1793 has sunset clause"; "DC applies Sunset Clause on a (Z) -> Lands up for AUCTION"; "(Z) files a case in DA". Then "WHR WHAT if J = DC, Then conflict of interest, :. security of property (sad face) for (Z)". Some words ("WHR") are [unclear]. Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-1793) introduced the most systematic judicial reform of the early period. He is rightly called the father of civil services, but his influence on the judiciary was equally significant. #### 2.5.1 Why did Cornwallis 86-93 reform the judiciary? He had just introduced the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS1793), creating a new class of large zamindars as private property owners. For this to work, zamindars needed secure property rights: courts they could trust, and revenue officials who could not harass them. An officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions. So Cornwallis 86-93 properly implemented Separation of Powers at the level of the DC: the District Collector was stripped of all judicial powers and confined to revenue collection and administration. Teacher: "Imagine": PS1793 has a sunset clause (on his board, applying it lands the zamindar's estate up for auction). Suppose the DC applies the sunset clause on a zamindar (Z) and his land goes up for auction. The zamindar files a case in the Diwani Adalat. What if the judge is the same DC? Then there is a conflict of interest, and security of property falls for the zamindar (he draws a sad face). That is why the DC could no longer be a judge. Beside it, in yellow: Cornwallis 86-93 = AUTHORITARIAN, therefore he removed Indians from all senior positions (the other side of the same reform). Mnemonic: Land-lords need Law-lords: why the DC lost the gavel. Decode: PS1793 made zamindars owners with a sunset clause; a DC who auctions an estate and then judges the owner's appeal has a conflict of interest; so Cornwallis 86-93 made the DC revenue-only (separation of powers, Prelims 2010 answer (c)). Why it sticks: the new landlords wanted a different man in the judge's chair. Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 2.5). "By a regulation in 1793, the DC was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. Why?" Correct: (c) absolute power in one person was undesirable (separation of powers; the post-PS1793 zamindar class needed independent courts). (a) efficiency of revenue collection is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. (b) "judicial power must be European-only, revenue can be Indian" is wrong: Cornwallis 86-93 in fact removed Indians from all senior positions, including revenue. (d) "judicial work demanded deep India knowledge" is a partial truth, not the principal motivation.  Teacher's board: 1793 CW 86-93 CODE. CIVIL (underlined) and CRIMINAL. At the SUBA: SDA, "CJ: GG: CJ", SNA. At the DIVISION level [Bengal divided into 4 Divisions]: "4 Provincial Courts of appeal" with an arrow up to the SDA; a yellow bracket "Patna, MURSHIDABAD, CALCUTTA, DACCA" joined to "4 COURTS OF CIRCUIT" with an arrow up to the SNA. At the DISTRICT: DA and CITY COURTS with arrows up to the Provincial Courts. MOFUSSIL: MCs crossed out. NA crossed out on the criminal side. Right: a yellow circle "Week 1 District 1, W2 D2, W3 D3, W4 D4" back to Week 1, captioned "a Court of Circuit in a Division". #### 2.5.2 In civil matters  Cornwallis Code 1793: Civil Matters. Typeset: 18 Mofussil courts replaced by Diwani Adalats at district level and City Courts; 4 divisions Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta, Dacca with a Provincial Court of Appeal in each; appeal track District DA and City Courts, then Provincial Court of Appeal, then SDA (shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta); personal laws continued, PS1793 governed land revenue disputes; Charter Act 1793 codified all Bengal regulations, written orders compulsory, laws printed in vernaculars. Teacher's ink: under "Charter Act 1793", "By Br (P)" with P circled; at the right, rotated, "1781 code by HASTINGS 78-85 | apply only on Bengal, + can be changed by future GG"; at the bottom "Difference is of issuing AUTHORITY: 1781 - GG (Be); 1793 - Br (P)". The 18 Mofussil courts were replaced by Diwani Adalats at the district level and City Courts for urban areas. Bengal was divided into four divisions: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta and Dacca, and a Provincial Court of Appeal was set up in each. Appeals: district Diwani Adalats and City Courts, then the Provincial Court of Appeal, then the Sadar Diwani Adalat, shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Personal laws of Hindus and Muslims continued in civil matters. PS1793 governed land revenue disputes. Per Charter Act 1793, all regulations for governing Bengal were codified, written orders made compulsory and laws printed in the vernaculars so people could know their rights. Teacher: The Code of 1781 versus the Code of 1793: the difference is the ISSUING AUTHORITY. The 1781 code (by Hastings, applying only to Bengal) was issued by the GG (in Bengal), so a future GG could change it. The 1793 Code came through the Charter Act 1793, so it was issued by the British Parliament (the circled P) and carries more weight. Next to the Charter Act 1793 row he writes "By Br (P)": British Parliament. A code on slide 22. The teacher's ink reads "HASTINGS 78-85" (the last digits are [unclear] and look like 78); every typed slide and the handout write Hastings 73-85. This notebook keeps 73-85. Check your own notebook. Mnemonic: Four divisions, Pat's Mother Cooks Dal: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta, Dacca. Decode: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta, Dacca: the four divisions of Bengal, each with one Provincial Court of Appeal (civil) and one Court of Circuit (criminal). Civil ladder: District DA or City Court, then Provincial Court, then SDA (now in Calcutta). Why it sticks: P-M-C-D in the board's order; four divisions, four courts, four courts. Mnemonic: 1781 by the GG can be undone; 1793 by Parliament cannot. Decode: the Code of 1781 (Hastings 73-85, Bengal only) came from the GG and could be changed by a future GG; the Cornwallis 86-93 Code came through the Charter Act 1793 (British Parliament). The difference is the issuing authority. Why it sticks: higher the issuer, stronger the law. #### 2.5.3 In criminal matters  Cornwallis Code 1793: Criminal Matters. Typeset: abolished Faujdari/Nizamat Adalats at district level; 4 Provincial Courts of Circuit in the 4 divisions (a Court of Circuit physically moves around its division hearing cases in rotation); appeal from Courts of Circuit to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat; Islamic law with British modifications became Anglo-Muhammadan law, applied for about 70 years until the Indian Penal Code 1860. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines under "Anglo-Muhammadan law" and "Indian Penal Code 1860"; to the right "[* CPC 1859 | IPC 1860 | CrPC 1861]". Faujdari / Nizamat Adalats at the district level were abolished. Four Provincial Courts of Circuit were set up in the four divisions. A Court of Circuit is a court that physically moves around its division, hearing cases in different areas in rotation. This eliminated the need for a district-level criminal court. Appeals from the Courts of Circuit went to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Islamic law continued in criminal matters, but with British legal modifications. This hybrid was Anglo-Muhammadan law. For about 70 years, until the Indian Penal Code 1860, courts applied it. Teacher: The circle on slide 21: a Court of Circuit spends week 1 in district 1, week 2 in district 2, week 3 in district 3, week 4 in district 4, then returns to week 1. It is a travelling bench, so no district needs its own criminal court. He underlines Anglo-Muhammadan law and IPC 1860 and adds the three codes: CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (see Section 2.7). Mnemonic: Circuit = circle: week 1 district 1, week 2 district 2. Decode: 4 Courts of Circuit (Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta, Dacca) rotate through the districts of a division; Nizamat Adalat at district abolished; appeal goes to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat; law = Anglo-Muhammadan until IPC 1860 (about 70 years). Why it sticks: the court goes round like a wheel, a week in each district. #### 2.5.4 Anglo-Muhammadan law in practice: three examples (handout only, no class notes) Handout only (no class notes). The slide (23) stops at the name "Anglo-Muhammadan law"; the three examples below come from the handout alone.   Example   Islamic law (strict Hanafi)   British modification by Cornwallis 86-93    --- --- ---    A: weapon rule replaced by intent rule   Whether a killing was capital murder depended on the weapon used: a sharp iron instrument (sword) meant murder; strangling, drowning or a heavy stone was often a lesser crime (the instrument was not "designed" to draw blood)   He abolished this loophole: the intent of the accused decides, not the instrument. This matches the modern principle of mens rea     B: the end of "blood money" (Diyat)   Murder was largely a private dispute between families: the victim's heirs could pardon the killer for financial compensation (blood money, Diyat)   Relatives could no longer pardon a murderer. This set the principle that a major crime is an offence against the State, not just a private injury     C: abolition of mutilation   The standard punishment for serious theft or dacoity was amputation of a hand or foot   The EIC completely outlawed mutilation and replaced it with hard labour and rigorous imprisonment, typically 7 to 14 years   Mnemonic: I-D-M: Intent, Diyat, Mutilation: three loopholes shut. Decode: Intent (not the weapon) decides murder (mens rea); Diyat (blood money) ends, so relatives cannot pardon (crime = offence against the State); Mutilation ends, replaced by 7 to 14 years of hard labour and rigorous imprisonment. Why it sticks: the three are the old Islamic rule, then the new British rule: weapon, family, limb became intent, State, jail. #### 2.5.5 Personnel and a new profession: lawyers  Cornwallis 1793: Personnel and a New Profession. Typeset: Cornwallis 86-93 removed Indians from all senior positions and all courts were headed by European officials; Kazis and Muftis retained only as assistants; Naib Nazim office abolished; lawyers now permitted, creating the Indian lawyer class; with PS1793 (land a tradeable commodity) also a class of property dealers. Teacher's ink: beside the Kazis and Muftis row "[NA ABOLISHED]"; a yellow underline under "new professional class, the Indian lawyer"; at the right "* CW 86-93 / Father of" with a fork to "CS" and "PROPERTY Dealers", a short word under the fork that reads like "SHO" [unclear], and "LAWYER" at the bottom right inside one large bracket. Cornwallis 86-93 was authoritarian. He removed Indians from all senior positions. All courts were headed by European officials. Kazis and Muftis were retained only as assistants, not judges. The office of Naib Nazim was abolished. One progressive change: lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts. This created a new professional class, the Indian lawyer, and, along with PS1793 (which made land a tradeable commodity), also a class of property dealers. Teacher: "[NA ABOLISHED]": the Nizamat Adalat at district level is gone. "Cornwallis 86-93, father of: CS (civil services), property dealers, lawyer." One man, three offspring. Under the fork there is a short word that reads like "SHO" (the station house officer, which would be his police Daroga of Section 4.3): [unclear: check your notebook]. Mnemonic: Father of three: C-P-L. Decode: Cornwallis 86-93 is the father of Civil services, Property dealers and Lawyers. Authoritarian: Indians out of all senior posts; Kazis and Muftis only assistants; Naib Nazim abolished. Why it sticks: CPL is the rank of a corporal, a small officer with three stripes. #### 2.5.6 Why the new system increased litigation (class slide only, not in the handout)  Why the New System Increased Litigation (typeset, no ink). After PS1793 litigation increased because of the Cornwallis Code of 1793, which in practice made the system inefficient. (1) Separation of Powers, the key reason: the DC lost all judicial and magisterial powers; earlier the Collector swiftly and informally resolved revenue disputes on the spot, after 1793 they had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats. (2) Abolition of court fees: abolished to make justice "accessible", it flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits; reimposed just 2 years later, in 1795. (3) Creation of a legal profession: formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals meant cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed. Lecture 20, slide 25 only (the handout does not carry this table). The slide gives three reasons litigation rose after PS1793, with no ink on it.   Reason   What happened    --- ---    1. Separation of Powers (key reason)   The DC lost all judicial and magisterial powers. Earlier the Collector could resolve revenue disputes swiftly and informally on the spot; after 1793 every such dispute had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats     2. Abolition of court fees   Cornwallis 86-93 initially abolished court fees to make justice "accessible," which instantly flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits. Fees were reimposed just 2 years later, in 1795     3. A legal profession   Formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals: cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed   Mnemonic: S-F-L: Separation, Fees, Lawyers: why courts clogged. Decode: Separation of powers (key reason: disputes moved from the Collector's table to the court), Fees abolished (free justice flooded courts; fees back in 1795, two years later), Lawyers (Vakils) plus a rigid ladder of appeals: delay. Why it sticks: free entry, a long queue and a paid advocate in front of it. Mnemonic: Free in 93, fee back in 95. Decode: court fees were abolished with the 1793 Code and reimposed in 1795. Why it sticks: the two numbers differ by 2, and so do the two years. 2.6 Judicial system in Ryotwari areas  Judicial System in Ryotwari Areas. Typeset: the Bengal model of separated judicial and revenue functions worked in a zamindari system; in Ryotwari areas the ryot is the direct landowner; problem = very many small landowners and so very many land disputes, district courts physically distant; Madras 1814 on Munro's advice the separation was ended, the European DC and his subordinates given judicial powers; greater Indianisation at the lower judiciary; downside = concentration of power in one official; Bombay 1819 Elphinstone. Teacher's ink: top right, with a line to "zamindari", "WHR no of Landowners are less"; in the Downside row "+ his Juniors"; right margin "DC > 300 (currency sign unclear)", a vertical word "INDIANS" with a bracket to 300, 200, 100 and a drawn triangle (unlabelled); lower right, "Oppression by MIRASIDARS revealed" with an arrow to "MADRAS TORTURE Commission REPORT 1855". The Bengal model of separated judicial and revenue functions worked in a zamindari system. In Ryotwari areas, where the ryot is recognised as the direct landowner, conditions were very different: A very large number of small landowners meant a very large number of land-related disputes. District courts were physically distant for poor ryots in villages. Madras, 1814: the Bengal system was replaced on Munro's advice. Separation of judicial and revenue powers was ended. The European DC and his subordinates were given judicial powers so disputes could be resolved at the ground level. (Less paperwork, less travel, faster justice, at least in theory.) This led to greater Indianisation at the lower judiciary, because the DC's subordinates included Indian officials. The downside: enormous concentration of power in one official. The DC now collected taxes, maintained order and judged disputes, including disputes arising from his own tax collection decisions. Bombay, 1819: the same Ryotwari system was applied by Elphinstone, a follower of Munro's philosophy. Teacher: Why Bengal separated and Madras merged: "WHR (where) the number of landowners is LESS" (the line points at "zamindari"): in a zamindari area there are few big landowners, so few disputes and a distant court is workable. In a ryotwari area the landowners are many, so the courts must come to the village. On the downside row he adds "+ his juniors": the DC's juniors (the subordinates, including Indians) also gain judicial powers. The Madras Torture Commission Report of 1855 is his example of what the concentrated power led to: "oppression by Mirasidars revealed." The pyramid of 300, 200 and 100 beside the word INDIANS [unclear: the currency sign and the triangle are not labelled; check your notebook] seems to show pay or rank scales for Indians below a DC above 300. Same Commission, two homes. The handout mentions the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855 in the police section (4.3.2) as the exposure of the atrocities of revenue officials after the Daroga system failed in Madras. The teacher hangs it on the Ryotwari judicial system (a DC with all powers, plus juniors) and writes Mirasidars (the village landholders of Madras). Learn the fact once, 1855, Madras Torture Commission, oppression exposed, and use it in either answer. Mnemonic: Zamindari splits, Ryotwari merges: Munro 14, Elphinstone 19. Decode: few big landowners (zamindari) means separate judge and collector; many small ryots means the DC judges too. Madras 1814 (on Munro's advice), Bombay 1819 (Elphinstone, a follower of Munro). Gain: faster justice, more Indians below. Loss: one official holds tax, order and judgement (Madras Torture Commission 1855). Why it sticks: M-14 then B-19, the two Presidencies in age order after Bengal. 2.7 Charter Act 1833 (judicial impact)  Charter Act 1833: Judicial Impact. Typeset: single legislature (the GG of India the single central legislative authority, laws apply equally to Indians and Britishers); Law Member (Thomas Macaulay); Law Commission 1834, codification substantially complete by 1837; the codes CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861; subordinate judicial posts below District Judge opened to Indians; impact on the common Indian. Teacher's ink: next to the codes row "PERSONAL Laws CONTD in PERSONAL MATTERS"; next to the Indians row "[Indianization of Lower (J)]"; next to the impact row "[WESTERN EDU 1835]". The Charter Act of 1833 made the GG of India the single central legislative authority for all of British India, and the laws passed were to apply equally to Indians and Britishers alike. (A major shift: one law for everyone, regardless of race.) One Law Member was added to the GG's Council: Thomas Macaulay was appointed, and a Law Commission (1834) was set up under him to codify all laws systematically. Codification was substantially complete by 1837, but full implementation came after 1857:   Code   Year    --- ---    Civil Procedure Code (CPC)   1859     Indian Penal Code (IPC)   1860     Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC)   1861   Subordinate judicial positions below the rank of District Judge were opened to Indians. Impact on the common Indian: justice became psychologically distant (new laws were western, complex and unfamiliar), physically distant for rural areas and financially distant (legal fees few could afford). The system was more systematic, but it served the educated and propertied far better than the poor. Teacher: "Personal laws continued in personal matters": even with the IPC, CPC and CrPC, marriage and inheritance stayed under Hindu and Muslim personal law. "Indianisation of the lower J": the opening of posts below District Judge is the lower judiciary's Indianisation (note how it follows the 1814 Madras Indianisation in Section 2.6). "Western Edu 1835": the new western, English-language law goes with western education from 1835 (Chapter 19: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture): the English-educated class is the one that could use the new courts. Mnemonic: 59-60-61: C-I-C, Civil, Indian Penal, Criminal. Decode: CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861, the three codes of the Law Commission (1834, Macaulay) that were drafted by 1837 but implemented only after 1857. Personal laws stayed in personal matters. Why it sticks: three codes, three years in a row, in the order Civil, Penal, Criminal procedure. Mnemonic: One GG, one law, one Law Member. Decode: Charter Act 1833: the GG of India is the single legislature for British India; laws apply to Indians and Britishers alike; the new Law Member is Macaulay, who heads the Law Commission 1834. Why it sticks: one, one, one: the Act is about unity. 2.8 Reforms by Bentinck 28-35 (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35)  Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35 Reforms. Circled "Concept": POLITY: (L) (E) (J), each circled and in a row. A vertical line divides the board; on the right, "Reality": circled E (top), circled L (lower left), circled J (lower right) arranged diagonally. Far right: "DC / senior CS in (E)", with an arrow down "POSTED [PUNISHMENT]" to "Divisional COURT". Teacher: Concept versus reality. In concept the polity has three equal organs: L (legislature), E (executive), J (judiciary). In reality the E is the top prestige: DC and senior civil servants want to be in E, and an inefficient officer is posted as a punishment to the Divisional Court. So the judiciary (J) was the dumping ground. This is the setup for why Bentinck 28-35 abolished those courts.  Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35, "Decs in (J)" (decisions in the judiciary). SDA at the top with two curved arrows going up to it; inside, "4 PCoA" crossed out with a big X; below, "DA (+) CITY COURTS", the + circled, with arrows from DA and City Courts up to the SDA, bypassing the crossed-out 4 PCoA. On the right: SNA with two curved arrows going up to it; "4 CoCircuits" crossed out; below, "NA", with arrows from NA up to the SNA. Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts: both the Provincial Courts of Appeal (civil) and the Courts of Circuit (criminal) that Cornwallis 86-93 had created. Why: these courts had become parking grounds for inefficient officers (punishment postings for non-performers), which contributed to high pendency. High-ranking officers also meant high State expenditure, so the courts were ended as a fiscal-prudence measure. Transfer: judicial powers and pending cases went to District Judges. Teacher: After Bentinck 28-35 the ladders are shorter: civil: District Diwani Adalat + City Courts go straight up to the SDA (the four Provincial Courts of Appeal are crossed out); criminal: Nizamat Adalat goes straight up to the SNA (the four Courts of Circuit are crossed out). He underlines "high State expenditure" on slide 30 and writes "86-93" (small, no name) beside "Cornwallis 86-93 had created": the courts he removed were Cornwallis 86-93's.  Reforms by William Bentinck (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35). Typeset: divisional courts abolished; why (parking grounds, high State expenditure); transfer to District Judges; 1835 court language: Persian replaced, vernaculars in lower courts and English in higher courts, legal backing via Act XXIX of 1837, anxiety among Muslim elites; NWP Adalats: SDA and SNA in the Northwest Provinces (portion of Awadh annexed 1801, full province status 1836). Teacher's ink: "86-93" beside Cornwallis; yellow underline under "high State expenditure"; a small "so" inserted before "people from this region"; top right two joined ovals "1801" with an arrow down to "NWP 1836" and "Bengal Presidency", with a yellow dotted line labelled "Distance". 1835, language of the courts: Persian was replaced: vernaculars in the lower courts and English in the higher courts. Legal backing: Act XXIX of 1837. The removal caused anxiety among Muslim elites, because Persian education had been an important pathway to administrative careers. Courts for the Northwest Provinces: he created a Sadar Diwani Adalat and a Sadar Nizamat Adalat in the Northwest Provinces (the portion of Awadh annexed in 1801, given full province status in 1836), so people from this region did not have to travel to Bengal to file appeals. Teacher: The NWP circle: 1801 (the Awadh portion annexed) leads down to NWP 1836, a province with full status; the other oval is the Bengal Presidency, and the dotted line between them is written "Distance." Appeals to Calcutta meant a long journey, so (his inserted word) the NWP got its own two Sadar courts. Mnemonic: Bentinck 28-35's Bin, Persian, North: B-P-N. Decode: Bin the divisional courts (Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit of Cornwallis 86-93: parking grounds, high expense, pendency); Persian out in 1835 (vernaculars below, English above; Act XXIX of 1837); North-West Provinces get their own Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats (1801 annexed, 1836 full status). Why it sticks: the three words in the order of the slide. Context on Persian (slide 31, typeset, no ink). Persian was introduced under the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century. It got a major boost when Humayun 30-40, to win military support from Persia's Safavid dynasty to reclaim his throne from the Suri Dynasty (1540-55), accepted the condition of promoting Persian. Akbar 56-05, with finance minister Todar Mal, made Persian compulsory for all administrative records. Mnemonic: S-H-A: Sultanate, Humayun 30-40, Akbar 56-05: how Persian won. Decode: Sultanate (13th century: introduced), Humayun (Safavid military help against the Suris 1540-55 in return for promoting Persian: boost), Akbar 56-05 with Todar Mal (compulsory for all administrative records). Bentinck 28-35 ended it in 1835. Why it sticks: S-H-A reads "Shah", a Persian title. 2.9 Indian High Courts Act 1861 and 2.10 the Federal Court (GOI Act 1935)  High Courts 1861 to Federal Court 1935 (typeset, with thin yellow dotted underlines under "Federal Court, the direct ancestor", "(Centre vs Province, Province vs Province)" and "appeals from High Courts"). Indian High Courts Act 1861: High Courts in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta in 1862; Calcutta High Court created by merging the Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat and the Supreme Court at Calcutta, ending the dual track; GOI Act 1935, implemented from 1937, a Federal Court, the direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court of India; role: inter-governmental disputes and appeals from High Courts; today's Supreme Court under the Constitution of India 1950. The Indian High Courts Act 1861 led to High Courts in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta in 1862. The Calcutta High Court was created by merging three existing courts: the Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat and the Supreme Court at Calcutta. This finally ended the dual-track system of separate courts for Indians and the British. The GOI Act 1935, implemented from 1937, established a Federal Court, the direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court of India. It dealt with inter-governmental disputes (Centre versus Province, Province versus Province) and heard appeals from High Courts. Today's Supreme Court, set up under the Constitution of India 1950, continues this role with expanded jurisdiction. Mnemonic: Three into one: SDA + SNA + SC = Calcutta High Court. Decode: the Indian High Courts Act 1861 (Act year 61) gave High Courts in Madras, Bombay, Calcutta in 1862 (court year 62); Calcutta merged the Sadar Diwani Adalat, Sadar Nizamat Adalat and Supreme Court. Then Federal Court 1935 Act, working 1937, is the ancestor of the Supreme Court (1950). Why it sticks: the dual track of Indian courts and the British Supreme Court finally becomes one road. Before 1772: two ladders (civil: Diwan, Pandits and Maulvis, Zamindar's Kachari; criminal: Naib Nazim, Kazi, Mufti, Faujdar); personal law in civil, Islamic law in criminal Dual Government 1765-72: Reza Khan heads both Diwani and Nizamat; revenue poor; law and order falls; famine 1770 1772 (Hastings 73-85): DC as civil judge; Kazi and Mufti kept under DC supervision; Governor and Council head the two Sadar Adalats 1773-74: 18 Mofussil courts; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), later Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823; Gentoo Code 1776, Hedaya 1791, Code of 1781 (warn) 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): DC loses judicial power; four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Indians out of senior posts; lawyers in (warn) 1814 and 1819: Madras and Bombay merge the DC's roles in Ryotwari areas 1833-37 (Bentinck 28-35 and Macaulay): divisional courts abolished; Persian replaced 1835; NWP Adalats; Law Commission 1834 (good) 1859-62: CPC, IPC, CrPC; High Courts 1862 end the dual track (good) 1937: Federal Court, ancestor of the Supreme Court of India (1950)
