Left list: "Nomination (OR) Examination?"; "if exam: UPSC (circled) OR NOT (circled), UPSC = Specialized Body"; "Syllabus: Indian / Western"; "exam Location: LONDON OR India and London"; "Age Limit: Low / High". Right list: "Civil Services (underlined) organization eg TODAY IAS IPS IFS IRS ..."; "Common exam OR Separate exam for each Service"; "TRAINING: on the job / Training Institute". Teacher: The seven design questions for any civil service, as his board lists them: (1) nomination or examination? (2) if exam, by a specialised body like the UPSC or not? (3) syllabus: Indian or Western? (4) exam location: London, or India and London? (5) age limit: low or high? (6) organisation of the services (today IAS, IPS, IFS, IRS and more): one common exam or a separate exam for each service? (7) training: on the job or in a training institute? Read the rest of the chapter as the EIC's answers to these seven, in order. Mnemonic: N-U-S-L-A, then C and T: the seven design questions. Decode: Nomination or exam, UPSC-type body or not, Syllabus (Indian or Western), Location (London or India), Age (low or high), Common exam or separate per service, Training (on the job or institute). Why it sticks: "Nusla" for the first five, then C and T for Common and Training.  Civil Services: What a "Service" Means. Typeset: employed versus service; service = pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion and removal, clear structure of seniority and accountability (the difference between an employee and a member of a cadre); the story = from chaotic patronage to a structured merit-based cadre, with the tension of how many Indians would be allowed in; early recruitment by nomination, posts purchased or handed out, EIC Directors lobbied British Parliamentarians with jobs for their sons. Teacher's ink: from the "Service =" row, "No CAREER LADDER" and "Total Discretion, i.e. employment and promotion". In any organisation officials may be simply employed, or organised into a service. A service means a pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion and removal, and a clear structure of seniority and accountability: the difference between being an employee and being a member of a cadre. The history of the EIC's civil services is a move from a chaotic, patronage-based system to a structured, merit-based administrative cadre, with an extra tension: how many Indians would be allowed in? Teacher: Without a service: "No career ladder" = "Total discretion," that is, total discretion in employment and in promotion. The boss alone decides who is hired and who is promoted. A service replaces discretion with rules. 3.2 Recruitment: from patronage to examination Initially EIC officials were recruited by nomination, not merit. Posts were either purchased or handed out through patronage. EIC Directors actively lobbied British Parliamentarians with offers of jobs for their sons. This bred corruption and incompetence. 3.3 Training  Training of Civil Servants (typeset, no ink): until 1800 essentially on the job; 1800-1806 Fort William College, Calcutta, set up by Wellesley 98-05 for training in Indian laws, customs and languages; 1806-1858 Haileybury College, London (East India College); 1858 onwards British universities.   Period   Training    --- ---    Until 1800   Essentially on the job     1800-1806   Fort William College, Calcutta, set up by Wellesley 98-05 for training in Indian laws, customs and languages     1806-1858   Haileybury College, London (East India College)     1858 onwards   British universities   Mnemonic: Fort 1800, Hailey 1806, University 1858: F-H-U. Decode: Fort William College, Calcutta (1800-06, Wellesley 98-05, Indian laws, customs, languages); Haileybury, London (1806-58); Universities in Britain (from 1858). Before 1800: on the job. Why it sticks: each college hands over in the year the next one starts: 1800, 1806, 1858. 3.4 Cornwallis 86-93: founder of civil services  Cornwallis, Founder of Civil Services: 2 Tiers. Teacher's ink under the title: "ORGanized employees into:". Table CCS versus UCS. CCS: like today's Group A; senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, a "covenant", with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing to India (yellow dotted underlines under "formal legal contract" and "called a covenant"); high defined pay, clear career path; under Cornwallis reserved strictly for Europeans (ink: a line down from "Europeans" to "Authoritarian"). UCS: like today's Group B; junior officers hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors (dotted underlines); lower pay, less formal; the space where Indians were allowed to serve, from clerical roles to Deputy Collectors and Deputy Magistrates by the 1830s-40s. Ink beside UCS: "Indians + British". Cornwallis 86-93 brought the first proper structure to the civil services. He organised ("ORGanised") EIC employees into two tiers:   Aspect   Covenanted Civil Service (CCS)   Uncovenanted Civil Service (UCS)    --- --- ---    Today's parallel   Like today's Group A   Like today's Group B     Who   Senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, a "covenant," with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing to India   Junior officers hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors     Pay and path   High defined pay, clear career path   Lower pay, less formal     Access   Under Cornwallis 86-93 reserved strictly for Europeans   The space where Indians were allowed to serve: at first very low-level clerical roles, then Deputy Collectors and Deputy Magistrates by the 1830s-40s as the empire grew and needed cheaper local administrators   Teacher: "Organised employees into...": this is what the word "service" means (Section 3.1): from a pool of employees to ranked cadres. Beside the CCS access cell: Europeans-only = "Authoritarian" (the same Cornwallis 86-93 who removed Indians from all senior judicial posts). Beside the UCS: "Indians + British": the UCS was not Indians-only; it held both, which is why it is the space where Indians could enter.  Cornwallis: What He Did and Did NOT Introduce (typeset, no ink). First proper structure: 2 tiers, CCS and UCS. Did NOT introduce: merit-based selection for entry; entry remained patronage-based (nomination by the EIC's Court of Directors) right until the Charter Act 1853. DID introduce merit at promotions: strict seniority, so EIC bosses in London could no longer push underqualified relatives into senior ranks over experienced officers. Salaries massively increased to reduce corruption. Curbed private trade by EIC officials. Separation of Powers: DC stripped of judicial powers in 1793. Why "founder": converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service.     What   Detail    --- --- ---    DID   Two tiers   CCS plus UCS: the first proper structure     DID   Strict seniority for promotions   London bosses could no longer push underqualified relatives over experienced officers (the slide calls it "Merit @ Promotions")     DID   Massively higher salaries   To reduce the incentive to be corrupt     DID   Curbed private trade by EIC officials   (see the Dastak and private trade story in Chapter 10)     DID   Separation of Powers   DC stripped of judicial powers in 1793     DID NOT   Merit-based selection for entry   Entry stayed patronage-based: nomination by the EIC's Court of Directors in London, right until the Charter Act 1853   This is why he is called the founder of civil services in India: he converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service. Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 3.4). "Who among the following GGs created the Covenanted Civil Service, which later became the Indian Civil Service?" Correct: (c) Cornwallis 86-93. (a) Hastings 73-85 is wrong: first GG of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773, introduced a judicial plan but not the CCS structure. (b) Wellesley 98-05 is wrong: set up Fort William College 1800 for CCS training but did not create the service structure. (d) Bentinck 28-35 is wrong: opened the UCS to Indians under the Charter Act 1833 and encouraged some senior Indian recruitment, but did not create the CCS. Also: the CCS was later renamed ICS in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94, per the Aitchison Commission 1887, NOT by the Indian Councils Act 1892. Mnemonic: Covenant in London = Group A; hired locally = Group B. Decode: CCS (Covenanted, signed a covenant with the Court of Directors in London, high pay, Europeans only under Cornwallis 86-93, like Group A) versus UCS (Uncovenanted, hired in India by the GG or governors, lower pay, where Indians served, like Group B). Why it sticks: "covenant" = a signed promise made before the ship sails. Mnemonic: Cornwallis 86-93: pay up, trade down, powers split, seniority rules; merit exam NOT till 1853. Decode: salaries massively raised; private trade curbed; separation of powers (DC without judicial power, 1793); strict seniority for promotion; and the one thing he did not do: merit-based entry (nomination by the Court of Directors until the Charter Act 1853). Why it sticks: four yes and one no; the no is the Prelims trap (Statement "he introduced a competitive exam" is false). 3.5 Charter Act 1833 and Bentinck 28-35  Charter Act 1833 and Bentinck 28-35, Charter Act 1853 (typeset, with yellow dotted underlines under "UCS to Indians" and under "first CSexam of CCS in 1855"). Charter Act 1833: opened the UCS to Indians to reduce administration cost by having Indians in junior roles; Bentinck 28-35 encouraged recruitment of Indians to some senior positions. Charter Act 1853, a landmark: mandated a CS exam for the CCS and Indians were eligible; 1854 Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommended exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service; Civil Services Commission 1854 (London) held the first CS exam of the CCS in 1855. The Charter Act of 1833 opened the Uncovenanted Civil Services to Indians, primarily to reduce administration cost by using cheaper Indian labour in junior roles. Bentinck 28-35 went slightly further and encouraged recruitment of Indians to some senior positions. 3.6 Charter Act 1853: the exam opened to Indians The Charter Act of 1853 was a landmark: it mandated a Civil Service Examination for the CS and Indians were eligible to appear. 1854: a Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommended replacing patronage-based recruitment with exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service. This led to the Civil Services Commission (1854) in London, which held its first examination in 1855.  Exam on Paper versus Access in Practice. Typeset: age limit ranged 18 to 23 and was kept deliberately low (1859 Crown reduced the maximum entry age to 23; 22 in 1860; 21 in 1866; 19 in 1876, implemented 1878 so as not to impact preparing aspirants); syllabus dominated by English Literature, designed to produce Macaulay's "Brown Sahibs"; venue London; for an Indian candidate: cost of travel to England, inferior preparation, a syllabus rewarding English cultural knowledge; first Indians: 1864 Satyendranath Tagore, 1867 four more. Teacher's ink: right of "Age limit" "To Prevent entry of Indians into CS."; beside the 1859 to 1876 lines "not imp"; under Syllabus "LITERATURE = SOURCE of VALUES"; beside the last row "CULTURE'S KNOWLEDGE" and "WESTERN (EDU) in Br BETTER THAN in INDIA"; yellow dotted underlines under "18 to 23" and "English Literature". Eligibility on paper did not mean access in practice:   Barrier   Detail    --- ---    Age limit   The maximum age ranged from 18 to 23, kept deliberately low. 1859: the Crown cut the maximum entry age to 23. Then 22 in 1860, 21 in 1866, and 19 in 1876 (implemented 1878 so as not to hit aspirants already preparing)     Syllabus   Dominated by English Literature, designed to produce what Macaulay called "Brown Sahibs": Indians educated in English culture and values, culturally loyal to Britain     Venue   Held only in London     For an Indian candidate   Cost of travel to England; inferior preparation compared with British candidates; a syllabus that rewarded English cultural knowledge over Indian     First Indians through   1864: Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) was the first Indian to clear the CCS exam. 1867: four more Indians cleared it   Teacher: Why low age, English Literature and a London exam? "To prevent entry of Indians into CS." The age ladder itself he marks "not imp" (do not memorise every step). "Literature = source of values": English Literature on the syllabus carried English values, which is how the Brown Sahib is made. And the last row's point in his words: the exam tested "culture's knowledge," and western education in Britain was better than in India, so a Briton had the advantage. Mnemonic: 53-54-55: law, committee, exam; then 64 and 67. Decode: 1853 Charter Act mandates the exam (Indians eligible); 1854 Macaulay's Select Committee and the Civil Services Commission (London); 1855 first exam; 1864 Satyendranath Tagore first Indian; 1867 four more. Why it sticks: three years in a row for the system, then the Indians arrive nine years later (64) and three years after that (67). Mnemonic: Age shrinks 23, 22, 21, then jumps to 19. Decode: 1859 max age 23 (Crown); 1860 22; 1866 21; 1876 19 (implemented 1878). The teacher marks this ladder "not imp"; the point is "to prevent entry of Indians". Why it sticks: a countdown by one, then a jump of two: 23, 22, 21, 19. Mnemonic: London exam, English Literature, low age: the three locks on the door. Decode: venue London (travel cost), syllabus English Literature ("Brown Sahibs", source of values), age 18 to 23, kept deliberately low (to prevent Indian entry). Why it sticks: three locks, three keys the Briton already had. 3.7 The fight for Indianisation (1860 onwards)  Fight for Indianisation (1860 +) and Statutory CS 1879. Typeset: from 1860 the WEMC began demanding Indianisation; two core demands: simultaneous exam in India and a higher maximum age limit; British response hostile (post-1857 insecure); Statutory CS 1879 (Lytton 76-80): Parliament gave directions in 1870 (link 1858 proclamation and Charter 1833); instead of an exam in India or a higher age, Lytton 76-80 brought lateral entry via nomination, rules framed in 1879 under GOI Act 1870, only loyalists selected; role of the SoSforIndia (the typed "ICS" is struck through and "CCS" written). Teacher's ink: under WEMC "Western educated middle class [1835+]"; beside the British response "1st exam in India, 1922"; yellow dotted underlines under "lateral entry", "Statutory CS" and "only loyalists"; beside the Statutory CS row "[unimportant ACT]". From 1860 the western-educated Indian middle class (WEMC), the very product of British educational policy, began demanding Indianisation of the civil services. Two core demands: Simultaneous examination in India (not just London). A higher maximum age limit. The British response was hostile. Post-1857 British administrators were insecure about Indian assertion and determined to keep Indians out of senior positions. Teacher: WEMC = Western Educated Middle Class [1835+]. The date is the western education of 1835 (see the "Western Edu 1835" note on slide 27): the class that demands entry is the one the British made. And on the same row, beside the British response, "1st exam in India = 1922" (the answer to demand 1, which came only with the GOI Act 1919; see Section 3.9). #### 3.7.1 The Statutory Civil Services Act (Lytton 76-80) Parliament had given directions for Indianisation in 1870. Instead of holding the exam in India or raising the age limit, Lytton 76-80 (Viceroy 1876-1880) brought lateral entry via nomination through the Statutory Civil Services Act. Under it loyal elite Indians could be nominated to posts previously reserved for CCS officers, but only carefully vetted, politically loyal individuals were selected. The statutory authority over the rules, regulations, syllabus and age limits for the civil service was vested in the Secretary of State for India after the GOI Act 1858. (The handout adds a note: books put responsibility on Lytton 76-80 for reducing the age limit and credit Ripon 80-84 for increasing it, because the SoSforIndia was greatly influenced by the GG's input, but that is not the legal truth.) Teacher: He links the 1870 directions to the 1858 Proclamation and the Charter 1833 (the "star" note on the slide), and labels the Statutory Civil Services Act "[unimportant ACT]." Underlined: lateral entry, Statutory CS, only loyalists. Learn it in one line: nomination of loyal elite Indians, instead of an exam in India. Handout versus slide on the Statutory Civil Services Act. The handout writes "Statutory Civil Services Act 1878 (under Lytton 76-80)" and says the Statutory Civil Services were "created 1878" (Section 3.7.2). The slide title and body write "Statutory CS 1879," with "rules framed in 1879 under GOI Act 1870." Reading them together: the Act is 1878 in the handout; the rules were framed in 1879 on the slide. The teacher calls it an "unimportant act," so memorise only Lytton 76-80, lateral entry, loyalists. Slide 40 strikes out "ICS" and writes "CCS" in the SoSforIndia row, while the handout says authority over the "Indian Civil Service." The slide's correction is the logical one (the service in 1858 was still the CCS; it became ICS only in 1892, Section 3.7.2). Mnemonic: Lytton 76-80 lets Loyalists Leap Laterally. Decode: instead of an exam in India or a higher age, Lytton 76-80 brought lateral entry by nomination (Statutory Civil Services Act, 1878 handout and 1879 slide), only loyal elite Indians, into posts reserved for CCS officers. Teacher: "unimportant act." Why it sticks: four L words, Lytton 76-80, loyal, lateral, leap. Mnemonic: Two demands: S-A, Simultaneous and Age. Decode: Simultaneous exam in India and a higher Age limit: demanded by the WEMC from 1860; first exam in India only in 1922. Why it sticks: two S-A demands, both refused for decades. Mnemonic: Ripon 80-84 raises, Lytton 76-80 lowers: but the law says SoS. Decode: guidebooks credit Lytton 76-80 for reducing the age limit and Ripon 80-84 for raising it; the legal truth is that the Secretary of State for India held the authority after the GOI Act 1858. Why it sticks: a see-saw with the Secretary of State holding the seat. Handout only (no class notes): Lecture 20 stops at slide 40, so everything from here to the end of the chapter comes from the handout alone #### 3.7.2 Aitchison Commission (1887) Dufferin 84-88 appointed it in 1886; the report came in 1887. It recommended dropping the terms "Covenanted" and "Uncovenanted" and dividing the services into three tiers: Imperial Civil Service (ICS), Provincial Civil Service (PCS) and Subordinate Civil Service. Implementation came in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 (NOT a provision of the Indian Councils Act 1892, a classic exam trap; see Chapter 28: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (Lord Cross Act), Section 9). CCS became ICS, UCS became PCS, and the Statutory Civil Services (created 1878) were abolished (partly through moderate nationalist pressure). The Provincial Civil Services were recruited through exams and selection held in India, to ensure greater Indian participation in administration. Mnemonic: 86 appoints, 87 reports, 92 executes: D-D, L-L. Decode: Dufferin 84-88 appointed the Aitchison Commission 1886; report 1887; implemented 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94: CCS to ICS, UCS to PCS (plus Subordinate), Statutory CS abolished. Not the Indian Councils Act 1892. Why it sticks: the two D's and two L's: Dufferin 84-88 appoints, Lansdowne 88-94 lands it. #### 3.8 Islington Commission (1912) Context in the national movement: Swadeshi Movement (1905-11), Delhi Conspiracy Case (1912), Ghadar Movement (1913-15), Home Rule Leagues (1916-18) and British wartime claims of fighting for democracy in WW I (1914-19). The Commission was set up in 1912 but published its report only in 1917. It recommended 25% Indians in senior positions, via exam and via promotion from the PCS. It rejected the nationalist demand for simultaneous examination in India, arguing that educational standards in India were not uniform enough. (The handout's reading of the real reason, unstated: the British feared an exam in India would produce more Indian candidates than they were comfortable with.) Mnemonic: Islington: 12 sets up, 17 reports; 25% yes, simultaneous exam no. Decode: 1912 set up, 1917 report; 25% Indians in senior posts (by exam and by promotion from the PCS); rejected a simultaneous exam in India. Why it sticks: a quarter in, the door to the Indian exam still shut. #### 3.9 Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms / GOI Act 1919 Context: Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919). The GOI Act 1919 mandated: Simultaneous examination in India (first held in 1922). A Public Service Commission for India (established in 1926). A gradual increase to 33% Indians in senior positions. The ICS was also restructured. Since the Act divided subjects between the Centre and the Provinces (Dyarchy), the ICS was split into All India Services (AIS) and Central Civil Services. (The AIS and Central Services structure of today is essentially this 1919 structure, continued and modified by the Constitution.) Mnemonic: 19 promises, 22 exam, 26 PSC, 33% posts. Decode: GOI Act 1919: simultaneous exam in India (first held 1922), Public Service Commission (established 1926), 33% Indians in senior posts; ICS split into AIS and Central services because of Dyarchy. Why it sticks: 19, 22, 26, 33: the years grow by 3, 4, then the percentage. #### 3.10 Lee Commission / Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services (1923) Context: Khilafat Movement (1920-24) and Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22). It had equal numbers of British and Indian members. Its report (1924) recommended:   Recommendation   Detail    --- ---    20% of senior positions   Filled by promotion from the PCS     40%   Indians via exam     40%   Europeans via exam     50:50 ratio   Between Indians and Europeans within 15 years via exam     Public Service Commission   As originally mandated by the GOI Act 1919, should be established     Structure   AIS (ICS, IPS, Indian Forest Service and so on), Central Services (Foreign Affairs, Customs, Railways and so on) and Provincial Services (Health, Education and so on)   Mnemonic: Lee: 20-40-40, then 50:50 in 15 years. Decode: Lee Commission 1923 (report 1924): 20% by promotion from the PCS, 40% Indians by exam, 40% Europeans by exam (total 100); 50:50 in 15 years via exam; set up the PSC already promised in 1919. Why it sticks: 20+40+40 fills the hundred, and the exam half then moves to equal. #### 3.11 GOI Act 1935 Context: Hindustan Republican Army (1924), CPI (1925), HSRA (1928), Anti-Simon agitations (1928), Lahore Conspiracy Case (1928), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34), Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930-33), the martyrdom of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Chandrashekhar Azad (1931). The Act made the federal distribution of subjects between Centre and Provinces a formal constitutional structure. It mandated a Federal Public Service Commission (set up in 1937, replacing the 1926 PSC, the direct predecessor of today's UPSC) and Provincial Public Service Commissions for each Province or group of Provinces. By 1947 more than 50% of civil service positions had been Indianised. On 26 January 1950 the Federal PSC became the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 378 of the Constitution. (Article 378 is a transition provision: it ensures membership of the British-era UPSC and State PSCs continued seamlessly. Articles 315 and 316 govern the UPSC and State PSCs. Article 312 governs All India Services.) Mnemonic: 378 transition, 315-316 commissions, 312 services. Decode: Article 378 moved the Federal PSC (set up 1937, GOI Act 1935) into the UPSC on 26 January 1950; Articles 315 and 316 govern the UPSC and State PSCs; Article 312 governs All India Services. By 1947 more than 50% of posts were Indianised. Why it sticks: 3-1-8 is the transition, 3-1-5 and 3-1-6 are the commissions, 3-1-2 the services: all start with 31. Early EIC: nomination, purchase and patronage; Directors lobby Parliamentarians for sons' jobs 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): CCS plus UCS, higher pay, private trade curbed, seniority for promotion; entry still by nomination Training: on the job until 1800; Fort William College 1800-06; Haileybury 1806-58; universities from 1858 1833: UCS opened to Indians (cheaper junior labour); Bentinck 28-35 encourages some senior posts (good) 1853-55: exam mandated, London-only; first exam 1855; Satyendranath Tagore 1864; four more 1867 (warn) 1860 onwards: Indians demand a simultaneous exam and a higher age; British hostile; Lytton 76-80 offers lateral entry (Statutory CS 1878-79) 1887-92: Aitchison; ICS, PCS, Subordinate by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 1912-17: Islington: 25% Indians, no simultaneous exam (good) 1919-26: GOI Act 1919: exam in India 1922, PSC 1926, 33% 1923-24: Lee: 20-40-40, 50:50 in 15 years (good) 1935-50: Federal PSC 1937; over 50% Indianised by 1947; UPSC under Article 378 on 26 January 1950

items.t: 4 · Police (handout only, no class notes)
items.x: Handout only (no class notes). Lecture 20 has no slides on the police, so there is no teacher ink in Sections 4 and 5. The teacher's title-slide verdict (few and rare Prelims questions) still applies. 4.1 The inherited system (pre-1781) The EIC treated law and order as extremely sensitive, so the Mughal system of policing was left untouched for the longest time. Under it in Bengal:   Level   Police authority    --- ---    Overall head   Naib Nazim (Deputy Subadar)     Rural districts (Sarkars)   Faujdars (Sarkar here means a sub-divisional unit, not government; the meaning differs by region)     Towns and urban areas   Kotwals     Villages   Zamindars held police duties and paid Village Watchmen from their own resources   Mnemonic: N-F-K-Z: top to bottom. Decode: Naib Nazim (head), Faujdar (rural Sarkars), Kotwal (towns), Zamindar (villages, pays the Village Watchmen). Why it sticks: four letters, four levels, from province down to village. 4.2 Warren Hastings 73-85's reforms of 1781 The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 had led to a sharp increase in crime. Hastings 73-85 replaced Faujdars with English Magistrates (DC/DM) in rural districts. Zamindars kept their police duties under the DM's supervision. The problem: very few DMs, and poor supervision of zamindars, who continued to oppress the masses freely. 4.3 The Daroga system of Cornwallis 86-93 (1793) Ended the police powers of zamindars: under PS1793 zamindars were to be agrarian capitalists, not local police authorities. Divided each district into thanas of 30 square miles each. Each thana was under a new officer, the Daroga (Indian), appointed and supervised by the DM. The English District Magistrate (DM) was made the absolute, supreme head of law and order within his district. Rather than an intermediary like an English Naib Nazim or an Inspector General, Cornwallis 86-93 centralised ultimate oversight of criminal and police administration in the GG and his Council. Chain of command: Darogas, then DM, then the central government. #### 4.3.1 DC and DM: two roles, usually one person In most of British India (and in India today) the District Collector and District Magistrate are the same person holding two roles. Cornwallis 86-93 separated the judicial function from this officer (the DC/DM lost the power to be a judge), but the revenue and law-and-order functions stayed combined:   Hat   Role   Mughal ancestor    --- --- ---    DC (revenue)   Collects land revenue, manages government land, maintains land records, collects various taxes   The Mughal Diwani / Amalguzar function     DM (law and order)   Heads the district's criminal administration; coordinates with the SP to keep peace, prevent riots and issue executive orders such as Section 144 of the CrPC   The Mughal Nizamat / Faujdari function   #### 4.3.2 Result: the Daroga-Zamindar nexus A Daroga-Zamindar nexus quickly developed: zamindars bribed Darogas and kept private armed men (lathiyals). The nexus became the primary instrument of oppression of the rural poor in the early 1800s. The British blamed "Indian corruption" rather than the structural weaknesses of the system. 1799: Wellesley 98-05 restored police powers to zamindars, in effect admitting the Daroga system had not worked. 1802: the Daroga system was extended to Madras but was later abolished there too because of its failures. The resulting atrocities of revenue officials were exposed by the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855, which led to corrective measures. Mnemonic: 30 square miles per thana, one Daroga, one DM on top: 93. Decode: 1793 Cornwallis 86-93: zamindars lose police powers; each district is cut into thanas of 30 square miles, each under an Indian Daroga appointed by the DM; the DM is supreme in the district; chain Daroga, DM, GG and Council. Failure: Daroga-Zamindar nexus, Wellesley 98-05 reverses in 1799, Madras tries it 1802, Torture Commission 1855. Why it sticks: the thana is the unit, the Daroga is the man, the DM is the boss. Mnemonic: DC collects, DM controls: Collector's two hats. Decode: DC = revenue (descendant of the Mughal Diwani / Amalguzar); DM = law and order (descendant of the Nizamat / Faujdari), with the SP, issues orders such as Section 144 of the CrPC; the judge's hat was taken off by Cornwallis 86-93 in 1793. Why it sticks: C for Collect, M for Maintain order; the third hat (judge) is gone. 4.4 The Police Act 1861 The Daroga system had failed. The British looked for a proven alternative and found it in the Irish Constabulary model: a centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force, effective in Ireland since 1787, designed as much for suppressing political agitation as for preventing ordinary crime. (The British were not primarily building a crime-prevention force; they were building a political control mechanism.) #### 4.4.1 Province-by-province road-test (pre-1861)   Province   Year   Detail    --- --- ---    Sindh   1843 (annexed)   Charles Napier, the military general who conquered Sindh, set up the Sindh Police on the Irish Constabulary model immediately after conquest     Punjab   1849   Post-annexation     Bombay   1853       Madras   1859     The 1st Police Commission (1860) was set up by Canning 56-62 under M.H. Court. It simply formalised what had already proved effective on the ground and borrowed heavily from the Sindh model when drafting the 1861 Police Act. A common UPSC trap: Charles Napier did NOT head the 1860 commission (many guidebooks wrongly say he did). Napier gave the blueprint (Sindh); M.H. Court's commission drew the national map using it. Mnemonic: Sindh 43, Punjab 49, Bombay 53, Madras 59: S-P-B-M. Decode: the Irish Constabulary model was road-tested in Sindh (1843, Charles Napier), Punjab (1849), Bombay (1853), Madras (1859); the 1st Police Commission 1860 (Canning 56-62, M.H. Court) copied Sindh; Napier did not head it. Why it sticks: the years climb 43, 49, 53, 59; "Court" in the name, Napier "gave the plan". #### 4.4.2 The Police Act 1861 The Police Act, 1861 was passed in March 1861 by the GG's Council (as last restructured by the Charter Act 1853). (The Indian Councils Act 1861 came in August 1861 and created the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC); do not mix them.) It created the provincial police structure across all provinces: each Province to have its own police organisation, with a clear hierarchy:   Post   In charge of   Reports to    --- --- ---    Inspector General (IG)   The provincial police   The Governor / Lieutenant Governor (LG)     Superintendent of Police (SP)   The district police   The DC / DM     Sub-Inspector (SI)   The thana   The SP (not to the DC as earlier)   Operational accountability ran upward through the police chain: SI, SP, IG. Political accountability ran to civilian authority: SP to DC/DM, IG to LG / Governor. This was only the organisational chart. In 1861 the British simply posted military officers or nominated European men into the senior posts: no formal cadre, no competitive exam, no unified service, just employees of provincial governments. The posts existed; the service did not yet. From 1857 onwards a "Police Raj" was created: Indians were excluded from all senior positions, and the emphasis was on effective policing, intelligence collection and political surveillance. Mnemonic: IG over SP over SI: Province, District, Thana. Decode: IG heads the province (reports to Governor / LG); SP heads the district (reports to DC/DM); SI heads the thana (reports to SP, not the DC). Police Act March 1861; the Indian Councils Act 1861 is August 1861. Why it sticks: I-S-S climbs down the map from big to small. #### 4.4.3 Formalisation into a structured cadre   Year   Step    --- ---    1893   First open competitive exam for senior police posts, held in London; top candidates became probationary Assistant Superintendents of Police under the Secretary of State for India     1902-03   Curzon 99-05 set up the 2nd Police Commission under Sir Andrew Fraser; report 1903. It organised superior police officers into one unified all-India cadre, the Imperial Police (IP) (informally the Indian Police); scheme implemented from about 1905     (Fraser's package)   Provincial Police Service (PPS) created, with a new rank Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) that accommodated Indians at officer level, always junior to the British IP. CID set up in every province, plus a central intelligence bureau, the Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of today's IB. But the IP itself stayed closed to Indians: Fraser did NOT recommend appointing Indians to it     1920   Direct entry into the IP officially opened to Indians (simultaneous exams in England and India from 1921), largely a result of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (GOI Act 1919)     By 1931   Only 20% of SPs were Indians     From 1939   More Indians posted as SP because British candidates were unavailable (recruited for World War II, 1939-45)     1948   The IP was administratively replaced by the Indian Police Service (IPS) by a Home Ministry resolution; statutory backing came from the All India Services Act, 1951   1861 built the structure, 1902-03 built the service, 1948-51 built the IPS. (Today's IPS is an All India Service under Article 312, with State police under State governments, directly inheriting the 1861 framework.) Mnemonic: 93 exam, 03 Fraser, 20 Indians in, 48 IPS, 51 Act. Decode: 1893 first police exam in London (probationary ASPs); 1902-03 Fraser (Curzon 99-05): Imperial Police, PPS and DySP, CID, DCI 1903, IP closed to Indians; 1920 IP opened (exams in both countries from 1921); 1931 20% SPs Indian; 1939 more Indian SPs (WWII); 1948 IPS by Home Ministry resolution; 1951 All India Services Act. Why it sticks: "1861 structure, 1902 service, 1948 IPS" is the three-line summary.

items.t: 5 · The three-pillar administrative legacy (handout only, no class notes)
items.x: The EIC's administrative evolution across judiciary, civil services and police shows a consistent pattern: structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle. Each major reform was triggered by a crisis (the Great Bengal Famine 1770, the 1857 revolt) or was a concession wrested by the Indian National Movement after sustained pressure. The British never voluntarily Indianised their administration beyond what was economically necessary (to reduce costs) or politically unavoidable (to manage nationalist pressure). They left behind, however inadvertently, a set of institutions that independent India would inherit, adapt and build upon: codified law, an organised civil service, a hierarchical police.   Pillar   Inherited (Mughal)   Foundational reform   Mid-19th century consolidation   Modern legacy    --- --- --- --- ---    Judiciary   Diwani Adalats (civil; Pandits and Maulvis) plus Nizamat Adalats (criminal; Kazis, Muftis, Faujdars)   Hastings 73-85's 1772 plan; 1774 Supreme Court at Calcutta; Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 with Anglo-Muhammadan law   Charter Act 1833 (Macaulay, Law Commission 1834) leading to CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861; High Courts Act 1861 (High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta 1862)   GOI Act 1935: Federal Court (1937), then Supreme Court of India 1950; CPC, IPC and CrPC replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS and BS     Civil services   Mansabdari nobility under Mughal patronage   Cornwallis 86-93 (1793): founder of CCS plus UCS; salaries raised; seniority for promotion   Charter 1853: exam mandated, Indians eligible (London only); ICS renamed by executive order 1892 (Lansdowne 88-94, per Aitchison 1887, NOT by ICA 1892)   Lee Commission 1923 leading to PSC 1926; GOI 1935 Federal PSC (1937) then UPSC 1950 (Article 378); AIS under Article 312     Police   Naib Nazim to Faujdars (rural) and Kotwals (towns), plus Zamindars (villages)   Hastings 73-85's 1781 reforms; Cornwallis 86-93's Daroga System 1793 (failed through the Daroga-Zamindar nexus)   Irish Constabulary road-test (Sindh 1843 Napier, Punjab 1849, Bombay 1853, Madras 1859); 1st Police Commission 1860 (M.H. Court) leading to the Police Act 1861 (March 1861)   2nd Police Commission 1902-03 (Fraser) leading to the Imperial Police (IP) cadre; 1948 Home Ministry resolution leading to the IPS; AIS Act 1951 plus Article 312   The handout's scrambled table. In the PDF this summary table is broken (words split across cells; the last cell of the judiciary row is cut). The version above is rebuilt from the readable pieces; the one unclear part is the final words of the judiciary "modern legacy" cell, which read "CPC/IPC/CrPC replaced 2024 by BNS/BNSS/BS" and are cut off after "BS" [unclear: check your handout page 193 for the full name]. The 2024 replacement appears only in this table. Mnemonic: Crisis or pressure: the British only moved when pushed. Decode: reforms came after the Great Bengal Famine 1770 or the 1857 revolt (crisis), or as a concession to the Indian National Movement (Indianisation: 1919, 1923, 1935); never beyond what cost or politics demanded. What was left: codified law, organised civil service, hierarchical police. Why it sticks: two triggers (crisis, pressure), three legacies (law, service, police).

items.t: Memory hooks: chapter in one breath
items.x: Mnemonic: The story of "Judge, Collector, Constable". Reza Khan wears two hats under the Dual Government (65-72) and the famine of 70 breaks law and order, so Hastings 73-85 takes over in 72: DC sits as civil judge, DC watches the Kazi; a Supreme Court for Britons (74). Then Cornwallis 86-93 splits the DC from the judge (93) because the new landlords need a fair court: four divisions (P-M-C-D), Circuit like a wheel, Intent not Weapon, Indians out and Lawyers in; he also fathers the CCS and UCS (Group A and B) with pay up, trade down, seniority yes, merit exam not yet. Bentinck 28-35 bins the divisional courts and Persian (35); Macaulay's codes (59-60-61) and High Courts (62) tidy the law; the Federal Court (37) points to the Supreme Court (50). The exam opens in 53-55 but with three locks (London, Literature, low age); Indians demand S and A; Lytton 76-80 offers loyalists a lateral door, Aitchison 87 and Lansdowne 88-94 rename (92), 1919 brings the exam to India (22), Lee says 20-40-40, 1935 gives the FPSC (37) and Article 378 the UPSC (50). The police: N-F-K-Z becomes DM plus Daroga (93), fails in the Daroga-Zamindar nexus; Sindh 43 becomes the Police Act 1861 (IG, SP, SI); Fraser 1902-03 builds the service; 1948-51 the IPS. Decode: 1765-72, 1772, 1774, 1793, 1835, 1859-62, 1853-55, 1892, 1919-22, 1923-24, 1935-37, 1950, 1861, 1902-03, 1948-51.
